areas.title: Oxidative stress biology & antioxidant supplements
areas.summary: Reactive oxygen species are normal signalling molecules at low levels (oxidative eustress) and damaging only in excess (distress). Defence is dominated by enzymes such as peroxiredoxins, glutathione peroxidases and the Nrf2-controlled glutathione system, not by dietary scavengers. Large RCTs show high-dose antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, cocktails) do not prevent disease and some cause harm. Plant compounds most likely help through mild Nrf2/hormetic signalling and gut effects, and ORAC-type 'antioxidant capacity' numbers are meaningless for health.

areas.title: Foods, drinks & dietary patterns
areas.summary: How specific foods, drinks and eating patterns change systemic oxidative stress in humans. The biggest dietary levers are not 'antioxidant superfoods' but avoiding chronic overfeeding, large high-glycemic and high-fat meal spikes, alcohol, processed meat and high-heat dry cooking, inside a Mediterranean-style pattern. Among individual foods, high-phenolic extra-virgin olive oil, cruciferous foods that actually deliver sulforaphane (sprouts, seed powder with active myrosinase, raw or mustard-dressed broccoli), filtered coffee, blueberries, cocoa flavanols and brewed green tea have the best human evidence. Polyphenol milligrams and ORAC scores do not predict benefit: these compounds work through different routes (Nrf2 electrophile signalling, gut-microbial metabolites, endothelial nitric oxide, blunting NADPH oxidase), most show thresholds and plateaus, and very few human trials measure validated oxidative-damage markers.

areas.title: Exercise, lifestyle & environment
areas.summary: Lifestyle and environment drive more of the body's oxidative load than any supplement. Not smoking, losing excess visceral fat, staying fit, keeping blood sugar in range and limiting alcohol produce the largest, best-documented drops in validated markers such as urinary F2-isoprostanes. Exercise works by hormesis: each session briefly raises ROS, which trains the body's own antioxidant systems, and megadose vitamin C/E can blunt that signal. Sleep, air quality, sun protection and gum health matter at a smaller scale, while hydrogen water, grounding, ozone therapy and IV glutathione lack credible evidence.

areas.title: Sperm health & DNA fragmentation
areas.summary: Sperm are unusually exposed to oxidative damage: their membranes are packed with oxidisable fatty acids, they have almost no cytoplasm for antioxidant enzymes, and they cannot repair oxidised DNA themselves, so the egg has to. High sperm DNA fragmentation (SDF) is linked to slower natural conception, roughly double the miscarriage risk and lower IVF/ICSI success. The biggest proven levers are treating a clinical varicocele, stopping smoking, avoiding testicular heat and exogenous testosterone, and ejaculating every 1-2 days; diet, weight and exercise help modestly. Over-the-counter 'male fertility' antioxidants have mostly failed in large, well-run trials (MOXI, FAZST), so they are a low priority, and megadoses may do harm.

areas.title: Egg (oocyte) quality & oxidative stress
areas.summary: Egg quality depends above all on age: chromosome errors driven by cohesin loss and declining mitochondrial function rise steeply after the mid-30s, and no lifestyle change or supplement has been shown to reverse that in humans. Within that limit, the biggest controllable factors are not smoking, avoiding obesity and heavy drinking, taking folic acid, and eating a Mediterranean-style diet in the ~3 months of follicle growth before conception or IVF. Antioxidant supplements, including CoQ10 and melatonin, have at best low-quality evidence for women, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

entries.headline: A pattern of supplemental folic acid, B12 and vitamin D plus low-pesticide produce, whole grains, dairy, soy and seafood was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD of adherence (top vs bottom quartile: +28 percentage points).

dose.effective: Folic acid supplement (>= 400-800 ug/day), adequate B12 and vitamin D, whole grains, dairy, soy foods, seafood instead of other meats, and lower-pesticide-residue fruit and vegetables.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of a score from a validated food-frequency questionnaire.
dose.timeframe: Diet in the year before treatment was measured.
dose.notes: Not related to estradiol, oocyte counts or endometrial thickness; associated with less clinical pregnancy loss.

entries.mechanism: Likely via one-carbon metabolism (folate/B12), vitamin D signalling and lower pesticide exposure rather than a direct antioxidant effect.
entries.interactions: Contains [folic-acid] and [vitamin-d]; overlaps with [mediterranean-diet] and [omega3-fish].
entries.caveats: Derived and tested in the same single US cohort (357 women) by the same group, which risks overfitting; needs independent replication or an RCT.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth odds per SD adherence
Live birth, top vs bottom quartile

entries.title: "Profertility" diet pattern (EARTH study)

timing.summary: Diet changes reach the embryo surprisingly fast: six weeks of a Mediterranean-style supplement before IVF changed embryo cleavage timing. The cohort linking a profertility diet to live birth measured diet over the year before treatment.

onset.text: Embryo cleavage changes after 6 weeks [tegg-kermack2020].

full.text: Not measured; folate components need months [tegg-crider2019].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Daily pattern; no schedule comparison.

timing.debate: The live-birth association is observational [tegg-gaskins2019]; the only RCT measured embryo morphokinetics, a surrogate [tegg-kermack2020].

egg.late_start: Six weeks was enough to change embryo kinetics [tegg-kermack2020], though not shown to change live birth.
egg.text: Diet in the year before ART was linked to live birth [tegg-gaskins2019]; 90 days is extrapolated from the follicle growth path.

audit.claim: The EARTH 'profertility' diet was associated with 53% higher odds of IVF live birth per SD.
audit.biases: Score derived and tested in the same single cohort (overfitting), food-frequency measurement error, and healthy-user confounding among fertility-clinic patients.
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication of the profertility score has appeared. Meta-analyses of diet patterns in ART find all studies at moderate-high risk of bias, with Mediterranean and profertility patterns each associated with live birth in individual studies [afert-kellow2022, afert-winter2023]; in EARTH itself the Mediterranean benefit plateaued above the second quartile [afert-gaskins2019].
audit.bottom_line: A healthy diet is reasonable, but no specific 'fertility diet' has been shown to cause more live births.

entries.headline: Choosing products labelled free of specific chemicals works for those chemicals (within 3-5 days: parabens -30 to -45%, triclosan and BP-3 -36%, MEP -22 to -27%), but 'clean' and 'natural' are unregulated marketing terms: 94% of 1,470 'clean' products contained at least one contact allergen, and no study shows a health benefit from switching.

dose.effective: Read the ingredient list for specific chemicals rather than trusting 'clean' or 'natural'. Prioritise leave-on products used on large areas (body lotion, sunscreen, body spray, foundation) and perfume. Prefer 'fragrance-free'. If you have eczema or sensitive skin, patch-test new 'natural' products (essential oils such as ylang-ylang and lemongrass are common allergens). A 3-5 day switch measurably lowers urine levels; a 1-month web-based programme sustained 9-24% reductions for parabens.
dose.studied_range: Interventions of 2 days to 1 month in teenage girls, young women and mothers.
dose.timeframe: Urinary levels drop within 2-5 days of switching.
dose.notes: The switch did not work in Korean girls who used few cosmetics to begin with, and some chemicals rose when unlabelled substitutes were present.

entries.mechanism: Removing the dominant source of short-half-life chemicals (parabens, phthalates, triclosan, BP-3) lowers urinary levels within days; it does not change persistent chemicals much.
entries.interactions: The practical tool for [parabens], [triclosan-triclocarban], [uv-filters], [fragrance-musks] and the phthalate part of [phthalates]; keep [sunscreen] use when switching.
entries.caveats: Intervention studies are short, mostly uncontrolled pre-post designs, and measure urine chemicals, not health. Labels are incomplete: product testing found many unlisted chemicals, including in 'alternative' products [epc-dodson2012].
entries.debate: Dermatologists warn that 'natural does not mean safe' and that clean-labelled products are loaded with botanical allergens [epc-rubin2019, epc-tran2022, epc-geier2022]. Environmental-health researchers argue that targeted label reading lowers exposure [epc-harley2016, epc-kim2021] and that precaution is justified given endocrine activity [epc-dodson2012], while noting individual action is limited and regulation would be fairer [epc-jovanovic2026]. A 2-day restriction failed overall in low users [epc-kang2025]. US law (MoCRA) now requires safety substantiation but sets no definition of 'clean' [epc-fdamocra, epc-filley2023].

key_numbers.label: 'Clean' products with at least one potential allergen
Propylparaben after 3 days of labelled-free products
MEP after 5 days without usual products

entries.title: 'Clean', 'natural' and 'free-of' product choices

timing.summary: Switching to products free of specific short-lived chemicals lowers their urine levels within 2-5 days, and the reduction lasts as long as the habit does. It does not change persistent chemicals.

onset.text: Reductions of 22-45% in MEP, parabens, triclosan and BP-3 after 3-5 days [epc-harley2016, epc-jovanovic2026]; no reduction in 2 days among low users [epc-kang2025].

full.text: A web-based programme sustained reductions over 1 month [epc-kim2021].

after_stopping.text: Not measured directly; given half-lives of hours to a day, levels return within days of resuming old products (extrapolated from [epc-shin2023, epc-sandborgh2006]).

frequency.text: The benefit lasts only while the low-exposure products are used every day.

timing.debate: Whether short switches work for everyone is contested: large drops in Latina teenagers and French young women [epc-harley2016, epc-jovanovic2026] versus no overall change in Korean girls who used few products [epc-kang2025].

entries.headline: Two days/week at 500-650 kcal matched continuous restriction for weight loss (-6.4 vs -5.6 kg at 6 months; -8.0 vs -9.0 kg at 1 year) and for HbA1c in type 2 diabetes, with more hunger and double the hypoglycaemia rate on glucose-lowering drugs.

dose.effective: 500 kcal (women) / 600 kcal (men) on 2 non-consecutive days per week, usual healthy eating on the other 5.
dose.studied_range: 400-650 kcal on 2 days/week for 3-12 months.
dose.too_much: Not for insulin or sulfonylurea users without medication adjustment (hypoglycaemia RR 2.05); not for pregnancy or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Weight changes within 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Low-calorie days do not usually produce deep ketosis because some food is eaten.

entries.mechanism: Weekly energy deficit with two short periods of very low intake; small extra falls in fasting insulin vs continuous restriction in one trial.
entries.interactions: Interchangeable with [calorie-restriction] and [alternate-day-fasting]; choose by preference. Benefits follow [weight-loss] and [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Few trials measured oxidative stress directly; any benefit is expected to follow weight loss.

key_numbers.label: Weight change at 6 months (vs -5.6 kg continuous)
Hypoglycaemia rate ratio on glucose-lowering drugs

entries.title: 5:2 diet (two low-calorie days per week)

timing.summary: Two low-calorie days a week produce weight loss that builds for about six months, matching continuous dieting. The benefits last only as long as the weight stays off.

onset.text: Not reported at early time points in the trials reviewed; weight loss was measured at 6 months [tbody-harvie2011].

full.text: Weight loss similar to continuous restriction at 6 months, then held over a further 6-month maintenance phase [tbody-harvie2011, tbody-sundfor2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured for 5:2 specifically; after structured diets people keep only 17-29% of lost weight at 4-5 years [tbody-anderson2001].

frequency.text: Two fasting days a week; no advantage over the same deficit spread daily [tbody-sundfor2018, tbody-allaf2021].

timing.debate: Fasting-specific benefits are proposed via the metabolic switch [tbody-anton2018], but trials matched for calories show no difference from continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021, tbody-sundfor2018].

audit.claim: 5:2 matches continuous restriction for weight loss with more hunger and hypoglycaemia on glucose-lowering drugs.
audit.biases: None beyond small, short trials.
audit.newer_evidence: One-year trials and meta-analyses agree [adiet-harvie2011, adiet-sundfor2018, adiet-semnaniazad2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Every dose is detoxified with glutathione: even 600-1200 mg speeds glutathione turnover, 4 g/day raised liver enzymes (ALT >3x normal) in 31-44% of healthy adults within two weeks, and overdose exhausts glutathione; the prenatal autism/ADHD association shrinks to nothing in sibling comparisons.

dose.effective: Occasional use at labelled doses (e.g. 500-1000 mg per dose) for pain or fever.
dose.studied_range: 50-1200 mg single doses (glutathione turnover); 4 g/day for 14 days (liver enzymes); 4 g/day for 12 weeks (resistance-training trial).
dose.too_much: Label maximum for healthy adults is 4 g/day; at that dose ALT rose in a third of healthy volunteers. Overdose is a medical emergency. People with low glutathione reserves (fasting, malnutrition, heavy alcohol use, liver disease) have less margin.
dose.timeframe: Glutathione drain is per dose; ALT rises appeared within days at 4 g/day and resolved after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. In pregnancy, follow the 2021 consensus advice: use it when medically indicated (fever needs treating), at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and check with a clinician before long-term use. Do not combine products that both contain acetaminophen.

entries.mechanism: A small fraction of each dose is oxidized by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which is neutralized by conjugation with glutathione; therapeutic doses measurably accelerate cysteine and glutathione turnover [med-lauterburg1987]. When glutathione runs out (overdose), NAPQI binds liver proteins and causes oxidative hepatocyte death, which is why the glutathione precursor N-acetylcysteine is the antidote. Acetaminophen also weakly inhibits COX and has anti-androgenic effects in rodent fetal testis [med-kristensen2011].
entries.interactions: Shares the glutathione pool with other detox demands; [n-acetylcysteine] replenishes cysteine for glutathione. [alcohol] and [calorie-restriction]/fasting reduce the safety margin. In older adults it did not blunt (and may have enhanced) gains from [resistance-training]. Often chosen instead of [nsaids] around conception and in pregnancy.
entries.caveats: Therapeutic-dose glutathione depletion in healthy people is transient and not shown to cause harm; ALT rises at 4 g/day resolved. Male-fertility signals (longer time to pregnancy) come from one cohort and were not seen when exposure was modelled continuously.
entries.debate: Pregnancy: a consensus statement of 91 scientists [med-bauer2021] and a 2025 Navigation Guide review (27 of 46 studies positive) [med-prada2025] urge precaution over neurodevelopmental risk; teratology experts warned against causal inference [med-alwan2022], and a 2.5-million-child Swedish sibling analysis found no association with autism, ADHD or intellectual disability (HR 0.98) [med-ahlqvist2024]. Male reproduction: Danish cohort and rat data link prenatal mild analgesics to cryptorchidism but the Finnish cohort did not [med-kristensen2011]; adult male urinary paracetamol was linked to longer time to pregnancy in the top quartile only [med-smarr2016]. Exercise: OTC acetaminophen enhanced muscle gains in older adults [med-trappe2011], while reviews warn COX inhibitors may impair adaptation in the young [med-lundberg2018].

key_numbers.label: Healthy adults with ALT >3x ULN on 4 g/day
Fecundability OR, top-quartile male urinary paracetamol

entries.title: Acetaminophen (paracetamol)

timing.summary: Every dose draws on glutathione within hours, since therapeutic doses of 600-1200 mg speed cysteine and glutathione turnover [tleg-lauterburg1987]. Daily 4 g raises ALT above three times normal in 31-44% of healthy adults within 2 weeks [tleg-watkins2006], and - importantly for timing - those elevations resolve by day 40 even if dosing continues [tleg-heard2014].

onset.text: Glutathione turnover rises within hours of a single therapeutic dose [tleg-lauterburg1987]. At 4 g/day, ALT elevations appear within 4-14 days [tleg-watkins2006, tleg-heard2014].

full.text: The liver-enzyme signal peaks within the first 2-3 weeks and then adapts: 77% of people on 4 g/day had no or only transient ALT elevation by day 16, and 47 of the 48 with raised ALT at day 16 normalised by day 40 while still taking the drug [tleg-heard2014].

after_stopping.text: ALT elevations resolve over days to a few weeks after stopping, and often lag behind the drug's disappearance from blood [tleg-watkins2006]. The glutathione drain itself is per dose and ends with the dose [tleg-lauterburg1987].

frequency.text: The exposure is per dose, so occasional use and continuous maximal use are different exposures: 4 g/day is where the enzyme signal appears [tleg-watkins2006], and that signal attenuates with continued dosing [tleg-heard2014]. In older adults, 4 g/day for 12 weeks during resistance training did not impair muscle gains [tleg-trappe2011].

sperm.late_start: No lead time has been established; the glutathione effect is per dose and ends with the dose [tleg-lauterburg1987].
sperm.text: No human study has measured semen outcomes against timing of acetaminophen use, so no window can be given.

egg.late_start: No evidence supports stopping ahead of conception for egg quality; the recognised concerns are about exposure during pregnancy, i.e. after conception.
egg.text: No measured time course for egg outcomes exists; in the miscarriage cohort acetaminophen users served as the indication control group rather than showing the NSAID-associated risk [tleg-li2018nsaid].

timing.debate: The clinical meaning of the fast ALT rise is disputed: it appears in a third to a half of healthy adults within 2 weeks [tleg-watkins2006], yet it resolves during continued dosing and no participant developed liver dysfunction [tleg-heard2014], which argues for adaptation rather than progressive injury. Whether the per-dose glutathione cost matters at ordinary intermittent doses has not been tested on any clinical outcome [tleg-lauterburg1987].

audit.claim: Acetaminophen is detoxified by glutathione and 4 g/day raises ALT; the prenatal autism/ADHD association shrinks to nothing in sibling comparisons.
audit.biases: Confounding by maternal fever, infection, pain and familial (genetic) factors; exposure misclassification.
audit.newer_evidence: The Swedish sibling analysis found no association (autism HR 0.98) [abody-ahlqvist2024]. A 2025 BMJ umbrella review rated the reviews reporting a link as low to critically low quality and noted associations vanish in sibling-controlled studies [abody-sheikh2025]; a 2026 meta-meta-analysis found small associations that attenuated toward null in higher-quality studies [abody-tayebihillali2026]. A 2025 Navigation Guide review still urged precaution [abody-prada2025].
audit.bottom_line: The best-controlled evidence does not support a causal link to autism or ADHD; use when indicated at the lowest effective dose.

entries.headline: EFSA concluded that dietary acrylamide (average adult intake 0.4-0.9 µg/kg body weight per day) is a concern for cancer based on animal data, but human meta-analyses are largely null, with weak signals only for kidney cancer and, in never-smokers, endometrial and ovarian cancer.

dose.effective: Fry, roast, bake and toast starchy foods to golden rather than dark brown; soak or blanch cut potatoes before frying; an air fryer produced about 90% less acrylamide than deep frying in one study.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes around 9-40 µg/day (median ~23 µg/day across studies).
dose.too_much: EFSA's margin-of-exposure approach treats any exposure as carrying some risk; no safe threshold is set because acrylamide's metabolite glycidamide is genotoxic. Adult 95th-percentile intake is 0.6-2.0 µg/kg bw/day.
dose.timeframe: Cancer: decades. Haemoglobin adducts reflect the last ~4 months of exposure.
dose.notes: Main sources: fried potatoes and crisps, coffee, biscuits, crackers, crispbread and toast. Coffee is a major source; its overall evidence is covered under [coffee].

entries.mechanism: Formed when the amino acid asparagine reacts with reducing sugars above ~120 °C (Maillard reaction) in low-moisture foods. CYP2E1 converts acrylamide to glycidamide, which forms DNA adducts; acrylamide also depletes glutathione and generates ROS, adding oxidative DNA damage and non-genotoxic effects.
entries.interactions: Shares Maillard chemistry with AGEs in [high-temperature-cooking]. Smoking is a much larger acrylamide source than diet, which is why cancer signals are sought in never-smokers. Air frying cuts acrylamide and oil intake ([oxidized-frying-oils]).
entries.caveats: Food questionnaires correlate only moderately with blood adducts (r ~0.3), so cohorts misclassify exposure and may hide or distort small effects. In pregnancy, higher cord-blood acrylamide adducts were linked to 132 g lower birth weight in a European study; this is observational.
entries.debate: Regulators: EFSA's 2015 opinion, reaffirmed in 2022, concluded that margins of exposure indicate a concern for cancer [kcc-efsa2015, kcc-efsa2022]. Epidemiology: pooled analyses find no association for most cancers [kcc-pelucchi2015, kcc-filippini2022] and an early Swedish study was null or even inverse [kcc-mucci2003], but the Netherlands Cohort Study found ovarian HR 1.78 and, in never-smokers, endometrial HR 1.99 [kcc-hogervorst2007], and a later meta-analysis supported small ovarian and endometrial risks in never-smokers [kcc-adani2020]. Biomarker studies split: adducts were linked to ER-positive breast cancer in Denmark [kcc-olesen2008] but not to ovarian cancer in EPIC [kcc-obonsantacana2016]. Critics of the null cohorts point to weak FFQ-adduct correlations [kcc-wilson2009].

entries.title: Acrylamide (browned starchy foods, coffee)

timing.summary: Acrylamide itself is gone within 3-4 days of a meal, so urinary markers reflect yesterday's cooking [tleg-goempel2017]. Haemoglobin adducts average the last few months because they ride on the red cell, and the health concern - cancer - plays out over decades, which is why no short intervention can show a benefit.

onset.text: Urinary mercapturic acid excretion rises within hours of an acrylamide-rich meal and is essentially complete in 72-96 hours [tleg-goempel2017]; haemoglobin adducts form in linear proportion to dose [tleg-fennell2005].

full.text: Adduct levels approach a plateau over the roughly 120-day life of the red cell, so a sustained change in cooking habits takes about 4 months to show fully in adducts; within-person adduct levels are otherwise stable over years [tleg-wilson2009]. The cancer endpoints that motivate concern accrue over decades.

after_stopping.text: Labelled acrylamide was cleared within 72-96 hours with no release from deep compartments [tleg-goempel2017], but adducts wash out only as the labelled red cells are replaced, over roughly 4 months. A measurable background excretion persisted on an acrylamide-minimised diet, implying the body makes some acrylamide itself - so you cannot get to zero [tleg-goempel2017].

frequency.text: Because exposure does not accumulate in tissue, what matters is the long-run average, not any single meal: an occasional batch of dark-roasted or well-browned food is irrelevant against the endogenous background [tleg-goempel2017]. Daily staples (coffee, bread, fried potato) dominate intake and therefore adducts [tleg-wilson2009].

timing.debate: The implication of the endogenous background is contested in practice: if the body generates 0.3-0.4 ug/kg/day of acrylamide regardless of diet [tleg-goempel2017], the achievable reduction from cooking changes is smaller than exposure-assessment models assume. Adducts also correlate only moderately (r about 0.3) with questionnaire intake, so studies disagree partly because they are measuring different time windows [tleg-wilson2009].

factors.name: Advanced sperm selection for ICSI (PICSI/hyaluronan, MACS, microfluidics, IMSI)

entries.headline: Selecting 'better' sperm lowers measured DNA fragmentation in the dish but has not raised live birth: PICSI in 2772 couples gave 27.4% vs 25.2% (NS), MACS and microfluidics trials are small and conflicting; HFEA rates PICSI black and SDF-guided selection grey.

dose.effective: Not routinely recommended (ESHRE); microfluidics 'can be considered'. If SDF is high, cheaper first steps are short abstinence and fixing causes.
dose.studied_range: Hyaluronan binding (PICSI), annexin-V magnetic beads (MACS), microfluidic chips, high-magnification morphology (IMSI).
dose.too_much: Extra cost per cycle; no safety signal.
dose.timeframe: Lab step on the day of ICSI.
dose.notes: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan selection probably slightly reduces miscarriage (RR 0.59, moderate certainty), a secondary outcome.

entries.mechanism: Mature sperm with intact chromatin bind hyaluronan; apoptotic sperm expose phosphatidylserine (removed by MACS); microfluidic channels select motile sperm without the ROS burst of centrifugation. All aim to deliver sperm with less oxidative DNA damage to the egg.
entries.interactions: Alternatives for high SDF: [short-abstinence], [varicocele] repair, [testicular-sperm-icsi]; the egg's repair capacity falls with [maternal-age], so effects might differ by female age.
entries.caveats: Lower DFI in the prepared sample does not translate into live births in trials so far.
entries.debate: A small single-centre RCT reported higher live birth with a microfluidic chip (46.8% vs 25%) [fer-aydin2022], but a 2026 RCT found lower DFI without better live birth [fer-huong2026]; MACS RCTs were null [fer-romany2014, fer-mantravadi2024]. HABSelect was null for live birth [fer-miller2019], while Cochrane 2026 finds a probable miscarriage reduction with hyaluronan selection [fer-garg2026]. ESHRE: not routine, microfluidics 'can be considered' [fer-eshre2023addons]; HFEA: PICSI black, SDF-guided selection grey [fer-hfea2026, fer-hfea2026sdf].

key_numbers.label: Term live birth, PICSI vs ICSI (HABSelect)

entries.title: Advanced sperm selection for ICSI (PICSI/hyaluronan, MACS, microfluidics, IMSI)

audit.claim: Selecting 'better' sperm lowers SDF in the dish but has not raised live birth; HFEA PICSI black, SDF-guided selection grey.
audit.biases: Small single-centre positive trials; surrogate outcome (DFI of prepared sample).
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2026: hyaluronan selection may make little difference to live birth (RR 1.09) and probably reduces miscarriage [afert-garg2026]; HABSelect null [afert-miller2019]. On the other side, an Egyptian 4-arm RCT in high-SDF couples reported higher ongoing pregnancy with PICSI and MACS than density-gradient preparation [afert-hozyen2022].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Aflatoxin from mouldy maize and peanuts causes an estimated 5-28% of liver cancers worldwide, multiplying hepatitis B risk, mostly in Africa and Asia; in Europe exposure is low but EFSA still flags concern, and children commonly carry several mycotoxins (deoxynivalenol above its tolerable intake in about a third of UK child samples).

dose.effective: Discard nuts, grains, dried fruit and spices that look or smell mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured; store them cool and dry and buy from reputable sources; get vaccinated against hepatitis B. In a trial in a high-exposure region, chlorophyllin 100 mg with each meal cut aflatoxin-DNA adducts by 55%.
dose.studied_range: High-exposure Chinese and African populations; European dietary exposure from peanuts, tree nuts, maize and dried figs.
dose.too_much: Aflatoxin B1 is a genotoxic carcinogen with no safe threshold; EFSA found margins of exposure of 29-5,000 (below 10,000 = concern).
dose.timeframe: Albumin adducts reflect the previous 2-3 months; urinary DNA adducts the last days; liver cancer risk accumulates over decades.
dose.notes: Exposure is highest where maize and peanuts are staples and storage is poor; in Europe and North America regulatory limits keep average intake low.

entries.mechanism: Aflatoxin B1 is activated by CYP enzymes to an epoxide that forms DNA adducts (TP53 codon 249 mutations) and generates ROS; detoxification depends on glutathione S-transferases, which Nrf2 activators such as sulforaphane induce.
entries.interactions: Sulforaphane from [broccoli-sprouts] tracked lower aflatoxin adducts in Qidong [efw-kensler2005]. Hepatitis B and alcohol multiply liver risk.
entries.caveats: Most outcome data come from high-exposure, high-hepatitis-B regions and do not translate directly to Western diets. Male-fertility data are a single 1994 Nigerian case-control study.
entries.debate: Liver cancer burden is well supported [efw-liu2010, efw-liu2012], and EFSA flags concern even in Europe [efw-efsa2020]. Growth: observational links with child stunting were not confirmed in a cluster RCT where aflatoxin-tested maize lowered exposure but not stunting [efw-hoffmann2018]. Reproduction: aflatoxin was found in semen of 40% of infertile vs 8% of fertile Nigerian men [efw-ibeh1994, efw-shuaib2010], unreplicated. Mycotoxin mixtures correlated with oxidative stress markers in a cross-sectional study [efw-aljaal2021].

entries.title: Aflatoxin and other mycotoxins

entries.headline: Acute alcohol raised urinary isoprostanes in a time- and dose-dependent way in healthy volunteers, tracking blood alcohol; red-wine polyphenols do not cancel this.

dose.effective: Less is better for oxidative stress; there is no antioxidant reason to drink.
dose.studied_range: Acute doses in a randomized placebo-controlled study; patients with alcoholic liver disease.
dose.too_much: Dose-dependent; heavy and binge drinking worst.
dose.timeframe: Hours.
dose.notes: Covered in more depth in the lifestyle section.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism by CYP2E1 generates ROS; acetaldehyde depletes glutathione; raised NADH/NAD+ alters mitochondrial redox; iron mobilisation.
entries.interactions: Negates the polyphenol benefit of [red-wine-resveratrol].
entries.caveats: Small acute study; chronic moderate intake data are confounded.
entries.title: Alcohol (dietary)

entries.headline: Alcohol raises lipid-peroxidation markers even at moderate intake (4 drinks/day of red wine raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine without alcohol); there is no antioxidant benefit from drinking.

dose.effective: Less is better. If drinking, stay at or below ~100 g alcohol/week (about 7 US standard drinks or 12 UK units), spread out, with alcohol-free days; avoid binges.
dose.studied_range: Experimental: 41 g/day (4 drinks) red wine for 4 weeks; acute dosing in volunteers; cohorts across 0 to >350 g/week.
dose.too_much: Mortality rose above ~100 g/week; heavy and binge drinking drive CYP2E1 induction and liver injury.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostane rise within 4 weeks of daily moderate drinking; acute rise after single doses.
dose.notes: The polyphenols in red wine did not offset the alcohol; dealcoholized wine performed better.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase and, with chronic use, by induced CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and H2O2. Acetaldehyde forms protein/DNA adducts and depletes glutathione; a high NADH/NAD+ ratio, iron mobilization and gut-derived endotoxin activating Kupffer-cell NADPH oxidase add to the load.
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking]. Can worsen [short-sleep] quality, [sleep-apnea] and [weight-loss] (alcohol is calorie-dense).
entries.caveats: The 'red wine is an antioxidant' story is not supported by biomarker data. Observational 'J-curves' for heart disease are confounded.
entries.title: Alcohol

entries.headline: Daily or heavy drinking lowers semen quality (about 33% lower concentration above 40 units/week); occasional light drinking shows little effect.

dose.effective: Keep intake at or below about 5 units (UK units, ~8 g alcohol each) per week while trying to conceive; avoid daily drinking.
dose.studied_range: From 0 to over 40 units/week in 1221 young Danish men; 15 cross-sectional studies (16,395 men).
dose.too_much: Adverse associations appear above ~5 units/week and are strongest above 25 units/week.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Binge drinking was not independently linked to semen in the Danish study, but heavy episodes are best avoided.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), lowers testosterone, raises estrogen and depletes antioxidants such as glutathione.
entries.interactions: Often clustered with [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Direct SDF data are scarce; most evidence is on conventional parameters and is cross-sectional.
entries.title: Alcohol

entries.headline: Heavier drinking lowers fertility, but under about 7 drinks a week effects on conception are small or undetectable; one IVF cohort saw 16% lower live birth at 4 or more drinks a week.

dose.effective: Ideally none while trying; if drinking, keep well under 4 drinks/week before and during IVF.
dose.studied_range: 0 to >= 14 servings/week; light <= 12.5 g ethanol/day vs >12.5 g/day.
dose.too_much: >= 4 drinks/week associated with lower IVF live birth (OR 0.84); >12.5 g/day (about one drink/day) with ~23% lower fecundability; ASRM: >2 drinks/day best avoided.
dose.timeframe: Preconception months; stop entirely once pregnancy is possible (fetal safety).
dose.notes: Data do not separate binge from regular drinking; binge drinking in the fertile window is probably worse.

entries.mechanism: Ethanol metabolism generates acetaldehyde and ROS (CYP2E1), disturbs estrogen and LH signalling, and depletes antioxidant reserves.
entries.interactions: Effects combine across partners in IVF (both drinking >= 4/week: OR 0.79).
entries.caveats: Studies conflict: a large Danish cohort found no effect below 14/week, and the EARTH IVF cohort found no effect of <= 12 g/day. The pregnancy-safety case for abstinence is stronger than the egg-quality case.
entries.title: Alcohol

timing.summary: Semen differences track habitual, mostly daily or heavy, drinking rather than occasional drinks. Recovery after stopping heavy drinking can be complete within about one spermatogenic cycle.

onset.text: Not measured in sperm; associations are with habitual intake over typical weeks, strongest above 25 units/week [tsperm-jensen2014].

full.text: Not measured; in a heavy chronic drinker, damage built up over years from abnormal morphology to azoospermia [tsperm-sermondade2010].

after_stopping.text: After stopping heavy drinking, semen was normal within 3 months in one documented case [tsperm-sermondade2010], which fits one spermatogenic cycle of about 64-76 days [tsperm-misell2006].

frequency.text: Differences appear mainly in daily versus occasional drinkers; moderate intake did not clearly harm semen [tsperm-ricci2017]. Concentration was 33% lower above 40 units/week [tsperm-jensen2014]. No study compared binge versus spread-out patterns for sperm DNA.

sperm.late_start: Cutting down 2-4 weeks before only reaches sperm already in late spermiogenesis and storage; whether that helps was never measured.
sperm.text: Heavy alcohol acted at meiosis (pachytene arrest) in the case report [tsperm-sermondade2010], so the full benefit needs a whole cycle (extrapolated).

egg.late_start: Alcohol clears within hours, so stopping 2 weeks before still removes exposure during final maturation, conception and the weeks before a pregnancy is recognised.
egg.text: In IVF, female drinking in the month before was linked to failure to conceive and in the week before to miscarriage [tegg-klonoffcohen2003]; four or more drinks a week before IVF lowered live birth odds by 16% [tegg-rossi2011]. Fewer than 14 drinks a week did not change natural fecundability [tegg-mikkelsen2016], but any drinking in pregnancy was linked to miscarriage (OR 1.19) [tegg-sundermann2019], so stopping before the conception cycle covers the unrecognised early weeks.

timing.debate: Cross-sectional data link habitual intake above 5 units/week to poorer semen [tsperm-jensen2014], while a meta-analysis found moderate intake did not clearly harm semen and only daily drinking mattered [tsperm-ricci2017]; neither measured a time course.

audit.claim: Alcohol raises lipid-peroxidation markers with no antioxidant benefit, observational J-curves are confounded, and less is better (at most ~100 g/week if drinking).
audit.biases: The classic J-curve compares drinkers with 'abstainers' that include sick quitters and former heavy drinkers (reverse causation), and light drinkers have healthier lifestyles and higher socioeconomic status (residual confounding) [abody-stockwell2016, abody-biddinger2022].
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analyses that separate lifetime abstainers and adjust for former-drinker bias find no mortality benefit of low-volume drinking (2016: RR 0.97 [abody-stockwell2016]; 2023, 107 cohorts: RR 0.93, not significant, with harm from 45 g/day [abody-zhao2023]). Mendelian randomization removes the U-shape: in 512,715 Chinese adults genotype-predicted intake raised stroke log-linearly [abody-millwood2019]; ADH1B carriers who drink less have less coronary disease [abody-holmes2014]; UK Biobank MR shows rising cardiovascular risk [abody-biddinger2022] and a linear rise in mortality [abody-kassaw2024]. WHO staff state no safe level for cancer can be set [abody-anderson2023]. On the other side, GBD 2020 still models a J-shaped burden curve for people over 40 (minimum risk 0.1-1.9 drinks/day) [abody-gbd2022], and a 2025 US National Academies review for the Dietary Guidelines re-examined moderate drinking and mortality [abody-nasem2025] (its graded conclusions could not be retrieved in this session). Caveat: non-linear MR methods used in some of these papers are themselves biased under common conditions [abody-burgess2023, abody-hamilton2024], so the cleanest genetic evidence is the linear and the China Kadoorie analyses.
audit.bottom_line: There is no good evidence that light drinking protects health: less is better. The ~100 g/week figure is a ceiling for current drinkers, not a safe dose.

entries.headline: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day cut ejaculate volume by 2.4 mL and caused complete anejaculation in 35% of healthy men, and 95% of sexually active silodosin users reported ejaculatory disorder; alfuzosin had no such effect.

dose.effective: Tamsulosin 0.4-0.8 mg/day; silodosin 8 mg/day (typical prostate doses).
dose.studied_range: Tamsulosin 0.8 mg/day vs alfuzosin vs placebo (healthy volunteers); silodosin in 91 men with BPH.
dose.too_much: Higher tamsulosin doses and silodosin have the strongest effect.
dose.timeframe: Immediate and reversible on stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men trying to conceive who take these drugs can ask about an alternative (alfuzosin did not affect ejaculation in the healthy-volunteer trial) or timing.

entries.mechanism: Alpha-1A blockade relaxes the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and bladder neck, reducing emission of semen; the tamsulosin trial found this was not explained by retrograde ejaculation [med-hellstrom2006]. This is a mechanical, not a redox, effect.
entries.interactions: Often combined with [finasteride-sperm] (5-ARIs) for prostate enlargement, which also lowers semen volume.
entries.caveats: Ejaculate volume and anejaculation matter for natural conception; sperm production itself is not shown to be harmed.
entries.debate: No substantive published debate found on the effect itself; the size differs by drug, with tamsulosin and silodosin affecting most men and alfuzosin none in a head-to-head trial [med-hellstrom2006, med-sakata2012].
entries.title: Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, silodosin) and ejaculation

timing.summary: Tamsulosin and silodosin act on the muscles that move semen, not on sperm production, so the effect is on within days. It should also wear off within days of stopping, though no study timed that.

onset.text: After 5 days of tamsulosin 0.8 mg, ejaculate volume fell 2.4 mL and 35% of men had no ejaculate [tsperm-hellstrom2006].

full.text: Present at the first check (day 5) [tsperm-hellstrom2006]; with silodosin 95% of sexually active men reported ejaculatory disorder [tsperm-sakata2012].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; because the effect is pharmacological on emission rather than on spermatogenesis, it should fade within days of stopping (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Effect occurs with every dose; alfuzosin did not reduce ejaculate volume and is the usual alternative [tsperm-hellstrom2006].

sperm.late_start: Switching or pausing (with a doctor) even 1-2 weeks before trying should restore ejaculation, since sperm production is not affected (extrapolated).
sperm.text: Acts on ejaculation, not on any stage of sperm development, so no 3-month lead time is needed.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: 600 mg/day ALA eases diabetic nerve-pain symptoms over weeks, but a 4-year trial missed its main endpoint with more serious adverse events, weight loss is only about 1.3 kg, and it can trigger insulin autoimmune hypoglycaemia in genetically susceptible people.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day orally for symptomatic diabetic neuropathy; 600 mg/day IV for 3 weeks in clinical settings
dose.studied_range: 300-1800 mg/day orally for 5 weeks to 4 years
dose.too_much: Doses above 600 mg/day add nausea, vomiting and vertigo without more benefit; insulin autoimmune syndrome reported 30-120 days after starting 600 mg/day in HLA-DRB1*04:03 or *04:06 carriers
dose.timeframe: Symptom relief within 3-5 weeks; no structural nerve benefit over 4 years
dose.notes: Not a general longevity supplement. The egg- and sperm-specific evidence is on the same page.

entries.mechanism: A mitochondrial enzyme cofactor (pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase). As a free supplement, ALA and its reduced form dihydrolipoate scavenge radicals, chelate metals, help recycle vitamins C and E and glutathione, and can activate Nrf2. Its thiol groups explain the immune reaction to insulin in susceptible people.
entries.interactions: May add to glucose-lowering drugs; watch for hypoglycaemia. Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine] as a thiol antioxidant.
entries.caveats: Neuropathy symptom trials are short and mostly from one network; the 4-year NATHAN 1 trial was negative on its primary endpoint. Unexplained low blood sugar in someone taking ALA warrants testing for insulin autoimmune syndrome.
entries.debate: Short trials and a meta-analysis show symptom relief, particularly with IV dosing [lon-ziegler2006, lon-mijnhout2012], while the long NATHAN 1 trial found no effect on the primary composite outcome, only on some secondary scores, and more serious adverse events on ALA (38% vs 28%) [lon-ziegler2011]. The meta-analysts themselves questioned the clinical relevance of oral dosing [lon-mijnhout2012]. Weight-loss effects are statistically significant but small [lon-kucukgoncu2017]. Case series show a rare but serious autoimmune risk [lon-gullo2014].

entries.title: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)

entries.headline: A systematic review reports some positive effects on oocyte maturation, embryo grade and endometriosis pain, but the trials are small and no live-birth benefit has been shown.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: Small trials, often combined with inositol or other agents.
dose.notes: Mostly from Italian combination-product studies.

entries.mechanism: Mitochondrial enzyme cofactor and redox-cycling antioxidant that regenerates glutathione, vitamins C and E.
entries.interactions: Usually given with [myo-inositol].
entries.caveats: Evidence base is too weak to recommend.
entries.title: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA)

timing.summary: Alpha-lipoic acid is in and out of the blood within a few hours, yet daily dosing eased neuropathy symptoms within 5 weeks. Four years of daily use did not change the main nerve-damage endpoint, so the benefit is symptomatic and lasts only while it is taken.

onset.text: Blood levels peak 0.5-1 h after a dose and halve every ~0.5 h [tnut-breithaupt1999]; symptom scores were clearly lower at the 5-week assessment [tnut-ziegler2006].

full.text: Symptom relief was established by 5 weeks; no further structural nerve benefit appeared over 4 years [tnut-ziegler2011].

after_stopping.text: Blood levels are gone within hours; how long symptom relief persists after stopping was not measured.

frequency.text: Trials used one 600 mg dose a day, which gave the best benefit-to-side-effect balance despite the very short half-life [tnut-ziegler2006]; no trial compared intermittent schedules.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the disagreement is about whether 4 years of use helps nerves at all [tnut-ziegler2011] versus short-term symptom relief [tnut-ziegler2006].

audit.claim: 600 mg/day eases diabetic nerve-pain symptoms over weeks, but the 4-year NATHAN 1 trial missed its endpoint; small weight loss; rare insulin autoimmune hypoglycaemia.
audit.biases: Short symptom trials largely from one network [anut-mijnhout2012]; long trial null [anut-ziegler2011].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 network meta-analysis found the apparent superiority of sequential IV-then-oral regimens was a bias artefact, with IV ALA best for short-term symptoms [anut-shen2026].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Fasting (0-25% of needs) every other day gives the same 1-year weight loss as daily 25% restriction (-6.0% vs -5.3%), with more dropouts; calorie-matched ADF did not lower oxidative stress markers and lost less fat than daily restriction.

dose.effective: Fast days at ~500 kcal (about 25% of needs) or zero calories, alternating with ad libitum or ~125% days, for 8 weeks to 12 months.
dose.studied_range: 20-36 h fasts every other day; 3 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: Persistent hunger on fast days and high dropout (38% at 1 year). Hypoglycaemia risk with insulin or sulfonylureas.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 3-8 weeks.
dose.notes: Strict 36-h fasts raise beta-hydroxybutyrate even on eating days; a 20-h fast barely does (0.10 mmol/L).

entries.mechanism: Energy deficit plus repeated 20-36 h fasts that lower insulin and raise fat oxidation and ketones; in a long-term cohort ADF lowered sICAM-1, LDL and T3.
entries.interactions: Matches [calorie-restriction] and [five-two-diet]; benefits follow [weight-loss]. Food quality on eating days still matters; a [mediterranean-diet]-style pattern is a sensible base.
entries.caveats: The large falls in isoprostanes, carbonyls and nitrotyrosine (Johnson 2007) came from an uncontrolled study of 10 people. Templeman 2021: ADF without a deficit did nothing, and with a deficit lost less fat than daily CR. The network meta-analysis edge for ADF (-1.29 kg) is trivial.

key_numbers.label: Weight at 12 months, ADF vs control
Fat mass change, ADF at matched deficit (vs -1.75 kg daily CR)

entries.title: Alternate-day fasting

timing.summary: Fasting days start changing insulin action within about two weeks, but the main effect, weight loss, builds over about six months and then levels off. When fasting stops, the gains last only as long as the lost weight stays off.

onset.text: Insulin-mediated glucose uptake improved after 15 days of every-other-day 20-h fasts even without weight loss [tbody-halberg2005]; a 20-h fast raises ketones only slightly (0.10 mmol/L), whereas strict 36-h fasts raised BHB even on eating days after 4 weeks [tbody-stekovic2019].

full.text: Weight loss reached about -6.8% at 6 months and was -6.0% at 12 months, the same as daily 25% restriction [tbody-trepanowski2017].

after_stopping.text: Not measured specifically after stopping ADF. In general, 4-5 years after structured weight-loss programmes people kept only 17-29% of the weight they had lost [tbody-anderson2001], and weight-related benefits fade with regain.

frequency.text: The schedule itself (fast every other day) adds nothing measurable over the same calorie deficit spread daily: weight, insulin and CRP matched daily restriction at 6 and 12 months [tbody-trepanowski2017, tbody-allaf2021]. Pick whichever pattern can be sustained.

timing.debate: A strict 36-h ADF trial reported improved ageing markers and ketones on eating days [tbody-stekovic2019], but a year-long trial found no advantage over daily restriction, with more dropouts [tbody-trepanowski2017], and Cochrane found no meaningful difference from continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021].

audit.claim: ADF gives the same 1-year weight loss as daily restriction with more dropouts; calorie-matched ADF did not lower oxidative stress markers.
audit.biases: The early oxidative-stress result came from an uncontrolled 10-person study.
audit.newer_evidence: Trepanowski 2017 and Templeman 2021 stand [adiet-trepanowski2017, adiet-templeman2021]; the 2025 network meta-analysis found only a small ADF edge [adiet-semnaniazad2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

factors.name: Aluminium, cast iron, stainless steel and glazed pottery

entries.headline: Acidic food leaches metals from cookware: new stainless steel raised nickel and chromium in tomato sauce about 35-fold, artisanal scrap-aluminium pots can leach enough lead to raise children's blood lead, lead-glazed pottery leaches lead, and cast iron adds iron (helpful in deficiency, unhelpful in iron overload).

dose.effective: Avoid lead-glazed or decorative ceramics and artisanal scrap-aluminium pots for cooking; don't cook or store acidic or salty foods (tomato, citrus, vinegar) for long in uncoated aluminium; season new stainless steel pans (leaching falls after about six uses) and use them for acidic dishes rather than storing food in them; people with nickel allergy may prefer enamelled or glass for acidic stews; cast iron is fine for most people but avoid it if you have haemochromatosis.
dose.studied_range: Laboratory cooking with acidic simulants and tomato sauce; iron-pot trials in low- and middle-income countries.
dose.too_much: About 88 ug nickel and 86 ug chromium per serving of tomato sauce after ten uses of stainless steel. EFSA tolerable weekly intake for aluminium 1 mg/kg body weight; food alone supplies about half of it for average German adults. Lead leaching >250 ug/L from about 1 in 10 artisanal aluminium pots.
dose.timeframe: Leaching happens per meal; stainless-steel leaching falls over the first six cooking cycles.
dose.notes: Commercial anodised aluminium and enamelled pots leach little. Iron cookware raised haemoglobin in some trials in anaemic populations, but a fish-shaped iron ingot did not help Cambodian women where iron deficiency was uncommon.

entries.mechanism: Acids dissolve metal ions from cookware surfaces. Iron and nickel can catalyse Fenton chemistry; lead and aluminium impair antioxidant enzymes; nickel triggers allergic inflammation in sensitised people.
entries.interactions: Cast iron interacts with [iron-deficiency] (helps) and [iron-excess] (avoid). Lead from pots adds to [lead-drinking-water] and [lead-spices]. Non-stick alternatives: [nonstick-cookware].
entries.caveats: Mostly laboratory leaching with aggressive simulants; few human biomarker studies. The aluminium-Alzheimer hypothesis rests on weak and conflicting data.
entries.debate: Aluminium and dementia: aluminium in drinking water was associated with cognitive decline and dementia in the PAQUID cohort [efw-rondeau2009], but antacid users, who take in far more aluminium, had no excess Alzheimer's disease [efw-virk2015]; aggregated exposure can exceed EFSA's intake limit [efw-tietz2019]. Iron cookware: some trials raised haemoglobin [efw-alves2019], a well-run RCT of an iron ingot did not [efw-rappaport2017]. Lead from pots: lab studies find dangerous leaching from scrap-aluminium [efw-weidenhamer2023, efw-binkhorst2025] and glazed pottery [efw-castellanos2026], though the authors note test conditions may be harsher than real cooking [efw-binkhorst2025].

entries.headline: A 4-day broad-spectrum antibiotic course wiped out much of the gut microbiota in healthy men; most of it recovered within 6 weeks, but 9 common species were still missing in most men at 6 months.

dose.effective: Not applicable: take antibiotics when clinically indicated, for the prescribed course.
dose.studied_range: Meropenem, gentamicin and vancomycin for 4 days in 12 healthy men.
dose.too_much: Repeated or unnecessary courses; effects on polyphenol-converting bacteria are not quantified.
dose.timeframe: Near-baseline recovery in about 1.5 months; some species absent at 180 days.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop a prescribed antibiotic course early on the basis of microbiome concerns. A fibre- and plant-rich diet supports recovery generally, but no specific post-antibiotic protocol is proven.

entries.mechanism: Gut bacteria convert many dietary polyphenols into the metabolites that are actually absorbed, so a depleted microbiome may temporarily change what people get from polyphenol-rich foods; after antibiotics, enterobacteria and pathobionts bloom and butyrate producers and bifidobacteria fall [med-palleja2018].
entries.interactions: Relevant to the benefits of [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol foods; [ppi-acid-suppressants] shift the microbiome more than antibiotics at population level [med-imhann2016]. Treating [genital-tract-infection] with antibiotics can lower seminal ROS.
entries.caveats: Evidence is from a small study in young men; health consequences of the residual changes are unknown.
entries.debate: The same data support both resilience (near-full recovery in 6 weeks) and a lasting imprint (species still missing at 6 months) [med-palleja2018]; at population level, PPI effects on the microbiome exceeded those of antibiotics [med-imhann2016]. No direct human outcome data link these changes to oxidative stress.
entries.title: Antibiotics and the gut microbiome

timing.summary: A short course does its damage in 3-4 days and most of it repairs within about 6 weeks, but not all of it: after a 4-day broad-spectrum cocktail, nine common species were still undetectable at 180 days [tleg-palleja2018], and a 7-day clindamycin course left Bacteroides diversity altered for up to 2 years [tleg-jernberg2007].

onset.text: Diversity collapses within 3-4 days of starting the drug [tleg-dethlefsen2011], and a 4-day cocktail wiped out much of the gut community [tleg-palleja2018].

full.text: The disruption is complete by the end of a typical course; the open question is recovery rather than onset [tleg-palleja2018, tleg-dethlefsen2011].

after_stopping.text: Recovery starts within a week of the last dose and reaches near-baseline at about 1.5 months, but nine common species were still missing at 180 days [tleg-palleja2018]; repeated ciprofloxacin courses left communities stabilised in an altered state [tleg-dethlefsen2011], and clindamycin effects on Bacteroides clones and resistance genes persisted up to 2 years [tleg-jernberg2007].

frequency.text: Each course carries its own incomplete recovery, and repeated courses do not simply repeat the same curve - the second ciprofloxacin course produced a different and less complete recovery than the first [tleg-dethlefsen2011]. Spacing courses does not restore what is lost [tleg-palleja2018].

sperm.late_start: Unknown: no study links antibiotic timing to semen outcomes. If a course is clinically needed, take it.
sperm.text: No measured semen time course exists; the 90-day figure is simply one spermatogenic cycle and is extrapolated, not evidence-based.

timing.debate: How much of the microbiome really fails to come back, and whether it matters, is unsettled: one study found near-complete recovery in 6 weeks with nine species missing at 6 months [tleg-palleja2018], another found persistent altered states and incomplete recovery between individuals [tleg-dethlefsen2011], and a third found 2-year persistence of resistance genes and clonal shifts [tleg-jernberg2007]. What helps recovery is also contested: probiotics delayed and left incomplete the mucosal recovery compared with spontaneous recovery, while autologous faecal transplant restored it within days [tleg-suez2018].

factors.name: Antioxidant supplements during chemotherapy or radiotherapy

entries.headline: In a radiotherapy RCT, vitamin E (with beta-carotene initially) nearly tripled second primary cancers during supplementation (HR 2.88), and antioxidant use during breast-cancer chemotherapy was linked to more recurrence (HR 1.41); older reviews found no loss of efficacy, so the default is: do not take high-dose antioxidants during treatment without the oncology team.

dose.effective: None recommended during active treatment without oncologist approval; food sources are not the concern.
dose.studied_range: Alpha-tocopherol 400 IU/day with or without beta-carotene 30 mg/day (head and neck radiotherapy); self-reported vitamins A, C, E, carotenoids, CoQ10 (breast chemotherapy).
dose.too_much: Any high-dose antioxidant supplement concurrent with radiation or ROS-generating chemotherapy; smokers having radiotherapy are the clearest risk group.
dose.timeframe: Risk concentrated during the supplementation/treatment period.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Tell the oncology team about every supplement, including 'fertility' antioxidant blends used during fertility preservation.

entries.mechanism: Radiotherapy and many chemotherapy drugs kill tumour cells partly through ROS; antioxidants could protect tumour cells as well as normal tissue, though some trials suggest selective protection of normal tissue [med-lawenda2008].
entries.interactions: A special case of [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail], [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] risks; relevant to [chemo-radiation] and fertility preservation; [n-acetylcysteine] and [coq10] are commonly self-prescribed in this setting.
entries.caveats: The breast-cancer data are observational and the result for antioxidants was borderline (CI 0.98-2.04). Some specific agents are used under oncology supervision to reduce toxicity; this is not covered here.
entries.debate: Caution camp: an RCT showed more second cancers with vitamin E during radiotherapy [med-bairati2005], a JNCI review concluded antioxidants should be discouraged [med-lawenda2008], and SWOG S0221 linked antioxidant use to recurrence [med-ambrosone2020]. Reassurance camp: a systematic review of 19 RCTs found no decrease in chemotherapy efficacy and often fewer toxicities, though trials were underpowered [med-block2007], and a 49-RCT review judged harm unclear except for smokers on radiotherapy [med-yasueda2016].

Recurrence HR, antioxidant use during chemo

entries.title: Antioxidant supplements during chemotherapy or radiotherapy

timing.summary: The worry is a time window: antioxidants taken while radiotherapy or chemotherapy is working. In the clearest trial, excess second cancers appeared only while vitamin E was being taken and not after it stopped.

onset.text: Excess second primary cancers appeared during the supplementation period (radiotherapy plus 3 years; HR 2.88) [tnut-bairati2005]; exact onset in days not reported.

full.text: Not applicable; the harm signal was confined to the supplementation period [tnut-bairati2005].

after_stopping.text: After supplementation stopped the rate of second cancers was not higher (HR 0.41) and 8-year cancer-free proportions were similar [tnut-bairati2005].

frequency.text: Avoid high-dose antioxidant supplements from before treatment starts until it ends unless the oncology team agrees; use both before and during chemotherapy was linked to more recurrence [tnut-ambrosone2020].

timing.debate: Timing is unsettled: the randomised trial saw harm only during supplementation [tnut-bairati2005], while the observational chemotherapy study could not separate use before treatment from use during it [tnut-ambrosone2020].

audit.claim: Vitamin E during radiotherapy nearly tripled second cancers (HR 2.88) and antioxidant use during breast chemotherapy was linked to more recurrence (HR 1.41); default is no high-dose antioxidants during treatment without the oncology team.
audit.biases: The breast-cancer HR is observational (self-reported use, confounding by indication and by who chooses supplements) and borderline (CI 0.98-2.04) [anut-ambrosone2020]. The radiotherapy result is an RCT but in head-and-neck patients, mostly smokers [anut-bairati2005].
audit.newer_evidence: No large RCT has settled the question. Mechanistic work strengthened the plausibility: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung-tumour progression [anut-sayin2014] and promoted metastasis via BACH1 in mice [anut-wiel2019]. The precautionary default is reasonable.
audit.bottom_line: Still sound advice; the human evidence is one RCT plus observational data, backed by consistent animal data.

factors.name: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)

entries.headline: The Cochrane review of 63 trials found only low- to very-low-quality evidence that antioxidants help subfertile women, several included trials have since been retracted, and ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF.

dose.effective: No antioxidant product or dose is proven to raise live birth in women.
dose.studied_range: Trials of NAC, melatonin, L-arginine, myo-inositol, carnitine, selenium, vitamins C/E/D, B complex, CoQ10 and omega-3, usually for 1-3 cycles.
dose.too_much: No clear harms in pooled data (miscarriage OR 1.13, GI effects OR 1.55, both NS), but in animals blocking ROS impairs ovulation, so more is not better.
dose.timeframe: Trials typically 1-3 months.
dose.notes: Cochrane's headline OR for live birth (1.81) rests on very-low-quality, small, often unregistered trials; treat it as unreliable. A 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'concern' trials in the review.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavengers cannot reach the mitochondrial sites where oocyte ROS are generated at meaningful concentrations, and ROS are required for LH-triggered ovulation; the 'antioxidant paradox' applies.
entries.interactions: Specific agents are listed separately: [coq10], [melatonin], [myo-inositol], [n-acetylcysteine], [vitamin-c-e-combined], [l-carnitine], [alpha-lipoic-acid], [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements], [nmn-nad]. Antioxidants for the male partner are a different question.
entries.caveats: Supplement marketing for 'egg quality' far outruns the evidence. Spending on lifestyle basics and folic acid is better supported.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, antioxidants vs control (very low quality)

entries.title: Antioxidant supplements in general (for the female partner)

timing.summary: No trial has measured how long antioxidant supplements take to act on the egg. Taken during the IVF cycle they lower oxidative markers in follicular fluid, but live-birth evidence is weak and partly retracted.

onset.text: Follicular oxidative-damage markers fell when melatonin or vitamin E was taken during the treatment cycle [tegg-tamura2008]; exact duration not reported.

full.text: Not measured; covering the ~85-day preantral-to-ovulatory path is an extrapolation [tegg-gougeon1986].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No trial compared schedules.

timing.debate: Cochrane finds low- to very-low-quality evidence; seven included trials were later retracted, although editors judged the conclusions unchanged [tegg-showell2020].

egg.late_start: Starting in the cycle of IVF can still change follicular fluid [tegg-tamura2008], but not the earlier growth of the oocyte.
egg.text: Extrapolated from follicle growth time [tegg-gougeon1986]; the Cochrane review finds only low-quality evidence of benefit [tegg-showell2020].

audit.claim: Cochrane (63 trials) found only low to very low quality evidence; several included trials since retracted; ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in IVF.
audit.biases: Integrity: Cochrane's March 2026 editorial note lists 7 retracted and 2 'expression of concern' trials in the review; editors judge the main conclusion unchanged but the N-acetylcysteine vs L-carnitine comparison loses all data once El Sharkwy 2019 is removed [afert-showell2020, afert-elsharkwy2019]. Other retracted antioxidant fertility trials include CoQ10 with clomiphene in PCOS [afert-elrefaeey2014]. Trials are small, unregistered and use surrogate outcomes.
audit.newer_evidence: No large trustworthy RCT has since shown a live-birth gain. Cochrane-wide trustworthiness work shows such problems are common and are missed by Risk-of-Bias tools [afert-wilkinson2025].
audit.bottom_line: Be cautious: once retracted trials are removed, the evidence is weaker than the headline odds ratio suggests.

factors.name: Antioxidants added to IVF culture media

entries.headline: A single sibling-oocyte RCT (133 patients) found more good day-3 embryos (50% vs 41%) with acetyl-L-carnitine, NAC and alpha-lipoic acid in the medium and higher ongoing pregnancy only in a 35-40 subgroup; no live-birth trial, no HFEA rating.

dose.effective: Unproven; a lab choice, not something patients take.
dose.studied_range: Acetyl-L-carnitine, N-acetyl-L-cysteine and alpha-lipoic acid (A3) at micromolar levels in G-Series media.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation to blastocyst (days 0-6).
dose.notes: This is the one place an antioxidant acts directly on the embryo in a dish, free of oral bioavailability problems.

entries.mechanism: Embryos in culture are exposed to light, atmospheric handling and metabolic ROS without the oviduct's antioxidant defences; direct scavenging and glutathione support may reduce lipid peroxidation and DNA damage. Low oxygen (5%) culture is the established way to limit this.
entries.interactions: Separate from oral antioxidants, which ESHRE does not recommend ([female-antioxidant-supplements], [male-antioxidant-combination]).
entries.caveats: Industry-developed media; the positive outcomes are surrogates or subgroups.
entries.debate: The trial's developers conclude antioxidants 'may improve' embryo viability [fer-gardner2020]; ESHRE's review of oral antioxidants found no reliable live-birth gain and does not recommend antioxidant therapy in ART, and culture-media supplements remain unendorsed [fer-eshre2023addons]. No independent replication found.

factors.name: Arsenic in well and tap water

entries.headline: About 2.1 million Americans drink well water above the 10 ug/L arsenic limit; arsenic is an established carcinogen at high levels, and at low-moderate levels each 20 ug/L is linked to about 9-16% more cardiovascular disease, while a randomized program of point-of-use filters cut urinary arsenic by 47-55%.

dose.effective: Test private well water for arsenic (and uranium) at least once, and again if the area is known for arsenic; if above 10 ug/L, install a certified point-of-use reverse-osmosis or arsenic-adsorption filter for drinking and cooking water and maintain it, or use another source. Cooking rice and pasta in high-arsenic water adds to intake.
dose.studied_range: Well water from <1 to several hundred ug/L; US cohorts mostly 1-50 ug/L.
dose.too_much: WHO/EU/US limit 10 ug/L. Fetal loss and infant death rose above 50 ug/L in Bangladesh. EFSA's reference point is 0.06 ug/kg body weight per day of inorganic arsenic (all sources).
dose.timeframe: Urinary arsenic falls over days to weeks after switching water; cardiovascular and cancer risks reflect years.
dose.notes: Arsenic in water is tasteless and odourless; only testing finds it. Boiling does not remove it.

entries.mechanism: Inorganic arsenic binds thiols, depletes glutathione, inhibits DNA repair and generates ROS during its methylation; arsenic-exposed populations show higher urinary 8-OHdG and comet-assay damage [efw-devizcaya2009, efw-fujino2005]. It also causes endothelial dysfunction and epigenetic changes.
entries.interactions: Rice is the other main source ([arsenic-rice]); arsenic and [uranium-drinking-water] often co-occur in wells; selenium and folate status affect arsenic methylation ([folic-acid]). See [heavy-metals] for other toxic metals.
entries.caveats: Low-level cardiovascular associations weaken after adjusting for diabetes, hypertension and kidney function, which may be mediators or confounders [efw-moon2013]. Cancer risk below about 100 ug/L is disputed. Semen data are mostly small cross-sectional studies; a meta-analysis's pooled concentration and motility differences were not significant [efw-akhigbe2024b].
entries.debate: Low-level harm: dose-response meta-analysis shows CVD risk without a threshold [efw-moon2017]; the Strong Heart Study links low-moderate arsenic to CVD [efw-moon2013]; EFSA judges current dietary exposure a health concern [efw-efsa2024]. Doubt: meta-analyses found no lung or bladder cancer increase up to 150 ug/L [efw-boffetta2019] or at low levels in never-smokers [efw-mink2008]; the 2019 analysis's lead author declared work as a litigation expert [efw-boffetta2019]. Pregnancy: fetal loss rose above 50 ug/L [efw-rahman2007], but a later Bangladesh cohort found a stage-dependent pattern suggesting survival bias [efw-ahmed2019].
