factors.name: Assisted hatching (laser or chemical zona opening)

entries.headline: Across 14 RCTs reporting live birth, assisted hatching made no clear difference (OR 1.09, 0.92-1.29) and may raise multiple pregnancy (OR 1.38); ESHRE does not recommend it and HFEA rates it grey.

dose.effective: Not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Laser, acid Tyrode's or mechanical thinning/opening of the zona pellucida before transfer.
dose.too_much: Possible embryo damage; more multiple pregnancies and monozygotic twinning.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer day.
dose.notes: Often still used routinely for frozen embryos or older women without trial support.

entries.mechanism: Assumes embryos fail to escape a hardened zona pellucida (e.g. after freezing or with age).
entries.interactions: Trophectoderm biopsy for [pgt-a-egg] already opens the zona.
entries.caveats: Very low to low quality trials with publication bias.
entries.debate: Some clinicians argue for subgroups (frozen embryos, older women, thick zona), but no high-quality subgroup evidence exists [fer-lacey2021]; HFEA and ESHRE do not support it [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Assisted hatching (laser or chemical zona opening)

audit.claim: Assisted hatching made no clear live-birth difference (OR 1.09) and may raise multiples; HFEA grey.
audit.biases: Low-quality trials with publication bias.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2021 conclusion unchanged [afert-lacey2021]; HFEA grey as of Sep 2026 [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Astaxanthin modestly lowers blood MDA in small trials and extended median lifespan 12% in male (not female) ITP mice, but no human trial shows a clinical or aging benefit.

dose.effective: No proven clinical dose; trials commonly used 4-12 mg/day of natural astaxanthin
dose.studied_range: 2-24 mg/day approved by different regulators; 35 of 87 human studies used 12 mg/day or more
dose.too_much: No safety concerns in 87 human studies of natural astaxanthin (35 at 12 mg/day or more); EFSA's ADI of 2 mg/day was derived from synthetic astaxanthin in rats
dose.timeframe: Biomarker changes at 8-12 weeks
dose.notes: Fat-soluble; take with a meal. Salmon and shrimp supply small amounts. The sperm-specific evidence is on the same page.

entries.mechanism: A red xanthophyll carotenoid that spans cell membranes and quenches singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals; in models it also activates Nrf2. The ITP classified it as an Nrf2 activator.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with other carotenoids. High-dose beta-carotene harmed smokers ([beta-carotene-supplement]); astaxanthin has no such signal but has never been tested in trials of that size.
entries.caveats: The MDA result is mostly from TBARS-type assays, which are non-specific. Many trials are small and industry-supplied.
entries.debate: Proponents cite a meta-analysis showing reduced MDA and, in diabetes, IL-6 [lon-ma2022], improved exercise performance with training [lon-liu2024], and the ITP male lifespan extension [lon-harrison2024]; Ames lists it as a putative 'longevity vitamin' [lon-ames2018]. Skeptics note the absence of any clinical outcome trial, the male-only mouse effect, and that cognition outcomes were null or marginal [lon-liu2024]. Regulators disagree on safe intake: EFSA's 2 mg/day versus a review arguing natural astaxanthin is safe at 12 mg/day or more [lon-brendler2019].
entries.title: Astaxanthin

entries.headline: One tiny trial (30 men) found 16 mg/day astaxanthin lowered seminal ROS and reported more pregnancies; never replicated at scale.

dose.effective: 16 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 16 mg/day, 3 months.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Carotenoid that spans lipid bilayers and quenches singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals.
entries.interactions: Similar role to [tomatoes-lycopene].
entries.caveats: 11 vs 19 analysed men; pregnancy result very fragile; industry-supplied product.
entries.title: Astaxanthin

entries.headline: Three small RCTs (PCOS, poor responders, endometriosis; 6-12 mg/day for 6-12 weeks) reported more mature (MII) oocytes and high-quality embryos, but the PCOS trial found no difference in pregnancy rates and none reported live births.

dose.effective: 6-12 mg/day for 40 days to 12 weeks before ovarian stimulation.
dose.studied_range: 6-12 mg/day, 40 days to 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No safety signal in these short trials.
dose.timeframe: 6-12 weeks before stimulation.

entries.mechanism: Raised serum antioxidant capacity and granulosa-cell Nrf2/HO-1/NQO1 expression, and lowered follicular-fluid IL-6, IL-8 and cell-free DNA.
entries.interactions: Compare [female-antioxidant-supplements], [coq10] and [astaxanthin].
entries.caveats: Oocyte and embryo grades are surrogates; the trials are small; no live-birth data; independent replication is needed.
entries.title: Astaxanthin before IVF/ICSI

timing.summary: Astaxanthin has a blood half-life of about 16 hours, so daily intake reaches a steady blood level within a few days. How long tissue levels or any benefit take to build or fade has not been measured in humans.

onset.text: Plasma levels rise within hours of a dose (half-life ~16 h) [tnut-odeberg2003].

full.text: Extrapolated: a steady plasma level after about 3-4 days of daily intake (5 half-lives); fertility trials ran 6-12 weeks without time-course data.

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated: plasma falls to near baseline within about 3-4 days; tissue persistence not measured.

frequency.text: The 16-hour half-life favours daily intake with a fatty meal (lipid formulations raised absorption 1.7-3.7-fold) [tnut-odeberg2003]; no schedule comparisons exist.

sperm.late_start: Not measured; a start 2-4 weeks before would only reach sperm in their final maturation.
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; with plasma at steady state in days, the lead time is set by sperm development, not loading (extrapolated).

egg.late_start: Not measured; small trials started 6-12 weeks before stimulation.
egg.text: Extrapolated: the ovulatory follicle's cohort starts differentiating about 85 days before ovulation [tnut-gougeon1986], so starting about 3 months ahead covers the growing follicle.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: General: modest MDA lowering, ITP male lifespan +12%. Sperm: one 30-man trial lowered seminal ROS and reported more pregnancies. Egg: three small RCTs reported more mature oocytes and embryos.
audit.biases: Tiny, industry-supplied trials [anut-comhaire2005]; MDA by non-specific assays [anut-ma2022].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of three human trials found no significant improvement in any semen parameter versus placebo, while animal studies were strongly positive [anut-dehpahni2026]. Egg-side rankings remain very low certainty [anut-du2025].
audit.bottom_line: For sperm the pooled human evidence is now null; impact should be 0.

factors.name: B vitamins (folic acid, B6, B12) to protect the ageing brain

entries.headline: In older people with mild cognitive impairment, folic acid 0.8 mg + B6 20 mg + B12 0.5 mg slowed brain shrinkage by about 30% (53% when homocysteine was above 13 umol/L) in the VITACOG trial, but 11 trials in about 22,000 mostly unselected people showed no effect on cognitive aging.

dose.effective: VITACOG regimen: folic acid 0.8 mg + vitamin B6 20 mg + vitamin B12 0.5 mg daily, for people with MCI and plasma homocysteine above about 11-13 umol/L.
dose.studied_range: VITACOG 2 years; high-dose regimens up to folic acid 5 mg + B6 25 mg + B12 1 mg in Alzheimer disease trials.
dose.too_much: The high-dose Alzheimer trial reported more depression-related adverse events. Correct B12 deficiency medically rather than masking it with folic acid alone.
dose.timeframe: Brain-atrophy differences over 2 years.
dose.notes: Benefit in VITACOG appeared only in people with higher homocysteine and, in post hoc analyses, only when baseline omega-3 (EPA+DHA) levels were good. A homocysteine blood test identifies who might benefit.

entries.mechanism: Folate, B12 and B6 drive homocysteine remethylation and transsulfuration (the route to cysteine and glutathione). High homocysteine promotes oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction and NMDA-receptor excitotoxicity and impairs methylation; omega-3 fats may need adequate methylation capacity to be incorporated into brain phospholipids, a proposed basis for the interaction.
entries.interactions: Interacts with omega-3 status ([omega3-fish]): B vitamins slowed atrophy only in those with high baseline omega-3. Overlaps with [folic-acid] (fertility use) and [multivitamin-mineral], which supplies smaller amounts.
entries.caveats: VITACOG was small (168 people with MRI) and the strongest effects are subgroup and post hoc findings. In established Alzheimer disease, B vitamins did not help.
entries.debate: The VITACOG group and an international consensus statement argue homocysteine is a modifiable dementia risk factor and that trials failed because they enrolled people with normal homocysteine or used cognitive tests too insensitive over short periods [skb-smith2010, skb-douaud2013, skb-smith2018]. Clarke and colleagues' meta-analysis of 11 trials (about 22,000 people) excluded benefits larger than 1 month of cognitive aging per year [skb-clarke2014], and high-dose B vitamins failed in Alzheimer disease [skb-aisen2008]. The omega-3 interaction [skb-jerneren2015, skb-oulhaj2016] comes from secondary analyses of the same small trial and has not been independently replicated.

key_numbers.label: Brain atrophy, B vitamins vs placebo

entries.title: B vitamins (folic acid, B6, B12) to protect the ageing brain

timing.summary: Folic acid lowers homocysteine over weeks, but the brain-atrophy benefit seen in people with mild cognitive impairment and high homocysteine was measured over 2 years. Folate status falls back within months of stopping, while B12 stores last years.

onset.text: Plasma folate rises from the first month and plateaus at about 3 months of daily folic acid [tnut-hao2008].

full.text: Slower brain atrophy was measured after 24 months (0.76% vs 1.08% per year) [tnut-smith2010].

after_stopping.text: Blood folate fell rapidly over 3 months after stopping [tnut-hao2008]; B12 stores (1-5 mg) take years to run down [tnut-ods2025b12]; persistence of the brain effect not measured.

frequency.text: Trials used daily doses; splitting a daily folic acid dose made no difference to blood folate [tnut-hao2008].

timing.debate: The 2-year atrophy benefit in high-homocysteine MCI [tnut-smith2010] contrasts with trials of 1-2 years (and up to 5-10 years) showing no cognitive benefit in broader groups [tnut-ods2025b12]; it is unknown whether longer treatment or earlier timing would matter.

audit.claim: In MCI with high homocysteine, folic acid + B6 + B12 slowed brain atrophy about 30% (53% if homocysteine >13 umol/L) in VITACOG, while 11 trials in ~22,000 people showed no effect on cognitive ageing.
audit.biases: The strongest effects are subgroup and post hoc findings from one 168-person MRI trial [anut-smith2010]; brain atrophy is a surrogate. The homocysteine-dementia link comes largely from cohorts, where homocysteine also marks kidney function, B12 status, smoking and vascular disease (residual confounding).
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization tested the causal chain directly: genetically predicted homocysteine, serum folate and vitamin B12 were not associated with Alzheimer disease [anut-larsson2017], which undercuts the premise that lowering homocysteine prevents dementia. The 11-trial meta-analysis remains null [anut-clarke2014], although proponents dispute it [anut-garrard2015, anut-smith2018].
audit.bottom_line: B vitamins correct deficiency and lower homocysteine, but causal evidence that this protects cognition is weak; treat VITACOG as a hypothesis for high-homocysteine MCI.

entries.headline: At 20-30 mg/day, beta-carotene raised lung cancer by 18-28% and total mortality by 8-17% in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers. No benefit for anyone, and USPSTF recommends against it.

dose.effective: None as a supplement. Food carotenoids (carrots, leafy greens, sweet potato) are a different matter.
dose.studied_range: 6 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX mix) to 20-30 mg/day (ATBC, CARET, HPS)
dose.too_much: 20-30 mg/day: lung cancer RR 1.16-1.28, stomach cancer RR 1.34; harm concentrated in smokers and asbestos workers.
dose.timeframe: Excess lung cancer appeared within the 4-8 year trial periods
dose.notes: CARET combined it with 25,000 IU retinol; Cochrane also found dose-related mortality with vitamin A. Smokers should avoid all beta-carotene and vitamin A supplements.

entries.mechanism: At pharmacological doses in a smoke-oxidised lung, beta-carotene lowers lung retinoic acid and RARβ signalling, and raises AP-1/cyclin D1 proliferation signals. In ferrets, a ~30 mg/day-equivalent dose caused squamous metaplasia and a ~6 mg/day-equivalent dose did not. This is a clear example of dose- and context-dependent pro-oxidant harm.
entries.interactions: The harm is amplified by [tobacco-smoking] and asbestos exposure. Part of [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] and HPS regimens.
entries.caveats: Observational studies linked high blood beta-carotene to lower cancer risk, probably because it marks high fruit and vegetable intake. Supplements reversed this. Multivitamins with small amounts (a few mg) have not shown this harm.
entries.title: Beta-carotene supplements

timing.summary: Beta-carotene has a plasma half-life of about 5 weeks and its harm in smokers outlasted the pills. In one trial the excess faded within 4-6 years of stopping; in the other, excess lung cancer persisted for at least 6 years.

onset.text: Plasma beta-carotene builds with a half-life of about 37 days [tnut-burri2001]; excess lung cancer emerged during 5-8 years of supplementation in trials [tnut-virtamo2003, tnut-goodman2004].

full.text: Not applicable (harm); trial exposures were 4-8 years.

after_stopping.text: ATBC: excess risk gone 4-6 years after stopping [tnut-virtamo2003]; CARET: lung cancer and mortality RR stayed above 1 for 6 years, while cardiovascular excess faded quickly [tnut-goodman2004].

frequency.text: No schedule makes high-dose beta-carotene pills safe for smokers or asbestos-exposed people [tnut-goodman2004].

timing.debate: ATBC found the excess faded within 4-6 years of stopping [tnut-virtamo2003], whereas CARET found lung-cancer and mortality excess persisting through 6 years, especially in women [tnut-goodman2004].

audit.claim: 20-30 mg/day beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18-28% and mortality 8-17% in smokers and asbestos workers; no benefit for anyone; USPSTF recommends against it.
audit.biases: This is the textbook case of an observational association reversed by trials: high blood beta-carotene marked a fruit- and vegetable-rich, non-smoking lifestyle (residual confounding by diet and smoking), and supplements caused harm [anut-atbc1994, anut-omenn1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Post-trial follow-ups show the excess lung cancer faded after stopping in ATBC (18-year RR 1.04) [anut-virtamo2014] but persisted, non-significantly, in CARET, especially in women (RR 1.12) [anut-goodman2004]. A 2021 Mendelian randomization of 768,121 people found genetically higher beta-carotene had no effect on coronary disease (OR 1.03) [anut-luo2021], consistent with the null HPS trial. USPSTF reaffirmed grade D in 2022 [anut-uspstf2022].
audit.bottom_line: Still correct: beta-carotene supplements help nobody and harm smokers; the risk appears to fade some years after stopping.

entries.headline: BPA and its replacements BPS and BPF clear with half-lives of about 6-7 hours, so urine tracks the last meal: a can of soup a day took urinary BPA from 1.1 to 20.8 ug/L and a 7-day low-plastic diet cut it 60%, but human disease links are observational and regulators disagree by up to 20,000-fold on the safe dose.

dose.effective: Avoid canned food and canned drinks (canned soup daily: urinary BPA 20.8 vs 1.1 ug/L; cans vs PET bottles: +22%); retire old hard polycarbonate bottles (+69% in a week); eat fresh food (3 days: BPA -66%; 7-day randomized low-plastic diet: -60%). Decline paper receipts or hold them briefly, and never right after hand sanitizer or lotion (2 hours of handling raised urinary BPA from 1.8 to 5.8 ug/L, prevented by gloves; sanitizer before handling plus finger food gave serum free BPA of about 7 ng/mL within 90 minutes). Treat 'BPA-free' as possibly BPS or BPF, not bisphenol-free.
dose.studied_range: Interventions from one meal to 3 weeks in 20-103 people; outcomes are urinary bisphenols. US medians 2013-14: BPA 1.24 ug/L, BPS 0.37, BPF 0.35.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2023) tolerable daily intake 0.2 ng/kg body weight/day, cut 20,000-fold from 4 ug/kg on immune (Th17) effects in mice; average and high diets exceed it 100-1,000-fold. Germany's BfR proposed a TDI 1,000-fold higher, and the US FDA kept its higher limits. The EU banned BPA in food contact materials by Regulation 2024/3190 (most uses from 20 July 2026, some to January 2028).
dose.timeframe: Urinary BPA peaks 2-4 hours after a canned meal and is back to baseline within about 24 hours; after skin contact with receipts it peaks later (8-12 hours) and is still raised at 24 hours.
dose.notes: A single spot urine is close to useless for ranking people's usual BPA exposure (ICC 0.12 in pregnancy; one sample attenuated a dose-response by 69%, and about 18 samples were needed to cut that bias to 10%).

entries.mechanism: Bisphenols act on nuclear and membrane estrogen signalling and have anti-androgenic activity in vitro and in animals. In 482 pregnant women with repeated samples, an IQR rise in urinary BPA went with 5-9% higher 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane and 9% higher IL-6. EFSA's critical effect is immune: expansion of pro-inflammatory Th17 cells in mice. BPS and BPF show hormonal potency of the same order as BPA in vitro and in animals.
entries.interactions: Comes from the same canned and packaged foods as [phthalates] and the plastic contact that sheds [microplastics]. Ultra-processed diets raise BPF along with several phthalates. Fertility evidence is in [bisphenols] and [bisphenols]; soy intake modified BPA associations in one IVF cohort ([soy]).
entries.caveats: Human outcome studies rely on one or two spot urines for a chemical with an hours-long half-life, so exposure misclassification is severe. Mortality and cardiometabolic links come from NHANES-type cross-sections or cohorts with one sample, open to confounding by diet, income and obesity (BPS was higher in heavier men). Many endpoints and metabolites are tested. Industry-funded guideline studies and academic studies reach different conclusions, partly because they test different endpoints. Falling BPA has been offset by rising BPS (US: BPA -15%, BPS +20% after California's Prop 65 listing).
entries.debate: Safe dose: EFSA's 20,000-fold TDI cut [ept-efsa2023] is endorsed by academic endocrinologists [ept-vomsaal2024, ept-zoeller2023] but opposed by the European Medicines Agency and Germany's BfR, which proposed a TDI 1,000-fold higher based on sperm counts and rejected the Th17 endpoint [ept-zoeller2023, ept-kortenkamp2024]; the US FDA kept its higher limits [ept-vomsaal2024]. A consultant-written letter arguing EFSA's evidence did not support a lower TDI was withdrawn by the journal [ept-prueitt2023] and should not be relied on. The NTP CLARITY-BPA guideline study found no consistent effects except at the top dose [ept-camacho2019], while the linked academic studies on the same animals reported effects at the lowest dose, often non-monotonic [ept-heindel2020]. Half-life: dosing studies give about 6 hours [ept-thayer2015, ept-teeguarden2011], but NHANES BPA barely fell with fasting (apparent half-life 43 hours), implying non-food sources [ept-stahlhut2009], which receipt studies support [ept-ehrlich2014, ept-hormann2014]. Interventions: fresh food, a pilot RCT and the PERTH RCT lowered urinary BPA [ept-rudel2011, ept-hagobian2017, ept-harray2026], but a real-world teenager diet had no effect [ept-galloway2018] and a catered diet backfired [ept-sathyanarayana2013]. Substitutes: BPS and BPF show BPA-like hormonal activity and reproductive-toxicity signals [ept-rochester2015, ept-denbraversewradj2020, ept-mhaoutykodja2024]. Mortality: top-tertile BPA had HR 1.49 for all-cause death in NHANES [ept-bao2020], from 344 deaths and one urine sample.

entries.title: Bisphenols (BPA, BPS, BPF, BPAF)

entries.headline: Pooled studies find at most a slight link between urinary BPA and lower sperm concentration and count, and a motility link vanished after publication-bias correction; a 190-man clinic study tied BPA to 10% more Comet DNA damage, but a 418-man population cohort found higher BPA with slightly less DNA fragmentation, so the DNA-damage claim is unconfirmed.

dose.effective: Same steps as [bisphenols]: fewer canned foods and drinks, no old polycarbonate bottles, decline or briefly handle receipts (not after hand sanitizer), fresh food. Start about 3 months before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA medians about 0.5-1.9 ug/L in general-population and clinic studies; much higher in Chinese BPA factory workers.
dose.too_much: No semen threshold established. Germany's BfR based its proposed BPA TDI (1,000-fold above EFSA's 0.2 ng/kg/day) on sperm-count declines after adult exposure.
dose.timeframe: Urinary BPA turns over within a day; any sperm effect would need about one spermatogenic cycle (roughly 3 months).
dose.notes: Clear harm is seen mainly at occupational exposures; at everyday levels results are inconsistent.

entries.mechanism: Estrogenic and anti-androgenic activity (higher SHBG and estradiol, lower bioactive androgens in pooled data), with oxidative stress proposed but not measured in the semen studies cited here.
entries.interactions: Co-exposed with [phthalates]; BPS associations were concentrated in overweight men ([excess-adiposity]).
entries.caveats: Single spot urines for a chemical with a 6-hour half-life (ICC about 0.1-0.2), clinic populations, many endpoints, and possible publication bias.
entries.debate: For: men with workplace exposure had 3-4 times the risk of low concentration and count, persisting at environmental levels [ept-li2011]; in a clinic, an IQR rise in BPA went with 23% lower concentration and 10% more Comet DNA damage [ept-meeker2010]; a 2024 meta-analysis found small falls in concentration and count [ept-lu2024]; detectable BPS went with lower concentration, mainly in overweight men [ept-ghayda2019]. Against: a meta-analysis of 2,399 men found only a weak motility link that disappeared after publication-bias correction and called it clinically negligible [ept-castellini2022]; in the population-based LIFE study the only finding among 35 semen measures was less DNA fragmentation with higher BPA [ept-goldstone2015]; in 158 young Spanish men there was no overall link with DNA fragmentation [ept-kiwittcardenas2021]. Regulators split on whether adult sperm effects should set the safe dose [ept-kortenkamp2024].

entries.title: Bisphenols (BPA, BPS) and sperm

entries.headline: BPA disrupts the meiotic spindle of mouse eggs and of human eggs matured in a dish, and an early study of 84 IVF patients found 12% fewer eggs per log unit of urinary BPA, but the larger follow-up of the same clinic (256 women, 375 cycles) found no link with egg yield, embryo quality or live birth; a 2025 meta-analysis links BPA to lower fertilization rates only.

dose.effective: Same steps as [bisphenols]: avoid canned food and drinks and polycarbonate, minimise receipts (not after hand sanitizer), fresh food. The mouse data point to the final weeks of egg growth as most sensitive, so keep it up through the cycle of retrieval or conception.
dose.studied_range: Urinary BPA geometric means about 1.5-2.5 ug/L in IVF cohorts; in-vitro oocyte studies used 20 ng/mL to 20 ug/mL.
dose.too_much: No human threshold established; EFSA TDI 0.2 ng/kg/day (2023).
dose.timeframe: Urinary BPA falls within a day of removing a source; follicle growth spans about 85 days, with recruitment of the ovulatory follicle 15-20 days before ovulation.
dose.notes: BPS, BPF and BPAF show similar oocyte effects in animal and in-vitro studies, with little human data.

entries.mechanism: Estrogen-receptor activity and interference with microtubules: in mice, low-dose BPA during the final stages of oocyte growth caused meiotic aneuploidy; in discarded human oocytes BPA reduced maturation and disturbed spindles and chromosome alignment dose-dependently; in IVF patients higher BPA went with lower peak estradiol in one cohort.
entries.interactions: Co-exposed with [phthalates]. In one IVF cohort, BPA associations with live birth appeared only in women eating no soy ([soy]), an unreplicated effect-modification finding.
entries.caveats: Small single-clinic cohorts, one or two spot urines per cycle (BPA ICC about 0.1), many endpoints. The aneuploidy data are from mice, and a second mouse study did not reproduce them; in-vitro oocytes were ones that had already failed to mature.
entries.debate: For: fewer oocytes and lower peak estradiol with BPA in 84 women [ept-moklin2010]; a trend to more implantation failure (top quartile OR 2.11, CI 0.84-5.31) [ept-ehrlich2012]; lower fertilization rates and fewer good embryos in a 2025 meta-analysis [ept-yuan2025]; lower AMH and clinical pregnancy in a 2026 meta-analysis [ept-majdi2026]; 11 of 21 human studies in a scoping review linked BPA to lower follicle counts or oocyte yield [ept-peters2024]; dose-dependent spindle damage in human oocytes in vitro [ept-machtinger2013] and aneuploidy in mice [ept-hunt2003]. Against: the expanded EARTH cohort found no association with any IVF outcome [ept-minguezalarcon2015]; the 2025 meta-analysis found no link with pregnancy or implantation [ept-yuan2025]; a mouse study with single, 7-day and 7-week dosing found no oocyte aneuploidy [ept-pacchierotti2008]; the soy-modification finding [ept-chavarro2016] is a subgroup result.

entries.title: Bisphenols and egg quality / IVF

timing.summary: BPA and BPS have half-lives of about 6-7 hours [ept-thayer2015, ept-oh2018], so a canned meal shows up within hours and is gone in a day [ept-peng2019]. Receipts are slower: skin uptake peaks 8-12 hours after handling and is still raised at 24 hours [ept-ehrlich2014].

onset.text: Urinary BPA peaks about 2.75-4 hours after a BPA-containing meal [ept-teeguarden2011, ept-peng2019] and 8-12 hours after handling receipts [ept-ehrlich2014]. A fresh-food diet cut urinary BPA 66% in 3 days [ept-rudel2011] and a low-plastic diet 60% in 7 days [ept-harray2026].

full.text: The new level is reached within about 1-7 days [ept-rudel2011, ept-harray2026].

after_stopping.text: Terminal half-life of unconjugated BPA about 6.2 hours [ept-thayer2015], BPS 6.8 hours [ept-oh2018]; canned-meal BPA was back to baseline by 24 hours [ept-peng2019].

frequency.text: Every canned or plastic-packaged meal re-exposes you [ept-carwile2011, ept-peng2019]; avoidance works only while maintained. Because one urine sample captures a single day, about 18 samples were needed to rank a person's average BPA exposure well [ept-vernet2019].

timing.debate: Dosing studies give a half-life of about 6 hours [ept-thayer2015, ept-teeguarden2011], but NHANES urinary BPA barely fell with fasting, implying an apparent population half-life of 43 hours from non-food sources or storage [ept-stahlhut2009]; dermal routes (receipts, especially after hand sanitizer) are slower than oral ones [ept-ehrlich2014, ept-hormann2014].

sperm.late_start: A late start lowers current exposure within days but covers only the final maturation of sperm already in production.
sperm.text: Lead time set by the 64-day cycle plus epididymal transit [ept-heller1963]; semen associations themselves are inconsistent [ept-castellini2022, ept-goldstone2015].

egg.late_start: If the mouse data apply, the final 2-4 weeks (dominant follicle and meiotic resumption) are the most important to cover, so a late start is not wasted [ept-hunt2003, ept-gougeon1986].
egg.text: About 85 days of follicle growth set the full lead time [ept-gougeon1986]; the meiotic window is the last part of it [ept-hunt2003].

entries.headline: Black tea's catechins are largely converted to theaflavins and thearubigins; in the same smoker trial where green tea cut 8-OHdG, black tea had no effect, although in the UK Biobank drinking 2 or more cups a day was associated with 9-13% lower mortality.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit shown; normal intake (2-4 cups) is fine.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 4 months.
dose.notes: Folin values for black tea are similar to green tea, but the compounds differ.

entries.mechanism: Theaflavins/thearubigins and catechins, extensively metabolised by gut bacteria.
entries.interactions: Reduces non-heme iron absorption when taken with meals.
entries.caveats: Cohort associations with mortality and cardiovascular outcomes (UK Biobank, 498,043 adults) are observational; portion size and strength were not measured. Tea is one of the flavan-3-ol foods that lower blood pressure in pooled RCTs, but most of those trials used green tea or cocoa.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality HR, 2-3 cups/day vs none (UK Biobank)

entries.title: Black tea

timing.summary: Black tea improved flow-mediated dilation within a week of daily drinking, but a single day of tea did not lower 24 h blood pressure. The blood-pressure benefit that the same group saw needed months of regular intake.

onset.text: FMD was higher after 1-week periods of twice-daily black tea, even at 100 mg flavonoids/day [tfood-grassi2009].

full.text: One day of tea did not change 24 h BP, whereas 6 months of regular intake did [tfood-hodgson2013].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Benefits came from daily drinking [tfood-grassi2009, tfood-hodgson2013].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Black tea showed no oxidative-DNA benefit in a smoker RCT, while UK Biobank links 2+ cups/day with 9-13% lower mortality.
audit.biases: The mortality figure is from a single baseline questionnaire in a health-conscious volunteer cohort (healthy-user bias, residual confounding) [adiet-inouechoi2022]. Diet-intake genetic instruments partly capture education and taste, so tea MR studies are weak [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No trial has tested black tea on hard outcomes. Pooled RCTs of flavan-3-ol foods show a small blood-pressure effect (about -2.8 mmHg), mostly from cocoa and green tea [adiet-lagou2025]. The only oxidative-damage RCT remains null for black tea [adiet-hakim2003].
audit.bottom_line: Black tea is harmless; its link with lower mortality may be confounded, so 'neutral' is the fair rating.

entries.headline: As rich in polyphenols as blueberries (mostly cyanidin-3-glucoside and ellagitannins), but the only human feeding trial measured fat oxidation and insulin sensitivity, not oxidative stress; benefits are inferred from other anthocyanin foods.

dose.effective: A 150 g serving is a reasonable berry portion by analogy with blueberry trials; 600 g/day was used in the one controlled feeding study.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 7 days (1500 mg flavonoids/day).
dose.timeframe: Days to weeks.
dose.notes: Ellagitannins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, and people differ in whether they produce them.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites (gut-derived phenolic acids, urolithins) acting on endothelium and inflammation.
entries.interactions: Interchangeable with [blueberries] and [berries-other] as a berry serving; little reason to think combining berries beyond ~1 cup/day adds much for oxidative stress.
entries.caveats: No RCT on oxidative-stress markers. In a 600 g/day feeding study blackberries lowered 24-h respiratory quotient and insulin AUC in overweight men.
entries.title: Blackberries

timing.summary: No timing study exists for blackberries themselves. By analogy with other anthocyanin berries, effects should come within hours of eating and fade within about 2 days.

onset.text: Extrapolated from blueberries: vascular effects at 1-2 h and 6 h [tfood-rodriguezmateos2013].

full.text: Not measured for blackberries.

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated: anthocyanin metabolites clear within about 48 h [tfood-czank2013].

frequency.text: Extrapolated from berry trials that used daily intake [tfood-curtis2019].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Polyphenol-rich, but only one feeding trial, on metabolism not oxidative stress.
audit.biases: Inference by analogy.
audit.newer_evidence: Nothing newer found beyond the feeding study [adiet-solverson2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: One cup (150 g) a day improved endothelial function over 6 months in metabolic syndrome, while half a cup did nothing; several trials show lower oxidized LDL, monocyte ROS or DNA oxidation.

dose.effective: 150 g fresh (1 cup) daily, or ~22-25 g freeze-dried powder.
dose.studied_range: 75-350 g fresh-equivalent/day for 6 weeks to 6 months; acute doses of 319-1791 mg blueberry polyphenols.
dose.timeframe: Acute FMD rise at 1-2 h and 6 h; chronic effects by 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Acute FMD rose with dose up to ~766 mg blueberry polyphenols and then plateaued. Frozen wild blueberries count. Juice with added sugar is not equivalent.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanins are poorly absorbed intact; benefits track circulating phenolic metabolites (many made by gut bacteria) that lower neutrophil NADPH oxidase activity and improve nitric-oxide-dependent vasodilation. Not direct radical scavenging in plasma.
entries.interactions: Within-class saturation: little extra acute benefit above ~766 mg polyphenols per serving, so megadoses of berry extract are unlikely to add much. Mechanistically complementary to [broccoli-sprouts] (Nrf2) and [extra-virgin-olive-oil].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (n=18-115) and often industry-funded; oxidative-marker results are inconsistent across the 45 human studies reviewed, while vascular function results are the most consistent. A 75 g/day dose was ineffective. Insulin resistance, blood pressure and plasma thiols did not change in the 6-month trial. Cognitive trials are positive but small: a single 1-cup-equivalent wild blueberry drink preserved memory and executive function over 8 h in 35 middle-aged adults, and 6 months of powder improved processing speed in 86 older adults with mild cognitive decline.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography (highbush, sum of compounds)
FMD gain with 150 g/day for 6 months

entries.title: Blueberries

timing.summary: Blueberries improve artery function in two waves, at 1-2 h and 6 h, as phenolic metabolites circulate; some metabolites stay in blood up to 48 h. A cup a day for 6 months kept a sustained improvement, while half a cup did nothing.

onset.text: FMD rose at 1-2 h and again at 6 h after blueberry polyphenols [tfood-rodriguezmateos2013].

full.text: Sustained FMD and arterial-stiffness improvements after 6 months of 150 g/day [tfood-curtis2019]; intermediate time points not reported.

after_stopping.text: Anthocyanin metabolites persist up to 48 h, with half-lives of 12-52 h [tfood-czank2013]; vascular persistence after stopping was not measured.

frequency.text: The positive 6-month trial used a cup every day [tfood-curtis2019]; metabolites clear within about 2 days [tfood-czank2013].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: One cup a day improved endothelial function over 6 months; small trials show oxidative-marker and cognitive benefits.
audit.biases: Small trials, often industry-funded, with many outcomes (multiplicity) [adiet-curtis2019].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs in healthy people confirmed better FMD (+1.11 points) but found no effect on blood pressure, executive function or mood [adiet-he2026].
audit.bottom_line: Vascular benefit holds; the cognitive claims should be presented as unconfirmed.

factors.name: Broccoli seed powder / seed extract with active myrosinase

entries.headline: Seeds are the most concentrated glucoraphanin source; taken with their own (or added mustard) myrosinase they convert roughly 30-40% to sulforaphane, about double to quadruple glucoraphanin alone, but outcome trials with plain seed powder are scarce.

dose.effective: Enough assayed powder to supply roughly 100-200 µmol glucoraphanin a day with active enzyme, which at 30-40% conversion yields on the order of 30-80 µmol sulforaphane; this brackets the effective Qidong detox dose and the 50-150 µmol doses used in clinical trials.
dose.studied_range: Single doses of glucoraphanin-rich seed extract with or without myrosinase in bioavailability studies; seed-and-sprout extract tablets with myrosinase supplied the sulforaphane in several psychiatric trials (e.g. 100 µmol/day for 18 weeks).
dose.too_much: Not established. GI upset (nausea, loose stools) is the main dose-limiting effect of concentrated broccoli preparations.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites peak within hours and are mostly gone in 8-12 h, so effects are pulsatile with once-daily dosing.
dose.notes: Stir into cool or room-temperature water, yogurt or juice and wait a few minutes; never cook it. Less stomach acid (e.g. proton pump inhibitors) and enteric coating increased conversion in one pilot, suggesting acid can blunt plant myrosinase. A pinch of seed powder or mustard powder on cooked broccoli restores some conversion, the same principle as [mustard-seed-myrosinase]. Potency of bulk seed powder is rarely assayed.

entries.mechanism: Same KEAP1-Nrf2 electrophile mechanism as sprouts; the powder supplies both substrate (glucoraphanin) and enzyme (myrosinase). Without active myrosinase, conversion falls to whatever the person's gut bacteria (e.g. Bacteroides with the BT2159-2156 operon) can do.
entries.interactions: Mechanistically redundant with [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. Combining an enzyme-active source with a glucoraphanin-only source increases total delivery (65% vs 60% recovery, earlier peak). If seed powder already provides an effective dose, cooked [broccoli-mature] adds little extra sulforaphane but still adds fiber and micronutrients. See the saturation discussion in the deep-dive.
entries.caveats: Bioavailability data come from small volunteer groups. No trial has shown that seed powder lowers validated oxidative-damage markers (F2-isoprostanes, 8-oxo-dG) in healthy people. Bulk products vary and are seldom tested for glucoraphanin and enzyme activity.

key_numbers.label: Bioavailability with active plant myrosinase vs glucoraphanin alone
Seed extract + mustard myrosinase, sulforaphane bioavailability
Seed extract without added myrosinase, sulforaphane bioavailability

entries.title: Broccoli seed powder / seed extract with active myrosinase

timing.summary: With active myrosinase, seed powder behaves like sprouts: a sulforaphane pulse within hours that is cleared in about a day, with downstream enzyme effects lasting a few days. Without the enzyme, conversion depends on gut bacteria and is slower, lower and more drawn out.

onset.text: Sulforaphane from seeds or sprouts with active enzyme appears within hours and is 3-4 times more bioavailable than glucoraphanin without enzyme [tfood-fahey2015]; enzyme induction follows within a day (extrapolated from sprout data [tfood-egner2014]).

full.text: No time course with seed powder itself; sprout and beverage trials reached their full detox effect within a day [tfood-egner2014].

after_stopping.text: Sulforaphane is cleared within about a day [tfood-ye2002]; enzyme-mediated protection fades over 2-5 days by analogy with sprout data [tfood-talalay2007, tfood-kensler2012].

frequency.text: Preformed sulforaphane gives a bolus, while glucoraphanin without enzyme gives a slower, steadier exposure [tfood-egner2011]. No trial has compared daily with intermittent seed powder; daily is what was tested in sprout and extract trials.

timing.debate: Whether a steady low exposure (glucoraphanin converted by gut bacteria) or a sharp peak (preformed sulforaphane) is better is unresolved; Egner et al. propose blends [tfood-egner2011], while the greater, more consistent delivery with active enzyme [tfood-fahey2015] favours the bolus form.

audit.claim: Seed powder with active myrosinase converts 30-40% to sulforaphane but outcome trials are scarce.
audit.biases: Pharmacokinetic studies only; products vary.
audit.newer_evidence: Concentrated sulforaphane trials at 150 umol/day failed to change Nrf2 or oxidative markers in haemodialysis [adiet-ribeiro2024] and a broccoli sprout extract trial in prediabetes missed its primary endpoint, with benefit confined to exploratory responder subgroups [adiet-dwibedi2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; outcome benefit is unproven.

entries.headline: The richest whole-food source of glucoraphanin plus its own active myrosinase; daily sprout preparations reliably deliver sulforaphane and raised benzene detoxication by about 60% in randomized trials, but proof of lower oxidative damage or better clinical outcomes in healthy people is thin.

dose.effective: About 30-70 g fresh sprouts a day (a loose handful to roughly a cup), eaten raw and chewed well. In Qidong the effective beverage gave 600 µmol glucoraphanin + 40 µmol sulforaphane a day, and only a dose producing about 25 µmol of urinary sulforaphane metabolites per day clearly worked.
dose.studied_range: 16-200 g fresh sprouts per serving; 30 g/day for 10 weeks; 70 g/day (420 µmol glucoraphanin) for 8 weeks; 100 g/day for 3 days; sprout beverages 400-600 µmol glucoraphanin/day for 1-12 weeks.
dose.too_much: No toxicity at trial doses, including a 12-week thyroid safety analysis. Very large amounts are bitter and can cause bloating or loose stools.
dose.timeframe: Plasma sulforaphane peaks about 1-2 h after eating and falls with a half-life of about 2 h; detox-enzyme effects appear within days and held for 12 weeks without tolerance.
dose.notes: Chew thoroughly (chewing raised absorbed dose by about half vs swallowing whole). Do not cook: sprouts' own myrosinase is what makes them 3-4x better than glucoraphanin without enzyme. Glucoraphanin content varies by seed lot and cultivar; 70 g of the sprouts used in one trial held 420 µmol (about 6 µmol/g). Grow or buy from a reputable source, because raw sprouts carry a food-safety (bacterial) risk.

entries.mechanism: Chewing mixes glucoraphanin with myrosinase, releasing sulforaphane, a small electrophile that reacts with sensor cysteines on KEAP1 (notably C151). KEAP1 can then no longer tag Nrf2 for destruction, so Nrf2 accumulates and switches on ARE genes: NQO1, HO-1, GSTs, glutamate-cysteine ligase (glutathione synthesis), thioredoxin reductase. This is an indirect, catalytic antioxidant effect, not radical scavenging. Secondary actions seen in cells include reduced NF-kB DNA binding and HDAC inhibition (also seen in human blood cells after a sprout meal).
entries.interactions: Directly redundant in mechanism with [broccoli-seed-powder] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. Human data show absorption scales linearly from 25 to 200 µmol, a detox threshold near 25 µmol/day excreted, dose-dependent airway enzyme induction up to 200 g sprouts, and no tolerance over 12 weeks; but blood-cell markers did not rise further between 100 and 200 µmol/day. So adding sprouts on top of a large supplement dose probably gives diminishing Nrf2 returns, while adding them to a small dose probably helps. No human trial tests stacking. Sulforaphane is a far stronger and more bioavailable Nrf2 inducer than [turmeric-curcumin]; [coffee] and [aerobic-exercise-moderate] activate Nrf2 weakly and act through many other routes, so they are not made redundant. Mature [broccoli-mature] and [cruciferous-other] add fiber, folate, vitamin C and indole glucosinolates that sprouts lack.
entries.caveats: Many positive results are small or uncontrolled (e.g. lower IL-6 and CRP after 30 g/day for 10 weeks with no control group). Short sprout courses failed in asthma (100 g/day for 3 days), ozone-induced airway inflammation, and a calorie-challenge study, and 4 weeks of sulforaphane did nothing in COPD lungs. Conversion of any glucoraphanin that escapes plant myrosinase depends on gut bacteria and varies 1% to more than 40% between people. Benefits for hard outcomes are unproven.

Fresh sprouts vs myrosinase-treated extract, absorbed sulforaphane
Urinary sulforaphane metabolites at lowest effective detox dose

entries.title: Broccoli sprouts (fresh, raw, chewed)

timing.summary: Each serving gives a short sulforaphane pulse (plasma half-life about 2 h), but the enzymes it switches on are long-lived proteins, so the protective effect lasts roughly 1-3 days and then fades. Detox effects appear on day 1 of daily dosing and hold for 12 weeks without tolerance, and they are gone within about 5 days of stopping.

onset.text: Plasma sulforaphane peaks about 1 h after a dose [tfood-ye2002]; benzene detoxication was already up 61% on day 1 [tfood-egner2014], and nasal NQO1/HO-1/GST mRNA rose 2-3-fold after 3 daily doses [tfood-riedl2009].

full.text: Detox biomarkers reach their full effect within the first day and stay flat for 12 weeks [tfood-egner2014]; induced skin NQO1 keeps stacking over the first few daily doses (1.5-fold after one, 4.5-fold after three) [tfood-dinkovakostova2007]. Clinical endpoints in trials were read at 8-18 weeks [tfood-yanaka2009, tfood-singh2014].

after_stopping.text: The drug itself is mostly excreted within 8-24 h [tfood-ye2002]. Protection in human skin was 32% at 48 h and 10% at 72 h after the last dose [tfood-talalay2007], and pollutant-detox biomarkers were back to baseline after a 5-day washout [tfood-kensler2012]. Clinical gains reversed over 4-8 weeks off treatment [tfood-singh2014, tfood-yanaka2009].

frequency.text: Every positive human trial dosed daily, and daily dosing showed no tolerance over 12 weeks [tfood-egner2014]. Because induced enzymes persist 1-3 days (NQO1 protein half-life over 18 h [tfood-siegel2001]; protection decays over 2-3 days [tfood-talalay2007, tfood-gao2001]), every other day probably keeps much but not all of the effect; no human trial has compared schedules, and every-other-day dosing worked in mice [tfood-xu2016]. Splitting the same daily amount into two doses raised plasma exposure but not blood-cell markers [tfood-atwell2015].

timing.debate: How long the effect lasts is contested by method: cell and skin studies show enzyme-mediated protection persisting for days [tfood-gao2001, tfood-talalay2007], while the Qidong crossover found no carryover after 5 days [tfood-kensler2012]. Nrf2 induces its own inhibitor KEAP1, which predicts damping with constant stimulation [tfood-lee2007], yet 12 weeks of daily dosing showed no attenuation [tfood-egner2014]. Some argue for blending glucoraphanin and sulforaphane to get both a peak and steady exposure [tfood-egner2011], but split dosing changed no blood-cell marker [tfood-atwell2015].

audit.claim: Sprouts reliably deliver sulforaphane and raised benzene detoxication ~60% in RCTs, but proof of lower oxidative damage or clinical benefit in healthy people is thin.
audit.biases: Small trials, many from a few groups; a pattern of striking small positive trials followed by null replications [adiet-houghton2016].
audit.newer_evidence: The Qidong detoxication trials hold [adiet-egner2014]. Elsewhere sulforaphane's record is mixed: the 2014 autism trial (44 men) [adiet-singh2014] was not replicated on primary outcomes in 2021, 2023 or a 108-child 2024 trial [adiet-zimmerman2021, adiet-magner2023, adiet-ou2024]; 150 umol/day did nothing to Nrf2, inflammation or MDA in haemodialysis [adiet-ribeiro2024]; COPD was null [adiet-wise2016]; a 2025 prediabetes trial of sprout extract missed its primary endpoint [adiet-dwibedi2025].
audit.bottom_line: Sprouts are a sound way to get sulforaphane, but clinical benefits are unproven and several replications have failed.

factors.name: Cadmium and lead in cocoa and dark chocolate

entries.headline: Cadmium and lead rise with cocoa content: 43% of 72 US dark chocolate and cocoa products exceeded California's lead limit and 35% the cadmium limit per serving (97% were below FDA's lead reference level), and organic products were higher; no study has measured health effects from chocolate itself.

dose.effective: Treat dark chocolate as an occasional food (about one serving, 20-30 g, a day at most), rotate brands, prefer brands that publish heavy-metal testing, and be more careful with high-cocoa products for children and in pregnancy. West African cocoa tends to be lower in cadmium than some Latin American cocoa.
dose.studied_range: Cadmium 0.004-3.15 mg/kg and lead up to 0.38 mg/kg in US products.
dose.too_much: EFSA cadmium tolerable weekly intake 2.5 ug/kg body weight; California Prop 65 MADLs 0.5 ug/day lead and 4.1 ug/day cadmium; FDA lead reference 8.8 ug/day for women of childbearing age, 2.2 ug/day for children.
dose.timeframe: Lead in blood has a mean life of about a month; cadmium accumulates in kidney with a half-time of decades.
dose.notes: Cadmium comes mainly from soil, lead mostly from contamination after harvest (drying, shipping, processing).

entries.mechanism: Cadmium binds thiols, displaces zinc in antioxidant enzymes, depletes glutathione and promotes lipid peroxidation; it accumulates in kidney and is linked to cardiovascular disease and sperm DNA damage in observational studies [efw-peana2022, efw-chowdhury2018, efw-branch2021].
entries.interactions: Weigh against the flavanol benefits in [cocoa-flavanols]. Smoking ([tobacco-smoking]) is a far bigger cadmium source than chocolate. Other dietary metals: [lead-spices], [arsenic-rice]; overall burden [heavy-metals].
entries.caveats: All data are product concentrations, not human biomarkers or outcomes; Prop 65 limits are very conservative. Product testing is sporadic and varies by batch.
entries.debate: Concern: a substantial share of products exceed Prop 65 per serving [efw-hands2024], cadmium rises with cocoa percentage [efw-abt2018], and cadmium has a 30-year kidney half-time [efw-elinder1976]. Context: medians were below even conservative limits and 97% were below FDA's lead reference [efw-hands2024]; FDA scientists frame it as a mitigation issue still being studied [efw-abt2020]; no study links chocolate intake to metal-related disease.

Products over Prop 65 cadmium limit per serving

entries.title: Cadmium and lead in cocoa and dark chocolate

entries.headline: Moderate coffee or tea does not clearly affect semen quality; caffeinated soft drinks and energy drinks look worse.

dose.effective: Up to about 2-3 cups of coffee per day appears fine.
dose.studied_range: 28 observational studies, nearly 20,000 men.
dose.too_much: Avoid large intakes from colas and energy drinks.
dose.notes: Some studies linked caffeine to sperm aneuploidy and DNA breaks, but findings are inconsistent.

entries.mechanism: Coffee polyphenols are antioxidant; caffeine effects on sperm DNA are uncertain.
entries.interactions: Separate from [refined-sugar-high-glycemic].
entries.caveats: Observational and inconsistent; residual confounding by smoking.
entries.title: Coffee and caffeine

entries.headline: Moderate caffeine shows little or no effect on conceiving; cohort studies link high intake in pregnancy to miscarriage (about 7% per 100 mg/day), but this is likely partly confounded by pregnancy nausea, and two Mendelian randomization studies found no causal effect of coffee on miscarriage.

dose.effective: Keep under 200 mg/day (about 1-2 cups of brewed coffee) while trying and in pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: <50 to >700 mg/day.
dose.too_much: > 500 mg/day linked to lower fertility (ASRM); in pregnancy, 350-699 mg/day RR 1.40 and >= 700 mg/day RR 1.72 for pregnancy loss.
dose.timeframe: Matters most from conception onward.
dose.notes: Keep fertility and miscarriage data separate: preconception intake was not associated with miscarriage in a large Danish cohort; early-pregnancy intake was.

entries.mechanism: Adenosine-receptor antagonism; effects on ovulation and tubal function are speculative. Not primarily an oxidative-stress factor.
entries.interactions: Coffee and tea are also polyphenol sources; there is no evidence that this offsets or adds to the caffeine effect on fertility. For general (non-pregnancy) oxidative-stress effects of coffee, see [coffee].
entries.caveats: Observational and confounded by pregnancy nausea (women with healthier pregnancies feel sick and drink less coffee). Male caffeine intake >= 300 mg/day was associated with lower fecundability in one cohort.

key_numbers.label: Miscarriage risk per +100 mg/day in pregnancy

entries.title: Caffeine (high intake)

timing.summary: Caffeine clears within a day (half-life about 3 h, about 8 h on the pill, up to 10 h late in pregnancy), so its effect is about current intake. What matters for the egg side is keeping intake moderate around conception and in early pregnancy; evidence that preconception intake matters is mixed.

onset.text: Blood levels peak within about an hour of a dose; half-life about 3 h in non-pregnant women [tegg-knutti1982] and 7.9 h on oral contraceptives [tegg-abernethy1985].

full.text: Steady state with daily intake within 1-2 days (about five half-lives; extrapolated).

after_stopping.text: Cleared within 1-2 days of stopping; slower in pregnancy as half-life lengthens toward 10.5 h [tegg-knutti1982].

frequency.text: It is the daily total that matters: early-pregnancy intake of 100-299 mg/day was linked to miscarriage [tegg-hahn2015], with about 7% higher risk per 100 mg/day [tegg-chen2016].

timing.debate: Hahn and colleagues found preconception caffeine unrelated to miscarriage but early-pregnancy intake related [tegg-hahn2015], whereas the LIFE study linked more than two caffeinated drinks a day before conception, by either partner, to pregnancy loss [tegg-bucklouis2016]. Leviton argued the miscarriage link reflects nausea of healthy pregnancies reducing coffee intake [tegg-leviton2002]; the dose-response meta-analysis acknowledged possible residual confounding [tegg-chen2016].

egg.late_start: Cutting down even in the cycle of conception reaches full effect within a day or two, because caffeine does not accumulate.
egg.text: Caffeine acts on the conceptus and early pregnancy rather than on oocyte growth: intake in the year before IVF was not linked to live birth [tegg-abadia2017], and preconception intake was not linked to miscarriage in one cohort [tegg-hahn2015].

audit.claim: Moderate caffeine has little effect on conceiving; the clearer risk is miscarriage once pregnant, rising about 7% per 100 mg/day.
audit.biases: Reverse causation and confounding by the pregnancy signal: healthy pregnancies cause more nausea and food aversion, so women with viable pregnancies drink less coffee; smoking is a further confounder, and the source meta-analysis flags incomplete adjustment for both and possible publication bias [afert-chen2016]. One case-control study found the association survived adjustment for nausea [afert-giannelli2003].
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization, which avoids the nausea problem, found no effect of genetically predicted coffee drinking on pregnancy loss in UK Biobank and FinnGen (OR 0.96, 0.87-1.06), while the same method did detect harm from smoking (OR 1.31) [afert-yuan2021]; a 2023 MR and genetic-risk-score study likewise found no effect on miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth [afert-britonunes2023]. In the Norwegian MoBa cohort, triangulation with MR found consistent effects on time to conception only for smoking and BMI [afert-wootton2023]. Caveat: the MR instruments index habitual coffee intake in the general population, not caffeine dose in early pregnancy.
audit.bottom_line: Caffeine probably does little to fertility, and the miscarriage link may be largely confounded by pregnancy nausea; staying under about 200 mg/day in pregnancy remains a reasonable precaution, but the risk figure should not be read as causal.

entries.headline: In CALERIE, the only long-term RCT of calorie restriction in healthy non-obese adults, prescribed 25% CR (about 12% achieved) for 2 years lowered urinary F2-isoprostanes by 13-27%, LDL, blood pressure, CRP and insulin resistance, at the cost of some bone and lean mass.

dose.effective: A sustained moderate deficit of ~10-15% of energy needs; CALERIE participants achieved 11.9% (about 300 kcal/day) and lost ~7.5 kg.
dose.studied_range: 25% CR prescribed for 6 months to 2 years in non-obese and overweight adults.
dose.too_much: Bone density fell at spine and hip and fat-free mass fell ~2.2 kg over 2 years in CALERIE; extreme CR risks malnutrition and amenorrhoea. Not for underweight people, pregnancy or eating disorders.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostane reductions present at 12 months and sustained at 24 months; DNA damage reduced at 6 months.
dose.notes: In overweight people weight loss itself drives much of the effect. Long-term CR does not lower IGF-1 in humans unless protein intake also falls (~0.95 g/kg/day).

entries.mechanism: Lower energy flux reduces mitochondrial ROS production per day (metabolic adaptation of 80-120 kcal/day beyond weight loss, lower T3), lower insulin signalling, less adipose inflammation, and hormetic upregulation of defences.
entries.interactions: Opposite of [overfeeding]. The comparator against which all fasting protocols should be judged: [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting] and [five-two-diet] match but do not beat it when calories are equal. Combine with [resistance-training] and adequate protein and calcium to protect bone and lean mass. Overlaps with [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: Long-term adherence is hard; most people benefit from avoiding surplus rather than strict CR. Effects on DNA-methylation aging clocks were small (DunedinPACE only). Lean, active women risk crossing into low energy availability; see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy].
entries.title: Calorie restriction

timing.summary: Moderate calorie restriction lowers oxidative and metabolic markers within months, reaches its full effect over about a year, and holds while restriction continues. After stopping, about half the lost weight returned within two years, but people were still lighter than at the start.

onset.text: The earliest measured point in the long trials was 6 months, when fasting insulin and DNA damage were already lower [tbody-heilbronn2006]; earlier time points were not measured for oxidative markers.

full.text: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were lower at 12 months and the reduction held at 24 months of ~12-15% achieved restriction [tbody-ilyasova2018].

after_stopping.text: Two years after CALERIE ended, participants had regained 54% of the 9 kg they lost, yet weight and fat mass stayed below baseline and below controls [tbody-marlatt2017]. Whether oxidative markers stayed low was not measured.

frequency.text: Studied as a continuous daily deficit; intermittent schedules give similar weight loss for the same deficit [tbody-allaf2021].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the main uncertainty is whether the marker changes are due to restriction itself or simply weight loss [tbody-heilbronn2006, tbody-ilyasova2018].

audit.claim: In CALERIE, ~12% calorie restriction for 2 years lowered F2-isoprostanes, LDL, BP, CRP and insulin resistance, with some bone and lean loss.
audit.biases: Randomized; main limits are adherence and generalisability to lean young adults.
audit.newer_evidence: CALERIE secondary analyses confirm isoprostane falls [adiet-ilyasova2018], cardiometabolic gains [adiet-kraus2019] and only a small effect on one epigenetic pace-of-aging measure [adiet-waziry2023].
audit.bottom_line: One of the best-supported claims in the group.

entries.headline: Regular cannabis use is associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation and chromosome abnormalities in small studies.

dose.effective: Stop regular use at least 3 months before trying.
dose.studied_range: Regular users vs non-users in 54 infertile men.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Smoking cannabis also delivers combustion oxidants similar to tobacco.

entries.mechanism: THC acts on endocannabinoid receptors in the testis and sperm, disturbing the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, spermatogenesis and mitochondrial function.
entries.interactions: Often co-used with tobacco [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Exploratory, small, retrospective data; confounding by tobacco is likely.
entries.title: Cannabis

timing.summary: Human data tie lower counts to cannabis use more than once a week in the previous 3 months, but there is no human time course for onset or recovery. In monkeys, stopping THC gave only partial recovery.

onset.text: Not measured in humans; the association was with use in the previous 3 months [tsperm-gundersen2015].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured in humans. In rhesus macaques, testis volume returned only to 73% of baseline after THC was stopped [tsperm-hedges2023].

frequency.text: Use more than once a week was linked to 28% lower concentration; use once a week or less was not clearly linked [tsperm-gundersen2015].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; stopping late cannot undo effects on cells that passed meiosis while exposed, if the reported aneuploidy link is real [tsperm-verhaeghe2020].
sperm.text: Reported effects on aneuploidy and DNA fragmentation point to meiosis and spermiogenesis [tsperm-verhaeghe2020], so a full cycle is the minimum lead time (extrapolated).

timing.debate: A large Danish study linked weekly-plus use to lower counts [tsperm-gundersen2015], but a US fertility-clinic cohort found higher concentrations in men who had ever smoked marijuana [tsperm-nassan2019]; recovery data come only from monkeys [tsperm-hedges2023].

audit.claim: Regular cannabis use is associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation and chromosome abnormalities in small studies.
audit.biases: Confounding by tobacco co-use, alcohol and lifestyle; differences in abstinence time before sampling; small clinic samples.
audit.newer_evidence: The cited study is small and exploratory [abody-verhaeghe2020]. A meta-analysis of 9 studies found no significant association with abnormal semen (RR 1.16, 0.84-1.60) or testosterone [abody-belladelli2021]; newer cross-sectional studies found inconsistent associations [abody-belladelli2023] and apparent motility differences explained by abstinence time [abody-zufferey2024].
audit.bottom_line: Human evidence that cannabis damages sperm is weak and inconsistent; stopping before conception is a reasonable precaution, not a proven fix.

entries.headline: Carnosine and anserine (meat dipeptides) lowered HbA1c by about 0.8% and waist by 3.5 cm in a meta-analysis of mostly small trials, and anserine slightly slowed decline in one 30-person MCI trial; anti-glycation claims are mainly experimental.

dose.effective: Carnosine 2 g/day (glucose pilot); anserine 500 mg/day (cognition pilot)
dose.studied_range: About 0.5-2 g/day for 8-12 weeks; beta-alanine (the precursor) is used to raise muscle carnosine
dose.too_much: No serious adverse events reported in the small trials
dose.timeframe: Effects measured at 12 weeks
dose.notes: Oral carnosine is partly broken down in blood by carnosinase. Meat and fish are the dietary sources.

entries.mechanism: Histidine-containing dipeptides buffer acid in muscle, chelate copper and zinc, quench reactive carbonyls and inhibit advanced glycation end-product formation, and scavenge hypochlorous acid in experimental systems.
entries.interactions: Relevant mainly to [glycemic-control]; no evidence it adds to diet and exercise measures.
entries.caveats: Human trials are few and small; the glycaemic meta-analyses pooled heterogeneous populations, and one included only four human studies.
entries.debate: Two meta-analyses report glycaemic benefits [lon-menon2020, lon-matthews2021], supported by a 30-person pilot [lon-decourten2016] and mechanistic reviews [lon-boldyrev2013]. The evidence base is thin (Matthews rated human certainty moderate but on four studies) and effects shrank in low-bias trials [lon-menon2020]; the cognition evidence is a single small Japanese trial [lon-masuoka2021]. No critical commentary was found, which reflects limited attention rather than consensus.
entries.title: Carnosine and anserine

timing.summary: Carnosine stored in muscle is very stable: after loading (via beta-alanine) it fell only 2-4% a week. Time courses for oral carnosine or anserine themselves have not been measured.

onset.text: Not measured for oral carnosine; beta-alanine raised muscle carnosine over 5-6 weeks [tnut-baguet2009].

full.text: Extrapolated from beta-alanine loading: weeks to months [tnut-baguet2009].

after_stopping.text: Muscle carnosine returned to baseline 6-15 weeks after stopping beta-alanine [tnut-baguet2009]; extrapolated to carnosine supplements.

frequency.text: No schedule data; the slow muscle washout suggests occasional missed days matter little (extrapolated) [tnut-baguet2009].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Carnosine/anserine lowered HbA1c ~0.8% in a meta-analysis of small trials; anti-glycation mainly experimental.
audit.biases: Effects shrank in low-bias trials [anut-menon2020]; few human studies [anut-matthews2021].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer large trial found.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Carrots and carotenoid-rich vegetables (vs beta-carotene pills)

entries.headline: Carotenoid-rich foods are associated with lower oxidative DNA and lipid damage, but isolated beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer and mortality in smokers (CARET), a textbook antioxidant paradox.

dose.effective: Regular orange/yellow and green vegetables eaten with some fat; a medium carrot (~60 g) provides ~5 mg beta-carotene.
dose.studied_range: Food: cohort and feeding studies. Supplements: 30 mg beta-carotene + 25,000 IU retinol daily (CARET).
dose.too_much: Beta-carotene supplements in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers: lung cancer RR 1.28, all-cause death RR 1.17. Beta-carotene supplements raised mortality in Cochrane analysis.
dose.notes: Absorption needs dietary fat: salads with full-fat dressing delivered much more carotenoid than reduced-fat or fat-free versions.

entries.mechanism: Carotenoids quench singlet oxygen and lipid peroxyl radicals in membranes and lipoproteins; at high doses in high-oxygen, smoke-exposed lungs beta-carotene can act as a pro-oxidant.
entries.interactions: Absorption improved by [extra-virgin-olive-oil], avocado.
entries.caveats: Food associations are observational. The supplement results are the reason not to translate food carotenoid data into pills.
entries.title: Carrots and carotenoid-rich vegetables (vs beta-carotene pills)

timing.summary: Blood and skin carotenoids build over weeks and fade over weeks to months, because plasma half-lives are 4-11 weeks. Eating carotenoid-rich vegetables most days keeps levels high; no single day matters much.

onset.text: Plasma carotenoids rise within days of higher intake (lycopene dosing for 8 days) [tnut-cohn2004].

full.text: Plasma and skin carotenoids were up more than 200% after 8 weeks of a high vegetable-fruit diet [tnut-jahns2014]; half-lives of 26-76 days imply a full plateau takes about 3-6 months (extrapolated) [tnut-burri2001].

after_stopping.text: Plasma fell back to baseline within about 3 weeks of a low-carotenoid diet and skin within about 10 weeks [tnut-jahns2014]; depletion half-lives 26-76 days [tnut-burri2001].

frequency.text: Long half-lives mean intake averaged over weeks counts, not daily timing; eat with some fat (extrapolated) [tnut-burri2001].

timing.debate: Short dosing studies give lycopene half-lives of about 5-9 days [tnut-cohn2004], whereas long depletion studies give about 26 days [tnut-burri2001], reflecting a fast plasma pool and a slow tissue reservoir.

audit.claim: Carotenoid foods are linked to less oxidative damage, but beta-carotene pills raised lung cancer and mortality in smokers.
audit.biases: The food associations are observational; the supplement result is the classic case where randomized trials overturned cohort-based expectations [adiet-omenn1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane confirms beta-carotene supplements increase mortality [adiet-bjelakovic2012].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; a model antioxidant-paradox entry.

entries.headline: Gonadotoxic chemotherapy and ovarian radiation destroy the egg reserve directly; less than 2 Gy is estimated to kill half of human oocytes.

dose.effective: Fertility-preservation counselling before treatment; egg or embryo freezing is standard care.
dose.too_much: Oocyte LD50 estimated at < 2 Gy; chemotherapy risk depends on drug (e.g. cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin), cumulative dose and age.
dose.timeframe: Primordial-follicle oocytes die within 12-24 h of gonadotoxic drug exposure, so preservation must happen before treatment.
dose.notes: GnRH agonists may be offered (e.g. breast cancer) but are not a substitute for proven preservation methods.

entries.mechanism: DNA double-strand breaks in primordial-follicle oocytes trigger apoptosis; radiation generates ROS and direct DNA damage.
entries.interactions: No antioxidant has been shown to protect human ovaries from chemotherapy.
entries.caveats: This is a medical-referral factor, not a lifestyle one.
entries.title: Chemotherapy and pelvic radiation

timing.summary: Chemotherapy and testicular radiation hit dividing spermatogonia and spermatocytes; sperm DNA damage and counts are worst 3-6 months after treatment. Recovery takes 1-2 years for milder regimens and up to 5 years or never for harsher ones.

onset.text: Worst DFI and sperm counts at the first follow-ups, 3-6 months after treatment [tsperm-paoli2015, tsperm-bujan2013].

full.text: Lowest values at 3-6 months [tsperm-bujan2013]; DFI 28% at 3 months versus 18% before treatment [tsperm-paoli2015].

after_stopping.text: DFI improved by 12-24 months [tsperm-paoli2015]; count recovered by 12 months after two or fewer BEP cycles but not after radiotherapy or more cycles [tsperm-bujan2013]; aneuploidy normalised by about 18 months but persisted for some chromosomes to 24 months [tsperm-tempest2008]; after cisplatin about 50% of men recover by 2 years and 80% by 5 years [tsperm-howell2005].

frequency.text: Not applicable; damage depends on drug class and cumulative dose [tsperm-howell2005].

sperm.late_start: Nothing done in the last weeks repairs this; bank sperm before treatment starts [tsperm-oktay2018].
sperm.text: Because damaged stem cells and spermatocytes keep feeding the pipeline, genetic counselling is advised for conceptions up to 2 years after starting chemotherapy [tsperm-tempest2008].

egg.late_start: Conceiving soon after treatment uses oocytes that were growing during chemotherapy: in mice this gave more pregnancy failure and malformations, normalising by about 12 weeks [tegg-meirow2001]; in women, conception within 1 year of starting chemotherapy was linked to more preterm birth [tegg-hartnett2018].
egg.text: Waiting about a year after chemotherapy before conceiving avoided the excess preterm risk (2 years after chemoradiation) [tegg-hartnett2018]. AMH falls by about 20-90% at 12 months depending on regimen (76% after breast-cancer chemotherapy) and recovers partly between 6 and 24 months [tegg-balachandren2026, tegg-mailliez2022]. Eggs or embryos frozen before treatment avoid the problem [tegg-oktay2018]; ovarian or uterine radiation above 10 Gy raises stillbirth and neonatal death regardless of wait [tegg-signorello2010].

timing.debate: Studies agree on worst damage at 3-6 months; they differ on whether DFI ends lower than before treatment after chemotherapy (yes in [tsperm-paoli2015]) and on how long aneuploidy lasts (18 vs 24 months in [tsperm-tempest2008]).

entries.headline: Trihalomethanes from chlorinated water are linked to bladder cancer in men (pooled OR 1.24 above 1 ug/L, 1.44 above 50 ug/L; about 5% of EU bladder cancers if causal), but an early miscarriage signal (OR 1.8) was not confirmed in a larger study designed to test it, and links with birth weight and preterm birth are close to null.

dose.effective: If your utility reports high total trihalomethanes (above about 50-80 ug/L), drink water from a carbon-filter pitcher or under-sink carbon filter (a pitcher plus fridge storage removed about 92% of THMs and 66% of haloacetic acids) or let water stand in an open jug in the fridge. Showers and baths give more THM uptake than drinking: ventilate the bathroom and keep hot showers shorter.
dose.studied_range: Tap-water THM about 1-100+ ug/L; EU mean about 12 ug/L.
dose.too_much: Regulatory limits: 80 ug/L total THM (US), 100 ug/L (EU). Birth-defect associations appeared above about 60 ug/L THM in a dose-response meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: THMs leave the blood within hours; bladder cancer associations reflect decades of exposure.
dose.notes: Disinfection prevents far more disease than by-products cause; never avoid treated water for untreated sources. Boiling removes volatile THMs but not most haloacetic acids.

entries.mechanism: Chlorine reacts with organic matter to form THMs and haloacetic acids. Brominated THMs are activated by GSTT1 to mutagens. In pregnant women, blood THMs and urinary haloacetic acids tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoprostane and HNE-MA across repeated samples [efw-liu2020].
entries.interactions: Sperm data: [disinfection-byproducts]. Filtration for other contaminants: [water-filtration]. Swimming pools add exposure.
entries.caveats: Exposure is usually assigned from utility averages, missing showering, bathing and swimming (which raised bladder cancer risk independently [efw-villanueva2007]). The bladder cancer link appears in men but not women [efw-villanueva2004]. The EU burden estimate assumes causality [efw-evlampidou2020].
entries.debate: Miscarriage: a California cohort found OR 1.8 for heavy drinkers of high-THM water [efw-waller1998], but a three-site US study built to test this found no effect (OR 1.1) [efw-savitz2006] and no longer time to pregnancy [efw-maclehose2008]. Birth outcomes: a meta-analysis found little or no association with low birth weight or preterm birth [efw-grellier2010], while a newer dose-response meta-analysis reports defects above about 60 ug/L [efw-deiana2025]. Bladder cancer: pooled case-control studies support an association [efw-villanueva2004, efw-villanueva2007], but cohort data are scarce.

entries.title: Chlorination by-products (trihalomethanes) in tap water

entries.headline: Chinese studies measuring blood trihalomethanes found lower sperm count and concentration (including repeated-measure data in 1,199 men), but the largest study using tap-water levels (642 cases, 926 referents in England and Wales) found no link (OR 1.01 per 10 ug/L).

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention tested. If your water is high in THMs, a carbon-filter pitcher or under-sink filter for drinking and shorter, ventilated showers lower exposure ([disinfection-byproducts]).
dose.studied_range: Blood THMs in Chinese men; tap-water THM 0-100 ug/L in UK and US studies.
dose.too_much: Not defined; associations appeared within regulatory ranges.
dose.timeframe: Blood THMs fall within hours; sperm effects would take at least ~64 days (one round of spermatogenesis) to change [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Blood THM reflects only the last few hours of showering and drinking.

entries.mechanism: Brominated THMs and haloacetic acids produce oxidative stress and lower testosterone in animal studies; GST genotypes modify metabolism.
entries.interactions: General exposure and reduction: [disinfection-byproducts].
entries.caveats: Positive studies come largely from one Wuhan research group; blood THM is a snapshot; many THM species and semen endpoints were tested.
entries.debate: Harm: blood THMs tracked lower sperm count in 1,199 donors [efw-chen2020] and in other Wuhan samples [efw-zeng2014, efw-zeng2013]; an early US study found fewer normal-morphology sperm with high ingestion [efw-fenster2003]. No harm: the England and Wales case-referent study found none [efw-iszatt2013].
