factors.name: Choosing and storing cooking oils (stability over smoke point)

entries.headline: For high-heat cooking, how resistant an oil is to oxidation matters more than its smoke point: olive oils (including extra-virgin) lasted 24-27 hours of domestic deep-frying before reaching the 25% polar-compound limit versus 15 hours for a PUFA-rich blend, and PUFA-rich oils form more toxic aldehydes, though cohort data show no heart-disease difference between olive- and sunflower-oil frying.

dose.effective: For frying and roasting, use oils low in polyunsaturates and/or rich in antioxidants: extra-virgin or refined olive oil, high-oleic sunflower or safflower, or rapeseed/canola; keep PUFA-rich oils (sunflower, corn, soybean, flaxseed, walnut) mainly for low-heat or cold use. Store oils closed, in the dark, away from the stove, in tin, bag-in-box or dark glass; use within a few months of opening.
dose.studied_range: Domestic deep-frying for up to 27 h; heating at 180-190 °C for up to 36 h; household-use storage over 40 days; dark storage for 18 months at room temperature vs 4 °C.
dose.too_much: Oil that smokes, smells acrid or has darkened and thickened is degraded; discard it.
dose.timeframe: Oxidation products accumulate within the first hours of frying and over months of storage.
dose.notes: Smoke point mostly reflects free fatty acids and refining, not oxidative stability. EVOO keeps oleic acid, sterols and squalene during heating though phenols and tocopherols decline. A widely cited 2018 industry-linked comparison of oils under heating appeared in a non-indexed journal and is not used as evidence here; its main conclusion agrees with the indexed studies above.

entries.mechanism: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (linoleic, alpha-linolenic) have bis-allylic hydrogens that oxidize far faster than oleic acid; heat, oxygen, light and trace metals drive hydroperoxide formation and breakdown into aldehydes such as 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal and acrolein. Phenols and tocopherols in virgin oils slow the chain reaction. Light-driven photo-oxidation (chlorophyll as sensitiser) and warmth degrade phenols during storage.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [extra-virgin-olive-oil] (phenolic benefits). Not in conflict with [seed-oils-linoleic-acid]: seed oils are fine as a dietary fat, but the most PUFA-rich ones are the poorest choice for repeated high-heat use ([oxidized-frying-oils]). Cooking vegetables in EVOO transfers olive phenols into them.
entries.caveats: Evidence is oil chemistry, not human outcomes. Oils vary by cultivar, refining and freshness, and frying conditions in studies differ from home cooking. Coconut oil is very stable to heat but rich in saturated fat that raises LDL.
entries.debate: Olive-oil frying studies show good stability and retention of minor compounds [kcc-casal2010, kcc-allouche2007], and PUFA-rich oils form more aldehydes in NMR studies [kcc-guillen2009, kcc-ampem2023]; Grootveld argues PUFA-rich oils should not be recommended for high-heat frying at all [kcc-grootveld2022]. On the other side, the Spanish EPIC cohort found no difference in coronary risk between people frying in olive versus sunflower oil [kcc-guallarcastillon2012], so the health relevance of these chemistry differences is unproven. Storage studies agree that PET bottles, light and warmth speed phenol loss and peroxide formation [kcc-sordini2026, kcc-crupi2025].

entries.title: Choosing and storing cooking oils (stability over smoke point)

timing.summary: Switching oil changes what forms in the pan tonight - there is no build-up phase and no washout. The only slow clocks are in the bottle and the fryer: oils degrade over hours of frying (olive oils lasted 24-27 hours versus 15 for a PUFA-rich blend) [tleg-casal2010] and over months of storage.

onset.text: Immediate: the oil you cook in determines the oxidation products in that meal, and the postprandial difference is measurable within hours - repeatedly heated sunflower oil raised postprandial oxidative-stress and DNA-repair markers while virgin olive oil did not [tleg-rangel2017].

full.text: No cumulative effect to reach; the practical 'full effect' is replacing habitual high-heat PUFA frying, which changes every subsequent meal [tleg-rangel2017, tleg-casal2010].

after_stopping.text: Reverting to a less stable oil restores the exposure with the next meal; nothing is retained [tleg-rangel2017].

frequency.text: Per cooking session. The useful schedule rules are about the oil's own clock: discard frying oil well before it darkens and smells (olive oils reached the 25% polar-compound limit after 24-27 hours of domestic deep-frying, a PUFA-rich blend after 15) [tleg-casal2010], and store oil cool and dark.

timing.debate: Whether the oil-stability difference matters for health is unresolved: postprandial marker trials favour virgin olive oil [tleg-rangel2017] and chemistry favours monounsaturated oils for frying [tleg-casal2010], but a large cohort frying in olive or sunflower oil found no difference in coronary events [tleg-guallar2012], and blood linoleic acid is associated with lower, not higher, cardiovascular risk [tleg-marklund2019].

factors.name: Chronic high-volume endurance training and low testosterone (exercise-hypogonadal male condition)

entries.headline: Men with years of very high endurance volumes (e.g. ~100+ km/week running, elite triathlon) can develop persistently low testosterone without raised LH, and small studies show lower motility, more immature sperm and high DNA fragmentation (~20% in elite triathletes), though changes rarely fall below WHO thresholds.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and training very high volumes, cut back toward moderate volumes for about 3 months, eat enough to match training (avoid low energy availability), and keep cycling under about 5 h/week.
dose.studied_range: High-mileage runners ~108 km/week vs ~54 km/week vs sedentary; elite triathletes in championship preparation; endurance athletes in cross-sectional and short training studies (280 athletes across 13 studies).
dose.too_much: Hormonal and semen changes appeared at high-mileage running (~100+ km/week) and elite triathlon training, not at moderate volumes.
dose.timeframe: Spermatogenesis takes ~74 days, so allow about 3 months after reducing load; testosterone recovers when energy balance and load normalise, sometimes over months.
dose.notes: Recreational activity is associated with equal or better semen quality ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]). Men with low testosterone should not self-treat with testosterone, which shuts down sperm production ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]).

entries.mechanism: Chronic training load and low energy availability suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulses (functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), lowering testosterone; high cortisol, systemic and seminal inflammation (more round cells/leukocytes), scrotal heat and oxidative stress during heavy training may add sperm DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [cycling] (saddle pressure, heat) and [overtraining-ultraendurance]; the female counterpart is [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake support recovery.
entries.caveats: Evidence is small, cross-sectional and mostly in elite athletes; whether low testosterone reflects dysfunction or an adaptive readjustment is debated, and few studies measure fertility (pregnancy) outcomes.
entries.debate: Hackney's group describes a persistent 'exercise-hypogonadal male condition' with possible spermatogenesis effects [exr-lane2019, exr-hackney2008], supported by lower testosterone and semen quality in high-mileage runners [exr-desouza1994], high DNA fragmentation in elite triathletes [exr-vaamonde2018], and lower libido at the highest training loads [exr-hackney2017]; the IOC REDs consensus and a review of male runners link it to low energy availability [exr-mountjoy2023, exr-cupka2023]. But Hackney himself argues some cases may be adaptive rather than pathological [exr-hackney2020]; a systematic review found semen changes in endurance athletes rarely clinically relevant [exr-aerts2024]; a meta-analysis found most activity has no major semen effect, with harm limited to elite levels [exr-ibanezperez2019]; and in large preconception cohorts male vigorous activity was not consistently associated with couples' fecundability [exr-wise2025].
entries.title: Chronic high-volume endurance training and low testosterone (exercise-hypogonadal male condition)

timing.summary: Low testosterone from endurance training builds over years of high volume, while seminal oxidative stress rises within weeks of an intensive block. That oxidative stress was still raised a month after training stopped; full recovery has not been timed.

onset.text: Seminal ROS and malondialdehyde were raised by week 8 of intensive cycling training [tsperm-maleki2014].

full.text: Keeps building: the hormonal condition is seen in men with years of chronic endurance training [tsperm-lane2019].

after_stopping.text: Seminal ROS and antioxidant capacity were still abnormal 30 days after a 16-week block ended [tsperm-maleki2014]; recovery of semen after cutting volume has not been measured.

frequency.text: This is about very high volume: runners at about 108 km/week had lower testosterone and motile counts, those at 54 km/week did not [tsperm-desouza1994].

sperm.late_start: A taper in the last weeks may lower seminal oxidative stress for stored sperm, but it was still raised after 30 days in the one study [tsperm-maleki2014].
sperm.text: Hormonal suppression affects spermatogonia and spermiation, so a full cycle at reduced volume is needed (extrapolated).

timing.debate: Small studies show high SDF in triathletes despite normal hormones [tsperm-vaamonde2018], while reviews stress that the condition is uncommon and limited to long-term high-volume athletes [tsperm-lane2019]; a widely cited 2009 treadmill RCT on this question was retracted [tsperm-safarinejad2009]. The only time-course data come from one author group (Hajizadeh Maleki/Tartibian) whose other exercise-and-semen trials have been retracted [tsperm-maleki2014], so these timings are provisional.

entries.headline: Activated neutrophils and macrophages are a major regulated source of oxidants, and ROS and NF-kB amplify each other, so persistent inflammation keeps oxidative stress high.

dose.effective: Treat the source (adiposity, smoking, infection, autoimmune or periodontal disease).
dose.timeframe: Not specified in these studies
dose.notes: Antioxidant supplements have not reduced inflammatory cardiovascular outcomes in large trials.

entries.mechanism: NOX2 and myeloperoxidase in phagocytes generate superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid that damage endothelium and tissue. ROS modulate NF-kB activation, and NF-kB targets regulate ROS production.
entries.interactions: Fed by [excess-adiposity], [tobacco-smoking] and [glycemic-control]. Nrf2 activation can counter NF-kB-driven inflammation.
entries.caveats: Inflammation is also protective acutely. The target is chronic, unresolved inflammation.
entries.title: Chronic low-grade inflammation

timing.summary: CRP is a fast-moving marker: it falls within weeks to a few months of treating a source of inflammation - about 0.37 mg/L within 1-3 months of periodontal therapy [tleg-demmer2013] and about 0.13 mg/L per kilogram of weight lost [tleg-selvin2007]. The clinical payoff is much slower: lowering inflammation with canakinumab cut cardiovascular events by 15% over a median 3.7 years [tleg-ridker2017].

onset.text: Marker changes appear within weeks: periodontal treatment lowered CRP measurably at the earliest post-treatment measurement, typically 1-3 months [tleg-demmer2013], and statins cut CRP by 37% within the treatment period [tleg-ridker2008].

full.text: CRP reductions plateau over 1-6 months with the treated source [tleg-demmer2013, tleg-selvin2007], but the event reduction from targeting inflammation accrued over a median 3.7 years in CANTOS [tleg-ridker2017].

after_stopping.text: Markers rebound quickly when the suppression stops: CRP and IL-6 rose above treated levels within 3-7 days of abruptly stopping a statin, independently of LDL [tleg-li2006statin]. Untreated sources of inflammation (gums, visceral fat) resume driving oxidant production as soon as they return [tleg-mittal2014].

frequency.text: Inflammation responds to continuous rather than episodic measures, because the mediators turn over in hours to days: activated neutrophils and macrophages generate oxidants while the stimulus is present, and ROS and NF-kB amplify each other [tleg-mittal2014]. The practical lever is removing sources (gum disease, excess adiposity, smoke) rather than timing a treatment.

timing.debate: Whether CRP is a target or just a thermometer is the long-running dispute. CANTOS lowered CRP without changing lipids and reduced events, supporting causality [tleg-ridker2017], but only one of three doses met the significance threshold and fatal infections increased. Weight-loss and periodontal CRP reductions are consistent [tleg-selvin2007, tleg-demmer2013], yet trials lowering CRP in those ways have not demonstrated event reductions.

audit.claim: Activated immune cells are a major oxidant source and persistent inflammation keeps oxidative stress high; treat the source.
audit.biases: CRP associations with heart disease were confounded; CRP is a marker, not a cause.
audit.newer_evidence: Genetically raised CRP does not raise coronary risk [abody-ccgc2011], but the IL-6 receptor pathway is causal by MR [abody-il6r2012], and trials confirm that blocking inflammation lowers events: canakinumab (HR 0.85) [abody-ridker2017] and colchicine in chronic coronary disease (HR 0.69) [abody-nidorf2020]. Colchicine started after acute MI did not help (HR 0.99) [abody-jolly2025].
audit.bottom_line: Inflammation is a proven cause of cardiovascular events, though not every anti-inflammatory works in every setting, and CRP is a marker rather than a target.

factors.name: Citrus flavanones (hesperidin: oranges, orange juice, supplements)

entries.headline: 500 mg/day hesperidin or 500 mL/day orange juice lowered diastolic blood pressure and improved endothelial function in small crossover trials, and a meta-analysis finds modest lipid, glucose and systolic BP effects above 500 mg/day.

dose.effective: 500 mg/day hesperidin, or 500 mL/day orange juice.
dose.studied_range: Hesperidin 500 mg/day or more for 3 weeks to over 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar; whole oranges are a better default.
dose.timeframe: 3-4 weeks for blood pressure and FMD; over 12 weeks for lipids.
dose.notes: Hesperidin carries a sugar that gut bacteria must remove before absorption, so responses vary between people.

entries.mechanism: Hesperetin metabolites stimulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase (via Akt/AMPK, H2O2-dependent signalling in endothelial cells) and reduce adhesion-molecule expression.
entries.interactions: Vascular route overlaps [cocoa-flavanols]; oranges also count toward [vitamin-c-foods].
entries.caveats: Trials are small and short; the FMD benefit was shown in metabolic syndrome; most supplement trials are not independently replicated.

key_numbers.label: FMD on hesperidin vs placebo (metabolic syndrome)

entries.title: Citrus flavanones (hesperidin: oranges, orange juice, supplements)

timing.summary: Hesperidin needs gut bacteria to free it, so blood levels peak late (5-7 h) and are gone by 24 h. Microvascular function improved only at that peak, while diastolic blood pressure was lower after 4 weeks of daily orange juice or hesperidin.

onset.text: Flavanone metabolites appear at 3 h, peak at 5-7 h [tfood-manach2003]; microvascular reactivity improved at the hesperetin peak [tfood-morand2011].

full.text: Diastolic BP was lower after 4 weeks of 500 mL/day orange juice or hesperidin [tfood-morand2011].

after_stopping.text: Flavanones return to baseline within 24 h [tfood-manach2003]; BP persistence not measured.

frequency.text: Fasting microvascular function did not improve, only post-dose function did [tfood-morand2011], so the effect depends on regular intake.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: 500 mg/day hesperidin or orange juice lowered diastolic BP in small crossover trials; meta-analysis shows modest effects.
audit.biases: Small, short, partly industry-linked trials.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2025 meta-analysis is current [adiet-heidari2025, adiet-morand2011].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: A palpable varicocele is the single largest common driver of high SDF, adding roughly 10-14 percentage points on average.

dose.effective: Clinical (palpable, grade 1-3) varicocele found on physical exam; ultrasound-only (subclinical) varicoceles matter much less.
dose.studied_range: Present in roughly 40% of infertile men; meta-analyses compare men with vs without varicocele.
dose.too_much: Higher grades and bilateral varicoceles tend to do more damage, but the grade-SDF relationship is inconsistent.
dose.timeframe: Damage accumulates over years; after repair SDF falls over 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Ask a urologist for a scrotal exam if SDF is high, semen is abnormal or there is a dull ache or visible veins.

entries.mechanism: Venous pooling raises testicular temperature and causes hypoxia and reflux of adrenal/renal metabolites; this drives mitochondrial ROS, NADPH oxidase activity in leukocytes and lipid peroxidation, producing 8-OHdG and strand breaks in poorly protaminated sperm.
entries.interactions: Heat from [sauna] and [everyday-scrotal-heat] adds to the varicocele's thermal load. Smoking [tobacco-smoking] in varicocele patients compounds oxidative stress. The fix is [varicocele-repair], not supplements.
entries.caveats: Many men with varicocele are fertile; it is a problem mainly when semen or SDF is abnormal. Varicocele and SDF studies are mostly cross-sectional.
entries.title: Clinical varicocele (enlarged scrotal veins)

timing.summary: A clinical varicocele adds about 14 points of sperm DNA fragmentation and can keep worsening semen over years. Timing of repair is covered under varicocele repair.

onset.text: Not timed.

full.text: Keeps worsening: initially normal semen deteriorated when re-tested 9-96 months later [tsperm-chehval1992].

after_stopping.text: Not applicable; see the varicocele-repair record.

frequency.text: Not applicable.

timing.debate: The evidence for progression is a 13-man series [tsperm-chehval1992]; the size of the SDF excess (+13.6 points) comes from pooled cross-sectional data [tsperm-szabo2023].

audit.claim: A palpable varicocele is the largest common driver of high SDF, adding roughly 10-14 points.
audit.biases: Cross-sectional comparisons in men attending infertility clinics (selection into care: men with varicocele and normal fertility are rarely tested); detection depends on examination; varicocele correlates with age and duration.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2023 risk-factor meta-analysis of 190 studies confirmed varicocele as the largest SDF association (+13.6 points) [afert-szabo2023]. Before-after data show SDF falls after repair (about 6.7 points at 3 months, 12.4 at 6 months), with a dose-response by grade, which supports causation [afert-szabo2025].
audit.bottom_line: The varicocele-SDF link holds and repair lowers SDF, which supports a causal role; the open question is how much that changes live birth (see varicocele-repair).

entries.headline: Cocoa flavanols reliably improve endothelial function (EFSA-authorised at 200 mg/day) and lower blood pressure in pooled RCTs; in the 21,442-person COSMOS trial, 500 mg/day did not significantly cut total CVD events (HR 0.90) or improve cognition overall, though memory improved in people with low habitual flavanol intake.

dose.effective: 200 mg cocoa flavanols/day: about 2.5 g high-flavanol cocoa powder or 10 g high-flavanol dark chocolate (EFSA).
dose.studied_range: 200-900 mg flavanols/day; COSMOS 500 mg/day (80 mg epicatechin) for a median 3.6 years.
dose.too_much: Chocolate brings sugar, fat and calories; extracts avoid these. Ordinary chocolate flavanol content varies widely and is rarely labelled.
dose.timeframe: FMD rises within hours; chronic improvement plateaued after ~2 weeks.
dose.notes: Epicatechin is the key active monomer; blood-pressure effects were larger above 50 mg epicatechin/day.

entries.mechanism: (-)-Epicatechin and its structurally related metabolites drive the vascular effect: an extract with 130 mg epicatechin improved FMD while a procyanidin-rich, low-epicatechin extract did not. They raise endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability and reduce NADPH-oxidase-driven superoxide; procyanidins are mostly degraded by gut bacteria to valerolactones. A high-flavanol drink prevented the post-meal and post-exercise rise in GC-MS F2-isoprostanes.
entries.interactions: Shares flavan-3-ols with [green-tea], apples and grapes; FMD gains appear regardless of dose in meta-analysis, implying a plateau.
entries.caveats: Most vascular trials are short and many were funded by cocoa companies. COSMOS primary endpoints (CVD events; memory at 1 year in COSMOS-Web; global cognition in COSMOS-Clinic) were null, and the CVD-death and low-flavanol memory findings are secondary or subgroup results. A 6-month PAD trial improved walking distance by 43 m but was a 44-person phase II study. Direct oxidative-damage markers are seldom measured.

entries.title: Cocoa flavanols / high-flavanol dark chocolate

timing.summary: Each flavanol dose improves artery function within 2 h, and daily intake also raises the fasting baseline within 3-8 days, without tolerance over 30 days. The gain is gone a week after stopping, and in a 6-month trial walking improved much more 2.5 h after a dose than 24 h after.

onset.text: FMD peaks about 2 h after a dose [tfood-heiss2007, tfood-schroeter2006].

full.text: Fasting FMD rose on days 3, 5 and 8 of daily intake [tfood-heiss2007]; 30 days of thrice-daily cocoa kept both the raised baseline and the post-dose rises, with no tachyphylaxis [tfood-balzer2008].

after_stopping.text: Fasting FMD was back to baseline after a 1-week cocoa-free washout [tfood-heiss2007]; in PAD, the walking gain was 42.6 m at 2.5 h but only 18 m at 24 h after the last dose [tfood-mcdermott2020].

frequency.text: The effect is largely dose-timed: trials used one to three doses a day [tfood-heiss2010, tfood-balzer2008], and benefit faded by 24 h [tfood-mcdermott2020]. In COSMOS a third of the cocoa group did not reach expected biomarker levels, and adherence-based analyses showed larger effects [tfood-ottaviani2025].

timing.debate: Short trials show reliable vascular effects [tfood-sun2019], but the 3.6-year COSMOS trial missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.90) [tfood-sesso2022]; a biomarker re-analysis by investigators including industry-affiliated authors argues poor adherence and background flavanol intake hid a larger effect [tfood-ottaviani2025].

audit.claim: Cocoa flavanols improve FMD and lower BP; in COSMOS 500 mg/day did not significantly reduce total CVD events or cognition overall.
audit.biases: Many vascular trials are short and cocoa-industry funded; COSMOS's CVD-death benefit is a secondary outcome [adiet-sesso2022].
audit.newer_evidence: COSMOS ancillary work (2025) found an 8.4%/year relative fall in hsCRP but no change in IL-6 or TNF-alpha [adiet-li2025]; COSMOS-Clinic cognition was null [adiet-vyas2024]. Vascular benefits remain consistent in pooled RCTs [adiet-hooper2012, adiet-lagou2025].
audit.bottom_line: Strong for vascular function and blood pressure; unproven for heart attacks, strokes or cognition.

entries.headline: CoQ10 at 200-300 mg/day modestly raises sperm motility and concentration, but there is no evidence it raises pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 200 mg/day (ubiquinone or ubiquinol) with a fat-containing meal for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 200-300 mg/day for 3-6 months.
dose.too_much: Well tolerated; may interact with warfarin.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Men with low baseline motility and low seminal CoQ10 responded best.

entries.mechanism: Electron carrier in the mitochondrial electron transport chain and lipid-soluble antioxidant in sperm midpiece membranes.
entries.interactions: Common ingredient in [male-antioxidant-combination] products.
entries.caveats: Meta-analysis of 3 small RCTs; no live-birth data; SDF rarely measured.
entries.title: Coenzyme Q10

entries.headline: The best-studied 'egg quality' supplement: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs retrieved (median 4 vs 2) and good embryos in young poor responders, and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day (200 mg three times daily) for 60 days before IVF (Xu 2018 RCT).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in the Xu RCT; pooled RCTs (5 trials, 449 women) used varying regimens.
dose.too_much: No harms reported in these trials.
dose.timeframe: At least 2 months before stimulation; ideally covering the ~3-month follicle-growth window.
dose.notes: Fat-soluble. Evidence is mainly in poor responders/low ovarian reserve; no good data in women with normal reserve.

entries.mechanism: CoQ10 carries electrons in the mitochondrial respiratory chain and is a lipid-phase antioxidant. Ageing oocytes in mice and women express less of the CoQ-synthesis enzymes PDSS2 and COQ6; in mice CoQ10 restored oocyte mitochondrial function and reduced spindle defects.
entries.interactions: Mechanistically overlaps with [nmn-nad] (both target mitochondrial ageing). Often bundled with [melatonin] and [myo-inositol] in commercial products, which prevents attributing effects.
entries.caveats: Small trials; the Xu RCT was open-label without placebo and excluded 17 non-compliant women. ESHRE does not recommend antioxidant therapy in IVF. Not shown to reduce aneuploidy in humans.

key_numbers.label: Cumulative live birth, CoQ10 vs control (NS)

entries.title: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone/ubiquinol)

timing.summary: CoQ10 has a plasma half-life of about 33 hours, so blood levels plateau within about a week of daily dosing and fall back over a similar period. Fertility benefits were measured after 2-6 months because sperm and follicles take that long to develop.

onset.text: Plasma CoQ10 peaks 6-7 h after a dose, with a second peak at 24 h [tnut-tomono1986].

full.text: Plasma rose for about 7 days and then stayed level [tnut-martucci2019]; seminal and sperm CoQ10 were raised at 6 months [tnut-balercia2009].

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated from the 33 h half-life: plasma near baseline in about a week; it was fully back by 8 months, the only time measured [tnut-ikematsu2006, tnut-bhagavan2006].

frequency.text: A 33-hour half-life suits once-daily dosing with fat; the IVF trial split 600 mg into three doses [tnut-xu2018], but no trial compared schedules.

sperm.late_start: Not measured; plasma loads in a week, but only late-stage sperm would be exposed.
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; the 6-month trial raised CoQ10 inside sperm cells [tnut-balercia2009].

egg.late_start: Not measured; shorter pretreatment has not been tested.
egg.text: The positive IVF trial gave CoQ10 for 60 days before stimulation [tnut-xu2018]; the ovulatory follicle's cohort starts differentiating about 85 days before ovulation [tnut-gougeon1986], so 2-3 months is the evidence-based lead time.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; trials simply chose 2-6 months.

audit.claim: Egg: 600 mg/day for 60 days before IVF increased eggs and good embryos in young poor responders and meta-analyses show higher clinical pregnancy (OR ~2.2-2.4) but no significant live-birth gain. Sperm: modest motility gains, no pregnancy evidence.
audit.biases: Small, often open-label single-centre trials (Xu 2018 excluded non-compliant women) [anut-xu2018]; such fertility-supplement trials are prone to integrity problems, as shown for PCOS ovulation-induction trials that did not share data [anut-bordewijk2020] and for one author's 14 RCTs [anut-mol2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Egg: a 2026 meta-analysis of three small trials (326 women) reported higher live birth in poor responders (OR 2.28) [anut-schutz2026], whereas a 2026 RCT in poor responders found more oocytes but no difference in pregnancy [anut-abdelrahman2026]; ESHRE still does not recommend antioxidant add-ons [anut-eshre2023]. Sperm: a 2025 meta-analysis reported clinical pregnancy OR 6.02 from 9 small studies [anut-bakri2025], an implausibly large effect, while broader 2025 and 2022 syntheses found no pregnancy or live-birth benefit from any supplement [anut-michaelsen2025, anut-deligny2022].
audit.bottom_line: CoQ10 is the most promising egg-quality supplement, but the live-birth evidence is three small trials; it is reasonable to try in poor responders, not proven.

entries.headline: The biggest single polyphenol (chlorogenic acid) source in many Western diets; small RCTs at 3-4 cups/day lowered DNA strand breaks and isoprostanes, and cohorts link 3-4 cups/day with ~15% lower mortality, though Mendelian randomization studies do not confirm that the mortality benefit is causal.

dose.effective: 3-4 cups (about 750 mL) per day of paper-filtered coffee.
dose.studied_range: 200-800 mL/day, from 8 hours to 4 weeks in intervention trials.
dose.too_much: Unfiltered coffee (French press, boiled, Turkish) raises LDL cholesterol through cafestol/kahweol; ~10 mg cafestol is in 2-3 cups of cafetiere coffee. Caffeine limits apply in pregnancy (see fertility sections).
dose.timeframe: DNA strand-break reduction detectable 2 h after the first cup; sustained at 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Paper filters retain the diterpenes. Decaffeinated coffee was also associated with lower mortality, so caffeine is not the whole story. Roast level shifts the compound mix (dark roast: less chlorogenic acid, more N-methylpyridinium).

entries.mechanism: Chlorogenic (caffeoylquinic) acids are partly absorbed in the small intestine and extensively metabolised by gut bacteria to dihydrocaffeic and ferulic acid derivatives; coffee also contains roast-derived compounds such as N-methylpyridinium. Trials show raised glutathione (consistent with induced antioxidant defences) and fewer DNA strand breaks rather than higher plasma 'antioxidant capacity'.
entries.interactions: Shares chlorogenic acids with [eggplant], [blueberries] and artichoke. Caffeine and fertility: covered elsewhere.
entries.caveats: Effects on plasma antioxidant capacity, antioxidant enzymes and lipid/protein damage are unclear across 26 intervention studies; the clearest signal is DNA protection and glutathione. Some positive trials were industry-sponsored. Pregnancy: high intake associated with low birth weight and pregnancy loss. When trying to conceive or pregnant, keep total caffeine under about 200 mg/day; see [caffeine-fertility].

Reduction in spontaneous DNA strand breaks vs water (4 wk, 750 mL/day)
