entries.title: Coffee (paper-filtered)

timing.summary: Coffee lowered background DNA strand breaks within 2 h of the first cup, and four weeks of 3-4 cups a day held a 27% reduction. Chlorogenic acid metabolites arrive in two waves (about 1 h and after 4 h) and clear within a day, so the effect depends on regular intake.

onset.text: DNA strand breaks fell within 2 h of the first cup [tfood-bakuradze2016]; chlorogenic acid metabolites peak within 1 h and again after 4 h [tfood-stalmach2009].

full.text: A cumulative reduction of about a third over 8 h of repeated cups [tfood-bakuradze2016]; 27% lower than water after 4 weeks [tfood-bakuradze2015].

after_stopping.text: Not measured for DNA damage. Caffeine's blood-pressure tolerance regresses within hours of abstinence [tfood-shi1993].

frequency.text: Benefit was shown with cups spread through the day, every day [tfood-bakuradze2016, tfood-bakuradze2015]. Tolerance to caffeine's pressor effect builds and fades within hours, so regular drinkers see little blood-pressure rise while occasional drinkers see more [tfood-shi1993].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Paper-filtered coffee at 3-4 cups/day lowers DNA strand breaks and isoprostanes in RCTs, and cohorts show the lowest mortality at 3-4 cups/day.
audit.biases: The mortality curve rests on cohorts, where non-drinkers include people who stopped for health reasons (reverse causation, 'sick quitters') and coffee tracks smoking and socioeconomic status (residual confounding) [adiet-poole2017]. The DNA strand-break trials are small, short and partly industry-linked [adiet-bakuradze2015].
audit.newer_evidence: Kim 2019 found the inverse association held within never-smokers and other strata, which argues against simple smoking confounding [adiet-kim2019]. But Mendelian randomization using caffeine-intake variants found no genetic link with ischaemic heart disease or mortality (2016) [adiet-nordestgaard2016], and a 2022 review of all coffee MR studies found no support for causal protection against mortality, heart disease, stroke, diabetes or obesity, only for gallstones [adiet-nordestgaard2022]. UK Biobank shows a U/J shape, with higher CVD risk above 6 cups/day and in non-drinkers [adiet-zhou2019], and similar U-shaped mortality associations for decaf, instant and lightly sweetened coffee [adiet-liu2022], a pattern consistent with healthy-user effects as well as with non-caffeine compounds. Coffee MR has its own problem: caffeine-metabolism variants change how much people drink but also how fast they clear it, so null MR is not decisive. The 2023 CRAVE randomized n-of-1 trial found no rise in atrial ectopy but more ventricular ectopy and less sleep on coffee days [adiet-marcus2023].
audit.bottom_line: Coffee up to about 3-4 cups a day is safe for most adults and may be mildly beneficial, but the 15-17% lower mortality in cohorts is probably partly confounded and is not confirmed by genetic studies.

entries.headline: Regular winter swimmers show higher baseline antioxidant enzymes (a hormesis signal), but human evidence for health benefits is small and inconsistent, and cold plunges right after strength training blunt muscle gains.

dose.effective: If you do it: brief immersions (seconds to a few minutes) in cold water, with acclimatization and never alone; keep it away from (at least several hours after) strength sessions.
dose.studied_range: Winter-swimming studies over a season; post-exercise CWI 10 min after each strength session for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: Cold shock and arrhythmia risk on sudden immersion, especially with heart disease; hypothermia.
dose.timeframe: Antioxidant adaptations seen after a winter season.
dose.notes: Each plunge itself causes acute oxidative stress; adaptation follows repetition.

entries.mechanism: Cold triggers a catecholamine surge and increased metabolic rate (brown-fat thermogenesis), generating a transient ROS pulse that may up-regulate glutathione, SOD and catalase. Post-exercise cooling reduces blood flow and anabolic signalling.
entries.interactions: Blunts adaptations to [resistance-training] if done immediately after.
entries.caveats: Winter swimmers are a self-selected healthy group; most studies are small, single-sex and uncontrolled. Reviews rate many claimed benefits as resting on weak or anecdotal data.
entries.title: Cold-water immersion and winter swimming

timing.summary: A cold plunge right after strength training dampens muscle-building signals for one to two days, and done after every session for 7-12 weeks it leaves smaller muscle gains. Repeated cold exposure on its own can raise insulin sensitivity within about ten days, but long-term health effects are unproven.

onset.text: After one session, cold immersion reduced satellite-cell and anabolic signalling at 24-48 h [tbody-roberts2015] and mTORC1 signalling at 1 h [tbody-fyfe2019]; 10 days of mild cold acclimation raised insulin sensitivity ~43% in type 2 diabetes [tbody-hanssen2015].

full.text: Smaller gains in muscle mass after 7-12 weeks of post-session immersion [tbody-fyfe2019, tbody-roberts2015, tbody-malta2021]. Higher antioxidant enzymes in seasoned winter swimmers come from cross-sectional data [tbody-siems1999].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; whether blunted hypertrophy is regained later was not tested.

frequency.text: Keep cold plunges away from strength sessions. No trial tested how many hours of separation is enough; the 24-48 h anabolic window [tbody-roberts2015] suggests separating by at least several hours or using cold on non-lifting days (extrapolated). Endurance adaptations were not harmed [tbody-malta2021].

timing.debate: For endurance training, some argue post-exercise cooling may even enhance mitochondrial adaptation [tbody-ihsan2021], while an umbrella review rates the certainty of all cold-water findings as low to very low [tbody-berjisian2026].

audit.claim: Winter swimmers show higher antioxidant enzymes, but human evidence for health benefits is small and inconsistent.
audit.biases: Self-selected healthy winter swimmers; unblinded trials with expectancy effects.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 studies found an acute inflammatory response and a transient stress reduction at 12 h only [abody-cain2025]; the largest RCT cut self-reported sickness absence by 29% but not illness days [abody-buijze2016].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: benefits are modest, short-lived or self-reported.

entries.headline: Three large placebo-controlled RCTs (MOXI 2020, FAZST 2020 with 2370 men, SUMMER 2025 with 1171 men) found no gain in live birth or pregnancy from male antioxidant/vitamin supplements; SUMMER saw fewer pregnancies in months 4-6 (15.5% vs 21.5%).

dose.effective: No dose has proven benefit for live birth. If used, choose a modest-dose product (roughly vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 IU, selenium 100-200 ug, zinc 15-25 mg, folate 400-1000 ug, CoQ10 100-200 mg, L-carnitine 1-2 g) for 3 months, not stacked products.
dose.studied_range: MOXI: vitamin C 500 mg, vitamin E 400 mg, selenium 0.2 mg, L-carnitine 1000 mg, zinc 20 mg, folic acid 1000 ug, lycopene 10 mg daily for 3-6 months. Cochrane: 20 different antioxidants in 90 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Stacking several products or megadoses risks reductive stress ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]); antioxidants cause more mild GI upset (OR 2.70).
dose.timeframe: Trials use 3-6 months.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: counsel that supplements are of questionable clinical utility. EAU: insufficient evidence for widespread empirical use. Yet in a global survey 85.6% of reproductive specialists prescribed them.

entries.mechanism: Intended to scavenge seminal ROS and support antioxidant enzymes; only helpful if a man actually has oxidative stress and a deficiency.
entries.interactions: Not a substitute for removing the source of ROS ([tobacco-smoking], [varicocele], [genital-tract-infection]). May blunt hormetic benefits of [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Cochrane 2022: live birth OR 1.43 but very low certainty and null when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed; MOXI live birth was 15% vs 24% with placebo (not significant, small). A 6-month RCT in men with DFI >=25% also found no DFI change. Supplements may help a subgroup with proven oxidative stress, but no validated test identifies them.

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR (all trials, very low certainty)

entries.title: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidant supplements

timing.summary: Where antioxidants were reported to work, changes showed after 2-3 months, but the best-designed trials saw no change in DNA fragmentation at 3 or 6 months. No trial tested whether a short course in the final weeks helps.

onset.text: Shortest positive result: TUNEL SDF fell from 22.1% to 9.1% after 2 months of vitamins C and E [tsperm-greco2005c]; null at 3 months in MOXI [tsperm-steiner2020].

full.text: Not established: DFI did not change over 6 months in a placebo-controlled RCT [tsperm-stenqvist2018], and folic acid plus zinc for 6 months slightly raised it [tsperm-schisterman2020].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: All trials used daily dosing; none compared schedules [tsperm-deligny2022].

sperm.late_start: No trial measured a course shorter than 2 months; a post-testicular (epididymal) effect would act fast in theory, but this is unproven.
sperm.text: Trials run for one cycle or more (2-6 months) [tsperm-greco2005c, tsperm-steiner2020]; any benefit would need cells to pass through the vulnerable late stages while supplemented (extrapolated).

timing.debate: Small trials report fast falls in SDF within 2-3 months [tsperm-greco2005c, tsperm-tunc2009], while larger placebo-controlled trials found no change at 3-6 months [tsperm-steiner2020, tsperm-stenqvist2018, tsperm-schisterman2020]; Cochrane rates the evidence very low certainty [tsperm-deligny2022].

audit.claim: Combination 'male fertility' antioxidants have at best weak, biased evidence; the best RCT (MOXI) found no gain in semen, DNA fragmentation or live birth.
audit.biases: Small single-centre trials at high risk of bias, surrogate outcomes (semen parameters, seminal MDA) instead of live birth, industry-made products, and research-integrity problems in the trial base: Cochrane's apparent live-birth gain disappears when high-risk-of-bias trials are removed [afert-deligny2022], and trustworthiness checks of Cochrane-included RCTs flag about a quarter for authenticity concerns that Risk-of-Bias tools do not catch [afert-wilkinson2025]. Positive meta-analyses come from groups with long-standing advocacy for antioxidant therapy and mostly report pregnancy rather than live birth [afert-agarwal2023].
audit.newer_evidence: Two large placebo-controlled trials have since reported. FAZST (2020, 2370 men): folic acid plus zinc did not change live birth (34% vs 35%) or semen quality and slightly raised DNA fragmentation [afert-schisterman2020]. SUMMER (2025, 1171 men, 21 Dutch centres): 6 months of an antioxidant/B-vitamin product did not raise ongoing pregnancy (33.8% vs 37.5%) and pregnancy was lower in the 4-6 month window when any effect should appear (15.5% vs 21.5%) [afert-deligny2025]. These confirm MOXI (live birth 15% vs 24%) [afert-steiner2020]. On the other side, a 2023 meta-analysis of 45 RCTs reports higher spontaneous pregnancy but no live-birth or SDF effect [afert-agarwal2023]; 2025-2026 meta-analyses find small SDF falls (about 4 points) and better semen numbers but at very low certainty with prediction intervals crossing zero [afert-szabo2025, afert-melhem2026]. HFEA rates antioxidants after SDF testing grey [afert-hfea2026sdf].
audit.bottom_line: The three largest, best-run trials (MOXI, FAZST, SUMMER) all found no live-birth benefit from male supplements, and two hinted at harm. Treat them as unproven and not worth paying for to improve fertility.

entries.headline: Combined with resistance training, 3-5 g/day creatine adds about 1.4 kg lean mass and modest strength in older adults; memory effects are small and contested, the antioxidant role is mechanistic only, and long trials in Parkinson and Huntington disease were null.

dose.effective: 3-5 g/day creatine monohydrate (or about 0.1 g/kg/day), taken with resistance training
dose.studied_range: 3-20 g/day (20 g/day for 5-7 days as an optional loading phase); 10 g/day for 5 years in Parkinson disease; up to 40 g/day in Huntington disease
dose.too_much: No kidney harm in healthy people at studied doses; serum creatinine rises slightly as a by-product, which is not kidney injury. People with kidney disease should involve their doctor. Very high doses cause more gastrointestinal upset.
dose.timeframe: Muscle stores fill in about a week with loading or about 3-4 weeks at 3-5 g/day; lean-mass gains seen over 7-52 weeks of training
dose.notes: Monohydrate is the studied and cheapest form. Vegetarians start with lower stores and may respond more on memory tests. A single 0.35 g/kg dose (about 25 g) was used in the sleep-deprivation study, far above normal use.

entries.mechanism: Creatine and phosphocreatine buffer ATP through creatine kinase, which matters in tissues with high, fluctuating energy demand (muscle, brain). Cell and animal studies suggest direct scavenging of some radicals and indirect protection of mitochondria, but these antioxidant effects have not been shown to matter in humans.
entries.interactions: Its benefit for muscle depends on training; pair with [resistance-training]. No known antagonism with exercise adaptation, unlike [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]. Often combined with [coq10] in sarcopenia proposals without outcome data.
entries.caveats: Persistent myths (kidney damage, dehydration, cramps, hair loss) are not supported by the trial evidence. Water retention adds 1-2 kg body weight early on. Neurodegeneration trials at high doses were negative. Creatine is not a longevity drug: there is no human lifespan or aging-rate data.
entries.debate: For muscle, meta-analyses agree that creatine plus training beats training alone in older adults [lon-devries2014, lon-chilibeck2017]. For cognition, positive meta-analyses report memory gains mainly in older adults [lon-prokopidis2023, lon-xu2024], but a letter argued the Prokopidis analysis double-counted data and may be a false positive [lon-eckert2023], and an earlier systematic review found no effect in young people and inconsistent results across domains [lon-avgerinos2018]. Antioxidant claims rest on mechanistic reviews [lon-sestili2011]. Hopes for neuroprotection were tested and failed in large RCTs [lon-kieburtz2015, lon-hersch2017]. Note that the main safety reviews come from sports-nutrition authors, some with industry ties [lon-kreider2017, lon-antonio2021], although an independent meta-analysis also found no renal harm [lon-desouzaesilva2019].

key_numbers.label: Extra lean mass with training (older adults)

entries.title: Creatine monohydrate

timing.summary: Muscle creatine can be filled in about 6 days with a 20 g/day loading phase or in about 4 weeks at 3 g/day, reaching the same level. After stopping, muscle stores drift back to baseline over about a month.

onset.text: Muscle uptake is fastest in the first 2 days of high-dose loading [tnut-harris1992].

full.text: About 20% higher muscle creatine after 6 days at 20 g/day or 28 days at 3 g/day [tnut-hultman1996].

after_stopping.text: Muscle creatine declined gradually and was back to baseline by 30 days [tnut-hultman1996].

frequency.text: Loading is optional; 3 g/day reaches the same level in about 4 weeks and 2 g/day maintains it [tnut-hultman1996].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: With resistance training 3-5 g/day adds ~1.4 kg lean mass in older adults; memory effects small and contested; neurodegeneration trials null.
audit.biases: Safety and position statements come partly from industry-linked sports-nutrition authors [anut-kreider2017]; the memory meta-analysis was criticised for double counting [anut-prokopidis2023, anut-eckert2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 meta-analysis again found small memory gains (SMD 0.31) [anut-xu2024]; muscle and null-neuroprotection findings are unchanged [anut-chilibeck2017, anut-ninds2015].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Curcumin supplements (enhanced absorption)
aliases: Curcumin supplements for PCOS and egg quality

entries.headline: Enhanced-absorption curcumin (micellar, cyclodextrin, phytosome, colloidal) modestly lowers CRP (~0.6 mg/L) and MDA and reduces knee-osteoarthritis pain about as much as an NSAID in short trials, but the trial base is small, heterogeneous and low quality, and rare idiosyncratic liver injury is now well documented.

dose.effective: Osteoarthritis: 1500 mg/day Curcuma extract (the ibuprofen-comparison trial) or ~180 mg/day curcumin as Theracurmin, for 4-12 weeks. Biomarkers: ~600 mg/day curcuminoids or more (often with piperine) for at least 4-8 weeks; micellar or gamma-cyclodextrin forms deliver more curcumin per mg.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (nanomicelle) to 8 g/day (standard powder) in trials; single doses up to 12 g tolerated.
dose.too_much: EFSA ADI 3 mg/kg/day (about 210 mg/day at 70 kg), which many products exceed. Liver injury (hepatocellular or cholestatic hepatitis, latency 1-4 months, one US death) has been linked to high-dose, high-bioavailability products and is strongly associated with HLA-B*35:01; 3 of 7 implicated US products also contained piperine. GI upset at gram doses.
dose.timeframe: Pain effects within 2-8 weeks; biomarker changes at 4-12 weeks; fasting plasma curcuminoids reached ~50 nmol/L after 3 weeks of meal-time micellar dosing.
dose.notes: Free (unconjugated) curcumin is barely detectable in blood even with advanced formulations; most 'fold-increase' claims compare total conjugates after enzymatic hydrolysis and use different assays, so brand comparisons are not reliable. Best head-to-head data favour micelles (57-185x) and gamma-cyclodextrin (30-39x); phytosome ~8-29x; piperine adds little to conjugate exposure in the head-to-head study but inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes. Take with meals.

entries.mechanism: Claimed: Nrf2 activation via KEAP1 Cys151 (Michael acceptor), NF-kB inhibition, direct radical scavenging and iron chelation. Reality check: these effects appear in cells at 1-20 uM, whereas oral dosing gives low-nanomolar free curcumin and mostly glucuronide/sulfate conjugates that are inactive in cell assays. Curcumin also degrades rapidly and is a known pan-assay interference compound, so many in-vitro 'hits' are suspect. Clinical effects that do appear (OA pain, CRP) may come from gut-local actions, minor metabolites, or bias, and the mechanism in humans is not established.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [sulforaphane-supplements], [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder] on Nrf2; sulforaphane is far more potent and bioavailable, and there are no human data on combining them, so adding curcumin for Nrf2 is likely redundant (inference). Its distinct use case is symptomatic osteoarthritis pain. No human evidence that curcumin blunts training adaptations the way high-dose vitamins C/E do ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); this is untested rather than disproven. Pharmacokinetic interactions: curcumin inhibits intestinal BCRP (sulfasalazine exposure up 3.2x) and CYP/P-gp in vitro; piperine raises phenytoin levels. Short studies found no change in INR on warfarin or bleeding time on antiplatelets, but caution is still advised with anticoagulants. Belongs to the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] category.
entries.caveats: The field carries an integrity problem: a leading curcumin laboratory has dozens of retracted papers, and one glycaemic meta-analysis was itself retracted. Most positive trials are small, short, single-centre and often from a few research networks; meta-analyses show very high heterogeneity and GRADE certainty is low. Larger or Western trials are frequently null (FAP adenomas, radiation dermatitis, prostate cancer, Alzheimer's disease, micellar curcumin on CRP/lipids). Liver injury is rare but real; stop and test liver enzymes if jaundice, dark urine or fatigue appear. Avoid with gallstones or bile-duct obstruction (curcumin contracts the gallbladder), with marginal iron stores (iron chelation in mice), and in pregnancy (no safety data at supplement doses).

key_numbers.label: Relative AUC, micellar vs native (500 mg)
HLA-B*35:01 carriers among US turmeric liver-injury cases

entries.title: Curcumin supplements (enhanced-bioavailability extracts)

entries.headline: One small Iranian RCT (56 completers) found 80 mg/day nanomicelle curcumin for 10 weeks improved sperm count, concentration and motility plus seminal-redox and inflammation markers; there are no human data on DNA fragmentation, varicocele, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: 80 mg/day curcumin as nanomicelle for 10 weeks in the only RCT.
dose.studied_range: 80 mg/day (single human RCT); animal varicocele studies used 4-100 mg/kg.
dose.too_much: Not established for sperm. In vitro, curcumin added directly to sperm blocks motility and capacitation in a concentration-dependent way (it has been studied as a vaginal contraceptive), although such concentrations are not reached in semen after oral dosing. General supplement risks (liver injury, drug interactions) apply.
dose.timeframe: At least one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days); the RCT ran 10 weeks.
dose.notes: Human DNA-fragmentation benefits come only from adding curcumin to freezing medium in the lab (cryopreservation), not from oral use. Varicocele data are from rats only (mechanistic).

entries.mechanism: Proposed: lowering seminal lipid peroxidation (MDA) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-a, CRP) and Nrf2-driven antioxidant enzymes in testis. Human mechanistic support is limited to blood TAC/MDA changes in one trial.
entries.interactions: Likely overlaps with other antioxidant approaches such as [n-acetylcysteine]; no head-to-head or combination trials. Redundant with [sulforaphane-supplements] on the Nrf2 axis (inference). Not comparable to culinary [turmeric-curcumin].
entries.caveats: A single small trial from one country, without pregnancy outcomes, cannot support a recommendation; it does not show more pregnancies. The in-vitro anti-motility effect argues against assuming 'more is better'. Check for publication bias as further Iranian trials appear.

key_numbers.label: Dose in the only human RCT
Curcumin in freezing medium that reduced post-thaw DNA fragmentation

entries.title: Curcumin supplements for sperm quality

entries.headline: In PCOS, several small RCTs and meta-analyses show curcumin modestly lowers fasting glucose (~3-4 mg/dL), insulin and HOMA-IR, without consistent effects on lipids, testosterone, LH/FSH or weight, and no trial has measured ovulation, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: PCOS trials: 500-1500 mg/day standard curcumin or ~80 mg two to three times daily as nanocurcumin, for 8-12 weeks.
dose.studied_range: 80-240 mg/day nanocurcumin to 1500 mg/day standard curcumin; endometriosis-ART trial 120 mg/day nanomicelle for 10 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not established. EFSA ADI (3 mg/kg/day) rests on a multigeneration reproductive-toxicity study (reduced F2 body-weight gain). Mouse oocytes exposed to curcumin showed impaired maturation and embryo development. No human safety data in pregnancy at supplement doses.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic effects at 8-12 weeks; an oocyte matures over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Glycaemic benefit is small compared with metformin; one 200-woman factorial trial found curcumin plus metformin better than either alone. Stopping high-dose supplements once pregnancy is possible is a precautionary inference, not a tested rule.

entries.mechanism: Improved insulin sensitivity and lower inflammation/oxidative stress would plausibly help the ovarian environment in PCOS; animal studies show curcumin can preserve follicle reserve but other animal studies show direct harm to oocytes and embryos, so the net effect on eggs is unknown.
entries.interactions: Additive to metformin in one trial. Alternative or adjunct to [myo-inositol], which has a larger PCOS evidence base; no head-to-head trials. Treat [pcos] and [glycemic-control] first with lifestyle and established drugs. Same liver and drug-interaction cautions as [curcumin-supplements].
entries.caveats: All PCOS and endometriosis trials found here were small and mostly from Iran; meta-analyses pool 3-8 trials with high heterogeneity for HOMA-IR. A small endometriosis-ART trial reported more mature oocytes and good embryos but needs replication; a separate endometriosis RCT found no pain benefit. Oocyte-quality claims rest on conflicting animal data (mechanistic).

key_numbers.label: Fasting glucose change in PCOS (5 RCTs)

entries.title: Curcumin supplements for PCOS and egg quality

timing.summary: Enhanced-absorption curcumin builds a measurable fasting blood level within 3 weeks of taking it with each meal. Semen changes were seen after 10 weeks; liver injury, when it happens, appears 1-4 months in.

onset.text: Fasting plasma curcuminoids reached 49 nmol/L within 3 weeks of micellar dosing with meals [tfood-kocher2016]; Nrf2-target mRNA in leukocytes peaks 4-6 h after a dose [tfood-cheng2019].

full.text: Semen and inflammation changes at 10 weeks [tfood-alizadeh2018]; lipid and inflammation markers did not change by 6 weeks in hyperlipidemia [tfood-kocher2016].

after_stopping.text: Conjugate half-life about 7 h [tfood-vareed2008]; clinical persistence not measured.

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily, often with each meal [tfood-kocher2016, tfood-alizadeh2018]. Liver injury linked to turmeric products had a latency of 1-4 months [tfood-halegoua2023].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; the trial measured only at 10 weeks.
sperm.text: The single RCT ran 10 weeks, about one spermatogenic cycle [tfood-alizadeh2018]. Sperm take about 64 days (range 42-76) from labelled precursor to ejaculate [tfood-misell2006], and the classic ~74-day estimate is uncertain by about a week [tfood-amann2008], so a diet change needs roughly 2.5-3 months to reach every stage of the sperm in a given ejaculate.

egg.late_start: Unknown; PCOS trials measured metabolic markers, not eggs.
egg.text: PCOS trials improved glucose and insulin [tfood-abdelazeem2022]; no egg or IVF outcome data. A follicle grows for several months before ovulation, including about 70 days from the preantral stage to 2 mm [tfood-gougeon2010], so anything acting on the growing follicle needs roughly 3-4 months to cover the whole final growth phase.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Enhanced-absorption curcumin modestly lowers CRP and MDA and eases knee-osteoarthritis pain like an NSAID in short trials, but trials are small and low quality, the field has integrity problems, and liver injury is documented.
audit.biases: Curcumin is a PAINS/IMPS compound with poor bioavailability [anut-nelson2017]; meta-analyses pool small, heterogeneous, often single-country trials, and an overview rated 37 of 48 knee-OA outcomes extremely low quality [anut-chen2025]. Larger Western trials are often null [anut-kocher2016].
audit.newer_evidence: Pooled CRP and OA estimates [anut-dehzad2023, anut-wang2021] are unchanged; a 2025 network meta-analysis ranked curcumin top for oocyte outcomes in infertile women, but at very-low certainty [anut-du2025], an example of rankings built on weak trials.
audit.bottom_line: Short trials of enhanced-absorption curcumin show modest CRP and knee-pain benefits, but the trials are small and low quality, the field has integrity problems, and liver injury is documented.

entries.headline: The best-proven way to prevent oxidative skin aging: in the Nambour RCT, daily sunscreen stopped measurable photoaging (24% less aging than discretionary use over 4.5 years), cut squamous-cell tumours by 39%, and was followed by half as many melanomas over the next 10 years.

dose.effective: Broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher applied every morning to the face, neck, arms and hands, as in the Nambour trial; reapply after swimming, heavy sweating or long periods outdoors.
dose.studied_range: SPF 15+ broad-spectrum, daily for 4.5 years, adults 25-75 (photoaging analysis in those under 55); melanoma follow-up 10 years after the trial ended.
dose.too_much: No harm was seen in the trial. All six common organic filters are absorbed into blood above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL screening threshold after one application; the clinical significance is unknown.
dose.timeframe: Photoaging differences after 4.5 years; melanoma differences emerged over the following decade.
dose.notes: Sunscreen filters block photons before they generate ROS; they are not antioxidants. Iron-oxide (tinted) sunscreens also block visible light, which improved melasma in one RCT. Sunscreen is one part of sun protection alongside shade, clothing and timing.

entries.mechanism: Organic and mineral UV filters absorb or scatter UVB and UVA, preventing direct DNA photoproducts and the UVA-driven singlet oxygen and superoxide that lead to 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and AP-1/MMP-mediated collagen breakdown. Standard filters do little against visible light and near-infrared; adding antioxidants to sunscreen reduced IR-A-induced MMP-1 in one small trial.
entries.interactions: Works on the cause of [uv-sun-exposure]. [topical-vitamin-c] and other topical antioxidants are add-ons, not substitutes. Oral [beta-carotene-supplement] added nothing in the same trial. Sunscreen does not meaningfully lower vitamin D status at normal use ([vitamin-d]).
entries.caveats: The only long-term RCT is Nambour (one Australian community, high UV). The melanoma result rests on 11 versus 22 cases and was borderline (P=0.051). Sunscreen did not reduce basal-cell carcinoma.
entries.debate: Observational meta-analyses of mostly case-control studies found no association between sunscreen use and melanoma (OR 1.10) [skb-silva2018], feeding claims that sunscreen does not prevent skin cancer. Rueegg and colleagues showed that adjusting for sun exposure, sunburn and skin type consistently shifts estimates toward protection, and that the only RCT showed HR 0.49 [skb-rueegg2019, skb-green2011]: sun-seeking, fair-skinned people use more sunscreen, which confounds the observational data. Safety: systemic absorption of organic filters [skb-matta2020] prompted calls for more toxicology, but no harm has been shown. Vitamin D concerns are addressed by [skb-passeron2019].
entries.title: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen

timing.summary: This is the clearest example in the group of a benefit that keeps growing and then outlives the habit. Daily sunscreen for 4.5 years produced no detectable increase in photoageing and 24% less ageing than discretionary use [tleg-hughes2013]; squamous-cell tumour rates were still about 40% lower 8 years after the trial ended [tleg-vanderpols2006], and melanomas were halved over the following decade [tleg-green2011].

onset.text: Protection against the acute insult is immediate - tretinoin and sunscreen both act on the same MMP induction that starts within hours of exposure [tleg-fisher1997]. Visible improvement in photoageing scores was reported from week 12 of daily use, though in an uncontrolled study [tleg-randhawa2016].

full.text: The randomized photoageing difference was measured over 4.5 years [tleg-hughes2013], and squamous-cell tumour rates fell 39% over the same trial [tleg-green1999]. The cancer benefit kept growing after the trial: SCC still about 40% lower at 8 years post-trial [tleg-vanderpols2006] and melanoma halved at 10 years [tleg-green2011].

after_stopping.text: Remarkably, the benefit persisted after the enforced daily use ended: both the SCC reduction (8 years) and the melanoma reduction (10 years) were measured in the post-trial period, because prevented DNA damage cannot come back [tleg-vanderpols2006, tleg-green2011]. New unprotected exposure, of course, starts accumulating again.

frequency.text: Daily is what was tested and daily is what worked: the trial compared daily application with discretionary use, and only the daily arm showed the photoageing and tumour benefits [tleg-hughes2013, tleg-green1999]. Discretionary use was the comparator, not a second effective schedule.

timing.debate: The melanoma result is contested. The trial follow-up found melanomas halved [tleg-green2011], but a meta-analysis of observational studies found no overall protective association between sunscreen use and melanoma, attributing the discrepancy to confounding by sun sensitivity and exposure behaviour [tleg-rueegg2019]. The trial's photoageing outcome also had missing data and modest power [tleg-hughes2013].

audit.claim: In the Nambour RCT daily sunscreen reduced photoaging and squamous-cell cancer and was followed by half as many melanomas.
audit.biases: Observational null results are confounded by sun-seeking, fair-skinned people using more sunscreen.
audit.newer_evidence: The RCT follow-up (melanoma HR 0.50) [abody-green2011] and the bias analysis showing adjustment moves estimates toward protection [abody-rueegg2019] outweigh the unadjusted null meta-analysis [abody-silva2018].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Damp and visible mould are linked to 30-50% more respiratory and asthma outcomes and about 30% more new asthma; repairing damp homes reduced adult wheeze (OR 0.64) in Cochrane-reviewed studies. Claims that indoor mould causes systemic "mycotoxin illness" diagnosed by urine tests are unproven.

dose.effective: Fix leaks and rising damp; keep indoor humidity down; use bathroom and kitchen extract fans; dry laundry outside or vented; clean small mould patches with detergent and water and dry the area; get professional remediation for large or hidden mould; insulate and heat cold walls.
dose.studied_range: Visible mould, damp spots, water damage or mould odour in homes, schools and offices.
dose.too_much: No dose threshold; mould odour carried the highest new-asthma estimate (1.73).
dose.timeframe: Symptoms improved within months of remediation in controlled before-after studies.
dose.notes: Do not rely on direct-to-consumer urine mycotoxin tests: CDC called them unvalidated.

entries.mechanism: Fungal spores, fragments and microbial products act through allergic (IgE) and innate immune pathways; damp also feeds dust mites and bacteria. Oxidative stress is shown for some mycotoxins in cell and animal studies only (mechanistic).
entries.interactions: Damp homes are often cold, poorly ventilated and low-income, and often have gas heaters ([gas-stoves]); insulation and better heating improved health in New Zealand trials [eia-howdenchapman2007, eia-howdenchapman2008]. Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers humidity.
entries.caveats: Damp and mould are reported by occupants, and symptomatic people may notice and report mould more. Poverty, crowding and cold confound. Remediation trials cannot be blinded. No fertility data.
entries.debate: The respiratory association is consistent across meta-analyses [eia-fisk2007, eia-quansah2012] and supported by remediation studies [eia-sauni2015] and WHO guidance [eia-who2009mould]. The contested ground is systemic illness: an allergy society position paper finds many hypothesized mould illnesses unproven [eia-bush2006], CDC warned against unvalidated urine mycotoxin tests [eia-kawamoto2015], while critics argue that an earlier occupational-medicine statement minimizing mould effects was shaped by litigation-related conflicts of interest [eia-craner2008].

key_numbers.label: Increase in respiratory/asthma outcomes with damp and mould
Adult wheeze after repairing mould damage

entries.title: Damp and mould at home

timing.summary: Living with damp is linked to new asthma over years [eia-quansah2012]; repairing damage and insulating improved wheeze and respiratory symptoms within a winter or two in remediation and insulation trials [eia-sauni2015, eia-howdenchapman2007].

onset.text: New-onset asthma accrued over the follow-up of cohort studies [eia-quansah2012].

full.text: Insulation reduced wheeze and days off school over one winter [eia-howdenchapman2007]; remediation studies measured symptoms months to years later [eia-sauni2015].

after_stopping.text: Not measured precisely; symptoms improved after remediation in before-after studies [eia-sauni2015].

frequency.text: Fix the building; ongoing humidity control and ventilation keep it fixed.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Across 30 RCTs DASH lowers blood pressure by about 3/2.5 mmHg (more with high salt intake and in younger people); one small study also showed less lipid-induced F2-isoprostane rise, and no trial has yet measured heart attacks or strokes.

dose.effective: 8-10 servings/day of fruit and vegetables, low-fat dairy, whole grains, nuts and legumes, low sodium and sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4 weeks per diet in a 24-person crossover study.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Blood pressure benefits of DASH are well established in larger trials; oxidative data are small.

entries.mechanism: High potassium, fiber and plant polyphenols; reduced sodium lowers vascular NADPH oxidase activity.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Oxidative-stress data come from one small study.
entries.title: DASH diet

timing.summary: DASH lowers blood pressure within a week, and most of the effect is there by then, unlike salt reduction, which keeps working for at least 4 weeks. How fast blood pressure rises again after stopping was not measured.

onset.text: Systolic BP 4.4 mmHg lower than control after 1 week [tfood-juraschek2017]; changes evident within 2 weeks in hypertensives [tfood-conlin2000].

full.text: No further fall after week 1 in DASH-Sodium [tfood-juraschek2017]; effect held through 8 weeks of feeding [tfood-appel1997].

after_stopping.text: Not measured in the feeding trials.

frequency.text: The effect comes from the current diet [tfood-juraschek2017], so it lasts only as long as the eating pattern does.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: DASH lowered BP ~8/7 mmHg and blunted lipid-induced F2-isoprostane rise in one small study; evidence rated limited.
audit.biases: The oxidative-stress claim rests on a single 2003 study [adiet-lopes2003]; the blood-pressure effect is randomized and replicated.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2020 meta-analysis of 30 RCTs (5,545 people) found DASH lowered BP by 3.2/2.5 mmHg, moderate-quality evidence [adiet-filippou2020]. The 2025 Cochrane review found too few trials with events to say whether DASH prevents heart attack or stroke [adiet-bensaaud2025].
audit.bottom_line: DASH is a proven blood-pressure diet (moderate evidence), though the average effect is smaller than the 8 mmHg in the cited study and hard-outcome trials are lacking.

entries.headline: Cochrane (2024, moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders (OR 1.30, NS); testosterone pre-treatment looks more promising (OR 2.53). ESHRE does not recommend DHEA.

dose.effective: Not recommended. A typical trial dose was 75 mg/day before and during the IVF cycle.
dose.studied_range: 75 mg/day (Wiser 2010) and similar regimens.
dose.too_much: Androgenic side effects (acne, hair growth); a hormone, use only under medical supervision.
dose.timeframe: Started before the IVF cycle and continued during stimulation in trials.
dose.notes: Network meta-analysis showed higher clinical pregnancy with DHEA (OR 2.46), but the larger Cochrane pooled analysis with live birth as outcome did not.

entries.mechanism: Androgen precursor proposed to increase FSH sensitivity of small antral follicles; not an antioxidant.
entries.interactions: Compare [coq10] in the same poor-responder population.
entries.caveats: Early small trials (e.g. 33 women) overstated benefit.
entries.title: DHEA in poor responders

timing.summary: DHEA raises blood and follicular DHEA-S within weeks, but any effect on the ovary would have to act on follicles still months from ovulation. Uncontrolled data show AMH climbing with 1-4 months of use, while the one 12-week placebo-controlled trial and the Cochrane review found no real gain.

onset.text: Serum and follicular DHEA-S rise on treatment [tegg-yeung2014]; uncontrolled AMH gains appear over 30-120 days [tegg-gleicher2010].

full.text: Uncontrolled series used a mean 17.6 weeks [tegg-barad2006]; no plateau measured in a controlled trial.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Trials used 25 mg three times daily or 75 mg once daily [tegg-yeung2014, tegg-wiser2010]; no schedule comparison exists.

timing.debate: Gleicher and Barad report AMH and embryo gains that grow with months of use [tegg-gleicher2010, tegg-barad2006], and one small RCT reported higher live birth [tegg-wiser2010]; a placebo-controlled 12-week trial found nothing [tegg-yeung2014] and Cochrane 2024 finds little or no live-birth difference [tegg-naik2024]. For androgens generally, Polyzos argues short courses miss the early follicle stages where androgens act [tegg-polyzos2018], while a small RCT found 3-4 weeks of testosterone gel better than 2 [tegg-kim2014].

egg.late_start: A course started 2-4 weeks before stimulation can only reach follicles already in the antral stage; no trial shows this helps.
egg.text: If used, start at least 12 weeks before stimulation, the duration of the main placebo-controlled trial [tegg-yeung2014], so that exposure covers the preantral-to-antral path; even then the expected benefit is small or none [tegg-naik2024].

audit.claim: Cochrane 2024 (moderate certainty): DHEA probably makes little or no difference to live birth in poor responders; testosterone looks more promising.
audit.biases: Research-integrity problems in the trial base: two DHEA RCTs in poor responders have been retracted, Elprince 2020 (retracted 2024) and Kotb 2016 (140 women, retracted 2026) [afert-elprince2020, afert-kotb2016, afert-kotb2016ret]; pooled estimates published before 2026 may contain such trials. Early small trials overstated benefit.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2024 (28 RCTs): DHEA OR 1.30 (0.95-1.76); testosterone OR 2.53 [afert-naik2024]. A 2025 meta-analysis restricted to POSEIDON-defined low reserve found testosterone the only adjuvant linked to higher live birth (OR 2.19) [afert-conforti2025], while a 2025 network meta-analysis found no significant live-birth differences among hormonal add-ons [afert-etrusco2025]. HFEA rates androgens grey [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: DHEA does not reliably help; the testosterone signal is real enough to test properly but not established.

factors.name: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

entries.headline: Most dietary polyphenols reach the colon and only work after gut bacteria convert them, and people differ widely in this; a fiber intake of 25-29 g/day is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease.

dose.effective: 25-29 g fiber/day or more from varied plants (whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts).
dose.studied_range: Cohorts (185 studies) and 58 RCTs.
dose.too_much: Increase gradually to limit bloating.
dose.timeframe: Microbiome shifts in days; outcomes long-term.
dose.notes: 'High' vs 'low excretor' and 'producer vs non-producer' metabotypes (urolithins, equol) explain part of why the same food works differently in different people.

entries.mechanism: Microbial catabolism turns anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, chlorogenic acids and ellagitannins into smaller phenolic acids, valerolactones and urolithins that are absorbed and circulate for up to 48 h; fermentation yields short-chain fatty acids that support barrier integrity and lower inflammation.
entries.interactions: Determines how much benefit you get from [blueberries], [coffee], [cocoa-flavanols], [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], and how much glucoraphanin converts to sulforaphane ([sulforaphane-supplements]). Antibiotics abolish microbial glucoraphanin conversion.
entries.caveats: Mechanisms are well described; direct evidence that changing the microbiome lowers systemic oxidative stress in humans is limited.

key_numbers.label: Fiber intake with greatest risk reduction
Anthocyanin relative bioavailability incl. metabolites (13C tracer)

entries.title: Dietary fiber and the gut microbiome

timing.summary: The gut microbiome shifts within a day of a diet change and snaps back within about 2 days of returning to the old diet, while a person's basic enterotype stays put. Over generations, fiber deprivation can permanently lose microbes in mice.

onset.text: Community composition changed within 24 h [tfood-wu2011] and within 1 day of the new food reaching the gut [tfood-david2014].

full.text: Fiber-degrading capacity rose over a 17-week high-fiber diet, with person-specific responses [tfood-wastyk2021].

after_stopping.text: The microbiota reverted to its original structure 2 days after a short diet ended [tfood-david2014]; in mice, losses reversed within one generation but became permanent over several [tfood-sonnenburg2016].

frequency.text: Because the community follows the last few days of food [tfood-david2014], fiber needs to be eaten every day to keep fiber-feeding microbes active.

timing.debate: Short feeding studies show fast, reversible change [tfood-david2014, tfood-wu2011], whereas a mouse study shows cumulative, irreversible loss over generations [tfood-sonnenburg2016]; an 8-week whole-grain trial produced no major microbiome change at all [tfood-roager2019].

audit.claim: 25-29 g/day fibre is linked to 15-30% lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease; most polyphenols need gut bacteria.
audit.biases: Observational mortality data share the healthy-user problem [adiet-satija2015].
audit.newer_evidence: The Lancet series combined cohorts with trials showing that higher fibre lowers weight, blood pressure and cholesterol, giving the association a causal pathway [adiet-reynolds2019].
audit.bottom_line: Well supported; the link from the microbiome to oxidative stress remains the weak part.

entries.headline: Vaping causes less oxidative stress than smoking but more than not using anything: a single e-cigarette acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a, and dual use is worse than smoking alone.

dose.effective: Best: use neither. For a smoker who cannot otherwise quit, a complete switch lowers toxicant exposure; dual use should be avoided.
dose.studied_range: Acute single-session crossover; large cross-sectional cohort (PATH); 24-week switching RCT.
dose.too_much: Dual use (vaping plus smoking) had 9% higher F2-isoprostanes than smoking only.
dose.timeframe: Acute effects within minutes; switching changes over weeks.
dose.notes: Long-term data are still limited.

entries.mechanism: Heated propylene glycol/glycerol forms carbonyls (formaldehyde, acrolein), and coils release metals; nicotine activates NOX2. Exposure to radicals is far lower than from combustion.
entries.interactions: Only reduces harm versus [tobacco-smoking] if it fully replaces cigarettes.
entries.caveats: Long-term independent data are limited; the acute study tested one session in healthy adults, and the cohort data are cross-sectional.
entries.title: E-cigarettes (vaping)

timing.summary: Daily e-cigarette users had lower sperm counts in one large study, but nothing is known about how quickly this appears or reverses.

onset.text: Not measured; daily users had 91 versus 147 million total sperm [tsperm-holmboe2020].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Daily use was the exposure studied [tsperm-holmboe2020].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: By analogy with smoking cessation, at least one spermatogenic cycle (extrapolated).

timing.debate: Users of e-cigarettes were often also smokers, and the authors note possible residual confounding [tsperm-holmboe2020].

audit.claim: Vaping causes less oxidative stress than smoking but more than nothing; dual use is worse than smoking alone.
audit.biases: Most vapers are current or former smokers, so cohort harms attributed to vaping are confounded by smoking history and timing (reverse causation).
audit.newer_evidence: Biomarkers: exclusive vapers have 10-98% lower toxicant exposure than smokers but more than never users, and dual users the most [abody-goniewicz2018]; acute vaping raises oxidative markers [abody-carnevale2016]. Outcomes: in PATH, exclusive vaping was not associated with incident CVD (HR 1.00) while smoking and dual use were (about 1.5) [abody-berlowitz2022]. A 2019 paper linking vaping to heart attacks was retracted in 2020 because it never established whether the infarctions came before or after vaping started [abody-bhatta2019]. Cochrane finds e-cigarettes help smokers quit better than NRT [abody-lindson2025].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: vaping is not harmless but much less toxic than smoking; quitting both is best.

entries.headline: Egg freezing works best young and in volume: with 10-15 eggs frozen at 35 or under, cumulative live birth reached ~85% vs a ~36% plateau at 36+, but only 9-38% of women ever return to use their eggs, and success after 40 is low.

dose.effective: Freeze at 35 or younger if possible and aim for about 10-15 mature eggs (often 2+ stimulation cycles); at least 8-10 for reasonable success, and expect lower odds per egg when older.
dose.studied_range: Vitrified mature (MII) eggs; mean freezing age in cohorts 36-38.
dose.too_much: Ovarian hyperstimulation, procedure risks and cost of repeated cycles and storage; diminishing returns after 40.
dose.timeframe: One stimulation cycle takes about 2 weeks; eggs keep for years in liquid nitrogen.
dose.notes: Per-egg efficiency is low (about 6% overall per thawed egg) and falls with age at freezing; freezing age, not using age, sets the odds.

entries.mechanism: Vitrification halts egg ageing: aneuploidy risk is fixed at the age of freezing (see [maternal-age]); about 75-85% of eggs survive warming.
entries.interactions: Planning uses [amh-ovarian-reserve-egg] to predict egg yield; later use often involves [pgt-a-egg] (not proven helpful).
entries.caveats: Outcome data come from small numbers of returning users; models (Goldman, Doyle) are partly extrapolated from fresh IVF.
entries.debate: Advocates argue it extends reproductive autonomy and that women should freeze younger [fer-goold2009, fer-cobo2016review]; clinic authors also note it is most cost-effective at 37-38, when biological success is lower [fer-cobo2016review]. Ethicists warn employer-paid schemes may pressure women [fer-mertes2015], and follow-up shows most eggs are never used (38% return at 10-15 years; 15% in Sweden) [fer-blakemore2021, fer-wennberg2019]. ASRM calls it ethically permissible with honest counselling and says live birth cannot yet be predicted precisely [fer-asrm2024ethics, fer-asrm2021oc].

key_numbers.label: Cumulative live birth plateau, frozen at <=35 (10-15 eggs)
Cumulative live birth plateau, frozen at >=36 (~11 eggs)
Women returning to use eggs (10-15 y)
Overall egg-to-baby efficiency per vitrified egg

entries.title: Egg freezing (planned / 'social' oocyte cryopreservation)

timing.summary: Freezing stops the egg's clock: what counts is the age at freezing and the number of mature eggs, not how long they stay in storage. Results fall sharply when eggs are frozen at 36 or older.

onset.text: One stimulation cycle; several may be needed to bank 8-10 mature eggs [tegg-cobo2016].

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Stored vitrified material keeps for years: in 58,001 blastocysts, storage up to 11 years did not affect live birth [tegg-cobo2024].

frequency.text: One or more stimulation cycles, ideally before 36: live birth per patient was 50% at <=35 vs 22.9% at >=36 [tegg-cobo2016].

timing.debate: A large single-group analysis found no effect of storage time on vitrified blastocysts [tegg-cobo2024]; a multicentre retrospective study found lower pregnancy with longer storage [tegg-zhang2021]. Both concern embryos; storage-time data for eggs are thinner.

audit.claim: Egg freezing works best young and with 10-15 eggs (~85% cumulative live birth at 35 or under), but only 9-38% of women return to use eggs.
audit.biases: Outcome data come from the minority who return (selection: returners differ in age and prognosis), single-centre series from leading clinics (the 85% figure), and models extrapolated from fresh IVF.
audit.newer_evidence: Two 2024 meta-analyses give pooled figures: about 11% of women return (median 7-year follow-up) and live birth per returning woman is about 28-29% [afert-hirsch2024, afert-kirubarajan2024]; 52% if eggs were frozen at 35 or younger and 19% at 40+ [afert-hirsch2024]. A large US clinic cohort found 43% cumulative live birth overall and over 70% only with 20+ mature eggs frozen before 38; extra freezing cycles did not independently help beyond the egg count [afert-cascante2024].
audit.bottom_line: The age and egg-number message holds, but pooled per-woman success is lower than the best single-clinic figures: roughly half at 35 or younger and one in five at 40+.

entries.headline: Eggplant skin's nasunin is a strong superoxide scavenger and iron chelator in test tubes, and the flesh is rich in chlorogenic acid, but there is no human evidence that eggplant lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: No human dose for oxidative stress exists; eat it as a normal vegetable with the skin on.
dose.studied_range: One RCT used 1.2 g/day eggplant powder for 12 weeks (blood pressure outcome, attributed to acetylcholine, not antioxidants).
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Phenol-Explorer has only a Folin value (61 mg/100 g) for whole purple eggplant. Chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic (>65% of phenolic acids) but content varies widely by cultivar and fruit segment. Frying in oil soaks up a lot of fat.

entries.mechanism: In vitro: nasunin (delphinidin-3-(p-coumaroylrutinoside)-5-glucoside) scavenges superoxide and inhibits hydroxyl radical generation mainly by chelating ferrous iron; chlorogenic acid is metabolised much like coffee chlorogenic acids.
entries.interactions: Chlorogenic acid overlaps with [coffee], which supplies far more per serving.
entries.caveats: The nasunin data are from rat brain homogenate and ESR assays at micromolar concentrations that dietary anthocyanins do not reach intact in human tissues. A 12-week RCT of eggplant powder lowered blood pressure in stressed adults, but the authors attribute it to choline esters (acetylcholine), not antioxidants.
entries.title: Eggplant (skin: nasunin; flesh: chlorogenic acid)

timing.summary: There are no human data on eggplant and oxidative stress, so nothing is known about timing. The only evidence is test-tube antioxidant activity of nasunin.

onset.text: Not measured in humans [tfood-noda2000].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No human evidence to base a schedule on.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: In a 767-patient JAMA trial with euploid embryos, timing transfer by receptivity testing gave no benefit (live birth 58.5% vs 61.9%); HFEA rates it red and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Endometrial biopsy in a mock cycle, gene-expression panel, then 'personalised' transfer timing.
dose.too_much: Extra biopsy (pain, bleeding, rare perforation), a mandatory freeze-all, delay and cost.
dose.timeframe: Adds at least one mock cycle.
dose.notes: Distinct from standard hysteroscopy or treatment of a diagnosed uterine problem.

entries.mechanism: Proposes that some women have a shifted 'window of implantation' detectable by endometrial transcriptomics.
entries.interactions: Often combined with [pgt-a-egg] and [endometrial-scratch-egg] after failed transfers.
entries.caveats: The non-significant direction of the main trial was toward lower live birth.
entries.debate: The test developer's own RCT reported higher per-protocol cumulative live birth (71.2% vs 55.4%) but no intention-to-treat difference and about 50% dropout [fer-simon2020]; the independent JAMA trial was null [fer-doyle2022]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Endometrial receptivity testing (ERA and similar)

audit.claim: Receptivity-timed transfer gave no benefit in a 767-patient JAMA RCT; HFEA red, ESHRE not recommended.
audit.biases: The positive evidence is developer-run (per-protocol analysis with ~50% dropout) and observational meta-analyses with methodological errors [afert-wilkinson2024].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 8 studies found no live-birth difference (OR 1.38, 0.79-2.41) [afert-arian2023]; methodologists used ERA reviews as a case study of fatal flaws in observational meta-analyses [afert-wilkinson2024]. The JAMA RCT result stands (58.5% vs 61.9%) [afert-doyle2022]; HFEA red [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: No newer evidence supports receptivity testing.

entries.headline: The 1364-woman PIP trial found identical live birth with and without a scratch (26.1% vs 26.1%); Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28), so at best a small benefit, at the cost of a painful extra procedure.

dose.effective: Not recommended for routine use (ESHRE). Trials used a pipelle biopsy in the luteal phase of the cycle before transfer.
dose.studied_range: One or two pipelle passes, day 3 of the preceding cycle to day 3 of the transfer cycle (PIP).
dose.too_much: Median pain 3.5/10; small infection and bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: Cycle before embryo transfer.
dose.notes: HFEA amber for most IVF patients, grey for recurrent implantation failure.

entries.mechanism: Hypothesis: controlled injury triggers a local inflammatory and wound-healing response (cytokines, macrophages) that improves endometrial receptivity.
entries.interactions: Often offered alongside [endometrial-receptivity-egg] or [immune-addons-egg] after failed transfers; none has been shown to add up.
entries.caveats: Early small trials were strongly positive; several trials have had data-integrity questions. Benefit, if any, is a few percentage points.
entries.debate: The IPD meta-analysis of 13 integrity-checked RCTs found higher live birth (OR 1.29, 1.02-1.64) [fer-vanhoogenhuijze2023], but its sensitivity analyses crossed 1 and it was publicly criticised [fer-aktoz2024]. The large pragmatic PIP trial was flat [fer-lensen2019] and Cochrane 2026 rates the effect unclear [fer-perera2026]. HFEA rates it amber [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE does not recommend routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Endometrial scratching before IVF

timing.summary: The scratch is timed to the cycle before embryo transfer, on the theory that tissue repair makes the lining more receptive in the next cycle. The largest trial, which scratched anywhere from the previous cycle to day 3 of the transfer cycle, found identical live birth.

onset.text: Done between day 3 of the preceding cycle and day 3 of the transfer cycle [tegg-lensen2019]; most trials used the luteal phase of the previous cycle [tegg-perera2026].

full.text: The hypothesised effect is confined to the next cycle; never measured directly.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Single procedure per IVF attempt.

timing.debate: An individual-participant meta-analysis found higher live birth (OR 1.29) [tegg-vanhoogenhuijze2023], challenged in a critical appraisal [tegg-aktoz2024]; the 1364-woman PIP trial found 26.1% vs 26.1% [tegg-lensen2019] and Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear [tegg-perera2026].

egg.late_start: Not applicable; it targets the endometrium, not the egg.
egg.text: Acts on the endometrium in the transfer cycle, not on the oocyte [tegg-perera2026].

audit.claim: PIP found identical live birth; Cochrane 2026 calls the effect unclear (OR 1.12); several trials have had integrity questions.
audit.biases: Early positive trials were small and some came from groups whose work has since been retracted: two Egyptian scratch RCTs were retracted in 2024 [afert-maged2018, afert-helmy2017], within a wider pattern of integrity problems in women's-health trials from single institutes [afert-bordewijk2020a, afert-mol2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2026 restricted its primary analysis to low-risk-of-bias trials and found an unclear effect (OR 1.12, 0.98-1.28) [afert-perera2026]; the 1364-woman PIP trial found 26.1% live birth in both arms [afert-lensen2019]. HFEA yellow [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: At best a small benefit, judged now on trustworthy trials only.

entries.headline: Endometriosis is an inflammatory, pro-oxidant condition linked to fewer and less mature eggs and lower oocyte mitochondrial content, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth rates (OR 0.98) once eggs are retrieved.

dose.effective: Specialist management; surgery for endometrioma before IVF did not improve live birth (OR 0.90) and may reduce ovarian reserve.
dose.notes: Discuss fertility preservation and surgery timing with a reproductive specialist.

entries.mechanism: Peritoneal and follicular inflammation, iron from repeated bleeding (free-iron Fenton chemistry) and granulosa-cell ROS impair follicle development and oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Antioxidant supplements have been tried, but none has convincing live-birth data ([female-antioxidant-supplements]).
entries.caveats: Evidence on egg quality is mostly from small biological studies; the main clinical effect is fewer oocytes and more cancelled cycles rather than lower live birth per transfer.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, endometrioma vs none

entries.title: Endometriosis

timing.summary: Endometriosis acts over years, and its main timing decisions are about treatment before IVF. Surgery on endometriomas lowers AMH and it does not recover; three to six months of GnRH-agonist suppression before IVF, once standard, is no longer supported.

onset.text: Not applicable (chronic condition).

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: AMH loss after endometrioma cystectomy persisted at long-term follow-up with no recovery over time [tegg-murdock2025].

frequency.text: Not a dosing question.

timing.debate: Older guidance endorsed 3-6 months of pituitary down-regulation before IVF; the 2019 Cochrane update found very low-quality evidence and could not confirm benefit, and ESHRE 2022 reversed the recommendation [tegg-georgiou2019, tegg-michaeli2022]. Some clinicians argue subgroups may still benefit [tegg-michaeli2022].

egg.late_start: Surgery before IVF did not change live birth or egg numbers [tegg-hamdan2015], so there is no lead time to gain by operating first.
egg.text: Long-term (3-6 month) GnRH agonist before IVF has uncertain effect on live birth [tegg-georgiou2019], and guidelines have withdrawn the recommendation [tegg-michaeli2022].

audit.claim: Endometriosis is pro-oxidant and linked to fewer eggs, but women with endometrioma have similar IVF live birth (OR 0.98); surgery before IVF did not help.
audit.biases: Mostly retrospective comparisons; egg-quality claims rest on small biological studies.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2021 meta-analysis again found fewer oocytes but similar live birth with endometrioma [afert-alshehre2021], consistent with the 2015 review [afert-hamdan2015].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Higher blood ergothioneine (mainly from mushrooms) is linked to 14% lower mortality per SD in a Swedish cohort, and the body has a dedicated transporter for it, but supplement trials are tiny and show only trends.

dose.effective: No proven supplement dose; eating mushrooms regularly is the practical source
dose.studied_range: Supplements 5-25 mg/day for weeks; 25 mg three times weekly for one year in an MCI pilot
dose.too_much: EFSA judged synthetic ergothioneine safe at proposed levels, including in pregnancy and for young children (NOAEL 800 mg/kg/day in animals)
dose.timeframe: Blood levels rise within days and the compound is retained for weeks
dose.notes: Mushrooms are by far the richest food source; mushroom intake was linked to modestly lower all-cause mortality in cohort studies.

entries.mechanism: A sulfur-containing histidine derivative made only by fungi and some bacteria. Humans absorb and concentrate it through the OCTN1 (SLC22A4) transporter in red cells, immune cells and other tissues. It scavenges radicals and chelates metals, and may act mainly under oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Comes packaged with fibre and other compounds in mushrooms; overlaps with diet-pattern benefits such as [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Blood ergothioneine is a marker of a health-conscious diet, so cohort links may be confounded. Supplement trials measured biomarkers in small groups; the MCI pilot had 19 participants.
entries.debate: Halliwell and Ames argue ergothioneine may be a 'longevity vitamin' because the body actively concentrates it and levels fall with age and cognitive decline [lon-halliwell2018, lon-ames2018, lon-cheah2016]; the Malmo cohort found strong links with lower mortality [lon-smith2020]. But the cohort authors identified it as a marker of a healthy food pattern, the mushroom-mortality meta-analysis showed only a small association (RR 0.94) and a null NHANES estimate [lon-ba2021], and supplementation produced mostly non-significant biomarker changes [lon-cheah2017]. The only cognitive trial is a 19-person pilot [lon-yau2024].

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality HR per SD higher ergothioneine

entries.title: Ergothioneine (mushrooms)

timing.summary: Ergothioneine is actively absorbed and held on to by the body, with less than 4% lost in urine. Exact build-up and wash-out times were not reported in the verified abstract.

onset.text: Plasma and whole-blood levels rose significantly after oral dosing [tnut-cheah2017]; exact timing not given in the abstract.

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured in verified data; low urinary loss suggests slow clearance (extrapolated) [tnut-cheah2017].

frequency.text: Extrapolated: strong retention suggests regular mushroom intake a few times a week maintains levels; no schedule trials.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Higher blood ergothioneine is linked to 14% lower mortality per SD in a Swedish cohort, but supplement trials are tiny.
audit.biases: Blood ergothioneine marks a health-conscious diet (residual confounding) [anut-smith2020, anut-ba2021].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer trial beyond the 19-person pilot was found.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Evening and night-time light (room light, screens, light while sleeping)

entries.headline: Ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99% of people and shortened melatonin by about 90 minutes, half-maximal suppression occurs at only ~25 lux, sleeping with a light or TV on was linked to 17-33% more weight gain and obesity, and one night at 100 lux raised next-morning insulin resistance.

dose.effective: In the 3 hours before bed keep light at the eye below about 10 lux melanopic EDI (dim, warm lamps below eye level); keep the bedroom as dark as possible (≤1 lux melanopic EDI; blackout curtains or an eye mask); reduce screen brightness and use low-melanopic (warm) display settings, or stop screens before bed.
dose.studied_range: Room light <200 lux vs <3 lux for 8 h before bed; 10-2,000 lux for 5 h; ~4 h of e-reader use for 5 nights; 100 lux during one night of sleep; habitual bedroom light ≥3 lux.
dose.too_much: Sleeping with a TV or ceiling light on; bright overhead lighting or full-brightness screens late in the evening.
dose.timeframe: Melatonin suppression within minutes to hours; circadian delay after a few evenings; metabolic effects after one night.
dose.notes: Brightness matters more than screen colour filters: in one trial, iPhone Night Shift did not improve sleep, and blue-blocking glasses have indeterminate effects on sleep. See also [morning-light]. Melatonin supplements are covered under [melatonin].

entries.mechanism: Melanopsin-driven signals from the retina inhibit pineal melatonin synthesis and phase-delay the clock. Melatonin is a direct radical scavenger and induces antioxidant enzymes and DNA repair; suppressing it, plus sympathetic activation during lit sleep, worsens insulin sensitivity. Follicular fluid melatonin protects oocytes from oxidative stress in laboratory studies.
entries.interactions: Delays the melatonin rise that makes [late-eating] worse for glucose; adds to [shift-work-circadian]; contributes to [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Health-outcome links (obesity, diabetes, mortality) are observational and confounded by urban living, income, sleep and mental health. Sperm data are one small cross-sectional study of men at a fertility clinic and one ecological study of outdoor light at night; we did not create a separate sperm factor. No human study has tied evening light to egg quality, although melatonin protects oocytes in laboratory work.
entries.debate: Laboratory trials consistently show melatonin suppression and circadian delay [kcc-gooley2011, kcc-phillips2019, kcc-chang2015, kcc-schollhorn2023], and one night of lit sleep impaired insulin sensitivity [kcc-mason2022]; cohorts link light at night to obesity, diabetes and mortality [kcc-park2019, kcc-obayashi2013, kcc-windred2024a, kcc-windred2024b]. A letter argued the e-reader findings overstate real-life relevance and the authors defended them [kcc-zeitzer2015, kcc-changczeisler2015]; screen-colour fixes have weak support (Night Shift [kcc-duraccio2021]; blue-blocking glasses indeterminate [kcc-singh2023]); and cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding [kcc-windred2024a]. Sperm associations [kcc-green2020, kcc-tian2024] are preliminary.

entries.title: Evening and night-time light (room light, screens, light while sleeping)

timing.summary: Evening light suppresses melatonin within minutes to hours and shifts the body clock later over a few evenings; one night of sleeping with the light on worsened next-morning insulin resistance. These effects reverse within days once evenings are kept dim and days bright.

onset.text: Room light before bed delayed melatonin onset in 99% of people and shortened melatonin by ~90 min the same night [tbody-gooley2011]; one night at 100 lux during sleep raised next-morning insulin resistance [tbody-mason2022].

full.text: Five evenings of e-reader use delayed the circadian clock and lengthened sleep onset [tbody-chang2015].

after_stopping.text: Natural light re-anchored the clock within a weekend (about 69% of a week's shift) and fully within a week [tbody-stothard2017, tbody-wright2013].

frequency.text: Effects act night by night, so dim evenings need to be a nightly habit; a single bright evening resets only partially within days.

timing.debate: Laboratory effects within days are clear [tbody-chang2015], but a published letter argued that these lab findings may not reflect real-life exposure [tbody-zeitzer2015].

audit.claim: Evening room light suppresses and delays melatonin; light while sleeping is linked to weight gain, diabetes and insulin resistance, but outcome links are observational.
audit.biases: Bright nights travel with urban living, poor sleep, shift work and illness (confounding, reverse causation).
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 UK Biobank analysis of 88,905 sensor wearers linked the brightest nights to more coronary disease (aHR 1.32), heart failure and AF, robust to adjustment for SES and polygenic risk [abody-windred2025], extending the 2024 mortality analysis [abody-windred2024]; both are from the same group and remain observational.
audit.bottom_line: The melatonin physiology is trial-based; links to disease have grown but are still observational.

entries.headline: Fat mass tracks systemic oxidative stress. BMI was one of the strongest independent correlates of urinary F2-isoprostanes in 2,828 Framingham participants, through adipose NADPH oxidase and inflammation.

dose.effective: Reducing excess fat mass (see lifestyle area for specifics).
dose.timeframe: Not specified in these studies
dose.notes: Mechanistic and cross-sectional human evidence. Intervention data are covered by the lifestyle area.

entries.mechanism: In expanded adipose tissue, free fatty acids activate NADPH oxidase and antioxidant enzymes fall, raising ROS. This disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1) and drives systemic low-grade inflammation through NF-kB. Nutrient excess also raises mitochondrial superoxide.
entries.interactions: Compounds [glycemic-control] and [chronic-inflammation]. Supplements do not offset it.
entries.caveats: Most human data are associations. The causal chain is supported by mouse NOX-inhibitor experiments.
entries.title: Excess body fat (especially visceral adiposity)

entries.headline: Obese men are more often infertile and have lower IVF live-birth rates; the BMI-SDF link is real but smaller and less consistent than for smoking or varicocele.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30, ideally 18.5-25; waist reduction matters more than the scale number.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories from <18.5 to >=40.
dose.too_much: Risk rises steeply above BMI 35-40 (odds of oligo/azoospermia 2.04 in morbid obesity). Impaired glucose tolerance was linked to +13.8 points SDF.
dose.timeframe: Lifestyle weight loss over 3-6 months has improved semen in trials.
dose.notes: Very underweight (BMI <18.5) also trends toward worse semen.

entries.mechanism: Excess adipose tissue raises aromatase activity (lower testosterone, higher estradiol), systemic inflammation and insulin resistance, increases scrotal fat and temperature, and raises seminal ROS.
entries.interactions: Improves with [weight-loss], [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [mediterranean-diet]. Often co-occurs with poor sleep and sugary drinks.
entries.caveats: In the SDF meta-analysis only class I obesity showed a small, borderline increase (SMD 0.23). Confounding by diet, activity and diabetes is substantial.
