entries.title: Obesity and metabolic dysfunction

entries.headline: Obesity (BMI >= 30) is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth (RR 0.85), worse with PCOS, and with an inflamed, lipid-rich follicular environment.

dose.effective: Aim for BMI under 30 and ideally 18.5-24.9; in PCOS, even 5% weight loss improved hormones and cycles.
dose.studied_range: BMI categories 18.5-24.9 vs >= 30 kg/m2 in meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Underweight (BMI < 18.5) and very low energy availability also impair ovulation (see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]).
dose.timeframe: Follicular environment reflects the preceding ~3 months.
dose.notes: Donor-egg data did not change the overall conclusion, suggesting both egg and uterine effects.

entries.mechanism: Higher follicular fluid insulin, triglycerides, lactate and CRP; lipid accumulation in oocytes causes ER stress, reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and cumulus-cell apoptosis (lipotoxicity).
entries.interactions: Compounds [pcos] and [glycemic-control]. Weight-loss evidence is in [weight-loss]. Vigorous exercise was not harmful in women with BMI >= 25 ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).
entries.caveats: Associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease. Weight-loss RCTs before IVF have not raised IVF live birth (see [weight-loss]).

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, BMI >= 30 vs normal

entries.title: Obesity (BMI 30 or higher)

timing.summary: Excess fat shapes the follicle's environment continuously: follicular fluid mirrors blood insulin, lipids and CRP. In mice, oocyte damage outlasted 8 weeks of diet reversal; in women, 3-6 months of pre-IVF weight loss did not raise live birth, though it restored ovulation in PCOS.

onset.text: Builds over years of excess fat; not measured as an onset.

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: In mice, spindle and mitochondrial defects persisted after 8 weeks of normal diet despite normal weight and glucose [tegg-reynolds2015]; partial recovery with diet plus exercise [tegg-xinyan2025]. Human recovery time unknown.

frequency.text: Not a dosing question; see weight-loss.

timing.debate: Whether oocyte effects of obesity reverse is contested: mouse studies show persistence after diet reversal [tegg-reynolds2015, tegg-xinyan2025], while human trials of preconception weight loss show improved ovulation and natural conception [tegg-best2017] but no IVF live-birth gain [tegg-einarsson2017, tegg-mutsaerts2016].

egg.late_start: Follicular fluid tracks current blood chemistry [tegg-valckx2012], so metabolic gains in the final month can still reach the follicle environment, but mouse data suggest earlier damage to oocytes is not undone quickly.
egg.text: Obesity lowers IVF live birth (RR 0.85) [tegg-sermondade2019] and alters preovulatory follicular fluid [tegg-robker2009]; 16 weeks is the duration of the PCOS trials in which weight loss improved ovulation and live birth [tegg-legro2015].

audit.claim: Fat mass tracks systemic oxidative stress, obesity lowers male fertility and is associated with about 15% lower IVF live birth.
audit.biases: The 'obesity paradox' arises from smoking, illness-related weight loss (reverse causation) and collider bias [abody-horita2023]; fertility associations are confounded by PCOS and metabolic disease.
audit.newer_evidence: Among 3.95 million never-smokers free of disease, mortality was lowest at BMI 20-25 and rose log-linearly above 25 [abody-gbmc2016]. The 2019 non-linear MR J-curve [abody-sun2019] was revised in 2024 because its method's assumption failed; the reanalysis showed clear harm above BMI 25 and weak evidence of harm below 20 [abody-burgess2024], although non-linear MR remains error-prone [abody-hamilton2024]. MR supports genetically higher BMI and waist-hip ratio causing PCOS and other reproductive conditions [abody-venkatesh2022]. The IVF association holds [abody-sermondade2019].
audit.bottom_line: Excess fat is a cause, not just a marker, of disease and reproductive disorders; the obesity paradox is largely an artefact.

factors.name: Exercise snacks and vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity (VILPA)

entries.headline: In non-exercisers, three 1-2 minute bursts of vigorous everyday activity a day (stairs, fast uphill walking, carrying loads) were associated with 38-40% lower mortality and 48-49% lower cardiovascular death, and small RCTs show stair or sprint 'snacks' raise VO2peak modestly (about 4% for sprint snacks); the cohort data may overstate the benefit.

dose.effective: 3-5 bouts a day of about 1 minute of vigorous effort (fast stair climbing, e.g. 60 steps; brisk uphill walking; 20-second sprints), totalling about 3-5 min/day; or 6 x 1-min hard intervals before meals.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to ~10 VILPA bouts/day (median 3-5); RCTs: 3 x 60-step stair climbs or 3 x 20-s sprints, 3 days/week for 6 weeks.
dose.too_much: None known; the mortality curve flattened beyond about 8 bouts/day.
dose.timeframe: VO2peak gains in 6 weeks; glucose effects the same day.
dose.notes: A practical entry point for people who do not exercise. Benefit for cardiovascular events was clearer in women than men in UK Biobank.

entries.mechanism: Brief vigorous efforts produce the same metabolic, calcium and ROS signals as interval training (AMPK, PGC-1alpha), raise heart rate near maximum, and improve post-meal glucose uptake.
entries.interactions: A stepping stone to [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [cardiorespiratory-fitness]; breaks up [sedentary-time]; pre-meal snacks complement [post-meal-walking].
entries.caveats: VILPA data come from wrist accelerometers in UK Biobank volunteers (healthier than average) and one smaller US sample; people able to climb stairs fast may simply be healthier. RCTs are small (9-28 people) and short.
entries.debate: The UK Biobank analyses report large, near-linear benefits for mortality, cancer and cardiovascular events [exr-stamatakis2022, exr-stamatakis2023, exr-stamatakis2025, exr-ahmadi2023]. A US national replication found a similar 44% lower mortality, but when people with prevalent heart disease or cancer were excluded the confidence intervals mostly crossed 1, consistent with reverse causation [exr-koemel2026]. Training studies confirm fitness gains but they are modest and small [exr-jenkins2019, exr-little2019], and pre-meal snacks improved glucose in only 9 people [exr-francois2014]. Proponents frame snacks as proof-of-concept rather than a replacement for guidelines [exr-islam2022]. The related 'weekend warrior' pattern is better supported: concentrating activity into 1-2 days gave similar mortality and cardiovascular associations to spreading it out [exr-odonovan2017, exr-dossantos2022, exr-khurshid2023, exr-kim2025].

entries.title: Exercise snacks and vigorous intermittent lifestyle activity (VILPA)

timing.summary: Short vigorous bursts lower that day's blood sugar, and done several times a day for six weeks they modestly raise fitness. Like other exercise, the effect needs repeating to persist.

onset.text: Six 1-min intense intervals before meals lowered the next 24 h of glucose [tbody-francois2014].

full.text: VO2peak rose after 6 weeks of 3 daily stair-climb or sprint snacks [tbody-jenkins2019, tbody-little2019]; longer trials are lacking.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; by analogy with other training, gains would fade within weeks [tbody-mujika2000b] (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Sprints spread across the day raised fitness about as much as the same sprints done in one session [tbody-little2019]; the glucose effect is per meal, so snacks before or after main meals are the logical timing [tbody-francois2014].

timing.debate: Cohort data link three 1-2 min daily bursts to 38-40% lower mortality [tbody-stamatakis2022], far more than the modest fitness gains seen in 6-week trials [tbody-jenkins2019] would predict.

audit.claim: Three 1-2 minute vigorous bouts a day are associated with 38-40% lower mortality; the cohort data may overstate the benefit.
audit.biases: Reverse causation: people who can climb stairs fast are healthier; UK Biobank volunteers are healthier than average.
audit.newer_evidence: The UK Biobank estimate [abody-stamatakis2022] was replicated in US NHANES wearables data, but confidence intervals mostly crossed 1 once people with heart disease or cancer were excluded (2026) [abody-koemel2026].
audit.bottom_line: Short vigorous bursts raise fitness modestly in small trials; the large mortality reduction seen in cohorts is probably inflated.

factors.name: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

entries.headline: A ketone-ester drink raises blood BHB to ~2-4 mmol/L within an hour, and salts or C8 oil raise it much less. Acute doses lower glucose by ~0.5 mmol/L and give a small cognitive benefit, but they do not improve exercise performance, and the anti-inflammatory story is contradictory in humans.

dose.effective: Ketone monoester ~0.3-0.5 g/kg (about 12-27 g BHB) gives a peak BHB of ~2.8-4 mmol/L for 2-4 h. Ketone salts ~12-24 g BHB give ~1 mmol/L. C8 (tricaprylin) 20 mL twice daily gives ~0.3-0.5 mmol/L. A 15 g twice-daily MCT drink was used in the 6-month MCI trial.
dose.studied_range: Single doses up to 714 mg/kg monoester; 25 mL (26.8 g) monoester three times daily for 28 days in healthy adults; 12 g BHB before meals for 14 days in obesity; 30 g/day MCT for 6 months.
dose.too_much: Gut upset (nausea, cramps, diarrhoea) at high doses, worse with salts and MCT. Salts carry a large sodium/potassium load and half the BHB is the less useful L-isomer. Avoid with SGLT2 inhibitors or type 1 diabetes without medical advice.
dose.timeframe: Peak at 30-60 min, back to baseline within 3-4 h; no lasting ketosis without repeated dosing.
dose.notes: A meal cuts the peak by about a third. Ketone esters taste harsh and cost several dollars per serving at retail (a market observation, not from a study). They give ketones without carbohydrate restriction, so they do not reproduce the low-insulin, weight-loss and low-glucose milieu of the diet.

entries.mechanism: Supplies D-BHB directly. In the short term it lowers hepatic glucose output, free fatty acids and lipolysis (HCAR2), and gives the brain an alternative fuel. HDAC inhibition and NLRP3 blockade are cell and mouse findings. In humans, a single dose increased monocyte caspase-1 activation, while 14 days of pre-meal dosing decreased it.
entries.interactions: No human trials measure oxidative-damage markers. It does not replace [ketogenic-diet] for epilepsy. Glucose lowering adds to diabetes drugs. For athletes, pre-race ketone drinks impaired a time trial; post-session ester during overload training is the one positive signal.
entries.caveats: A meta-analysis of 13 RCTs found no performance effect (g = -0.05). The cognitive meta-analysis effect is small (SMD 0.29) across heterogeneous trials. Most trials are industry-linked, small and short. Vendor claims about 'burning fat' are backwards: exogenous BHB suppresses lipolysis.

entries.title: Exogenous ketones (ketone esters, ketone salts, MCT/C8 oil)

timing.summary: A ketone ester drink raises blood ketones within an hour and they are back to baseline within a few hours; nothing builds up with daily use. Any glucose benefit lasts only as long as the dosing continues.

onset.text: Peak ketones within 1-2 h of a monoester dose [tbody-clarke2012].

full.text: No cumulative build-up: three drinks a day for 28 days gave the same post-drink rises without changes in weight, glucose or lipids [tbody-sotomota2019]; pre-meal dosing for 14 days lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-walsh2021].

after_stopping.text: Ketones fall back within a few hours of each dose (half-life roughly 1-3 h) [tbody-clarke2012].

frequency.text: Effects last hours, so they need dosing before each meal to matter for glucose [tbody-walsh2021]; there is no evidence for intermittent schedules.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Ketone esters raise BHB, acutely lower glucose and give a small cognitive benefit, but do not improve performance.
audit.biases: Mostly small, industry-linked trials [anut-valenzuela2020].
audit.newer_evidence: The 2026 cognition meta-analysis (SMD 0.29) is already cited [anut-bonnechere2026]; nothing newer changes the picture.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Outside testosterone shuts down the brain's signal (LH/FSH) to the testes and can drop sperm counts to zero; recovery takes months to over a year.

dose.effective: Any exogenous testosterone or anabolic steroid, including gels, injections and 'cycles'.
dose.studied_range: Androgen regimens used for male contraception reliably suppress sperm output.
dose.too_much: Long-term, high-dose and long-acting preparations recover slowest.
dose.timeframe: Median recovery to 20 million/mL about 3.4 months after contraceptive-style androgen use; after steroid abuse, often 6-12+ months, sometimes incomplete.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: do not prescribe testosterone to men who want current or future fertility. Do not stop abruptly without medical advice; urologists can use hCG, SERMs or aromatase inhibitors to restart production.

entries.mechanism: Negative feedback suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH; intratesticular testosterone collapses, halting spermatogenesis (endocrine, not primarily oxidative).
entries.interactions: Overrides any benefit from diet or supplements. Often combined with other harmful exposures in body-building (high-dose supplements, stimulants).
entries.caveats: Not an SDF factor in the usual sense: it mainly lowers sperm number, often to azoospermia. Included because it is the most common avoidable cause of severe male-factor infertility in young men.
entries.title: Exogenous testosterone (TRT) and anabolic-androgenic steroids

timing.summary: Outside testosterone switches off the brain's signal to the testes and sperm counts fall within weeks, mainly because sperm stop being released. Recovery after stopping takes a median of about 3.4 months after contraceptive doses and over a year after steroid abuse.

onset.text: Sperm counts fell to 10% of baseline in about 24 days on 200 mg testosterone enanthate weekly [tsperm-mclachlan2002]; most men were azoospermic or severely oligozoospermic by 6 months [tsperm-who1995].

full.text: Suppression to under 3 million/mL in 96-98% of men within 6 months [tsperm-who1995].

after_stopping.text: Median 3.4 months to 20 million/mL; 67% recovered by 6 months, 90% by 12 and 100% by 24 [tsperm-liu2006]; after anabolic steroid abuse, sperm output took about 14 months on average [tsperm-shankara2020] and can take over a year [tsperm-rajmil2024].

frequency.text: Any regular use suppresses spermatogenesis; shorter-acting preparations and shorter use recovered faster [tsperm-liu2006].

sperm.late_start: Stopping 2-4 weeks before achieves nothing for that cycle; recovery takes months.
sperm.text: Acts on spermatogonial maturation and spermiation [tsperm-mclachlan2002]; plan on 6-24 months after stopping [tsperm-liu2006, tsperm-shankara2020].

timing.debate: Contraceptive-trial data show full recovery within 24 months [tsperm-liu2006], whereas steroid abusers recover more slowly and sometimes incompletely, with residual small testes [tsperm-shankara2020, tsperm-rajmil2024].

entries.headline: In the 200-man EUROLIVE RCT, oxidized LDL fell with olive-oil phenolic content at 25 mL/day, and the EU authorises an LDL-protection claim at 5 mg hydroxytyrosol per 20 g; PREDIMED's Mediterranean diet with EVOO cut major CVD events by ~30%, but that trial tested the whole diet, not the oil alone.

dose.effective: 20-25 g (about 2 tablespoons) per day of a high-phenolic EVOO meeting >= 5 mg hydroxytyrosol + derivatives per 20 g.
dose.studied_range: 25 mL/day for 3 weeks (EUROLIVE); ~1 L/week per household in PREDIMED for years.
dose.too_much: Calories (about 120 kcal per tablespoon).
dose.timeframe: Measurable LDL changes within 3 weeks.
dose.notes: Use as the main culinary fat, raw on food or for moderate-heat cooking; phenolics decline with storage, light and heat. Refined olive oil has a fraction of the phenolics.

entries.mechanism: Hydroxytyrosol and its secoiridoid precursors (oleacein/3,4-DHPEA-EDA, oleuropein aglycone) bind to LDL and protect its lipids from oxidation; high oleic acid content makes membranes and LDL less oxidizable than PUFA-rich oils; modest Nrf2 and anti-inflammatory effects.
entries.interactions: Best evidence when it replaces butter, refined seed oils or [oxidized-frying-oils]. Improves carotenoid absorption from [tomatoes-lycopene] and [leafy-greens]. Core component of [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Short trials use LDL oxidation markers rather than outcomes; PREDIMED was re-analysed after randomisation irregularities (results held). Phenolic content varies enormously between oils and labels rarely state it. In the 50-person OLIVAUS crossover, 60 mL/day of high- vs low-polyphenol oil for 3 weeks gave no significant between-treatment difference, with oxLDL falling only within the high-polyphenol arm (more in abdominal obesity), so effects in healthy people are modest. The throat sting of fresh oil comes from oleocanthal, a COX inhibitor with ibuprofen-like activity in vitro; its clinical relevance at culinary doses is unknown.

entries.title: Extra-virgin olive oil (high-phenolic)

timing.summary: Olive oil phenols peak in blood within an hour and have a half-life of about 2.5 h, but daily use lowered oxidized LDL within 3 weeks. Cardiovascular-event benefit in PREDIMED accrued over about 5 years.

onset.text: Hydroxytyrosol peaks 32-53 min after 25 mL virgin olive oil, half-life 2.43 h [tfood-mirocasas2003].

full.text: Oxidized LDL and HDL changed within 3-week periods in proportion to phenol content [tfood-covas2006]; oxidized LDL fell at 3 months in PREDIMED [tfood-fito2007]; CVD events were lower over a median 4.8 years [tfood-estruch2018].

after_stopping.text: Not directly measured; EUROLIVE assumed reversal within its 2-week washouts [tfood-covas2006].

frequency.text: Phenols clear within hours [tfood-mirocasas2003]; trials used 25 mL every day [tfood-covas2006].

timing.debate: PREDIMED's long-term benefit is debated after its 2013 report was retracted and republished because of randomization problems [tfood-agarwal2019, tfood-estruch2018].

audit.claim: High-phenolic EVOO lowers oxidized LDL (EUROLIVE), carries an EU health claim, and PREDIMED's EVOO arm cut major CVD events by ~30%; evidence rated strong.
audit.biases: PREDIMED tested a whole Mediterranean diet plus free oil against low-fat advice, so it cannot isolate EVOO, and its randomization problems weaken it [adiet-estruch2018, adiet-agarwal2019]. Olive-oil cohorts are subject to healthy-user and socioeconomic confounding; in US cohorts olive oil was no better than other vegetable oils combined [adiet-guaschferre2022].
audit.newer_evidence: EUROLIVE's surrogate result (oxidized LDL falling with phenol content) still stands [adiet-covas2006]; the 2022 OLIVAUS crossover found smaller, partly within-arm effects [adiet-sarapis2022]. Cochrane rated the PREDIMED-type evidence low quality for mortality [adiet-rees2019]. No trial has compared high- vs low-phenolic oil on clinical events.
audit.bottom_line: EVOO is a good default fat with a real but modest effect on LDL oxidation; the 30% event reduction belongs to the whole PREDIMED diet, not to the oil alone.

entries.headline: In PCOS, intermittent fasting lowered weight (-4.25 kg) and free androgen index and raised SHBG, but no more than calorie restriction; in lean women a 72-h fast made 2 of 7 cycles anovulatory, and fasting beyond the overnight period in late pregnancy rapidly produces ketosis.

dose.effective: With PCOS and excess weight: an 8-10 h eating window or daily calorie restriction for 8+ weeks, whichever is easier to keep. Without excess weight: avoid deliberate energy deficit while trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: 72-h follicular-phase fasts; 5-12 weeks of 6-10 h TRE in PCOS; Ramadan in pregnancy.
dose.too_much: Energy availability below ~30 kcal/kg lean mass/day disrupts LH pulses; multi-day fasts in lean women can block ovulation. In pregnancy avoid fasting beyond the overnight period (18-h fasts cause ketonaemia).
dose.timeframe: Androgen and menstrual changes in PCOS over 5-8 weeks; follicle effects within one cycle.
dose.notes: Normal-weight women tolerated a 3-day fast without cycle disruption; lean women (<=20% body fat) did not.

entries.mechanism: In insulin-resistant PCOS, lower insulin raises SHBG and lowers ovarian androgen output. In lean women, energy deficit slows GnRH/LH pulsatility (hypothalamic suppression). In pregnancy, 'accelerated starvation' raises maternal ketones that cross the placenta.
entries.interactions: Works through the same route as [weight-loss] in [pcos]. Stacking fasting with heavy training risks [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]. Prenatal nutrient needs (e.g., [folic-acid]) are harder to meet in short eating windows.
entries.caveats: PCOS evidence is five small studies; the only RCT comparing early TRE with calorie restriction (Talebi 2024) found no difference. Ramadan pregnancy meta-analyses show no birth-weight effect but are observational and lack mortality data; the IQ-ketone link (Rizzo 1991) is correlational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change with IF in PCOS (meta-analysis)
Energy availability threshold for LH disruption
PCOS women with improved menstrual regularity after 5 weeks of 8-h TRE

entries.title: Fasting, ovulation, PCOS and pregnancy

timing.summary: Deep energy deficit acts on the hypothalamus within days: LH pulses slow and a cycle can become anovulatory, but the effect is limited to the cycle in which it happens. Milder intermittent fasting in PCOS works through weight and androgens over 5-8 weeks.

onset.text: LH pulsatility disrupted after 5 days below 30 kcal/kg lean mass [tegg-loucks2003]; a 72-h fast cut LH pulses 19% in lean women [tegg-alvero1998].

full.text: PCOS: weight, free androgen index and SHBG improved over 5 weeks of time-restricted eating [tegg-li2021] and in trials pooled by [tegg-ranneh2025].

after_stopping.text: LH changes reverse after refeeding; in normal-weight women a 3-day fast did not change ovulation [tegg-olson1995]. Effects confined to the affected cycle (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Avoid multi-day fasts or very low energy availability in the 2-3 weeks before ovulation or egg retrieval, especially if lean [tegg-alvero1998]. No trial compared fasting schedules for fertility.

timing.debate: Normal-weight women tolerated a 3-day mid-follicular fast without ovulation changes [tegg-olson1995], whereas lean women had anovulation in 2 of 7 fasted cycles [tegg-alvero1998]; body fat appears to set the threshold.

egg.late_start: Stopping a deep fast restores LH pulses within days, so the next cycle is usually unaffected.
egg.text: The sensitive window is the follicular phase of the conception or IVF cycle, when LH pulses drive the dominant follicle [tegg-alvero1998, tegg-loucks2003].

entries.headline: No trial shows fasting improves sperm; a 48-h fast cut LH by ~64% and lowered testosterone, 16:8 TRE lowered testosterone in trained men, and a retrospective IVF study found lower progressive motility (30% vs 38%) in samples produced during Ramadan.

dose.effective: None established. If overweight, the benefit comes from losing weight by any method; daily 12-14 h overnight fasts appear harmless.
dose.studied_range: 48-h fasts, 8 weeks of 16:8 TRE, Ramadan (dawn-to-sunset fasting for a month), three 5-day FMD cycles.
dose.too_much: Multi-day fasts suppress the reproductive axis within 48 h; avoid them during the ~74-day window before conception attempts or semen analysis.
dose.timeframe: Hormone changes within 48 h; semen effects would need one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days).
dose.notes: Ramadan meta-analysis found no average change in testosterone, LH or FSH, so daily dawn-to-dusk fasting is probably neutral for hormones.

entries.mechanism: Acute energy deficit slows hypothalamic GnRH/LH pulsatility and lowers testosterone and IGF-1; dehydration and circadian disruption during Ramadan may affect semen volume and motility.
entries.interactions: Weight loss in men with obesity improves semen quality; see [weight-loss] and [excess-adiposity]. Poor sleep during late-night eating periods overlaps with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Human sperm data are a 21-man 1986 study, a 97-man retrospective IVF cohort, and an 18-man FMD pilot. Rodent studies of fasting and sperm are not transferable.
entries.title: Fasting and sperm (Ramadan, TRE, multi-day fasts)

timing.summary: A 48-hour fast suppresses the hormone signal to the testes within two days. Semen produced during and in the 70 days after a month of daily fasting had lower motility, but recovery has not been timed.

onset.text: LH fell from 2.94 to 1.07 IU/L, with lower FSH and testosterone, after 48 h of fasting [tsperm-cameron1991].

full.text: Not measured for semen.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; samples during Ramadan and the 70 days after showed lower progressive motility (30% vs 38%) [tsperm-engel2023].

frequency.text: No trial shows a sperm benefit; repeated or prolonged fasting in the months before a sample is where harm signals appear [tsperm-engel2023].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: Hormone suppression affects spermatogonial development and spermiation, so avoiding long fasts for about one cycle before is the cautious choice (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Three monthly 5-day cycles (~1,100 then ~700 kcal/day, low protein) lowered weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 vs usual diet in one 100-person trial; no direct oxidative stress endpoints, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest.

dose.effective: 5 consecutive days per month of a plant-based, low-protein, low-sugar, higher-unsaturated-fat diet (~1,100 kcal on day 1, ~700 kcal on days 2-5), for 3 cycles.
dose.studied_range: 3 monthly cycles in generally healthy adults; 3 cycles over 4 months in men with poor semen quality.
dose.too_much: Same exclusions as fasting: pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, diabetes medication without supervision.
dose.timeframe: Changes measured after 3 cycles (3 months).
dose.notes: Benefits were concentrated in people with elevated baseline risk; low protein is probably what lowers IGF-1.

entries.mechanism: Mimics fasting signals (low insulin, IGF-1 and amino acids) while supplying some food; in mice, cycles triggered regeneration on refeeding and extended lifespan.
entries.interactions: Effects overlap with [weight-loss]; IGF-1 lowering is also achieved by moderate protein reduction under [calorie-restriction].
entries.caveats: Small number of trials, largely from one group with a commercial product; the 2.5-year 'biological age' reduction is an exploratory secondary analysis.
entries.title: Fasting-mimicking diet (5-day low-calorie, low-protein cycles)

timing.summary: Three monthly five-day cycles lowered weight, IGF-1 and blood pressure, and in a voluntary follow-up these changes had largely persisted about three months after the last cycle. This rests on one company-linked trial with no control during follow-up.

onset.text: Changes were measured only after three monthly cycles, 5-7 days after returning to normal eating [tbody-wei2017].

full.text: Measured after 3 cycles (3 months) [tbody-wei2017]; whether more cycles add more is unknown.

after_stopping.text: Effects on weight, waist, IGF-1 and blood pressure persisted for about 3 months (mean 3.2) after the final cycle in the 50 people followed up [tbody-wei2017].

frequency.text: Tested as 5 days per month for 3 months [tbody-wei2017]; no trial compared other spacing.

timing.debate: The trial authors note that lifestyle changes during follow-up may explain the persistence, and the lead developer holds a commercial interest in the diet [tbody-wei2017]; intermittent schemes generally match simple calorie restriction [tbody-allaf2021].

audit.claim: One 100-person trial showed lower weight, BP and IGF-1; the developer has a commercial interest.
audit.biases: Single research group with a commercial product; biological-age result exploratory [adiet-wei2017, adiet-brandhorst2024].
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication found in this search.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate; the conflict-of-interest caveat is the key point.

entries.headline: Age is by far the dominant, non-modifiable driver of egg quality: fecundity falls from about 32 and faster after 37, and the share of women with no chromosomally normal embryo rises from 2-6% (age 26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.

dose.effective: Not modifiable. The practical lever is time: ACOG/ASRM advise expedited evaluation after 6 months of trying from age 35, and immediate evaluation over 40.
dose.studied_range: Aneuploidy data from embryos of women aged ~22-47; egg chromosome-segregation data from ages 9-43.
dose.timeframe: Gradual decline from the early 30s, steep after ~37; no lifestyle change reverses it.
dose.notes: Lifestyle can avoid adding damage on top of age, but no diet or supplement has been shown to restore the chromosomal quality of older eggs in humans. Egg freezing at a younger age and IVF with PGT-A or donor eggs are the only interventions that address age directly.

entries.mechanism: Eggs are arrested in meiosis for decades. Cohesin that holds sister chromatids together is laid down before birth and is not renewed, so it erodes with age, causing chromosome mis-segregation (aneuploidy). In parallel, oocyte mitochondria become less efficient (less ATP, more mtDNA instability), CoQ10-synthesis enzymes and NAD+ levels decline (animal data), and spindle assembly becomes error-prone.
entries.interactions: Age magnifies almost every other harm: [tobacco-smoking] and [excess-adiposity] effects are layered on a declining baseline. Diet associations such as [mediterranean-diet] were seen only in women under 35 in one cohort. Supplements aimed at mitochondria ([coq10], [nmn-nad]) target the age mechanism but have no human live-birth proof.
entries.caveats: Aneuploidy also rises slightly in the very young (U-curve), but this is a minor effect compared with the rise after the mid-30s. Ovarian reserve tests (AMH, antral follicle count) predict egg number and response to stimulation, not egg quality; a woman with high AMH at 42 still has age-typical aneuploidy rates. Claims that any supplement 'reverses egg ageing' are not supported by human data.

key_numbers.label: Age at which fecundity starts falling

entries.title: Female age (oocyte ageing)

timing.summary: Egg ageing builds over decades and nothing reverses it: the follicle pool shrinks and chromosome cohesion, laid down before birth, decays. Embryo aneuploidy rises steadily after the mid-20s and fecundity falls faster after 37.

onset.text: Aneuploidy rises predictably after about 26 [tegg-franasiak2014]; fecundity falls from about 32 [tegg-acog2014].

full.text: Keeps growing: the share of women with no euploid embryo was 2-6% at 26-37, 33% at 42 and 53% at 44 [tegg-franasiak2014].

after_stopping.text: Irreversible; only egg freezing at a younger age stops the clock.

frequency.text: Not a dosing question.

timing.debate: Mouse studies report reversal of age-related oocyte decline with CoQ10 [tegg-benmeir2015] or NAD+ precursors [tegg-bertoldo2020]; human trials have not shown equivalent effects (CoQ10 aneuploidy trial underpowered [tegg-bentov2014]). Aneuploidy also follows a U-curve, higher in the youngest [tegg-gruhn2019].

egg.late_start: No intervention shown in humans to reverse it.
egg.text: The relevant clock is age at retrieval or freezing [tegg-cobo2016]; by 40 only about 3% of the original follicle pool remains [tegg-wallace2010].

audit.claim: Female age is the dominant driver of egg quality; women with no euploid embryo rise from 2-6% (26-37) to 33% at 42 and 53% at 44.
audit.biases: Embryo-biopsy data come from IVF patients (selection), but the age gradient is replicated in egg chromosome studies from a wide age range, so confounding is not a plausible explanation.
audit.newer_evidence: The trophectoderm-biopsy numbers are as stated [afert-franasiak2014], and direct study of egg chromosome segregation shows an age U-curve driven by cohesion loss [afert-gruhn2019].
audit.bottom_line: Nothing newer challenges this; age remains the single biggest factor in egg quality.

factors.name: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

entries.headline: A fever of 39-40 C for even 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.

dose.effective: Body temperature around 38.5-40 C for 1 day or more.
dose.studied_range: Case report: 2 days at 39-40 C followed for 79 days.
dose.timeframe: DFI up 24-36% at days 15-37, back toward baseline by about day 79; plan semen tests or ART cycles at least ~3 months after a high fever if possible.
dose.notes: Fever control with paracetamol/acetaminophen is reasonable; there is no evidence that it prevents the sperm effect.

entries.mechanism: Whole-body hyperthermia warms the testes, impairing late spermatogenesis and chromatin protamination and increasing heat-shock and apoptotic signalling.
entries.interactions: Same mechanism as [sauna]. A semen test taken within 3 months of a fever may overstate long-term problems.
entries.caveats: Evidence is mostly case reports and small series; the effect is temporary.
entries.title: Fever and acute febrile illness (including flu, COVID-19)

timing.summary: A fever of 39-40 C damages the sperm that are in meiosis and spermiogenesis at the time, so DNA damage shows in semen 2-5 weeks later and counts fall for about 2 months. Values return to normal about 2-3 months after the fever, as after COVID-19.

onset.text: DFI up 24% at day 15 and 36% at day 37 after a 2-day fever [tsperm-sergerie2007]; 36% denatured DNA 18 days after a 1-day fever [tsperm-evenson2000].

full.text: Worst DNA changes around days 18-37 after the fever [tsperm-evenson2000, tsperm-sergerie2007].

after_stopping.text: DFI fell back by days 58-79 and count was normal by day 79 [tsperm-sergerie2007]; after COVID-19, abnormal counts fell from 37% of men within a month to 6% after 2 months, with recovery estimated at about 3 months [tsperm-donders2022, tsperm-stigliani2022].

frequency.text: Each fever day during meiosis or spermiogenesis lowered later concentration by about 7-9% [tsperm-carlsen2003].

sperm.late_start: A fever in the last week before a sample mostly spares sperm already stored; a fever 2-5 weeks before hits the sperm that will be ejaculated then [tsperm-carlsen2003, tsperm-evenson2000].
sperm.text: If possible, plan semen tests or IVF/ICSI cycles about 3 months after a high fever, when the damaged cohort has passed [tsperm-sergerie2007].

timing.debate: Most COVID-19 cohorts found recovery by about 3 months [tsperm-donders2022, tsperm-stigliani2022], but one year-long cohort described slower, immune-driven recovery in some men [tsperm-depuydt2023]; the fever DNA time courses rest on single-case reports [tsperm-sergerie2007, tsperm-evenson2000].

audit.claim: A fever of 39-40 C for 2 days can raise DNA fragmentation and cut sperm count for 2-3 months before recovering.
audit.biases: Evidence is case reports and observational illness studies (the illness, medicines and weight loss travel with the fever).
audit.newer_evidence: The original case data stand [afert-sergerie2007]; a 2024 meta-analysis of COVID-19 found lower sperm concentration, count and motility during or soon after infection, mostly short-term [afert-cannarella2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds; plan semen tests or ART about 3 months after a high fever where possible.

entries.headline: Hair-loss-dose finasteride (1 mg) left semen unchanged in 181 young men, but prostate doses (finasteride 5 mg, dutasteride 0.5 mg) cut total sperm count about 30%, and subfertile men on finasteride saw counts rise on average 11.6-fold after stopping.

dose.effective: Finasteride 1 mg/day (hair loss) or 5 mg/day (prostate); dutasteride 0.5 mg/day.
dose.studied_range: Finasteride 1 mg/day for 48 weeks (RCT); finasteride 5 mg and dutasteride 0.5 mg for 1 year (RCT); mean 1 mg/day for ~57 months (subfertile men).
dose.too_much: Prostate doses and dutasteride have larger effects (semen volume -29.7% on dutasteride); men who are already oligospermic appear most vulnerable even at 1 mg.
dose.timeframe: Counts fell by 26 weeks; recovery after stopping over months (one spermatogenic cycle is ~74 days).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Men with low counts who are trying to conceive and use finasteride for hair loss can ask about pausing it; a repeat semen analysis about 3 months after stopping shows whether it was a factor.

entries.mechanism: Blocking conversion of testosterone to DHT (by 73% with finasteride 5 mg and 94% with dutasteride) reduces prostate and seminal-vesicle secretions and modestly impairs epididymal sperm maturation; testosterone itself rises slightly [med-amory2007].
entries.interactions: Unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids], 5-ARIs do not shut down LH/FSH. Often used alongside [alpha-blockers-sperm] for prostate enlargement, which adds ejaculatory problems.
entries.caveats: The dramatic recovery data come from 27 men who presented with infertility, a selected group; healthy men on 1 mg show no average change.
entries.debate: In healthy young men, 1 mg finasteride did not affect spermatogenesis [med-overstreet1999]; in subfertile men on similar doses, counts rose sharply after stopping [med-samplaski2013], suggesting a vulnerable subgroup. Prostate doses produced mild, mostly reversible falls [med-amory2007].

key_numbers.label: Total sperm count change, finasteride 5 mg (26 wk)
Total sperm count change, dutasteride (26 wk)
Average count increase after stopping (subfertile men)

entries.title: Finasteride & dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors)

timing.summary: Prostate-dose finasteride and dutasteride cut sperm counts by about a third by 6 months, with largely reversible changes. Hair-loss doses had no effect in healthy young men but some subfertile men improved dramatically after stopping.

onset.text: Total count down 29-34% at the first check, 26 weeks, with 5 mg finasteride or 0.5 mg dutasteride [tsperm-amory2007].

full.text: Largest fall at 26 weeks; smaller at 52 weeks [tsperm-amory2007].

after_stopping.text: Smaller residual differences 24 weeks after stopping [tsperm-amory2007]; in subfertile men on about 1 mg, counts rose 11.6-fold after stopping (time not given) [tsperm-samplaski2013]. One cycle of about 64 days is the minimum wait [tsperm-misell2006].

frequency.text: Daily drug; 1 mg daily for 48 weeks did not change semen in 181 healthy young men [tsperm-overstreet1999].

sperm.late_start: Stopping 2-4 weeks before is too late to change counts; recovery was assessed at 24 weeks.
sperm.text: For subfertile men with low counts, stopping about 3-6 months before trying is reasonable [tsperm-samplaski2013, tsperm-amory2007].

timing.debate: A large RCT found no semen effect of 1 mg [tsperm-overstreet1999], while a clinic series of subfertile men on about 1 mg saw counts rise 11.6-fold after stopping [tsperm-samplaski2013]; the difference may be susceptibility in already-subfertile men.

factors.name: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

entries.headline: Fisetin cleared senescent cells and extended lifespan in one mouse study, but the NIA Interventions Testing Program found no lifespan extension and no placebo-controlled senolytic trial in humans has reported results; food supplies milligrams, while trials test about 1.4 g doses.

dose.effective: None established.
dose.studied_range: Senolytic trials: 20 mg/kg/day for 2 consecutive days (about 1.4 g for a 70 kg adult), repeated intermittently; one small continuous trial used 200 mg/day for 12 weeks.
dose.too_much: High-dose human safety data are limited; flavonols alter the bioavailability of some drugs (see [quercetin]).
dose.notes: All flavonols and flavones together averaged about 17 mg/day in a Japanese diet, so eating strawberries cannot approach trial doses.

entries.mechanism: In cell and mouse models fisetin triggers apoptosis of senescent cells by disabling their anti-apoptotic defences, lowering the inflammatory SASP. Any antioxidant action in vivo is weak and short-lived.
entries.interactions: Same flavonol class as [quercetin]. The human senolytic data so far come from dasatinib plus quercetin, a drug combination, not from fisetin.
entries.caveats: The widely quoted mouse lifespan result was not reproduced by the multi-site ITP. The Mayo AFFIRM-LITE trial (started 2018) is still listed as enrolling in 2026. Senescent cells also help wound healing, so clearing them is not risk-free. The only completed RCTs are a small trial in obese men measuring adipokines and an unrelated stroke trial.

key_numbers.label: Total flavonol + flavone intake, Japanese women

entries.title: Fisetin (senolytic flavonol supplement; traces in strawberries)

timing.summary: Fisetin is promoted for 'hit-and-run' senolytic dosing: a few days of high doses to kill senescent cells, which then take weeks to reaccumulate. This schedule worked in one mouse study, failed in the NIA lifespan test, and is untested in published human outcome trials.

onset.text: In humans, unformulated fisetin gives very low plasma levels over 12 h [tnut-krishnakumar2022]; senolytic effects in humans not measured.

full.text: Not measured in humans.

after_stopping.text: The hypothesised benefit would persist for weeks because senescent cells reaccumulate slowly [tnut-kirkland2020]; not shown for fisetin in humans.

frequency.text: Mouse studies used acute or intermittent courses [tnut-yousefzadeh2018]; the NIA program found no lifespan gain with its schedule [tnut-harrison2024]; no human schedule is established.

timing.debate: Intermittent fisetin extended mouse lifespan in one lab [tnut-yousefzadeh2018] but not in the multi-site NIA Interventions Testing Program at the dose and schedule used [tnut-harrison2024].

audit.claim: Fisetin extended mouse lifespan in one lab but not in the ITP; no placebo-controlled senolytic trial has reported in humans.
audit.biases: Single-lab mouse result [anut-yousefzadeh2018] versus multi-site ITP null [anut-harrison2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Through 2026 only protocols have appeared, including a triple-blind low-dose trial on suPAR [anut-tavenier2026]; no senolytic efficacy results are published.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Flame retardants (PBDEs and organophosphate replacements)
aliases: Flame retardants and IVF / female fertility

entries.headline: Old PBDEs are fading from bodies but persist for years, and their organophosphate replacements are in almost every urine sample; PBDEs carry the best human evidence (about 3.7 IQ points per 10-fold higher prenatal exposure), while oxidative-stress and fertility links are small, inconsistent single-cohort findings.

dose.effective: Wash hands before eating and after handling electronics or foam (urinary metabolites fell by up to about half in a week); wet-mop and HEPA-vacuum to cut dust; when replacing pre-2014 sofas or foam, choose TB117-2013 products labelled flame-retardant-free (replacement lowered dust levels of all measured flame retardants). Replacing only the foam works too.
dose.studied_range: Dust TPHP/TDCIPP up to 1.8 mg/g in US homes; urinary OPFR metabolites (BDCIPP, DPHP) detected in 85-95% of people; serum PBDEs fell up to 80% between 2005 and 2016 in a Boston cohort.
dose.too_much: No validated harm threshold. PBDE IQ link is per 10-fold exposure; e-waste and older California homes (TB117 foam) had the highest exposures.
dose.timeframe: OPFR metabolites clear within days (urine reflects the last day or so); PBDE serum half-lives are about 1-4 years depending on congener.
dose.notes: Urinary OPFR metabolites vary by season (BDCIPP about 2-fold higher in summer) and between days; hand-wipe levels predict urine better than dust levels do.

entries.mechanism: PBDEs resemble thyroid hormones and lower thyroxine; in cells and animals both PBDEs and organophosphate esters raise mitochondrial ROS and lipid peroxidation. In humans, PBDE mixtures tracked higher urinary 8-isoprostane in pregnancy [eia-sehgaln2025] and OPE metabolites tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoprostane and MDA in small panels [eia-ingle2020ox, eia-li2026ope], but NHANES found no link between serum PBDEs and blood oxidative markers [eia-yuan2017].
entries.interactions: Shares the dust exposure route with [phthalates] and [pfas]; the same hand-washing and wet-cleaning steps cut several at once (see [house-dust]). Thyroid effects overlap with iodine status.
entries.caveats: Most human studies are small and cross-sectional, use a single urine sample for chemicals with hours-long half-lives, and test many metabolites against many outcomes. Phasing out commercial penta- and octa-BDE (2004 in the US) [eia-sjodin2020] replaced one problem with another class (organophosphate esters such as TDCIPP, TPHP, TCIPP) that has far less toxicity data: a textbook regrettable substitution. California's 2014 switch to a fabric smolder standard (TB117-2013) made flame-retardant-free furniture possible [eia-rodgers2021], but older furniture keeps emitting for years.
entries.debate: Fertility associations point in opposite directions: PBDEs predicted longer time to pregnancy in a low-income Californian cohort [eia-harley2010], a finding disputed in a published letter [eia-goodman2010]; follicular BDE-153 predicted failed implantation in 65 IVF patients [eia-johnson2012], yet in 215 EARTH patients serum BDE-153 predicted higher implantation and live birth [eia-ingle2020]. For organophosphate replacements, the large EARTH IVF signal [eia-carignan2017] has not been replicated in an independent IVF cohort, and semen findings range from weak and inconsistent [eia-ingle2018] to positive in Chinese clinic men [eia-li2023ope]. Oxidative-stress links are positive in small panels [eia-ingle2020ox, eia-li2026ope, eia-sehgaln2025] but null in NHANES [eia-yuan2017]. The neurodevelopment evidence is the most settled [eia-lam2017].

entries.title: Flame retardants (PBDEs and organophosphate replacements)

entries.headline: Higher dust TPHP went with 19% lower sperm concentration in 50 clinic men and PBDEs with lower motility in small studies, but the largest US fertility-clinic cohort found only weak, inconsistent links, and no study shows a sperm DNA-fragmentation effect.

dose.effective: Hand-washing before meals and wet cleaning lowered flame-retardant metabolites within a week; replace old foam furniture when practical.
dose.studied_range: Urinary OPFR metabolites in 220 EARTH men; dust TPHP and TDCPP in 50 men; serum PBDEs in 52-153 men.
dose.timeframe: Exposure during the roughly 74 days of spermatogenesis is what counts; OPFR body levels fall within days, PBDEs over years.
dose.notes: Strong co-exposure with phthalates and organophosphate pesticides; the one large Chinese "OPE" signal was driven by pesticide metabolites.

entries.mechanism: Thyroid and androgen disruption and Sertoli-cell oxidative stress in animals; in young men BDE-47 tracked motility but not sperm chromatin damage [eia-albert2018].
entries.interactions: See [flame-retardants]; overlaps with [phthalates] and [pesticides].
entries.caveats: Small samples, single urine samples, multiple metabolites and outcomes, and clinic populations. Paternal OPFRs were linked to fewer fertilized eggs and top-quality embryos in IVF, but not to live birth after adjusting for the female partner [eia-carignan2018].
entries.debate: Positive associations in small studies [eia-meeker2010, eia-abdelouahab2011, eia-yu2018] and a large Chinese clinic study [eia-li2023ope] versus weak and inconsistent results in 220 EARTH men [eia-ingle2018] and a 796-donor study where the mixture signal came from pesticide, not flame-retardant, metabolites [eia-tang2025]; borderline associations without DNA damage in healthy young men [eia-albert2018, eia-siddique2022].

key_numbers.label: Sperm concentration per IQR dust TPHP

entries.title: Flame retardants and semen quality

entries.headline: In 211 IVF patients, the highest quartile of urinary organophosphate flame-retardant metabolites went with 38% lower live birth per cycle, but this has not been independently replicated, and PBDE findings in IVF point in opposite directions.

dose.effective: Hand-washing before eating and after handling electronics, wet cleaning and HEPA vacuuming lowered urinary OPFR metabolites within a week; avoid sitting on or handling crumbling pre-2014 foam.
dose.studied_range: Summed urinary OPFR metabolites (BDCIPP, DPHP, ip-PPP) in EARTH, 2005-2015; serum and follicular PBDEs in 65-215 IVF patients.
dose.timeframe: OPFRs: body levels fall within days, so the weeks of stimulation and transfer are modifiable. PBDEs: years.
dose.notes: OPFR urinary metabolites vary by season and day; one or two samples per cycle were used.

entries.mechanism: Animal and cell data suggest endocrine disruption and impaired embryo development; human mechanisms in the ovary are unstudied.
entries.interactions: See [flame-retardants]; co-exposure with [phthalates] and [pfas] in dust.
entries.caveats: Single academic clinic; many outcomes tested; exposure measured in urine during treatment. The small Taiwanese AMH study [eia-lien2025] had very wide confidence intervals.
entries.debate: OPFRs: a large EARTH association with lower fertilization, implantation, pregnancy and live birth [eia-carignan2017] versus no replication so far and only small cross-sectional AMH data [eia-lien2025]. PBDEs: longer time to pregnancy in one cohort [eia-harley2010] disputed in a letter [eia-goodman2010]; follicular BDE-153 linked to failed implantation [eia-johnson2012] versus serum BDE-153 linked to higher implantation and live birth in a larger cohort [eia-ingle2020].

key_numbers.label: Live birth, highest vs lowest OPFR quartile

entries.title: Flame retardants and IVF / female fertility

timing.summary: Two very different clocks: organophosphate replacements leave the body within days, so their urine levels respond within a week to hand-washing and cleaning [eia-gibson2019], while old PBDEs have serum half-lives of about 1-4 years [eia-sjodin2020]. Swapping out old foam lowers house-dust levels over 6-18 months [eia-rodgers2021].

onset.text: Urinary OPFR metabolites track hand-wipe contact on the same days (moderate to high 5-day reliability, ICC 0.51-0.81) [eia-hoffman2015].

full.text: Body PBDE burden reflects years of dust exposure; it fell up to 80% across a decade after the 2004 phase-out in an IVF cohort [eia-ingle2020].

after_stopping.text: OPFR metabolites fell within one week of instructed cleaning or hand-washing [eia-gibson2019]; PBDEs halve only every 0.9-4.1 years depending on congener [eia-sjodin2020].

frequency.text: Because OPFR exposure is continuous and clears quickly, the behaviours (hand-washing before meals, regular wet cleaning) need to be habitual; one big clean-up does not last [eia-gibson2019].

sperm.late_start: Cutting OPFR intake works within days, so even 2-4 weeks of hand-washing and cleaning lowers exposure during spermiogenesis, but whether that changes semen quality is unknown.
sperm.text: Spermatogenesis takes roughly 64-74 days plus epididymal transit [eia-heller1964], so a change acts fully on sperm ejaculated about 3 months later. PBDE body stores cannot be lowered on that timescale [eia-sjodin2020].

egg.late_start: OPFR levels respond within a week [eia-gibson2019], so exposure during stimulation and transfer, where the EARTH association was measured [eia-carignan2017], is still modifiable.
egg.text: The ovulatory follicle begins its final growth about 85 days before ovulation [eia-gougeon1986]. The OPFR-IVF association used urine collected during the treatment cycle [eia-carignan2017].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the uncertainty is whether the exposures matter at all for fertility [eia-ingle2018, eia-ingle2020].

entries.headline: Fluoride above 1.5 mg/L (twice the 0.7 mg/L used in fluoridation) is consistently linked to lower child IQ (NTP 2024, moderate confidence), but whether fluoridation-level exposure lowers IQ is contested, and the dental benefit of fluoridation today is smaller than once thought (about a quarter of a decayed tooth per child).

dose.effective: If your well water exceeds 1.5 mg/L, use reverse osmosis or another source, especially in pregnancy and for infant formula. At fluoridation levels (0.7 mg/L), a cautious option during pregnancy and for formula-fed infants is to use low-fluoride water for formula; keep brushing with fluoride toothpaste (spit, don't swallow).
dose.studied_range: Drinking water 0.1 to >4 mg/L; maternal urinary fluoride 0.1-3 mg/L.
dose.too_much: WHO guideline 1.5 mg/L; fluorosis of aesthetic concern in about 12% of people at 0.7 mg/L. A pooled benchmark analysis put a possible threshold for prenatal neurotoxicity at about 0.3-0.45 mg/L in urine.
dose.timeframe: Plasma fluoride clears in hours; skeletal stores accumulate over years; neurodevelopmental sensitivity is in pregnancy and infancy.
dose.notes: Carbon pitcher filters do not remove fluoride; reverse osmosis, activated alumina or distillation do.

entries.mechanism: At high doses fluoride inhibits enzymes, induces oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in animal brain and testis; human mechanistic evidence was judged too limited by NTP [efw-ntp2024].
entries.interactions: Fluoride often co-occurs with arsenic in some groundwater ([arsenic-drinking-water]). Reverse osmosis that removes fluoride also removes nitrate, arsenic and PFAS ([water-filtration]).
entries.caveats: Most studies (64 of 74 in the main meta-analysis) are cross-sectional, mostly from endemic-fluorosis areas in China and India with co-exposures (arsenic, iodine deficiency) and poor adjustment; North American cohorts measure single urine samples in pregnancy and found sex-specific effects that differ between studies.
entries.debate: Harm at higher exposure is broadly accepted: NTP found moderate-confidence evidence above 1.5 mg/L [efw-ntp2024] and a meta-analysis found IQ 1.63 points lower per mg/L urinary fluoride [efw-taylor2025]. At fluoridation levels: Canadian and Los Angeles cohorts link maternal fluoride to lower IQ in boys and to behaviour problems [efw-green2019, efw-malin2024], and a three-cohort benchmark analysis suggests a low threshold [efw-grandjean2024]; the NTP authors defend these findings [efw-taylor2025b]. Against: an editorial urged caution because the evidence rests on high-exposure, high-risk-of-bias studies [efw-levy2025]; a meta-analysis at fluoridation levels found no IQ effect [efw-kumar2023]; the Dunedin cohort found none [efw-broadbent2015]; a Spanish cohort found better scores in boys [efw-ibarluzea2022]. Benefit: Cochrane finds only a small, uncertain contemporary caries benefit [efw-iheozorejiofor2024], while Calgary saw more decay after stopping fluoridation [efw-mclaren2022].

entries.title: Fluoride in drinking water

entries.headline: The largest male supplement trial (FAZST, 2370 couples) found folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth, and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Not recommended for male fertility.
dose.studied_range: 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg elemental zinc daily for 6 months.
dose.too_much: SDF 29.7% vs 27.2% with placebo (+2.4 points); more GI symptoms. Long-term zinc above ~40 mg/day can cause copper deficiency.
dose.timeframe: 6 months studied.
dose.notes: Correcting a genuine zinc or folate deficiency via diet is still sensible.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism and DNA methylation; zinc stabilises sperm chromatin and is an antioxidant enzyme cofactor. High doses did not help replete men.
entries.interactions: High-dose folate overlaps with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] concerns.
entries.caveats: Population was general infertility patients, not selected for deficiency.
entries.title: Folic acid + zinc

timing.summary: Six months of folic acid plus zinc did nothing for semen or live birth and slightly raised sperm DNA fragmentation. With no benefit, timing only matters for stopping.

onset.text: Semen was assessed at 6 months; no improvement, DNA fragmentation 2.4 points higher [tnut-schisterman2020].

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Not recommended for male fertility at any schedule [tnut-schisterman2020].

sperm.late_start: No benefit to gain.
sperm.text: If taken, stopping about one sperm-development cycle before trying would clear any effect on sperm DNA (extrapolated); Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: FAZST (2370 couples) found folic acid + zinc did nothing for semen or live birth and slightly raised DNA fragmentation.
audit.biases: Large, well-run RCT with live birth as outcome [anut-schisterman2020]; population not selected for deficiency.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 50 studies found no supplement, including zinc and folate, improved pregnancy or live birth in men [anut-michaelsen2025].
audit.bottom_line: Still the best-quality null result in male fertility supplements.

entries.headline: Folic acid is mandatory preconception care (400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects) and is also consistently associated with better fertility: 15% higher fecundability and 20 percentage points higher IVF live birth at > 800 ug/day supplemental folate.

dose.effective: 400-800 ug/day folic acid, started before conception (ideally 3 months ahead) and continued through early pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Supplemental folate < 400 to > 800 ug/day (cohorts).
dose.too_much: Higher doses only on a clinician's advice for specific indications.
dose.timeframe: Before conception for neural tube protection; 3 months covers follicle development.
dose.notes: Usually taken as a prenatal multivitamin. Diet folate (leafy greens, legumes) is good but does not replace the supplement.

entries.mechanism: Folate supports one-carbon metabolism: DNA synthesis and repair, methylation and homocysteine clearance. Elevated homocysteine in follicular fluid is linked to poorer embryo quality.
entries.interactions: Core of [profertility-diet]; may buffer the [outdoor-air-pollution] association in one cohort.
entries.caveats: Fertility benefits are observational; the neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reason enough to take it.
entries.title: Folic acid / folate

timing.summary: Plasma folate rises within weeks and plateaus at 3 months, but red-cell folate, the marker linked to neural tube protection, takes a median 36 weeks to reach steady state. The neural tube closes 22-26 days after fertilisation, so folic acid must be on board before conception, ideally months before.

onset.text: Plasma folate rises within the first month [tegg-hao2008].

full.text: Plasma folate plateaus at 3 months [tegg-hao2008]; RBC folate steady state median 36 weeks (27-52) [tegg-crider2019].

after_stopping.text: Blood folate falls rapidly within 3 months of stopping, faster after higher doses [tegg-hao2008].

frequency.text: Daily: single and split doses gave the same blood levels, but 4 mg once weekly raised plasma folate far less than 0.4 mg daily (142% vs 259%) [tegg-hao2008].

timing.debate: Agreement that folic acid must start before conception [tegg-uspstf2023]; the optimal lead time differs by outcome, about 1.1 months for non-cardiac malformations versus 2.2 months for heart defects [tegg-dong2023], while red-cell kinetics argue for longer [tegg-crider2019]. Fertility associations (fecundability, IVF) are observational [tegg-cueto2016, tegg-gaskins2014].

egg.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks before conception still raises plasma folate before the neural tube closes, but RBC folate will be far from steady state [tegg-crider2019].
egg.text: The lowest malformation risk was with folic acid started about 1.5 months (1.1-1.9) before conception and continued about 4 months [tegg-dong2023]; IVF live birth was higher with >800 ug/day supplemental folate [tegg-gaskins2014].

audit.claim: Folic acid 400-800 ug/day prevents neural tube defects and is consistently associated with better fertility (15% higher fecundability, +20 points IVF live birth at >800 ug/day).
audit.biases: Fertility associations are observational and prone to healthy-user bias (supplement users plan pregnancies and have healthier habits).
audit.newer_evidence: The neural-tube benefit is RCT-proven and reaffirmed by USPSTF 2023 [afert-uspstf2023]. The only randomised fertility data come from the Hungarian periconceptional multivitamin trial (0.8 mg folic acid), which found more conceptions and more multiple births [afert-czeizel1994]. The EARTH IVF association remains a single cohort [afert-gaskins2014]. In men, folic acid plus zinc did not improve live birth (FAZST) [afert-schisterman2020].
audit.bottom_line: Take it for neural tube protection; any fertility gain is plausible but not proven and should not be presented as established.

entries.headline: Perfume use roughly triples urinary monoethyl phthalate (from the fragrance fixative diethyl phthalate) and synthetic musks like galaxolide build up in blood and breast milk of users; the clearly proven harm is contact allergy (about 2% of Europeans), while endocrine effects of musks are weak and mostly in vitro.

dose.effective: Choose 'fragrance-free' leave-on products ('unscented' can still contain masking fragrance); if you wear perfume, spray clothes rather than large skin areas; avoid air fresheners and ventilate after cleaning with scented products, especially on high-ozone afternoons. Labelled-free products cut urinary MEP by 27% in 3 days.
dose.studied_range: Perfume, deodorant and lotion use within 6-24 h before urine collection; blood musk levels up to 4,100 ng/L (galaxolide).
dose.too_much: No systemic harm threshold known. For allergy, the EU requires about 80 fragrance allergens to be named above 0.001% in leave-on and 0.01% in rinse-off products (transition to 2026-2028); the US fragrance-allergen labelling rule required by MoCRA has not been issued.
dose.timeframe: MEP rises within hours of use and falls within days; lipophilic musks persist longer (half-life not well measured).
dose.notes: 'Fragrance' on a label can hide dozens of undisclosed chemicals; many detected chemicals were not on labels in product testing.

entries.mechanism: Diethyl phthalate, used to fix fragrance, is metabolised to MEP, which tracked higher urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane in pregnancy alongside other phthalates [epc-ferguson2015]. Polycyclic musks are very weakly estrogenic but anti-estrogenic, anti-androgenic and anti-progestagenic in cell assays [epc-vanderburg2008]. Terpene fragrances react with indoor ozone to form formaldehyde and fine particles for hours [epc-carslaw2022].
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [phthalates] (diethyl phthalate) and [indoor-combustion-smoke]-type indoor air quality; see [clean-beauty-labels] and [parabens].
entries.caveats: Survey reports that a third of adults get symptoms from fragranced products are self-reported online data [epc-steinemann2016]. Nitro musks have been largely replaced and blood levels fell versus the 1990s [epc-hutter2009]. Breast-milk musk intake by infants is lower than for legacy pollutants such as PCBs [epc-reiner2007].
entries.debate: Some researchers call fragranced products a primary indoor pollutant with broad health effects [epc-steinemann2016]; general-population patch testing finds clinically relevant fragrance allergy in about 0.8-1.9% [epc-diepgen2015]. Reviews of musks range from 'no evidence for substantial human risk' [epc-kafferlein1998] to calls for epidemiology given animal and cell signals [epc-taylor2014]. Older women carry higher musk levels, possibly from more skin-cream use [epc-hutter2010].

entries.title: Fragrance chemicals and synthetic musks

timing.summary: The phthalate part of fragrance (diethyl phthalate) clears within days, but lipophilic synthetic musks accumulate in blood and fat, and levels were higher in older women. Musk half-lives in people have not been measured well.

onset.text: Urinary MEP rose sharply with cologne or perfume use within 6 h of collection [epc-nassan2017].

full.text: Musks keep accumulating with long-term use; older women had higher plasma musks than younger women [epc-hutter2010]. Time course not measured.

after_stopping.text: MEP fell 22-27% within 3-5 days of switching products [epc-harley2016, epc-jovanovic2026]; musk washout not measured.

frequency.text: Less frequent and less skin-area use of fragranced leave-on products lowers both MEP and musk exposure; no schedule has been tested.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps sperm fresher: each extra day of abstinence adds about 0.65 points of SDF, and a second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 35% to 24%.

dose.effective: Ejaculate (intercourse or otherwise) every 1-2 days through the fertile window and beyond. For ART with high SDF, ask about a sample after 1 day or a second sample 1-4 hours after a first ejaculation.
dose.studied_range: Abstinence from 1-4 hours to 7+ days; 2-day cut-off in RCT meta-analysis.
dose.too_much: Volume and total count fall with very frequent ejaculation, but for natural conception daily intercourse is not harmful.
dose.timeframe: Immediate: works on the next ejaculate.
dose.notes: Diagnostic labs usually specify 2-7 days of abstinence and SDF guidelines suggest 2-5 days before a test; follow the lab's instructions when testing, and use short abstinence for conception attempts and ART samples.

entries.mechanism: Shortens the time sperm sit in the epididymis, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS and stored sperm accumulate oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Cheapest and fastest lever; a non-invasive alternative to [testicular-sperm-icsi]. Works alongside slower changes that act on sperm production.
entries.caveats: One large meta-analysis of risk factors found no significant abstinence effect, and absolute reductions in healthy men are small (about 2-3 points). The biggest drops are in men with high baseline SDF or abnormal semen.

key_numbers.label: SDF increase per extra day of abstinence
SDF in second sample 3 h later

entries.title: Frequent ejaculation (short abstinence, 1-2 days)

timing.summary: Shortening the time sperm sit in storage lowers DNA fragmentation within hours to a day, because damage accumulates after sperm leave the testis. The benefit is lost again as abstinence lengthens.

onset.text: A second sample 3 hours after the first cut SDF from 34.6% to 23.7% [tsperm-dahan2021]; 1-day abstinence normalised high SDF in 91% of men [tsperm-pons2013].

full.text: Immediate; the next ejaculate benefits [tsperm-gosalvez2011, tsperm-pons2013].

after_stopping.text: SDF rises about 0.65 points per extra day of abstinence [tsperm-logiudice2024]; IUI pregnancy fell beyond about day 3 [tsperm-du2024].

frequency.text: Ejaculation every 1-2 days keeps storage short; for an ART sample, 1 day of abstinence (or a second sample after 1-4 hours) [tsperm-pons2013, tsperm-barbagallo2022]. Very short abstinence lowers volume and count [tsperm-du2024].

sperm.late_start: This is the main intervention that works fully in the final days: up to three 1-day-abstinence samples normalised SDF [tsperm-pons2013].
sperm.text: Acts on the epididymal storage window, not on sperm production.

timing.debate: Meta-analyses of short-abstinence studies find lower SDF [tsperm-logiudice2024, tsperm-du2024], but a broader SDF risk-factor meta-analysis found no significant effect of abstinence period [tsperm-szabo2023], and the benefit is clearest in men with abnormal semen [tsperm-barbagallo2022]; pregnancy data are mostly retrospective [tsperm-gupta2021].

audit.claim: Ejaculating every 1-2 days keeps SDF lower; a second sample 3 hours later cut SDF from 35% to 24%.
audit.biases: Most data are within-man before-after comparisons (regression to the mean when men are selected for high SDF) and small ART studies.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 dose-response meta-analysis of 85 studies found short abstinence lowered DFI modestly in healthy men (-2.4 points) [afert-du2024], and a 2023 meta-analysis linked a second ejaculate within 4 hours to higher ART live birth [afert-barbagallo2023]. The 2023 risk-factor meta-analysis found no significant SDF difference by abstinence period [afert-szabo2023].
audit.bottom_line: Short abstinence is cheap and probably helpful, with small average effects.

entries.headline: Doubling produce from 5.8 to 12 servings/day for 2 weeks reduced lymphocyte 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes, but another controlled trial found 600 g/day had no effect on oxidative DNA damage in healthy non-smokers; cohorts show lower mortality with more produce, but a 2021 analysis of 26 cohorts found the benefit levels off at about 5 servings/day [adiet-wang2021] (an earlier meta-analysis put the plateau near 800 g/day).

dose.effective: At least 5 servings (400-500 g)/day from diverse botanical families; benefit above ~5 servings is uncertain.
dose.studied_range: 600 g/day for 24 days; 12 servings/day for 14 days.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Diversity across plant families mattered in the positive trial; benefit was larger in people with low baseline carotenoids.

entries.mechanism: Many compounds acting through different routes (Nrf2 electrophiles, gut metabolites, vitamin C/carotenoids, nitrate, fiber, potassium).
entries.interactions: The null Danish trial suggests healthy people with adequate defences may already be near a ceiling for oxidative DNA damage.
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials conflict; cohort benefits may partly reflect healthier lifestyles.

entries.title: High fruit and vegetable intake

entries.headline: Low-pesticide fruit and vegetables (2.8+ servings a day) are linked to much higher sperm counts; high-residue produce is not.

dose.effective: At least 3 servings/day; wash produce and favour lower-residue choices.
dose.studied_range: <1.1 to >=2.8 servings/day of low-to-moderate-residue produce.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Benefit is likely part of the overall dietary pattern.

entries.mechanism: Food-level vitamin C, folate, carotenoids and polyphenols support seminal antioxidant defences without the megadoses that cause reductive stress.
entries.interactions: See [pesticides] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Total fruit and vegetable intake was unrelated to semen in the same study; the finding depended on pesticide residue classification.

key_numbers.label: Higher total count, >=2.8 servings/day low-residue produce

entries.title: Fruit and vegetables

timing.summary: Doubling produce intake lowered oxidative DNA and lipid damage markers within 2 weeks in one trial, but 600 g a day for 24 days did nothing in healthy nonsmokers. Disease benefits in cohorts reflect years of intake.

onset.text: Lymphocyte and urinary 8-OHdG and urinary isoprostanes fell after 14 days at 12 servings/day [tfood-thompson1999].

full.text: Mortality associations reflect long-term intake up to ~800 g/day [tfood-aune2017]; no trial mapped the plateau.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; 24 days of complete produce depletion did not raise oxidative DNA damage either [tfood-moller2003].

frequency.text: Benefits are associated with habitual daily intake [tfood-aune2017].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: High-pesticide-residue produce was associated with lower sperm count in semen collected up to 18 months after diet assessment [tfood-chiu2015]. Sperm take about 64 days (range 42-76) from labelled precursor to ejaculate [tfood-misell2006], and the classic ~74-day estimate is uncertain by about a week [tfood-amann2008], so a diet change needs roughly 2.5-3 months to reach every stage of the sperm in a given ejaculate.

timing.debate: Short-term trials disagree: 14 days of doubled produce lowered oxidative markers [tfood-thompson1999], while 24 days of 600 g/day did not [tfood-moller2003].

audit.claim: Doubling produce lowered some oxidative markers but another trial was null; cohorts show lower mortality up to ~800 g/day; low-pesticide produce linked to higher sperm counts.
audit.biases: Produce intake marks wealth, education, non-smoking and exercise (healthy-user, residual confounding); FFQ measurement error is large [adiet-trepanowski2018, adiet-satija2015]. The sperm finding depends on a pesticide-residue classification in one cross-sectional study [adiet-chiu2016].
audit.newer_evidence: The largest dose-response analysis (2021, 1.9 million people) found mortality benefit plateaued at about 5 servings/day (~400 g), with no extra benefit above that and none from starchy vegetables or juice [adiet-wang2021], lower than the ~800 g in the 2017 analysis [adiet-aune2017]. The oxidative-marker trials remain split [adiet-moller2003].
audit.bottom_line: Eating about 5 servings a day is well supported; benefits beyond that are uncertain and some of the cohort association is likely confounding.

factors.name: G6PD deficiency (oxidant drug and fava bean sensitivity)

entries.headline: An X-linked enzyme defect carried by roughly 400-500 million people; carriers are usually well but can hemolyze after fava beans, high-risk drugs (dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, methylene blue) or very high IV vitamin C, so knowing your status changes what you must avoid.

dose.effective: One G6PD activity test (or genotype) before high-risk drugs or IV vitamin C infusions, especially with African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Asian ancestry. If deficient: avoid fava beans and CPIC high-risk drugs.
dose.studied_range: CPIC 2022 classification of drugs by systematic review: high risk (dapsone, methylene blue, pegloticase, primaquine, rasburicase, tafenoquine, toluidine blue), medium (nitrofurantoin), low-to-no risk (vitamin C at standard doses, vitamin K, many sulfonamides).
dose.too_much: Very high-dose IV vitamin C (gram-level infusions) can trigger hemolysis in deficient people; methylene blue, sometimes sold as a 'mitochondrial' or nootropic supplement, is classed high risk.
dose.timeframe: Hemolysis typically starts within 1-3 days of the trigger and resolves after it is removed.
dose.notes: Activity tests can read falsely normal during or right after a hemolytic episode; heterozygous women may have intermediate activity and still hemolyze.

entries.mechanism: G6PD makes NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway; NADPH keeps glutathione reduced. Red cells have no other NADPH source, so oxidant drugs, fava-bean glycosides (vicine, convicine) or infection-related oxidants overwhelm glutathione, oxidize hemoglobin into Heinz bodies and destroy the cells.
entries.interactions: Pro-oxidant effects of megadose vitamin C (see [vitamin-c-supplement]) and of high-dose antioxidant stacks ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]) matter here because ascorbate can act as an oxidant in the presence of iron and oxygen. Infections ([febrile-illness]) are themselves triggers.
entries.caveats: Most carriers are lifelong asymptomatic; this is about avoiding specific triggers, not about general oxidative stress. Ordinary dietary antioxidants and standard-dose vitamin C are not a concern.
entries.debate: Regulatory warnings conflict and evidence for many listed drugs is sparse; CPIC authors disagreed about the strength of the nitrofurantoin evidence [tst-gammal2023], while older reviews list a broader range of triggers [tst-cappellini2008]. CPIC classes standard-dose vitamin C as low-to-no risk [tst-gammal2023], but a systematic review of IV vitamin C flags hemolysis at very high doses and supports pre-infusion G6PD testing [tst-alangari2026].
entries.title: G6PD deficiency (oxidant drug and fava bean sensitivity)

entries.headline: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in hypertensives (about -8.7/-6.1 mmHg) and a meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs reports lower MDA and higher antioxidant enzymes, but these markers are weak and the trials low quality.

dose.effective: Culinary: 1-2 cloves/day crushed and left 10 min before cooking; supplement trials used aged garlic extract or powder.
dose.studied_range: 80-4000 mg/day garlic preparations for 2-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Supplements can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Red onions are a major dietary source of quercetin (onion chromatography total ~140 mg/100 g in Phenol-Explorer).

entries.mechanism: Organosulfur compounds (allicin breakdown products, S-allylcysteine) activate Nrf2 and raise hydrogen sulfide signalling; onion quercetin.
entries.interactions: Another mild Nrf2 inducer; much weaker than sulforaphane.
entries.caveats: TAC and TBARS-type MDA are non-specific oxidative markers; effect sizes in the meta-analysis (Hedges' g up to 13.8) are implausibly large, a sign of small heterogeneous studies.
