entries.title: Garlic and onions

timing.summary: Garlic supplements lower blood pressure in trials lasting weeks, and cholesterol effects needed more than 2 months. Persistence after stopping is not known.

onset.text: BP lowering in trials of a few weeks or more [tfood-ried2016].

full.text: Cholesterol lowering required more than 2 months of intake [tfood-ried2016].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Trials gave garlic daily [tfood-ried2016].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Garlic supplements lower BP in hypertensives; oxidative-marker meta-analysis is weak.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials with implausibly large effect sizes on oxidative markers [adiet-askari2021].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found [adiet-ried2016].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Gas burners raise indoor NO2 and emit benzene (2.8-6.5 ug per minute, 10-25 times electric); gas cooking is linked to about 30% higher odds of childhood asthma, and removing indoor gas combustion cut asthma symptoms in randomized heater trials, but the size of the stove effect is fiercely contested.

dose.effective: Switching to induction or electric removes the source (kitchen NO2 -51% at 3 months in a randomized trial; 21 to 6 ppb in an asthma before-after study). Otherwise: use a range hood that vents outdoors on high, cook on back burners, open a window, and use a HEPA-plus-activated-carbon purifier (NO2 -27%). Never use a gas oven or burners to heat the home.
dose.studied_range: NO2 emissions about 7.8 ng/J; US stoves add about 4 ppb to long-term NO2 on average; benzene from burners 2.8-6.5 ug/min; leaking idle stoves also release benzene.
dose.too_much: WHO 2021 annual NO2 guideline is 10 ug/m3 (about 5.3 ppb); gas stoves alone add about 75% of that on average and can exceed the 1-h US standard (100 ppb) within minutes in small, unventilated kitchens.
dose.timeframe: Indoor NO2 falls within a week of swapping the stove; asthma control improved within 2-3 months in an uncontrolled study.
dose.notes: Exposure is four times higher in homes under 800 ft2 than over 3000 ft2. A hood that recirculates rather than vents outside does little for NO2.

entries.mechanism: NO2 is a free-radical gas that oxidizes airway-lining lipids and antioxidants and drives airway inflammation; benzene is a haematotoxic carcinogen metabolized to quinones that redox-cycle. In 144 COPD patients, low indoor NO2 (median 6.8 ppb) did not track urinary 8-OHdG or MDA [eia-mchugh2023], so systemic oxidative-stress effects at typical levels are unproven.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [indoor-combustion-smoke] (which also covers wood); a carbon-filter purifier ([hepa-air-purifier]) helps, a plain HEPA unit does not remove NO2. Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) is the cheap partial fix.
entries.caveats: Most stove-asthma studies are cross-sectional with self-reported exposure, and gas-stove homes differ in income, housing size, crowding and damp. The 12.7% attributable-fraction figure assumes causality. The 2026 stove-swap study had no control group, so regression to the mean and seasonal change could explain part of the improvement. Industry-funded reviews reach conclusions opposite to the independent emission and epidemiology studies (see debate).
entries.debate: One side: a meta-analysis of 41 studies found OR 1.32 for gas cooking and childhood asthma with no publication bias [eia-lin2013], used to estimate that 12.7% of US childhood asthma is attributable to gas stoves [eia-gruenwald2022], and emissions work shows NO2 and benzene at levels above health benchmarks [eia-lebel2022, eia-kashtan2023, eia-kashtan2024]. The other side: a systematic review by a consultancy that has worked for gas-industry clients judged the literature too weak and biased for causal conclusions [eia-li2023gas], an American Gas Association-funded commentary rejected the attributable fraction [eia-li2024gas], an independent commentary called it an example of questionable research practices [eia-cox2023], and the 47-country ISAAC analysis did not find a clear gas-cooking association [eia-wong2013]. The most causal evidence comes from removing unflued gas heaters, not stoves [eia-pilotto2004, eia-howdenchapman2008].

entries.title: Gas and propane stoves (NO2, benzene)

timing.summary: NO2 peaks within minutes of lighting a burner [eia-lebel2022] and benzene lingers in bedrooms for hours after the stove is off [eia-kashtan2023]. Replacing the stove lowers indoor NO2 at once and kept it 51% lower at 3 months [eia-paulin2014]; asthma control improved over 2-3 months [eia-sehgal2026].

onset.text: Kitchens without ventilation can exceed the 1-h NO2 standard within a few minutes of cooking [eia-lebel2022].

full.text: Asthma control and NO2 were reassessed 2-3 months after electric stoves were installed [eia-sehgal2026]; removing unflued school heaters reduced symptoms within one 12-week winter [eia-pilotto2004].

after_stopping.text: Benzene stayed elevated for hours after the stove was turned off [eia-kashtan2023]; nothing accumulates in the body, so the exposure ends with the source.

frequency.text: Dose follows each cooking session; extraction must run every time and continue for a while afterwards because benzene lingers [eia-kashtan2023]. A non-venting hood did not lower NO2 [eia-paulin2014].

timing.debate: The before-after stove-swap timing has no control group, so seasonal change could explain part of the 2-3-month improvement [eia-sehgal2026]; randomized heater-removal trials support a within-winter effect [eia-pilotto2004, eia-howdenchapman2008].

entries.headline: Active infection and white cells in semen are linked to higher ROS and SDF; one uncontrolled study saw SDF fall by a third after antibiotics, but the only RCT found leukocytospermia often resolves without them.

dose.effective: Leukocytospermia is defined as >=1 million white cells/mL; even 0.2-1 million/mL has been linked to higher ROS and SDF.
dose.studied_range: Antibiotic courses guided by culture/PCR; follow-up about 4 months.
dose.timeframe: In one study SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after ~3.8 months of treatment; pregnancy rates were higher in couples who tried after rather than during treatment.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: if round cells exceed 1 million/mL, distinguish white cells from immature germ cells before treating. Treat confirmed infection; do not give empiric antibiotics for every abnormal semen test.

entries.mechanism: Activated neutrophils and macrophages produce superoxide via NADPH oxidase (NOX2) at rates far above sperm, overwhelming seminal antioxidants and attacking sperm membranes and DNA.
entries.interactions: [febrile-illness] from the same infection adds thermal damage. Antioxidants are not a substitute for treating infection.
entries.caveats: A large meta-analysis found overall effects of Chlamydia and HPV on SDF negligible, so the strongest data are from symptomatic or culture-positive cases. Evidence comes from small observational studies.
entries.title: Genital tract infection and leukocytospermia

timing.summary: Chlamydia or Mycoplasma infection triples sperm DNA fragmentation, and antibiotic treatment lowered it by about a third over a few months. Couples who tried after finishing treatment did much better than those who tried during it.

onset.text: Not timed.

full.text: SDF fell from 37.7% to 24.2% after 3.8 +/- 2.2 months of antibiotic treatment [tsperm-gallegos2008].

after_stopping.text: Not applicable to treatment; reinfection would restart the damage.

frequency.text: A prescribed antibiotic course; no schedule comparisons.

sperm.late_start: Treating late still reduces white-cell ROS on stored sperm, but in the one cohort pregnancy was 12.5% during treatment versus 85.7% after it [tsperm-gallegos2008].
sperm.text: Infection-related ROS acts mainly in the genital tract after the testis, but measured SDF improvement took about 2-6 months [tsperm-gallegos2008].

timing.debate: A large meta-analysis found the overall SDF effect of Chlamydia negligible [tsperm-szabo2023], unlike the threefold rise in one clinic cohort [tsperm-gallegos2008].

audit.claim: Active infection and white cells in semen raise ROS and SDF; treating a proven infection can lower SDF by about a third.
audit.biases: The 'one third' fall comes from an uncontrolled before-after study [afert-gallegos2008]: men are selected for high SDF and abnormal tests, so some fall is expected from regression to the mean and spontaneous resolution.
audit.newer_evidence: The only RCT of antibiotics for leukocytospermia found frequent spontaneous resolution and no benefit of doxycycline or co-trimoxazole over no treatment [afert-yanushpolsky1995]. The 2023 SDF meta-analysis found Chlamydia and HPV effects on SDF negligible overall [afert-szabo2023].
audit.bottom_line: Treat a confirmed infection for its own sake, but do not expect a reliable SDF drop; leukocytes alone often clear without antibiotics.

factors.name: GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide)
aliases: GLP-1 drugs before conception (PCOS, contraception, washout)

entries.headline: Semaglutide and tirzepatide cut body weight by about 15-21% in 68-72-week trials, semaglutide cut major cardiovascular events by 20% in people with heart disease and overweight (SELECT), and they lower CRP, but roughly a quarter to a third of weight lost is lean mass unless resistance training is added.

dose.effective: Semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly (obesity dose); tirzepatide 5, 10 or 15 mg once weekly, reached by gradual dose escalation.
dose.studied_range: Semaglutide 2.4 mg/week for 68 weeks (STEP 1); tirzepatide 5-15 mg/week for 72 weeks (SURMOUNT-1); liraglutide 1.2-3 mg/day in older and fertility studies.
dose.too_much: Lean mass made up about 35% of weight lost on semaglutide and 25% on tirzepatide; older or frail people risk sarcopenia. GI side effects are the main reason for stopping (4.5% vs 0.8% on placebo for semaglutide).
dose.timeframe: Weight and inflammatory markers fall over months, with weight plateauing around 1-1.5 years; in STEP 4, switching to placebo after 20 weeks regained 6.9% of body weight by week 68.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. To protect muscle, pair the drug with resistance training (lean-mass share fell to ~17.5% with lifestyle plus resistance training) and adequate protein. Women: see the egg entry for contraception and the label's 2-month semaglutide washout before trying to conceive.

entries.mechanism: Most of the redox benefit likely comes from losing visceral fat, which lowers adipose NADPH oxidase activity, inflammatory cytokines and insulin resistance; GLP-1 receptor signalling may also have direct anti-inflammatory effects. In a 40-RCT meta-analysis the CRP fall tracked blood-pressure and insulin-resistance improvement rather than HbA1c [med-bray2021]. The drugs slow gastric emptying, which is why they can change absorption of oral medicines [med-fda-zepbound2023].
entries.interactions: Delivers the benefits of [weight-loss] in people with [excess-adiposity]; improves [glycemic-control]. Combine with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean-mass loss. Alternative or add-on to [metformin] in [pcos]. In obese men with low testosterone it raised testosterone and preserved sperm, unlike [testosterone-anabolic-steroids]. Very-low-calorie intake on these drugs overlaps with [calorie-restriction].
entries.caveats: The MDA (lipid peroxidation) result rests on only 3 trials in the 2026 meta-analysis; IL-6 and TNF-alpha effects were not significant. Weight is regained after stopping (STEP 4). Long-term data on muscle function and bone in younger people are limited. Supply via compounded or unregulated products is outside the evidence base.
entries.debate: Inflammation/oxidative stress: one meta-analysis calls the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant evidence strong [med-bray2021], while a 2026 update finds consistent CRP and adiponectin effects but variable IL-6/TNF-alpha and a thin MDA evidence base [med-kanbay2026]. Lean mass: reviewers argue the loss is proportional and adaptive, with better muscle quality [med-neeland2024], and a 2026 meta-analysis found the lean-mass share similar to diet-based weight loss [med-eisa2026]; another 2026 systematic review found muscle-related losses exceeded prespecified benchmarks in about two thirds of incretin trials [med-batsis2026]. Sperm: a small RCT found GLP-1 treatment maintained diet-induced sperm-count gains [med-andersen2022] and semaglutide improved morphology in hypogonadal diabetic men [med-gregoric2025], but systematic reviews note no change in healthy men and too few trials to judge [med-deameh2026, med-peel2026].

entries.title: GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide, tirzepatide)

entries.headline: In PCOS with obesity GLP-1 drugs add modest weight loss (BMI -1.4 kg/m2 in 11 RCTs) but a fertility benefit is unproven; tirzepatide cut oral-contraceptive peak levels by 59%, and the semaglutide label says stop at least 2 months before trying to conceive.

dose.effective: Semaglutide or liraglutide in PCOS trials, usually 12-26 weeks before ovulation induction or IVF, followed by a drug-free gap.
dose.studied_range: Liraglutide 1.2 mg/day with metformin for 12 weeks then a 4-week washout before IVF (pilot RCT); 11 RCTs of GLP-1 add-on in PCOS.
dose.too_much: Continuing into pregnancy: the labels warn of possible fetal harm (from animal data) and human data on continued use are limited. Oral contraceptives may fail during tirzepatide start-up and dose escalation.
dose.timeframe: Semaglutide: discontinue >=2 months before a planned pregnancy (label). Tirzepatide: use non-oral or back-up contraception for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (label).
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan the washout and contraception with the prescriber; weight loss itself can restore ovulation, so unplanned pregnancies occur. Stop the drug and inform the prescriber if pregnancy is found.

entries.mechanism: Weight loss and lower insulin reduce ovarian androgen excess and can restore ovulation; GLP-1 receptors are also present in reproductive tissues. Delayed gastric emptying lowers and delays absorption of oral contraceptive hormones, most with tirzepatide after the first doses [med-fda-zepbound2023, med-skelley2024].
entries.interactions: An option alongside [metformin] and lifestyle in [pcos] and [excess-adiposity]; produces [weight-loss]. St John's wort is another cause of oral-contraceptive failure ([supplement-drug-interactions]). Folic acid ([folic-acid]) should start before the washout ends.
entries.caveats: Fertility trials are small, short and mostly use liraglutide; there are no large trials of semaglutide or tirzepatide with live birth as the outcome.
entries.debate: Benefit: a pilot RCT found higher IVF pregnancy rates with liraglutide plus metformin than metformin alone despite similar weight loss [med-salamun2018], and GLP-1 agonists beat metformin for weight and insulin sensitivity in PCOS [med-han2019]; but the 2026 guideline-informing meta-analysis found only modest weight loss and insufficient evidence for reproductive outcomes [med-forslund2026]. Safety: large cohorts found no excess malformations versus insulin [med-cesta2024] and no consistent safety signal [med-ozbek2026], with preterm-birth signals confined to women with diabetes [med-hviid2026]; an AJOG review argues malformation data cannot be trusted without glycaemic-control data and recommends contraception for all users [med-drummond2025].

Ethinyl estradiol Cmax fall after tirzepatide 5 mg

entries.title: GLP-1 drugs before conception (PCOS, contraception, washout)

timing.summary: GLP-1 drugs act over months on weight, and the weight comes back after stopping. Semaglutide has a one-week half-life and lingers 5-7 weeks, so the label says stop at least 2 months before trying to conceive; tirzepatide also cuts oral-contraceptive levels for 4 weeks after each dose step.

onset.text: Weight falls progressively through the 16-week dose escalation and beyond [tegg-wilding2022]; onset not reported separately.

full.text: Weight loss continued to week 68 in STEP 1 (17.3%) [tegg-wilding2022].

after_stopping.text: Semaglutide stays in circulation 5-7 weeks after the last dose [tegg-fda-wegovy2021]; two-thirds of lost weight returned within a year [tegg-wilding2022].

frequency.text: Once-weekly injection; tirzepatide reaches steady state after 4 weeks [tegg-fda-zepbound2023].

timing.debate: The washout rule rests on animal data and pharmacokinetics; large cohorts found no rise in malformations after periconceptional exposure (aRR 0.95 vs insulin) [tegg-cesta2024] and no consistent harm signal [tegg-ozbek2026], and preterm-birth links were confined to women with diabetes [tegg-hviid2026]. Fertility benefit beyond weight loss is unproven; the positive pilot had 28 women [tegg-salamun2018].

egg.late_start: Stopping 2-4 weeks before conception leaves meaningful drug in circulation into early pregnancy (half-life about 1 week) [tegg-fda-wegovy2021].
egg.text: Stop semaglutide at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy [tegg-fda-wegovy2021]; a pilot IVF trial used 12 weeks of liraglutide followed by a 4-week drug-free gap [tegg-salamun2018].

audit.claim: Semaglutide and tirzepatide cut weight by 15-21% and lower CRP and MDA, with lean-mass loss unless resistance training is added.
audit.biases: RCT evidence; main concerns are industry funding and surrogate outcomes for the redox claims.
audit.newer_evidence: Beyond weight [abody-wilding2021], SELECT (17,604 people with CVD and overweight, no diabetes) showed 20% fewer major cardiovascular events (HR 0.80), with twice as many stopping for adverse events (16.6% vs 8.2%) [abody-lincoff2023].
audit.bottom_line: The case for GLP-1 drugs now includes hard cardiovascular outcomes, not only weight and markers; the MDA evidence remains thin.

entries.headline: 3 g of glycine at bedtime reduced next-day fatigue in small sleep-restriction studies, and a high-glycine diet extended mouse lifespan by only 4-6%; there are no human aging-outcome trials.

dose.effective: 3 g taken about an hour before bed (sleep studies)
dose.studied_range: 3 g/night in sleep studies; about 100 mg/kg/day (about 7 g at 70 kg) as part of GlyNAC; 8% of diet in mice
dose.too_much: Well tolerated at gram doses in trials; long-term safety of multi-gram daily use has not been formally assessed
dose.timeframe: Sleep effects measured over 1-3 nights
dose.notes: Glycine is abundant in collagen and gelatin. For glutathione support, see [glynac].

entries.mechanism: Glycine is one of the three amino acids of glutathione, and red-cell glycine is low in older adults. In rats it promotes sleep by acting on NMDA receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, widening skin blood vessels and lowering core temperature. In mice it may also offset methionine excess, which is one proposed reason the ITP glycine diet extended life.
entries.interactions: Combined with [n-acetylcysteine] it forms [glynac]. Any glutathione effect is likely limited to people with low baseline status.
entries.caveats: Sleep data come from small, short studies, mostly from one research group. The mouse lifespan effect was small and the dose (8% of the diet) is not comparable to supplement use.
entries.debate: The ITP glycine result is one of the more rigorous mouse lifespan studies (three sites, both sexes) but the effect was small [lon-miller2019]. Human sleep evidence is a few small trials from one group [lon-bannai2012] with a rat mechanism [lon-kawai2015]; no independent replication or critique was found, which reflects how little the question has been studied.
entries.title: Glycine

timing.summary: Glycine is taken about an hour before bed and its measured effect is on the next day's fatigue. Nothing suggests it builds up or carries over.

onset.text: 3 g at bedtime reduced fatigue the next day during 3 nights of sleep restriction [tnut-bannai2012].

full.text: Effect present from the first nights [tnut-bannai2012].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; extrapolated to wear off within a day.

frequency.text: Used on the nights it is needed; no evidence that daily use builds benefit [tnut-bannai2012].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: 3 g glycine at bedtime reduced next-day fatigue in small studies; ITP mouse lifespan +4-6%; no human ageing trials.
audit.biases: Small, single-group sleep studies [anut-bannai2012].
audit.newer_evidence: No new randomized sleep trial was found in 2024-2026 searches; the ITP result stands [anut-miller2019].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: In small trials from one Baylor group, about 7 g glycine plus 9 g NAC daily restored glutathione and improved many aging markers in older adults, but a 114-person industry RCT at lower doses found no rise in glutathione.

dose.effective: Glycine 1.33 mmol/kg/day + cysteine 0.81 mmol/kg/day as NAC (about 100 mg/kg glycine + 130 mg/kg NAC, roughly 7 g + 9 g/day at 70 kg)
dose.studied_range: Weight-based doses for 2-24 weeks in the Baylor trials; 2.4, 4.8 or 7.2 g/day total (1:1) for 2 weeks in the Nestle trial
dose.too_much: Long-term safety beyond 24 weeks not established; NAC carries the same tumour-promotion caution in mice as [n-acetylcysteine]
dose.timeframe: Changes reported at 16-24 weeks; benefits faded within 12 weeks of stopping
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to older adults with low glutathione; young adults already have normal glutathione synthesis. Over-the-counter GlyNAC products usually supply far less than the trial doses.

entries.mechanism: Supplies both limiting precursors (cysteine and glycine) for glutathione synthesis, which is reduced with aging. Older adults in the original study had about half the red-cell glutathione and synthesis rate of young adults, and 2 weeks of precursors restored both and lowered F2-isoprostanes.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine] and [glycine]. Probably redundant in people with high protein intake and normal glutathione. Not a substitute for oral or IV glutathione, see [iv-glutathione].
entries.caveats: The positive trials are tiny (8 older adults open-label; 24 in the RCT), come from a single group, and measured many outcomes, which raises the chance of false positives. The striking mouse lifespan gain (24%) came from a single-lab study in one inbred strain, not the multi-site ITP design. No hard outcomes.
entries.debate: The Baylor group reports broad benefits: corrected glutathione, lower oxidative stress, better mitochondrial fuel oxidation, insulin sensitivity, gait speed and strength [lon-sekhar2011, lon-kumar2021, lon-kumar2023], and longer life in mice [lon-kumar2022]. A larger Nestle-run RCT in 114 healthy older adults found GlyNAC at up to 7.2 g/day for 2 weeks did not raise glutathione or the GSH:GSSG ratio; only a post-hoc subgroup with high oxidative stress and low glutathione responded [lon-lizzo2022]. The doses and duration were lower than in the Baylor trials, so the two are not a direct contradiction, but the null primary result shows benefit is not universal. Both sides have commercial interests: Nestle Health Science holds patents and licences on glycine-plus-NAC use [lon-lizzo2022].

key_numbers.label: Glutathione rise in older adults (2 weeks)

entries.title: Glycine + N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC)

timing.summary: In older adults with low glutathione, GlyNAC restored red-cell glutathione within 2 weeks and wider markers over 16-24 weeks; benefits had faded 12 weeks after stopping. In a larger trial of healthy older adults, 2 weeks raised glutathione only in those who started low.

onset.text: Red-cell glutathione up 95% after 2 weeks in glutathione-deficient older adults [tnut-sekhar2011].

full.text: Wider improvements were reported at 16 and 24 weeks [tnut-kumar2023, tnut-kumar2021].

after_stopping.text: Benefits had declined at the check 12 weeks after stopping (earlier points not measured) [tnut-kumar2021].

frequency.text: All trials dosed daily; no intermittent schedules tested.

timing.debate: One group found glutathione restored within 2 weeks [tnut-sekhar2011] and broad benefits at 16 weeks [tnut-kumar2023], but an industry RCT found no rise after 2 weeks except in people with high oxidative stress and low baseline glutathione [tnut-lizzo2022].

audit.claim: In small Baylor trials ~7 g glycine + 9 g NAC restored glutathione and improved ageing markers, but a 114-person Nestle RCT at lower doses found no glutathione rise.
audit.biases: Single-group positive trials with many outcomes [anut-kumar2023]; the null trial was industry-run at lower doses and shorter duration [anut-lizzo2022]; both sides have commercial interests.
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication was found through 2026.
audit.bottom_line: Still unproven: the trials are small and the largest one was null.

entries.headline: Glyphosate is in the urine of most people (geometric means about 0.1-0.4 ug/L, mainly from grains and legumes); IARC calls it 'probably carcinogenic' while EFSA and ECHA found no carcinogenic hazard, the largest farmer cohort found no lymphoma excess, and urinary glyphosate tracked modestly higher 8-OHdG and MDA (about 15-20%) in farmers.

dose.effective: For the general public the main source is diet: an all-organic diet cut urinary glyphosate by about 70% within 3-6 days in an uncontrolled study, but only modestly in a randomized trial and not at all for people living within 0.5 km of sprayed fields. Glyphosate is systemic, so washing and peeling remove little. Home and garden users: wear gloves and long sleeves when mixing and spraying (farmers who did had about half the urinary levels).
dose.studied_range: General-population urine about 0.1-0.4 ug/L; farmers after spraying about 0.9 ug/L geometric mean, with peaks of about 20-30 ug/g creatinine.
dose.too_much: EU acceptable daily intake 0.5 mg/kg body weight per day; urinary data suggest typical exposure is under 3% of it [efw-vicini2021]. No human threshold for harm has been identified.
dose.timeframe: Urinary half-life roughly 7-18 hours; levels fall within days of changing diet or stopping spraying.
dose.notes: Commercial formulations contain surfactants (e.g. POEA) that are more toxic to cells than glyphosate alone; most human studies measure only glyphosate.

entries.mechanism: In cell and animal studies glyphosate and its formulations raise ROS, lipid peroxidation and DNA damage and disturb mitochondrial function; IARC judged the genotoxicity evidence strong. In humans, urinary glyphosate was associated with higher urinary 8-OHdG and MDA in farmers [efw-chang2023] and in rural Taiwanese adults [efw-ko2025], and with mosaic loss of chromosome Y in heavy users [efw-chang2023b].
entries.interactions: Exposure-reduction overlaps with [organic-food]; residues in grains are a reason some people avoid [whole-grains], but no evidence suggests that trade-off is worthwhile. Sperm data are in [glyphosate]. Other pesticide classes: [organophosphates], [pyrethroids], [neonicotinoids].
entries.caveats: Almost all human outcome data come from occupational exposure, which is 10-100 times higher than dietary exposure. Single spot urines misclassify exposure. Cross-sectional NHANES analyses linking glyphosate to sex hormones, cognition or grip strength [efw-wu2025] test many outcomes in one dataset and cannot establish direction. The pregnancy-length signal from small cohorts [efw-parvez2018, efw-lesseur2022] did not replicate in a cohort of about 1,800 [efw-ashleymartin2025]. The organic-diet study showing a 70% drop was small, uncontrolled and partly advocacy-funded [efw-fagan2020].
entries.debate: Hazard classification: IARC classed glyphosate as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) on limited human evidence for non-Hodgkin lymphoma, sufficient animal evidence and strong genotoxicity evidence [efw-guyton2015], whereas EFSA's 2023 review found no critical areas of concern and accepted ECHA's conclusion that it is not carcinogenic [efw-efsa2023]. Epidemiology: the 54,251-person Agricultural Health Study found no NHL excess [efw-andreotti2018]; a meta-analysis using the highest-exposure groups found 41% higher NHL risk [efw-zhang2019], but a re-analysis showed this depends on exposure and lag choices, with RR 1.05 for ever-exposure [efw-kabat2021]. A 2025 lifetime rat study at the EU ADI reported multiple tumours [efw-panzacchi2025]. Integrity: an influential 2000 safety review concluding no human health concern was retracted in 2025 [efw-williams2000, efw-williams2025]. Oxidative stress: urinary glyphosate tracked 8-OHdG in farmers and rural adults [efw-chang2023, efw-ko2025] but only AMPA, not glyphosate, tracked 8-OHdG in children [efw-makris2022].

entries.title: Glyphosate (Roundup) residues

entries.headline: Glyphosate has been measured in seminal plasma at about four times blood levels, where it tracked 8-OHdG and MDA in 128 infertile French men, but no study links typical dietary glyphosate to semen quality, and in vitro it cut motility only at concentrations far above real exposure.

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention has been tested. Practical steps are the general ones in [glyphosate]: gloves and long sleeves when spraying, and organic grains and legumes if you want to cut dietary intake.
dose.studied_range: Seminal plasma glyphosate in infertile men (French cohort); 0.36 mg/L in vitro.
dose.too_much: Not defined for sperm. Occupational spraying without protection gives the highest exposure.
dose.timeframe: Glyphosate clears from urine within days, but any effect on sperm would take at least one round of spermatogenesis (about 64 days, plus epididymal transit) to appear or reverse [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Most animal reproductive studies use formulations with surfactants, which are more toxic than glyphosate itself.

entries.mechanism: In vitro and in animals, glyphosate-based herbicides damage sperm membranes (largely via surfactants), lower testosterone production in Leydig cells and raise testicular ROS. In men, seminal glyphosate tracked seminal 8-OHdG and men with detectable glyphosate had higher total oxidant status and MDA [efw-vasseur2024].
entries.interactions: General exposure data and reduction steps: [glyphosate]. Often co-occurs with other pesticides in farm work ([pesticides], [organophosphates]).
entries.caveats: One cross-sectional study of infertile men without a fertile comparison group or adjustment for other pesticides; ELISA-based oxidative markers. The in vitro study used 0.36 mg/L, far above environmental levels, and found no DNA-fragmentation effect [efw-anifandis2018].
entries.debate: Pro-harm: glyphosate concentrates in seminal plasma and tracks oxidative DNA damage there [efw-vasseur2024]; NHANES urinary glyphosate was cross-sectionally associated with lower sex steroids and AMH [efw-wu2025]. Against: in vitro, glyphosate lowered motility only at high concentrations and did not raise DNA fragmentation [efw-anifandis2018]; EFSA and ECHA concluded glyphosate is not a reproductive toxicant [efw-efsa2023].
entries.title: Glyphosate and sperm

entries.headline: Four cups a day of decaffeinated green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers over 4 months, and 4 cups/day lowered plasma MDA/HNE in metabolic syndrome; across 145 RCTs, flavan-3-ol foods including tea lower blood pressure by about 3/2 mmHg and improve FMD, while evidence on oxidative damage in healthy non-smokers stays weak.

dose.effective: About 4 cups (~1 L) per day of brewed green tea.
dose.studied_range: 4 cups/day for 8 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: Brewed tea is considered safe at usual intakes (90-300 mg EGCG/day; heavy drinkers up to ~866 mg/day); rare idiosyncratic liver injury reported. See [green-tea-extract] for the supplement risk.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: EGCG bioavailability is low and variable; plasma half-life ~3.4 h. Ring-fission valerolactone metabolites appear 3-15 h later.

entries.mechanism: Catechins (EGCG, EGC, EC) and their microbial valerolactone metabolites; at physiological doses mild Nrf2 signalling and effects on endothelium rather than plasma radical scavenging.
entries.interactions: Flavan-3-ols overlap with [cocoa-flavanols]. Tea with meals reduces non-heme iron absorption (relevant to [iron-excess] and to iron-deficient people). Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, 980 mg/day of green-tea polyphenols did not appear to blunt antioxidant-enzyme adaptation in sprinters.
entries.caveats: The smoker trial used decaf tea and showed no benefit for black tea. Smokers have high baseline oxidative damage, so the effect may not generalise. Concentrated extracts are a different exposure: free EGCG exposure rose by more than 60% after 4 weeks of 800 mg once-daily dosing, and in a 12-month RCT in 1021 women, high-dose green tea extract caused moderate or worse liver-test abnormalities in 5.1% (see [green-tea-extract]).

entries.title: Green tea (brewed)

timing.summary: Tea catechins peak 1-2 h after a cup and are mostly gone within 8 h, so each cup is a short pulse. Lower oxidative DNA damage in smokers was seen after 4 months of 4 cups a day.

onset.text: Catechins peak at 1.3-1.6 h with half-lives of 1.7-3.4 h; over 90% of urinary EGC/EC is excreted within 8 h [tfood-lee2002].

full.text: Urinary 8-OHdG was 31% lower after 4 months of 4 cups/day in heavy smokers [tfood-hakim2003].

after_stopping.text: Catechins clear within a day [tfood-lee2002]; persistence of the DNA-damage effect was not measured.

frequency.text: Because catechins clear within hours [tfood-lee2002], benefits seen in trials came from several cups every day [tfood-hakim2003].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Four cups/day of green tea cut urinary 8-OHdG by 31% in heavy smokers and flavan-3-ol foods lower blood pressure slightly, but evidence in healthy non-smokers is weak.
audit.biases: The headline trial is in heavy smokers with high baseline damage; generalising to non-smokers risks overstatement [adiet-hakim2003]. Cohort tea associations are prone to healthy-user confounding and genetic instruments for tea are weak [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 145 RCTs confirms a small blood-pressure and FMD effect of flavan-3-ols [adiet-lagou2025]. The 12-month Minnesota Green Tea Trial showed liver-enzyme rises with high-dose extract, underlining that extracts are a different exposure from brewed tea [adiet-yu2017].
audit.bottom_line: Brewed green tea is safe and has small vascular benefits; claims of broad antioxidant protection in healthy people remain unproven.

entries.headline: 30 g/day milled flaxseed lowered systolic BP by about 10 mmHg in a 110-patient RCT, but across 33 trials the average fall is about 3 mmHg, larger in hypertension and with longer use; lignans and ALA both appear to contribute.

dose.effective: 30 g/day milled flaxseed (roughly 3-4 tablespoons).
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day in foods for 6 months.
dose.timeframe: Months.
dose.notes: Use milled seed; enterolignans rose 2-50-fold on the milled-flax diet.

entries.mechanism: Secoisolariciresinol diglucoside is converted by gut bacteria to enterodiol and enterolactone; ALA and its oxylipins also lower blood pressure. Plasma ALA tracked systolic and diastolic pressure, lignans tracked diastolic.
entries.interactions: ALA overlaps only partly with [omega3-fish]. Lignans also come from [whole-grains]. In PREDIMED, lignan intake was among the subclasses most strongly linked to lower mortality.
entries.caveats: One main RCT, in peripheral artery disease patients; replication in the general population is limited. Enterolactone production depends on the microbiome.
entries.title: Ground flaxseed (lignans plus alpha-linolenic acid)

timing.summary: Flax lignans are turned into enterolactone by gut bacteria; it peaks about 20 h after eating and has a half-life of about 13 h, so it accumulates with daily intake. Blood pressure was about 10 mmHg lower after 6 months of 30 g a day.

onset.text: Enterolignans appear in plasma 8-10 h after intake and enterolactone peaks at about 20 h [tfood-kuijsten2005].

full.text: Systolic BP was about 10 mmHg lower after 6 months of 30 g/day milled flax (earlier time points not reported in the abstract) [tfood-rodriguezleyva2013].

after_stopping.text: Enterolactone mean residence time is about 36 h and most is excreted within 3 days [tfood-kuijsten2005]; BP persistence not measured.

frequency.text: Enterolignans reach steady state with intake 2-3 times a day [tfood-kuijsten2005]; the BP trial used daily flax [tfood-rodriguezleyva2013].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: 30 g/day milled flaxseed lowered systolic BP by ~10 mmHg (15 in hypertensives), one of the largest BP effects of any food.
audit.biases: A single trial in peripheral artery disease patients; large effects in single small trials tend to shrink [adiet-rodriguezleyva2013, adiet-schoenfeld2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 33 trials (2,427 people) found an average -3.2/-2.6 mmHg, with very high heterogeneity; effects were larger at >=30 g/day, >20 weeks and in hypertension [adiet-li2023].
audit.bottom_line: Flaxseed probably lowers blood pressure a little (about 3 mmHg on average); the 10-15 mmHg figure is the best case from one trial.

entries.headline: Claims that touching the ground supplies 'antioxidant electrons' have no credible mechanism and rest on small, mostly unblinded studies by proponents.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Walking barefoot outdoors is harmless and pleasant if you enjoy it.
dose.studied_range: Small studies of grounding mats/patches over nights to weeks.
dose.notes: No validated oxidative biomarker improvement in rigorous trials.

entries.mechanism: Proposed mechanism (free electrons neutralizing radicals) is not physiologically plausible: radical chemistry occurs inside cells and is buffered by enzymes and glutathione.
entries.interactions: None.
entries.caveats: The main review is by advocates; independent replication is lacking.
entries.title: Grounding / earthing

timing.summary: There is no credible measured effect on oxidative stress, so there is no time course to describe. Claims come from small proponent studies.

onset.text: Not measured in credible controlled studies [tbody-chevalier2012].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No evidence-based schedule.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: Growth hormone for poor responders in IVF

entries.headline: Growth hormone adds about 1.4 eggs in poor responders, and Cochrane pooling suggests more live births (OR 1.77) but at very low certainty; the only placebo-controlled trial focused on live birth (LIGHT) found 14.5% vs 13.7%, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely. Trials used about 4-12 IU/day subcutaneously during stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Various regimens, often started in the preceding luteal phase.
dose.too_much: Expensive (often the costliest drug in the cycle); fluid retention, joint pain.
dose.timeframe: During ovarian stimulation.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

entries.mechanism: GH and IGF-1 enhance granulosa-cell FSH sensitivity and steroidogenesis; proposed to improve egg competence and mitochondrial function.
entries.interactions: Same population as [dhea], [coq10] and [prp-ovarian-egg]; none has proven live-birth benefit.
entries.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; LIGHT stopped early (113 women), so it was underpowered.
entries.debate: Cochrane pooled 8 small poor-responder trials and found more live births (OR 1.77, 1.17-2.70) but rated it very low certainty [fer-sood2021]; the placebo-controlled LIGHT trial found no difference [fer-norman2019]. ESHRE lists GH among adjuncts not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Live birth OR in poor responders (Cochrane, very low certainty)

entries.title: Growth hormone for poor responders in IVF

timing.summary: Growth hormone is given only during the stimulation cycle, so it acts on the antral window of one cycle. Neither the poor-responder placebo trial nor a larger trial in normal responders found a live-birth gain.

onset.text: Started on day 1 of stimulation and continued to retrieval [tegg-mourad2025, tegg-norman2019].

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Not applicable.

frequency.text: Daily injections during stimulation in trials [tegg-mourad2025].

timing.debate: Cochrane pooling suggests more live births in poor responders but at very low certainty [tegg-sood2021], against null placebo-controlled trials [tegg-norman2019, tegg-mourad2025]; whether longer pretreatment would help has not been tested in a large trial.

audit.claim: Growth hormone adds about 1.4 eggs in poor responders; Cochrane suggests more live births at very low certainty; LIGHT was null; ESHRE does not recommend it.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials, mostly unblinded and from single centres; oocyte number is a surrogate.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs (4131 poor responders) found no live-birth differences among hormonal add-ons, with GH ranked best only for oocyte numbers [afert-etrusco2025]. Cochrane 2021 and LIGHT stand [afert-sood2021, afert-norman2019].
audit.bottom_line: More eggs, no proven extra babies.

factors.name: GSTM1 / GSTT1 null genotype and isothiocyanate handling

entries.headline: Roughly half of people lack both GSTM1 copies; null carriers handle broccoli's sulforaphane differently and in one cohort gained the most lung-cancer protection from isothiocyanates, but results conflict and the advice (eat crucifers) is the same whatever the genotype.

dose.effective: No test needed. Whatever the genotype, regular cruciferous vegetables (for example 1/2 cup broccoli sprouts or a serving of crucifers most days) are the lever.
dose.studied_range: Crossover feeding with standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli; urinary isothiocyanate cohort of 18,244 men; case-control meta-analysis of 6,934 men for infertility.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane pharmacokinetics differ within hours; any cancer association reflects years of intake.
dose.notes: Consumer 'detox' panels often report GSTM1 status; it should not drive supplement purchases.

entries.mechanism: GSTM1 and GSTT1 conjugate isothiocyanates and electrophilic toxins to glutathione for excretion. Null carriers may keep sulforaphane in circulation longer (more Nrf2 activation) or form less of the conjugated metabolites, depending on the study.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; may modify the effect of [tobacco-smoking] carcinogens.
entries.caveats: Associations with male infertility and endometriosis come from case-control studies with population heterogeneity and possible publication bias; no intervention study uses genotype to change outcomes.
entries.debate: In Shanghai men, isothiocyanate protection was concentrated in GSTM1-null and double-null carriers [tst-london2000], whereas a crossover study suggested GSTM1-positive people retain different sulforaphane metabolites that might give them more benefit [tst-gasper2005], and a 114-person feeding study found genotype made little difference to excretion [tst-steck2007]. GSTM1 null was associated with male infertility in a meta-analysis [tst-wu2013], but a broad meta-analysis of endometriosis polymorphisms found GSTT1, not GSTM1, among the more robust signals [tst-mear2020].

entries.title: GSTM1 / GSTT1 null genotype and isothiocyanate handling

entries.headline: Chronic periodontitis is associated with lower systemic antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde, and periodontal treatment lowers oxidative markers.

dose.effective: Brush twice daily, clean between teeth daily, and get professional cleaning and periodontal treatment if gums bleed or recede.
dose.studied_range: Non-surgical periodontal therapy studies with >=6 weeks follow-up.
dose.timeframe: Markers improved within 6 weeks to months after treatment.
dose.notes: Smoking and diabetes strongly worsen periodontitis.

entries.mechanism: Chronic bacterial infection recruits neutrophils that release superoxide, hypochlorous acid and other oxidants locally, with spill-over systemic inflammation.
entries.interactions: Worsened by [tobacco-smoking] and poor [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Most data are from saliva and gum fluid; systemic effects are less consistent and few trials are randomized.
entries.title: Gum disease (periodontitis)

timing.summary: Periodontal treatment gets worse before it gets better: flow-mediated dilation fell and inflammatory markers rose 24 hours after intensive treatment, then endothelial function was better than controls at 60 days and clearly better at 180 days [tleg-tonetti2007]. HbA1c in people with diabetes falls by about 0.4 percentage points by 3-4 months and the benefit is still there at 12 months [tleg-simpson2022].

onset.text: A transient worsening first: 24 hours after intensive periodontal treatment, flow-mediated dilation was 1.4% lower and endothelial-activation markers higher than with routine care [tleg-tonetti2007]. Benefit emerges from about 1-2 months: CRP was about 0.37 mg/L lower at the earliest post-treatment measurement, typically 1-3 months [tleg-demmer2013], and FMD was 0.9% better at 60 days [tleg-tonetti2007].

full.text: By 180 days, flow-mediated dilation was 2.0% better than control care [tleg-tonetti2007]; HbA1c fell 0.43 percentage points at 3-4 months, 0.30 at 6 months and 0.50 at 12 months [tleg-simpson2022], and one 12-month trial found 0.6 points [tleg-daiuto2018]. Oxidative markers in saliva and gingival fluid improve over the same months [tleg-dasilva2018].

after_stopping.text: Not directly measured, but periodontitis recurs without maintenance, and the systemic markers track the periodontal state - the improvement in endothelial function correlated with the improvement in periodontal health [tleg-tonetti2007]. Untreated periodontitis is associated with persistently lower antioxidant capacity and higher malondialdehyde [tleg-liu2014].

frequency.text: Daily home care plus scheduled professional maintenance: the trials deliver an intensive course and then maintenance, and the systemic benefit tracks sustained periodontal health rather than the single treatment episode [tleg-tonetti2007, tleg-simpson2022]. Expect a bad 24-48 hours after intensive treatment.

timing.debate: The metabolic benefit is contested on both size and reality. Cochrane found a 0.43-point HbA1c reduction at 3-4 months from 30 trials with moderate certainty [tleg-simpson2022] and a UK trial found 0.6 points at 12 months [tleg-daiuto2018], but the large multicentre US Diabetes and Periodontal Therapy Trial was stopped for futility with no HbA1c difference at 6 months despite improved periodontal measures [tleg-engebretson2013]. The CRP effect is small and only seen against no-treatment controls, not active comparators [tleg-demmer2013].

audit.claim: Periodontitis is associated with lower antioxidant capacity and higher MDA, and treatment lowers oxidative markers.
audit.biases: Smoking, diabetes and SES drive both gum disease and systemic disease (confounding); smoking causes periodontitis by MR [abody-larsson2022].
audit.newer_evidence: The marker association stands [abody-liu2014]. Systemic-outcome trials conflict: periodontal therapy did not lower HbA1c in a 514-person RCT [abody-engebretson2013] but lowered it by 0.6% in a 264-person 12-month RCT [abody-daiuto2018]; Cochrane found insufficient evidence on cardiovascular prevention [abody-liu2019].
audit.bottom_line: Treating gum disease is worthwhile for the mouth; systemic benefits remain unproven.

factors.name: Hair dyes, relaxers and straightening treatments

entries.headline: Frequent chemical straightener use went with 1.8-2.6 times higher uterine cancer in the Sister Study (not replicated overall in the Black Women's Health Study) and slightly lower fecundability (FR 0.89 in former users); permanent hair dye showed no overall cancer increase in 117,200 nurses; formaldehyde- and glyoxylic-acid smoothing treatments carry acute risks.

dose.effective: If you use relaxers or straighteners, use them less often (risk was highest above 4 uses a year), avoid scalp burns and broken skin, and avoid keratin/'Brazilian' smoothing treatments that release formaldehyde, even when labelled formaldehyde-free, and glyoxylic-acid straighteners. Salons need local exhaust ventilation. For permanent dyes, current evidence does not call for avoiding them for cancer reasons; patch-test for dye (PPD) allergy.
dose.studied_range: Self-reported use in the prior 12 months or over years (Sister Study, Black Women's Health Study, Nurses' Health Study, PRESTO).
dose.too_much: Uterine cancer HR 2.55 with straighteners more than 4 times in the prior year (Sister Study); formaldehyde up to 1.19 ppm in salon air during smoothing treatments, at or above occupational limits. FDA's proposed formaldehyde ban has been under White House review since August 2026 and is not in effect.
dose.timeframe: Acute kidney injury after glyoxylic-acid straightening appeared at a median of 2 days; cancer associations reflect years of use.
dose.notes: Products marketed to Black women often contain unlabelled parabens, diethyl phthalate and other endocrine disruptors, and relaxer use is concentrated in Black women, so exposure and disease disparities overlap.

entries.mechanism: Formaldehyde (released from methylene glycol in smoothing products) is genotoxic and forms DNA-protein crosslinks; relaxers contain endocrine-active chemicals (parabens, phthalates, cyclosiloxanes) [epc-helm2018], and scalp burns may raise absorption [epc-wise2012]. Glyoxylic acid is absorbed and converted to oxalate, causing crystal nephropathy [epc-robert2024]. Oxidative-stress evidence is mechanistic only.
entries.interactions: Shares ingredients with [parabens] and [fragrance-musks]; occupational exposure overlaps with [nail-products-solvents].
entries.caveats: Product use is self-reported and product contents unknown; Sister Study participants have a sister with breast cancer; follow-up analyses tested many cancer sites with little dose-response [epc-bailey2026]; fibroid analyses may be biased by misclassification [epc-ogunsina2025]. Absolute uterine cancer risk is low, so even a doubled relative risk is a small absolute change. Litigation surrounds this topic on both sides.
entries.debate: Positive: uterine cancer HR 1.80 [epc-chang2022], breast cancer with permanent dye in Black women HR 1.45 [epc-eberle2020], fibroids IRR 1.17 [epc-wise2012], lower fecundability [epc-wise2023]. Null or mixed: no overall uterine cancer link in 44,798 Black women, only in postmenopausal heavy users [epc-bertrand2023]; permanent dye unrelated to most cancers in nurses [epc-zhang2020] and to bladder cancer in a meta-analysis [epc-turati2014]; hairdressers had no excess of breast or uterine cancer [epc-ogunsina2026]. An independent systematic review called evidence insufficient [epc-farooq2024]; a review by a private risk-consulting firm concluded relaxers are not a cancer risk factor [epc-hernandez2025]. Regulation: FDA's formaldehyde ban is still a pending proposal [epc-fda2026hair].

key_numbers.label: Uterine cancer, straighteners more than 4x/year (Sister Study)
Uterine cancer, heavy relaxer use, all ages (BWHS)

entries.title: Hair dyes, relaxers and straightening treatments

timing.summary: Acute harms (formaldehyde irritation, glyoxylic-acid kidney injury) appear within days of a treatment, while cancer and fertility associations reflect years of use. How long risk persists after stopping is not known; former relaxer users still had slightly lower fecundability.

onset.text: Acute kidney injury after glyoxylic-acid straightening appeared at a median of 2 days [epc-aamir2025]; airborne formaldehyde peaks during the treatment itself [epc-pierce2011].

full.text: Cancer associations relate to frequent use over years (20+ years in postmenopausal women [epc-bertrand2023]); not a defined plateau.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; former relaxer users had fecundability ratio 0.89 versus never users [epc-wise2023], so any effect may outlast use.

frequency.text: Uterine cancer risk was highest with more than 4 straightener uses a year [epc-chang2022]; fewer treatments and no scalp burns are the practical levers [epc-wise2012].

egg.late_start: Stopping late avoids acute formaldehyde and chemical exposure in early pregnancy, but whether it restores fecundability is unknown.
egg.text: No study measured how fecundability changes after stopping; former users still showed slightly lower fecundability [epc-wise2023]. The 100 days follows the follicle growth period [epc-gougeon1986] (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Toxic metals deplete glutathione and drive oxidative damage; even at normal background levels, urinary cadmium tracked oxidative DNA damage in non-smokers.

dose.effective: Do not smoke (the main cadmium source); test well water for arsenic; check old homes for lead paint and pipes; choose low-mercury fish (salmon, sardines) over high-mercury species (swordfish, king mackerel, shark).
dose.studied_range: Observational studies at background and occupational exposure levels.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposures and contaminated water are the main high-dose risks.
dose.timeframe: Body burdens of cadmium and lead decline slowly (years).
dose.notes: Chelation 'detox' for people without documented poisoning is not supported.

entries.mechanism: Cadmium, lead and arsenic bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inhibit antioxidant enzymes; redox-active metals (iron, copper) generate hydroxyl radical via Fenton chemistry; arsenic can generate H2O2.
entries.interactions: Cadmium exposure is largely from [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Spot-urine biomarker studies are prone to confounding: in one study the strongest metal associations were for essential selenium and copper.
entries.title: Heavy metals: lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury

entries.headline: Higher follicular-fluid mercury (above ~0.5 ug/L) and lead were associated with lower IVF live birth (lead RR 0.68) in a small study; cadmium exposure comes mainly from smoking.

dose.effective: Favour smaller, lower-mercury fish over large predatory fish (e.g. shark, swordfish); do not smoke (main cadmium source).
dose.studied_range: Follicular fluid Hg, Pb, Cd, As in 56 IVF patients.
dose.too_much: Follicular fluid Hg > ~0.51 ug/L associated with lower biochemical pregnancy and live birth.
dose.notes: Keep eating fish: the omega-3 benefit is real; choose low-mercury species.

entries.mechanism: Metals bind thiol groups, deplete glutathione and inactivate antioxidant enzymes; cadmium and lead can displace essential metals and promote Fenton-type ROS generation.
entries.interactions: Trades off against [omega3-fish] (fish is the main source of both); [tobacco-smoking] supplies cadmium.
entries.caveats: One small cohort; associations were non-linear and imprecise.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, higher follicular lead

entries.title: Heavy metals (mercury, lead, cadmium)

timing.summary: Each toxic metal has its own clock, and they differ by a factor of a thousand: arsenic clears in days [tleg-buchet1981], methylmercury in about 2-3 months [tleg-yaginuma2012], lead in blood in about a month but in bone over 16 years [tleg-rabinowitz1976, tleg-nilsson1991], and cadmium over 14-24 years [tleg-suwazono2009]. Stopping an exposure therefore pays off within a week for arsenic and within a season for mercury, but barely at all within a planned pregnancy for lead and cadmium.

onset.text: Blood and urine respond quickly to intake: a single arsenic dose is 46-78% excreted in urine within 4 days [tleg-buchet1981], and blood mercury rose from 6.7 to 26.9 ng/g over 14 weeks of eating fish to the tolerable weekly intake [tleg-yaginuma2012].

full.text: Blood mercury plateaus within roughly 3-4 months of a constant fish intake (about 3 half-lives) [tleg-yaginuma2012], while cadmium and lead keep accumulating in kidney and bone for decades [tleg-suwazono2009, tleg-nilsson1991].

after_stopping.text: Methylmercury: blood half-life 57-94 days, so about 3 months to halve and ~6 months to quarter [tleg-yaginuma2012]. Lead: blood half-time 34 days but a 13-year component from the skeleton, with bone lead falling with a 16-year half-time [tleg-nilsson1991, tleg-rabinowitz1976]. Cadmium: urinary half-life 13.6-23.5 years [tleg-suwazono2009]. Arsenic: days [tleg-buchet1981].

frequency.text: For mercury the relevant quantity is average weekly intake over the preceding 2-3 months, so an occasional tuna steak matters much less than a weekly habit [tleg-yaginuma2012]. For cadmium the dominant modifiable source is smoking, and population cadmium fell as smoking fell [tleg-tellezplaza2012]; for lead and cadmium there is no schedule that clears an existing burden.

sperm.late_start: Cutting high-mercury fish 2-4 weeks before conception removes only about a quarter of blood mercury; it is still worth doing but most of the benefit needs 3-6 months [tleg-yaginuma2012]. Lead and cadmium cannot be meaningfully lowered in that time.
sperm.text: Blood mercury needs 2-3 half-lives (about 4-6 months) to fall substantially [tleg-yaginuma2012], which is longer than the 74-90 day spermatogenic cycle, so the lead time is set by metal kinetics rather than by sperm development.

egg.late_start: Switching to low-mercury fish in the month before an IVF cycle produces only a small fall in blood and follicular-fluid mercury; it does not undo years of accumulation.
egg.text: Follicular-fluid mercury above about 0.5 ug/L and higher lead were associated with lower IVF live birth [tleg-butts2021]. Mercury responds over months [tleg-yaginuma2012]; lead can even rise in pregnancy and lactation as the skeleton releases stored lead [tleg-gulson2003].

timing.debate: Crude versus background-corrected methylmercury half-lives differ almost two-fold (94 vs 57 days), and the authors argue the crude value is more practical [tleg-yaginuma2012]. Cadmium half-life estimates range from 13.6 to 23.5 years depending on sex and creatinine adjustment [tleg-suwazono2009]. Whether bone lead release during pregnancy is large enough to matter clinically is debated; the isotope work suggests about a third of maternal blood lead comes from the skeleton, more on low calcium intake [tleg-gulson2003].

factors.name: Heavy vigorous exercise & low energy availability (women)

entries.headline: In lean women, 5 or more hours a week of vigorous exercise was associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception; exercising to exhaustion or on most days was linked to 2-3 times the odds of fertility problems.

dose.effective: If trying to conceive and lean, cap vigorous exercise below ~5 h/week and swap some for moderate activity; eat enough to keep regular cycles.
dose.studied_range: Vigorous activity 0 to >= 5 h/week (Danish cohort); frequency/intensity categories (Norwegian cohort).
dose.too_much: >= 5 h/week vigorous: FR 0.68 in lean women; exercising most days: 3.2-fold odds of fertility problems; exercising to exhaustion: 2.3-fold.
dose.timeframe: Cycle recovery after restoring energy balance can take months.
dose.notes: Missed or irregular periods in an active woman are a red flag for low energy availability (hypothalamic suppression).

entries.mechanism: Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility (functional hypothalamic amenorrhea), lowering estrogen and ovulation; this is an energy-signalling problem more than an oxidative one.
entries.interactions: No adverse association in women with BMI >= 25, for whom activity helps ([aerobic-exercise-moderate], [weight-loss]). Different from acute oxidative damage after ultra-endurance events ([overtraining-ultraendurance]); in general health, vigorous exercise in normal amounts is beneficial ([hiit-vigorous-exercise]).
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; vigorous exercise was not associated with worse IVF outcomes in the EARTH cohort.
entries.title: Very intense exercise and low energy availability (RED-S)

timing.summary: Under-fuelling hard training disrupts the reproductive hormone pulse within five days, and menstrual disturbance follows. Eating about 330 kcal a day more restored cycles in most women who recovered within three to six months.

onset.text: LH pulsatility was disrupted within 5 days once energy availability fell below 30 kcal/kg lean mass per day [tbody-loucks2003].

full.text: Not measured prospectively; cycle disturbance develops over months of low energy availability [tbody-mountjoy2023].

after_stopping.text: With ~330 kcal/day more food, 67% of recoveries happened within 3 months and 78% within 6 months, in a 12-month trial [tbody-desouza2021].

frequency.text: Lean women trying to conceive: vigorous exercise of 5+ h/week was linked to lower fecundability [tbody-wise2012]; energy intake must match training every day [tbody-mountjoy2023].

egg.late_start: Eating more and cutting volume 2-4 weeks before may restore LH pulses within days [tbody-loucks2003], but regular ovulation usually needs months [tbody-desouza2021].
egg.text: Restoring energy balance acts on the hypothalamic signal for follicle growth; since most menstrual recoveries took up to 6 months [tbody-desouza2021] and the follicle grows ~85 days [tbody-gougeon1986], start early.

timing.debate: Very active women had more fertility problems [tbody-gudmundsdottir2009, tbody-wise2012], yet the most intensely active women were not more often childless at follow-up [tbody-gudmundsdottir2009], suggesting the harm is reversible.

audit.claim: In lean women, 5+ h/week of vigorous exercise is associated with about 32% lower monthly chance of conception.
audit.biases: Self-reported activity; possible confounding by low energy availability and underlying menstrual disorders; single cohorts.
audit.newer_evidence: No newer causal study was found; the evidence remains the Danish and Norwegian cohorts [abody-wise2012, abody-gudmundsdottir2009], with the 2023 IOC consensus describing low energy availability as a cause of reproductive dysfunction [abody-mountjoy2023].
audit.bottom_line: Reasonable but limited; the mechanism (energy deficiency) is better established than the exercise-hours threshold.

factors.name: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

entries.headline: Their biggest proven effect is in the pan: a polyphenol-rich spice mix cut malondialdehyde in cooked burgers by 71% and in the eaters' urine by 49%, and herb marinades cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%.

dose.effective: Generous use in cooking, especially in meat dishes and marinades (about a tablespoon of dried herbs per meal); 14 g spice blend in a meal in one trial.
dose.studied_range: Single meals; marinating steaks 1 h before grilling at 204 °C.
dose.too_much: None established at culinary amounts.
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Per gram, dried cloves, oregano and other herbs top every polyphenol table, but servings are small.

entries.mechanism: Rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid and carnosol inhibit lipid oxidation and Maillard/HCA chemistry in food and in the stomach, so fewer oxidized lipids are absorbed; a spice blend also lowered postprandial insulin and triglycerides.
entries.interactions: Counteracts [high-temperature-cooking] and [processed-red-meat] oxidation products. Here direct scavenging is plausible because the reaction happens in the food and gut, where concentrations are high.
entries.caveats: Meal studies are tiny (n=6-11) and short.

key_numbers.label: MDA reduction in spiced vs plain burger meat
Urinary MDA reduction after spiced burger
Total HCA reduction, Caribbean herb marinade

entries.title: Herbs and spices (oregano, rosemary, cloves, cinnamon, etc.)

timing.summary: Spices act mostly in the pan: they cut oxidation products formed while cooking and lowered the eaters' urinary MDA after that meal. There is no build-up or carryover.

onset.text: Same meal: meat MDA -71% and urinary MDA -49% after a spiced burger [tfood-li2010].

full.text: Complete within the meal [tfood-li2010].

after_stopping.text: No carryover beyond the meal.

frequency.text: Use with each meal that needs it, especially grilled or fried meat [tfood-li2010].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: HFE hemochromatosis (C282Y homozygosity) and iron overload

entries.headline: About 1 in 156 people of northern European descent are C282Y homozygotes; untreated iron loading caused documented organ disease in about 28% of homozygous men (about 1% of women in one cohort, more in UK Biobank), and regular blood removal to a ferritin below 50-100 ug/L prevents it.

dose.effective: Test transferrin saturation and ferritin; if TSAT >45% (women) or >50% (men) with ferritin >200/300 ug/L, genotype HFE. In C282Y homozygotes, phlebotomy (typically 400-500 mL blood) to ferritin <50 ug/L during induction, then maintenance at <100 ug/L.
dose.studied_range: Diagnostic thresholds and phlebotomy targets from EASL 2022 and ACG 2019 guidelines; outcomes from cohorts of 31,192 (Melbourne) and 451,243 (UK Biobank) people.
dose.too_much: Over-phlebotomy to iron deficiency causes fatigue and anemia; ferritin targets exist for that reason. Avoid iron supplements and iron-fortified 'antioxidant' blends, and avoid high-dose vitamin C supplements, which increase non-heme iron absorption.
dose.timeframe: Iron accumulates over decades (disease usually after 40 in men, after menopause in women); induction phlebotomy takes months, then lifelong maintenance.
dose.notes: Ferritin above 1,000 ng/mL at diagnosis marks higher risk of advanced liver fibrosis. C282Y/H63D compound heterozygotes rarely develop disease without fatty liver, diabetes or excess alcohol. High ferritin with normal TSAT is usually fatty liver, alcohol or inflammation, not hemochromatosis.

entries.mechanism: Loss of HFE function lowers hepcidin, so the gut absorbs and macrophages release too much iron; transferrin saturates and non-transferrin-bound iron enters liver, pancreas, heart and joints. Labile iron catalyzes Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical), driving lipid peroxidation, fibrosis and cell death.
entries.interactions: Alcohol and fatty liver multiply liver damage, see [alcohol] and [excess-adiposity]. Iron supplements and multivitamins with iron are contraindicated (see [iron-excess], [multivitamin-mineral]); megadose [vitamin-c-supplement] raises iron absorption. Diabetes in homozygotes interacts with [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Genotype alone is not disease: penetrance is incomplete and much lower in women, who lose iron through menstruation and pregnancy. Heterozygotes (single C282Y) do not need treatment. Consumer genotyping that reports HFE should be confirmed clinically with iron studies before any action.
entries.debate: UK Biobank found C282Y homozygosity caused substantial incident morbidity in both men (15.7% vs 5.0%) and women (10.1% vs 3.4%) and argued for expanded early case-finding [tst-pilling2019], whereas an earlier cohort found documented disease in only 1.2% of homozygous women [tst-allen2008] and USPSTF judged evidence insufficient to estimate benefit from population genetic screening [tst-whitlock2006]. Ferritin's accuracy for detecting overload is rated very low certainty [tst-garciacasal2021].

key_numbers.label: Liver disease odds in homozygotes (UK Biobank)

entries.title: HFE hemochromatosis (C282Y homozygosity) and iron overload

timing.summary: Iron overload in HFE haemochromatosis builds over decades and is reversed by repeated blood removal over months, followed by lifelong maintenance. Stopping maintenance lets iron build up again.

onset.text: Iron loading accumulates over years to decades; not timed in the verified sources.

full.text: Treatment target: ferritin below 50 ug/L in the induction phase, then below 100 ug/L [tnut-easl2022]; months of phlebotomy are needed (extrapolated from donation data) [tnut-kiss2015].

after_stopping.text: Maintenance is lifelong because loading resumes [tnut-easl2022]; re-accumulation speed not measured here.

frequency.text: Phlebotomy frequency is set clinically to reach and keep ferritin targets [tnut-easl2022].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Diabetes raises urinary isoprostanes and hyperglycaemia drives mitochondrial superoxide and AGEs; a much-cited small study tied isoprostanes to glucose swings (r = 0.86, 21 patients), but larger CGM studies in type 1 and type 2 diabetes found no such link.

dose.effective: Limit post-meal glucose excursions and keep glucose in the normal range (see food and lifestyle areas).
dose.timeframe: Acute: postprandial window (hours); chronic: years
dose.notes: Dietary AGEs from dry-heat cooking add to the endogenous load (10- to 100-fold more than uncooked).

entries.mechanism: Excess glucose makes the mitochondrial ETC overproduce superoxide, which activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways. AGEs bind RAGE, activating NOX and NF-kB. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia transiently raise oxidative stress and impair endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Compounds [excess-adiposity]. Antioxidants taken with a meal can attenuate postprandial oxidative stress, but this has not translated into supplement benefits.
entries.caveats: The Monnier study is small (21 patients). The extent to which glucose swings matter in non-diabetic people is less established.
entries.title: High blood glucose and post-meal glucose spikes

entries.headline: Type 2 diabetes was associated with ~75% higher urinary 8-iso-PGF2a, which tracked day-to-day glucose swings (r = 0.86) more than HbA1c; reducing glucose spikes is a meaningful lever.

dose.effective: Keep fasting glucose and HbA1c in the normal range (individualized targets with diabetes); limit post-meal spikes with fibre-rich whole foods, fewer refined carbohydrates, and a short walk after meals.
dose.studied_range: Case-control comparison using continuous glucose monitoring.
dose.too_much: Large post-meal excursions and sustained hyperglycemia.
dose.timeframe: Glucose swings respond within days; HbA1c over ~3 months.
dose.notes: Exercise and weight loss are the main non-drug tools.

entries.mechanism: High glucose overloads mitochondria, causing superoxide overproduction that activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways; AGE-RAGE binding further activates NADPH oxidase and NF-kB.
entries.interactions: Improved by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [resistance-training], [weight-loss] and [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Monnier 2006 was small (21 patients); the 'swings matter more than average glucose' idea is supported mechanistically but outcome trials targeting variability are limited.
entries.title: Blood-sugar control and diabetes

entries.headline: Women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes have 24-36% lower fecundability; in mice, maternal diabetes damages oocyte mitochondria and raises egg aneuploidy.

dose.effective: Good glycaemic control before conception (managed with the diabetes team); weight loss and physical activity for insulin resistance.
dose.timeframe: Preconception optimisation over at least 3 months covers one full cycle of follicle growth.
dose.notes: Preconception glucose control is also critical for reducing birth-defect risk.

entries.mechanism: Hyperglycaemia increases mitochondrial superoxide and advanced glycation end-products; in diabetic mice oocytes show abnormal mitochondrial structure, lower ATP and TCA metabolites, spindle defects and aneuploidy, and the defective mitochondria are passed to the embryo.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: Oocyte mechanism data are from animals; human data are fecundability associations.
entries.title: Diabetes and insulin resistance

timing.summary: Glucose spikes raise oxidative stress within an hour or two, HbA1c takes about three months to show a change, and glycation of long-lived proteins accumulates over years. Good control early has a 'legacy' effect that protected against heart attacks and death for up to 24 years after the trials ended.

onset.text: A glucose load doubled leukocyte ROS at 2 h [tbody-mohanty2000]; after glucose was normalised, fasting glucose fell with a half-time of ~6 days and fructosamine ~12 days [tbody-tahara1995].

full.text: HbA1c fell with a half-time of ~35 days, so a new steady state takes about 3 months [tbody-tahara1995]; skin collagen glycation was 30% lower after ~5 years of intensive control [tbody-monnier1999], reflecting years-long collagen turnover [tbody-verzijl2000].

after_stopping.text: HbA1c differences vanished within a year after UKPDS, yet lower microvascular risk persisted and lower heart attacks and death emerged [tbody-holman2008], with no sign of waning at 24 years [tbody-adler2024]; DCCT intensive therapy cut cardiovascular events 42% over 17 years [tbody-nathan2005].

frequency.text: Glucose excursions act meal by meal and day by day [tbody-mohanty2000, tbody-ceriello2008], so control has to be continuous; the long glycation turnover means earlier is better.

egg.late_start: Lowering glucose in the last weeks still helps the periovulatory egg and early embryo, but HbA1c and birth-defect risk reflect the preceding ~3 months.
egg.text: Birth-defect risk rose with HbA1c measured within 3 months around conception [tbody-ludvigsson2018]; HbA1c needs ~3 months to settle [tbody-tahara1995] and the ovulatory follicle grows for ~85 days [tbody-gougeon1986]. Diabetes is linked to lower fecundability [tbody-whitworth2011].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; only the final maturation stage would be covered.
sperm.text: Extrapolated from the ~64-day sperm production time [tbody-misell2006]; direct timing data in men are lacking.

timing.debate: Glucose swings, more than HbA1c, tracked oxidative stress in type 2 diabetes [tbody-monnier2006] and in clamp studies [tbody-ceriello2008], but in type 1 diabetes glucose variability was not associated with urinary isoprostanes [tbody-wentholt2008].

audit.claim: In type 2 diabetes urinary 8-iso-PGF2a tracked glucose variability (r = 0.86) rather than HbA1c, so reducing spikes is a meaningful lever.
audit.biases: The headline rests on 21 patients (small-study and selection effects); later studies with continuous glucose monitoring did not replicate it.
audit.newer_evidence: No relationship between glucose variability and urinary isoprostanes was found in type 1 diabetes (2008) [abody-wentholt2008] or in well-controlled type 2 diabetes (2011) [abody-siegelaar2011], although diabetes itself raised isoprostanes. On outcomes, targeting HbA1c below 6.0% in ACCORD increased mortality (HR 1.22) [abody-accord2008], so 'normal range' targets need individualising.
audit.bottom_line: High glucose and diabetes are harmful, but the specific claim that glucose swings drive oxidative stress more than average glucose rests on one small study that failed to replicate.

entries.headline: Higher ferritin consistently predicts type 2 diabetes (about +22% per 100 ug/L) and Mendelian randomization supports a causal diabetes link, but the heart-disease side of the 'iron hypothesis' failed: genetic data even suggest slightly less coronary disease with higher iron, and the one phlebotomy RCT (FeAST) was null on its primary outcome.

dose.effective: No target has been validated by trials. Practical reading: ferritin roughly 30-200 ug/L (women) or 30-300 ug/L (men) with normal transferrin saturation is unremarkable; persistently high ferritin together with high transferrin saturation warrants medical evaluation for haemochromatosis rather than self-treatment.
dose.studied_range: FeAST lowered mean ferritin from ~123 to ~80 ng/mL by phlebotomy over ~4.5 years.
dose.too_much: Pathological overload (haemochromatosis, transfusion) damages liver, pancreas, heart, joints and gonads.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls over months with phlebotomy or donation; disease associations accrue over years.
dose.notes: Ferritin is also an acute-phase protein: inflammation, obesity, fatty liver, alcohol and infection all raise it, so a single high value often reflects inflammation rather than iron. Check CRP and transferrin saturation alongside.

entries.mechanism: Iron stored in ferritin is safe; danger comes from the small labile iron pool that catalyses Fenton chemistry and drives ferroptosis (iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when GPX4/glutathione defences fail). Hepatic and pancreatic iron may impair insulin secretion and action. Serum ferritin itself partly leaks from damaged cells, which ties it to oxidative stress independently of stores.
entries.interactions: Blood donation lowers stores [blood-donation]. Red meat raises heme iron intake [processed-red-meat]. Interpreting ferritin requires accounting for [chronic-inflammation], [excess-adiposity] and alcohol; high ferritin co-travels with [glycemic-control] problems. Avoid iron pills when stores are high [iron-excess].
entries.caveats: Observational ferritin-disease links are heavily confounded because ferritin rises with inflammation and fatty liver. Do not induce iron deficiency in pursuit of 'low ferritin': [iron-deficiency] carries real harms. Haemochromatosis genetics is covered elsewhere.
entries.debate: Supporting a harmful role: Sullivan's hypothesis [nut-sullivan1981], ferritin-diabetes meta-analyses [nut-jiang2019, nut-kunutsor2013, nut-zhao2012], MR showing iron raises diabetes risk [nut-wang2021, nut-liu2024] and shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021], and FeAST's secondary cancer reduction [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: prospective studies found no ferritin-CHD association [nut-danesh1999, nut-sempos2000], FeAST was null on its primary endpoints [nut-zacharski2007] with an editorial calling the evidence far from ironclad [nut-hu2007] and another doubting the cancer result [nut-edgren2008], MR suggests higher iron is mildly protective for coronary disease [nut-gill2017, nut-liu2024] and hypercholesterolemia [nut-gill2019], and ferritin may mostly mark cell damage [nut-kell2014, nut-depalma2010]. Reviewers have long called the iron-heart question unresolved [nut-wood2004].
