entries.title: High iron stores (high-normal ferritin)

timing.summary: Iron stores change slowly: removed iron takes months to replace, and lowering stores by phlebotomy takes repeated sessions. Disease associations with high ferritin reflect years of exposure, and a multi-year phlebotomy trial was null.

onset.text: Stores fall immediately with blood removal; disease links accrue over years (not timed here).

full.text: Phlebotomy every 6 months for several years did not reduce mortality or cardiovascular events [tnut-zacharski2007].

after_stopping.text: Without iron, stores remained below baseline 168 days after a single donation in most donors [tnut-kiss2015].

frequency.text: No validated schedule for lowering ferritin in people without haemochromatosis [tnut-zacharski2007].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Ferritin predicts diabetes and MR supports a causal diabetes link, but the iron-heart hypothesis failed.
audit.biases: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant (confounding by inflammation and fatty liver).
audit.newer_evidence: MR indicating higher iron slightly lowers coronary risk [abody-gill2017]; no new trial has changed this.
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Pooled over 78 RCTs, antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04). A 20,536-person trial of vitamin E + C + beta-carotene found no effect at all. Around exercise they block training benefits.

dose.effective: None.
dose.studied_range: e.g. vitamin E 600 mg + C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg/day (HPS); vitamin C 1,000 mg + E 400 IU/day (exercise studies)
dose.too_much: Any dose at these levels: no benefit; beta-carotene, vitamin A and vitamin E components carry the documented harms.
dose.timeframe: Exercise-blunting effect within 4 weeks; mortality signal over years
dose.notes: Raising blood vitamin levels does not mean oxidative damage was reduced; HPS raised levels 'substantially' with zero outcome change.

entries.mechanism: Suppresses ROS signals needed for adaptation (insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, endogenous antioxidant enzyme induction). In tumours, lowering ROS can release p53-dependent brakes and increase metastasis (mouse data). Endogenous enzymatic defences do not respond to extra dietary antioxidants once someone is replete.
entries.interactions: Antagonises the adaptive (hormetic) benefits of exercise. Contains [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] harms. Redundant with endogenous defences.
entries.caveats: Marketing often cites ORAC or 'total antioxidant capacity' values, which USDA abandoned in 2012 because they have no demonstrated in-vivo relevance.
entries.title: High-dose 'antioxidant formula' supplements (vitamin C + E + beta-carotene/A, etc.)

entries.headline: Too much antioxidant can loosen sperm chromatin: one study saw DFI fall 19% but decondensation rise 23%, and high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: Avoid taking several fertility products at once or doses well above the RDA (e.g. vitamin C >1 g, zinc >40 mg, folic acid >1 mg) without a specific indication.
dose.studied_range: Antioxidant vitamins with zinc and selenium for 90 days (human); dose-escalation of vitamin C, zinc, folate, carnitine (mice).
dose.too_much: This factor is the 'too much' end of [male-antioxidant-combination].
dose.timeframe: Over one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: FAZST's small SDF increase with 5 mg folic acid + 30 mg zinc is consistent with this concern.

entries.mechanism: Sperm chromatin compaction depends on oxidative formation of protamine disulphide bridges in the epididymis, and capacitation needs a controlled ROS burst. Excess reductants (especially vitamin C) can reduce these disulphide bonds and blunt physiological ROS signalling.
entries.interactions: Opposes the benefits sought from [male-antioxidant-combination] and [vitamin-c-e-combined]; also relevant to [l-carnitine].
entries.caveats: Human evidence is one small uncontrolled study plus indirect trial data; the mouse data may not transfer. Plausible but unproven.
entries.title: Megadose or stacked antioxidants ('reductive stress')

timing.summary: High-dose antioxidants blunted training adaptations within 4 weeks, and the small mortality excess comes from trials lasting years. In sperm, a 90-day course lowered DNA breaks but loosened chromatin.

onset.text: Vitamin C 1 g plus E 400 IU blocked exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gains over 4 weeks [tnut-ristow2009].

full.text: Mortality signal from trials of median 2 years (28 days to 12 years) [tnut-bjelakovic2012].

after_stopping.text: For beta-carotene and vitamin E the excess faded 4-6 years after stopping in ATBC [tnut-virtamo2003].

frequency.text: No schedule is shown to be safe or useful; avoid megadoses around training [tnut-ristow2009, tnut-bjelakovic2012].

sperm.late_start: Not measured.
sperm.text: A 90-day course raised sperm decondensation 23% [tnut-menezo2007]; to clear it, stop about one sperm-development cycle before trying (extrapolated) [tnut-misell2006].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Across 78 RCTs antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); HPS found nothing; they blunt training; high doses may loosen sperm chromatin.
audit.biases: The pooled mortality RR depends on trial selection; the vitamin E component is disputed [anut-abner2011, anut-berry2009]. The sperm harm rests on an uncontrolled study and mice [anut-menezo2007, anut-moazamian2025].
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization of 768,121 people found genetically higher circulating antioxidants (retinol, carotenoids, ascorbate, tocopherols) did not lower coronary disease [anut-luo2021], supporting 'no benefit' independent of trial selection. Mouse work extended the tumour concern from progression to metastasis via BACH1 [anut-wiel2019]. For sperm, MOXI [anut-steiner2020] and a 2025 meta-analysis [anut-michaelsen2025] found no live-birth benefit, while a 2026 meta-analysis found semen-parameter gains of very low certainty [anut-melhem2026].
audit.bottom_line: No benefit is well established; a small mortality harm is likely for beta-carotene and possible but disputed for the mix as a whole.

factors.name: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)

entries.headline: Gram-level vitamin C plus vitamin E, and 150-250 mg/day resveratrol, blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs (e.g. 45% smaller VO2max gain with resveratrol; lean-mass gain 1.4% vs 3.9% with C+E in older men), although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength overall.

dose.effective: Avoid routine supplementation at about 500-1000 mg/day vitamin C plus 235-400 IU vitamin E, or 150-250+ mg/day resveratrol, during training blocks. Get antioxidants from food. Correct true deficiencies (e.g. low vitamin C or low glutathione status) under guidance.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin C 500-1000 mg/day plus vitamin E 117.5-400 IU (4-12 weeks); resveratrol 150-250 mg/day (4-8 weeks); NAC 1200-2400 mg/day orally or IV infusion; quercetin ~1000 mg/day.
dose.too_much: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E/day removed the insulin-sensitivity gain of 4 weeks' training in one trial; 1000 mg C plus 235 mg E blocked mitochondrial-protein gains and blunted bone-density gains in older men.
dose.timeframe: Effects appeared within 4-12 weeks of combined training and supplementation.
dose.notes: Timing has not been directly tested: blunting occurred both with daily dosing and when doses were taken just before and after sessions, so moving the pill a few hours away from workouts is not proven to help. Food-level intakes (fruit, vegetables, tea, cocoa) have not shown this effect. Acute NAC or other antioxidants before a single competition is a different question from chronic use during training.

entries.mechanism: Exercise ROS (largely NOX2-derived H2O2) act as second messengers that activate Nrf2, PGC-1alpha, MAPKs (p38, JNK, ERK) and insulin-signalling adaptations. Flooding cells with reducing agents can blunt this signal, reducing induction of SOD2, GPx, COX4 and mitochondrial biogenesis and hypertrophy signalling. Redundant pathways mean the blunting is partial and inconsistent.
entries.interactions: Directly undermines [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training]. See the general supplement entries [vitamin-c-supplement], [vitamin-e-supplement], [isolated-polyphenol-supplements], [n-acetylcysteine] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Trials are small (11-54 people), use different doses and outcomes, and many find molecular blunting without performance loss. Isoflavones may even help lean-mass gains. NAC may help people with low glutathione.
entries.debate: Pro-blunting: vitamin C/E abolished insulin-sensitivity gains [exr-ristow2009], blocked mitochondrial-protein increases [exr-paulsen2014a, exr-gomezcabrera2008], blunted hypertrophy signalling [exr-paulsen2014b], lean-mass gains [exr-bjornsen2016] and bone gains in older men [exr-stunes2017]; resveratrol blunted VO2max, blood pressure and lipid improvements [exr-gliemann2013] and HIIT power gains [exr-scribbans2014], and impaired training effects on muscle oxidative and inflammatory markers [exr-olesen2014]; NAC infusion blunted adaptive signalling [exr-petersen2012]. Against: other RCTs found no effect on endurance adaptation or insulin sensitivity [exr-yfanti2010, exr-yfanti2011] or only partial cellular effects [exr-morrison2015]; a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found no significant effect on VO2max (SMD -0.14), endurance, lean mass or strength [exr-clifford2020], and a strength-specific review found no effect on strength [exr-dutra2020]. Critics argued the resveratrol data do not show 'mainly negative' effects [exr-smoliga2013], and a polyphenol meta-analysis found resveratrol's harm non-significant (SMD -0.54) and isoflavones possibly helpful [exr-martineznegrin2022]. Underneath sits the question of whether exercise ROS are necessary at all: without any supplement, men with the smallest exercise-induced oxidative stress adapted least [exr-margaritelis2018], while reviews still weigh how essential the ROS signal is versus redundant pathways [exr-powers2024, exr-merry2016b]. A 'personalised' camp argues antioxidants help only deficient people: NAC improved performance only in men with low glutathione [exr-paschalis2018, exr-margaritelis2018b]. Narrative reviews converge on 'no benefit, possible harm' for chronic megadoses [exr-merry2016b, exr-mason2020, exr-higgins2020, exr-nikolaidis2012].

entries.title: High-dose antioxidant supplements during training (vitamin C/E, resveratrol, NAC)

timing.summary: High-dose vitamin C and E start blunting training signals within weeks, because they flatten the exercise ROS pulse that triggers adaptation, and the blunting of mitochondrial and muscle gains shows up over 1-3 months. Vitamin C saturates the blood within days, while vitamin E builds slowly over months.

onset.text: Four weeks of 1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during training abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity and antioxidant-enzyme expression [tbody-ristow2009]; plasma vitamin C saturates at ~1000 mg/day [tbody-levine1996].

full.text: Blunted mitochondrial proteins after 11 weeks [tbody-paulsen2014] and smaller lean-mass gain after 12 weeks [tbody-bjornsen2016]; vitamin E took 16 weeks to reach its maximal effect on F2-isoprostanes [tbody-roberts2007].

after_stopping.text: Not measured. Vitamin C excess is excreted within days [tbody-levine1996]; vitamin E builds and probably clears more slowly [tbody-roberts2007]. Whether blunted adaptations catch up after stopping has not been tested.

frequency.text: Blunting was seen both with daily dosing [tbody-paulsen2014] and with doses taken only around strength sessions [tbody-bjornsen2016]; no trial has compared taking the same dose far from sessions, so timing away from training is not a proven fix [tbody-gonzalez2026].

timing.debate: Trials showing blunted adaptations [tbody-ristow2009, tbody-gomezcabrera2008, tbody-paulsen2014] conflict with trials and a meta-analysis showing no loss of VO2max, endurance or strength gains [tbody-yfanti2010, tbody-clifford2020]; molecular markers are blunted more consistently than performance [tbody-morrison2015].

audit.claim: Gram-level vitamin C + E and 150-250 mg resveratrol blunted molecular and some functional training adaptations in several RCTs, although meta-analyses find no significant loss of VO2max, endurance or strength.
audit.biases: Small trials (11-54 people), many outcomes and selective emphasis on molecular markers inflate apparent blunting; trials on both sides are cited [anut-ristow2009, anut-clifford2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 RCT found 12 weeks of the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ did not alter exercise-induced redox signalling or gene responses in older muscle [anut-broome2025], showing that not every antioxidant blunts signalling. Polyphenol meta-analysis still shows a non-significant tendency for resveratrol to impair adaptation [anut-martineznegrin2022].
audit.bottom_line: The balanced claim holds: chronic gram doses are not useful during training and may blunt adaptation, but performance loss is not proven.

entries.headline: EFSA (2018) concluded that 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases in RCTs; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury, especially in multi-ingredient products.

dose.effective: No oxidative-stress benefit beyond brewed tea has been shown.
dose.studied_range: Supplements supply 5-1000 mg EGCG/day.
dose.too_much: >= 800 mg EGCG/day as a supplement (EFSA). Multi-ingredient products caused more severe injury.
dose.timeframe: Liver injury latency averaged ~6 months for green-tea-only products and ~6 weeks for multi-ingredient ones.
dose.notes: Brewed tea at traditional intakes is considered safe.

entries.mechanism: At high concentrations EGCG becomes pro-oxidant (generating H2O2) and hepatotoxic; patient susceptibility factors appear important.
entries.interactions: Do not combine with other hepatotoxic supplements.
entries.caveats: Absolute risk is low given wide use, but the dose threshold is clear from trials.

key_numbers.label: Typical EGCG from brewed green tea

entries.title: High-dose green tea extract (EGCG pills)

timing.summary: High-dose extract (about 800 mg EGCG a day) raises liver enzymes after a median of about 3.5 months, and the liver recovers about a month after stopping. Once-daily bolus dosing makes exposure climb over the first weeks.

onset.text: Liver-function abnormalities appeared a median 106 days (range 56-365) after starting ~843 mg EGCG/day [tfood-yu2017]; EFSA links ≥800 mg/day to transaminase rises [tfood-efsa2018].

full.text: EGCG exposure (AUC) rose over 60% after 4 weeks of once-daily 800 mg, but not with 400 mg twice daily [tfood-chow2003].

after_stopping.text: ALT returned to normal a mean 32 days (13-92) after stopping, and rose again in most women who restarted [tfood-yu2017].

frequency.text: Avoid high-dose extracts; if used, a split dose avoids the exposure build-up seen with a single daily bolus [tfood-chow2003].

timing.debate: EFSA sets the transaminase threshold at 800 mg EGCG/day from supplements [tfood-efsa2018], but idiosyncratic injury has a different, unpredictable timing that a dose threshold does not capture.

audit.claim: EFSA (2018): 800 mg EGCG/day or more from supplements significantly raises liver transaminases; extracts also cause rare severe liver injury.
audit.biases: Case series are subject to reporting bias, but the threshold is from RCTs [anut-efsa2018].
audit.newer_evidence: The largest RCT behind the threshold, the Minnesota Green Tea Trial (1075 women, 843 mg EGCG/day for a year), raised ALT in 6.7% vs 0.7% on placebo, with 1.3% serious ALT events [anut-dostal2015]; a 2023 analysis linked a UGT1A4 genotype to much larger ALT rises [anut-acosta2023].
audit.bottom_line: Holds, with a concrete trial number readers can use: about 1 in 15 women on 843 mg/day EGCG developed raised ALT.

factors.name: High-temperature dry cooking of meat (HCAs, PAHs, AGEs)

entries.headline: Grilling, broiling and pan-frying meat until well done or charred forms heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and PAHs, and people in the top intake category have about 15-20% higher odds of colorectal adenoma in meta-analyses; dry heat also multiplies food AGEs 10-100-fold, but the largest cohort and the most rigorous low- vs high-AGE diet trials found no effect.

dose.effective: Cook meat to a safe internal temperature without charring: moderate pan or grill heat (about 160-180 °C rather than 200-250 °C), turn every minute, cut off blackened parts, microwave patties 1-3 min first and pour off the juice, marinate before grilling, and use moist heat (stewing, braising, poaching, steaming) for much of your meat.
dose.studied_range: Cooking-chemistry studies at 160-250 °C; adenoma meta-analyses comparing top vs bottom HCA intake; AGE trials from a single meal to 1 year with 2.7- to 5-fold differences in CML intake.
dose.too_much: Regular well-done or very-well-done grilled red meat: each 10 g/day was linked to 29% higher odds of colorectal adenoma in one case-control study (rare/medium meat: 10%, not significant).
dose.timeframe: Cancer associations reflect years of habit; AGE-diet trials looked for effects over 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.notes: Poultry and fish form HCAs too (grilled chicken breast is often high). Vegetables, grains and fruit form essentially no HCAs. PAHs come mostly from fat dripping onto flames and from smoke, so leaner cuts, a raised grill rack and removing char help. Brown, crusty grain and nut products are the biggest AGE sources in LC-MS databases, not only meat.

entries.mechanism: Above about 150 °C, creatine/creatinine, free amino acids and sugars in muscle react to form HCAs such as PhIP and MeIQx; CYP1A2 N-hydroxylation and NAT2/SULT esterification turn them into DNA-binding species. PAHs such as benzo(a)pyrene form from fat pyrolysis; CYP1A1/1B1 activation to diol epoxides and quinone redox cycling produce DNA adducts and ROS. Maillard chemistry forms AGEs (CML, CEL, MG-H1); absorbed AGEs can bind RAGE and activate NADPH oxidase and NF-kB, although how much dietary AGE reaches tissues is debated.
entries.interactions: Adds to the risks of [processed-red-meat]. Reduced by [marinating-meat] and [herbs-spices]. Endogenous AGE formation from [glycemic-control] and [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] probably matters more than dietary AGEs. Related starchy-food chemistry is covered under [acrylamide].
entries.caveats: HCA exposure estimates come from questionnaires about doneness and cooking method, which are crude. Typical HCA intakes are far below the doses that cause tumours in rodents. Most low-AGE trial benefits come from one research group using an ELISA-based food database; independent groups using mass-spectrometry databases and blinded designs mostly found no effect. The egg link is indirect: AGEs in follicular fluid track poorer IVF outcomes and a small PCOS crossover found a high-AGE diet raised testosterone and oxidative stress, but no trial has tested cooking method on egg quality.
entries.debate: HCA epidemiology: meta-analyses of mostly case-control data find modest positive associations with colorectal adenoma and cancer [kcc-martinezgongora2019, kcc-chiavarini2017], and the NIH-AARP cohort linked MeIQx and DiMeIQx to colorectal cancer [kcc-cross2010], but the 165,717-person Multiethnic Cohort found no association for meat or HCAs [kcc-ollberding2012], and Sugimura argued that HCA content in ordinary meals is too low to explain human cancer alone [kcc-sugimura2004]. Dietary AGEs: the Vlassara/Uribarri group reported large improvements in insulin resistance and 8-isoprostanes on low-AGE diets [kcc-vlassara2016, kcc-uribarri2011] and a blinded crossover from another group found better insulin sensitivity [kcc-decourten2016], whereas 6-week, 2-week and 4-week trials found no effect on endothelial function, inflammation or glucose metabolism [kcc-semba2014, kcc-baye2017, kcc-linkens2022], habitual AGE intake measured by LC-MS/MS was not linked to microvascular or glucose outcomes [kcc-linkens2022b, kcc-linkens2023], and systematic reviews rate the evidence as low quality [kcc-kellow2013, kcc-clarke2016].

entries.title: High-temperature dry cooking of meat (HCAs, PAHs, AGEs)

timing.summary: The chemistry is per-meal and the biomarkers clear in a day - heterocyclic amines from a fried-meat meal are largely excreted within 24 hours [tleg-reistad1997] - but a high-AGE meal measurably impaired vascular function within 2-6 hours [tleg-negrean2007]. The cancer and metabolic risks attributed to browning build over years of habit, and the best controlled diet trials of 2-6 weeks found nothing.

onset.text: A high-AGE meal cut flow-mediated dilation by 36% at 2-6 hours in people with type 2 diabetes versus 21% for an identical low-AGE meal [tleg-negrean2007]; heterocyclic amines appear in urine the same day and are largely gone within 24 hours [tleg-reistad1997].

full.text: Two weeks of a low-AGE diet raised insulin sensitivity on clamp in one crossover trial [tleg-decourten2016], but 4-6 week trials found no effect [tleg-linkens2022, tleg-semba2014]. Colorectal adenoma associations with heterocyclic amine intake (OR about 1.20) reflect years of cooking habit [tleg-gongora2019].

after_stopping.text: Urinary HCA markers are gone within about a day [tleg-reistad1997] and the postprandial vascular effect resolves within hours [tleg-negrean2007]; cumulative cancer risk, by definition, does not reverse quickly.

frequency.text: Because nothing accumulates, it is the everyday cooking method that matters - the occasional charred steak is a rounding error against a daily habit of frying and grilling to well done. Lower-temperature and moist methods, shorter high-heat times and marinating all act on the same meal [tleg-salmon1997, tleg-smith2008].

egg.late_start: A late switch to gentler cooking changes exposure immediately, but there is no trial evidence that it changes egg quality at any notice.
egg.text: Serum and follicular-fluid AGEs were associated with fewer oocytes and lower ongoing pregnancy in an IVF cohort, and dietary AGE intake changes within days [tleg-negrean2007]; whether reducing it over a follicle-growth window (about 3-4 months) helps has not been tested.

timing.debate: The dietary-AGE story is the main dispute, and it is about duration as well as direction: a 2-week crossover found better insulin sensitivity on a low-AGE diet [tleg-decourten2016], while a 4-week randomized trial in 73 people [tleg-linkens2022] and a 6-week trial in healthy adults [tleg-semba2014] found no effect on insulin sensitivity, vascular function or inflammation despite confirmed differences in intake. Heterocyclic amine associations with adenoma are modest and based on intake estimation [tleg-gongora2019].

entries.headline: Cycling 5 or more hours a week is linked to lower sperm concentration; moderate cycling is not a concern.

dose.effective: Under about 5 hours/week is fine; above that, use a well-fitted saddle, padded shorts and rest days.
dose.studied_range: Cycling >=5 h/week vs no regular exercise (2261 men); 16 weeks of intensive road training (24 cyclists).
dose.too_much: Intensive training raised seminal inflammatory cytokines, with some semen changes persisting 30 days after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Recovery may need more than 30 days; plan ~3 months.
dose.notes: Combine with general exercise advice ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).

entries.mechanism: Perineal pressure, scrotal heat and friction, plus inflammation and oxidative stress from very high training loads.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: Observational; the training study comes from a group with several retracted papers.

key_numbers.label: Odds of low concentration, cycling >=5 h/week

entries.title: High-volume cycling

timing.summary: Any effect of heavy cycling on sperm would act on sperm still developing in the testis, so changes would show and fade on the timescale of sperm production, about two to three months. No study has measured this time course directly.

onset.text: Not measured; the association is cross-sectional (5+ h/week linked to low sperm concentration) [tbody-wise2011].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured in cyclists. Extrapolated from sperm production: newly made sperm reach the ejaculate after ~64 days (42-76) [tbody-misell2006], so allow about 3 months after cutting back.

frequency.text: The association appears only above about 5 h/week [tbody-wise2011]; moderate cycling is not a concern, and overall activity was linked to better semen [tbody-gaskins2015].

sperm.late_start: Cutting back 2-4 weeks before only spares the final maturation of sperm already formed; the benefit, if any, is unknown.
sperm.text: Heat or saddle pressure would act on developing sperm; the ~64-day production time [tbody-misell2006] sets a 2-3 month lead time (extrapolated).

timing.debate: One fertility-clinic cohort linked 5+ h/week of cycling to low sperm concentration [tbody-wise2011], while young men with more overall activity had better counts [tbody-gaskins2015]. A cycling-training trial from an author group with several retracted exercise-semen trials was deliberately not used.

entries.headline: Better ventilation dilutes every indoor-sourced pollutant and improved sleep quality in small bedroom trials; whether CO2 itself (at 1,000-3,000 ppm) impairs thinking is contested, with blinded studies split, so treat a CO2 monitor as a ventilation gauge, not a toxin meter.

dose.effective: As a rule of thumb, keep bedroom and living-room CO2 mostly below about 1,000 ppm (a cheap NDIR CO2 monitor shows this): open a window or trickle vent at night, run kitchen and bathroom extract fans that vent outdoors, and keep mechanical ventilation (MVHR) filters clean. On high outdoor-pollution days, close windows and rely on filtration instead.
dose.studied_range: Bedrooms at about 660-835 vs 2,400-2,600 ppm CO2; offices at 12 vs 24 L/s per person; chamber CO2 600-5,000 ppm.
dose.timeframe: Air changes within hours; sleep and next-day effects within days.
dose.notes: Outdoor air also brings in traffic and wildfire pollution, so in polluted cities ventilation and filtration have to be balanced.

entries.mechanism: Not directly antioxidant: ventilation lowers indoor NO2, formaldehyde, VOCs, radon, humidity and airborne infection, reducing airway oxidant and inflammatory load. CO2 at indoor levels is not toxic in the classical sense; bioeffluents and other co-pollutants may explain the symptoms seen in poorly ventilated rooms.
entries.interactions: The shared fix for [gas-stoves], [vocs-formaldehyde], [damp-mould] and partly [radon]; trades off against [outdoor-air-pollution] on bad days, when [hepa-air-purifier] is the better tool.
entries.caveats: Trials are small, short, and often unblinded to the smell of stale air. Office sick-leave data are observational. No fertility data.
entries.debate: Pure-CO2 studies conflict: decision-making fell at 1,000 and 2,500 ppm in one blinded chamber study [eia-satish2012] and cognitive scores rose sharply with better ventilation and fewer VOCs [eia-allen2016], but adding pure CO2 up to 3,000 ppm did nothing when bioeffluents were removed [eia-zhang2017], NASA-style testing up to 5,000 ppm found no dose-response [eia-scully2019], and children sleeping at 2,000-3,000 ppm showed no next-morning cognitive change [eia-klausen2023]. Bedroom ventilation improved sleep in students [eia-stromtejsen2016]. A multidisciplinary review found consistent links between low ventilation and sick-building symptoms, sick leave and allergy [eia-sundell2011, eia-milton2000].

key_numbers.label: Short-term sick leave, lower vs higher office ventilation

entries.title: Home ventilation and indoor CO2

timing.summary: Ventilation changes air within hours; in bedroom trials sleep and next-day performance improved within a week of lower CO2 [eia-stromtejsen2016]. Effects vanish when ventilation drops again.

onset.text: Chamber effects on symptoms and some tasks appeared within a 4-h exposure to reduced ventilation [eia-zhang2017].

full.text: Sleep quality improved within each 1-week ventilation condition [eia-stromtejsen2016].

after_stopping.text: Air quality reverts within hours; no lasting effect expected.

frequency.text: Ventilate every night and while cooking or showering; the benefit follows current air quality [eia-stromtejsen2016].

timing.debate: Whether CO2 itself acts within hours is disputed: effects at 1,000 ppm in one chamber study [eia-satish2012] versus none for pure CO2 up to 3,000-5,000 ppm in others [eia-zhang2017, eia-scully2019].

factors.name: Home water filtration (reverse osmosis, activated carbon)

entries.headline: Where tap water carries PFAS, reverse-osmosis and well-maintained carbon filters remove much of it and home-filter users in a contaminated county had lower serum PFAS, but real-world filter testing is thin, short-chain PFAS slip through more easily, and there is no human evidence that filtering changes microplastic body burden.

dose.effective: Most worthwhile when local water reports show PFAS, especially in the ~10-100 ng/L range or above (where water clearly raises blood levels, most consistently PFHxS). Options: under-sink reverse osmosis, or a carbon-block filter certified for PFOA/PFOS reduction; change cartridges on schedule.
dose.studied_range: Lab and certification tests of point-of-use devices; only five real-life tap studies; observational serum comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Serum PFAS falls slowly after exposure stops (roughly 13-26% per year for PFHxS, PFOS, PFOA).
dose.notes: Neglected activated-carbon cartridges can release captured PFAS back into water. Below ~10 ng/L the benefit for blood levels is uncertain. Filtering does not affect PFAS from food or consumer products.

entries.mechanism: Reduces intake rather than acting on oxidative stress directly: activated carbon adsorbs long-chain PFAS, ion-exchange resins bind anionic PFAS, and reverse osmosis membranes reject most PFAS molecules.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [pfas] serum testing; the elimination side (donation, sequestrants) is covered there. For bottled water vs tap and plastics see [microplastics].
entries.caveats: Serum benefit is shown only by observational comparisons in a heavily contaminated area. Device performance varies by product, PFAS chain length and maintenance.
entries.debate: Benefit size depends on water levels: a 2026 evidence summary found clear water-to-blood links at 10-100 ng/L but inconsistent ones below ~10 ng/L [env-tefera2026], whereas a California study found detectable PFAS in general public supplies raised serum PFHxS ~80% [env-fillman2026]. Filters: home-filter users had lower serum PFAS [env-cuffney2023], and stopping contaminated water lowers serum over years [env-li2018], but a review warns real-world performance is poorly characterized and short-chain PFAS are harder to remove [env-mackeown2024].

key_numbers.label: Higher serum PFHxS with PFAS detected in treated public water
Real-life studies of point-of-use PFAS removal

entries.title: Home water filtration (reverse osmosis, activated carbon)

timing.summary: The filter works the day you install it, but your blood takes years to notice. Serum PFAS fall only about 13-26% a year once the contaminated supply is replaced [tleg-li2018pfas], so a point-of-use filter is an investment with a multi-year payback rather than a quick fix [tleg-cuffney2023].

onset.text: Water concentrations drop as soon as a working filter is in line [tleg-mackeown2024]; the first measurable change in serum takes months, because the body burden is leaving at 13-26% a year [tleg-li2018pfas].

full.text: Serum levels approach the new, lower steady state over several years: halving takes 2.7-5.3 years depending on the compound [tleg-li2018pfas]. Home-filter users in a contaminated county had lower serum levels of all seven PFAS measured, a cross-sectional snapshot of that slow process [tleg-cuffney2023].

after_stopping.text: If the filter is removed or left unmaintained, exposure resumes immediately and serum levels climb again; exhausted activated carbon can even release PFAS back into the water [tleg-mackeown2024].

frequency.text: Continuous use plus maintenance on schedule: the benefit comes from every glass, and a neglected carbon filter can be worse than none [tleg-mackeown2024]. Reverse osmosis and ion exchange remove more, and short-chain PFAS slip through more easily [tleg-mackeown2024].

sperm.late_start: Installing a filter a month before conception will not change serum PFAS measurably for that cycle; it is a long-horizon measure that also protects a later pregnancy and breastfeeding.
sperm.text: The lead time is set by PFAS elimination (half-lives of years) rather than by sperm development [tleg-li2018pfas].

timing.debate: Real-world filter performance is thinly evidenced: only five real-life point-of-use studies exist, performance varies with maintenance, and short-chain PFAS are poorly removed [tleg-mackeown2024]. The serum evidence is cross-sectional and cannot separate filter use from other habits [tleg-cuffney2023]. For microplastics there is no evidence that filtering changes any measured body burden [tleg-lane2026].

factors.name: Hormonal contraception and return of fertility

entries.headline: About 83% of women conceive within 12 months of stopping contraception of any type; injectables delay return of normal fertility by about 5-8 cycles, the patch about 4, the pill or ring about 3, IUDs and implants about 2, and total years of use do not matter.

dose.effective: Not applicable; the question is the delay after stopping.
dose.studied_range: 22 studies of 14,884 women; prospective cohort of 17,954 women trying to conceive.
dose.too_much: Injectable progestin (DMPA) has the longest delay (FR 0.65).
dose.timeframe: Pill, ring: ~3 cycles; patch: ~4; injectable: 5-8; IUD and implant: ~2.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Plan stopping injectables several months before wanting to conceive. Start folic acid before stopping contraception (see folic-acid).

entries.mechanism: Hormonal methods suppress ovulation; the delay reflects time for the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis to resume normal cycles, longest with depot injections that persist in the body. No evidence that past use damages eggs.
entries.interactions: Oral contraceptive efficacy is reduced by St John's wort ([supplement-drug-interactions]) and during tirzepatide initiation ([glp1-agonists]). [folic-acid] should begin before stopping.
entries.caveats: Neither study measured egg quality directly; return of fertility is the outcome.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis found no significant delay overall or by method [med-girum2018], whereas a large prospective cohort found short method-specific delays, longest after injectables [med-yland2020]; both agree long-term use does not reduce eventual fertility.

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio after injectables vs barrier

entries.title: Hormonal contraception and return of fertility

timing.summary: Hormonal contraception pauses ovulation without using up eggs, and fertility returns within a few cycles of stopping. The delay is about 2 cycles for IUDs and implants, 3 for the pill or ring, 4 for the patch and 5-8 for injectables; years of use do not matter.

onset.text: Not applicable (contraceptive effect starts within the first cycle).

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Normal fertility returns after about 2 cycles (IUD, implant) to 3 (pill, ring), 4 (patch) and 5-8 cycles (injectable) [tegg-yland2020]; AMH normalises within 2 months of stopping the pill [tegg-landersoe2020].

frequency.text: Not a dosing question.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; studies agree on a short delay, with injectables the outlier [tegg-yland2020, tegg-girum2018].

egg.late_start: Conceiving in the first cycles after stopping is common and not harmful; about 83% conceive within 12 months [tegg-girum2018].
egg.text: Stop pill, ring or patch about 3 cycles, and injectables 5-8 cycles, before the time you hope to conceive to avoid the expected delay [tegg-yland2020]; duration of prior use does not matter [tegg-girum2018].

factors.name: House dust control (wet cleaning, HEPA vacuuming, hand-washing)

entries.headline: Dust is a reservoir for phthalates, flame retardants, PFAS and lead that young children swallow at about 60-70 mg a day; one week of wet cleaning or hand-washing roughly halved some flame-retardant metabolites, but dust control alone has not lowered children's blood lead or improved mite-allergic asthma in trials.

dose.effective: Wet-mop hard floors and damp-dust weekly; vacuum with a sealed HEPA vacuum; shoes off at the door; wash children's hands before eating and after floor play; replace crumbling foam; tailor allergen and smoke control to the specific sensitivities of a child with asthma.
dose.studied_range: Gibson 2019: one week of instructed cleaning, hand-washing, or both. Dust ingestion: 36-72 mg/day in infants and young children, 12-32 mg/day in adults.
dose.timeframe: Hand and urine levels of short-lived chemicals drop within a week; persistent chemicals (PBDEs, PFAS, lead) change over months to years.
dose.notes: Dust control is an exposure-reduction measure; no trial shows a health or fertility benefit from dust control on its own.

entries.mechanism: Not an oxidative intervention in itself: it lowers intake of dust-borne chemicals (see [flame-retardants], [phthalates], [pfas], [heavy-metals]) and allergens that drive airway inflammation.
entries.interactions: The cheapest shared lever for [flame-retardants], [phthalates], [microplastics] and lead. Avoid adding spray cleaners ([cleaning-products]) while doing it.
entries.caveats: Intervention studies are small, short and measure exposure markers, not health. Education-only lead programmes fail; removing the source (lead paint, contaminated soil) matters more than cleaning. Dust levels of short-lived chemicals vary day to day.
entries.debate: Cochrane found that household education and dust-control interventions did not lower children's blood lead [eia-nussbaumerstreit2020] and that mite-control measures did not help mite-allergic asthma [eia-gotzsche2008] (a review Cochrane now flags as outdated). Against that, a multifaceted, individually tailored home programme in 937 inner-city children cut allergen levels and symptom days for two years [eia-morgan2004], and a small cleaning/hand-washing trial lowered flame-retardant biomarkers [eia-gibson2019]. The difference is likely between single generic measures and targeted, multi-component ones.

key_numbers.label: Asthma symptom days per 2 weeks, tailored home intervention vs control

entries.title: House dust control (wet cleaning, HEPA vacuuming, hand-washing)

timing.summary: Dust-control and hand-washing lower short-lived chemical biomarkers within a week [eia-gibson2019], and replacing old foam lowers dust flame retardants over 6-18 months [eia-rodgers2021]. A tailored allergen programme kept asthma symptoms lower for a year after it ended [eia-morgan2004].

onset.text: Urinary flame-retardant metabolites fell after one week of cleaning or hand-washing [eia-gibson2019].

full.text: Dust flame retardants fell 6-18 months after furniture or foam replacement [eia-rodgers2021]; asthma symptom days were lower during the intervention year [eia-morgan2004].

after_stopping.text: Symptom benefit persisted through the year after a tailored home intervention [eia-morgan2004]; for short-lived chemicals, exposure presumably returns within days of stopping (not measured).

frequency.text: Wet cleaning weekly and hand-washing before every meal; the trial combined both for a week [eia-gibson2019].

timing.debate: Whether dust control changes blood lead at all is contested: education and dust control did not lower blood lead in Cochrane-reviewed trials [eia-nussbaumerstreit2020].

factors.name: Household cleaning products (sprays, bleach, quaternary ammonium disinfectants)

entries.headline: Weekly use of cleaning sprays was linked to about 50% more new adult asthma, and women who cleaned at home lost lung function about 3.6 mL/yr faster over 20 years; quaternary ammonium disinfectants cut fertility in mice, but human fertility data are thin and conflicting.

dose.effective: Use liquids on a cloth instead of sprays; use soap or detergent and water for routine cleaning and keep disinfectants (bleach, quats) for genuine need (illness, raw meat); never mix bleach with acids or ammonia; ventilate while cleaning; microfibre cloths and wet-mopping remove dust without chemicals.
dose.studied_range: ECRHS: cleaning sprays at least weekly (42% of participants) up to 4+ days a week.
dose.too_much: Asthma risk was dose-dependent: RR 1.49 for weekly sprays and 2.11 for physician-diagnosed asthma with sprays on 4+ days a week.
dose.timeframe: Lung function differences accumulated over 20 years; asthma incidence over the multi-year ECRHS follow-up and over 2 years in NutriNet-Sante.
dose.notes: "Green" products were also associated with asthma symptoms in a 30,000-person cohort, so the label is not a guarantee; fragranced green products still emit terpenes.

entries.mechanism: Hypochlorite, chloramines and quats are airway irritants that oxidize lung-lining fluid and trigger neutrophilic inflammation; repeated low-level injury is the proposed route to asthma and lung-function decline. Quats inhibit mitochondrial function and raise inflammatory cytokines in cells; in 43 people, blood QACs tracked higher cytokines and lower mitochondrial function [eia-hrubec2021].
entries.interactions: Terpene-based cleaners add to [vocs-formaldehyde]. Wet cleaning is still worth doing for [house-dust]; the issue is sprays and disinfectant overuse, not cleaning.
entries.caveats: Exposure is self-reported in all large cohorts. People with early asthma may avoid sprays (reverse causation would bias toward null) or clean more because of allergies. Professional cleaners have lower income and more smoking. QAC fertility harm is shown only in mice; in humans the only reproductive data are on nurses, where a retrospective study found 2-fold late miscarriage with disinfectants [eia-lawson2012] but a prospective one did not [eia-ding2021].
entries.debate: Respiratory harm is consistently found in independent cohorts [eia-zock2007, eia-svanes2018, eia-dumas2019, eia-pachecodasilva2026], although healthcare-worker studies are all at high risk of bias [eia-romerostarke2021]. For quats and fertility, academic mouse studies found subfertility in both sexes [eia-melin2014, eia-melin2016, eia-kirkpatrick2025], while industry steering committees disputed the first study [eia-hostetler2015] and a review relying on unpublished guideline studies rated those mouse studies unreliable and found no reproductive toxicity at expected exposures [eia-desesso2021]. A multi-institution review calls QACs a class of emerging concern [eia-arnold2023]. Bleach use was linked to more childhood infections in a cross-sectional study [eia-casas2015], which cannot exclude that families with sick children clean more.

key_numbers.label: New asthma with weekly spray use
FEV1 decline, women cleaning at home

entries.title: Household cleaning products (sprays, bleach, quaternary ammonium disinfectants)

timing.summary: The respiratory harm of cleaning sprays accumulates slowly: new asthma over the multi-year ECRHS follow-up [eia-zock2007] and faster lung-function decline over 20 years [eia-svanes2018]. Whether stopping reverses it has not been measured.

onset.text: Two-year changes in spray and irritant use tracked asthma symptom incidence and deterioration in NutriNet-Sante [eia-pachecodasilva2026]; ECRHS counted new asthma over its multi-year follow-up [eia-zock2007].

full.text: Accelerated FEV1 decline was measured across 20 years [eia-svanes2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Risk rose with frequency: weekly sprays RR 1.49, sprays on 4+ days a week RR 2.11 for diagnosed asthma [eia-zock2007]. Use disinfectants occasionally, for specific need.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Cochrane 2020 found about 21% more live births with hyaluronan transfer medium, but a 2026 meta-analysis found no significant gain (RR 1.14; 1.06 in low-bias trials); HFEA rates it amber and it raises twins if more than one embryo is transferred.

dose.effective: Hyaluronan 0.5 mg/mL in the transfer medium, with single embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 mg/mL ('functional') vs 0-0.125 mg/mL controls.
dose.too_much: Multiple pregnancy RR 1.45 when more than one embryo is transferred.
dose.timeframe: Embryo is placed in the medium minutes to hours before transfer.
dose.notes: Benefit seen with women's own eggs, not clearly with donor eggs.

entries.mechanism: Hyaluronan is abundant in uterine fluid at implantation; proposed to help embryo-endometrium adhesion via CD44 and to make the medium more viscous.
entries.interactions: Multiple-pregnancy risk interacts with the number of embryos transferred.
entries.caveats: Many trials are older, small and industry-linked; the effect appears in autologous fresh transfers more than frozen ones.
entries.debate: Cochrane (moderate certainty) and a 2022 meta-analysis find a live-birth gain with women's own eggs [fer-heymann2020, fer-heymann2022], and ESHRE recommends it [fer-eshre2023addons]. HFEA judges the evidence conflicting and rates it amber [fer-hfea2026], and in Cochrane's low-risk-of-bias subset the miscarriage benefit disappears [fer-heymann2020].

key_numbers.label: Number needed to treat, own eggs

entries.title: Hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium ('embryo glue')

audit.claim: Hyaluronan transfer medium is the one add-on with a plausible live-birth gain (Cochrane RR 1.21), so ESHRE recommends it with single embryo transfer; HFEA amber.
audit.biases: Many older, small, industry-linked trials at high risk of bias; the benefit shrinks in low-risk-of-bias analyses [afert-heymann2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 24 RCTs found live birth RR 1.14 (0.99-1.31, not significant), shrinking to 1.06 (0.85-1.31) when high-risk-of-bias trials were excluded, and rated certainty very low [afert-rocha2026]. Cochrane 2020 still reports RR 1.21 at moderate certainty [afert-heymann2020]. The HFEA keeps it yellow/amber (unclear) [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Any gain is small and uncertain; it is cheap and probably harmless with single-embryo transfer, but not proven.

entries.headline: Being dehydrated increased muscle H2O2 after resistance exercise in one small study; there is no evidence that drinking extra water beyond thirst lowers oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Drink to thirst; aim for pale-yellow urine; replace fluids lost in heavy sweating.
dose.studied_range: One crossover study with 24 h fluid restriction.
dose.too_much: Overdrinking (hyponatremia) is a risk in endurance events.
dose.notes: 'Alkaline' or 'structured' water claims have no support.

entries.mechanism: Dehydration raises cell stress and may increase ROS production in exercising muscle.
entries.interactions: Relevant to [overtraining-ultraendurance] and [sauna].
entries.caveats: Evidence is a single small study; 'flushing out toxins' with water is not a real antioxidant mechanism.
entries.title: Hydration

timing.summary: Dehydration is an acute state: 24 h of fluid restriction raised muscle H2O2 during exercise. Rehydrating should reverse it within hours, though that was not measured.

onset.text: Raised muscle H2O2 and stress signalling after 24 h of fluid restriction [tfood-luk2025].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; recovery with rehydration is expected within hours to a day (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Drink to thirst every day; dehydration effects are acute [tfood-luk2025].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Molecular hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies, but human trials are small and show at most modest effects on lipids, not established oxidative-stress benefits.

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress. Trials used ~0.5-1.5 L/day of hydrogen-rich water.
dose.studied_range: Pilot RCTs of weeks to 6 months.
dose.too_much: Appears safe.
dose.notes: Hydrogen escapes quickly from water once opened.

entries.mechanism: H2 reacts selectively with hydroxyl radical and peroxynitrite; may also signal via Nrf2. Doses from drinking water are tiny and transient.
entries.interactions: No known interactions.
entries.caveats: Most trials are small and come from a few research groups; the telomere result came from a 40-person pilot with many outcomes, and the lipid meta-analysis pooled only 7 small studies.
entries.title: Hydrogen-rich water / molecular hydrogen

timing.summary: Hydrogen from hydrogen-rich water shows up in breath within minutes and is gone soon after. Any effect would have to come from repeated brief exposures.

onset.text: Breath hydrogen peaks 10-15 minutes after drinking [tnut-shimouchi2009].

full.text: Peak at 10-15 minutes [tnut-shimouchi2009].

after_stopping.text: Breath hydrogen fell rapidly back to baseline; the small area under the curve (2-9 ppm-hours) implies roughly an hour (extrapolated) [tnut-shimouchi2009].

frequency.text: Not recommended; exposure is brief whatever the schedule [tnut-shimouchi2009].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Hydrogen scavenges hydroxyl radicals in lab and animal studies; human trials are small with modest lipid effects, not established oxidative-stress benefits.
audit.biases: Small trials from few groups [anut-todorovic2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 blinded RCT in chronic mountain sickness found 8 weeks of hydrogen-rich water raised MDA versus placebo and did not reduce oxidative damage [anut-zhang2026a].
audit.bottom_line: Holds, and the newest controlled trial points against an antioxidant benefit.

factors.name: ICSI when sperm are normal (non-male-factor ICSI)

entries.headline: With normal sperm count and motility, ICSI did not beat conventional IVF in a 1064-couple Lancet RCT (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS; fertilisation failure 5% vs 6%), yet US registry data show two-thirds of non-male-factor cycles use it; ESHRE and ASRM advise against routine use.

dose.effective: Use conventional IVF when semen is normal; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
dose.studied_range: Sibling and randomised comparisons with WHO-normal semen.
dose.too_much: Extra cost and lab time; skips natural sperm selection at the egg's surface.
dose.timeframe: Fertilisation day.
dose.notes: Distinct from ICSI for genuine male factor, where it is the standard of care.

entries.mechanism: ICSI bypasses sperm binding and penetration; it rescues fertilisation when sperm cannot do this, but adds nothing when they can.
entries.interactions: Often combined with [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm]; high SDF is not by itself an indication for ICSI over IVF.
entries.caveats: Observational data even suggest slightly lower live birth with ICSI in non-male-factor cycles, but confounding is likely.
entries.debate: Some clinicians use ICSI routinely to avoid the small risk of total fertilisation failure; the Dang RCT found no difference in failure or live birth [fer-dang2021], and registry data found no benefit and slightly lower live birth (aRR 0.95) [fer-boulet2015]. ASRM and ESHRE advise against routine use [fer-asrm2020icsi, fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Live birth, ICSI vs conventional IVF (normal sperm)

entries.title: ICSI when sperm are normal (non-male-factor ICSI)

audit.claim: With normal semen, ICSI does not beat conventional IVF; reserve ICSI for male factor, prior fertilisation failure, PGT cycles or very few eggs.
audit.biases: Registry comparisons are confounded by indication; clinicians' belief that ICSI prevents total fertilisation failure drives use in poor-prognosis groups without trial support.
audit.newer_evidence: The Dang 2021 Lancet RCT stands (live birth 35% vs 31%, NS) [afert-dang2021]. A 2023 RCT in exactly the 'very few eggs / older women' group (age >=40 and/or <=4 oocytes, 336 cycles) found ICSI gave lower fertilisation (53% vs 62%) and no better live birth, and clearly worse results when both applied [afert-fancsovits2023].
audit.bottom_line: ICSI for normal sperm adds cost without benefit, including for older women and low egg numbers.

factors.name: Immunological tests and treatments (IVIG, intralipids, steroids, NK-cell testing)

entries.headline: No good evidence that 'immune' tests or treatments help IVF: a 715-woman RCT found prednisone did not raise live birth and increased early loss and preterm birth; HFEA rates IVIG and steroids red and intralipids grey.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research or a diagnosed autoimmune disease treated for its own sake.
dose.studied_range: IVIG 0.2-0.5 g/kg infusions; intralipid 20% infusions; prednisolone/dexamethasone around implantation.
dose.too_much: IVIG is a blood product (thrombosis, kidney injury, allergy); steroids raise infection risk, blood pressure and possibly preterm birth; intralipids can cause allergy in soy/egg-allergic people.
dose.timeframe: Given before and after embryo transfer.
dose.notes: Uterine or blood natural-killer-cell tests have no validated link to IVF outcome.

entries.mechanism: Premise that maternal immune cells (especially NK cells) reject the embryo; immune rejection of the fetus 'rarely, if ever, happens' according to HFEA.
entries.interactions: Often sold after recurrent implantation failure; ESHRE's RIF recommendations do not support immunomodulators [fer-eshre2023rif].
entries.caveats: Positive small trials and meta-analyses exist but are low quality.
entries.debate: A meta-analysis mixing RCTs and case-control studies reported higher live birth with IVIG (RR 1.62) [fer-li2013] and a 102-woman RCT reported higher live birth with intralipid (28.8% vs 10%) [fer-singh2019]. Cochrane is uncertain about glucocorticoids (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71) [fer-boomsma2022]; HFEA (red/grey) and ESHRE reject these treatments [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons, fer-eshre2023rif].
entries.title: Immunological tests and treatments (IVIG, intralipids, steroids, NK-cell testing)

audit.claim: No good evidence that immune testing or treatments help IVF; HFEA red for IVIG and steroids, grey for intralipids.
audit.biases: Positive data come from small or mixed-design studies (IVIG meta-analysis pooling case-control studies; a single 102-woman intralipid RCT).
audit.newer_evidence: A 715-woman JAMA RCT (2023) in recurrent implantation failure found prednisone did not raise live birth (37.8% vs 38.8%) and increased biochemical pregnancy loss (17.3% vs 9.9%) and preterm delivery (11.8% vs 5.5%) [afert-sun2023]. Cochrane remains uncertain for glucocorticoids (OR 1.37, 0.69-2.71) [afert-boomsma2022]. HFEA red for IVIG and steroids [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: The best trial of steroids found no benefit and signals of harm: avoid immune add-ons outside a trial.

entries.headline: Fitness is one of the strongest predictors of survival: each 1-MET higher VO2max (about 3.5 mL/kg/min) is associated with 11-17% lower mortality, and the least fit have about 4x the risk of the most fit, with no upper limit; but genetic analyses question how much of this is caused by fitness itself.

dose.effective: Aim to move out of the bottom fifth for your age and sex, then keep improving: each +1 MET counts. Combine 150+ min/week of aerobic activity with 1-2 weekly interval sessions (e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax); add sessions or intensity if fitness does not budge.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: fitness from under 5 to over 14 METs on treadmill tests; training studies: 60-300 min/week for 6-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: No upper limit of benefit was seen for measured fitness, even at the 98th percentile (elite).
dose.timeframe: VO2max rises measurably within 4-8 weeks of training; fitness change over years tracks mortality.
dose.notes: The lowest mortality in 750,302 veterans was at about 14 METs (roughly 49 mL/kg/min). In older adults (70-77 years), being moderately fit gave most of the benefit. 'Non-responders' to standard programs responded when weekly time or intensity was raised.

entries.mechanism: Training raises stroke volume, blood and haemoglobin volume, capillary density and muscle mitochondrial content (PGC-1alpha), via the same redox-signalling and hormesis pathways as [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. High fitness travels with lower blood pressure, visceral fat, insulin resistance and inflammation, all chronic ROS sources.
entries.interactions: Built by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and even [exercise-snacks]; strength gains appear to feed fitness ([resistance-training]). Lower body fat raises VO2max per kg ([weight-loss]).
entries.caveats: Baseline fitness and trainability partly reflect genes, body composition and health status, so people with undiagnosed disease test as 'unfit'. Most data come from people referred for treadmill tests. VO2max in mL/kg/min also falls with fat mass, so part of the signal is adiposity.
entries.debate: Proponents point to large, consistent cohorts with graded associations and no upper limit [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022, exr-kodama2009, exr-han2022, exr-lang2024], an AHA call to treat fitness as a vital sign [exr-ross2016], and evidence that improving fitness over time tracks lower mortality [exr-imboden2019]. Skeptics note that a two-sample Mendelian randomization found genetically predicted VO2max was not causally associated with longevity, while activity, lean mass and lower fat did raise VO2max [exr-kjaergaard2025], that genetic analyses point from strength to fitness rather than the reverse [exr-norris2024], that the certainty of the meta-analytic evidence is very low to moderate [exr-lang2024], and that the only long-term exercise RCT in older adults did not reduce mortality significantly [exr-stensvold2020]. In older adults, benefit may plateau above moderate fitness [exr-tari2025]. Trainability is also debated: non-response to standard doses disappears at higher doses [exr-montero2017] or intensities [exr-ross2015].

entries.title: Improving cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max)

timing.summary: Fitness rises measurably within 2-3 weeks of training and keeps rising for months with enough dose, and the mortality benefit comes from fitness held for years. It is lost faster than it is gained: recent gains disappear within about a month off.

onset.text: VO2peak rose 17.5% after 14 daily sessions [tbody-egan2013] and VO2max was higher within 3 weeks of training three times a week [tbody-murias2010].

full.text: Still rising at 12 weeks [tbody-murias2010]; people who do not respond at low doses respond when weekly training is increased [tbody-montero2017]. Over 5-6 years, gaining or keeping fitness was associated with 30-44% lower mortality than losing it or staying unfit [tbody-blair1995, tbody-lee2011].

after_stopping.text: VO2max fell 7% within 3 weeks and 16% by 8 weeks in trained people [tbody-coyle1984]; recently acquired gains are completely lost after more than 4 weeks [tbody-mujika2000b]; even 2 weeks of very low step counts cut VO2max 7% [tbody-kroghmadsen2010].

frequency.text: Two sessions a week at unchanged intensity maintained a training-induced VO2max rise for 15 weeks [tbody-hickson1981, tbody-spiering2021]; cutting intensity by a third did not [tbody-hickson1985].

timing.debate: Cohorts tie changes in fitness to mortality [tbody-lee2011, tbody-laukkanen2016], but Mendelian randomization found no clear causal effect of genetically higher VO2max on longevity [tbody-kjaergaard2025].

audit.claim: Each 1-MET higher VO2max is associated with 11-17% lower mortality with no upper limit, though genetic analyses question causality.
audit.biases: Fitness is partly heritable and lowered by undiagnosed disease and fat mass, so measured fitness marks health as well as training (genetic confounding, reverse causation) [abody-karvinen2015].
audit.newer_evidence: Large treadmill cohorts continue to show strong graded associations [abody-mandsager2018]. Against a large causal effect: genes shared between fitness and survival [abody-karvinen2015], a 2025 two-sample MR finding genetically predicted VO2max not causal for longevity [abody-kjaergaard2025], and no significant mortality reduction in the Generation 100 training trial [abody-stensvold2020].
audit.bottom_line: Fitness is an excellent risk marker; how much raising your own VO2max extends life is uncertain.

entries.headline: I3C (200-400 mg/day) and DIM reliably shift estrogen metabolism toward 2-hydroxylation, and I3C regressed cervical precancer in one 30-woman trial, but no trial shows fewer cancers, DIM lowered active tamoxifen metabolites, and high-dose I3C caused liver tumours in male mice and uterine cancer in female rats.

dose.effective: No outcome-based dose; 200-400 mg/day I3C or 300 mg/day DIM shifted estrogen metabolites.
dose.studied_range: I3C 200-1200 mg/day; DIM 150 mg twice daily for up to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Do not combine with tamoxifen (endoxifen fell). NTP found carcinogenicity at high gavage doses. DIM plasma levels plateau above about 1000 mg I3C.
dose.timeframe: Estrogen metabolite shift within 1 month.
dose.notes: I3C itself never reaches the blood; it condenses in stomach acid, and DIM is the only product detected in plasma. Eating crucifers gives a much smaller version of the same shift.

entries.mechanism: Acid-condensation products of I3C (chiefly DIM) activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and induce CYP1A enzymes that hydroxylate estradiol at C-2 rather than C-16; they are also weak Nrf2 inducers.
entries.interactions: Synergistic or additive with isothiocyanates (sulforaphane, PEITC) in cell Nrf2 assays. Food sources overlap [cruciferous-other] and [broccoli-mature]. Drug interaction with tamoxifen.
entries.caveats: The urinary 2:16-hydroxyestrone ratio is a surrogate with an uncertain link to cancer risk. The cervical trial is small and unreplicated. Higher catechol-estrogen levels could have long-term downsides. Marketing for 'estrogen detox' outruns the data.

key_numbers.label: Complete CIN regression on I3C (8 of 17) vs placebo (0 of 10)
Plasma DIM Cmax plateau (1000 mg I3C)

entries.title: Indole-3-carbinol (I3C) and DIM supplements

timing.summary: I3C shifts estrogen metabolism toward 2-hydroxylation within a week, through enzyme induction. The one lesion-regression trial ran 12 weeks; persistence after stopping was not measured.

onset.text: Urinary estrogen metabolites shifted after 1 week in men (and at 2 months in women) [tfood-michnovicz1997].

full.text: CIN regression was assessed at 12 weeks [tfood-bell2000].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily [tfood-michnovicz1997, tfood-bell2000].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: I3C/DIM shift estrogen metabolism, but no trial shows fewer cancers; DIM lowered tamoxifen metabolites; I3C carcinogenic in rodents.
audit.biases: Surrogate urinary ratio; small cervical trial.
audit.newer_evidence: No newer outcome trial; the DIM-tamoxifen RCT and NTP data stand [anut-thomson2017, anut-ntp2017].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

entries.headline: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but had no systemic effect in another; gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma, though the quality of that evidence is debated.

dose.effective: Use range hoods vented outdoors when cooking (especially on gas), keep wood stoves well-sealed and burning cleanly, avoid open fireplaces as daily heat, and ventilate.
dose.studied_range: Chamber studies: 3-4 h at 220-354 µg/m³ wood-smoke particles.
dose.too_much: Exposure in poorly vented homes with daily solid-fuel burning (much higher in low-income countries using biomass).
dose.timeframe: Airway markers changed within hours.
dose.notes: Electric or induction cooking removes the NO2 source.

entries.mechanism: Combustion particles and gases (NO2, aldehydes, PAHs) generate airway ROS and inflammation; NO2 is itself an oxidant.
entries.interactions: Similar pathways to [outdoor-air-pollution]; mitigated by [hepa-air-purifier] for particles.
entries.caveats: Controlled wood-smoke studies are small and inconsistent. The gas-stove literature is mostly cross-sectional; a 2013 meta-analysis found OR 1.32 for asthma while a 2023 review judged the evidence too low-quality for causal conclusions.
entries.title: Indoor combustion: wood stoves, fireplaces, gas cooking

timing.summary: Burning things indoors acts within hours: a 4-hour wood-smoke exposure raised airway oxidative markers [tleg-barregard2008], and the exposure stops when the fire or burner does. Fixing the source works on two timescales - indoor NO2 falls within a week of replacing a gas stove [tleg-paulin2014], while symptom and health changes take a couple of months [tleg-sehgal2026].

onset.text: Four hours of 240-280 ug/m3 wood smoke raised malondialdehyde in exhaled breath condensate and alveolar nitric oxide [tleg-barregard2008]. HEPA/carbon purifiers cut kitchen NO2 immediately by 27%, and stove replacement by 51% at 3 months [tleg-paulin2014].

full.text: Exposure changes are complete within days to weeks of fixing the source [tleg-paulin2014]; clinical change takes longer - asthma control improved over the 2-3 months after gas stoves were swapped for electric [tleg-sehgal2026], and community wheeze reports fell over the winters after a wood-stove change-out [tleg-noonan2011].

after_stopping.text: Acute airway effects resolve within hours to a day of leaving the smoke [tleg-barregard2008]. Reverting to the old appliance restores the exposure immediately, since nothing is stored.

frequency.text: The dose is per burn, so the frequency of fires and gas cooking is what matters. Extraction that actually vents outdoors is necessary: in a randomized comparison, installing a ventilation hood over an unvented gas stove did not measurably lower NO2, while replacing the stove or adding HEPA/carbon purifiers did [tleg-paulin2014].

timing.debate: Whether modest wood-smoke exposures do anything systemic is contested: one chamber study found airway oxidative stress within hours [tleg-barregard2008] while another, at similar particle levels, found no effect on oxidative DNA damage, inflammation or microvascular function [tleg-forchhammer2012]. The gas-cooking and childhood-asthma literature is likewise disputed, with a systematic review by consultancy-affiliated authors judging 66 studies too weak for causal inference [tleg-li2023gas], while the stove-replacement study is uncontrolled and before-after [tleg-sehgal2026].

audit.claim: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but not systemic markers in another, and gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma though the evidence quality is debated (general impact 2, limited).
audit.biases: Gas-cooking studies are mostly cross-sectional with self-reported exposure and residual confounding by income, crowding, damp and smoking [eia-li2023gas]; reviewers critical of the evidence were consultancy- or industry-linked [eia-li2023gas, eia-li2024gas]. Stove-swap evidence is an uncontrolled before-after design open to regression to the mean and seasonal change [eia-sehgal2026]. Chamber studies are small and short [eia-barregard2008, eia-forchhammer2012].
audit.newer_evidence: Randomized cookstove trials in low-income countries are the big update: switching biomass to LPG cut personal PM2.5 from about 71 to 24 ug/m3 yet did not change birth weight (2022) [eia-clasen2022] or severe infant pneumonia (2024) [eia-mccollum2024], and cleaner biomass stoves did not reduce child pneumonia (2017) [eia-mortimer2017]. In rural US wood-stove homes, air filters and education did not reduce child respiratory infections, although infections rose with measured PM2.5 (2022) [eia-walker2022], and wood-stove changeouts did not lower indoor PM2.5 while filters cut it 63% (2017) [eia-ward2017]. On gas: replacing gas with electric stoves lowered NO2 51% in an RCT (2014) [eia-paulin2014] and improved asthma control in an uncontrolled study (2026) [eia-sehgal2026]; gas burners emit benzene (2023) [eia-kashtan2023]; removing unflued gas heaters reduced asthma symptoms in randomized trials [eia-pilotto2004, eia-howdenchapman2008].
audit.bottom_line: Reducing smoke is worthwhile, but partial reductions (still above WHO levels) have not delivered clinical benefit in large trials, and newer stoves alone did not lower indoor particles where filters did.

entries.headline: HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by roughly half to two-thirds and lower blood pressure by about 2-4 mmHg and some inflammatory markers within days, but longer trials in children with asthma, pregnant women and older adults have mostly found no clinical benefit.

dose.effective: Run a HEPA purifier sized for the room (check its clean-air delivery rate) continuously in the bedroom and main living space when outdoor or indoor PM2.5 is elevated, with windows closed.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 48 h to 1 week of real vs sham purification in dormitories with outdoor PM2.5 roughly 40-100 µg/m³.
dose.timeframe: Effects within 48 h to 1 week; they disappear when purification stops.
dose.notes: Benefits are largest where indoor air is polluted; in clean-air regions the gain is small.

entries.mechanism: Removes redox-active particles before they reach the lungs, reducing airway NADPH-oxidase activation, inflammatory cell activation and systemic lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: Counters [outdoor-air-pollution] and [indoor-combustion-smoke]; does not remove gases like NO2 unless the unit has activated carbon.
entries.caveats: Trials were short, in young healthy Chinese students exposed to high pollution; long-term clinical outcomes are not yet shown.
entries.title: Indoor HEPA air purification

timing.summary: A HEPA purifier is a tap, not a treatment: oxidative and inflammatory markers and blood pressure improve within 48 hours to a week of switching it on [tleg-chen2015, tleg-wang2021], and the benefit goes away when it is switched off. Nothing accumulates, so it has to run continuously to do anything.

onset.text: Forty-eight hours of real versus sham filtration cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% and lowered myeloperoxidase by 33% along with blood pressure [tleg-chen2015]; one week lowered urinary 8-isoprostane, exhaled nitric oxide and diastolic pressure [tleg-wang2021].

full.text: Pooled sham-controlled home trials lasting a median of 13.5 days found about a 4 mmHg fall in systolic blood pressure with no sign that longer studies did better [tleg-walzer2020], so the effect appears to plateau within about 2 weeks.

after_stopping.text: Crossover designs are the evidence: markers and blood pressure return toward baseline during sham periods, i.e. within days of filtration stopping [tleg-chen2015, tleg-wang2021].

frequency.text: Continuous operation in the rooms where you spend most time, especially the bedroom. Because the biological effect follows the exposure within days, intermittent use buys only intermittent benefit; filters also need maintenance to keep working.

sperm.late_start: Unknown. Filtration changes exposure the same day, but any semen effect would require the full spermatogenic cycle, and the only study to try it (a year of indoor purification in infertile men) found no improvement [tleg-paradisi2009].
sperm.text: Air-pollution exposure windows for sperm span the 90 days before ejaculation [tleg-sun2020], so a purifier would in principle need to run for that whole period; this has not been tested successfully [tleg-paradisi2009].

egg.late_start: Running a purifier only during ovarian stimulation targets the window with the strongest observational signal [tleg-gaskins2019], but no trial has tested this.
egg.text: Filtration lowers exposure immediately [tleg-chen2015]; whether that improves IVF outcomes has not been tested, and the one pregnancy trial of HEPA filters found no overall birth-weight benefit [tleg-barn2018].

timing.debate: How much the short-term marker changes mean is contested. One meta-analysis found a 4 mmHg systolic fall [tleg-walzer2020] and another found only 2.3 mmHg with no change in CRP or endothelial function and graded the certainty as very low, explicitly warning against strong claims [tleg-xia2021]; a third found 7% lower CRP and 13% lower IL-6 [tleg-wittkopp2022]. The only hard-outcome trial, HEPA filters through pregnancy in a highly polluted city, missed its primary endpoint [tleg-barn2018].

audit.claim: Sham-controlled crossover trials show HEPA purifiers halve indoor PM2.5 and lower oxidative and inflammatory markers and blood pressure within days (general impact 3, moderate).
audit.biases: Most positive trials are 2-day to 2-week crossovers in young adults in very polluted Chinese cities, measuring surrogate markers with many outcomes tested [eia-chen2015, eia-wang2021]; GRADE certainty for cardiovascular outcomes is very low [eia-xia2021]. Small-study and publication bias are likely in a field of short, small surrogate trials.
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analyses agree on a small systolic BP fall of about 2-4 mmHg (2020-2021) [eia-walzer2020, eia-xia2021] and 7% lower CRP and 13% lower IL-6 (2022) [eia-wittkopp2022], and a Detroit seniors trial found -3.2 mmHg over 3 days (2018) [eia-morishita2018]. But longer or clinical-outcome trials are mostly null: 4 weeks of bedroom HEPA did not change home BP in older adults (2026) [eia-brook2026]; 12 weeks of HEPA in 164 children with asthma cut PM2.5 64% with no improvement in symptoms or lung function (2025) [eia-qiu2025]; filters did not reduce child respiratory infections in wood-stove homes (2022) [eia-walker2022]; and HEPA cleaners in pregnancy in Ulaanbaatar did not raise birth weight overall (2018) [eia-barn2018]. The only fertility attempt (1 year of purification in 10 infertile men) found no semen improvement [eia-paradisi2009].
audit.bottom_line: Purifiers reliably cut indoor particles and nudge short-term blood pressure and inflammation markers, but trials of weeks to months have not shown clinical benefit outside very polluted settings. Worth using during smoke events, high-pollution periods or with indoor sources, not as a proven health intervention.

entries.headline: Radon raises lung cancer risk about 16% per 100 Bq/m3 of long-term exposure with no safe threshold; for a lifelong non-smoker that is roughly 0.4% to 0.7% lifetime risk at 0 vs 400 Bq/m3, but for smokers it is 10% to 16%, so testing and fixing high homes matters most for smokers and ex-smokers.

dose.effective: Test your home with a passive detector for at least 3 months (lowest lived-in floor); if above 100 Bq/m3 (WHO reference level; US EPA action level 148 Bq/m3 = 4 pCi/L) install sub-slab depressurisation (more than 80% reduction in most remediated homes) or improve under-floor ventilation; quit smoking, which removes most of the radon-related risk.
dose.studied_range: European controls averaged 97 Bq/m3; 11% of homes were above 200 and 4% above 400 Bq/m3.
dose.too_much: WHO: national reference level 100 Bq/m3, not above 300 Bq/m3.
dose.timeframe: Risk reflects exposure 5-34 years before diagnosis; the excess risk from past exposure fades over decades rather than months.
dose.notes: Radon is unrelated to how clean or modern a home looks; levels vary by geology and by house, so only measurement tells.

entries.mechanism: Radon decay products deposit in airways and emit alpha particles that produce dense ionization tracks, double-strand DNA breaks and reactive oxygen species, including in neighbouring (bystander) cells; ROS generation is one proposed basis of the synergy with tobacco smoke [eia-sethi2012]. Antioxidants have not been shown to modify the risk.
entries.interactions: Multiplicative with [tobacco-smoking] (about 25 times higher absolute risk in smokers at the same radon level). Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers radon modestly; sub-slab systems work better.
entries.caveats: Lung cancer is the only established outcome. No fertility or pregnancy effects are established at residential levels. Single short-term tests misclassify annual exposure.
entries.debate: Pooled case-control studies with measured home radon in Europe and North America found a linear, no-threshold increase consistent with miner data [eia-darby2005, eia-krewski2005]. A county-level ecological analysis found the opposite (more radon, less lung cancer) and was used to argue for a threshold or protective hormesis [eia-cohen1995]; re-analysis showed the same negative correlation for all smoking-related cancers but not others, i.e. confounding by smoking [eia-puskin2003]. For smokers, modelling shows quitting reduces radon-related risk more than mitigation does [eia-mendez1998].
