Lifetime risk to 75, smoker at 400 Bq/m3

entries.title: Indoor radon

timing.summary: Radon acts on a decades-long clock: lung cancer risk reflects home exposure 5-34 years earlier [eia-darby2005]. Mitigation lowers indoor radon within days of installing a sub-slab system [eia-groveskirkby2008], but past exposure keeps contributing risk for years.

onset.text: Risk was estimated from radon in homes lived in 5-34 years before diagnosis [eia-darby2005].

full.text: Risk keeps rising with cumulative exposure over decades [eia-darby2005, eia-krewski2005].

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated: excess risk from past exposure fades over decades, not months, since the relevant window extends to 34 years back [eia-darby2005]. Indoor radon itself drops by more than 80% after sub-slab depressurisation in most homes [eia-groveskirkby2008].

frequency.text: Test once for at least 3 months (retest after renovations); mitigation is a one-off installation that runs continuously [eia-whoradonfs].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the dispute is about low-dose risk [eia-cohen1995, eia-puskin2003].

entries.headline: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction, and carry a higher coronary risk per gram than any other fat.

dose.effective: As close to zero as possible from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts and controlled feeding studies.
dose.too_much: Any regular intake from partially hydrogenated oils.
dose.timeframe: Years.
dose.notes: Now banned or restricted in many countries; still present in some imported or older products.

entries.mechanism: Altered lipoprotein metabolism and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), endothelial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Often co-occurs with [oxidized-frying-oils] in fried fast food.
entries.caveats: The oxidative-stress component is one part of a broader cardiometabolic harm.
entries.title: Industrial trans fats

timing.summary: The lipid damage from trans fat shows up in 3 weeks: at 10% of energy it lowered HDL by 0.17 mmol/L and raised LDL within a 3-week feeding period [tleg-mensink1990]. Population-level removal paid off within about 3 years - Denmark's ban was followed by about 14 fewer cardiovascular deaths per 100,000 per year [tleg-restrepo2016], and New York's restrictions by 6-8% fewer heart attacks and strokes after 3 or more years [tleg-brandt2017].

onset.text: Blood lipid changes are measurable within the first weeks of a change in intake: a 3-week diet period was enough to show the full HDL and LDL effect [tleg-mensink1990].

full.text: Lipids reach a new steady state within about 3-4 weeks [tleg-mensink1990]; cardiovascular event rates in populations changed detectably 3 years after restrictions [tleg-brandt2017, tleg-restrepo2016]. Tissue trans fatty acids follow adipose turnover, a half-life of 200-270 days [tleg-strawford2004].

after_stopping.text: Lipid profile recovers over weeks once intake stops [tleg-mensink1990], while trans fatty acids already stored in adipose wash out over months to years, by the same kinetics as other fatty acids [tleg-strawford2004, tleg-arner2011].

frequency.text: This is a dose-average exposure rather than an acute one: what matters is habitual grams per day, since the lipid effect was demonstrated with 3 weeks of sustained intake [tleg-mensink1990]. There is no 'safe day' structure to exploit.

timing.debate: The feeding-trial lipid effect is uncontested; the speed of the population benefit is where interpretation varies, since both the Danish and New York analyses are natural experiments relying on synthetic or neighbouring controls and on the assumption that nothing else changed in the same 3-year window [tleg-restrepo2016, tleg-brandt2017].

audit.claim: Industrial trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL, promote inflammation and carry the highest coronary risk per gram of any fat.
audit.biases: Much of the original evidence was cohort-based, open to confounding by fast-food diets [adiet-mozaffarian2006b].
audit.newer_evidence: A natural experiment in New York State showed counties that restricted trans fat had a 6.2% extra drop in MI and stroke admissions versus comparable counties (2017) [adiet-brandt2017], a design that sidesteps individual confounding. The 2025 Burden of Proof review rated the dose-response evidence two stars, with at least 3% higher IHD risk across usual intakes [adiet-haile2025].
audit.bottom_line: The harm is about as well established as any diet finding; most countries have now removed most industrial trans fat, so the practical risk is lower than before.

factors.name: Inorganic arsenic in rice and rice products

entries.headline: Rice is the main dietary source of inorganic arsenic (urinary arsenic rises 14% per quarter cup in children; infant rice cereal tripled infant urinary arsenic), and cooking in excess water or parboiling then absorbing removes 45-73%, but eating rice was not linked to cardiovascular disease in large US cohorts.

dose.effective: Rinse rice, then either cook it like pasta in 6-10 parts water and drain (about 45% less inorganic arsenic) or parboil 5 min in fresh water, drain, and finish with absorption (54% less in brown, 73% in white). Vary grains (oats, barley, quinoa, buckwheat) rather than relying on rice; limit rice cakes, rice milk and rice cereal for infants and toddlers; basmati and jasmine tend to be lower.
dose.studied_range: Usual rice intake from <1 to >5 servings a week; rice with 100-300 ug/kg arsenic.
dose.too_much: EFSA reference point 0.06 ug/kg body weight per day (margin of exposure 0.4-2 for European adults = concern). Genotoxic effects were seen with staple rice >200 ug/kg arsenic in West Bengal.
dose.timeframe: Urinary arsenic reflects the last few days of intake; cancer risk is lifetime.
dose.notes: Brown rice has more arsenic than white (in the bran) but also more fibre and minerals; excess-water cooking loses some potassium, magnesium and B vitamins. Cooking with arsenic-contaminated water adds arsenic.

entries.mechanism: Paddy rice takes up arsenite from flooded soil via silicon transporters. Inorganic arsenic depletes glutathione, generates ROS during methylation and impairs DNA repair; high-arsenic rice eaters had more urothelial micronuclei [efw-banerjee2013].
entries.interactions: Adds to [arsenic-drinking-water]. Brown rice vs white trades fibre ([whole-grains]) against arsenic. Gluten-free diets often rely heavily on rice.
entries.caveats: Urinary arsenic includes organic arsenic from seafood unless speciated. No cohort has linked usual rice intake to a hard outcome; cancer risk estimates are extrapolated from drinking-water studies.
entries.debate: Exposure is clear [efw-davis2012, efw-wei2014, efw-karagas2016, efw-mantha2017] and EFSA judges European exposure a health concern [efw-efsa2024]. Outcome data are reassuring so far: no CVD increase with >=5 servings a week in US cohorts [efw-muraki2015], though genotoxic markers rose with high-arsenic staple rice in India [efw-banerjee2013]. Brown rice: higher arsenic [efw-scott2025] versus higher nutrients [efw-menon2021].

key_numbers.label: Urinary arsenic rise per 1/4 cup rice (children)
Inorganic As removed: parboil + absorb (white rice)
Inorganic As removed: parboil + absorb (brown rice)

entries.title: Inorganic arsenic in rice and rice products

entries.headline: Intermittent fasting helps mainly by making people eat less: across 99 RCTs it beat ad libitum eating, but matched calorie restriction about equally (Cochrane: -0.56 kg difference over 3-12 months), and calorie-matched trials show no fasting-specific drop in oxidative stress markers.

dose.effective: Any form you can sustain that produces a modest energy deficit: an 8-10 h daily eating window, alternate-day fasting (~500 kcal or zero on fast days), or 2 days/week of 500-600 kcal (5:2). See [time-restricted-eating], [alternate-day-fasting], [five-two-diet].
dose.studied_range: Daily fasts of 12-20 h, 24-36 h alternate-day fasts, 2 days/week at ~25% of needs, for 3 weeks to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Daily eating windows under ~6 h and multi-day fasts increase lean-mass loss; not for pregnancy, eating disorders, underweight, type 1 diabetes, or insulin/sulfonylurea users without medical adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Weight and insulin changes within 4-12 weeks; oxidative stress markers follow weight loss.
dose.notes: Fasting length matters physiologically (ketones barely rise before ~20 h), but for health outcomes the total energy deficit matters far more than the pattern.

entries.mechanism: Energy deficit and weight loss lower insulin, adipose inflammation and mitochondrial ROS production. Longer fasts add a metabolic switch to fatty acids and ketones; beta-hydroxybutyrate can inhibit class I HDACs and induce FOXO3A and metallothionein (mouse data). Early eating windows align intake with circadian insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Effects largely overlap with [calorie-restriction] and [weight-loss]; benefits are biggest with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control] problems. Pair with [resistance-training] and adequate protein to limit lean loss. Diet quality still matters: fasting does not offset [overfeeding] on eating days. Late, short windows can shorten sleep; see [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Most claims about autophagy, 'cellular cleanup' and longevity come from rodents. Calorie-matched trials (Templeman 2021, Liu 2022, Peters 2025) found no fasting-specific benefit. Only modified alternate-day fasting for BMI reached high-quality evidence in an umbrella review, and IF is associated with fat-free mass loss. The early eTRF oxidative stress result (n = 8) was driven partly by worsening on the control schedule.

key_numbers.label: IF vs continuous restriction, weight at 3-12 months (Cochrane)
ADF vs continuous restriction, weight (network meta-analysis)

entries.title: Intermittent fasting (umbrella: TRE, alternate-day, 5:2, periodic)

timing.summary: Some glucose and insulin effects appear within days, but the main benefit is weight loss building over about six months and matching ordinary dieting. Benefits fade as weight returns.

onset.text: Four days of early time-restricted eating lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-jamshed2019]; 15 days of alternate 20-h fasts improved insulin action [tbody-halberg2005].

full.text: Weight loss plateaued by 6-12 months and matched daily restriction [tbody-trepanowski2017, tbody-liu2022].

after_stopping.text: Not measured specifically; long-term weight maintenance after any diet is poor [tbody-anderson2001].

frequency.text: Daily windows, alternate days and 2 days a week all perform about like continuous restriction [tbody-allaf2021]; choose by sustainability.

timing.debate: Early time-restricted feeding improved insulin sensitivity and oxidative stress without weight loss in 5 weeks [tbody-sutton2018], but isocaloric 8-h windows for 2 weeks [tbody-peters2025] and calorie-matched TRE over 12 months [tbody-liu2022] showed no extra benefit.

audit.claim: Intermittent fasting works mainly by reducing calories; it matches calorie restriction and shows no fasting-specific oxidative benefit.
audit.biases: Early positive findings came from uncontrolled or tiny studies; calorie-matched designs remove confounding by energy deficit [adiet-templeman2021].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 BMJ network meta-analysis of 99 RCTs [adiet-semnaniazad2025] and a 2025 meta-analysis of 20 isocaloric RCTs [adiet-hamsho2025] found IF not superior to continuous restriction, with more hunger. Calorie-matched TRE (Liu 2022, Peters 2025) added nothing [adiet-liu2022c, adiet-peters2025]; Cochrane agrees [adiet-allaf2021].
audit.bottom_line: Confirmed: fasting schedules are a way to eat less, not a separate antioxidant intervention.

entries.headline: Two RCTs in poor responders found no gain in euploid embryos (one null on every outcome, one with ~1.5 more mature eggs over three retrievals); HFEA rates it red for safety and lack of evidence, and ESHRE does not recommend it.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: Autologous PRP injected transvaginally into each ovary, usually 1-3 months before stimulation.
dose.too_much: Needle injection under anaesthesia: infection, bleeding, anaesthetic risk; no standard preparation.
dose.timeframe: Claims of effect within 1-3 months; not borne out in RCTs.
dose.notes: Marketed for low AMH, perimenopause and premature ovarian insufficiency.

entries.mechanism: Platelet growth factors (PDGF, VEGF, TGF-beta) are claimed to activate dormant follicles or improve the ovarian microenvironment; no human evidence of new or better eggs.
entries.interactions: Does not change [maternal-age]-driven aneuploidy; compare [growth-hormone-ivf-egg] and [dhea] in the same poor-responder population.
entries.caveats: Most supporting studies are uncontrolled case series.
entries.debate: The double-blind Barrenetxea RCT found slightly more cumulative mature eggs (10.45 vs 8.91) but identical euploid blastocysts [fer-barrenetxea2024]; the PROVA RCT found no effect at all [fer-herlihy2024]. Cochrane rates the evidence very low certainty [fer-vaidakis2024]; HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: Mature eggs per cycle, PRP vs control (PROVA)

entries.title: Intraovarian platelet-rich plasma ('ovarian rejuvenation')

timing.summary: Ovarian PRP is promoted with the claim that it wakes dormant follicles, which would take months to show. A trial that followed three retrievals after injection found at most one or two more eggs and no more chromosomally normal embryos.

onset.text: Effect, if any, appeared only by the third consecutive retrieval [tegg-barrenetxea2024].

full.text: Not established.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Single injection in trials.

timing.debate: One RCT reported slightly more mature eggs cumulatively over three retrievals [tegg-barrenetxea2024]; the PROVA RCT found no change in eggs, euploid blastocysts, AMH or AFC [tegg-herlihy2024].

audit.claim: Two RCTs in poor responders found no gain in euploid embryos; HFEA red.
audit.biases: Supporting data are uncontrolled case series.
audit.newer_evidence: PROVA RCT null [afert-herlihy2024]; Cochrane very low certainty [afert-vaidakis2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

factors.name: Intrauterine hCG infusion before embryo transfer

entries.headline: An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of the 7 trustworthy RCTs (2244 women, 2026) found no effect on live birth (OR 0.99); the earlier 'benefit' came only from trials that failed integrity checks.

dose.effective: Not recommended. The only positive subgroup used >=500 IU before cleavage-stage transfer.
dose.studied_range: 100-1000 IU urinary or recombinant hCG infused minutes to days before transfer.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Not on the HFEA rating list.

entries.mechanism: hCG made by the embryo signals to the endometrium (angiogenesis, immune tolerance, decidualisation); infusion aims to mimic this early.
entries.interactions: Irrelevant to most current cycles, which use blastocyst transfer.
entries.caveats: Most trials at high risk of bias, with very high heterogeneity.
entries.debate: Cochrane rated the cleavage-stage >=500 IU benefit as moderate quality [fer-craciunas2018]; ESHRE judged the evidence conflicting and does not recommend it [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Intrauterine hCG infusion before embryo transfer

audit.claim: Cochrane found a live-birth benefit only for day-3 transfers with >=500 IU and no evidence for blastocyst transfer; ESHRE does not recommend it.
audit.biases: The Cochrane subgroup benefit came from trials later found untrustworthy: in a 2026 IPD meta-analysis none of the trials that did not provide individual data met trustworthiness criteria, and those trials alone produced the positive effect [afert-zou2026]. This is a textbook example of research-integrity bias inflating a meta-analysis [afert-li2020].
audit.newer_evidence: IPD meta-analysis (2026) of 7 trustworthy RCTs, 2244 women: live birth OR 0.99 (0.83-1.19), clinical pregnancy OR 1.04; untrustworthy non-IPD trials showed OR 1.87 for pregnancy (P for interaction 0.005) [afert-zou2026]. Cochrane 2018 had rated the cleavage-stage subgroup moderate quality [afert-craciunas2018].
audit.bottom_line: Intrauterine hCG does not work; the apparent benefit came from unreliable trials.

entries.headline: Pooled small trials suggest higher pregnancy after implantation failure, but the only low-risk-of-bias trial showed no clear effect on live birth (OR 1.10, 0.38-3.14); HFEA rates intrauterine PRP red for every indication.

dose.effective: Not recommended outside research.
dose.studied_range: 0.5-1 mL autologous PRP infused into the uterus 1-2 days before transfer or in the proliferative phase.
dose.too_much: Infection, bleeding, allergic reaction; preparations unstandardised.
dose.timeframe: Embryo-transfer cycle.
dose.notes: Marketed for thin endometrium, recurrent implantation failure and Asherman's syndrome.

entries.mechanism: Growth factors claimed to thicken the endometrium and promote angiogenesis and receptivity.
entries.interactions: Usually offered alongside other implantation add-ons ([endometrial-scratch-egg], [immune-addons-egg]).
entries.caveats: Positive pooled results come from high-risk-of-bias trials.
entries.debate: Including all trials, Cochrane found higher live birth/ongoing pregnancy (OR 2.38) but rated it very low certainty and the low-risk trial was null [fer-vaidakis2024]. HFEA red [fer-hfea2026prp]; ESHRE not recommended [fer-eshre2023addons].
entries.title: Intrauterine platelet-rich plasma

audit.claim: Pooled small trials suggest benefit but the only low-risk trial was null; HFEA red.
audit.biases: High-risk-of-bias trials drive the pooled effect.
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane 2024 and HFEA as cited [afert-vaidakis2024, afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: IV glutathione is cleared from blood with a half-life of ~14 minutes; oral glutathione raised blood stores 17-35% in one 6-month RCT, but no trial shows clinical benefit for oxidative stress.

dose.effective: Not recommended. Oral trial used 250-1000 mg/day for 6 months; levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping.
dose.studied_range: IV: single 2 g/m² infusion pharmacokinetics; oral: 6-month RCT.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown; usual infusion risks apply to IV use.
dose.timeframe: IV effect gone within about an hour; oral effect builds over months and reverses within a month.
dose.notes: Cells make their own glutathione from cysteine, glycine and glutamate; exercise, sleep and not smoking support it.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous glutathione is broken down in plasma and by gamma-glutamyl transferase into amino acids; cells resynthesize glutathione internally.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle factors that preserve glutathione: avoiding [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol], [short-sleep] correction.
entries.caveats: Biomarker increases do not equal health benefit; no outcome trials.
entries.title: Intravenous (IV) or oral glutathione

timing.summary: Intravenous glutathione gives only a brief spike; modelling suggested redosing every 3-7 hours to keep its breakdown products up. Oral glutathione raised blood stores slowly over 1-6 months in one trial, but levels returned to baseline within a month of stopping, and a 4-week trial saw nothing.

onset.text: Oral: blood glutathione up at the first check, 1 month [tnut-richie2015]; 4 weeks of 1 g/day showed no change in another trial [tnut-allen2011].

full.text: Still rising at 6 months (30-35% on 1 g/day) [tnut-richie2015].

after_stopping.text: Oral: back to baseline by a 1-month washout [tnut-richie2015]. IV: modelling suggested redosing every 3.4-7 h to sustain metabolites [tnut-hong2005].

frequency.text: Not recommended; IV effects are too brief to matter and oral effects need continuous daily use [tnut-richie2015, tnut-hong2005].

timing.debate: A 6-month trial found oral glutathione raised body stores [tnut-richie2015], whereas a 4-week trial found no change [tnut-allen2011]; duration may explain the difference.

audit.claim: IV glutathione is cleared in ~14 minutes; oral raised stores 17-35% in one RCT; no clinical benefit shown.
audit.biases: Biomarker-only outcomes [anut-richie2015].
audit.newer_evidence: No outcome trial found; PK unchanged [anut-aebi1991].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Mild iodine deficiency is linked in cohorts to slower conception and lower child verbal IQ, but a randomised trial of iodine in mildly deficient pregnant women found no IQ benefit; avoid deficiency rather than supplement high.

dose.effective: RDA 150 ug/day (220 pregnancy, 290 lactation). Iodised salt, dairy, eggs and seafood are main sources. The American Thyroid Association recommends a 150 ug/day iodine supplement (as potassium iodide) before and during pregnancy and lactation.
dose.studied_range: Observational urinary iodine:creatinine ratios (<50 to >150 ug/g).
dose.too_much: UL 1100 ug/day (IOM) or 600 ug/day (EFSA). Kelp supplements, amiodarone and contrast media can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism in susceptible people.
dose.timeframe: Thyroid stores build over months; fetal brain depends on maternal thyroxine in the first trimester.
dose.notes: At risk: vegans and people avoiding dairy, fish and iodised salt (sea salt and specialty salts are usually not iodised), pregnancy, regions without salt iodisation (e.g. UK).

entries.mechanism: Iodine is the substrate for thyroid hormones, which set mitochondrial metabolic rate and drive fetal brain development. Thyroid hormone synthesis itself uses H2O2 (thyroid peroxidase), protected by selenium-dependent GPx.
entries.interactions: Selenium supports thyroid peroxidase protection and deiodinases [selenium-supplement]. Delivered by most prenatal multivitamins [multivitamin-mineral].
entries.caveats: Fertility data come from a single cohort of 501 women; no RCT tests iodine for conception or child IQ in mildly deficient populations.
entries.debate: Observational data link mild deficiency to child cognition [nut-bath2013] and slower conception [nut-mills2018], prompting calls for action [nut-stagnarogreen2013] and supplement recommendations [nut-alexander2017, nut-korevaar2026]. The counterweight is that iodine has a U-curve too: excess can trigger thyroid dysfunction [nut-sohn2024], and the Mills result needs replication, as the authors themselves note [nut-mills2018].

key_numbers.label: Low child verbal IQ, maternal iodine <150 ug/g
Global share with inadequate iodine intake (food only)

entries.title: Iodine status

timing.summary: The thyroid stores iodine, so status reflects months of intake, and a sudden increase in early pregnancy can transiently raise TSH. Women who had used iodised salt for years before pregnancy had better thyroid function than those who started supplements in early pregnancy.

onset.text: Not measured as an onset.

full.text: Thyroid stores build over months (not precisely measured); long-term iodised salt users (>2 years) fared best [tegg-moleti2011].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Daily intake; no schedule comparison.

timing.debate: A systematic review found insufficient evidence that iodine supplementation in mildly deficient pregnancy helps thyroid function or child cognition, and called for trials accounting for preconception stores [tegg-dineva2020]; observational data favour early, long-term intake [tegg-moleti2011, tegg-mills2018].

egg.late_start: Starting 150 ug iodine only in early pregnancy reduced low-FT4 but raised TSH, possibly a "stunning" effect of the abrupt change [tegg-moleti2011].
egg.text: Moderate-to-severe iodine deficiency was linked to 46% lower fecundability [tegg-mills2018]; the 90-day lead is extrapolated from the advice to start "several months" before conception [tegg-moleti2011].

audit.claim: Even mild iodine deficiency matters around conception: very low urinary iodine cut fecundability 46%, and mildly deficient UK mothers' children had higher odds of low verbal IQ (OR 1.58).
audit.biases: Measurement error (single spot urine for a nutrient that varies day to day, acknowledged by the authors) and residual confounding [afert-mills2018, afert-bath2013].
audit.newer_evidence: The only adequately powered RCT in mildly deficient pregnant women (832 women, 2017) found 200 ug/day iodine did not improve child IQ or executive function [afert-gowachirapant2017]; a 2020 meta-analysis found no cognitive effect in pooled RCTs and insufficient evidence for supplementation recommendations [afert-dineva2020]. A 2019 IPD meta-analysis of 6180 mother-child pairs found UI/Creat <150 ug/g not significantly linked to IQ, with a curvilinear verbal-IQ association limited to the first trimester [afert-levie2019]. The fecundability finding has not been replicated [afert-mills2018].
audit.bottom_line: Avoiding real deficiency is sensible (iodised salt, dairy, a prenatal with iodine), but trials have not shown that topping up mild deficiency improves children's IQ, and the fertility link is a single study.

entries.headline: Iron deficiency is one of the world's leading nutritional harms: even without anaemia it causes fatigue (iron cut fatigue scores 48% vs 29% placebo in women with ferritin <50 ug/L), and in pregnancy anaemia is linked to ~30% more low birthweight and ~60% more preterm birth.

dose.effective: Treat documented deficiency: typical oral regimens give 40-100 mg elemental iron once daily or on alternate days for about 3 months, then recheck ferritin; 80 mg/day for 12 weeks was used in the fatigue RCT. Prevention: RDA 8 mg/day (men, postmenopausal women), 18 mg/day (menstruating women), 27 mg/day (pregnancy); vegetarians need ~1.8x more because non-heme iron is less bioavailable.
dose.studied_range: Oral iron 60-80 mg/day in most adult trials; prenatal 30-60 mg/day.
dose.too_much: Continuing high-dose iron after repletion pushes stores up [iron-excess]; IOM UL 45 mg/day (GI effects) applies to healthy people, not to supervised treatment.
dose.timeframe: Haemoglobin rises within 2-4 weeks; ferritin repletion takes ~3 months; fatigue improved by 12 weeks.
dose.notes: At-risk groups: heavy menstrual bleeding, pregnancy, infants and adolescents, vegans/vegetarians, frequent blood donors, endurance athletes, coeliac disease and other GI disease, bariatric surgery, chronic PPI use. In men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency needs investigation for GI blood loss.

entries.mechanism: Iron is needed for haemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial cytochromes and iron-sulfur clusters, catalase and many DNA-synthesis enzymes. Deficiency impairs oxygen delivery and mitochondrial energy production, immunity and brain neurotransmitter synthesis. It is not an 'antioxidant' state: anaemia is itself associated with oxidative stress in red cells.
entries.interactions: Frequent donation can cause it [blood-donation]. Vitamin C-rich foods with meals raise non-heme absorption [vitamin-c-foods]; tea and coffee with meals reduce it [green-tea] [coffee]. For fertility relevance see [iron-egg].
entries.caveats: Ferritin is the best single test but is falsely raised by inflammation; in that setting transferrin saturation <20% helps. Cognitive benefits of iron in non-anaemic people are less certain than fatigue benefits.
entries.debate: That deficiency harms health is not contested [nut-pasricha2021]. Debate centres on thresholds and on non-anaemic deficiency: fatigue benefits appeared in an RCT [nut-vaucher2012] and a 2025 meta-analysis found psychiatric and cognitive gains only in iron-deficient participants [nut-fiani2025], while an earlier review judged cognitive trials small and weak [nut-falkingham2010]. In pregnancy, Cochrane supports routine iron [nut-finkelstein2024] but also notes more haemoglobin above 130 g/L [nut-penarosas2015], and high maternal haemoglobin/ferritin are themselves linked to gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia [nut-young2023, nut-khambalia2016].

key_numbers.label: Fatigue reduction, iron vs placebo (ferritin <50 ug/L)

entries.title: Iron deficiency (with or without anaemia)

timing.summary: Oral iron raises haemoglobin within weeks, but refilling ferritin stores takes about 3 months. Each dose raises hepcidin for about 24 hours, so alternate-day dosing absorbs better per dose with fewer side effects, though clinical trials show similar end results.

onset.text: With iron, 80% haemoglobin recovery took about 32 days after blood loss [tnut-kiss2015]; hepcidin rises within 24 h of a dose [tnut-moretti2015].

full.text: Ferritin rose 11 ug/L and fatigue fell after 12 weeks of 80 mg/day [tnut-vaucher2012]; 90 days daily or 180 days alternate-day gave ferritin ~44 ug/L [tnut-vonsiebenthal2023].

after_stopping.text: If losses continue, deficiency returns: after 90 days of daily iron then placebo, 11.4% were iron-deficient at 6 months vs 3.0% with alternate-day dosing spread over 6 months [tnut-vonsiebenthal2023].

frequency.text: Single morning doses on alternate days absorb 40-50% better per dose [tnut-stoffel2017, tnut-stoffel2020] and cause fewer gut effects at equal total dose [tnut-vonsiebenthal2023]; split twice-daily dosing adds nothing [tnut-moretti2015].

timing.debate: Isotope studies favour alternate-day dosing [tnut-stoffel2017, tnut-stoffel2020], but clinical trials and a meta-analysis found similar haemoglobin and ferritin with daily dosing, with a non-significant edge to daily for haemoglobin [tnut-pasupathy2023, tnut-dhanvijay2025, tnut-vonsiebenthal2023].

audit.claim: Iron deficiency causes fatigue even without anaemia, and iron reduced fatigue in an RCT.
audit.biases: RCT-based; deficiency harms are not seriously confounded.
audit.newer_evidence: The fatigue RCT [abody-vaucher2012] and the 2021 Lancet seminar [abody-pasricha2021] stand.
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Pathological iron overload (thalassaemia, haemochromatosis) causes hypogonadism in about half of affected men and more sperm DNA damage; in ordinary men, higher seminal iron tracks with poorer motility, but there is no evidence that normal dietary iron harms sperm.

dose.effective: Men do not need iron supplements unless deficient; men with known iron overload need chelation or phlebotomy started early.
dose.studied_range: Median ferritin 2251 ug/L in thalassaemic men; observational seminal iron levels.
dose.too_much: Iron overload disorders: hypogonadism in ~47% of men, azoospermia in ~18% of those assessed.
dose.timeframe: Earlier chelation was associated with less sperm DNA damage.
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to men with thalassaemia, transfusion dependence or untreated haemochromatosis.

entries.mechanism: Iron deposits in the pituitary and testis; free iron catalyses Fenton chemistry and lipid peroxidation in polyunsaturated-rich sperm membranes; ferroptosis markers (low GPX4) appear in poor-motility sperm.
entries.interactions: Do not take iron-containing multivitamins without need [iron-excess]. Antioxidant supplements have not been tested in this group [male-antioxidant-combination].
entries.caveats: Evidence comes from tiny case series and case-control studies; seminal iron correlations are confounded by infection and leukocytes.
entries.debate: A systematic review of iron-overload disorders documents frequent hypogonadism and sperm abnormalities [nut-carlomagno2026], and a small study linked overload to sperm DNA damage [nut-perera2002]. Seminal iron correlates with poorer sperm quality [nut-ammar2019], but no study shows that dietary iron in non-overloaded men affects sperm; this extrapolation is unsupported.

key_numbers.label: Hypogonadism in men with iron overload
Median ferritin, thalassaemic men with sperm DNA damage

entries.title: Iron overload and sperm

timing.summary: Iron overload damages the testis and pituitary over years, and later start of chelation was linked to more sperm DNA damage. How fast sperm improve after iron is lowered has not been measured.

onset.text: Not measured; damage accumulates with years of overload [tsperm-carlomagno2026].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; later onset of chelation was associated with more sperm DNA damage [tsperm-perera2002].

frequency.text: Not applicable.

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: If iron is being lowered, at least one spermatogenic cycle of good control before a semen test or conception attempt is the minimum (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: In the Nurses' Health Study II, women taking iron supplements had 40% less ovulatory infertility, but two newer cohorts of 4662 pregnancy planners found no consistent link except in women prone to deficiency; correcting deficiency matters, extra iron does not.

dose.effective: Check ferritin before trying to conceive; if low, treat (see [iron-deficiency]). Prenatal vitamins typically supply 27 mg/day, matching the pregnancy RDA.
dose.studied_range: Dietary and supplemental non-heme iron intakes in cohorts; heme iron showed no association.
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day outside treatment; high ferritin in pregnancy is associated with gestational diabetes.
dose.timeframe: Repletion takes about 3 months, similar to the ~3-month follicle development window.
dose.notes: Heavy menstrual bleeding and short cycles are common causes of low iron in women trying to conceive.

entries.mechanism: Iron supports mitochondrial energy production and oxygen delivery to developing follicles. At the other extreme, iron overload in follicular fluid (seen in endometriosis) triggered granulosa-cell ferroptosis and poor oocyte maturation in mouse models, a mechanistic warning against excess.
entries.interactions: Usually delivered via prenatal multivitamins together with folic acid [folic-acid] [multivitamin-mineral]. Endometriosis creates local iron overload [endometriosis].
entries.caveats: Observational and self-reported; women who take supplements differ in many ways. No RCT of iron for fertility in non-anaemic women exists.
entries.debate: Positive: NHS II found iron supplements lowered ovulatory infertility (RR 0.60) [nut-chavarro2006]. Null-to-modest: PRESTO and Snart Foraeldre found no consistent association, with benefit limited to supplement users in North America and women with heavy menses [nut-hahn2019]. Mechanistic data point the other way for local excess [nut-ni2022], and iron-overload disorders cause amenorrhoea [nut-carlomagno2026].
entries.title: Iron status and ovulatory fertility

timing.summary: Correcting iron deficiency takes about 3 months of supplements to rebuild ferritin, and stores drain again over months after stopping. Alternate-day dosing absorbs better per dose and causes fewer side effects than daily dosing.

onset.text: Absorption is immediate; each dose raises hepcidin for about a day, lowering absorption of the next [tegg-stoffel2017].

full.text: Median ferritin about 44 ug/L after 90 days of daily 100 mg iron in iron-depleted women [tegg-vonsiebenthal2023].

after_stopping.text: Iron deficiency re-emerged in about 11% within 3 months of stopping daily iron [tegg-vonsiebenthal2023].

frequency.text: Alternate days: 22% vs 16% fractional absorption [tegg-stoffel2017], same ferritin at equal total dose with fewer GI side effects [tegg-vonsiebenthal2023]; splitting into twice-daily doses gave no gain [tegg-stoffel2017].

timing.debate: Nurses Health Study II linked iron supplements to less ovulatory infertility [tegg-chavarro2006], but two newer cohorts found no consistent link except in women prone to deficiency [tegg-hahn2019].

egg.late_start: Starting a month before still raises iron, but ferritin will not be fully restored.
egg.text: Repletion takes about 3 months [tegg-vonsiebenthal2023]; correcting deficiency, not adding extra iron, is what links to fertility [tegg-hahn2019].

audit.claim: Iron supplements were linked to less ovulatory infertility in NHS II, but newer cohorts found no consistent link; correct deficiency, extra iron does not help.
audit.biases: Healthy-user bias among supplement takers; self-reported intake.
audit.newer_evidence: Mendelian randomization found no causal effect of iron markers on infertility [afert-guo2024]. A Finnish before-after study reported more live births after IV iron in deficient women, but without a control group it is confounded by time and continued treatment [afert-tulenheimo2025]. Earlier cohorts as cited [afert-chavarro2006, afert-hahn2019].
audit.bottom_line: Correct iron deficiency, but don't take extra iron if your stores are normal.

entries.headline: Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as metabolites. Effects in human trials are small and mostly on biomarkers, and no outcome benefit is established for capsules.

dose.effective: Not established for outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Tens to hundreds of mg/day in short biomarker studies
dose.timeframe: Transient plasma exposure after each dose
dose.notes: Bioavailability varies over 100-fold by compound (urinary recovery 0.3-43%); isoflavones and gallic acid are best absorbed, proanthocyanidins and anthocyanins worst.

entries.mechanism: Direct scavenging in plasma is implausible at these concentrations. Likely actions are mild electrophilic Nrf2 activation, modulation of NF-kB and endothelial signalling, and local effects in the gut, where much of the dose and its microbial metabolites act.
entries.interactions: May act additively with other Nrf2 activators in vitro; human interaction data are lacking. The rise in plasma antioxidant capacity after polyphenol foods is mostly uric acid.
entries.caveats: Cell-culture 'antioxidant' effects are often artefacts of polyphenols oxidising in culture media. Whole foods with the same polyphenols carry fibre and other components.

key_numbers.label: Peak plasma metabolites per 50 mg dose

entries.title: Isolated polyphenol capsules (quercetin, resveratrol, grape-seed, etc.)

timing.summary: Most polyphenols peak in blood within a few hours at low micromolar levels and are cleared within a day, so any capsule effect is pulsatile. A few gut-derived metabolites (lignans, anthocyanin breakdown products) last 1-2 days.

onset.text: Plasma metabolites peak within hours at 0-4 µmol/L [tfood-manach2005].

full.text: Not applicable; no outcome benefit established.

after_stopping.text: Most clear within a day; some colonic metabolites persist 1-2 days [tfood-manach2005, tfood-czank2013, tfood-kuijsten2005].

frequency.text: No outcome-based schedule exists [tfood-manach2005].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Polyphenols reach only 0-4 umol/L in plasma; effects small and mostly on biomarkers.
audit.biases: Cell-culture artefacts [anut-halliwell2008].
audit.newer_evidence: Bioavailability limits [anut-manach2005] are unchanged; MR found no coronary benefit from genetically higher circulating antioxidants [anut-luo2021].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Most IVF add-ons do not raise live birth: the UK HFEA gives none of 17 rated add-ons a green light for 'having a baby', ESHRE (2023) recommends only hyaluronan transfer medium, and several (PGT-A, endometrial receptivity testing, IVIG, steroids, PRP) carry red ratings for cost, lost embryos or safety.

dose.effective: Default: a standard IVF/ICSI cycle with no paid extras. The only add-on ESHRE recommends is hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium (0.5 mg/mL) combined with single embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: Add-ons typically cost a few hundred to several thousand GBP/USD per cycle; 82% of Australian IVF patients used at least one.
dose.too_much: Stacking several add-ons multiplies cost and, for invasive ones (PRP, immunotherapy, endometrial biopsy, PGT-A biopsy), risk, without evidence of additive benefit.
dose.timeframe: Per IVF cycle.
dose.notes: Ask the clinic three questions for any extra: what is the HFEA/ESHRE rating, what RCT showed more live births, and what does it cost. Money saved is often better spent on an extra standard cycle.

entries.mechanism: Add-ons target embryo selection (PGT-A, time-lapse), implantation (scratching, embryo glue, hCG, receptivity tests, immune treatments), egg yield or quality (growth hormone, DHEA, PRP, mitochondria, antioxidants) or sperm selection (PICSI, MACS, microfluidics). Most rest on plausible biology or surrogate outcomes (eggs retrieved, embryo grade, pregnancy per transfer) rather than live birth per woman.
entries.interactions: See the individual entries: [endometrial-scratch-egg], [embryo-glue-egg], [assisted-hatching-egg], [time-lapse-egg], [pgt-a-egg], [intrauterine-hcg-egg], [immune-addons-egg], [endometrial-receptivity-egg], [prp-ovarian-egg], [prp-intrauterine-egg], [growth-hormone-ivf-egg], [mitochondrial-augment-egg], [culture-antioxidants-egg], [dhea], [sperm-selection-icsi-sperm], [icsi-non-male-factor-sperm]. Oral antioxidants before IVF are covered in [female-antioxidant-supplements] and [male-antioxidant-combination].
entries.caveats: Absence of evidence is not proof of no effect for a small subgroup, but the burden of proof should sit with the seller. Per-transfer success rates (common in clinic marketing) can rise while live birth per started cycle falls.
entries.debate: Regulators and evidence reviewers (HFEA, ESHRE, Cochrane, Oxford CEBM) conclude that most add-ons lack proof [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons, fer-heneghan2016]; ESHRE noted none of its 42 recommendations rested on high-quality evidence. Clinicians and patients often argue that add-ons offer hope where standard care has failed, and surveys show use is widespread and partly patient-driven, though most users later reported regret [fer-lensen2021survey]. Specific add-ons have their own debates (scratching, PGT-A, embryo glue, growth hormone); see their entries.

key_numbers.label: Australian IVF patients who used an add-on
HFEA add-ons rated green for live birth

entries.title: IVF add-ons (overview)

audit.claim: Most IVF add-ons do not raise live birth; HFEA gives no green rating for having a baby and ESHRE recommends little.
audit.biases: Add-on evidence is dominated by small trials, per-transfer reporting, industry funding and trustworthiness problems: in the intrauterine hCG field every trial that would not share data failed integrity checks and only those trials showed benefit [afert-zou2026]; similar patterns were found in PCOS trials [afert-bordewijk2020b].
audit.newer_evidence: The HFEA list reviewed 28 Sep 2026 still has no green rating for live birth (yellow for scratch, embryo glue and freeze-all; red for ERA, IVIG, steroids, PRP and PGT-A; black for time-lapse and PICSI) [afert-hfea2026]. ESHRE notes none of its 42 add-on recommendations rests on high-quality evidence [afert-eshre2023]. New RCTs since 2023 (prednisone, PGT-A in male factor, IPD of intrauterine hCG) were all null for live birth [afert-sun2023, afert-lin2025, afert-zou2026].
audit.bottom_line: The overview holds and has been reinforced by newer trials.

entries.headline: Cutting carbohydrate to roughly 20-50 g/day raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate to about 0.5-3 mmol/L; it is a proven epilepsy therapy and lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP in the short term, but direct evidence that it lowers oxidative damage in humans is thin, and LDL/apoB can rise sharply in lean people.

dose.effective: Under ~20-50 g/day total carbohydrate (about 5-10% of energy), protein around 1.2-2 g/kg, fat to appetite; aim for blood BHB 0.5-3 mmol/L. Build it around non-starchy vegetables, olive oil, nuts, seeds, fish, eggs and avocado rather than processed meat and butter.
dose.studied_range: Epilepsy: classic 4:1 diet or modified Atkins 10-20 g/day carbohydrate for >= 3 months. Type 2 diabetes: < 20-50 g/day for 6 months to 5 years. Weight/metabolic trials: 2 weeks to 2 years.
dose.too_much: Ketoacidosis needs BHB >= 3 mmol/L plus acidosis; healthy people on diet alone rarely exceed ~3 mmol/L, but SGLT2-inhibitor users, people with type 1 diabetes, and breastfeeding women can tip into ketoacidosis. Not for pregnancy or trying to conceive without specialist care, fatty-acid oxidation disorders, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, porphyria, eating disorders, or people on insulin or sulfonylureas without medication adjustment.
dose.timeframe: Ketones rise within days (a fast alone gives ~1 mmol/L by 24-48 h), and stable ketosis was confirmed at ~4 weeks in one RCT. Muscle fat-oxidation adaptation takes 5-6 days to a few weeks, glycaemic effects take weeks, and seizure benefit is judged at ~3 months.
dose.notes: Fingerstick blood BHB is the reference measurement. Breath acetone is a reasonable non-invasive proxy. Urine strips read only acetoacetate, fade as the kidney adapts, and are best in early-morning or post-dinner urine. Check lipids including apoB at baseline and 6-12 weeks.

entries.mechanism: Low insulin releases fatty acids that the liver converts to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). In cells and mice, BHB inhibits class I HDACs, which up-regulates FOXO3a, MT2, catalase and MnSOD. This result failed to replicate in one cell study. BHB also blocks NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and activates HCAR2 (GPR109A). Ketone oxidation shifts the mitochondrial NAD and coenzyme Q redox couples. In rats, ketogenic feeding causes a brief burst of mitochondrial H2O2 and 4-HNE that activates Nrf2 and raises glutathione, which looks like hormesis. In humans the clearer routes are lower glucose and insulin, fewer glycaemic excursions, weight loss and lower triglycerides. High fatty-acid supply can raise mitochondrial H2O2 emission, and acetoacetate can generate superoxide in vitro.
entries.interactions: Overlaps heavily with [calorie-restriction] and [intermittent-fasting] because all three raise ketones and cause weight loss. Most metabolic benefit runs through [weight-loss] and better [glycemic-control], and through removing [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] foods. Against [mediterranean-diet], the crossover trial found equal HbA1c, but keto raised LDL and cut fibre. A Mediterranean-style keto (olive oil, fish, vegetables) is the reasonable middle ground. Usually lowers fibre and bifidobacteria, working against [dietary-fiber-microbiome]. Impairs high-intensity endurance economy, so it is a poor fit for competitive [hiit-vigorous-exercise] or racing; [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [resistance-training] are maintained. BHB and sulforaphane ([broccoli-sprouts]) both act on HDACs and Nrf2 in lab models. That overlap is an inference: no human data show synergy or redundancy. In PCOS see [ketogenic-diet]. For a less restrictive option see [low-carb-diet].
entries.caveats: Human oxidative-stress data are small and short. In 20 women, 2 weeks raised total antioxidant status but did not change MDA, SOD or catalase. Children on the diet had higher brain glutathione, but that study was cross-sectional. In an isocaloric metabolic-ward study keto did not speed fat loss, and in an inpatient crossover people ate ~690 kcal/day more on animal-based keto than on a plant-based low-fat diet. Weight-loss advantage over low-fat diets is about 1 kg at a year. Diabetes benefits are largest at 3-6 months and fade by 12 months in RCT pooling. The Virta data are non-randomised. LDL rose about 41 mg/dL in lean people and fell in people with BMI >= 35. The 'lean mass hyper-responder' coronary-plaque data are cross-sectional, and the follow-up paper that claimed apoB did not predict plaque progression was retracted in 2026. Animal-based low-carb patterns are associated with higher mortality and plant-based ones with lower. Other risks: kidney stones (~6%), thiamine, folate, magnesium and iodine gaps, constipation, and poorer bone-turnover markers in athletes. Unhealthy versions (processed meat, little fibre) undo much of the case.

entries.title: Ketogenic diet (nutritional ketosis)

entries.headline: In men with obesity, very-low-calorie ketogenic diets raised total testosterone by ~6.75 nmol/L (normocaloric keto by ~1 nmol/L), in proportion to weight lost. No human trial has measured semen quality on keto; the only semen data are from obese mice.

dose.effective: Weight loss via a supervised very-low-calorie ketogenic diet (8-14 weeks) in men with obesity-related low testosterone, then a sustainable diet.
dose.studied_range: 7 studies, 230 participants; mostly uncontrolled before-after designs of 8-14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid weight loss and very-low-calorie protocols need medical supervision. LDL may rise in lean men.
dose.timeframe: Testosterone changes within 8-12 weeks; any semen effect would need at least one ~74-day spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Probably a weight-loss effect rather than a ketone effect. Higher-fat diets keep testosterone a little higher than low-fat diets (SMD ~0.38), independent of keto.

entries.mechanism: Weight loss lowers aromatase activity and insulin resistance, which releases hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal suppression. In obese mice an MCT-based ketogenic diet lowered testicular lipid peroxidation and raised glutathione peroxidase.
entries.interactions: Essentially a subset of [weight-loss] / [excess-adiposity]. General effects are under [ketogenic-diet].
entries.caveats: No controlled human semen data. The testosterone meta-analysis pools mostly uncontrolled studies, and the gains track weight loss and age. The animal data compare keto with a high-fat high-cholesterol obesogenic diet, not with a healthy diet.
entries.title: Ketogenic diet (male fertility)

entries.headline: In overweight women with PCOS, ketogenic and low-carb diets cut weight (~5 kg more than other diets), LH and insulin resistance and appear to improve cycles and ovulation. In mice, though, ketone levels typical of keto slow embryo development and a gestational keto diet harms offspring, so the case for staying ketotic while trying to conceive is weak.

dose.effective: For overweight PCOS: 8-12 weeks of a ketogenic diet (< 20-50 g/day carbohydrate, often Mediterranean-style) or a moderate low-carbohydrate diet (< 45% of energy) aimed at weight loss. Then move to a sustainable lower-glycaemic diet with folate-rich foods plus a folic-acid supplement before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: PCOS trials: 45 days to 24 weeks, ketogenic (< 20-50 g/day) and very-low-energy ketogenic protocols; low-carb RCTs < 45% energy for > 4 weeks.
dose.too_much: Not recommended once trying to conceive or in pregnancy outside specialist care (epilepsy). Avoid in lean PCOS without weight to lose. Restricted carbohydrate intake was linked to half the dietary folic acid and 30% higher odds of neural tube defects.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal and menstrual changes over 8-24 weeks, alongside weight loss.
dose.notes: Grade honestly: most PCOS data are uncontrolled before-after studies or small RCTs. Pregnancy and live-birth data are anecdotal (2 conceptions in an 11-woman pilot). Benefits are hard to separate from weight loss.

entries.mechanism: Lower insulin reduces ovarian theca androgen production and raises SHBG. Weight loss lowers adipose inflammation and lipotoxicity. In PCOS mice, BHB reduced granulosa-cell inflammation and apoptosis. Against that, BHB at ~2 mmol/L (keto-diet levels) disturbed embryo glycolysis and histone acetylation and reduced viability in mouse embryo culture. A maternal keto diet raised BHB in oviduct fluid and delayed blastocyst development.
entries.interactions: Works through [weight-loss] and [glycemic-control]; see [pcos] / [pcos]. Can be combined with [myo-inositol]. Folate intake drops when grains are cut, so pair with [folic-acid]. General-health effects are under [ketogenic-diet] and [low-carb-diet].
entries.caveats: Meta-analyses (2019-2026) agree on weight, insulin and LH but are inconsistent on androgens and lipids, with high heterogeneity. Two RCTs found no weight advantage over a matched low-calorie diet. Low-carb diets help reproductive outcomes in pooled PCOS RCTs, but the evidence is mostly not specific to ketosis. There are no human oocyte-quality data. The cautionary data (embryo, gestation, offspring lifespan) are mouse studies at diets more extreme than human keto, and the neural-tube association is observational.

key_numbers.label: Weight change vs other diets in PCOS
Ovulatory infertility RR, highest vs lowest carb intake

entries.title: Ketogenic / low-carbohydrate diet (PCOS and conception)

timing.summary: Ketosis starts within a day or two of cutting carbohydrate and the body's fuel use adapts within about a week, faster than often claimed; LDL can rise within three weeks. Glycaemic benefits peak around six months and shrink by a year, and the metabolic adaptation reverses within days of eating carbohydrate again.

onset.text: The switch to fat and ketones begins beyond ~12 h without carbohydrate [tbody-anton2018] (a 20-h fast gave only 0.10 mmol/L BHB [tbody-halberg2005]); exercise fat oxidation reached chronic-adapted levels after 5-6 days [tbody-burke2021].

full.text: LDL rose after 3-4 weeks in lean adults [tbody-retterstol2018, tbody-buren2021]; diabetes remission, weight and triglyceride benefits were greatest at 6 months and diminished by 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

after_stopping.text: Metabolic adaptations washed out in a similar 5-6 days [tbody-burke2021].

frequency.text: Ketosis depends on continuous restriction; occasional carbohydrate meals reverse it, and adaptation is quickly lost [tbody-burke2021].

timing.debate: Benefits at 6 months diminish by 12 months as adherence falls [tbody-goldenberg2021], and LDL rises within weeks in lean people [tbody-buren2021, tbody-retterstol2018]; the common claim that 'keto-adaptation' takes many weeks is contradicted by adaptation in 5-6 days in elite athletes [tbody-burke2021].

audit.claim: Keto is proven for epilepsy and improves HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP short-term; LDL can rise in lean people; animal-based patterns link to higher mortality.
audit.biases: The low-carb mortality data are cohort-based and confounded by what replaces carbohydrate [adiet-seidelmann2018].
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analysis confirms LDL rises in lower-BMI people [adiet-sotomota2024]; an inpatient trial showed higher energy intake on animal-based keto [adiet-hall2021]. Seidelmann (2018) found a U-shaped carbohydrate-mortality curve, higher mortality when carbohydrate was replaced by animal fat and protein, lower when replaced by plant sources [adiet-seidelmann2018]. The PCOS and testosterone effects track weight loss [adiet-arsenaki2026, adiet-furini2023]. The 2026 KETO-CTA paper was retracted.
audit.bottom_line: Keto works for epilepsy and improves HbA1c and triglycerides short-term; LDL can rise, especially in lean people, and replacing carbohydrate with animal rather than plant fat and protein tracks higher mortality.

entries.headline: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials, with no demonstrable effect on pregnancy; very high doses damaged sperm DNA in mice.

dose.effective: 1-2 g/day L-carnitine (often with 0.5-1 g acetyl-L-carnitine) for 3-6 months.
dose.studied_range: 8 RCTs, mostly 2 g/day L-carnitine + 1 g acetyl-L-carnitine.
dose.too_much: In healthy mice, moderate-to-high carnitine doses caused severe sperm DNA fragmentation and lower pregnancy rates (reductive stress).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Can cause fishy body odour and GI upset; raises TMAO.

entries.mechanism: Transports fatty acids into mitochondria for sperm energy; antioxidant properties in the epididymis.
entries.interactions: Included in MOXI (1 g), which was null. See [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Small, heterogeneous trials; pregnancy not improved.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

entries.headline: Evidence for women is weak; the most-cited positive RCT (L-carnitine 3 g/day in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) has been retracted.

dose.effective: No proven dose for female fertility.
dose.studied_range: 3 g/day in the retracted PCOS trial.
dose.notes: Male-factor evidence is separate and somewhat better.

entries.mechanism: Shuttles long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, which oocytes use for energy.
entries.interactions: Included in [female-antioxidant-supplements] analyses.
entries.caveats: Retraction of the main trial removes the main human evidence.
entries.title: L-carnitine / acetyl-L-carnitine

timing.summary: Carnitine supplements are poorly absorbed and quickly cleared from blood, but muscle carnitine rose only after 24 weeks of daily intake with carbohydrate. Sperm motility gains appeared after 2-6 months.

onset.text: Sperm motility improved after 2-month treatment periods in a crossover trial [tnut-lenzi2003].

full.text: Muscle carnitine up 21% only after 24 weeks [tnut-wall2011]; sperm trials ran 6 months [tnut-lenzi2004].

after_stopping.text: Plasma excess is cleared quickly by the kidney (body turnover 38-119 h) [tnut-rebouche2004]; tissue and sperm persistence not measured.

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily; rapid renal clearance of high plasma levels argues against large infrequent doses (extrapolated) [tnut-rebouche2004].

sperm.late_start: Two months of treatment already improved motility in a crossover trial [tnut-lenzi2003].
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; trials used 2-6 months [tnut-lenzi2003, tnut-lenzi2004].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Carnitines improve sperm motility and morphology in small trials with no pregnancy effect; the main positive female RCT is retracted.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials [anut-khaw2020]; the PCOS trial was retracted [anut-ismail2014, anut-ejogrb2023] and the Cochrane female review included later-retracted trials [anut-showell2020].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis again found carnitine improves motility but no supplement improves pregnancy or live birth [anut-michaelsen2025]. Carnitine is converted by gut microbes to TMAO, which accelerated atherosclerosis in mice [anut-koeth2013], a reason not to take it without a clear indication.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat

entries.headline: Everyday heat sources raise scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration, but direct SDF data are thin.

dose.effective: Laptop on a desk, not the lap; looser underwear (boxers); stand or walk for a few minutes every 30-60 min; heat protection or breaks for hot jobs (bakers, welders, drivers).
dose.studied_range: Laptop sessions of 60 min; scrotal temperature +1 C within 11-28 min.
dose.too_much: A laptop on closed thighs raised scrotal temperature 2.6-2.8 C in 60 min; lap pads did not prevent it.
dose.timeframe: Benefits, if any, would appear after one spermatogenic cycle (~3 months).
dose.notes: Sitting with legs apart reduces the rise. Heated car seats are plausible but unstudied for sperm.

entries.mechanism: Mild, repeated scrotal hyperthermia: same thermal pathway as saunas but smaller in size.
entries.interactions: Additive with [sauna] and [varicocele].
entries.caveats: Underwear and laptop data are cross-sectional or physiological (temperature) studies; the underwear association was partly explained by FSH. Occupational heat is a recognised risk but studies are older and confounded.

key_numbers.label: Scrotal temp rise, laptop on lap (60 min)
Higher sperm concentration in boxer wearers

entries.title: Laptops on the lap, tight underwear, long sitting, occupational heat

timing.summary: A small, sustained rise in testis and epididymis temperature raises sperm DNA fragmentation within about 3 weeks, before counts fall. Everything returned to baseline about 10 weeks after the heat stopped.

onset.text: With +2 C for 15 h/day, DFI rose by day 20 and HDS by day 34 [tsperm-ahmad2012]; abnormal morphology rose by day 34 [tsperm-abdelhamid2019]. A laptop on the lap warms the scrotum 2.6-2.8 C within an hour [tsperm-sheynkin2005].

full.text: Effects were established by day 34 and stayed raised for the rest of 120 days of heating [tsperm-ahmad2012].

after_stopping.text: Abnormal forms persisted 45 days after heating stopped; all parameters were back to baseline by day 73 [tsperm-abdelhamid2019, tsperm-ahmad2012].

frequency.text: The experiments used hours of heat every day; boxer wearers had higher counts in a cross-sectional study [tsperm-minguez2018]. No study tested how few hours per week are harmless.

sperm.late_start: Removing heat in the last 2-3 weeks protects late spermatids and stored sperm, where DFI rose within 20 days [tsperm-ahmad2012], but cells heated earlier will still come through.
sperm.text: Heat acts on meiosis, spermiogenesis and the epididymis [tsperm-abdelhamid2019], so the full benefit needs about 10 weeks [tsperm-ahmad2012].

timing.debate: The time course comes from 5 volunteers per study [tsperm-ahmad2012, tsperm-abdelhamid2019]; whether ordinary laptops or underwear reach enough heat for long enough is inferred from temperature [tsperm-sheynkin2005] and cross-sectional data [tsperm-minguez2018], not from trials.

audit.claim: Everyday heat raises scrotal temperature 1-3 C; boxer wearers have about 25% higher sperm concentration; SDF data thin.
audit.biases: Cross-sectional fertility-clinic data; underwear choice correlates with body size and lifestyle; self-report.
audit.newer_evidence: The underwear study itself found differences attenuated after adjustment for FSH, suggesting a compensatory pathway rather than pure confounding [afert-minguez2018]; no trial of changing underwear or laptop use has reported.
audit.bottom_line: Low-cost advice with plausible physiology; effect on fertility unproven.

factors.name: Late eating (meal timing relative to the body clock)

entries.headline: The same carbohydrate load taken 1 hour rather than 4 hours before bedtime raised glucose by 8% and cut insulin by 7% in an 845-person crossover trial (worse in MTNR1B risk-gene carriers), and late eating raised hunger and lowered energy expenditure in a tightly controlled trial, but weight-loss trials of meal timing are mixed and direct oxidative-stress evidence is lacking.

dose.effective: Finish the main meal at least 3-4 hours before habitual bedtime; put more of the day's food earlier (breakfast and lunch) and keep dinner lighter.
dose.studied_range: Evening meals 4 h vs 1 h before bedtime; dinner at 18:00 vs 22:00; calorie splits of 700/500/200 vs 200/500/700 kcal; 45:35:20% vs 20:35:45% across meals.
dose.too_much: Habitual eating close to or during biological night (night-shift eating, late dinners near bedtime).
dose.timeframe: Acute glucose effects at the next meal; weight differences in 4-20 week trials.
dose.notes: Fasting window length is a separate question ([time-restricted-eating], [intermittent-fasting]); here the issue is clock time relative to your own sleep. Late chronotypes and night workers have a later biological night, so 'late' is relative.

entries.mechanism: Insulin sensitivity and beta-cell responsiveness are higher in the biological morning; melatonin rises in the evening and, acting on beta-cell MT2 receptors (encoded by MTNR1B), suppresses insulin release, so food eaten when melatonin is high produces bigger glucose excursions. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and lipaemia activate NADPH oxidase and mitochondrial ROS production.
entries.interactions: Interacts with [evening-light-exposure] (which delays melatonin onset) and [shift-work-circadian]. Worst for people with impaired [glycemic-control]. Overlaps with eating-window approaches in [time-restricted-eating].
entries.caveats: Many cohort findings come from Spanish populations with late main meals and from weight-loss clinics. Isocaloric weight-loss trials show smaller or no effects. Oxidative stress endpoints have rarely been measured; one early time-restricted feeding trial lowered 8-isoprostane but changed the eating window as well as timing.
entries.debate: Supporting: acute crossover trials show poorer glucose tolerance with late meals [kcc-garaulet2022, kcc-lopezminguez2018, kcc-gu2020], night-time glucose tolerance is worse than daytime in a meta-analysis [kcc-leung2020], late eating raised hunger and lowered energy expenditure [kcc-vujovic2022], late eaters lost less weight in clinics [kcc-garaulet2013, kcc-dashti2021], and a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found 1.2 kg more weight loss with earlier intake [kcc-young2023]. Sceptical: a 4-week controlled crossover found no difference in energy expenditure or weight loss between morning- and evening-loaded diets [kcc-ruddickcollins2022], an earlier meta-analysis found no weight difference between small and large dinners [kcc-fong2017], and early vs late isocaloric time-restricted eating did not change insulin sensitivity or oxidative stress markers [kcc-peters2025].

key_numbers.label: Glucose AUC, late vs early evening load
Insulin AUC, late vs early evening load
Extra weight loss with earlier intake (9 RCTs)
Lower weekly weight loss in late eaters

entries.title: Late eating (meal timing relative to the body clock)

timing.summary: Eating close to bedtime worsens that meal's glucose handling the same evening, and a few days of late eating raises hunger and lowers energy expenditure. Moving meals earlier reverses this from the next meal.

onset.text: The same glucose load 1 h rather than 4 h before habitual bedtime gave higher glucose and lower insulin [tbody-garaulet2022]; late isocaloric eating raised hunger and lowered energy expenditure within days [tbody-vujovic2022].

full.text: Acute; no build-up beyond the days studied has been shown.

after_stopping.text: Effects are tied to each meal's timing; extrapolated to reverse from the next earlier meal.

frequency.text: A nightly habit matters; occasional late meals have only same-night effects.

timing.debate: Laboratory studies show acute harm from late meals [tbody-garaulet2022, tbody-vujovic2022], but 2 weeks of early versus late 8-h eating windows at intended equal calories did not change insulin sensitivity [tbody-peters2025].

audit.claim: Late carbohydrate loads worsen glucose tolerance (more in MTNR1B carriers); weight-loss timing trials are mixed; no oxidative data.
audit.biases: Cohort findings on late eaters are confounded by sleep, chronotype and shift work.
audit.newer_evidence: Both sides: the acute crossover trial [adiet-garaulet2022] and front-loading meta-analysis [adiet-young2023] versus a null controlled crossover [adiet-ruddickcollins2022] and isocaloric early vs late TRE [adiet-peters2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and current.

factors.name: Lead from service lines and plumbing

entries.headline: Lead service lines raise children's blood lead even when utilities meet the 15 ppb action level; Flint's 2014 water switch doubled the share of young children with elevated blood lead (2.4% to 4.9%), and certified carbon-block filters brought filtered water below 0.5 ug/L lead in over 97% of Flint samples.

dose.effective: Find out from your utility whether your home has a lead service line. If so, or if a water test shows lead: use an NSF/ANSI-53 certified filter for lead (and NSF-42 for particles) for all drinking and cooking water and for infant formula, change cartridges on time, use only cold water for cooking, and run the tap until it turns cold after water has stood for hours. Full (not partial) line replacement is the long-term fix.
dose.studied_range: Water lead from <1 to >150 ug/L; children's blood lead 1-10 ug/dL.
dose.too_much: No safe level of lead is known. CDC's blood lead reference value for children is 3.5 ug/dL; the US action level for water has been 15 ug/L, but blood lead rose even when utilities met it. FDA's interim dietary reference is 8.8 ug/day for women of childbearing age.
dose.timeframe: Blood lead mean life about 35 days; bone stores last decades and are released in pregnancy and menopause.
dose.notes: Partial service-line replacement can disturb pipes and temporarily raise lead; changes in water chemistry (as in Flint and Washington DC) can release lead suddenly.

entries.mechanism: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and glutathione-related enzymes, displaces zinc and calcium, and generates oxidative stress; it impairs neurodevelopment without a known threshold and raises blood pressure and cardiovascular mortality in adults [efw-lanphear2018].
entries.interactions: Other lead sources: [lead-spices], lead-glazed pottery and some cookware ([metal-cookware]), old paint and dust. Iron and calcium deficiency increase lead absorption ([iron-deficiency]). Overall metal burden: [heavy-metals].
entries.caveats: Water is one of several lead sources and its share varies by house. Flint blood-lead data are ecological. Fertility and fetal-death effects of the Flint crisis are contested.
entries.debate: Flint blood lead: one analysis found the share of children with elevated levels doubled after the switch [efw-hannaattisha2016], whereas a 2006-2016 trend analysis called the 2014-2015 rise consistent with random variation within a long decline [efw-gomez2018]. Flint fertility: an economics analysis found a 12% fall in fertility and lower birth weight [efw-grossman2019]; a biokinetic and vital-records analysis found the drop within normal variation and no excess fetal deaths [efw-roy2022]. Service lines: lead lines raised blood lead even at compliant water levels, and partial replacement did not help [efw-brown2011, efw-levallois2018].

factors.name: Lead in spices (turmeric, cinnamon, imported spices)

entries.headline: Lead chromate is added to some turmeric and was found in ground cinnamon that poisoned at least 566 people (mostly toddlers) via applesauce pouches in 2023; over 30% of spices collected in New York City lead investigations exceeded 2 ppm, and enforcement in Bangladesh cut adulterated turmeric from 47% to 0%.

dose.effective: Buy spices from established brands sold in regulated markets rather than bulk or unlabelled spices brought from abroad; be wary of unusually bright yellow turmeric; check recall notices; if a child has raised blood lead, ask about spices, remedies and cosmetics.
dose.studied_range: Spice lead from undetectable to >1,000 ug/g; outbreak cases median blood lead 7.2 ug/dL.
dose.too_much: FDA interim reference levels: 2.2 ug/day lead for children, 8.8 ug/day for women of childbearing age; CDC child reference value 3.5 ug/dL.
dose.timeframe: Blood lead falls with a mean life of about a month after the source is removed; bone lead persists for years.
dose.notes: Turmeric supplements are another possible source; buy products with third-party testing.

entries.mechanism: Lead chromate adds both lead (glutathione depletion, enzyme inhibition, neurotoxicity) and hexavalent chromium (an oxidant and carcinogen).
entries.interactions: Affects [turmeric-curcumin] and [herbs-spices] users; other lead sources are [lead-drinking-water] and [metal-cookware]; see [heavy-metals].
entries.caveats: Evidence is from surveillance, case series and market testing; the frequency of contamination in mainstream Western supermarket spices is low but not well quantified.
entries.debate: Little scientific disagreement: the harm is documented in outbreaks [efw-troeschel2025, efw-cataldo2026] and market surveys [efw-hore2019, efw-forsyth2024], and enforcement worked [efw-forsyth2023]. The open question is how often regulated-market spices are contaminated; surveillance relies on case-driven sampling [efw-porterfield2024].
