entries.title: Lead in spices (turmeric, cinnamon, imported spices)

entries.headline: Nitrate-rich greens and beetroot lower systolic blood pressure in short trials (about 4 mmHg in a 2013 meta-analysis; a 2023 meta-analysis found 2.4 mmHg in healthy people and no clear effect in hypertension [adiet-zhang2023]), and greens are the main dietary source of lutein; green leafy vegetables are among the produce most consistently linked to lower CVD and mortality.

dose.effective: 1-2 cups raw or 1/2-1 cup cooked daily.
dose.studied_range: Nitrate trials: 2 h to 15 days, dose-dependent BP effect.
dose.timeframe: Hours (nitrate) to weeks.
dose.notes: Nitrate effects on blood pressure were dose-dependent in meta-regression.

entries.mechanism: Nitrate -> nitrite -> nitric oxide supplements endothelial NO and can offset superoxide-driven NO loss; lutein and zeaxanthin protect membranes; folate.
entries.interactions: Nitrate and cocoa flavanols had additive effects on endothelial function at dietary amounts ([cocoa-flavanols]); pair greens with fat for carotenoid absorption ([extra-virgin-olive-oil]).
entries.caveats: Nitrate BP trials are short and small; oxidative-stress markers seldom measured.

key_numbers.label: Systolic BP change with inorganic nitrate/beetroot
Systolic BP change with dietary nitrate, healthy adults (2023 meta-analysis)
Total polyphenols, chromatography, spinach (sum of compounds)

entries.title: Leafy greens (spinach, lettuce, rocket, chard)

timing.summary: Nitrate from leafy greens lowers blood pressure within 2.5-3 h, with some effect left at 24 h, and daily intake lowered home blood pressure within a week with no tolerance over 4 weeks. Blood pressure drifts back up within 2 weeks of stopping.

onset.text: Peak BP fall at 2.5-3 h after a nitrate load (about -10/-8 mmHg) [tfood-webb2008].

full.text: Home BP fell within 1 week of daily nitrate and stayed down for 4 weeks without tachyphylaxis [tfood-kapil2015].

after_stopping.text: About 6 mmHg systolic still lower at 24 h after a single dose [tfood-webb2008]; BP started returning toward baseline during a 2-week washout [tfood-kapil2015].

frequency.text: Effects peak hours after intake and fade over a day or so [tfood-webb2008]; daily intake held the reduction [tfood-kapil2015]. Pooled short trials show about -4.4 mmHg systolic [tfood-siervo2013].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Nitrate-rich greens and beetroot lower systolic BP by ~4 mmHg in short trials.
audit.biases: Short, small trials (7-30 people each in the 2013 meta-analysis) [adiet-siervo2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis found -2.4 mmHg systolic in healthy people and no significant fall in hypertensive patients, including 24-h ambulatory BP [adiet-zhang2023].
audit.bottom_line: Nitrate's blood-pressure effect is smaller than early trials suggested and may not hold in people with hypertension; greens remain a good food.

entries.headline: Good for glycemic control and fiber intake, which indirectly limits postprandial oxidative stress, but direct human oxidative-stress data are scarce; their very high Folin 'polyphenol' scores are largely an assay artefact.

dose.effective: About 1/2-1 cup cooked most days as part of a high-fiber pattern.
dose.studied_range: Part of dietary-pattern trials.
dose.notes: Black beans: Folin 1391 mg/100 g but only 54 mg/100 g by chromatography; lentils: Folin 3697 vs 10 mg/100 g. Folin reacts with proteins, sugars and other reducing substances.

entries.mechanism: Low glycemic load, fermentable fiber (short-chain fatty acids), modest polyphenols in seed coats.
entries.interactions: Replacing refined starch or processed meat with legumes reduces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [processed-red-meat] exposure.
entries.caveats: Mostly inferred from fiber and dietary-pattern data.
entries.title: Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas)

timing.summary: A cup of legumes a day as part of a low-GI diet lowered HbA1c by 0.5% and systolic pressure over 3 months. HbA1c itself integrates about 3 months of glucose, so this is roughly the earliest it can fully show.

onset.text: Not measured before the 3-month endpoint [tfood-jenkins2012].

full.text: HbA1c -0.5% at 3 months [tfood-jenkins2012]; HbA1c reflects about 3 months of glucose exposure (extrapolated from red-cell lifespan).

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: The trial asked for at least 1 cup a day [tfood-jenkins2012].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Legumes help glycaemic control and fibre intake; direct oxidative data are scarce.
audit.biases: Mortality associations are observational [adiet-zargarzadeh2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 32 cohorts found 6% lower all-cause mortality and lower stroke mortality with higher legume intake, but no association with CVD or cancer mortality; low-to-moderate certainty [adiet-zargarzadeh2023]. Substituting legumes, nuts or soy for red meat was associated with lower CHD [adiet-alshaar2020].
audit.bottom_line: Modest and consistent but small benefits.

factors.name: Losing excess body fat
aliases: Weight loss through diet and exercise (in men with obesity)
Weight loss when overweight or obese

entries.headline: Excess (especially visceral) fat is one of the strongest population drivers of oxidative stress; a 12-month diet-based weight-loss trial cut F2-isoprostanes by about 23%, and bariatric surgery lowers them further.

dose.effective: If BMI >=25 or waist is high, aim for 5-10% weight loss over 6-12 months via a sustained calorie deficit (e.g., ~500 kcal/day), ideally combined with exercise.
dose.studied_range: Duggan 2016: 12 months of reduced-calorie diet with or without exercise in women with BMI >25; CALERIE 2: prescribed 25% calorie restriction for 2 years in non-obese adults; sleeve gastrectomy in BMI >40.
dose.too_much: Very-low-calorie diets and rapid loss carry their own risks (gallstones, muscle loss) and need supervision.
dose.timeframe: Reductions visible by 6-12 months and scale with amount of weight lost.
dose.notes: Visceral fat matters more than subcutaneous fat. Calorie restriction lowered isoprostanes even in non-obese people.

entries.mechanism: Enlarged adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages produce ROS via NADPH oxidase, release free fatty acids that overload mitochondria, and secrete inflammatory cytokines. Obesity also causes insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. Weight loss reverses these sources.
entries.interactions: Works with [aerobic-exercise-moderate] (exercise adds fitness-related benefits); improves [glycemic-control] and [sleep-apnea].
entries.caveats: F2-isoprostanes vary with metabolic rate; one cohort found higher isoprostanes predicted less later weight gain, so interpret single measurements cautiously. Obesity is consistently linked to poorer sperm parameters (cross-link to fertility areas).
entries.title: Losing excess body fat (if overweight or obese)

entries.headline: Weight loss in obese men raises sperm concentration and motility and lowers DNA fragmentation (effect size about -0.7); lifestyle programmes beat bariatric surgery for semen.

dose.effective: Lose 5-15% of body weight over 3-6 months through diet plus exercise.
dose.studied_range: 12 studies, mean baseline BMI 45; residential programme with 15% median weight loss over 14 weeks.
dose.too_much: Rapid loss after bariatric surgery produced no clinically significant semen or DNA-damage improvement and may temporarily worsen semen; time conception carefully after surgery.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months; re-test semen after one spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: GLP-1 drugs and metformin: too little sperm data to judge.

entries.mechanism: Reverses aromatase-driven hypogonadism, lowers inflammation and insulin resistance, and reduces scrotal heat, lowering seminal oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Usually achieved via [mediterranean-diet] and [aerobic-exercise-moderate]; those may help independently of the weight lost.
entries.caveats: Mostly uncontrolled before-after studies in severely obese men; little live-birth data.

key_numbers.label: DFI effect size after weight loss

entries.title: Weight loss through diet and exercise (in men with obesity)

entries.headline: In overweight and obese women, diet-plus-exercise programmes increased natural pregnancy (RR 1.59) and ovulation, but two RCTs (LIFEstyle, Nordic trial) found that delaying fertility treatment for weight loss did not improve live birth from treatment.

dose.effective: 5-10% of body weight via a reduced-calorie diet plus aerobic exercise; >5% loss improved insulin and cycles in PCOS.
dose.studied_range: Mean losses 4.4 kg (LIFEstyle, 6 months) to 9.4 kg (12 weeks of 880 kcal/day low-calorie diet).
dose.too_much: Do not delay treatment for long in women over ~35: time lost costs egg quality ([maternal-age]).
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Weight loss increased spontaneous conceptions (10.5% vs 2.6% in the Nordic trial). Best for women not yet in IVF or with anovulation.

entries.mechanism: Lowers insulin and free androgens, raises SHBG, reduces follicular lipid and inflammatory load (lipotoxicity).
entries.interactions: Works with [aerobic-exercise-moderate] and [mediterranean-diet]; counteracts [excess-adiposity] and [pcos].
entries.caveats: LIFEstyle: 27.1% vs 35.2% healthy term singleton births, favouring prompt treatment, partly because the intervention arm delayed treatment by 6 months. Weight loss is still worthwhile for pregnancy health.

key_numbers.label: LIFEstyle healthy term birth, intervention vs prompt treatment
Nordic trial IVF live birth, weight loss vs IVF only

entries.title: Weight loss when overweight or obese

timing.summary: Weight loss keeps paying off over months for ovulation and natural conception, but trials of 3-6 months of weight loss before IVF did not raise live birth, partly because the delay costs time. The clearest benefit is in anovulatory PCOS.

onset.text: Metabolic markers change within weeks (not measured as an onset); ovulation gains were measured after 16 weeks [tegg-legro2015].

full.text: Keeps growing with more loss; trials ran 12 weeks to 6 months [tegg-einarsson2017, tegg-mutsaerts2016].

after_stopping.text: Benefits fade with weight regain (not measured for fertility).

frequency.text: Daily diet and activity.

timing.debate: A small RCT found 44% vs 14% live birth after 12 weeks [tegg-sim2014] and a meta-analysis found higher pregnancy (RR 1.59) [tegg-best2017], whereas three large trials of 12 weeks to 6 months found no IVF or treatment live-birth gain [tegg-einarsson2017, tegg-mutsaerts2016, tegg-legro2022].

egg.late_start: A 12-week programme still raised natural conception [tegg-einarsson2017] and pregnancy in a small trial [tegg-sim2014], but delaying IVF to lose weight did not raise live birth [tegg-mutsaerts2016].
egg.text: 16 weeks of weight loss improved ovulation and live birth in obese PCOS [tegg-legro2015, tegg-legro2016]; in unexplained infertility it did not [tegg-legro2022].

audit.claim: Losing excess fat cuts F2-isoprostanes; in women, weight-loss programmes raise natural conception but do not improve IVF live birth.
audit.biases: Observational weight loss mixes intentional loss with illness-driven loss (reverse causation), so trials are needed.
audit.newer_evidence: Look AHEAD's lifestyle weight loss did not reduce cardiovascular events (HR 0.95) [abody-lookahead2013]; bariatric surgery in the controlled SOS study lowered mortality (HR 0.77) [abody-carlsson2020]; semaglutide cut major cardiovascular events 20% in SELECT [abody-lincoff2023]. Fertility RCTs confirm no IVF live-birth gain [abody-mutsaerts2016, abody-einarsson2017].
audit.bottom_line: Large, sustained weight loss improves hard outcomes; modest lifestyle loss improves risk factors but has not cut heart events in a trial.

entries.headline: In high-risk pregnancies, aspirin 150 mg nightly from 11-14 weeks cut preterm pre-eclampsia from 4.3% to 1.6% (ASPRE); USPSTF recommends 81 mg/day after 12 weeks for people at high risk.

dose.effective: 81 mg/day after 12 weeks (USPSTF, US) or 150 mg at night from 11-14 weeks to 36 weeks (ASPRE regimen), only when screening shows high risk.
dose.studied_range: 50-150 mg/day in trials.
dose.too_much: May slightly increase postpartum haemorrhage; not for people with aspirin allergy or bleeding disorders.
dose.timeframe: Start before 16 weeks, ideally 12-14; continue to about 36 weeks.
dose.notes: A pregnancy medicine prescribed by the obstetric team, not a preconception supplement; mention prior pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney or autoimmune disease, IVF and twin pregnancy at booking.

entries.mechanism: Low-dose aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX-1 and thromboxane A2 while sparing prostacyclin, improving placental perfusion; it does not act as an antioxidant.
entries.interactions: Contrast with [antioxidants-preeclampsia-egg], which failed despite the oxidative-stress rationale.
entries.caveats: Benefit is for preterm, placenta-driven pre-eclampsia; little effect on term disease. Rated low on the egg-quality scale because it acts in pregnancy (placenta), not on eggs; its effect on preterm pre-eclampsia in high-risk pregnancies is large.
entries.debate: Dose is debated: ASPRE used 150 mg [fer-rolnik2017] while USPSTF recommends 81 mg [fer-uspstf2021]; Cochrane shows a modest 18% reduction across 77 trials (NNT 61) [fer-duley2019]. StopPRE found that stopping at 24-28 weeks in women with normal placental markers was non-inferior [fer-mendoza2023].
entries.title: Low-dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia

timing.summary: Low-dose aspirin is a pregnancy-window drug: started at 11-14 weeks and taken nightly to 36 weeks it cut preterm pre-eclampsia by about 60% in high-risk women. Whether it must start before 16 weeks is disputed; starting before conception did not raise live birth overall.

onset.text: Started at 11-14 weeks of gestation in ASPRE [tegg-rolnik2017].

full.text: Protection applies to the pregnancy while it is taken; ASPRE continued to 36 weeks [tegg-rolnik2017].

after_stopping.text: Antiplatelet effect wears off over days after stopping (platelet turnover); not studied as an outcome.

frequency.text: Daily; in the preconception EAGeR trial, benefit in per-protocol analysis needed at least 4-5 of 7 days [tegg-naimi2021].

timing.debate: A trial-level meta-analysis found aspirin started at <=16 weeks cut pre-eclampsia far more than later starts (RR 0.57 vs 0.81) [tegg-roberge2017]; an individual-participant meta-analysis of 32,217 women found no difference by start time (RR 0.90 both) [tegg-meher2017]. Preconception aspirin did not raise live birth overall in EAGeR [tegg-schisterman2014], though per-protocol reanalysis suggested benefit with adherence [tegg-naimi2021].

audit.claim: In high-risk pregnancies aspirin 150 mg nightly cut preterm pre-eclampsia from 4.3% to 1.6%; USPSTF recommends 81 mg.
audit.biases: Not applicable; RCT and IPD evidence.
audit.newer_evidence: ASPRE and the Cochrane IPD-based review stand [afert-rolnik2017, afert-duley2019]; the 75 vs 150 mg dose question remains under trial.
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Many adults eat below the magnesium requirement and PPIs raise the odds of low blood magnesium (OR 1.71); supplements modestly lower CRP in RCTs, mostly in people who start inflamed or depleted, but claims of a hidden 'magnesium crisis' driving heart disease go beyond the data.

dose.effective: RDA 400-420 mg/day men, 310-320 mg/day women. Leafy greens, legumes, nuts, seeds, whole grains, dark chocolate. If low intake or on PPIs/diuretics, 200-320 mg/day supplemental magnesium (citrate or glycinate) is reasonable.
dose.studied_range: Typically 250-500 mg/day elemental magnesium in RCTs; 320 mg/day in the sleep/CRP trial.
dose.too_much: UL for supplemental magnesium 350 mg/day (IOM) or 250 mg/day for readily dissociable salts (EFSA); diarrhoea first; avoid supplements in kidney failure.
dose.timeframe: Weeks to months.
dose.notes: Serum magnesium is a poor marker of body stores; risk groups include PPI and loop/thiazide diuretic users, type 2 diabetes, alcohol use disorder, GI disease, older adults.

entries.mechanism: Magnesium is required for ATP handling, glutathione synthesis (Mg-ATP-dependent enzymes), and stabilising membranes; deficiency in animals primes inflammatory cells and oxidative stress. It is not itself an antioxidant.
entries.interactions: Often co-depleted with other nutrients in diets high in refined foods [refined-sugar-high-glycemic]; relevant to [glycemic-control].
entries.caveats: Inflammation trials are small and heterogeneous; effects on oxidative-stress outcomes are not established.
entries.debate: An opinion review called subclinical magnesium deficiency a principal driver of cardiovascular disease and a public health crisis [nut-dinicolantonio2018] (lead author has a commercial book interest). RCT evidence is more modest: CRP falls in meta-analysis [nut-veronese2022] and benefits concentrated in people with baseline CRP >3 mg/L or low serum magnesium [nut-nielsen2010]. PPI-related hypomagnesaemia is consistent across observational studies [nut-srinutta2019].
entries.title: Magnesium status

timing.summary: About 300 mg/day for a month was enough to raise serum magnesium and lower blood pressure slightly in pooled trials. Serum levels rose mainly in people who started low.

onset.text: 1 month at 300 mg/day was sufficient to raise serum magnesium and lower BP [tnut-zhang2016].

full.text: Median trial duration 3 months; 7 weeks lowered CRP only in those with high CRP [tnut-zhang2016, tnut-nielsen2010].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily; no schedule comparisons [tnut-zhang2016].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Many adults eat below requirement; supplements modestly lower CRP; 'magnesium crisis' claims overreach.
audit.biases: Serum magnesium is a poor marker and low intake travels with poor diet (confounding).
audit.newer_evidence: MR found genetically higher serum magnesium associated with lower coronary disease (OR 0.88 per 0.1 mmol/L) [abody-larsson2018], modest support for a causal role, but no outcome trial exists.
audit.bottom_line: Holds; correcting low intake is reasonable, the cardiovascular benefit of supplements is unproven.

factors.name: Marinating meat before grilling or frying

entries.headline: A 1-hour herb-and-spice marinade cut heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88%, a vinegar-lemon-garlic marinade cut PhIP in grilled chicken by 92-99%, and a dark-beer marinade cut PAHs in charcoal-grilled pork by 53%, but these are food-chemistry results with no human health outcome data, and sugary marinades can raise some HCAs.

dose.effective: Marinate meat for at least 1 hour in an oil-plus-acid base (vinegar, lemon juice, beer or wine) with rosemary, thyme, oregano, garlic and onion; keep sugar low, especially for long cooking.
dose.studied_range: 1-hour commercial herb/spice marinades in oil, water and vinegar (steak, 204 °C); brown sugar/olive oil/vinegar/garlic/mustard/lemon marinade (chicken, 10-40 min grilling); 4-hour beer marinades (pork); oil marinades with up to ~30% onion and garlic (beef patties).
dose.too_much: No harm threshold; marinades heavy in sugar raised MeIQx more than 10-fold at long (30-40 min) grilling times.
dose.timeframe: Immediate (it changes what forms in the pan).
dose.notes: Pat meat roughly dry before grilling to limit flare-ups. Marinating complements, but does not replace, avoiding charring and lowering the cooking temperature.

entries.mechanism: Polyphenols such as carnosic acid, carnosol and rosmarinic acid (rosemary family) and sulfur compounds from garlic and onion scavenge the free radicals and carbonyl intermediates of Maillard pathways that lead to HCAs; acids and moisture lower surface temperature and AGE formation; antioxidant-rich marinades also quench radical steps in PAH formation.
entries.interactions: Works alongside lower temperatures and frequent turning (see [high-temperature-cooking]); overlaps with the in-pan antioxidant effect of [herbs-spices]. Fat-heavy marinades dripping onto coals can add PAHs.
entries.caveats: All evidence is from food analysis, not people. Results vary by marinade recipe, meat, cooking time and temperature, and HCA levels in some studies were low to begin with. No study shows that people who marinate have less cancer or lower oxidative damage.
entries.debate: Most cooking studies find large reductions [kcc-smith2008, kcc-salmon1997, kcc-viegas2014], but the same chicken study showed MeIQx rising more than 10-fold and mutagenicity rising at 40 minutes with a sugary marinade [kcc-salmon1997], and in fried patties lemon juice did little while garlic and onion drove the effect [kcc-gibis2007]. Whether lower HCA or PAH content translates into lower human cancer risk is itself contested [kcc-ollberding2012, kcc-sugimura2004].

key_numbers.label: MeIQx reduction with high garlic in oil marinade

entries.title: Marinating meat before grilling or frying

timing.summary: This is a one-off kitchen step with no biology to wait for: the marinade changes what forms during that cooking session, and the effect is over when the meal is. The only clock is the marinating time itself - 1 hour was enough for herb-spice marinades to cut heterocyclic amines 57-88% [tleg-smith2008], while beer marinades did better at 6 hours than at 2-4 [tleg-melo2008].

onset.text: Immediate and confined to the meal: a 1-hour herb-and-spice marinade cut total heterocyclic amines in grilled steak by 57-88% [tleg-smith2008], and a vinegar-lemon-garlic type marinade cut PhIP in grilled chicken by 92-99% [tleg-salmon1997].

full.text: Longer marinating helps up to a point: beer marinades cut heterocyclic amines by about 88% after 6 hours versus less at 2-4 hours [tleg-melo2008], and overnight teriyaki or turmeric-garlic marinades lowered PhIP and MeIQx [tleg-nerurkar1999].

after_stopping.text: Nothing persists: an unmarinated grill session produces the full complement of heterocyclic amines again [tleg-smith2008].

frequency.text: Only on the occasions you use high dry heat - that is the only time it does anything. Sugary marinades can backfire: a sugar-containing marinade cut PhIP by 92-99% but raised MeIQx more than ten-fold at long cooking times [tleg-salmon1997], and a honey barbecue sauce tripled PhIP [tleg-nerurkar1999].

timing.debate: All of this is food chemistry with no human health outcome, and the direction depends on the recipe: herb, spice, beer, wine and acid marinades lower heterocyclic amines [tleg-smith2008, tleg-melo2008], while sugar-rich marinades raise MeIQx several-fold [tleg-salmon1997] or PhIP three-fold [tleg-nerurkar1999]. No trial has measured whether any of it changes a biomarker in people, let alone cancer risk.

entries.headline: Raw broccoli delivers roughly 3-10x more sulforaphane than fully cooked broccoli because cooking destroys myrosinase; high-glucoraphanin varieties lowered LDL cholesterol 5-7% in two RCTs, but glucoraphanin in supermarket heads varies more than 100-fold.

dose.effective: About 200 g (2 cups) raw or very lightly steamed, chopped and chewed well, or cooked broccoli with about 1 g mustard powder added after cooking. In trials 400 g/week of high-glucoraphanin broccoli lowered LDL.
dose.studied_range: 200 g single servings (pharmacokinetics); 400 g/week for 12 weeks (LDL trials); 200 g cooked + daikon daily for 15 days; 300 mL high-glucoraphanin soup weekly for 12 months.
dose.timeframe: Sulforaphane peaks about 1.6 h after raw and about 6 h after cooked broccoli; LDL effects over 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Raw: 32-37% of the potential isothiocyanate reaches the urine; steamed or cooked: 3.4-10%. Heating to about 60 °C can increase sulforaphane by inactivating epithiospecifier protein (which otherwise diverts glucoraphanin to an inactive nitrile), but 70 °C and above destroys floret myrosinase. Rough arithmetic: an average head (0.38 µmol/g) gives about 76 µmol glucoraphanin per 200 g, or about 28 µmol absorbed sulforaphane raw vs about 3 µmol fully cooked.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation by sulforaphane plus fiber, folate, vitamin C and carotenoids. Mature heads also contain indole glucosinolates (yielding indole-3-carbinol and DIM), which sprouts largely lack and which act additively or synergistically with isothiocyanates on ARE genes in cell culture.
entries.interactions: If you already take a strong sulforaphane dose ([broccoli-seed-powder], [broccoli-sprouts], [sulforaphane-supplements]), cooked broccoli adds only a few µmol of extra sulforaphane, but raw broccoli can add a dose similar to the Qidong threshold, and the fiber, folate and indoles are not duplicated. Add [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when eating it cooked. Part of [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet] patterns.
entries.caveats: Head-to-head variation in glucoraphanin (<0.005 to 1.13 µmol/g) means any single serving may deliver little. Commercially frozen broccoli is blanched (heat-treated), so by the heating data it should be treated like cooked broccoli. Mortality associations for crucifers are observational.

key_numbers.label: LDL-C reduction, high-glucoraphanin broccoli 400 g/week, 12 wk
Circulating sulforaphane, high- vs standard-glucoraphanin soup

entries.title: Mature broccoli (raw or lightly cooked)

timing.summary: A raw broccoli meal gives a sulforaphane peak at about 1.6 h (cooked: about 6 h) that is cleared within a day. Yet trials using broccoli only a few times a week (400 g per week, or one soup portion weekly) still lowered LDL over 12 weeks and changed prostate gene expression over a year.

onset.text: Plasma sulforaphane peaks 1.6 h after raw and 6 h after cooked broccoli, with excretion half-lives of 2.4-2.6 h [tfood-vermeulen2008].

full.text: LDL fell 5-7% after 12 weeks of 400 g/week high-glucoraphanin broccoli [tfood-armah2015]; prostate gene-expression changes were attenuated over 12 months of weekly soup [tfood-traka2019]. Earlier time points were not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured for LDL or gene expression; the sulforaphane itself is cleared within a day [tfood-vermeulen2008].

frequency.text: The two outcome trials used broccoli a few times a week (400 g/week) or weekly [tfood-armah2015, tfood-traka2019], so daily intake is not required for these effects; no trial compared schedules.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Raw broccoli gives far more sulforaphane than cooked; high-glucoraphanin broccoli lowered LDL 5-7% in two RCTs.
audit.biases: LDL trials by one group using a commercial variety [adiet-armah2015].
audit.newer_evidence: No contradicting trials found; crucifer mortality associations remain weak-to-suggestive in umbrella review [adiet-li2022].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Mind-body practices reliably lower cortisol and blood pressure modestly, but evidence that they reduce oxidative damage comes from small, weakly controlled trials.

dose.effective: If you enjoy it: ~20-45 min sessions, most days (yoga trials typically 2-5 sessions/week for 8-12 weeks).
dose.studied_range: Yoga/MBSR trials of 6-16 weeks.
dose.timeframe: 8-12 weeks in most trials.
dose.notes: Physical yoga also counts as light exercise.

entries.mechanism: Lower sympathetic and HPA-axis activity reduces cortisol and catecholamines; gene-expression studies show down-regulation of NF-kB inflammatory pathways.
entries.interactions: Addresses [psychological-stress]; can improve [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Oxidative-marker trials are small (e.g., 29 people), often lack active controls, and use crude markers like malondialdehyde. Grade honestly as limited.
entries.title: Meditation, mindfulness and yoga

timing.summary: Most trials run 8-12 weeks and show modest falls in cortisol and blood pressure; one intensive 3-day retreat was followed by lower IL-6 four months later. Direct oxidative-stress time courses are not known.

onset.text: Not well measured; most trials assess only at the end of 8-12 week programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

full.text: Modest cortisol and blood-pressure reductions after typical 8-12 week programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

after_stopping.text: IL-6 was lower 4 months after a 3-day intensive retreat in stressed adults [tbody-creswell2016]; otherwise not measured.

frequency.text: Trials mostly used several sessions a week; no trial compared schedules.

timing.debate: A systematic review judged immune and inflammation effects tentative and heterogeneous [tbody-black2016], while a small RCT found lasting IL-6 reductions after a brief retreat [tbody-creswell2016].

audit.claim: Mind-body practices modestly lower cortisol and blood pressure; oxidative-damage evidence is weak.
audit.biases: Unblinded trials, expectancy and volunteer effects; passive controls inflate effects.
audit.newer_evidence: Meditation programmes give small-to-moderate improvements in anxiety and depression but are no better than active treatments [abody-goyal2014]; an IPD meta-analysis found distress fell (SMD -0.32) versus passive controls [abody-galante2023].
audit.bottom_line: Holds; psychological benefits are real but modest, oxidative claims remain unproven.

entries.headline: In PREDIMED (7447 high-risk adults) a Mediterranean diet with EVOO or nuts cut major CVD events by ~30%; sub-studies found larger falls in urinary 8-oxo-dG, more oxidation-resistant LDL and borderline lower F2-isoprostanes vs a low-fat diet.

dose.effective: Daily EVOO as the main fat, vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts (about 30 g), fish weekly, little red/processed meat or sweets.
dose.studied_range: 4.8 years median (PREDIMED); 1-year oxidative sub-studies.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative markers improved at 1 year; CVD events diverged within a few years.
dose.notes: The wine component is optional and not needed for the benefits.

entries.mechanism: Combines olive phenolics (LDL protection), high produce and fiber (gut metabolites), lower glycemic load, fewer AGEs and processed meats, and better fatty-acid profile.
entries.interactions: Contains most of the beneficial foods here; individual 'superfoods' add little on top of it.
entries.caveats: PREDIMED was retracted and republished after randomisation irregularities; re-analysed results held. Oxidative endpoints were secondary and in subsamples.

key_numbers.label: LDL oxidative modifications, EVOO arm vs control

entries.title: Mediterranean diet

entries.headline: Men who eat a Mediterranean or 'prudent' diet have better counts and motility (about +24 million sperm, +8.8 points motility), but fertility outcomes are untested.

dose.effective: Daily: vegetables (3+ servings), fruit (2+), whole grains, legumes several times a week, nuts (30-60 g), olive oil as main fat; fish 2+ times a week; little processed meat, sweets or sugary drinks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore tertiles; observational studies in 2558 men plus 2 small RCTs.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months for sperm-level effects.
dose.notes: The pattern matters more than any single 'superfood'.

entries.mechanism: Supplies dietary antioxidants (vitamin E, carotenoids, polyphenols), omega-3 fats, folate and zinc at food-level doses; lowers inflammation and insulin resistance.
entries.interactions: Contains [walnuts-nuts], [omega3-fish], [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [tomatoes-lycopene]; displaces [processed-meat] and [refined-sugar-high-glycemic].
entries.caveats: Almost all data are cross-sectional or cohort studies; SDF itself is rarely measured; high heterogeneity (I2 ~80-90%).

key_numbers.label: Sperm count difference (high vs low adherence)
Odds of abnormal semen, lowest vs highest tertile

entries.title: Mediterranean / 'prudent' dietary pattern

entries.headline: Women in the lowest third of Mediterranean-diet adherence had much lower IVF live birth (26.6% vs 48.8%) in a Greek cohort of women under 35, but pooled evidence is inconsistent and no RCT has tested it.

dose.effective: Daily vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, olive oil and nuts; fish 2+ times/week; little processed meat, sweets and refined snacks.
dose.studied_range: MedDietScore 0-55 (tertiles <= 30 vs >= 36); EARTH quartiles.
dose.timeframe: Adopt at least 3 months before trying or IVF.
dose.notes: In the US EARTH cohort, benefit plateaued after the second quartile: the gain comes from avoiding a poor diet rather than perfect adherence.

entries.mechanism: Supplies folate, vitamin B6, omega-3 and polyphenols, lowers homocysteine and systemic inflammation, and improves insulin sensitivity; higher blood and follicular-fluid folate/B6 were seen with this pattern.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [profertility-diet], [folic-acid] and [omega3-fish]; also supports [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: All observational; association seen only in women under 35 in one study and no association with oocyte yield or embryo quality. A 2023 meta-analysis judged the evidence insufficient for clinical application.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, lowest vs highest tertile

entries.title: Mediterranean-style diet

timing.summary: Lipid oxidation improves within 3 months and semen quality within 4 months, while lower cardiovascular events took years. Six weeks of a Mediterranean-style supplement before IVF already changed embryo development.

onset.text: Oxidized LDL -10.6 U/L at 3 months [tfood-fito2007]; embryo cleavage changes after 6 weeks of a Mediterranean-type intervention before IVF [tfood-kermack2020].

full.text: Major CVD events lower over a median 4.8 years (HR 0.69-0.72) [tfood-estruch2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: A whole daily eating pattern; effects in trials came from sustained adherence [tfood-estruch2018].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; the trial measured only after 4 months.
sperm.text: A 4-month Mediterranean diet plus exercise program improved sperm concentration, motility and morphology [tfood-montano2022]. Sperm take about 64 days (range 42-76) from labelled precursor to ejaculate [tfood-misell2006], and the classic ~74-day estimate is uncertain by about a week [tfood-amann2008], so a diet change needs roughly 2.5-3 months to reach every stage of the sperm in a given ejaculate.

egg.late_start: Six weeks of an omega-3, vitamin D and olive oil intervention changed embryo cleavage timing [tfood-kermack2020], so a late start may still help.
egg.text: Lower adherence before IVF was linked to lower live birth in women under 35 [tfood-karayiannis2018]. A follicle grows for several months before ovulation, including about 70 days from the preantral stage to 2 mm [tfood-gougeon2010], so anything acting on the growing follicle needs roughly 3-4 months to cover the whole final growth phase.

timing.debate: PREDIMED's timing of benefit and overall trustworthiness are disputed after its retraction and republication [tfood-agarwal2019, tfood-estruch2018].

audit.claim: PREDIMED cut major CVD events by ~30%; sub-studies found less oxidative damage; for sperm and IVF the data are observational.
audit.biases: PREDIMED was retracted and republished in 2018 after non-random allocation of household members and at some sites [adiet-estruch2018r]; critics question whether it can still be treated as a randomized trial [adiet-agarwal2019]. The control group got low-fat advice rather than a true low-fat diet, and free EVOO or nuts. Fertility associations are cohort and cross-sectional (healthy-user bias) [adiet-muffone2023].
audit.newer_evidence: Republished PREDIMED results held after excluding 1,588 irregular participants [adiet-estruch2018]. Cochrane (2019) judged evidence low quality for mortality, found fewer strokes, and excluded two secondary-prevention trials for data-reliability concerns [adiet-rees2019]; separately, the Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study carries a 2005 Lancet expression of concern [adiet-singh2002]. CORDIOPREV (2022), a 7-year RCT in 1,002 coronary patients, found ~25-28% fewer cardiovascular events than with a low-fat diet [adiet-delgadolista2022], adding to the Lyon trial [adiet-delorgeril1999]. For sperm, two small RCTs (2020, 2025) found modest improvements in count [adiet-caruso2020, adiet-ghasemi2025]; for IVF outcomes no RCT exists and a 2023 meta-analysis called the evidence insufficient [adiet-muffone2023].
audit.bottom_line: The Mediterranean diet remains the best-supported dietary pattern for heart disease, with two independent trials besides PREDIMED; effect sizes are uncertain and the fertility claims remain mostly observational.

entries.headline: As a sleep aid melatonin shortens sleep onset by about 7 minutes; claims that it is a powerful mitochondrial antioxidant come from cell and animal work, human antioxidant data are small biomarker trials, and real products contain anywhere from -83% to +478% of the labelled dose.

dose.effective: For sleep: 0.3-5 mg; 0.3 mg restored sleep efficiency in older insomniacs, and benefit in a dose-response meta-analysis plateaued near 4 mg taken about 3 hours before bedtime. No dose is proven to slow aging.
dose.studied_range: 0.1-12 mg/day in sleep trials; often 5-20 mg or more in antioxidant-biomarker trials
dose.too_much: 3 mg or more can cause next-day sleepiness and leave blood levels high into the morning; label content is unreliable; keep gummies away from children
dose.timeframe: Sleep effects from the first nights; biomarker trials ran weeks to months
dose.notes: Regulated as a drug in the UK and EU but sold as a supplement in the US and Canada. Choose products with third-party testing because content varies widely.

entries.mechanism: Melatonin is the pineal hormone that signals darkness to the circadian system through MT1/MT2 receptors. In cell and animal studies it and its metabolites scavenge radicals, and it may be made inside mitochondria and raise antioxidant enzymes. At sleep doses, blood levels are in the nanomolar range, far below concentrations used in many antioxidant experiments.
entries.interactions: Helps with circadian problems such as [shift-work-circadian] and jet lag more clearly than with insomnia. Does not replace fixing [short-sleep]. Egg-quality evidence is on the same page.
entries.caveats: The AASM suggests not using melatonin for chronic insomnia in adults. Products are poorly controlled: 71% of tested supplements were outside 10% of label and some contained serotonin; 22 of 25 gummies were mislabelled. US pediatric ingestions rose 530% in a decade, with two deaths reported.
entries.debate: Reiter and colleagues argue melatonin is 'one of evolution's best' mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, mainly from experimental data [lon-reiter2017]. A meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found lower MDA and protein carbonyls with melatonin [lon-ghorbaninejad2020], but these were heterogeneous patient studies with surrogate markers and no clinical outcomes. For sleep, meta-analyses show real but small effects [lon-ferracioliOda2013, lon-cruzsanabria2024], and the AASM guideline judged the evidence too weak to recommend it for chronic insomnia [lon-sateia2017]. Short-term safety looks good [lon-besag2019], but long-term placebo-controlled data are scarce [lon-besag2022].
entries.title: Melatonin

entries.headline: Melatonin is a natural follicular antioxidant; in IVF RCTs it raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg/embryo counts in pooled low-quality data, but not live birth (OR 1.38, NS), and a placebo-controlled dose trial saw no change in follicle numbers.

dose.effective: 3 mg/day at night during IVF stimulation was the dose used in the early Japanese studies; not proven.
dose.studied_range: 3 mg/day to 8 mg twice daily.
dose.too_much: Higher doses (up to 8 mg twice daily) did not add benefit; doses below and above showed no live-birth difference in Cochrane comparisons.
dose.timeframe: Usually from early follicular phase to egg retrieval.
dose.notes: Melatonin is a hormone with circadian effects; doses up to 8 mg twice daily did not cause daytime sleepiness in an IVF trial, but there is no reason to use high doses.

entries.mechanism: Concentrated in follicular fluid, scavenges hydroxyl radicals and stimulates antioxidant enzymes; follicular melatonin was inversely related to 8-OHdG oxidative DNA damage.
entries.interactions: Frequently combined with [myo-inositol]; a large combination trial was retracted in 2026.
entries.caveats: Trials are heterogeneous (PCOS to poor responders), small and low quality; the key Tamura data were non-randomized.
entries.title: Melatonin

timing.summary: Melatonin is gone from blood within hours (half-life about 45 min), but IVF trials gave it nightly through the stimulation cycle, when it lowered follicular oxidative markers. Effects on egg numbers and live birth are unproven.

onset.text: Peak about 50 min after an oral dose [tegg-harpsoe2015]; follicular oxidative markers lower within the treatment cycle [tegg-tamura2008].

full.text: Within one stimulation cycle (about 2 weeks) in trials [tegg-fernando2017].

after_stopping.text: Half-life about 45 min, so cleared within hours [tegg-harpsoe2015].

frequency.text: Nightly or twice daily (MIART used twice daily) from cycle day 2 to the day before retrieval [tegg-fernando2017]; no schedule comparison.

timing.debate: A meta-analysis found higher clinical pregnancy but not live birth [tegg-hu2020]; the placebo-controlled dose trial saw no change in follicle numbers [tegg-fernando2020], and the follicular-fluid study was not randomised [tegg-tamura2008].

egg.late_start: Starting at the beginning of the stimulation cycle matches the trials.
egg.text: Trials started in the early follicular phase or previous cycle and stopped at retrieval [tegg-fernando2017, tegg-tamura2008].

audit.claim: In IVF RCTs melatonin raised clinical pregnancy (OR 1.43) and egg counts in low-quality data but not live birth.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials; a widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin trial is retracted [afert-pacchiarotti2016]; live birth was reported by only 3 trials with low power [afert-hu2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No large live-birth RCT has appeared; the 2020 meta-analysis is still the main synthesis (live birth OR 1.38, 0.78-2.46, power 0.34) [afert-hu2020].
audit.bottom_line: Unproven for egg quality or live birth.

entries.headline: Metformin lowers glucose partly by mildly inhibiting mitochondrial complex I; in exercise trials it blunted some training gains (about half the VO2max gain in one study, less muscle growth in the MASTERS trial), it lowers vitamin B12 by about 19% over years, and in PCOS it helps ovulation but less than letrozole or clomiphene.

dose.effective: Usual prescribed range 500-2000 mg/day (e.g. 850 mg twice daily in the DPP). The exercise-blunting trials used 1700-2000 mg/day.
dose.studied_range: 500-3000 mg/day in exercise studies; 1700 mg/day (MASTERS); 2550 mg/day for 4.3 years (de Jager B12 trial); 1700 mg/day for up to 13 years (DPP/DPPOS).
dose.too_much: B12 deficiency risk rises about 13% per year of use; check B12 periodically on long-term use (deficiency roughly <150 pmol/L or <=203 pg/mL; borderline up to ~220 pmol/L or 298 pg/mL).
dose.timeframe: Training interactions appear within 12-16 weeks; B12 falls within 6 weeks to 3 months and deficiency accumulates over years; ovulation effects within a few cycles.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. People with diabetes, prediabetes or PCOS who take metformin should keep exercising: exercise still improves fitness and glucose on metformin, the blunting is partial and inconsistent, and the disease benefits of each are established. Ask about B12 testing on long-term use.

entries.mechanism: Metformin accumulates in mitochondria and inhibits respiratory-chain complex I, lowering the cell's energy charge and activating AMPK; it also acts through AMPK-independent, gut and lysosomal routes [med-owen2000, med-rena2017]. It suppresses NF-kB-linked inflammatory signalling independent of diabetes status [med-cameron2016]. Exercise adaptations depend partly on mitochondrial redox and energy-stress signals, and metformin abolished the exercise-induced rise in muscle mitochondrial respiration in older adults [med-konopka2019], a plausible way it can dampen a hormetic signal. B12 loss reflects reduced ileal absorption, raising homocysteine [med-dejager2010].
entries.interactions: May partially blunt adaptations to [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [hiit-vigorous-exercise] and [resistance-training] (a parallel to [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Improves [glycemic-control]. Main fertility use is in [pcos]. Long-term B12 depletion adds to that from [ppi-acid-suppressants]. [statins] have a similar exercise-interaction debate; [glp1-agonists] are the newer weight-and-glucose alternative.
entries.caveats: The blunting trials were mostly in healthy older adults or people with prediabetes taking metformin for research, not in people who need it for diabetes. Metformin is not an anti-aging supplement: TAME has not reported, and the survival advantage seen in one UK cohort was not reproduced in Danish twin data. Sperm data are tiny and uncontrolled.
entries.debate: Exercise blunting: RCTs found metformin reduced lean-mass and thigh-muscle gains [med-walton2019], VO2max and mitochondrial gains [med-konopka2019], and insulin-sensitivity gains [med-malin2012], and a 2026 meta-analysis of 9 trials found a modest VO2peak penalty (-1.19 mL/kg/min) and smaller blood-pressure falls [med-etayourtasun2026]; but other trials found no attenuation of glycaemic or fitness benefits [med-boule2013, med-pilmark2021, med-terada2019], and transcriptomic work suggests some aging-related muscle pathways may even be favourably shifted [med-kulkarni2020]. Longevity: TAME advocates cite metformin users outliving non-diabetic controls [med-barzilai2016, med-bannister2014]; a Danish twin and registry reanalysis found the opposite (IRR 1.32-1.64) [med-keys2022], and critics argue healthy-person benefit is unproven [med-konopka2019tame, med-miller2020]. Fathers: a Danish cohort linked paternal metformin during sperm development to birth defects (aOR 1.40) [med-wensink2022], but a larger Norway-Taiwan study controlling for diabetes severity found no association (pooled RR 0.89) [med-meng2024].

entries.title: Metformin

timing.summary: Metformin acts within days and clears within a day or two of stopping, but its interaction with exercise shows up over 3-4 months of training and its lowering of vitamin B12 accumulates over years. In UKPDS, early metformin use left a long-term legacy benefit.

onset.text: Half-life ~5 h with good kidney function [tbody-graham2011]; glucose effects begin within days of reaching dose (extrapolated from pharmacokinetics).

full.text: Blunted gains in insulin sensitivity, VO2max and mitochondrial respiration over 12 weeks of aerobic training [tbody-konopka2019] and in lean mass over 14 weeks of resistance training [tbody-walton2019]; B12 fell 19% over 4.3 years [tbody-dejager2010], with risk rising per year of use [tbody-aroda2016].

after_stopping.text: The drug itself clears within 1-2 days [tbody-graham2011]. In UKPDS, the cardiovascular and mortality benefit of early metformin persisted for 10-24 years after the trial [tbody-holman2008, tbody-adler2024].

frequency.text: Prescribed daily, usually split with meals. Whether separating doses from exercise sessions avoids blunting has not been tested.

timing.debate: Metformin blunted exercise adaptations in older adults [tbody-konopka2019, tbody-walton2019], yet carried a long legacy benefit in overweight people with type 2 diabetes [tbody-holman2008]; the two findings concern different populations.

audit.claim: Metformin blunts some training gains and lowers B12; it is not an anti-ageing supplement, and the UK survival advantage was not reproduced.
audit.biases: Immortal-time and time-window biases created illusory benefits in metformin cohorts [abody-suissa2012]; comparisons with non-diabetic controls are prone to selection and informative censoring.
audit.newer_evidence: The Bannister survival advantage [abody-bannister2014] reversed in Danish registry and twin data [abody-keys2022]. A 2025 target-trial emulation found metformin users more likely than sulfonylurea users to reach age 90 (HR 0.70), but against an active comparator that may itself be harmful and with acknowledged residual confounding [abody-shadyab2025].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: there is still no randomised evidence that metformin slows ageing in people without diabetes.

entries.headline: Promoted online as a mitochondrial enhancer, methylene blue did not extend mouse median lifespan in the ITP and its derivative failed a phase 3 Alzheimer trial, while it is a potent MAO-A inhibitor that can cause fatal serotonin toxicity with common antidepressants.

dose.effective: No proven anti-aging dose; medical uses (e.g. methaemoglobinaemia) are supervised IV doses of about 1-7.5 mg/kg
dose.studied_range: Single low oral doses in imaging studies; 195 mg/day in a bipolar trial; LMTM 8-250 mg/day in Alzheimer trials
dose.too_much: Severe serotonin toxicity reported at about 1 mg/kg in people taking serotonin reuptake inhibitors; high doses of the oxidized form can cause methaemoglobinaemia
dose.timeframe: Acute fMRI effects within an hour; no long-term benefit shown
dose.notes: Non-pharmaceutical-grade 'nootropic' products may contain impurities and are not standardized. Anyone on antidepressants should not take it without medical advice.

entries.mechanism: A redox dye that shuttles electrons between NADH and cytochrome c, bypassing complex I-III blocks in the respiratory chain; at low doses it enhanced cytochrome oxidase and memory in animal models. It is also a tight-binding MAO-A inhibitor, which is the basis of its main interaction risk.
entries.interactions: Dangerous with serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs, SNRIs, clomipramine) and other serotonergic drugs because of MAO-A inhibition.
entries.caveats: The human evidence for cognition is a 26-person single-dose imaging study; the Alzheimer phase 3 trial was negative. It is a prescription drug in medical use, and social-media dosing advice ignores its interaction profile.
entries.debate: Gonzalez-Lima and colleagues argue low-dose methylene blue enhances mitochondrial respiration and memory [lon-rojas2012], citing a small human fMRI study [lon-rodriguez2016]; a bipolar crossover trial found improved residual depression [lon-alda2017]. Against this, the ITP found no median lifespan effect in mice [lon-harrison2014], the 891-person phase 3 trial of the derivative LMTM was negative [lon-gauthier2016], and pharmacologists warn that all proposed doses reach MAO-A-inhibiting levels [lon-ramsay2007, lon-gillman2011]. Sponsor-employed authors later argued that the low-dose 'control' arm was itself pharmacologically active, which would mask a benefit [lon-vanmaanen2026]; this is a post-hoc, conflicted explanation that has not been confirmed by an independent trial.

key_numbers.label: Dose associated with severe serotonin toxicity

entries.title: Methylene blue (as a 'mitochondrial' longevity supplement)

timing.summary: Methylene blue acts within an hour and has a blood half-life of about 5 hours, so it is largely cleared within a day. Interaction risk with serotonergic drugs is a same-day issue.

onset.text: Brain fMRI and memory effects 1 hour after an oral dose [tnut-rodriguez2016].

full.text: Same as onset.

after_stopping.text: Terminal half-life about 5 h, so largely cleared in about a day (extrapolated) [tnut-peter2000].

frequency.text: No proven anti-ageing schedule [tnut-peter2000].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Methylmercury from large predatory fish can harm the developing brain at high intake (Faroe Islands), but in fish-eating populations the omega-3 and nutrient benefits outweigh it: children of mothers eating more than 340 g seafood a week did better, and mercury was not linked to cardiovascular disease in US cohorts.

dose.effective: Eat 2-3 servings (about 225-340 g) of fish a week, choosing low-mercury species (salmon, sardines, anchovies, herring, trout, pollock, shrimp); limit shark, swordfish, king mackerel, bigeye tuna, marlin and tilefish, especially in pregnancy and for children; check local advisories for freshwater fish you catch.
dose.studied_range: Maternal hair mercury about 0.1-10 ug/g; Seychelles mothers ate fish about 12 meals a week (mean hair 6.9 ppm).
dose.too_much: Deficits in Faroese children were seen even below 10 ug/g maternal hair mercury (where pilot whale was a source). Hair mercury >=2 ug/g was linked to MI in Finnish men eating freshwater fish.
dose.timeframe: Methylmercury blood half-life about 80 days; brain sensitivity is in pregnancy and early childhood.
dose.notes: Selenium in ocean fish may offset some mercury toxicity. Locally caught freshwater fish can be higher than commercial ocean fish; follow local advisories.

entries.mechanism: Methylmercury binds selenium and thiols, inhibits selenoenzymes (glutathione peroxidase, thioredoxin reductase) and promotes lipid peroxidation; Finnish men with high hair mercury had more antibodies to oxidised LDL [efw-salonen1995].
entries.interactions: Balance against [omega3-fish]. Follicular-fluid mercury and IVF are covered in [heavy-metals]. Selenium status ([selenium-supplement]) may modify toxicity.
entries.caveats: Fish intake confounds every mercury study: in a Polish clinic higher hair mercury went with better sperm concentration, likely because of fish nutrients [efw-minguezalarcon2018]. The Faroese exposure included pilot whale, which also carries PCBs.
entries.debate: Neurodevelopment: deficits in Faroese children [efw-grandjean1997] versus no consistent deficit in the high-fish Seychelles [efw-myers2003] and benefits with >340 g seafood a week in ALSPAC [efw-hibbeln2007, efw-golding2022]. Cardiovascular: higher MI risk with high hair mercury in Finland [efw-salonen1995] versus no association in two US cohorts [efw-mozaffarian2011] or NHANES [efw-sun2021]. Fertility: infertile couples had higher blood mercury [efw-choy2002] and predatory-fish eaters had fewer normal sperm [efw-ai2019], but hair mercury was unrelated to IVF outcomes [efw-wright2015] and positively related to sperm counts [efw-minguezalarcon2018]. A risk-benefit review concludes benefits exceed risks when high-mercury species are limited [efw-mozaffarian2006].

Coronary death reduction with 1-2 fish servings/week

entries.title: Methylmercury in fish

entries.headline: Plastic particles have been reported in blood, placenta, testis and brain, and one NEJM cohort linked plastic in carotid plaque to 4.5x more heart attacks, strokes and deaths, but the tissue numbers rest on a method that can mistake fat for polyethylene, and nothing yet shows that cutting exposure lowers body burden or risk.

dose.effective: No proven dose or intervention. Low-cost steps that cut measured particle release: don't microwave food, drinks or infant formula in plastic (up to 2 billion nanoparticles per cm2 in 3 min), prefer tap over bottled water where tap is safe (~240,000 particles/L in bottled water by single-particle imaging), use loose tea or non-plastic teabags (one plastic teabag at 95 C: ~15 billion particles), and vacuum regularly.
dose.studied_range: Estimated intake 39,000-52,000 particles/year from food (74,000-121,000 with inhalation); tissue concentrations reported from ~1.6 ug/mL (blood) to ~4,900 ug/g (brain) by pyrolysis GC/MS.
dose.timeframe: Unknown: uptake, clearance and half-lives of plastic particles in people have not been measured.
dose.notes: Exposure studies count particles released into water or food simulants in the lab; whether those particles are absorbed is unknown. No human study has tested whether any change lowers tissue levels.

entries.mechanism: In cells and animals, polystyrene and other particles trigger oxidative stress (mitochondrial ROS, NADPH oxidase), NLRP3/NF-kB inflammation, barrier disruption and immune changes; additives and adsorbed chemicals may contribute. Most experiments use pristine spheres at doses above estimated human exposure.
entries.interactions: Heated plastic food contact also leaches [phthalates]; household dust also carries flame retardants. No study has tested whether air purifiers or vacuuming lower microplastic body burden.
entries.caveats: Pyrolysis GC/MS cannot cleanly separate polyethylene and PVC signals from fats and other tissue components; microscopy-based methods in the same tissues find only a handful of particles. No study has met all basic quality-control criteria. Cross-sectional autopsy data cannot show cause (dementia brains may simply clear less).
entries.debate: Tissue burden: Py-GC/MS studies report milligram-per-gram plastic in brain [env-nihart2025], hundreds of ug/g in testis [env-hu2024] and placenta [env-garcia2024]. Against this, a validation study concluded Py-GC/MS is currently unsuitable for polyethylene and PVC in biological samples because of matrix interference [env-rauert2025]; lipid interference forces much higher polyethylene detection limits [env-almeida2026]; a QA/QC screen of 101 human studies found none met all essential criteria [env-lane2026]; analytical chemists published correspondence on the brain study [env-amonikh2025]; the brain paper required a correction for duplicated images and methods [env-nihart2025b]; and a comment on the testis study listed missing blanks and validation, to which the authors replied by trimming their reliable polymer list from 12 to 6 [env-uppu2025, env-hu2025]. Microscopy finds far fewer particles: 16 particles in 15 olfactory bulbs [env-amatolourenco2024]. Cardiovascular: plaque polyethylene predicted events (HR 4.53) [env-marfella2024], but this was one observational cohort measuring exactly the polymers (PE, PVC) that Py-GC/MS struggles with [env-rauert2025], and several letters were published with an author reply [env-glazier2024, env-wang2024, env-kalkman2024, env-holda2024, env-marfella2024b]. Mechanism: animal reproductive studies mostly report harm, but most lacked particle characterization or dose-response [env-due2026]. Exposure counts are also disputed: the teabag study drew a published comment [env-busse2020].

entries.title: Micro- and nanoplastics

timing.summary: Nobody has measured how long plastic particles stay in a human body, so no honest time course exists. Particles pass in stool within days of being eaten [tleg-schwabl2019], but whether anything is retained in tissue, for how long, and whether cutting exposure lowers a tissue burden are all unmeasured [tleg-lane2026].

onset.text: Not measured. Ingested particles appear in stool, which shows passage rather than uptake [tleg-schwabl2019]; intake has been estimated at tens of thousands of particles a year [tleg-cox2019].

full.text: Not measured. Organ concentrations were reported to be higher in 2024 than 2016 samples, which would imply slow accumulation, but the measurement method is disputed [tleg-nihart2025, tleg-monikh2025].

after_stopping.text: Not measured: there is no published human clearance half-life for micro- or nanoplastics, and no study has shown that reducing exposure lowers a measured body burden [tleg-lane2026].

frequency.text: No schedule can be justified from evidence. Avoiding bottled water is the one change with a quantified exposure difference (about 90,000 versus 4,000 particles a year) [tleg-cox2019], but no health or body-burden outcome has been measured.

sperm.late_start: Unknown: there is no measured lead time because there is no measured clearance.
sperm.text: Plastic particles have been reported in testis tissue with a correlation to lower sperm count, but this is a small autopsy series with contested methods and no timing information [tleg-lane2026, tleg-almeida2026].

timing.debate: The dispute is methodological and goes to the heart of the timing question. A widely reported study found rising micro- and nanoplastic concentrations in decedent brains [tleg-nihart2025]; a published letter argues the concentrations are implausible because the pyrolysis markers used for polyethylene cannot be distinguished from body lipids [tleg-monikh2025], an animal-tissue method study confirms that this causes false positives [tleg-almeida2026], and a quality-screening framework finds most human tissue studies fail basic contamination controls [tleg-lane2026]. The plaque-outcome cohort [tleg-marfella2024] rests on the same class of measurement.

audit.claim: Plastic particles are reported in blood, placenta, testis and brain and one NEJM cohort linked plaque plastic to 4.5-fold more cardiovascular events, but tissue numbers rest on a method prone to false positives and nothing shows that cutting exposure lowers body burden or risk (impact general 1, limited).
audit.biases: Measurement error and contamination: Py-GC/MS overcounts polyethylene and PVC in fatty matrices [ept-rauert2025, ept-almeida2026], and no human-tissue study met all essential QA/QC criteria [ept-lane2026]. Confounding and reverse causation in the plaque cohort (people with more plaque plastic may differ in many exposures); a single unreplicated cohort [ept-marfella2024, ept-marfella2024b].
audit.newer_evidence: No independent replication of the plaque-outcome association has appeared; newer studies are small cross-sections using the same Py-GC/MS approach, linking blood microplastics to acute coronary syndrome and inflammatory markers [ept-yang2024] and showing only moderate correlation between paired blood and plaque levels [ept-cui2025]. Methodological criticism has grown (2025-2026) [ept-monikh2025, ept-rauert2025, ept-almeida2026, ept-lane2026], and the brain paper was corrected [ept-nihart2025, ept-nihart2025b]. Published exposure figures check out against their sources (2.11 billion nanoplastics per cm2 in 3 minutes of microwaving [ept-hussain2023]; about 240,000 particles per litre of bottled water [ept-qian2024]; 11.6 billion micro- plus 3.1 billion nanoplastics per plastic teabag [ept-hernandez2019]; 39,000-121,000 particles a year [ept-cox2019]). Reproductive animal studies remain mostly of limited regulatory reliability [ept-due2026].
audit.bottom_line: Plastic particles have been reported in human tissue, but harm in people is unproven and the measurement method itself is under question.

entries.headline: Plastic particles have been reported in human testes (Py-GC/MS, mean 328 ug/g in 23 men) and in most semen samples (a few particles each by Raman or infrared), with hints of lower motility in studies of 40-45 men, but the testis method is disputed and there are no human data on sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: No proven intervention; use the general exposure steps in [microplastics] (don't heat food in plastic, prefer tap over bottled water where safe).
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional measurements in 6-45 men per study.
dose.timeframe: Unknown; any effect on sperm would take at least one ~74-day spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Different methods give incompatible numbers: Py-GC/MS reports mass (ug/g), spectroscopy counts a handful of particles.

entries.mechanism: In rodents, polystyrene micro/nanoplastics cross the blood-testis barrier, raise testicular ROS and inflammation and reduce sperm count and motility; human mechanistic data are lacking.
entries.interactions: Plastic particles carry phthalates and bisphenols ([phthalates]), which are hard to separate from particle effects.
entries.caveats: Tiny samples, no exposure gradient, no contamination-proof designs; motility differences were borderline (p=0.056) or between polymer types rather than exposed vs unexposed.
entries.debate: Presence: Py-GC/MS found plastic in every human testis [env-hu2024] and spectroscopy found particles in semen [env-montano2023, env-li2024, env-zhao2023, env-guo2025]. A published comment argued the testis study lacked blanks, controls and method validation [env-uppu2025]; the authors defended their digestion method but limited future work to 6 reliable polymers [env-hu2025]. Py-GC/MS polyethylene and PVC values in biological samples are vulnerable to false positives [env-rauert2025]. Harm: animal studies frequently report testicular damage but often lack dose and particle characterization [env-due2026].
entries.title: Microplastics in testis and semen

timing.summary: No time course exists: microplastics have been measured in testes, but not how fast levels change or how long any effect on sperm would last. The shape here is an assumption.

onset.text: Not measured.

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; tissue clearance rates in humans are unknown.

frequency.text: No evidence on exposure frequency.

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: Any effect on sperm production would need at least one cycle to change (extrapolated).

timing.debate: The testis measurement method behind the 328 ug/g figure [tsperm-hu2024] has been disputed in a published comment [tsperm-uppu2025].

audit.claim: Plastic is reported in human testes (mean 328 ug/g in 23 men by Py-GC/MS) and in most semen samples, with hints of lower motility in studies of 40-45 men, but the testis method is disputed and there are no human data on sperm DNA fragmentation (impact sperm 1, limited).
audit.biases: Cross-sectional designs with no exposure gradient; contamination and Py-GC/MS false positives for polyethylene and PVC [ept-rauert2025, ept-lane2026]; incompatible units across methods (ug/g vs particles); selection of fertility-clinic and varicocele patients; many polymer-by-endpoint comparisons.
audit.newer_evidence: Larger but still cross-sectional studies have appeared: 113 men in three Chinese regions (Raman; each extra polymer type detected went with lower count, concentration and motility) [ept-zhang2024]; 200 men (microplastics in 55.5% of semen; lower concentration only in a subgroup with frequent plastic-tableware use) [ept-qu2025]; 51 IVF couples (seminal PVC tracked lower motility, no effect on pregnancy) [ept-kong2025]; and a 98-man varicocele case-control using light microscopy [ept-ilki2026]. The earlier 45-man study's motility difference was p=0.056 [ept-guo2025]. The testis study's comment and reply stand [ept-hu2024, ept-uppu2025, ept-hu2025]. Still no human study of sperm DNA fragmentation. Follicular-fluid studies in women (44-51 patients) now report links with lower fertilization and ovarian reserve [ept-wang2025, ept-kong2025, ept-zhou2026], with the same method caveats; reviews conclude MNPs may be a reproductive hazard but cannot separate particle from additive effects [ept-wehrli2025, ept-due2026].
audit.bottom_line: Still a plausible but unproven sperm hazard: studies are bigger (up to 200 men) but all cross-sectional and method-limited, and no human DNA-fragmentation data exist.

factors.name: MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay)

entries.headline: Cohort studies linked high MIND-diet adherence to 53% lower Alzheimer incidence, but the 3-year randomized MIND trial (604 people) found no cognitive or brain-MRI benefit over a control diet with the same mild calorie restriction.

dose.effective: The MIND score rewards green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, berries, nuts, olive oil, whole grains, fish, beans and poultry, and penalizes red meat, butter and margarine, cheese, pastries and sweets, and fried or fast food.
dose.studied_range: Trial: MIND diet with mild caloric restriction versus a control diet with the same mild caloric restriction, 3 years, cognitively healthy adults 65+ with a family history of dementia. Cohorts: 4.5-12 years of follow-up.
dose.timeframe: No difference detectable after 3 years in the trial.
dose.notes: Both trial groups improved, so the trial compared MIND with another calorie-restricted diet, not with an unchanged diet.

entries.mechanism: Proposed: polyphenols (berries, leafy greens), folate, vitamin E, carotenoids and omega-3 fats limit neuronal lipid peroxidation and neuroinflammation and support vascular health; less saturated fat and fried food reduce dietary oxidation products and cardiometabolic risk.
entries.interactions: A hybrid of [mediterranean-diet] and [dash-diet]; emphasizes [blueberries] and [leafy-greens]. Weight loss and calorie restriction were confounded with diet in the trial.
entries.caveats: The observational evidence comes from food-frequency questionnaires in health-conscious cohorts and is prone to confounding and reverse causation (people in early cognitive decline change their diets). The MIND score was derived and first tested in the same cohort.
entries.debate: For: the original Rush cohort [skb-morris2015] and an Australian cohort [skb-hosking2019] found lower risk with high adherence, and a Mediterranean-diet RCT substudy improved cognitive composites [skb-vallspedret2015]. Against: the MIND RCT was null [skb-barnes2023], and a 20-year Swedish cohort of 28,025 people found no link between midlife diet quality (including Mediterranean adherence) and dementia [skb-glans2023]. Defenders argue 3 years is too short and the control group also improved its diet; critics reply that this is exactly why observational associations should not be read as causal.

entries.title: MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay)

timing.summary: Cognitive effects of diet are expected to build over years: the cohort link appeared over about 5 years of follow-up. The 3-year randomized trial found no difference against a calorie-matched control.

onset.text: No difference after 3 years in the randomized trial [tfood-barnes2023].

full.text: Cohort association over an average 4.7 years [tfood-morris2015].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: A whole daily eating pattern [tfood-morris2015].

timing.debate: Cohort data suggest slower decline over 4.7 years [tfood-morris2015], but the 3-year trial was null [tfood-barnes2023]; whether 3 years was too short or the cohort link was confounded is unresolved.

audit.claim: Cohorts linked MIND adherence to 53% lower Alzheimer risk, but the 3-year MIND RCT was null.
audit.biases: Reverse causation and food-questionnaire error apply; this is a textbook case of a cohort finding not replicated by a trial [adiet-barnes2023].
audit.newer_evidence: The 2023 NEJM MIND trial was null for cognition and MRI [adiet-barnes2023]. Diet MR is weak because food-intake genetics track education [adiet-cole2020].
audit.bottom_line: The cohort association should not be read as causal: the 3-year trial was null.

entries.headline: MitoQ 20 mg/day improved artery function in two small trials (older adults, kidney disease), but did not slow Parkinson disease over a year and slowed recovery after muscle-damaging exercise; SkQ1 has only eye-drop trials in humans.

dose.effective: MitoQ 20 mg/day (vascular trials)
dose.studied_range: MitoQ 20 mg/day for 2-6 weeks; 40-80 mg/day for 28 days (hepatitis C) and 12 months (Parkinson disease); single doses of 100-160 mg
dose.too_much: No serious toxicity reported; a single 100-160 mg dose did not raise urinary kidney-injury markers
dose.timeframe: Vascular effects at 4-6 weeks; DNA-damage protection after 3 weeks but not after a single dose
dose.notes: MitoQ is a proprietary product. SkQ1 has been tested in humans only as eye drops (Visomitin); oral SkQ1 has no published human trials.

entries.mechanism: A ubiquinone (MitoQ) or plastoquinone (SkQ1) attached to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium cation, which concentrates the antioxidant several hundred-fold in the mitochondrial matrix, aiming to quench mitochondrial superoxide and lipid peroxidation where ordinary antioxidants cannot reach.
entries.interactions: Like other antioxidants it may blunt adaptive signalling (see the mitohormesis mechanism); in one trial it delayed recovery after eccentric exercise. Compare [coq10], which suppressed muscle mitochondrial H2O2 similarly in a head-to-head trial.
entries.caveats: All human trials are small and short except the null Parkinson trial. Effects on urinary F2-isoprostanes, the best oxidative-damage marker, were absent in two trials. Rodent lifespan studies with SkQ1 depended heavily on housing and pathogen conditions.
entries.debate: Supporters point to improved flow-mediated dilation in older adults [lon-rossman2018] and chronic kidney disease [lon-kirkman2023], lower liver enzymes in hepatitis C [lon-gane2010], less exercise-induced DNA damage [lon-williamson2020], and its rationale as a targeted drug [lon-murphy2018]. Against this, a 12-month RCT in 128 people found no effect on Parkinson progression [lon-snow2010], MitoQ did not change mitochondrial function or F2-isoprostanes in middle-aged men [lon-pham2020], and it delayed strength recovery and raised creatine kinase after eccentric exercise [lon-broome2022]. SkQ1 rodent lifespan gains were strain- and vivarium-dependent [lon-anisimov2011], and its human evidence is limited to company-funded dry-eye trials [lon-petrov2016, lon-brzheskiy2015].
entries.title: Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (MitoQ, SkQ1)

timing.summary: MitoQ improved artery function after 6 weeks of daily use in older adults. Its human half-life and wash-out have not been published in verified sources.

onset.text: Not measured before 6 weeks; a large acute dose was used as a probe of mitochondrial ROS [tnut-rossman2018].

full.text: Flow-mediated dilation 42% higher after 6 weeks [tnut-rossman2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Trial used 20 mg once daily [tnut-rossman2018].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: MitoQ 20 mg/day improved artery function in two small trials, did not slow Parkinson disease, and slowed recovery after damaging exercise.
audit.biases: Small, short, company-linked trials [anut-rossman2018]; the one long trial was null [anut-snow2010].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 RCT of 12 weeks in older adults found MitoQ lowered muscle H2O2 emission capacity but changed neither respiration nor exercise redox signalling [anut-broome2025].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged: a biomarker effect without demonstrated functional benefit.

entries.headline: The only randomised trial of AUGMENT was discontinued after an interim analysis showed no benefit: fewer blastocysts (23% vs 41%) and the same live birth per transferred embryo (41.6% vs 41.2%), after an extra surgical ovarian biopsy.

dose.effective: Not recommended; ESHRE says mitochondrial replacement to improve egg quality is not recommended.
dose.studied_range: Mitochondria from the woman's own ovarian 'egg precursor' cells, injected with the sperm during ICSI.
dose.too_much: Requires laparoscopic ovarian cortex biopsy; unknown long-term safety for children.
dose.timeframe: One IVF cycle plus a prior biopsy.
dose.notes: Different from mitochondrial donation to prevent mtDNA disease, which is a regulated medical use.

entries.mechanism: Ageing eggs have fewer, less efficient mitochondria (see [maternal-age], [coq10]); adding 'young' mitochondria was meant to restore ATP supply for meiosis and early cleavage.
entries.interactions: Shares its rationale with [coq10] and [nmn-nad]; none has shown live-birth benefit in humans.
entries.caveats: Early positive reports were uncontrolled.
entries.debate: Researchers behind the technique note three early uncontrolled studies (104 patients) suggesting benefit [fer-tilly2020]; the randomised pilot found none and was discontinued [fer-labarta2019]. ESHRE does not recommend mitochondrial replacement for egg quality [fer-eshre2023addons].
