entries.title: Mitochondrial augmentation (AUGMENT autologous mitochondrial transfer)

entries.headline: Lab studies show phone radiation can raise ROS in semen in a dish, but human studies are inconsistent and show no dose-response with hours of use.

dose.effective: Low-cost precaution: keep the phone out of the front trouser pocket when possible.
dose.studied_range: In vitro exposure of semen samples; self-reported daily use in observational studies.
dose.timeframe: Unknown.
dose.notes: Treat as a weak, uncertain factor; far below smoking, heat or varicocele.

entries.mechanism: Proposed: RF energy and local heating increase mitochondrial ROS in sperm (shown in vitro), without clear DNA damage in the key in vitro study.
entries.interactions: Far smaller and less certain than heat sources in [everyday-scrotal-heat].
entries.caveats: One meta-analysis found no effect in human studies; another found associations but no dose-response, which argues against a strong causal effect. Confounding (sedentary habits, socioeconomic factors) likely.
entries.title: Mobile phone radiofrequency exposure

timing.summary: Studies found no relationship between hours of phone use and the size of any sperm effect. There is no time course to report.

onset.text: Not measured.

full.text: Not measured; the effect did not grow with more use [tsperm-kim2021].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No dose or time relationship with usage was found [tsperm-kim2021].

timing.debate: The same meta-analysis reports lower motility with exposure but no increase with more use [tsperm-kim2021], which weakens a causal reading.

audit.claim: Phone radiation raises ROS in semen in a dish, but human studies are inconsistent with no dose-response; keep the phone out of the front trouser pocket as a low-cost precaution (sperm impact 1, limited).
audit.biases: Self-reported phone use; heavy users differ in sedentary time, BMI and socioeconomic factors; in vitro studies expose neat semen at close range in conditions unlike pocket carriage [eia-agarwal2009]. Risk of bias for exposure assessment was high in most studies in the WHO reviews [eia-cordelli2024, eia-kenny2024].
audit.newer_evidence: The WHO-commissioned reviews (2024) found very uncertain evidence for any effect of duration of phone use on human semen and little or no effect of front-pocket carriage on semen or time to pregnancy [eia-kenny2024]; animal data suggested lower pregnancy rate (moderate certainty) and sperm count (low certainty), and in vitro human sperm data showed only a small effect on vitality and none on DNA (very low certainty) [eia-cordelli2024]. In 2,886 Swiss young men (2023), frequent use was linked to lower concentration and count, an association that faded over 2005-2018 as phones changed, with no pocket effect [eia-rahban2023]. Critics argue the WHO reviews cannot establish safety [eia-melnick2025].
audit.bottom_line: The evidence remains weak and uncertain. Keeping the phone out of a front pocket is harmless but not supported by human data.

entries.headline: Moving from no activity to 150-300 min/week is associated with 30-37% lower mortality in cohorts, but twin, genetic and trial data suggest much of that gap reflects genes and pre-existing illness; the benefits on fitness, blood pressure and glucose are proven in trials.

dose.effective: 150-300 min/week of moderate activity (brisk walking, easy cycling, swimming at a pace where you can talk but not sing), e.g. 30-45 min on 5 days, or roughly 7,000-10,000 steps/day. Splitting it into 1-2 longer sessions ('weekend warrior') appears about as good as spreading it out.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to 10+ times the 7.5 MET-h/week minimum (Arem 2015); 2,000-16,000 steps/day (step meta-analyses). Oxidative-stress RCTs: 45 min/day, 5 days/week at 60-75% HRmax for 12 months (Campbell 2010).
dose.too_much: No excess mortality even at 10 or more times the minimum (HR 0.69 vs inactive); the mortality curve plateaus at 3-5 times the minimum (about 450-750 min/week moderate). Very high lifelong endurance volumes raise questions about coronary calcium and atrial fibrillation (see [overtraining-ultraendurance]).
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity and antioxidant enzymes shift within weeks; resting F2-isoprostane reductions were seen at 12 months and only in women whose VO2max rose more than 15%. For sperm, allow one spermatogenic cycle (~74 days) plus maturation, about 3 months.
dose.notes: Fitness gain, not minutes logged, tracked the fall in oxidative markers. For older adults, mortality benefit levelled off around 6,000-8,000 steps/day; for younger adults around 8,000-10,000. Step speed added little once total steps were counted. Avoid gram-level vitamin C/E during training blocks ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).

entries.mechanism: Each session raises superoxide and H2O2 in working muscle, mainly from NADPH oxidase 2 at the cell membrane and to a lesser extent mitochondria. (Older views blamed mitochondrial leak; newer biosensor work identifies NOX2 as the main cytosolic source during moderate exercise, with xanthine oxidase also implicated.) These pulses oxidize KEAP1 and release Nrf2 (glutathione synthesis, SOD, catalase, HO-1), activate PGC-1alpha-driven mitochondrial biogenesis and AMPK/p38 signalling, and acutely boost GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake. Repeated pulses raise resting antioxidant capacity (mitohormesis), while reduced visceral fat, better glucose control and lower inflammation remove chronic ROS sources.
entries.interactions: Adds to [weight-loss] (diet-induced weight loss lowered F2-isoprostanes more than exercise alone). Improves [glycemic-control]. High-dose vitamin C/E, resveratrol or NAC around training can blunt molecular adaptations ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). Builds [cardiorespiratory-fitness]. Pairs with [resistance-training] for the largest mortality association. In men, very high cycling volumes are a separate issue ([cycling]); in lean women, heavy vigorous volumes can suppress ovulation ([vigorous-exercise-low-energy]).
entries.caveats: Mortality data are observational: healthier people exercise more, and sick people stop. Effects on resting oxidative markers in already-fit healthy people are small and inconsistent, and many trials use crude markers (MDA/TBARS, 'total antioxidant capacity'). A rise in oxidative markers right after a session is the signal, not damage. Sperm evidence: active men often have better counts, but a large Spanish study and a large preconception cohort found no consistent link; the strongest semen RCT comes from a group with other retracted papers.
entries.debate: How much of the observational 30-50% mortality reduction is causal is contested. Twin data show the association persists within twin pairs [exr-kujala1998], and modelling cumulative activity with lag time preserved a robust inverse dose-response [exr-lee2021]; but a newer twin analysis found that after accounting for familial factors and prevalent disease the benefit shrank to near zero, pointing to genetic confounding and reverse causation [exr-kankaanpaa2025]. The largest long-term RCT in older adults (Generation 100) found no mortality difference versus guideline advice, although controls were themselves active [exr-stensvold2020], and a critical review of ~50,000 RCT participants found no proven reduction in mortality or CVD [exr-ballin2021]. Supporters note that RCTs compare active with slightly-less-active people over short periods. For semen, positive cross-sectional data [exr-gaskins2015, exr-zou2018, exr-vaamonde2012] contrast with null findings [exr-minguezalarcon2014, exr-wise2011, exr-wise2025]; the main RCT [exr-hajizadehmaleki2017] comes from a group whose related trials were retracted.

entries.title: Regular moderate aerobic exercise

entries.headline: Active men have better sperm counts, and one large RCT found moderate continuous training improved sperm DNA integrity more than high-intensity training.

dose.effective: About 30-45 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise (brisk walking, jogging, swimming, gym cardio), 3-5 days a week, plus less TV/sitting time.
dose.studied_range: Moderate continuous, high-intensity continuous and interval training, 3 sessions/week for 24 weeks (280 men); >=15 h/week moderate-vigorous activity in observational data.
dose.too_much: Very high training loads and long-distance cycling may worsen semen ([cycling]); in the RCT moderate beat high-intensity.
dose.timeframe: Improvements by 12-24 weeks; benefits faded within about a month of stopping training.
dose.notes: Over 20 h/week of TV was linked to 44% lower concentration.

entries.mechanism: Regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase) via hormetic Nrf2 signalling, lowers inflammation, improves insulin sensitivity and weight.
entries.interactions: Supports [weight-loss]. High-dose antioxidant pills can blunt exercise adaptations in other tissues, a reason not to stack them.
entries.caveats: The key RCTs come from one Iranian group (Hajizadeh Maleki/Tartibian); its moderate-exercise trial in infertile men (Cytokine 2017) and its combined-exercise trial (J Strength Cond Res 2019) were retracted, so the remaining healthy-men trial should be treated with caution. Observational data are confounded.
entries.title: Moderate regular exercise (and less sitting)

entries.headline: Moderate activity (e.g. brisk walking, cycling) is linked to slightly higher fecundability (FR 1.18 at >= 5 h/week) and, in women with reproductive problems, exercise interventions roughly doubled pregnancy rates in small trials.

dose.effective: Regular moderate activity; >= 5 h/week of moderate activity was associated with slightly higher fecundability, and any activity type helped women with BMI >= 25.
dose.studied_range: Moderate activity < 1 to >= 5 h/week; intervention trials mainly in PCOS and obesity.
dose.too_much: See [vigorous-exercise-low-energy]: >= 5 h/week vigorous activity in lean women.
dose.timeframe: Insulin sensitivity improves within weeks; ovulatory changes over months.
dose.notes: Pre-IVF activity (median 2.8 h/week moderate-to-vigorous) was not harmful.

entries.mechanism: Improves insulin sensitivity and reduces inflammation; regular moderate exercise up-regulates endogenous antioxidant defenses (hormesis).
entries.interactions: Combines with [weight-loss] in overweight women.
entries.caveats: Intervention trials are few and small; the benefit is clearest in women with PCOS or overweight.

key_numbers.label: Pregnancy, PA intervention vs no therapy

entries.title: Moderate physical activity

timing.summary: Each session gives a burst of redox signalling and better glucose handling that lasts one to two days, while repeated sessions build fitness, mitochondria and antioxidant defences over weeks and the survival benefit tracks fitness kept up over years. Recently gained fitness fades within one to two months of stopping, so the habit matters more than any single block of training.

onset.text: Within hours: blood oxidative markers peak 1-4 h after hard exercise and settle within 24 h [tbody-michailidis2007]; PGC-1alpha and Nrf2 signals spike after each bout [tbody-perry2010, tbody-islam2020]; insulin sensitivity is raised the same day [tbody-mikines1988]. Muscle mitochondrial markers rise within the first week [tbody-egan2013].

full.text: VO2max rises within 3 weeks and was still climbing at 12 weeks (+18% young, +31% older men) [tbody-murias2010]; gains keep growing with more weekly dose [tbody-montero2017]. Mortality benefit accrues over years: men who went from unfit to fit over ~5 years had 44% lower mortality than those who stayed unfit [tbody-blair1995].

after_stopping.text: The single-bout insulin effect is gone after about 2-5 days [tbody-hawley2008, tbody-mikines1989]. Recently gained VO2max is completely lost after more than 4 weeks off [tbody-mujika2000b]; in long-trained people VO2max fell 7% in 3 weeks and settled 16% lower by 8 weeks, and muscle oxidative enzymes halved in ~12 days but stayed above sedentary levels [tbody-coyle1984].

frequency.text: Because one session's insulin-sensitising effect lasts roughly 48 h [tbody-hawley2008, tbody-mikines1988], exercising at least every second day keeps it continuous. Building fitness needs more than keeping it: after 10 weeks of training, 2 sessions a week at the same intensity maintained VO2max for 15 weeks [tbody-hickson1981, tbody-spiering2021], whereas lowering intensity did not [tbody-hickson1985].

sperm.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks before still improves insulin sensitivity and fitness quickly, but only reaches sperm in their last maturation steps; no trial shows semen changes that fast.
sperm.text: New sperm take about 64 days (42-76) to reach the ejaculate [tbody-misell2006], so a new programme needs 2-3 months to show in semen; the trial that improved semen in obese men ran 16 weeks [tbody-rosety2017]. Evidence is mostly observational [tbody-gaskins2015].

egg.late_start: Insulin sensitivity improves within days of starting, which may help the final follicle phase, but there is no direct trial evidence for a late start.
egg.text: The ovulatory follicle grows for about 85 days before ovulation [tbody-gougeon1986]; exercise likely acts through insulin sensitivity and weight, which change over weeks to months. Intervention trials in women with reproductive problems are few and small [tbody-mena2019].

timing.debate: Fitness gains are linked to lower mortality in cohorts [tbody-blair1995, tbody-lee2011], and starting in midlife looked as good as lifelong activity [tbody-saintmaurice2019], but Mendelian randomization questions whether fitness itself causes longevity [tbody-kjaergaard2025]. On frequency, the short-lived insulin effect argues for frequent sessions [tbody-hawley2008], yet people who do all their activity on 1-2 days have similar mortality to regular exercisers [tbody-odonovan2017, tbody-dossantos2022].

audit.claim: Going from no activity to 150-300 min/week is associated with roughly 30-37% lower mortality, with most gain in the first 7,000-8,000 steps/day.
audit.biases: Healthy-user and reverse causation: people with preclinical disease move less (activity fell up to 9 years before a dementia diagnosis [abody-sabia2017]); genetic confounding: the same genes influence activity, fitness and survival [abody-karvinen2015].
audit.newer_evidence: The 1998 Finnish twin study found the association persisted within twin pairs (OR 0.44) [abody-kujala1998], but later analyses of the same twin resource found no mortality difference in activity-discordant identical twins [abody-karvinen2015] and at most 7% lower mortality that faded after accounting for familial factors and prevalent disease (2025) [abody-kankaanpaa2025]. MR studies are null for coronary disease, stroke and mortality [abody-bahls2021, abody-han2026], though one MR supports vigorous activity lowering hypertension and type 2 diabetes [abody-zhao2024]. The only long-term RCT in older adults (Generation 100) found no significant mortality reduction, with an active control group [abody-stensvold2020], and RCTs of ~50,000 people show no mortality or CVD reduction [abody-ballin2021]. Cohort dose-response remains strong [abody-arem2015].
audit.bottom_line: Exercise clearly improves fitness, blood pressure and glucose, but the 30-37% mortality figure is an upper bound; the causal effect on death is probably smaller and its size is unknown.

entries.headline: Cutting carbohydrate to under ~130 g/day (below ~26% of energy) without necessarily reaching ketosis lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP over 3-6 months about as well as keto for many people. Weight loss matches low-fat diets at 12 months, and plant-based versions are linked to lower mortality.

dose.effective: About 50-130 g/day of carbohydrate, mostly from vegetables, legumes, nuts, berries and some intact whole grains, replacing refined starch and sugar. Protein and unsaturated fat fill the gap.
dose.studied_range: RCTs of < 130 g/day (or < 26-45% of energy) for 3-24 months; DIETFITS reached ~30% of energy from carbohydrate for 12 months.
dose.too_much: Below ~50 g/day it becomes a ketogenic diet, with the risks listed there. Patterns heavy in animal fat and processed meat are linked to higher mortality.
dose.timeframe: Glycaemic and triglyceride effects within weeks; benefits in diabetes trials shrink by 12 months unless adherence holds.
dose.notes: This is mostly the carbohydrate-quality message ([refined-sugar-high-glycemic]) plus some quantity restriction. It keeps the fibre and polyphenols that strict keto tends to drop.

entries.mechanism: Lower glycaemic load means smaller post-meal glucose and insulin spikes. That means less glucose-driven NADPH oxidase activation and less AGE formation, plus lower triglycerides and liver fat. Benefits on oxidative and inflammatory markers mostly track weight loss and glycaemic control rather than ketones.
entries.interactions: Largely the same benefit as [glycemic-control] and [weight-loss]. Compatible with [mediterranean-diet] and [dietary-fiber-microbiome]. In PCOS, low-carbohydrate diets were the best dietary subgroup for reproductive outcomes (see [ketogenic-diet]). A stricter version is [ketogenic-diet].
entries.caveats: In DIETFITS (609 adults), healthy low-carb and healthy low-fat diets gave the same 12-month weight loss. Lipid responses vary, and LDL can rise. The mortality data are observational, and the result depends on what replaces the carbohydrate.

key_numbers.label: Diabetes remission at 6 months, low-carb vs control
12-month weight change, healthy low-carb vs low-fat
Mortality HR per 20 percentiles, healthy low-carb score

entries.title: Moderate low-carbohydrate diet (non-ketogenic, ~50-130 g/day)

timing.summary: Lower glucose peaks start with the first meals, while HbA1c, weight and triglyceride benefits build over months, peaking around six months. They shrink by a year as adherence slips and reverse if the diet stops.

onset.text: Post-meal glucose and oxidative bursts depend on each meal's carbohydrate load [tbody-mohanty2000]; trials first measured HbA1c and weight at 3-6 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

full.text: Largest improvements at 6 months, diminished at 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; HbA1c would drift back over about 3 months given its ~35-day half-time [tbody-tahara1995] (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Effects depend on everyday meals; LDL can rise within 3 weeks on very low intakes in lean people [tbody-retterstol2018].

timing.debate: Remission and weight benefits seen at 6 months shrank to small or trivial by 12 months [tbody-goldenberg2021]; no substantive published debate on timing beyond this was found.

audit.claim: Moderate low-carb lowers HbA1c, triglycerides and CRP, matches low-fat for weight at 12 months, and plant-based versions are linked to lower mortality.
audit.biases: Mortality data are observational; questionnaire-based diet scores mix food quality with carbohydrate amount [adiet-shan2020].
audit.newer_evidence: DIETFITS showed equal weight loss for healthy low-fat and low-carb [adiet-gardner2018]; the ARIC/meta-analysis U-shape with plant vs animal substitution shows that the source of the replacement fat and protein matters [adiet-seidelmann2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate as written.

factors.name: Moringa leaf powder (moringin and related isothiocyanates)

entries.headline: Moringa leaves make unusually stable isothiocyanates, and 20 g of leaf powder blunted a post-meal glucose rise in people with diabetes, but a 2025 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs found no consistent effect on glucose, lipids or weight (very low certainty).

dose.effective: Not established; the acute glucose effect used 20 g leaf powder with a meal, and 4 g raised insulin secretion in healthy adults.
dose.studied_range: 1-20 g leaf powder; chronic RCTs of 2 weeks or more.
dose.too_much: Large doses are unpalatable; supplement isothiocyanate content is rarely stated.
dose.timeframe: Acute post-meal effects; chronic effects unproven.
dose.notes: Fresh leaves crushed in water let the leaf's own myrosinase form moringa isothiocyanates, which kept about 80% of their activity after 30 days at 37 C, far more stable than sulforaphane.

entries.mechanism: Moringa isothiocyanates are electrophilic Nrf2 activators and NF-kB/iNOS inhibitors in cells; in mice they suppressed liver gluconeogenesis. The leaf's polyphenols, fibre and minerals may also contribute to glucose effects.
entries.interactions: Same electrophile/Nrf2 route as [broccoli-sprouts] and [watercress-peitc]; stacking them mostly targets one pathway.
entries.caveats: Claims that moringin equals or beats sulforaphane rest on cell assays; there are no published human pharmacokinetic or Nrf2-target data for moringin. Continuous-glucose-monitor anecdotes are not trials. Human RCTs are small and heterogeneous.

key_numbers.label: Insulin secretion rise after 4 g leaf powder

entries.title: Moringa leaf powder (moringin and related isothiocyanates)

timing.summary: Moringa leaf powder blunted the blood-glucose rise of the meal it was eaten with, in people with diabetes. Longer-term effects are unproven, so there is no known build-up or persistence.

onset.text: Lower post-meal glucose increments at 90-150 min with 20 g leaf powder in the meal [tfood-leone2018].

full.text: Not measured beyond the single meal.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; the measured effect is confined to that meal.

frequency.text: Acts per meal [tfood-leone2018]; chronic benefit unproven.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Moringa showed an acute glucose effect but a 2025 meta-analysis found no consistent cardiometabolic effect.
audit.biases: Small heterogeneous trials.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2025 meta-analysis remains the latest [adiet-crisan2025].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Bright daytime, especially morning, light anchors the body clock earlier (a summer camping weekend gave ~69% of a full week's shift), light therapy modestly improves sleep problems, and among 88,905 UK Biobank sensor-wearers the brightest days were linked to 17-34% lower mortality, but these outcome links are observational.

dose.effective: Daytime light of at least 250 lux melanopic EDI at eye level, which typical indoor lighting often fails to reach but outdoor daylight easily exceeds; in practice, time outdoors in the first hours after waking and working near windows.
dose.studied_range: Camping in natural light for a weekend to a week; office workers with measured circadian light; light-therapy trials with light boxes for sleep problems.
dose.too_much: Never look directly at the sun; balance with skin UV protection ([uv-sun-exposure]).
dose.timeframe: Circadian shifts within days; sleep improvements within weeks.
dose.notes: Late chronotypes shifted the most toward solar time in the camping study.

entries.mechanism: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus; light in the early biological day advances the clock, strengthens rhythm amplitude and supports a timely, robust evening melatonin rise, which aligns metabolic, antioxidant and DNA-repair rhythms with behaviour.
entries.interactions: Complements dim evenings ([evening-light-exposure]); helps shift workers re-entrain ([shift-work-circadian]); supports sleep ([short-sleep]).
entries.caveats: Mortality and diabetes associations with light patterns come from a week of wrist-sensor data and could reflect health, mobility and time outdoors (exercise). Light-therapy meta-analysis showed publication bias and smaller effects in RCTs. Some of the leading cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding.
entries.debate: Camping and office studies show earlier, stronger rhythms with more daylight [kcc-wright2013, kcc-stothard2017, kcc-figueiro2017], and UK Biobank links brighter days to lower mortality [kcc-windred2024b]; an expert consensus sets daytime targets [kcc-brown2022]. Sceptics note the outcome data are observational with possible reverse causation (sick people go outside less), light-therapy effects are small with publication bias [kcc-vanmaanen2016], and some cohort authors disclose lighting-industry funding [kcc-windred2024b]. No trial has tested daylight exposure on oxidative-stress markers.

key_numbers.label: Recommended daytime light at the eye
Circadian shift from weekend camping, relative to a week
All-cause mortality, brightest-day decile (lower bound of range)

entries.title: Morning and daytime bright light

timing.summary: Bright daytime and morning light moves the body clock earlier within a weekend and fully within a week, and light therapy improves sleep problems over weeks. The clock drifts later again when daylight is lost.

onset.text: A summer weekend of natural light achieved ~69% of a week's circadian advance [tbody-stothard2017].

full.text: One week of natural light aligned the clock to sunrise and sunset [tbody-wright2013]; light therapy improved sleep problems in trials lasting weeks [tbody-vanmaanen2016].

after_stopping.text: Not measured directly; the delay seen in typical weekends under electric light [tbody-stothard2017] suggests the shift reverses within days.

frequency.text: The clock is reset daily, so daily outdoor light, especially early in the day, is needed.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Bright daytime light anchors the clock; UK Biobank brightest days were linked to 17-34% lower mortality, but these links are observational.
audit.biases: Reverse causation (sick people go outside less) and confounding by outdoor activity.
audit.newer_evidence: No new causal data; the main outcome study remains observational [abody-windred2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds as worded.

factors.name: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

entries.headline: Sprinkling 1 g powdered brown mustard on 200 g cooked broccoli raised sulforaphane metabolite excretion about 4.5-fold, and mustard-seed myrosinase doubled conversion of a broccoli seed extract (40% vs 19%).

dose.effective: About 1 g (roughly 1/2 teaspoon) powdered brown mustard per 200 g cooked broccoli, stirred in after cooking.
dose.studied_range: 1 g mustard powder with 200 g cooked broccoli (12 adults, crossover); mustard-seed powder with a glucoraphanin-rich seed extract (16 adults, crossover).
dose.timeframe: Same meal.
dose.notes: Add after cooking, once the food has cooled below steaming; heat inactivates mustard myrosinase too. Raw daikon radish (used to make Qidong's sulforaphane-rich beverage) or a pinch of broccoli seed powder works on the same principle.

entries.mechanism: Exogenous plant myrosinase hydrolyses glucoraphanin that survives cooking into sulforaphane in the meal and upper gut, instead of leaving it to variable colonic bacteria; then Nrf2 activation.
entries.interactions: Turns cooked [broccoli-mature] and [cruciferous-other] into meaningful sulforaphane sources and can boost glucoraphanin-only [sulforaphane-supplements]; same redundancy considerations as other Nrf2 inducers.
entries.caveats: Two small pharmacokinetic trials; no outcome data.

key_numbers.label: Urinary SF-NAC, cooked broccoli + 1 g mustard
Seed extract conversion with mustard myrosinase

entries.title: Mustard powder on cooked crucifers (myrosinase add-back)

timing.summary: Mustard powder works within the same meal: it restores the enzyme that cooking destroys and raised sulforaphane output from cooked broccoli about 4.5-fold over the next 24 h. It has no effect of its own beyond that meal.

onset.text: Same meal: sulforaphane metabolites in 24 h urine rose about 4.5-fold [tfood-okunade2018].

full.text: Complete within the 24 h after the meal [tfood-okunade2018].

after_stopping.text: No carryover beyond the meal it is added to.

frequency.text: Add it to each cooked crucifer meal; it only affects that meal [tfood-okunade2018].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Widely used in PCOS, but the Cochrane review rated the evidence very low quality and could not show a live-birth benefit (OR 2.42, 95% CI 0.75-7.83); the 2023 PCOS guideline review calls it limited and inconclusive.

dose.effective: Trials commonly used 4 g/day myo-inositol with 400 ug folic acid (e.g. the now-retracted Pacchiarotti trial); no dose is proven to raise live birth.
dose.studied_range: 11 of 13 Cochrane trials used myo-inositol as pre-treatment before IVF; 2 during ovulation induction.
dose.too_much: Mild GI effects; fewer GI effects than metformin.
dose.timeframe: Pre-treatment before IVF stimulation in most trials.
dose.notes: D-chiro-inositol may help ovulation per the guideline review, but evidence is very uncertain. One widely cited myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT (526 women) was retracted in 2026.

entries.mechanism: Inositol phosphoglycans act as second messengers for insulin and FSH signalling; may improve insulin sensitivity in PCOS.
entries.interactions: Alternative to or adjunct with metformin; often combined with [melatonin] and [folic-acid].
entries.caveats: Industry-linked trials, poor reporting and a retraction. Not relevant for women without PCOS.

key_numbers.label: Live birth, MI vs standard (2 RCTs)

entries.title: Myo-inositol (in PCOS)

timing.summary: In PCOS, inositol trials report a rise in estradiol within the first week and earlier first ovulation, with cycle regularity improving over about 3 months. Much of the early trial literature has since been retracted or flagged.

onset.text: E2 rose in the first week; first ovulation at 23.6 vs 41.8 days on placebo [tegg-gerli2003] (trial now under an expression of concern).

full.text: Trials typically ran about 14 weeks [tegg-gerli2003].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Usually twice daily; no schedule comparison.

timing.debate: A 2023 meta-analysis of 26 RCTs found more regular cycles (RR 1.79) [tegg-greff2023], but Cochrane rates the evidence very low quality [tegg-showell2018]; a key placebo trial was retracted in 2023 [tegg-gerli2007], a 2009 review retracted in 2025 [tegg-papaleo2025], and the 2003 trial carries a 2025 expression of concern [tegg-gerli2003].

egg.late_start: Ovulatory effects in PCOS may start within weeks [tegg-gerli2003], but evidence for egg quality is very low quality [tegg-showell2018].
egg.text: Extrapolated from trial durations and the follicle growth path; live-birth benefit is unproven [tegg-showell2018].

audit.claim: Widely used in PCOS, but Cochrane rates the evidence very low and cannot show a live-birth benefit; one myo-inositol plus melatonin RCT was retracted in 2026.
audit.biases: Industry links and integrity: a second key trial, Papaleo 2009 (myo-inositol and oocyte quality in ICSI), was retracted in 2025 at the request of the ASRM Publications Committee for an undisclosed conflict of interest with the supplement maker [afert-papaleo2009, afert-papaleo2009ret], alongside the retracted Pacchiarotti 2016 trial [afert-pacchiarotti2016]. PCOS fertility trials that did not share data were more often at high risk of bias and gave different pooled results [afert-bordewijk2020b]. Cochrane's apparent miscarriage reduction rested on one trial with an unusually high control miscarriage rate [afert-showell2018].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis reports higher mature-egg rates in PCOS IVF but no data strong enough for live birth [afert-zhang2025]; Cochrane's live-birth estimate remains OR 2.42 (0.75-7.83) [afert-showell2018].
audit.bottom_line: There is still no reliable evidence that myo-inositol raises live birth, and two influential trials are now retracted.

entries.headline: NAC raises glutathione and improved performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunts muscle repair signalling. In mouse cancer models it accelerated tumour growth and metastasis.

dose.effective: 1,200 mg/day (600 mg twice daily) for 30 days in people with low baseline glutathione
dose.studied_range: 1,200 mg/day for 30 days (performance trial); short courses in exercise-recovery studies
dose.too_much: No defined toxicity threshold at these doses, but caution in people with active or past cancer (mouse data) and around training (blunted adaptation).
dose.timeframe: Glutathione restored within 30 days in deficient individuals
dose.notes: Benefit depends on baseline redox status; there is no routine clinical test, and this is a research approach.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine, the limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis via glutamate-cysteine ligase. By raising GSH it can blunt redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR, NF-kB) needed for repair, and in tumour cells it can increase glutathione-dependent migration.
entries.interactions: Combined with glycine as [glynac]. Redundant with a high-protein diet rich in sulfur amino acids, and with Nrf2 activators that induce GCL. Antagonises exercise adaptation like [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Popular as a 'master antioxidant' supplement. Human outcome data in healthy people are lacking, and the tumour-promotion findings come from mice with existing tumours.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: NAC 600 mg/day for 3 months lowered SDF and improved motility in an uncontrolled study; no placebo-controlled live-birth data.

dose.effective: 600 mg/day for 3 months (studied dose).
dose.studied_range: 600 mg/day in 50 men with asthenoteratozoospermia.
dose.too_much: Higher doses add GI upset; no proven extra benefit.
dose.timeframe: 3 months.

entries.mechanism: Cysteine donor for glutathione synthesis; also reported to induce Nrf2 target genes in sperm.
entries.interactions: Part of many combination products.
entries.caveats: Before-after design without placebo. Some widely cited NAC/selenium RCTs come from an author several of whose other papers have been retracted; they are not used here.
entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)

entries.headline: In PCOS, NAC added to clomiphene improved ovulation and pregnancy vs placebo in small, biased trials, but it was inferior to metformin and live-birth data are thin.

dose.effective: 1.2 g/day (with clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS) in the original RCT.
dose.studied_range: 1.2 g/day in the main RCT; 8 RCTs (910 women) pooled in meta-analysis.
dose.timeframe: During ovulation-induction cycles.
dose.notes: A glutathione precursor; available as a supplement in some countries and a drug in others.

entries.mechanism: Supplies cysteine for glutathione synthesis; may improve insulin sensitivity.
entries.interactions: Compared against metformin and [l-carnitine] in trials; the NAC-vs-carnitine trial in the Cochrane review was flagged for integrity concerns.
entries.caveats: Many trials come from a few centres; high risk of selection, attrition and reporting bias. The 1.2 g/day trial's 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast is implausibly large.

key_numbers.label: Ovulation, NAC + clomiphene vs placebo + clomiphene

entries.title: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) in PCOS

timing.summary: NAC peaks in blood within 1-2 hours and has a half-life of about 6 hours, but restoring glutathione in deficient people took about 30 days of twice-daily dosing. Sperm studies used 3 months.

onset.text: Plasma peak 1-2 h, half-life ~6 h [tnut-holdiness1991].

full.text: 30 days of 600 mg twice daily restored glutathione in low-glutathione people only [tnut-paschalis2018].

after_stopping.text: Plasma NAC gone within about a day (extrapolated from 6 h half-life) [tnut-holdiness1991]; glutathione persistence not measured.

frequency.text: Trials split doses twice daily, which fits the 6-hour half-life (extrapolated) [tnut-paschalis2018, tnut-holdiness1991].

sperm.late_start: Not measured.
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; the (uncontrolled) sperm study used 3 months [tnut-jannatifar2019].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: NAC helps only people with low glutathione, blunts repair signalling in replete people, accelerated tumours in mice; small uncontrolled sperm data; PCOS trials small and biased.
audit.biases: The 49% vs 1% ovulation contrast in the key PCOS trial [anut-rizk2005] is implausible; PCOS trials from few centres carry integrity risk [anut-bordewijk2020, anut-thakker2015].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 RCT in vascular MCI found NAC added nothing to cardiac rehabilitation [anut-gallagher2026]. Mouse data now show NAC promoting metastasis as well as progression [anut-wiel2019]. The low-glutathione responder finding [anut-paschalis2018] has not been replicated in a larger trial.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged; NAC is not a general 'master antioxidant'.

entries.headline: NR and NMN reliably raise blood NAD+ (NR 1 g/day by about 140%), but most human trials found no gain in insulin sensitivity, muscle mitochondria or muscle function, and NR did not extend mouse lifespan in the ITP.

dose.effective: No dose has a proven clinical benefit; NR 300-1000 mg/day or NMN 250-600 mg/day raise blood NAD+
dose.studied_range: NR 100-2000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks; NMN 250-900 mg/day for up to about 12 weeks
dose.too_much: No serious adverse effects in trials up to NR 2 g/day for 12 weeks; long-term safety beyond months is unknown
dose.timeframe: Blood NAD+ rises within 2 weeks; no clinical effect has been consistently shown at any duration
dose.notes: Blood NAD+ is a marker of intake, not proof of tissue benefit; muscle NAD+ did not rise in some trials. In the US, FDA reversed its 2022 exclusion of NMN from the supplement definition in September 2025.

entries.mechanism: NAD+ is the cofactor for mitochondrial energy metabolism and the substrate of sirtuins and PARPs (DNA repair). NAD+ falls with age in rodent tissues. NR and NMN are vitamin B3 forms that feed NAD+ salvage synthesis. They are not antioxidants, but NAD+/NADH and NADPH balance underlies much of cellular redox control.
entries.interactions: Exercise raises muscle NAD+ synthesis naturally ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]). Plain nicotinamide and niacin also raise NAD+ but were rarely compared head-to-head. The egg-specific evidence is covered on the same page.
entries.caveats: Many trials are small, short, industry-funded and measure surrogate markers. The single strongly positive insulin-sensitivity trial had a large baseline liver-fat imbalance. Positive walking-distance and 'biological age' findings come from one trial that used an online age calculator of uncertain validity.
entries.debate: Supporters cite the Yoshino trial, in which NMN 250 mg/day raised muscle insulin sensitivity in 25 prediabetic women [lon-yoshino2021], a dose-ranging trial showing longer 6-minute walks [lon-yi2023], and anti-inflammatory signals [lon-elhassan2019, lon-brakedal2022]. Critics note the Yoshino groups differed sharply in baseline liver fat [lon-brenner2021], while trials of NR at 1-2 g/day found no improvement in insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial function or body composition [lon-dollerup2018, lon-dollerup2020, lon-remie2020] and a meta-analysis found no benefit for muscle mass or function in older adults [lon-prokopidis2025]. NR also failed to extend lifespan in the rigorous ITP mouse programme [lon-harrison2021]. Several key pharmacokinetic and safety trials were sponsored by the NR manufacturer [lon-trammell2016, lon-conze2019]. Reviews agree the compounds are safe short term and raise NAD+, but benefit is unproven [lon-freeberg2023].

key_numbers.label: Baseline liver fat, NMN vs placebo group

entries.title: NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)

entries.headline: NAD+ falls in ageing mouse eggs and NMN restored egg quality and fertility in aged mice, but there are no human data on egg quality, pregnancy or live birth.

dose.effective: No human fertility dose exists; all egg data are from mice.
dose.studied_range: Animal studies only.
dose.too_much: Unknown in pregnancy; safety in early embryos not studied in humans.
dose.notes: Marketed heavily as 'egg rejuvenation'; this is extrapolation from mice.

entries.mechanism: Raises NAD+, a cofactor for sirtuins (e.g. SIRT2) and mitochondrial metabolism; in aged mice restored spindle assembly, mitochondrial function and lowered ROS.
entries.interactions: Shares the mitochondrial-ageing target with [coq10]; sirtuin overlap with [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements].
entries.caveats: Mouse reproductive ageing differs from human (human egg aneuploidy is driven largely by cohesin loss over decades).
entries.title: NMN / NAD+ precursors (NMN, NR)

timing.summary: NR and NMN raise blood NAD+ metabolites within hours and roughly double blood NAD+ within about a week. Clinical effects, where seen at all, were measured after 6-10 weeks.

onset.text: Single NR or NMN doses raised NAD+ metabolites within hours [tnut-trammell2016, tnut-irie2020].

full.text: Blood NAD+ doubled by day 9 of NR [tnut-airhart2017]; muscle insulin sensitivity rose after 10 weeks of NMN [tnut-yoshino2021].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: All trials dosed daily; no intermittent comparisons [tnut-martens2018].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: NR and NMN raise blood NAD+, but most trials show no gain in insulin sensitivity, mitochondria or muscle; NR failed in the ITP; no human egg data.
audit.biases: Industry funding, surrogate outcomes and a baseline imbalance in the main positive NMN trial [anut-yoshino2021, anut-brenner2021].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 meta-analysis of 10 small RCTs found only a modest diastolic blood-pressure drop (-2.15 mmHg) [anut-zhang2026b]; the 2025 muscle meta-analysis remains null [anut-prokopidis2025]; ITP null for NR [anut-harrison2021].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged: raises a biomarker, no proven clinical benefit.

factors.name: Nail polish, gel lamps and salon solvents

entries.headline: For customers the measured exposures are brief: painting nails with a triphenyl-phosphate polish raised its urinary metabolite about 7-fold for 10-14 h, and UV gel-lamp light caused ROS-type DNA damage in cultured cells (no human data); the bigger concern is nail technicians, who breathe formaldehyde, toluene and benzene daily.

dose.effective: Customers: apply and dry polish in a ventilated space, choose polishes without triphenyl phosphate, toluene or formaldehyde if you paint often, and for UV/LED gel manicures put broad-spectrum sunscreen on the backs of the hands or use fingertip-free UV gloves. Technicians: local exhaust ventilation at the table, nitrile gloves (gloves blocked most triphenyl phosphate uptake), and respirators for acrylic work.
dose.studied_range: Single nail-painting sessions; 2-day measurements in nail technicians; air measurements in 6 salons.
dose.too_much: Formaldehyde exceeded the NIOSH recommended exposure limit in 1 of 6 Colorado salons; modelled 20-year occupational cancer risks exceeded EPA benchmarks. Men with high occupational solvent exposure had about 3-4 times the odds of low motile sperm count.
dose.timeframe: Urinary triphenyl-phosphate metabolite peaks 10-14 h after painting; workplace exposure accumulates over each shift.
dose.notes: 'Free-of' claims (3-free, 5-free and so on) refer to a few named chemicals only.

entries.mechanism: Solvents (toluene, xylene, ethyl acetate) and formaldehyde are irritants and, at occupational doses, reproductive and carcinogenic hazards; triphenyl phosphate is an organophosphate flame retardant/plasticizer with endocrine activity in animals. UV-A from nail dryers generated ROS, 8-oxoguanine damage, mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS-signature mutations in mouse and human cells [epc-zhivagui2023].
entries.interactions: Occupational overlap with [hair-dyes-relaxers]; UV-lamp damage is the same chemistry as [uv-sun-exposure].
entries.caveats: The UV-lamp study used cells, not people, and no epidemiological link to skin cancer exists. Salon air studies are small. Occupational solvent and fertility evidence is mixed.
entries.debate: For men, a Canadian case-referent study found high solvent exposure linked to low motile sperm counts in two clinic series [epc-cherry2001]; a systematic review judged solvent evidence for time to pregnancy equivocal [epc-snijder2012]. Reviewers call for better data on cosmetologists' reproductive risks [epc-pak2013]. For customers, cell evidence of UV-lamp DNA damage [epc-zhivagui2023] has no human outcome data either way.

entries.title: Nail polish, gel lamps and salon solvents

timing.summary: Polish chemicals are absorbed through the skin around the nails and peak in urine within half a day. Workplace solvent exposure repeats every shift; UV-lamp DNA damage in cells is permanent once mutations form.

onset.text: Urinary DPHP rose about 7-fold 10-14 h after nail painting [epc-mendelsohn2016]; technicians' urinary DPHP rose across a work shift [epc-estill2021].

full.text: Peak at 10-14 h after a single application [epc-mendelsohn2016].

after_stopping.text: Return to baseline not precisely measured; urine was followed for about 24 h in the glove substudy [epc-mendelsohn2016].

frequency.text: Each manicure is a short pulse; frequent painting or gel sessions and daily salon work multiply exposure. No schedule studies exist.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: About half of Americans have recent neonicotinoid exposure (higher in young children and in summer), but human health data are sparse: a systematic review found only suggestive, methodologically weak findings, and links to oxidative stress or sperm motility come from small cross-sectional studies.

dose.effective: Organic produce lowered urinary clothianidin by 83% in 6 days. Because neonicotinoids are systemic (taken up into the plant), washing removes little; peeling helps only for residues in the peel.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary neonicotinoids and metabolites (NHANES 2015-2016; Chinese cohorts).
dose.too_much: No human health threshold established.
dose.timeframe: Urinary half-lives 2.5-50 hours depending on compound.
dose.notes: Neonicotinoids are best known for harm to bees; their human health effects are largely unstudied.

entries.mechanism: Neonicotinoids bind nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (more weakly in mammals than insects); animal studies report oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and reproductive toxicity at high doses. In pregnant women a neonicotinoid metabolite contributed to associations with 8-OHdG [efw-wang2024].
entries.interactions: Co-exposure with [organophosphates] and [pyrethroids]. Organic diets ([organic-food]) lower intake; [washing-produce] does little for systemic pesticides.
entries.caveats: Single urines classify neonicotinoid exposure poorly (ICC 0.02-0.37; 16-172 samples needed per person) [efw-li2020]. One seminal-plasma study found lower motility with only one of several metabolites [efw-wang2022].
entries.debate: Exposure is common [efw-ospina2019, efw-zhang2022] and some cross-sectional studies link it to oxidative markers [efw-wang2024, efw-li2020] or motility [efw-wang2022], but the only systematic review judged the evidence too limited and weak to draw conclusions [efw-cimino2017]. No study has found a health outcome robust to repeated exposure measurement.

entries.headline: Shift work is linked to about 17% more cardiovascular events and roughly 10% more type 2 diabetes, and lab studies that flip sleep and meals by 12 hours raise glucose, blood pressure and inflammatory markers within days; night workers show more oxidative damage and lower antioxidant defences, though these data are cross-sectional.

dose.effective: Where possible limit consecutive nights and years of rotating nights; keep the day-sleep room dark and quiet; avoid large meals during the biological night (roughly midnight to 6 am); get bright light during the shift and wear dark glasses on the way home; keep a regular schedule on days off.
dose.studied_range: Lab misalignment for 3-10 days or 3 weeks of 28-hour days; cohorts with up to decades of rotating nights (≥3 night shifts/month).
dose.too_much: CVD risk rose ~7% per additional 5 years of shift work after the first 5 years; CHD risk rose with years of rotating nights and waned after stopping.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and blood-pressure effects within 3 days of misalignment; cardiometabolic disease over years.
dose.notes: Melatonin before day sleep is being tested for DNA repair (borderline result); see [melatonin]. Short or poor sleep often coexists ([short-sleep]).

entries.mechanism: Light at night suppresses melatonin and desynchronises the central clock from peripheral clocks in liver, muscle and fat. Misalignment lowers insulin sensitivity, raises blood pressure and inflammatory cytokines and disturbs clock-controlled antioxidant and DNA-repair genes (including Nrf2 targets and OGG1). Reduced night-time melatonin is proposed to impair repair of 8-oxoguanine.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [short-sleep], [evening-light-exposure] and [late-eating]; worsens [glycemic-control] and weight gain ([excess-adiposity]).
entries.caveats: Shift workers differ from day workers in income, smoking and health (healthy-worker and selection effects). Lower urinary 8-OH-dG during night work is interpreted as reduced repair rather than less damage, which is an assumption. Sperm and egg data are observational: rotating-shift men had ~11% lower sperm concentration and lower fecundity, and women on non-day shifts had 2.3 fewer mature oocytes at IVF, but a large nurse cohort found no effect of shift work on time to pregnancy.
entries.debate: IARC classifies night shift work as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) [kcc-iarc2019], yet a meta-analysis of 10 prospective studies found no association with breast cancer even after 30 years [kcc-travis2016]. Cardiometabolic associations are consistent [kcc-torquati2018, kcc-gan2015, kcc-gao2020, kcc-vetter2016] and supported by lab misalignment studies [kcc-scheer2009, kcc-morris2015, kcc-morris2016, kcc-buxton2012]. For oxidative stress, a cross-sectional study found worse markers in night workers but no link with social jetlag [kcc-teixeira2019]; the reduced-repair reading of 8-OH-dG [kcc-bhatti2016, kcc-bhatti2017] rests on an untested assumption and the melatonin trial was borderline [kcc-zanif2025]. Fertility: a meta-analysis linked shift work to menstrual disruption and infertility (with very high heterogeneity) [kcc-stocker2014], while nurses showed no effect on time to pregnancy [kcc-gaskins2015].

entries.title: Night-shift work and circadian misalignment

timing.summary: Living out of step with the body clock raises blood pressure and inflammation within three days, and these lab changes normalise within about nine days of regular sleep. Years of rotating night shifts carry a heart-disease risk that fades only gradually over years after quitting.

onset.text: Three days of 12-h misalignment raised 24-h blood pressure and IL-6, CRP and TNF-alpha by 3-29% [tbody-morris2016]; 10 days of a 28-h day raised glucose and blood pressure [tbody-scheer2009].

full.text: Coronary risk rose with years of rotating night shifts [tbody-vetter2016].

after_stopping.text: Lab metabolic changes normalised within 9 days of recovery sleep and re-entrainment [tbody-buxton2012]; the excess coronary risk waned with longer time since quitting shift work over years [tbody-vetter2016].

frequency.text: Limit consecutive nights and total years of rotating nights where possible.

egg.late_start: Unknown.
egg.text: Shift work is linked to menstrual disruption [tbody-stocker2014]; the lead time is extrapolated from follicle growth (~85 days) [tbody-gougeon1986].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Shift work is linked to about 17% more cardiovascular events and ~10% more diabetes; lab misalignment raises glucose and blood pressure within days.
audit.biases: Shift workers are more often in lower social classes and smoke more (residual confounding), and the healthy-worker survivor effect keeps the most resilient on nights.
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analysis supports a 17% CVD excess [abody-torquati2018], but in a cohort that adjusted for pre-employment risk and social class the IHD association disappeared (OR 1.04) [abody-yadegarfar2008]. For breast cancer, 10 prospective studies were null [abody-travis2016], while MR suggests morning chronotype protects [abody-richmond2019], implicating the body clock rather than shift work per se.
audit.bottom_line: The laboratory misalignment effects are real; the size of the long-term disease excess in shift workers is uncertain and partly social.

entries.headline: Large Danish and US cohorts link drinking-water nitrate well below legal limits (from about 4-9 mg/L nitrate, vs 50 mg/L EU / 44 mg/L US) to 16-50% more colorectal or colon cancer and slightly more preterm birth and neural tube defects, but meta-analyses disagree and the effects are small.

dose.effective: If you use a private well in a farming area, test it for nitrate yearly (and after floods). If nitrate is raised, use reverse osmosis or ion-exchange treatment or a different water source, especially for pregnancy and infant formula. Boiling concentrates nitrate; carbon filters do not remove it.
dose.studied_range: Tap-water nitrate from <1 to >50 mg/L nitrate (0-11 mg/L nitrate-N).
dose.too_much: Legal limits: 50 mg/L nitrate (EU, WHO) or 10 mg/L nitrate-N (US). Colorectal cancer risk rose from about 3.9 mg/L nitrate in Denmark; colon cancer HR 1.52 at >=9.25 mg/L.
dose.timeframe: Nitrate half-life in the body about 5 h; cancer associations reflect decades; birth outcomes relate to exposure during pregnancy.
dose.notes: Vegetable nitrate (beetroot, leafy greens) comes with vitamin C and polyphenols that block nitrosamine formation and was not linked to colorectal cancer; the concern is water and processed-meat nitrate/nitrite.

entries.mechanism: Ingested nitrate is reduced to nitrite by oral bacteria; in the stomach nitrite can form N-nitroso compounds that alkylate DNA. Vitamin C, vitamin E and polyphenols inhibit this nitrosation; red and processed meat promote it. Nitrite also oxidises haemoglobin (methaemoglobinaemia in infants) and nitrate competes with iodide uptake by the thyroid.
entries.interactions: Risk appeared stronger with smoking and high red-meat intake and weaker with high vitamin C, folate and flavonoid intake [efw-erichsen2025]; see [processed-meat], [vitamin-c-foods], [leafy-greens]. Agricultural well water often also carries [arsenic-drinking-water] or pesticides.
entries.caveats: Exposure is assigned from water-utility or well-zone data, not personal intake; rural residence, agricultural co-contaminants (atrazine, pesticides) and socioeconomic status confound. Many associations are near 1.0 (preterm OR 1.01-1.08), so residual confounding could explain them.
entries.debate: Harm below the limit: a Danish nationwide cohort found colorectal cancer risk rising from 3.87 mg/L [efw-schullehner2018], a Danish diet cohort found colon cancer HR 1.52 at >=9.25 mg/L [efw-erichsen2025], and reviews cite colorectal cancer, thyroid disease and neural tube defects [efw-ward2018]. Doubt: one meta-analysis found no colorectal link (OR 1.02) but a gastric-cancer link [efw-picetti2022], another judged the colorectal association weak, inconsistent and possibly confounded [efw-elwood2022], and a third found water nitrate unrelated to colorectal cancer [efw-hosseini2021]. Birth outcomes: a within-mother sibling design [efw-sherris2021] and national cohorts [efw-coffman2022, efw-chambers2026] found small preterm increases, and a meta-analysis found OR 1.05 for preterm and 1.51 for neural tube defects in case-control studies [efw-lin2023].

entries.headline: Older non-stick pans released small amounts of residual PFOA when heated (7-337 ng per pan, falling with use), newer coatings mostly release no detectable PFAS, and scratched pans shed PTFE particles; overheating can cause polymer fume fever, but no study links non-stick cookware use to blood PFAS or disease.

dose.effective: Use non-stick pans at low-to-medium heat, never preheat empty, use the extractor fan, use wooden or silicone utensils, and replace pans once the coating is scratched or flaking. For high-heat searing use cast iron, carbon steel or stainless steel. Keep pet birds out of the kitchen when cooking with non-stick pans.
dose.studied_range: Laboratory heating of pans at 179-250 C surface temperature; simulated cooking with abrasion.
dose.too_much: Overheated fluoropolymer coatings release fumes that cause polymer fume fever, usually self-limited within 12-48 h but potentially serious with heart or lung disease.
dose.timeframe: Fume symptoms within hours; any chronic effect unknown.
dose.notes: PFOA has been replaced in coating manufacture by alternatives such as GenX, which may be similarly toxic. 'Ceramic' (sol-gel silica) coatings are PTFE-free but wear faster; their particle release is barely studied. Microwave popcorn bags and grease-proof packaging are a more established PFAS source than pans.

entries.mechanism: Residual PFOA or replacement PFAS can off-gas from coatings; PTFE particles are chemically inert but, like other microplastics, may cause inflammation and oxidative stress in cell and animal studies.
entries.interactions: Main PFAS routes and testing are in [pfas]; particle exposure in [microplastics]. Packaging matters more: daily microwave popcorn tracked higher serum PFAS [efw-susmann2019]. Switching to metal pans raises different questions ([metal-cookware]).
entries.caveats: All evidence is from laboratory release tests, some by the manufacturer; no human biomonitoring study isolates cookware. PFAS emissions vary by brand and decline with use.
entries.debate: PFOA release: independent tests detected PFOA in the gas phase from heated pans [efw-sinclair2007], whereas DuPont scientists found none extractable under simulated cooking [efw-powley2005]; a 2024 study found no PFAS in 12 of 18 coated items [efw-wolf2024]; a perspective warns replacements may be similarly toxic [efw-sajid2017]. Particles: Raman imaging suggests thousands to millions of PTFE particles from a scratched pan [efw-luo2022], while a food-simulant study counted only a few thousand plastic particles a year from plastic cookware and none from non-plastic cookware [efw-cole2024].
