entries.headline: Daily maximal OTC ibuprofen (1200 mg) halved muscle growth from 8 weeks of strength training in young adults, yet similar doses did not hurt (and seemed to help) older adults; in young men daily ibuprofen produced compensated hypogonadism, and around ovulation NSAIDs can stop the follicle from rupturing.

dose.effective: Occasional use at labelled doses (e.g. ibuprofen 200-400 mg per dose) for pain or inflammation.
dose.studied_range: Ibuprofen 1200 mg/day for 8 weeks (young adults) or 12 weeks (older adults); ibuprofen 1600 mg/day and etoricoxib in women with arthritis.
dose.too_much: Chronic daily high doses are where training and testicular effects appear; GI bleeding, kidney and cardiovascular risks rise with dose and duration.
dose.timeframe: Training effects over 8-12 weeks; hormonal changes in men within weeks; ovulatory effects in the same cycle.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. If you take NSAIDs for a chronic condition and are trying to conceive or training for muscle, discuss timing (avoiding continuous use around ovulation) and alternatives with the prescriber.

entries.mechanism: NSAIDs block COX-1/COX-2 and prostaglandin synthesis. Prostaglandins help drive satellite-cell activity and muscle protein turnover after exercise [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018], are needed for follicle rupture at ovulation [med-stone2002], and influence Leydig-cell steroidogenesis; ibuprofen transcriptionally repressed testosterone production in human testis explants [med-kristensen2018].
entries.interactions: May blunt hypertrophy from [resistance-training] in young people (compare [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]). [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception. Fish oil ([omega3-fish]) is sometimes used for inflammatory pain without the ovulation issue.
entries.caveats: Occasional use is unlikely to matter for muscle. The testicular study is short-term with a hormonal (not semen) outcome. Ovulation data come mainly from women with inflammatory arthritis on continuous NSAIDs.
entries.debate: Muscle: maximal OTC ibuprofen blunted hypertrophy and strength in young adults [med-lilja2018], while ibuprofen or acetaminophen enhanced gains in older adults [med-trappe2011]; reviewers suggest age and growth potential explain the split and that occasional use is harmless [med-schoenfeld2012, med-lundberg2018]. Men: ibuprofen induced compensated hypogonadism [med-kristensen2018], but reviews note human semen data on NSAIDs are scarce and effects look smaller than for opioids [med-drobnis2017]. Women: see the egg entry for ovulation and miscarriage debates [med-micu2011, med-li2018, med-chen2024].
entries.title: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, COX-2 inhibitors)

entries.headline: Continuous NSAIDs around ovulation caused luteinized unruptured follicles (the egg is not released) in 35.6% of cycles vs 3.4% untreated in women with arthritis, mostly with the COX-2 drug etoricoxib, while ibuprofen 1600 mg/day caused none; NSAIDs around conception were also linked to miscarriage (aHR 1.89).

dose.effective: Occasional NSAID doses for period pain are not implicated; concern is continuous use spanning ovulation.
dose.studied_range: Continuous periovulatory etoricoxib, diclofenac and ibuprofen 1600 mg/day (arthritis cohort); any NSAID use around conception (miscarriage cohort).
dose.too_much: Continuous periovulatory COX-2 inhibitor use; use for >=15 days around conception (aHR 1.85 for miscarriage).
dose.timeframe: Ovulation returns in the next cycle after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Women with inflammatory conditions planning pregnancy can discuss avoiding continuous NSAIDs around mid-cycle with their rheumatologist.

entries.mechanism: COX-2-derived prostaglandins drive the enzymatic breakdown of the follicle wall at ovulation; blocking them lets the follicle luteinize without releasing the egg [med-stone2002, med-micu2011].
entries.interactions: [acetaminophen] is the usual alternative around conception; relevant to [endometriosis] and inflammatory arthritis, where NSAIDs are common.
entries.caveats: Ovulation data come from women with inflammatory arthritis and small case series; the miscarriage link is observational and confounded by the reasons for taking NSAIDs.
entries.debate: Ovulation: case series and a monitored-cycle cohort show reversible ovulatory failure [med-smith1996, med-micu2011, med-stone2002], but evidence is limited to small samples. Pregnancy: a prospective cohort linked periconceptional NSAIDs to miscarriage, even versus acetaminophen users [med-li2018], while a 2024 meta-analysis found the miscarriage association non-significant (OR 1.20) but birth defects modestly higher (OR 1.19) [med-chen2024].
entries.title: NSAIDs around ovulation and conception

timing.summary: NSAIDs act on different systems at completely different speeds. Around ovulation they can block follicle rupture within the same cycle, and ovulation returns in the next cycle after stopping [tleg-micu2011, tleg-smith1996]; muscle adaptation is blunted over 8 weeks of training [tleg-lilja2018]; and testicular hormone changes appear with daily dosing over weeks [tleg-kristensen2018].

onset.text: Ovulatory effects within a single cycle: periovulatory rofecoxib delayed follicular rupture beyond 48 hours after the LH peak in 4 of 6 women in the treated cycle [tleg-pall2001], and continuous NSAIDs produced luteinized unruptured follicles in 35.6% of cycles [tleg-micu2011]. Training adaptation is measurably blunted by 8 weeks [tleg-lilja2018].

full.text: The hypertrophy penalty accumulated over 8 weeks of training (quadriceps volume +3.7% on ibuprofen 1,200 mg/day versus +7.5% on low-dose aspirin) [tleg-lilja2018]; hormonal changes developed with continued daily dosing [tleg-kristensen2018]; ovulatory suppression is dose-dependent and present while the drug is taken [tleg-jesam2014].

after_stopping.text: Ovulation recovers in the next cycle: three women with recurrent luteinized unruptured follicles on NSAIDs ovulated normally in the cycle after stopping [tleg-smith1996], and cycles normalised after an 18-day meloxicam regimen ended [tleg-jesam2014]. Muscle adaptation presumably resumes, but this was not measured.

frequency.text: Dose and continuity matter more than any clever schedule. Continuous periovulatory dosing is what caused unruptured follicles, and the COX-2-selective etoricoxib was the main culprit while ibuprofen 1,600 mg/day caused none [tleg-micu2011]; in older adults, 12 weeks of 1.2 g/day ibuprofen or 4 g/day acetaminophen during training did not blunt and may have helped muscle gains [tleg-trappe2011]. Occasional single doses outside the fertile window are a different exposure from daily use.

sperm.late_start: Stopping daily NSAIDs weeks before conception removes the hormonal effect, which is reversible, but any effect already imprinted on developing sperm would take a spermatogenic cycle to clear.
sperm.text: The measured effect is endocrine (raised LH, lower testosterone/LH ratio) rather than on sperm counts [tleg-kristensen2018]; the 90-day figure is extrapolated from spermatogenesis length, not measured.

egg.late_start: Two weeks is enough: the effect is on follicle rupture in the current cycle, so stopping before the periovulatory window restores ovulation in that cycle [tleg-pall2001, tleg-smith1996].
egg.text: NSAIDs act locally on COX-2-dependent follicle rupture, so the sensitive window is the few days around the LH surge [tleg-pall2001, tleg-micu2011], and use around conception was also associated with a 1.89-fold higher miscarriage risk, with a dose-response by duration [tleg-li2018nsaid].

timing.debate: Effects depend on who is taking them: maximal over-the-counter ibuprofen halved hypertrophy in young adults [tleg-lilja2018], while the same doses did not blunt and appeared to enhance gains in older adults over 12 weeks [tleg-trappe2011]. Ovulatory blockade is drug-specific - mostly etoricoxib, with none on ibuprofen 1,600 mg/day [tleg-micu2011] - and even at the highest meloxicam dose over 20% of women ovulated normally [tleg-jesam2014]. The miscarriage association comes from an observational cohort with acetaminophen users as an indication control [tleg-li2018nsaid].

audit.claim: Daily high-dose ibuprofen blunts muscle growth in the young; continuous periovulatory NSAIDs can block follicle rupture, and NSAIDs around conception were linked to miscarriage (aHR 1.89).
audit.biases: Miscarriage studies are vulnerable to protopathic bias (NSAIDs taken for the pain of an impending miscarriage), immortal-time bias and confounding by indication.
audit.newer_evidence: The Kaiser cohort reported aHR 1.89 [abody-li2018], but a 65,457-pregnancy Israeli cohort found no independent association (aHR 1.10) [abody-daniel2014]; the same group showed that fixed-exposure analyses create immortal-time bias [abody-daniel2015a] and that NSAID dispensing spikes in the days before a miscarriage, with the association disappearing when those days are excluded [abody-daniel2015b]. A 2024 meta-analysis found the miscarriage association non-significant (OR 1.20) [abody-chen2024].
audit.bottom_line: The muscle and ovulation findings stand as limited evidence; the miscarriage signal is probably largely bias.

factors.name: Occupational solvents and chemical fumes (glycol ethers, dry-cleaning solvents, paints, formaldehyde)
aliases: Occupational solvents and sperm (glycol ethers, paints, formaldehyde)
Occupational solvents, disinfectants and formaldehyde: miscarriage and fertility

entries.headline: Workers exposed to solvents show higher lipid-peroxidation markers, and glycol ether exposure roughly doubled the odds of low motile sperm count; women exposed at work had more miscarriage in older, mostly retrospective studies. The risk is concentrated in specific jobs, not in ordinary home use.

dose.effective: If you work with solvents, paints, adhesives, dry-cleaning fluid, formaldehyde or disinfectants: use local exhaust ventilation and closed systems, wear the correct respirator and chemical gloves, ask your employer for safety data sheets, and when trying to conceive (either partner) or pregnant, ask for reassignment from high-exposure tasks.
dose.studied_range: Shipyard painters at 2-ethoxyethanol TWA 0-80.5 mg/m3; dry-cleaning operators; laboratory and pharmaceutical workers; formaldehyde-exposed workers.
dose.too_much: Occupational exposure limits do not account for reproductive effects; painters below biological exposure limits still showed oxidative changes.
dose.timeframe: Sperm effects reflect exposure in the roughly 3 months before the sample.
dose.notes: The most toxic glycol ethers (2-methoxy- and 2-ethoxyethanol) are now restricted in many countries, so older studies may overstate current risk in regulated workplaces.

entries.mechanism: Glycol ethers are metabolized to alkoxyacetic acids that are toxic to spermatocytes; toluene, perchloroethylene and formaldehyde raise lipid peroxidation and antioxidant enzyme activity in exposed workers [eia-moro2010, eia-li2024pce].
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [alcohol] in men with marginal semen; household VOCs at much lower levels are covered in [vocs-formaldehyde].
entries.caveats: Exposure is usually assigned by job title or expert rating, not measured. Manual work correlates with heat, smoking and lower income. Healthy-worker and recall bias affect miscarriage studies.
entries.debate: See [occupational-solvents] and [occupational-solvents]. A systematic review of 49 time-to-pregnancy studies found the evidence for solvents equivocal, unlike lead and pesticides [eia-snijder2012].

key_numbers.label: Low motile sperm count, high glycol ether exposure

entries.title: Occupational solvents and chemical fumes (glycol ethers, dry-cleaning solvents, paints, formaldehyde)

entries.headline: Men with high glycol ether or solvent exposure at work had 2-4 times the odds of low motile sperm count, and formaldehyde-exposed workers had lower motility; effects are sizeable for exposed workers but rest on case-referent and cross-sectional studies.

dose.effective: For about 3 months before trying to conceive, minimise exposure at work: local exhaust ventilation, respirator with organic-vapour cartridges, impermeable gloves, substitution of water-based products; ask for task reassignment if exposure is high.
dose.studied_range: Glycol ether exposure rated moderate/high by hygienists; shipyard painters 2-ethoxyethanol TWA mean 9.9 mg/m3; formaldehyde exposure index in Chinese factory workers.
dose.too_much: High glycol ether exposure: adjusted OR 2.25 for low motile count; high solvent exposure OR 2.9-3.8.
dose.timeframe: Sperm reflect roughly the last 74 days of exposure; the case-referent window was the 3 months before the clinic visit.
dose.notes: Hobby use (occasional painting, varnishing) in a ventilated space is far below the occupational exposures studied.

entries.mechanism: Alkoxyacetic acid metabolites of glycol ethers kill pachytene spermatocytes; solvents and formaldehyde raise lipid peroxidation, the main oxidative injury to sperm membranes.
entries.interactions: See [occupational-solvents]. Adds to heat ([everyday-scrotal-heat]) and smoking, which travel with manual work.
entries.caveats: Job-based exposure assessment; confounding by heat, smoking and alcohol (adjustment reduced the glycol ether OR from 2.54 to 2.25). The most toxic glycol ethers have been restricted.
entries.debate: Two independent case-referent series (Canada, UK) found dose-related associations [eia-cherry2001, eia-cherry2008] and painters had more oligospermia [eia-welch1988], but in the Canadian replication series moderate exposure showed no effect (OR 1.01) [eia-cherry2001], and the time-to-pregnancy literature for solvents is equivocal [eia-snijder2012]. Formaldehyde-motility findings come from two Chinese occupational studies with exposure indices [eia-wang2015fa, eia-lv2022] and await replication.

key_numbers.label: Low motile count, high glycol ether exposure
Low motile count, high solvent exposure (Montreal)

entries.title: Occupational solvents and sperm (glycol ethers, paints, formaldehyde)

entries.headline: Women exposed to organic solvents or formaldehyde at work had about 25-75% higher miscarriage risk in older, mostly retrospective studies (formaldehyde RR 1.76); a prospective nurse cohort found no miscarriage excess with high-level disinfectants, and time-to-pregnancy data for solvents are equivocal.

dose.effective: When trying to conceive and in early pregnancy, avoid high-exposure tasks (dry-cleaning machine operation, solvent-based painting and printing, histology/anatomy labs with formaldehyde, endoscope disinfection) or use closed systems, local exhaust and proper respirators; ask occupational health for an exposure assessment.
dose.studied_range: Dry-cleaning operators (perchloroethylene), laboratory and pharmaceutical workers, nurses using sterilizing agents, formaldehyde-exposed workers.
dose.too_much: Dry-cleaning operators: 17.1% miscarriage vs 10.9% unexposed; formaldehyde-exposed women RR 1.76.
dose.timeframe: The periconception and first-trimester weeks; exposure in the 3 months before conception was included in the dry-cleaning study.
dose.notes: The female-relevant signal is mostly miscarriage, not egg quality per se; no IVF data.

entries.mechanism: Solvents and formaldehyde raise lipid peroxidation and are genotoxic in animal studies; perchloroethylene-exposed women had higher MDA and altered cytokines [eia-li2024pce].
entries.interactions: See [occupational-solvents] and [cleaning-products].
entries.caveats: Self-reported exposure and outcome, recall bias in retrospective designs (women with a miscarriage recall exposures more), healthy-worker effects, and co-exposure to shift work and lifting.
entries.debate: Meta-analyses found a non-significant solvent-miscarriage trend (OR 1.25) with more malformations (OR 1.64) [eia-mcmartin1998] and higher miscarriage with formaldehyde (RR 1.76) while warning about recall and selection bias [eia-duong2011]; dry-cleaning operators [eia-doyle1997] and solvent-exposed lab workers [eia-attarchi2012] had more miscarriage. For disinfectants, a retrospective nurse study found 2-fold late miscarriage [eia-lawson2012] but a prospective one found none (HR 0.84) [eia-ding2021]. Time-to-pregnancy evidence for solvents is equivocal [eia-snijder2012].
entries.title: Occupational solvents, disinfectants and formaldehyde: miscarriage and fertility

timing.summary: Oxidative markers in exposed workers reflect current exposure [eia-moro2010, eia-li2024pce]; reproductive effects map to the 3 months of sperm production and the periconception weeks.

onset.text: Not measured as a time course; cross-sectional studies compare current workers [eia-moro2010].

full.text: Extrapolated for sperm: one spermatogenic cycle [eia-heller1964].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Minimise every work shift; exposure assessment in the key study covered the 3 months before the clinic visit [eia-cherry2008].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; later stages may still benefit, but no study measured recovery.
sperm.text: Spermatogenesis takes roughly 64-74 days plus epididymal transit [eia-heller1964], so a change acts fully on sperm ejaculated about 3 months later. The case-referent exposure window was the 3 months before the visit [eia-cherry2008].

egg.late_start: Avoiding exposure in early pregnancy remains important because the miscarriage signal concerns the first trimester [eia-doyle1997].
egg.text: Exposure during pregnancy or the 3 months before conception was counted in the dry-cleaning study [eia-doyle1997].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: Oily fish & omega-3
aliases: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Although EPA/DHA are highly peroxidizable, 3.4 g/day fish oil did not raise plasma F2-isoprostanes or MDA vs oleic or linoleic oils; long-chain omega-3s slightly reduce CHD events and lower triglycerides ~15%.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings of oily fish per week (salmon, sardines, mackerel), baked or poached rather than deep-fried.
dose.studied_range: 0.5 to >5 g/day long-chain omega-3 in RCTs (86 trials, 162,796 people).
dose.too_much: Cochrane found little or no effect of increased omega-3 on serious adverse events.
dose.timeframe: Weeks for triglycerides.
dose.notes: Oxidized (rancid) oils and deep-fried fish deliver dietary lipid oxidation products.

entries.mechanism: EPA/DHA alter membrane composition, eicosanoids and resolvins (anti-inflammatory); their double bonds are substrates for lipid peroxidation, so oxidized products in food or capsules matter more than the fats themselves.
entries.interactions: Eat with polyphenol-rich foods and avoid [oxidized-frying-oils]. TBARS rose with fish oil while F2-isoprostanes did not, illustrating how marker choice changes conclusions.
entries.caveats: Cochrane: little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or total CV events; modest CHD reduction is low-certainty.
entries.title: Oily fish and omega-3 fats

entries.headline: Fish eaters have higher sperm counts, and a small RCT of 1.5 g/day DHA lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel, herring) 2-3 times a week; if supplementing, about 1-1.5 g/day EPA+DHA.
dose.studied_range: 1.5 g/day DHA for 10 weeks (n=74); fish-oil use on >=60 days in 1679 young men; fish-intake quartiles.
dose.too_much: Above ~3 g/day EPA+DHA raises bleeding risk; choose low-mercury fish.
dose.timeframe: 10-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Swap processed meat for fish: the fish-sperm association was strongest when fish replaced processed red meat.

entries.mechanism: DHA is a key structural lipid of sperm membranes; supplementation raised seminal antioxidant capacity. Paradoxically more PUFA means more oxidisable substrate, so benefit depends on adequate antioxidant status.
entries.interactions: Pairs with [walnuts-nuts] (plant omega-3) and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Supplement trials are small; the Danish fish-oil study is cross-sectional; reviews note heterogeneity.

key_numbers.label: Total count, lowest vs highest fish quartile

entries.title: Fish and omega-3 fatty acids (food and fish oil/DHA)

entries.headline: Each 1% higher serum long-chain omega-3 was associated with 8% higher probability of IVF live birth; in mice omega-3-rich diets preserved egg quality into older age.

dose.effective: Eat lower-mercury fatty fish regularly as part of the diet; studies measured serum levels and dietary share rather than a fixed supplement dose (replacing 1% of energy from saturated fat with long-chain omega-3 was associated with RR 2.37 for live birth).
dose.studied_range: Serum omega-3 4.7% median (IQR 3.8-5.8%) of total fatty acids.
dose.too_much: High-mercury fish (see [heavy-metals]).
dose.timeframe: Adopt within the 3-month preconception window.
dose.notes: Human evidence is from observational IVF cohorts; no adequate RCT on live birth.

entries.mechanism: Incorporation into membranes, anti-inflammatory lipid mediators, possible effects on follicular steroidogenesis.
entries.interactions: Trade-off with [heavy-metals]; part of [mediterranean-diet] and [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Small cohort (100 women); mouse data on reproductive ageing have not been replicated in humans.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth probability per +1% serum LC omega-3

entries.title: Omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA from fish)

timing.summary: Omega-3s fill body pools at different speeds: plasma in days to weeks, red cells (the omega-3 index) over about 4-6 months, fat tissue over years. Because red cells integrate weeks of intake, doses taken 1-4 times a week still raise levels in proportion to the weekly total.

onset.text: Plasma EPA plateaus in 4-8 weeks (half-life 4.8 days) [tnut-katan1997]; plasma phosphatidylcholine responds within days [tnut-browning2012].

full.text: Red-cell EPA half-life 28 days, steady state ~180 days [tnut-katan1997]; omega-3 index 7.8% after 8 weeks of 2.2 g/day [tnut-cao2006]; adipose still rising at 12 months [tnut-browning2012].

after_stopping.text: Plasma falls within weeks; the red-cell index stayed relatively high 4 weeks after stopping [tnut-cao2006], and a 28-day half-life implies months to wash out (extrapolated) [tnut-katan1997].

frequency.text: Doses mimicking fish meals 1, 2 or 4 times a week produced dose-dependent incorporation [tnut-browning2012]; total weekly intake and body weight drive the omega-3 index [tnut-flock2013, tnut-patterson2015].

sperm.late_start: Seminal-plasma DHA rose and DNA fragmentation fell within 10 weeks [tnut-martinezsoto2016].
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; 3 months of DHA did not change sperm membrane DHA [tnut-conquer2000], and associations with testicular function were seen with use on 60+ of 90 days [tnut-jensen2020].

egg.late_start: Plasma levels rise within weeks, so a late start still lifts the serum levels linked to IVF success (extrapolated) [tnut-katan1997].
egg.text: Serum long-chain omega-3 on stimulation days 3-9 predicted live birth [tnut-chiu2018]; the ovulatory follicle's cohort starts differentiating about 85 days before ovulation [tnut-gougeon1986].

timing.debate: Three months of DHA did not reach sperm membranes [tnut-conquer2000], while 10 weeks lowered DNA fragmentation through seminal plasma without changing sperm lipids [tnut-martinezsoto2016]; it is unclear whether sperm benefit needs tissue loading at all.

audit.claim: Fish oil does not raise oxidative markers; long-chain omega-3 slightly reduces CHD; fish eaters have better sperm counts and a DHA RCT lowered SDF; serum omega-3 linked to IVF live birth.
audit.biases: Fish-eater associations are confounded by wealth and overall diet; fish also carries methylmercury, which may blunt cardiovascular benefit [adiet-mozaffarian2006]. Sperm and egg data are small trials and cohorts [adiet-martinezsoto2016, adiet-chiu2018].
audit.newer_evidence: VITAL (2019): 1 g/day omega-3 did not reduce major CVD events [adiet-manson2019]. Supplement trials raise atrial fibrillation risk by 25%, more above 1 g/day [adiet-gencer2021], echoed in UK Biobank fish-oil users without CVD [adiet-chen2024]. Cochrane remains low-certainty for CHD [adiet-abdelhamid2020]. A meta-analysis of small RCTs supports omega-3 for sperm count and motility [adiet-salashuetos2018].
audit.bottom_line: Eating oily fish once or twice a week is reasonable; high-dose supplements bring a small atrial-fibrillation risk and no clear heart benefit in healthy people.

entries.headline: Regular opioid use, including methadone, lowers testosterone by about 165 ng/dL in men, and reviews report lower semen quality and higher sperm DNA fragmentation; direct human semen studies are few and low quality.

dose.effective: Effects described with regular (daily) use of any opioid, including maintenance methadone.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional and cohort studies of chronic users; no dose-response trials.
dose.too_much: Higher doses and long-acting opioids appear worse; tramadol and tapentadol may cause less suppression.
dose.timeframe: Hormonal suppression develops with regular use; semen recovery after tapering is expected over months but is poorly studied.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Never stop opioids or methadone abruptly; tapering or switching must be supervised. Men on opioids with low testosterone who want children should not be treated with testosterone, which further suppresses sperm production.

entries.mechanism: Opioids suppress hypothalamic GnRH and hence LH and testosterone, increase aromatase, and act on opioid receptors in the testis and on sperm themselves [med-drobnis2017, med-bawor2015].
entries.interactions: Testosterone replacement ([testosterone-anabolic-steroids]) for opioid-induced low testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis; [glp1-agonists] raised testosterone without suppressing LH/FSH in obese men, though not studied in opioid users. [cannabis] is covered separately.
entries.caveats: Opioid users differ from controls in smoking, illness and other drug use, so semen findings are heavily confounded.
entries.debate: The testosterone effect is consistent across 17 studies, though heterogeneous and low quality [med-bawor2015]; the semen and DNA-fragmentation effects rest mainly on narrative review of small studies [med-drobnis2017]. No published study was found arguing opioids are harmless to sperm; the debate is about magnitude and reversibility.

key_numbers.label: Testosterone difference, opioid users vs controls

entries.title: Opioid painkillers & methadone

timing.summary: High-dose methadone and heroin keep testosterone low as long as they are taken, and testosterone tracked the dose during detoxification. Sperm recovery after tapering has not been timed.

onset.text: Not timed; testosterone is low during regular high-dose use (80-150 mg/day methadone) but not on low doses [tsperm-mendelson1975].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured for sperm; testosterone rose as methadone doses fell during detoxification [tsperm-mendelson1975].

frequency.text: Effect is dose-related; buprenorphine-treated men had normal testosterone [tsperm-bliesener2005].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: Low testosterone affects spermatogonial development and spermiation, so a full cycle after any change is needed (extrapolated); never stop opioid treatment abruptly without medical supervision.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: Oral nicotinamide (vitamin B3 amide) for skin-cancer prevention

entries.headline: In people with at least two previous non-melanoma skin cancers, nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily cut new skin cancers by 23% in a year (ONTRAC), but it did nothing in immunosuppressed transplant recipients (rate ratio 1.0), and the benefit stops when the pills stop.

dose.effective: 500 mg nicotinamide twice daily, taken continuously, in people at high risk (prior keratinocyte cancers or many actinic keratoses).
dose.studied_range: 500 mg twice daily for 12 months in RCTs; more than 30 days in the Veterans Affairs cohort.
dose.too_much: Well tolerated in trials; a meta-analysis found slightly more digestive side effects. Nicotinic acid (niacin) is a different compound and should not be substituted.
dose.timeframe: Actinic keratoses fell from 3 months; no carry-over benefit 6 months after stopping.
dose.notes: Observational VA data suggest the largest benefit (54% lower risk) when started after a first skin cancer. Topical 5% niacinamide is a separate, cosmetic use with modest effects on spots, redness and fine lines in an industry trial.

entries.mechanism: Nicotinamide is an NAD+ precursor. DNA repair after UV consumes NAD+ and cellular energy; nicotinamide enhances repair of UV-induced DNA damage and reduces UV-induced suppression of skin immunity, the proposed basis for fewer actinic keratoses and keratinocyte cancers.
entries.interactions: An add-on to [sunscreen], not a substitute. Shares NAD+ biology with [nmn-nad]. Unlike antioxidant cocktails ([high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]), it has positive RCT data for skin cancer.
entries.caveats: Evidence applies to high-risk people, not the general public. The pivotal trial lasted 12 months; long-term and melanoma data are lacking. It did not work in organ-transplant recipients, the group with the highest risk.
entries.debate: ONTRAC [skb-chen2015] and a meta-analysis (rate ratio 0.50, with heterogeneity explained by risk of bias) [skb-mainville2022] support use, and some guidelines recommend it. The transplant trial was flatly null [skb-allen2023], although it stopped early with only 158 participants. A large Veterans Affairs cohort found 14% lower risk overall and 54% when started early, but no overall benefit in transplant recipients [skb-breglio2025]; being observational, it is open to confounding by who gets prescribed nicotinamide.

key_numbers.label: Risk reduction when started after first skin cancer (cohort)

entries.title: Oral nicotinamide (vitamin B3 amide) for skin-cancer prevention

timing.summary: Nicotinamide reduced actinic keratoses from the first 3-month check and skin cancers over 12 months in high-risk people. The protection stopped when the pills stopped.

onset.text: Actinic keratoses 11% lower at 3 months [tnut-chen2015].

full.text: 20% fewer keratoses at 9 months; 23% fewer skin cancers over 12 months [tnut-chen2015].

after_stopping.text: No benefit remained in the 6 months after stopping [tnut-chen2015]; exact speed of loss not reported.

frequency.text: 500 mg twice daily, continuously [tnut-chen2015].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; benefit did not appear at all in transplant recipients over 12 months [tnut-allen2023].

audit.claim: In people with prior skin cancers, 500 mg twice daily cut new non-melanoma skin cancers 23% (ONTRAC); null in transplant recipients; benefit stops when pills stop.
audit.biases: The large VA cohort is open to confounding by indication [anut-breglio2025]; the RCTs are the anchor [anut-chen2015, anut-allen2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 randomized within-person study found nicotinamide raised the UVA burn threshold by 26% but did not reduce UVA-induced thymidine dimers [anut-faisal2026], so the mechanism is not simply less DNA damage.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Switching to organic food reliably cuts urinary pesticide metabolites within days (e.g. organophosphate metabolites down ~60-95%), but health benefits rest on observational cohorts (25% lower cancer in high organic consumers, absolute difference 0.6%) that are heavily confounded.

dose.effective: If budget allows, prioritize organic versions of produce that typically carry high residues; never eat less fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides.
dose.studied_range: Organic-diet interventions of about 1 week (urinary biomarkers); cohort comparisons of habitual organic intake.
dose.timeframe: Urinary metabolites fall within days; any disease effect would take years and is unproven.
dose.notes: Glyphosate fell with organic food only in people living away from fields; near farms, spray drift dominates.

entries.mechanism: Lowers dietary intake of organophosphate, pyrethroid and neonicotinoid residues, which in animals induce oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and endocrine disruption.
entries.interactions: Sperm-specific pesticide data are in [pesticides]; fertility diet patterns that favour low-residue produce are in [profertility-diet]. Overall produce intake ([high-fruit-vegetable-intake]) matters more than its organic status.
entries.caveats: Organic buyers are richer, leaner, more active and eat better diets; cohort adjustment cannot remove all of this. No long-term randomized trial with clinical outcomes exists.
entries.debate: Exposure: organic-diet trials consistently lower urinary pesticide metabolites [env-hyland2019, env-gonzalez2023], though glyphosate fell only modestly [env-hyland2023]. Outcomes: NutriNet-Sante linked high organic intake to 25% lower cancer risk [env-baudry2018] and organic produce substitution to lower postmenopausal breast cancer only [env-berlivet2026], but an accompanying commentary questioned whether this justifies the cost [env-hemler2018]. Reviews split: one reports lower cardiometabolic risk in prospective studies [env-poulia2025], another finds data too contradictory for any conclusion [env-komati2025]. Fertility: high-residue produce was linked to 26% lower IVF live birth in women [env-chiu2018] and lower fertilization in male partners [env-kazemi2025], but a 5,234-woman preconception cohort found no link with natural fecundability and evidence of reverse causation [env-wesselink2020].

Cancer HR, highest vs lowest organic intake
Lower IVF live birth, highest high-residue produce intake

entries.title: Organic food (lower pesticide residues)

timing.summary: Urinary pesticide metabolites fall within days of switching to organic food, because most current pesticides clear quickly. They would rise again within days of switching back; health effects, if any, would take years.

onset.text: Pesticide metabolites fell significantly between day 1 and day 6 of an organic diet [tfood-gonzalez2023], by up to 95% in a family study [tfood-hyland2019].

full.text: Reached within the first week [tfood-gonzalez2023, tfood-hyland2019].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; given the fast fall, levels would be expected to return within days of resuming conventional food (extrapolated).

frequency.text: Exposure tracks recent meals, so the reduction lasts only while the diet lasts [tfood-hyland2019].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: Organic UV filters in sunscreen (oxybenzone and others)

entries.headline: Organic sunscreen filters are absorbed: in FDA trials all six tested passed the 0.5 ng/mL safety-testing threshold after one application and oxybenzone reached 170-260 ng/mL, so FDA asked for more data and the EU capped oxybenzone at 2.2% for body products; no human harm has been shown, and the proven skin-cancer benefit of daily sunscreen ([sunscreen]) outweighs the uncertainty.

dose.effective: Keep using sunscreen daily. To cut filter absorption, pick mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide, titanium dioxide), the only filters FDA proposed as safe and effective; zinc oxide nanoparticles stayed on the skin surface in volunteers. Use clothing, hats and shade to shrink the area that needs sunscreen. If pregnant or trying to conceive, a mineral product is a reasonable precaution.
dose.studied_range: 2 mg/cm2 applied to 75% of body surface, 1-4 times a day for up to 4 days (FDA trials); 10% filter creams over 1-2 weeks (Danish trials).
dose.too_much: No human harm level is known. FDA's 0.5 ng/mL is a trigger for toxicology testing, not a harm threshold. EU limits: oxybenzone (BP-3) 6% face/hand/lip, 2.2% body, 0.5% as a formula protector; octocrylene 10% (9% sprays); 4-MBC banned from 2025.
dose.timeframe: In plasma 1-2 h after application; oxybenzone still excreted in urine 5 days after the last application.
dose.notes: Oxybenzone is also used to stabilise other cosmetics. US urinary BP-3 is 10-20 times European and Asian levels. Octocrylene can degrade to benzophenone in stored products.

entries.mechanism: BP-3 and its metabolite BP-1 are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic at human-relevant concentrations [epc-mustieles2023, epc-krause2012]; several filters activate the sperm CatSper calcium channel in vitro [epc-rehfeld2016]. BP-3 tracked 17% higher urinary isoprostane in pregnant women [epc-watkins2015], though not independently of phthalates in a larger study [epc-ferguson2019]. On the skin the net redox effect is protective: filters absorb UV before it generates ROS ([sunscreen], [uv-sun-exposure]).
entries.interactions: Weigh against [sunscreen] (strong benefit) and [uv-sun-exposure]. Sunscreens are also a major source of parabens [epc-nassan2017] ([parabens]). See [uv-filters].
entries.caveats: Urinary BP-3 is a marker of sun exposure and outdoor life, so outcome associations are badly confounded: in IVF patients, higher BP-3 went with better pregnancy rates among outdoor workers [epc-minguez2019b]. Short-term whole-body trials found no hormone changes [epc-janjua2004, epc-janjua2007]. A meta-analysis found no clear link between prenatal BP-3 and birth size [epc-zhong2020].
entries.debate: FDA's absorption trials [epc-matta2019, epc-matta2020] and its 2019 proposed rule [epc-fda2019] ask for more safety data, and a comprehensive review supports Europe's limits [epc-mustieles2023, epc-eu2022]; both FDA authors and that review say people should not stop using sunscreen. A study found octocrylene sunscreens generate benzophenone during storage [epc-downs2021]; a published letter disputed it [epc-surber2021]. A 2025 review links benzophenones to poorer sperm quality in some studies but stresses photoprotection [epc-jaskulak2025].

EU maximum oxybenzone in body products
Urinary BP-3 after 3 days of labelled-free products

entries.title: Organic UV filters in sunscreen (oxybenzone and others)

entries.headline: Mostly null: in the US LIFE study men's urinary BP-2 (not the main sunscreen filter BP-3) went with 31% lower couple fecundability and some poorer semen measures, while Spanish and Danish studies found no semen links overall; several filters trigger sperm calcium signalling in a dish.

dose.effective: Keep using sunscreen; if trying to conceive, prefer mineral (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) sunscreen and protective clothing to reduce absorbed filters.
dose.studied_range: Urinary benzophenones in 413-501 men (LIFE), young men in Spain and Denmark.
dose.too_much: No human threshold. In vitro calcium effects began at nanomolar to micromolar concentrations for some filters.
dose.timeframe: BP-3 is excreted over about 5 days after use; sperm effects, if any, would take a spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: The filters most linked to semen findings (BP-2, BP-8, 4-hydroxybenzophenone) are not the main ones in modern sunscreens.

entries.mechanism: Thirteen of 29 UV filters induced calcium influx in human sperm, nine via CatSper, mimicking progesterone and potentially disturbing timing of hyperactivation and the acrosome reaction [epc-rehfeld2016]; benzophenones are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic.
entries.interactions: Weigh against the [sunscreen] benefit; see [uv-filters].
entries.caveats: Many semen endpoints and several filters were tested per study, so isolated hits are expected by chance. Associations appeared only in men with skin-barrier (filaggrin) mutations in one study [epc-joensen2018].
entries.debate: Positive: male BP-2 and 4OH-BP with lower fecundability [epc-buck2014]; BP-2 and BP-8 with a few of 35 semen endpoints [epc-buck2015]; a 2025 review sees a benzophenone-sperm signal [epc-jaskulak2025]. Null or opposite: no semen associations for any BP filter in Spanish young men, only small FSH shifts [epc-adoamnei2018]; 4OH-BP with slightly lower DNA fragmentation [epc-kiwitt2024]; associations limited to filaggrin-mutation carriers [epc-joensen2018]. A systematic review called the male benzophenone-TTP link preliminary [epc-hipwell2019].

key_numbers.label: UV filters inducing sperm calcium signals in vitro

entries.title: Sunscreen UV filters and sperm

timing.summary: Organic UV filters reach the blood within hours of the first application and build up with repeated daily use; oxybenzone is still excreted days after the last application. Exposure is seasonal and tied to how much skin is covered.

onset.text: BP-3, 4-MBC and OMC appeared in plasma 1-2 h after the first application [epc-janjua2008]; all six FDA-tested filters exceeded 0.5 ng/mL on day 1 [epc-matta2020].

full.text: Plasma levels kept rising over 4 days of repeated application, with some 96-h levels above 24-h levels [epc-janjua2008, epc-matta2019].

after_stopping.text: BP-3 was still being excreted in urine 5 days after the last of 5 days of use [epc-gonzalez2006]; full washout time is not well defined.

frequency.text: Daily sunscreen is beneficial for skin (see the sunscreen factor); filter exposure scales with applications and body area, so mineral products and clothing reduce it without giving up protection [epc-mohammed2019].

timing.debate: Whether persistence after stopping reflects tissue accumulation is unsettled: 96-h levels exceeded 24-h levels in one study [epc-janjua2008], and BP-3 excretion continued for 5 days in another [epc-gonzalez2006].

sperm.late_start: Switching to mineral sunscreen a few weeks before still lowers filter levels in semen around conception, relevant to the in-vitro CatSper effect.
sperm.text: Spermatogenesis takes about 64 days plus epididymal transit [epc-heller1963], so a chemical that affected developing sperm would need roughly 2-3 months off exposure before a full cohort of unexposed sperm is ejaculated.

entries.headline: Prenatal organophosphate exposure is consistently linked to lower child IQ (about 7 points between top and bottom quintiles of maternal urinary metabolites in one cohort), the EU withdrew chlorpyrifos in 2020 after EFSA said no safe level could be set, and an organic diet cuts urinary organophosphate metabolites by 60-95% within a week.

dose.effective: Diet is the main non-farm source: switching to organic produce lowered a malathion metabolite 95% and the chlorpyrifos metabolite 61% in 6 days. Peel or wash produce (peeling removes most surface residues). Avoid indoor organophosphate sprays; if you farm or garden, wear gloves and long sleeves. In pregnancy, these steps matter most.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary dialkyl phosphates and TCPy; cord-blood chlorpyrifos (SD 4.61 pg/g) in the Columbia cohort; occupational exposure in farmworkers.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2019) could not set any safe exposure level for chlorpyrifos because of possible genotoxicity and developmental neurotoxicity. Child IQ deficits were seen at maternal metabolite levels within the general US range.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites clear within 1-2 days (chlorpyrifos metabolite half-life ~27 h); neurodevelopmental effects relate to exposure during pregnancy and appear years later.
dose.notes: Organophosphates are the class most clearly linked to harm at everyday exposure. Chlorpyrifos is banned in the EU; in the US its food uses have been restricted but regulation has changed several times.

entries.mechanism: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; at lower doses their oxon metabolites also deplete glutathione, raise lipid peroxidation and disrupt neural development by non-cholinergic routes. In pregnant women, urinary organophosphate metabolites tracked 8-OHdG and lipid-peroxidation markers across repeated samples [efw-wang2024].
entries.interactions: Sperm effects in occupational settings are summarized in [pesticides]. Co-exposure with [pyrethroids] and [neonicotinoids] is the norm. Organic diets ([organic-food]) and [washing-produce] lower intake; don't eat fewer fruit and vegetables ([high-fruit-vegetable-intake]).
entries.caveats: Spot urines vary greatly within a person (ICC <0.4) [efw-li2019], and urinary dialkyl phosphates also capture harmless preformed metabolites in food. Cohorts are few (New York, California, Mount Sinai) and the Columbia raw data have not been shared [efw-dourson2020]. Effect sizes per person are small but population-wide.
entries.debate: For harm: the Columbia (chlorpyrifos) and CHAMACOS (dialkyl phosphates) cohorts both found lower IQ at age 7 [efw-rauh2011, efw-bouchard2011]; a policy review recommended a class-wide phase-out [efw-hertzpicciotto2018]; EFSA found no safe level for chlorpyrifos [efw-efsa2019]. Regulatory integrity: an academic re-analysis found effects in raw industry neurotoxicity data that the summaries omitted [efw-mie2018], which a letter from authors including a Dow scientist disputed [efw-juberg2019]; neurotoxicity studies given to US EPA were not disclosed in the EU [efw-mie2023]. Against: a consultancy commentary could not reproduce the Columbia association from published figures and criticised the lack of data sharing [efw-dourson2020].

factors.name: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

entries.headline: Berry RCTs pooled together show small improvements in LDL, systolic blood pressure, glucose and TNF-alpha, and anthocyanin foods improve flow-mediated dilation; specific oxidative-stress effects are inconsistent.

dose.effective: About 1 cup (150 g) of mixed berries daily, or ~3 servings per week in cohort data.
dose.studied_range: Juices, powders and whole fruit in 22 RCTs (1251 people); cranberry juice dose-response trials.
dose.timeframe: Acute (hours) for FMD; weeks for lipids and blood pressure.
dose.notes: Chokeberry and blackcurrant are far denser in anthocyanins than strawberries, but higher content has not been shown to give proportionally more benefit.

entries.mechanism: Anthocyanin and ellagitannin metabolites; vitamin C in strawberries.
entries.interactions: Substitutes for [blueberries]; not additive beyond plateau.
entries.caveats: Meta-analytic effects are small (LDL -0.21 mmol/L, SBP -2.7 mmHg) and heterogeneous. Cohort link: >3 servings/week of blueberries plus strawberries tended toward lower MI risk in young women (not significant on its own).
entries.title: Other berries & cherries (strawberry, raspberry, chokeberry, blackcurrant, cranberry, cherries)

timing.summary: Berry anthocyanins act on blood vessels within hours and their metabolites linger in blood for up to 2 days. Lipid and blood-pressure effects in trials took weeks of regular intake.

onset.text: Vascular effects at 1-2 h and 6 h after berry polyphenols [tfood-rodriguezmateos2013].

full.text: Sustained vascular and HDL effects needed daily intake over months in the longest berry trial [tfood-curtis2019].

after_stopping.text: Anthocyanin metabolites persist up to 48 h [tfood-czank2013].

frequency.text: Effects track recent intake; daily or near-daily servings were used in trials [tfood-curtis2019].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Pooled berry RCTs show small improvements in LDL, BP, glucose and TNF-alpha; anthocyanin foods improve FMD.
audit.biases: Heterogeneous small trials [adiet-huang2016].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found; blueberry-specific 2026 data support FMD but not BP [adiet-he2026, adiet-fairliejones2017].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and appropriately modest.

factors.name: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)

entries.headline: Supply other isothiocyanates and indoles plus fiber and vitamins; in large cohorts the top fifth of crucifer intake had about 22% lower total mortality, and a controlled feeding trial lowered IL-6 by 19%, but oxidative-stress trials are few.

dose.effective: 1-2 servings (80-160 g) most days, some raw or lightly cooked; in a feeding trial a double dose (14 g/kg body weight, about 1 kg/day for a 70 kg adult) lowered IL-6.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; feeding studies 7-14 g/kg body weight per day for 14 days.
dose.too_much: Collards, Brussels sprouts and some Russian kale can contain enough goitrin to reduce thyroid iodine uptake if eaten in very large amounts; with adequate iodine, normal intakes show no adverse thyroid effects.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Same cooking rules as broccoli: chop and wait, eat some raw, steam briefly, or add mustard powder after cooking.

entries.mechanism: Isothiocyanates (Nrf2), indoles, fiber and micronutrients; induction of conjugating enzymes such as UGT1A1 and GSTs.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [broccoli-mature]; benefits from [mustard-seed-myrosinase] when cooked. Part of [high-fruit-vegetable-intake] and [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: Inverse associations with mortality and cancers are observational and mostly rated weak to suggestive in an umbrella review.

IL-6 change, double-dose crucifer diet vs vegetable-free
Goitrin threshold for reduced thyroid iodine uptake

entries.title: Other crucifers (kale, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, cauliflower)

timing.summary: Isothiocyanates from kale, cabbage and Brussels sprouts are short-lived like sulforaphane, but a 14-day controlled crucifer diet lowered IL-6. What happens after stopping was not measured.

onset.text: Serum IL-6 was 19% lower after 14 days of a double-dose crucifer diet; earlier time points were not measured [tfood-navarro2014].

full.text: Not measured beyond 14 days in feeding trials.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; isothiocyanates are cleared within a day [tfood-ye2002].

frequency.text: The feeding trial gave crucifers daily [tfood-navarro2014]; schedule comparisons do not exist.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Top-fifth crucifer intake is linked to ~22% lower mortality; a feeding trial lowered IL-6 19%.
audit.biases: The 22% figure is from Shanghai cohorts, observational [adiet-zhang2011]; the feeding trial's other markers were inconsistent [adiet-navarro2014].
audit.newer_evidence: Umbrella review rates most crucifer associations weak or suggestive [adiet-li2022].
audit.bottom_line: The associations are observational; treat them as plausible, not proven.

entries.headline: Fine particles raise oxidative and inflammatory markers within days; each 10 µg/m³ of short-term PM2.5 was linked to ~1.6% higher malondialdehyde. Individually modest, but it affects everyone in polluted areas.

dose.effective: Aim to live and exercise where annual PM2.5 is near the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³; on high-pollution days (AQI 'unhealthy') move hard exercise indoors or away from traffic, and use HEPA filtration indoors (see [hepa-air-purifier]).
dose.studied_range: Epidemiology across typical urban levels (roughly 10-100 µg/m³ PM2.5).
dose.too_much: WHO 2021: annual PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³ and peak-season 8-h ozone above 60 µg/m³ are associated with harm; no clear safe threshold.
dose.timeframe: Marker changes within hours to days of exposure.
dose.notes: Distance from heavy traffic and indoor filtration are the practical levers for individuals.

entries.mechanism: Particles carry transition metals and quinones that redox-cycle (Fenton chemistry), activate NADPH oxidase in airway and immune cells, and trigger systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Ozone directly oxidizes lung-lining lipids and proteins.
entries.interactions: Adds to [tobacco-smoking] and [secondhand-smoke]. Reduced by [hepa-air-purifier].
entries.caveats: Effect sizes on systemic markers are small per unit exposure; most evidence is observational. Air pollution is also linked to poorer semen quality (cross-link to sperm area).
entries.title: Outdoor air pollution (PM2.5, ozone, traffic)

entries.headline: Periods of high air pollution are linked to higher SDF (about +9.7 points across studies) even when other semen measures look normal.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure on high-pollution days (air-quality alerts): avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors, keep car windows closed in traffic.
dose.studied_range: Episodes at or above US air-quality standard limits (Teplice, Czech Republic); PM and NO2 in later studies.
dose.timeframe: Effects appear in sperm produced during and after exposure (~2-3 months later).
dose.notes: Individual control is limited; the effect size is a population average.

entries.mechanism: Fine particles and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons cause systemic oxidative stress and inflammation, and some PAH metabolites form DNA adducts in germ cells.
entries.interactions: Additive with [tobacco-smoking], which delivers similar compounds at much higher doses.
entries.caveats: Ecological and repeated-measures studies; exposure misclassification likely.
entries.title: Air pollution

entries.headline: Higher traffic-related NO2 exposure is associated with lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (e.g. OR 0.76 per 0.01 ppm after embryo transfer); effect sizes per person are modest and hard to separate from other urban factors.

dose.effective: Reduce exposure where practical: avoid exercising beside heavy traffic, use HEPA filtration indoors on high-pollution days.
dose.studied_range: Residential and IVF-lab NO2, ozone, PM2.5 and PM10 from monitoring models.
dose.too_much: No safe threshold established; associations were per 0.01 ppm (Legro) or 20 ppb (Gaskins) increase in NO2.
dose.timeframe: Exposure in the ~3 months before IVF was studied.
dose.notes: In one IVF cohort the NO2-live birth association was absent in women taking >= 800 ug/day supplemental folate (hypothesis-generating).

entries.mechanism: Inhaled particles and NO2 cause systemic inflammation and oxidative stress; PAHs adsorbed on particles are ovotoxic.
entries.interactions: Possible modification by [folic-acid]. Overlaps with [tobacco-smoking] (shared PAH exposure).
entries.caveats: All observational, with exposure estimated from home address. Individual control is limited; do not let this become a source of anxiety.

Lower odds of live birth per +20 ppb NO2 (folate < 800 ug/day)

entries.title: Air pollution (NO2, fine particles)

timing.summary: Air pollution acts on two clocks at once. Within 2 hours of a particle peak, heart attack risk rises [tleg-peters2001] and oxidative markers follow within hours to days [tleg-li2020pm]; over years, sustained differences in exposure change life expectancy [tleg-pope2009]. For sperm, the damaging exposure happened during the 0-90 days before the sample, with specific windows for specific pollutants [tleg-sun2020, tleg-russo2025].

onset.text: Myocardial infarction risk rose with fine particles in the previous 2 hours and again with the 24-hour average one day earlier [tleg-peters2001]; each 10 ug/m3 of short-term PM2.5 was associated with 1.6% higher malondialdehyde within days [tleg-li2020pm].

full.text: Cardiovascular and mortality risk reflects years of average exposure: a 10 ug/m3 lower PM2.5 over about two decades was associated with 0.61 more years of life expectancy [tleg-pope2009]. Semen effects reflect the full 74-90 day spermatogenic window [tleg-russo2025].

after_stopping.text: The acute component reverses within days once exposure falls, which is what purifier trials show [tleg-chen2015]. At population level, Dublin's coal ban was followed by a 15.5% fall in respiratory and 10.3% fall in cardiovascular deaths within months to a few years [tleg-clancy2002], though a larger follow-up and a reanalysis found much smaller or absent mortality effects [tleg-dockery2013, tleg-wittmaack2007].

frequency.text: What matters is cumulative dose plus avoiding peaks: both the acute (hours) and chronic (years) components are real, so reducing exposure on high-pollution days has a different (and faster) payoff than moving to cleaner air, which pays off over years [tleg-peters2001, tleg-pope2009].

sperm.late_start: A late start still helps: PM2.5 and ozone exposure during spermiation - the final days before release - was associated with lower count, concentration and motility, so even the last 2 weeks of reduced exposure acts on a sensitive stage [tleg-russo2025].
sperm.text: Distributed-lag analyses place the critical windows at development weeks 6-12 for PM10, weeks 10-11 for ozone and weeks 0-5 for SO2 [tleg-sun2020], and ozone during meiosis and spermiogenesis specifically affected morphology [tleg-russo2025]. Sperm DNA fragmentation rose after high-pollution periods within the same men [tleg-rubes2005].

egg.late_start: Ovarian stimulation is the most sensitive window identified, so reducing exposure in the 2 weeks of stimulation and up to retrieval is worth doing even if nothing was done earlier [tleg-gaskins2019].
egg.text: In 522 IVF cycles the association with failure was strongest for exposure during ovarian stimulation (42% higher odds of failing before retrieval per interquartile rise in NO2), not during later stages [tleg-gaskins2019].

timing.debate: The size and even existence of the fast population-level benefit is contested: the Dublin coal-ban analysis reported large mortality falls [tleg-clancy2002], the extended Irish analysis found respiratory but not cardiovascular or total mortality reductions [tleg-dockery2013], and a reanalysis attributed the original finding to influenza epidemics and secular trends [tleg-wittmaack2007]. For the egg, one real-world study linked NO2 to lower AMH [tleg-lamarca2020] while a 20-year cohort with repeated measurements found no association with AMH or age at menopause [tleg-zou2025].

audit.claim: Fine particles raise oxidative markers (about 1.6% higher MDA per 10 ug/m3), high-pollution periods add about 9.7 points of sperm DNA fragmentation, and NO2 is linked to lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (general 3, sperm 2, egg 2).
audit.biases: Exposure is estimated from home address (misclassification); area-level income, smoking and diet confound between-city comparisons [eia-fouks2025]; season and temperature confound semen studies (a US cohort lost its associations after adjusting for them) [eia-hansen2010]; semen meta-analyses have extreme heterogeneity (I2 about 96-99%) [eia-margiana2025]; IVF studies test many pollutants, windows and outcomes [eia-legro2010].
audit.newer_evidence: General: in 61 million Medicare beneficiaries, PM2.5 was associated with mortality even below US standards (2017) [eia-di2017]. Sperm: dose-response meta-analysis found about 1% lower motility per 10 ug/m3 PM2.5 but no PM2.5 effect on concentration (2023) [eia-xu2023]; other meta-analyses report small falls in concentration and motility [eia-qian2022, eia-margiana2025]; in 21,851 US semen samples PM2.5 was associated with higher DNA fragmentation, more in low-SES areas (2025) [eia-fouks2025]; and a nationwide Danish cohort of 526,056 men found 24% higher risk of an infertility diagnosis per 2.9 ug/m3 PM2.5 (2024) [eia-sorensen2024]. Egg: the same Danish cohort found no PM2.5-infertility link in 377,850 women [eia-sorensen2024]; a 20-year Dutch cohort with up to five AMH measurements found no association with NO2 or particles (2025) [eia-zou2025], against the earlier cross-sectional AMH finding [eia-lamarca2020]; men's exposure did not clearly affect IVF live birth (2026) [eia-russo2026].
audit.bottom_line: The general and male-fertility claims hold and the male side is stronger than when written (nationwide cohort data). The egg-side claims are weaker: the best longitudinal AMH study and the Danish female cohort are null, leaving IVF associations from a few clinic cohorts.

factors.name: Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, antral follicle count)

entries.headline: AMH and antral follicle count predict how many eggs IVF will retrieve (AUC ~0.78 for poor response) but not natural fertility or egg quality: women 30-44 with low AMH conceived as often as those with normal AMH (84% vs 75% by 12 cycles).

dose.effective: Useful before IVF or egg freezing to plan drug dose and expected egg numbers; not a 'fertility test' for women trying naturally.
dose.studied_range: Low AMH commonly <0.7-1.0 ng/mL (5-7 pmol/L); AFC = follicles 2-10 mm on day 2-5 ultrasound.
dose.too_much: Over-interpretation: a low AMH can push people into rushed IVF or costly egg freezing; a normal AMH can falsely reassure.
dose.timeframe: AMH can be drawn any cycle day; falls with hormonal contraception, so retest off it if results drive decisions.
dose.notes: Neither marker adds to age in predicting IVF live birth.

entries.mechanism: AMH is secreted by small growing follicles, so it tracks the number of follicles (quantity), whereas egg quality (euploidy) is driven mainly by age.
entries.interactions: Interpret with [maternal-age]; a young woman with low AMH has fewer but mostly euploid eggs. Relevant to [egg-freezing-egg] planning.
entries.caveats: Assays differ; AMH is high in PCOS and low on the pill.
entries.debate: A pilot cohort found low AMH cut day-specific fecundability (FR 0.38) [fer-steiner2011], but the larger Time to Conceive cohort and EAGeR found no link [fer-steiner2017, fer-zarek2015]; ASRM now says markers poorly predict reproductive potential independent of age [fer-asrm2020reserve]. For menopause, AMH is the best single predictor but too imprecise for individuals [fer-depmann2016, fer-finkelstein2020].

entries.title: Ovarian reserve testing (AMH, antral follicle count)

timing.summary: AMH mirrors the current pool of small antral follicles, so one blood test on any cycle day is enough. The main timing trap is hormonal contraception, which lowers AMH by about a quarter; values settle within 2 months of stopping the pill.

onset.text: Not applicable: AMH is a snapshot of the current antral pool, not a treatment.

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: After stopping long-term combined pills, AMH rose 53% and AFC 41%, plateauing by 2 months [tegg-landersoe2020].

frequency.text: Repeating AMH rarely adds anything: a low value predicts fewer eggs at IVF but not lower natural conception over 6-12 cycles [tegg-steiner2017].

timing.debate: A large direct-to-consumer cross-sectional dataset found AMH about 24% lower on the pill, ring and implant but only 7% lower on the hormonal IUD [tegg-hariton2021]; the prospective washout study puts the true suppression closer to 35% (53% rise after stopping) [tegg-landersoe2020]. Both agree that results on hormonal contraception underestimate reserve; they differ on size.

audit.claim: AMH and antral follicle count predict IVF egg yield but not natural fertility or egg quality.
audit.biases: Cohort studies are small for a modest effect (imprecision); the largest cohort was recruited from buyers of a commercial hormone test with self-reported pregnancy (selection, measurement error) and was run with company involvement [afert-nelson2024].
audit.newer_evidence: Follow-up of the Time to Conceive cohort (2023) found low AMH or high FSH unrelated to future live birth, infertility or fecundability [afert-harris2023], extending the 2017 null result [afert-steiner2017]. A 2024 cohort of 3150 women found a modest association (adjusted HR 0.77 for AMH <1 ng/mL; peak per-cycle conception 11% vs 14%) [afert-nelson2024]. A 2023 meta-analysis found AMH relates to cumulative IVF live birth without a threshold, and lacks data for natural conception [afert-peigne2023].
audit.bottom_line: A low AMH may slightly lower monthly chances, but most women with low AMH still conceive; it is not a fertility test.

entries.headline: Overeating by ~1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls; 6000 kcal/day caused systemic oxidative stress within 2-3 days; BMI is one of the strongest correlates of urinary isoprostanes in the population.

dose.effective: Eat to energy balance; avoid sustained surplus.
dose.studied_range: +1040 kcal/day for 28 days; ~6000 kcal/day for 1 week.
dose.too_much: Any chronic surplus that drives weight gain, especially visceral fat.
dose.timeframe: Oxidative stress rises within days of overfeeding.
dose.notes: Avoiding a surplus probably outweighs any single 'antioxidant food'.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient excess overloads mitochondrial electron transport, increasing superoxide; adipose tissue oxidative stress carbonylated GLUT4, impairing insulin action; adipose inflammation.
entries.interactions: Reversed by [calorie-restriction]; compounded by [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] and [alcohol].
entries.caveats: Overfeeding studies are short and small; the Framingham link is cross-sectional.

key_numbers.label: Weight gain in 1 week at ~6000 kcal/day
Weight gain after 28 days at +1040 kcal/day

entries.title: Excess calories / overfeeding and weight gain

timing.summary: Large calorie surpluses cause insulin resistance and oxidative stress within two to three days, before any inflammation, and moderate surpluses raise oxidative markers within a month. The damage lasts as long as the extra fat does.

onset.text: About 6000 kcal/day caused systemic insulin resistance and oxidative stress within 2-3 days [tbody-boden2015].

full.text: +1000 kcal/day for 28 days raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and muscle protein carbonyls [tbody-samochabonet2012]; with continued surplus weight keeps rising.

after_stopping.text: Not measured after overfeeding ends.

frequency.text: Even a few days of large surplus matter [tbody-boden2015].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Experimental overfeeding raises isoprostanes and carbonyls within days to weeks.
audit.biases: Small, short experiments; but they are experiments, so confounding is not the issue [adiet-samochabonet2012, adiet-boden2015].
audit.newer_evidence: No contradicting work found.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Very long or excessive exercise spikes oxidative damage markers (F2-isoprostanes up ~75% after a 50 km race; up to 7-fold in overreaching), and decades of high-volume endurance training are linked to more coronary calcium and about 2.5x the odds of atrial fibrillation, yet very fit and very active people still have the lowest mortality.

dose.effective: Train within a load you recover from: performance, sleep, mood and (for women) menstrual cycles should not decline over weeks. Build volume gradually and include easy weeks.
dose.studied_range: 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h); 12-week resistance block peaking at 14 t/week; 4-week progressive HIIT overload; lifelong volumes above 2000-3000 MET-min/week (roughly 3.5-5+ h/week of running) in coronary studies; 5+ Vasaloppet 90 km ski races.
dose.too_much: Oxidative/metabolic: daily very hard sessions for weeks impaired mitochondria and glucose tolerance. Cardiac: lifelong >2000 MET-min/week linked to more coronary plaque (OR 3.2); 5+ long-distance ski races to higher AF risk (HR 1.29). Male reproductive: chronic high mileage (~100+ km/week) linked to lower testosterone and semen quality ([endurance-hypogonadism-sperm]).
dose.timeframe: Acute marker spikes resolve within about 24 h after an ultramarathon; overreaching markers stayed high 96 h after sessions; cardiac remodelling and calcification reflect years to decades.
dose.notes: Occasional long events are not a health problem for trained people; chronic under-recovery is. Athletes with palpitations or a high calcium score should see a cardiologist rather than stop exercising.

entries.mechanism: Prolonged high oxygen flux plus muscle damage and immune activation (neutrophil NADPH oxidase, myeloperoxidase) overwhelm glutathione and vitamin E; ROS shift from signal to damage, and mitochondrial respiration falls. Repeated atrial stretch, high vagal tone and inflammation may remodel the atria (AF substrate); repeated haemodynamic and inflammatory stress may promote calcified plaque. Low energy availability suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
entries.interactions: Adequate sleep ([short-sleep]) and energy intake matter for recovery; in women see [vigorous-exercise-low-energy], in men [endurance-hypogonadism-sperm] and [cycling]. High-dose antioxidants do not solve this and may hinder adaptation ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]).
entries.caveats: Most oxidative data come from small samples of athletes. Coronary studies are cross-sectional, mostly in men, and measure plaque, not events. Spikes after an event do not prove long-term harm.
entries.debate: The 'extreme exercise J-curve' is contested. Hypothesis papers argue chronic extreme endurance training may cause atrial fibrosis, coronary calcification and arterial stiffening [exr-okeefe2012], and a Copenhagen cohort reported strenuous joggers' mortality was no better than sedentary people's (HR 1.97) [exr-schnohr2015], but that estimate was extremely imprecise (95% CI 0.48-8.14), and much larger cohorts found no excess mortality at 10x the guideline [exr-arem2015], benefit across all running doses [exr-lee2014] and no upper limit for fitness [exr-mandsager2018, exr-kokkinos2022]. Lifelong athletes do have more coronary plaque [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017, exr-mohlenkamp2008]; whether it is more benign (more calcified) [exr-aengevaeren2017, exr-merghani2017] or not [exr-debosscher2023] is disputed. Outcome data so far are reassuring: high-volume men with high CAC did not die more (HR 0.77, NS) [exr-defina2019], and high volume carried similar coronary-event risk but the lowest mortality [exr-berry2025]; Tour de France riders outlived the general population [exr-marijon2013]. For AF, athletes have higher odds (OR 2.46) [exr-newman2021, exr-andersen2013], and population data suggest a J-shape [exr-morseth2016, exr-morseth2018] with higher risk in very active men but lower in women [exr-kunutsor2021, exr-elliott2020], while moderate activity lowers AF [exr-mozaffarian2008, exr-mishima2021].

Odds of AF, athletes vs non-athletes

entries.title: Overtraining, ultra-endurance and lifelong very high exercise volumes

timing.summary: A single ultra-race doubles a lipid-peroxidation marker that returns to normal within a day, but weeks of excessive load without recovery cause sustained oxidative stress, mitochondrial impairment and performance loss. Recovery depends on reducing the load.

onset.text: F2-isoprostanes rose during a 50 km race [tbody-mastaloudis2001]; in a 4-week ramp, mitochondrial function fell in the highest-load week [tbody-flockhart2021].

full.text: A 3-week overtraining block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold still 96 h after the last session [tbody-margonis2007].

after_stopping.text: Single-race markers returned to baseline by 24 h [tbody-mastaloudis2001]; recovery from multi-week overreaching was not quantified in the trials reviewed.

frequency.text: Build load gradually; markers stayed high 4 days after sessions in an overtraining block [tbody-margonis2007].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: High-mileage runners had lower testosterone and poorer semen [tbody-desouza1994]; any reversal would follow the ~64-day production time [tbody-misell2006] (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the threshold between productive overload and overreaching is individual [tbody-flockhart2021, tbody-margonis2007].

audit.claim: Extreme volumes spike oxidative markers and raise coronary calcium and AF, yet very active people still have the lowest mortality.
audit.biases: Athletes self-select; coronary studies are cross-sectional; the 'extreme exercise J-curve' rests on tiny groups.
audit.newer_evidence: The Copenhagen strenuous-jogger estimate (HR 1.97) had a 95% CI of 0.48-8.14 [abody-schnohr2015], while pooled cohorts show no excess mortality even at 10x the guideline [abody-arem2015].
audit.bottom_line: Extreme training volumes spike oxidative markers and may raise coronary calcium and atrial fibrillation, but pooled cohorts show no excess mortality even at ten times the guideline amount.

entries.headline: Independent surveys found 50-83% of fish-oil supplements exceeded oxidation limits while an industry-run survey found most compliant; in RCTs, 7 weeks of heavily oxidized fish oil did not raise isoprostanes or HNE, but it lost the LDL-lowering benefit of fresh oil.

dose.effective: Choose plain capsules over flavoured liquids and children's products; prefer brands that publish third-party oxidation results (peroxide value, anisidine value, TOTOX); store closed, cool and dark, refrigerate liquids after opening, and discard any product that smells or tastes strongly fishy or rancid.
dose.studied_range: RCTs: 8 g/day fish oil (1.6 g EPA+DHA) at peroxide values ~4 vs ~18 meq/kg for 3-7 weeks; 30-day capsule trial in 52 women.
dose.too_much: Voluntary industry limits (GOED): PV ≤5 meq O2/kg, p-anisidine ≤20, TOTOX ≤26; pharmacopoeia limits are looser (PV 10, p-AV 30, TOTOX 50).
dose.timeframe: Oxidation accumulates during storage and after opening; lipid effects seen within 4-7 weeks.
dose.notes: Fishy taste is masked in flavoured products, which also interfere with standard oxidation assays. Eating oily fish avoids the issue ([omega3-fish]).

entries.mechanism: EPA and DHA have five and six double bonds and oxidize readily to hydroperoxides (measured as peroxide value) and then aldehydes and ketones (anisidine value). Oxidized lipids may reduce the omega-3 biological activity and, in theory, add dietary lipid peroxides; in practice, gut and liver metabolism appear to handle the amounts in capsules without raising systemic oxidative-stress markers.
entries.interactions: Relevant to anyone taking fish oil for [omega3-fish] benefits. Antioxidants added by manufacturers (tocopherols, rosemary extract) slow oxidation in the bottle; taking [vitamin-e-supplement] does not fix an already rancid oil.
entries.caveats: Lab methods and limits differ; several surveys had commercial affiliations on both sides. Human trials are short, small and in healthy people.
entries.debate: Albert and colleagues found 83% of New Zealand products over the peroxide limit and most below label EPA/DHA [kcc-albert2015], and a Canadian survey found 50% over limits [kcc-jackowski2015] (most authors were affiliated with an omega-3 company); a US analysis of three top sellers also found excess oxidation [kcc-mason2017]. The industry association GOED re-tested 47 New Zealand products and found 72-86% compliant [kcc-bannenberg2017]. On health effects, oxidized oil did not raise isoprostanes, HNE or CRP [kcc-ottestad2012], but it blunted lipid benefits in two trials [kcc-rundblad2017, kcc-garciahernandez2013].
