entries.title: Oxidized (rancid) fish-oil supplements

timing.summary: Taking heavily oxidised fish oil for 7 weeks did not raise oxidative-stress markers in healthy people. Oxidation is a storage problem of the product, not a dosing-time question.

onset.text: Plasma EPA+DHA rose equally with fresh and oxidised oil by 3-7 weeks; no oxidative-stress change at 3 or 7 weeks [tnut-ottestad2012].

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No schedule question; buy fresh product and store it cool and closed.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Independent surveys found 50-83% of fish-oil supplements over oxidation limits (industry survey: most compliant); 7 weeks of oxidized oil did not raise isoprostanes but lost the LDL benefit.
audit.biases: Both sides of the survey dispute have commercial affiliations [anut-albert2015, anut-bannenberg2017]; human trials are short and small [anut-ottestad2012, anut-rundblad2017].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer human outcome trial of oxidized oil was found. Large omega-3 outcome trials raise a separate dose-related atrial fibrillation risk regardless of oxidation [anut-gencer2021].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged and fairly stated.

entries.headline: Ozone is a strong oxidant and a regulated air pollutant; 'ozone therapy' is marketed as hormetic, but a Cochrane review could draw no firm conclusions even for its best-studied use (diabetic foot ulcers).

dose.effective: Not recommended for oxidative stress.
dose.studied_range: Clinical trials of ozone for wounds and other conditions; small and high risk of bias.
dose.too_much: Inhaled ozone is toxic to the lungs; WHO's peak-season 8-h outdoor guideline is 60 µg/m³.
dose.notes: Intravenous and blood-handling procedures carry their own procedural risks.

entries.mechanism: Ozone reacts with lipids to form ozonides, aldehydes and H2O2; proponents claim this triggers Nrf2-mediated hormesis.
entries.interactions: Opposite of [outdoor-air-pollution] advice: ozone exposure is a recognized harm.
entries.caveats: Hormesis claims are mechanistic; human outcome evidence is poor.
entries.title: Ozone therapy (autohemotherapy, ozone saunas)

timing.summary: There is no credible time course to report, because there is no established effect: Cochrane could draw no conclusions from the three small trials (212 participants) of ozone therapy for its best-studied indication, diabetic foot ulcers [tleg-liu2015ozone]. Meanwhile ozone's measured biology is that of an acute airway oxidant, where exposure effects are a matter of hours.

onset.text: Not measured for any claimed benefit [tleg-liu2015ozone]. As an inhaled oxidant, ozone's effects on airway and systemic oxidative markers are acute, within hours of exposure, like other oxidant air pollutants [tleg-li2020pm].

full.text: Not measured: no trial establishes a plateau because no benefit has been established [tleg-liu2015ozone].

after_stopping.text: Not measured [tleg-liu2015ozone].

frequency.text: No schedule can be recommended: the trials are too few, too small and at high risk of bias to support any dosing interval [tleg-liu2015ozone].

timing.debate: Proponents frame ozone exposure as hormetic - a brief oxidant stress that triggers adaptive antioxidant responses - but the only systematic evidence base, Cochrane's review of its best-studied use, found three small trials at high or unclear risk of bias and no firm conclusions [tleg-liu2015ozone]. Ozone is simultaneously regulated as a harmful air pollutant whose exposure raises oxidative markers [tleg-li2020pm], and no study has reconciled the two framings with a measured time course.

factors.name: Parabens in cosmetics and personal-care products

entries.headline: Almost everyone excretes methylparaben (99% of Americans), mainly from leave-on products like lotion, sunscreen and makeup; switching to paraben-free products cuts urine levels by 30-45% within 3-5 days, but harm at everyday exposure is unproven and the oxidative-stress and breast-tumour signals are weak.

dose.effective: Switch leave-on products used on large skin areas (body lotion, sunscreen, foundation) to paraben-free versions; rinse-off products matter less. Three days of products labelled paraben-free cut urinary methyl- and propylparaben by 44-45% in teenage girls; 5 days without usual products cut methylparaben by 30% in young women.
dose.studied_range: Urinary methylparaben medians about 50-130 ug/L in US and European adults; exposure-reduction studies of 2-5 days and a 1-month web-based behavioural RCT.
dose.too_much: No human harm threshold is established. EU limits: methyl- and ethylparaben 0.4% each (0.8% combined), propyl- and butylparaben 0.14%, five other parabens banned since 2014-2015. German 24-h urine data put about 5% of people above acceptable intake for single parabens under deliberately conservative assumptions.
dose.timeframe: Urine levels track use within hours and fall within 1-3 days of stopping (dermal half-life about 9-12 h).
dose.notes: Parabens are also in some foods and medicines. A single spot urine ranks paraben exposure moderately well (intraclass correlation about 0.4-0.5) because product habits are stable, better than for BPA. 'Paraben-free' products use other preservatives, some of which (methylisothiazolinone) caused an allergy epidemic.

entries.mechanism: Parabens are weak estrogen-receptor agonists, with potency rising with alkyl chain length (butyl > propyl > methyl), and are anti-androgenic in vitro. In sperm in vitro they raise mitochondrial and cytosolic ROS and oxidative DNA adducts [epc-samarasinghe2018]. In pregnant women, butyl- and propylparaben tracked 20-27% higher urinary isoprostane per interquartile increase [epc-watkins2015], but in a larger repeated-measures study parabens dropped out once correlated phthalates were modelled [epc-ferguson2019].
entries.interactions: Travels with phthalates and fragrance in the same products ([phthalates], [fragrance-musks]), which confounds single-chemical studies. Sunscreen is a major paraben source in men [epc-nassan2017], so switching to a paraben-free sunscreen keeps the [sunscreen] benefit. Paraben-preserved lubricants matter for semen samples ([lubricants-sperm]). See [parabens], [parabens], [clean-beauty-labels].
entries.caveats: Detection is not harm: no human study links everyday paraben levels to disease with consistency. Paraben levels are patterned by sex, ethnicity and product habits [epc-calafat2010, epc-smith2012], so outcome studies are open to socioeconomic and lifestyle confounding. Spot-urine reliability is debated: moderate in clinic cohorts [epc-smith2012, epc-dewalque2015], poor in a small controlled-use study [epc-huang2021]. A study reporting that cutting parabens and phthalates 'reversed' cancer-associated gene expression in breast aspirates [epc-dairkee2023] was uncontrolled and used surrogate markers; it does not show lower cancer risk.
entries.debate: Breast cancer: Darbre et al. found parabens in 20 breast tumours [epc-darbre2004]; the accompanying editorial and a letter stressed there was no normal-tissue comparison and that presence does not show causation [epc-harvey2004, epc-jeffrey2004]. Oxidative stress: positive pregnancy associations [epc-watkins2015] versus a larger analysis attributing them to phthalate co-exposure [epc-ferguson2019]. Risk assessment: German biomonitoring found a cumulative hazard index above 1 at the 95th percentile but called its assumptions most conservative [epc-moos2017]. Substitution: as the preservative methylisothiazolinone spread in cosmetics, contact allergy to it rose to 3.7% of patch-tested patients [epc-lundov2013] and halved again after EU restrictions [epc-uter2020], a reminder that 'free-of' products carry their own trade-offs.

Methylparaben change after 5 days without usual products

entries.title: Parabens in cosmetics and personal-care products

entries.headline: Studies of urinary parabens and semen disagree: the Boston clinic study (190 men) and a Japanese study found no link with semen quality, while a 795-man Chinese study and smaller Polish and Chinese studies reported lower count or motility or more DNA damage; no study shows that cutting parabens improves sperm.

dose.effective: Use paraben-free leave-on products, especially sunscreen and body lotion (their use within 6 h raised men's urinary parabens 66-156% and 79-147%). For semen collected for testing, IUI or IVF, avoid paraben-preserved lubricants ([lubricants-sperm]).
dose.studied_range: Single or duplicate spot urines in men from fertility clinics and preconception cohorts (n = 42-795).
dose.too_much: No human threshold. In vitro, methylparaben at concentrations used in clinical products and lubricants cut motility and raised ROS and oxidative DNA adducts.
dose.timeframe: Exposure clears within days; any effect on sperm would need about one spermatogenic cycle (roughly 2-3 months) to show.
dose.notes: Butylparaben, the most potent and least common paraben, carries most of the positive findings.

entries.mechanism: Parabens raise mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA adducts in human sperm in vitro, more with longer chains [epc-samarasinghe2018]; they are weakly estrogenic and anti-androgenic.
entries.interactions: Co-exposure with phthalates and BPA ([phthalates]); see [parabens] for sources and [lubricants-sperm].
entries.caveats: All human studies are cross-sectional or clinic-based, many on single urines, with mixtures of correlated chemicals and many semen endpoints tested (multiple-testing risk). Positive findings cluster in mixture models and for butylparaben, which is detected in only a minority of samples.
entries.debate: Null: no association with semen quality in 190 Boston men (butylparaben only with DNA damage) [epc-meeker2011], 42 Japanese men [epc-nishihama2017], or Spanish young men's DNA fragmentation [epc-kiwitt2024]; paternal parabens were not linked to IVF fertilization or live birth [epc-dodge2015]. Positive: lower motility and more abnormal forms and DNA stainability in 315 Polish men [epc-jurewicz2017], lower count and motility with a paraben mixture in 795 Chinese men [epc-shen2023], and butylparaben with comet-assay DNA damage [epc-li2026]. No meta-analysis exists.

key_numbers.label: Largest semen study (paraben mixture, lower count/motility)
Rise in men's urinary parabens with sunscreen use

entries.title: Parabens and sperm

entries.headline: In IVF (EARTH, 245 women) urinary parabens were unrelated to egg counts, embryo quality or live birth; in a 501-couple preconception cohort women's top-quartile methylparaben went with 34% lower fecundability, but continuous models were null and another cohort found butylparaben with higher fecundability.

dose.effective: Use paraben-free leave-on products (lotion, sunscreen, makeup) in the months before conception or IVF; a 3-5 day switch lowers urine levels 30-45%.
dose.studied_range: Urinary parabens in 143-511 women in IVF or preconception studies.
dose.too_much: No human threshold; women in the top quartile of methylparaben had fecundability odds ratio 0.66 in one cohort.
dose.timeframe: Exposure falls within days; the final growth of a follicle takes about 3 months.
dose.notes: Paraben levels are 25-45% lower in pregnancy than before it [epc-smith2012].

entries.mechanism: Weak estrogenic activity and oxidative stress in experimental ovarian models; follicular-fluid parabens are measurable [epc-dimitriadis2025].
entries.interactions: See [parabens]; co-exposure with phthalates and BPA ([phthalates]).
entries.caveats: Findings are quartile-specific and non-monotonic (e.g. only the third propylparaben quartile with lower antral follicle count [epc-jurewicz2020]); multiple chemicals and outcomes tested.
entries.debate: Null: IVF outcomes in EARTH [epc-minguez2016], mixtures overall [epc-minguez2019], follicular-fluid parabens [epc-dimitriadis2025]. Suggestive harm: top-quartile methyl- and ethylparaben and lower fecundability [epc-smarr2017]; a systematic review found preliminary support for female paraben exposure and longer time to pregnancy [epc-hipwell2019]. Opposite: with pooled daily urines, higher butylparaben went with higher fecundability [epc-rosenvollmar2023].

entries.title: Parabens, female fertility and IVF

timing.summary: Parabens are short-lived: urine levels track product use within hours and fall within a few days of switching. Levels stay fairly stable over months only because people keep the same product habits.

onset.text: Use of lotion or sunscreen within 6 h of urine collection strongly raised urinary parabens [epc-nassan2017]; dermal absorption peaks over several hours [epc-shin2023].

full.text: With daily use levels reach a steady state within a day or two, given a dermal half-life of about 9-12 h [epc-shin2023] (extrapolated).

after_stopping.text: 80-85% of an oral dose is excreted within 24 h [epc-moos2016]; switching to paraben-free products cut methylparaben 30-45% within 3-5 days [epc-harley2016, epc-jovanovic2026].

frequency.text: Every application adds a new pulse, so exposure depends on how often leave-on products are used; habits are stable enough that one urine sample ranks exposure moderately well over months [epc-smith2012].

timing.debate: Whether one spot urine captures long-term exposure is disputed: moderate reliability in clinic cohorts [epc-smith2012, epc-dewalque2015] versus poor reliability in a small controlled-use study [epc-huang2021].

sperm.late_start: Switching 2-4 weeks before still removes parabens from semen and from any sample collected with a lubricant for IVF or IUI, which is where direct-contact effects are shown.
sperm.text: Spermatogenesis takes about 64 days plus epididymal transit [epc-heller1963], so a chemical that affected developing sperm would need roughly 2-3 months off exposure before a full cohort of unexposed sperm is ejaculated.

egg.late_start: Switching 2-4 weeks before still lowers exposure during the final, rapid growth of the dominant follicle and in early pregnancy.
egg.text: The ovulated follicle began its final growth phase about 85 days earlier and is recruited 15-20 days before ovulation [epc-gougeon1986], so a follicle-level effect would need about 3 months off exposure to clear.

entries.headline: SDF rises steadily with age, with a clear jump after 50 (about +12.6 points on average), alongside more new mutations in offspring.

dose.effective: Not modifiable, but relevant to timing: SDF climbs from the 20s with no threshold; effects are largest from about age 45-50.
dose.studied_range: Men aged 20-80.
dose.too_much: Age >=50 associated with the largest SDF increase.
dose.timeframe: Lifelong, gradual.
dose.notes: Older men gain the most from removing other risk factors, because damage is additive. Partner's age matters too: older eggs repair paternal DNA damage less well.

entries.mechanism: Age-related decline in testicular antioxidant defence and mitochondrial function, more oxidative stress, less efficient apoptotic culling of damaged germ cells, and accumulating replication errors in spermatogonial stem cells.
entries.interactions: Combined with older maternal age, high SDF has a bigger effect on embryo quality and miscarriage (see [testicular-sperm-icsi]).
entries.caveats: Age is confounded with weight, illness and varicocele duration; the absolute risk to any one child remains low.
entries.title: Paternal age

timing.summary: Sperm DNA fragmentation rises gradually through adult life with no clear threshold, and more steeply after 50. It does not reverse.

onset.text: Trends begin in the early reproductive years, with no age threshold [tsperm-wyrobek2006].

full.text: Keeps growing; after age 50 SDF is on average 12.6 points higher [tsperm-szabo2023].

after_stopping.text: Not reversible; freezing sperm earlier is the only way to use younger sperm.

frequency.text: Not applicable.

timing.debate: Age clearly raises SDF [tsperm-wyrobek2006, tsperm-johnson2015], but aneuploidy did not rise with age in one cohort [tsperm-wyrobek2006], so not every sperm defect worsens on the same timescale.

audit.claim: SDF rises with age with a clear jump after 50 (+12.6 points), alongside more new mutations in offspring.
audit.biases: Older fathers differ in health, weight, varicocele duration and partner age (residual confounding by maternal age in IVF data); offspring-outcome associations can reflect parental psychiatric traits that delay parenthood.
audit.newer_evidence: Designs that control for confounding support a real effect. De novo mutations rise by about two per year of paternal age [afert-kong2012]. Swedish sibling comparisons (2.6 million births) found paternal-age associations with autism, psychosis and bipolar disorder as large as or larger than population estimates [afert-donofrio2014]. In donor-egg cycles, where egg age is fixed, live birth falls slightly and linearly with paternal age [afert-begon2023]; a 2022 meta-analysis of 32,484 cycles links paternal age over 40-50 to lower live birth and more miscarriage [afert-murugesu2022]. US birth data show 14% higher odds of preterm birth for fathers 45+ after adjusting for maternal age, with a modest population impact [afert-khandwala2018].
audit.bottom_line: Male age matters, with effects that are real but small for any single child; it adds to, and is much smaller than, the effect of female age.

entries.headline: In the lab, many lubricants (K-Y, Astroglide, olive oil, saliva) cut sperm motility and some raise DNA fragmentation, while isotonic 'sperm-friendly' gels (e.g. Pre-Seed) do not; yet in two cohorts (6,467 and 296 women) lubricant use did not lower the chance of conceiving.

dose.effective: For natural conception, lubricant choice appears not to matter in cohort data; if wanted, pick an isotonic 'fertility-friendly' product. For semen collection (semen analysis, IUI, IVF), use none or a clinic-approved isotonic lubricant (Pre-Seed did not change motility, ROS or DNA damage in a crossover trial).
dose.studied_range: In vitro lubricant concentrations of 5-12.5% in semen for 10 min to 4 h; cohorts of natural conception attempts.
dose.timeframe: In vitro motility falls within 10-30 minutes of contact.
dose.notes: Saliva is one of the worst performers in vitro. Paraben preservatives at lubricant concentrations raised sperm ROS in vitro.

entries.mechanism: Hyperosmolar, acidic or viscous gels and preservatives (parabens, glycerol) impair motility and can raise mitochondrial ROS and oxidative DNA adducts in vitro; isotonic, pH-matched gels avoid this.
entries.interactions: Relevant mainly when sperm quality is already marginal or for samples collected for assisted reproduction.
entries.caveats: In vitro tests expose washed sperm to lubricant directly, unlike intercourse where most sperm enter cervical mucus quickly. Cohort data rely on self-reported lubricant type; no randomized fertility trial exists.
entries.debate: Lab studies show many lubricants impair motility or chromatin [env-anderson1998, env-agarwal2008, env-tulandi1982, env-mackenzie2019], with 'sperm-friendly' products performing best [env-mowat2014, env-tomlinson2023] and parabens adding oxidative stress [env-samarasinghe2018]. Real-world data disagree with the lab: no lubricant type reduced fecundability in a 6,467-woman cohort [env-mcinerney2018] or in a smaller diary study [env-steiner2012]. Reviews conclude the question is unresolved and that a randomized trial is needed [env-mesen2014, env-gumerova2024].

key_numbers.label: Fecundability ratio, any lubricant in fertile window

entries.title: Personal lubricants and sperm

timing.summary: Some lubricants slow sperm within 30 minutes in a dish, so the effect, if any, is limited to the sperm they touch during that act. Nothing carries over, and in couples lubricant use did not lower the chance of conceiving.

onset.text: Motility fell after 30 minutes of contact in vitro with several lubricants [tsperm-agarwal2008].

full.text: Some products raised DFI over 4 hours in vitro [tsperm-agarwal2008].

after_stopping.text: No carry-over: only sperm in contact are affected.

frequency.text: Lubricant use in the fertile window did not change fecundability [tsperm-steiner2012]; a sperm-friendly product removes even the in-vitro concern [tsperm-agarwal2008].

sperm.late_start: Switching on the day is enough, because the effect is only on contact.
sperm.text: Acts on ejaculated sperm only, not on any developmental stage.

timing.debate: In-vitro motility and DFI effects [tsperm-agarwal2008] contrast with no effect on real-world conception [tsperm-steiner2012].

audit.claim: Many lubricants (K-Y, Astroglide, olive oil, saliva) impair sperm motility and some raise DNA fragmentation in vitro, isotonic 'sperm-friendly' gels such as Pre-Seed do not, yet lubricant use did not lower fecundability in two cohorts (6,467 and 296 women).
audit.biases: Measurement error: lubricant type was self-reported and not tied to specific acts [epc-mcinerney2018, epc-steiner2012]. Confounding by indication: women who need lubricant may have vaginal dryness or painful sex, which itself predicted longer time to pregnancy [epc-bond2025]; this would bias toward finding harm, so the null cohort results are reassuring rather than masking harm. Lab-to-life gap: in vitro tests mix 5-12.5% lubricant with sperm for minutes to hours, unlike intercourse [epc-mesen2014]. Reverse causation is unlikely. No industry-funded cohort was identified, but 'sperm-friendly' claims rest largely on lab tests of commercial products.
audit.newer_evidence: No new cohort or randomized trial since 2018. Two 2024 systematic reviews agree the lab harm is real and driven by osmolality and pH (many products exceed WHO's 380 mOsm/kg) but that only 2 of 24 studies were in vivo and evidence is insufficient for a guideline [epc-gumerova2024, epc-molin2024]. Newer lab studies complicate the 'sperm-friendly' label: Pre-Seed matched controls only after initial loss of motility [epc-pradit2025], all commercial gels including Pre-Seed reduced forward progression and only egg white did not [epc-markram2022], and 'sperm-safe' gels still cut motility at 1-2 h though less than pleasure gels [epc-tomlinson2023]. Older positive data for Pre-Seed stand [epc-agarwal2008, epc-agarwal2013].
audit.bottom_line: For natural conception, using lubricant does not appear to reduce the chance of pregnancy, and avoiding it if sex is painful may do more harm than good. For semen collected for testing, IUI or IVF, use none or a clinic-approved isotonic product; even 'fertility-friendly' gels are not perfectly neutral in the lab.

entries.headline: Farm workers exposed to organophosphate/carbamate pesticides have higher SDF; high-residue produce seems to cancel the benefit of fruit and vegetables.

dose.effective: Use protective equipment for occupational spraying; wash produce; choose lower-residue or organic options for high-residue items if affordable.
dose.studied_range: Occupational cholinesterase-inhibiting exposure; dietary residues by produce type.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Do not cut fruit and vegetables to avoid pesticides; the net effect of produce is positive or neutral.

entries.mechanism: Organophosphates generate ROS and lipid peroxidation in testis and disrupt the HPG axis.
entries.interactions: See [high-fruit-vegetable-intake].
entries.caveats: Small cross-sectional occupational studies; dietary findings come from one cohort.
entries.title: Pesticides (occupational and dietary)

timing.summary: Dietary pesticide biomarkers collapse within a day or two of switching to organic food and return just as fast when you switch back [tleg-lu2006, tleg-oates2014]. Any effect on sperm, in contrast, is governed by the 74-90 day spermatogenic cycle, and the one longitudinal study across a spraying season found no short-term change in semen quality [tleg-larsen1998].

onset.text: Urinary organophosphate metabolites fell to undetectable immediately - within the first day - after organic food replaced conventional food in children [tleg-lu2006]; a week of organic eating cut total dialkylphosphates by 89% in adults [tleg-oates2014] and 13 pesticide biomarkers by 60-95% in families [tleg-hyland2019].

full.text: Biomarker reduction is complete within about a week; there is no slower component, because these compounds do not accumulate [tleg-oates2014, tleg-hyland2019].

after_stopping.text: Metabolites returned to pre-intervention levels as soon as conventional food was reintroduced, within days [tleg-lu2006].

frequency.text: Benefit exists only on the days you eat low-residue food: the children's study showed the biomarker tracking the diet day by day [tleg-lu2006]. Choosing low-residue produce rather than avoiding produce is what the semen-quality data support - high-residue fruit and vegetables were not associated with better semen while low-to-moderate-residue ones were [tleg-chiu2016].

sperm.late_start: A 2-4 week start lowers current pesticide exposure within days but can only affect the last stages of sperm maturation; the mitotic and meiotic stages 1-3 months earlier are already past.
sperm.text: Occupationally exposed farm workers had higher sperm DNA fragmentation [tleg-miranda2013] and the heaviest organophosphate exposure tracked the lowest sperm counts with seasonal variation [tleg-reciovega2008], so a full spermatogenic cycle (74-90 days) is the sensible lead time even though the biomarker responds in days.

timing.debate: Occupational cross-sectional studies find worse sperm chromatin and counts with organophosphate exposure [tleg-miranda2013, tleg-reciovega2008], but the one prospective within-person study across a spraying season found sperm concentration fell equally in spraying and non-spraying farmers, with no exposure-related change [tleg-larsen1998]. The dietary evidence is biomarker-only: no trial has shown that an organic diet changes any clinical or fertility outcome [tleg-oates2014, tleg-hyland2019].

entries.headline: PFAS stay in blood for years (half-lives 2.7-5.3 years) and are linked to weaker vaccine responses, higher cholesterol, lower birth weight and some cancers; NASEM advises testing likely-exposed people with extra screening above 2 and 20 ng/mL, and regular plasma or blood donation measurably lowered serum PFOS in an RCT.

dose.effective: If likely exposed (contaminated water, firefighting foam, PFAS work), ask for a serum test: NASEM sum of 7 PFAS <2 ng/mL = usual care; 2-20 ng/mL = cut exposure plus lipid screening; >20 ng/mL = also thyroid testing and kidney/testicular cancer and ulcerative colitis checks. Cut intake by treating contaminated tap water ([water-filtration]). To speed elimination: plasma donation every 6 weeks for 12 months lowered PFOS by 2.9 ng/mL (blood every 12 weeks: 1.1 ng/mL); prescription cholestyramine 4 g three times daily for 12 weeks lowered PFOS by 60% in highly exposed adults.
dose.studied_range: Donation RCT in firefighters with PFOS >=5 ng/mL; cholestyramine trials in residents with PFOS ~50-190 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: EFSA tolerable weekly intake: 4.4 ng/kg body weight per week for PFOA+PFNA+PFHxS+PFOS; NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased risk.
dose.timeframe: Years: after clean water was supplied, serum PFHxS, PFOS and PFOA fell only 13%, 20% and 26% per year.
dose.notes: Donate blood or plasma only if eligible and for its own sake; PFAS reduction is a side benefit. Bile-acid sequestrants have GI side effects and interfere with absorption of other drugs; trials are small and only in highly exposed people. Women eliminate some PFAS faster (menstruation, pregnancy, breastfeeding).

entries.mechanism: PFAS bind serum albumin and liver fatty-acid proteins, activate PPAR-alpha and other nuclear receptors, alter lipid and bile-acid handling, and in cells and animals raise ROS and modulate NF-kB and immune cell signalling. Human oxidative-stress marker data are mixed.
entries.interactions: Blood or plasma donation also lowers iron stores (relevant to [iron-excess]). Bile-acid sequestrants block enterohepatic recycling of PFAS. Shares food-contact and water routes with [phthalates].
entries.caveats: Most health links are observational; kidney function, menstruation, pregnancy and breastfeeding all change serum PFAS and can create reverse-causation artefacts. Elimination studies measure blood levels, not health outcomes.
entries.debate: Clinical relevance: NASEM concluded PFAS are linked to cancers, thyroid dysfunction, cholesterol changes and lower birth weight and set serum action levels [env-nasem2022]; EFSA based its intake limit on reduced vaccine antibodies in children [env-efsa2020, env-grandjean2012]. On cholesterol, a 2025 bias-focused meta-analysis found positive pooled links driven by cross-sectional studies, with longitudinal estimates near null [env-hussey2025]. Oxidative stress: PFOS tracked higher 8-isoprostane in pregnancy [env-siwakoti2024] and 8-OHdG in adults [env-lin2020], but a meta-analysis found PFAS-oxidative stress associations mostly inconsistent [env-chen2023]. Elimination: donation lowers PFOS [env-gasiorowski2022] and sequestrants lower it more [env-moller2024, env-andersson2025], but no study shows a health benefit, and the firefighter treatment-program data are uncontrolled [env-delaere2025]. A fibre trial hinted at falling long-chain PFAS but only in a secondary analysis [env-schlezinger2025].

entries.title: PFAS ('forever chemicals')

timing.summary: PFAS are the clearest example of an exposure that outlives the exposure: once in the blood they leave at roughly 13-26% a year, so serum levels fall with half-lives of 2.7-5.3 years [tleg-li2018pfas]. Nothing you change this month will be visible this month, and for a pregnancy planned within a year the body burden you already carry is essentially fixed unless you take deliberate steps to remove it.

onset.text: No acute effect to measure. Serum concentration climbs for as long as intake exceeds elimination, which is why body burden tracks years of drinking water or occupational exposure rather than recent meals [tleg-li2018pfas].

full.text: Serum levels only reach steady state after years on a constant intake, because the elimination half-life is years [tleg-li2018pfas]; this is extrapolated from the kinetics, not directly measured. The other legacy persistent organics behave the same way or worse: intrinsic human half-lives are 11.5-15.5 years for the main PCB congeners [tleg-ritter2011], and dioxin and furan half-lives run to years or decades, lengthening with age and body fat [tleg-milbrath2009].

after_stopping.text: After contaminated water was replaced, serum PFHxS, PFOS and PFOA fell 13%, 20% and 26% per year, i.e. half-lives of 5.3, 3.4 and 2.7 years [tleg-li2018pfas]. Blood or plasma donation over 12 months lowers PFOS measurably [tleg-gasiorowski2022], and 12 weeks of cholestyramine cut serum PFOS by 60% [tleg-moller2024] or 38% with colesevelam [tleg-andersson2025]; treated firefighters cleared PFOS at 41% a year versus 12% in those just observed [tleg-delaere2025].

frequency.text: Avoidance is continuous, not episodic: because elimination is so slow, each year of exposure adds to a burden that takes years to shed. For people with high measured levels, NASEM advises exposure reduction plus lipid screening between 2 and 20 ng/mL summed PFAS [tleg-nasem2022]; the drug and donation interventions are the only measures shown to speed elimination, and they take months [tleg-moller2024, tleg-gasiorowski2022].

sperm.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks, or even 3 months, before conception changes serum PFAS by only a few percent - too little to matter. The only short-horizon option is to stop adding (filtered water, no fluorinated gear or treated textiles) and accept the existing burden.
sperm.text: A semen-quality meta-analysis found consistent associations of PFAS with lower progressive motility and more sperm DNA fragmentation [tleg-dinisio2026], but with a 2.7-5.3-year half-life a meaningful reduction needs years, not one spermatogenic cycle [tleg-li2018pfas].

egg.late_start: Nothing useful can be achieved in the last weeks before an IVF cycle; filtering drinking water still prevents further accumulation and matters for a later pregnancy and for breastfeeding.
egg.text: PFAS elimination takes years [tleg-li2018pfas], so the exposure relevant to an egg retrieved next month was accumulated over the preceding decade. Deliberate lowering (plasma donation, bile-acid sequestrants) takes 3-12 months and has not been tested for fertility outcomes [tleg-gasiorowski2022, tleg-moller2024].

timing.debate: How fast PFAS leave the body is itself contested: apparent half-lives from populations with ongoing exposure are much longer than the 2.7-5.3 years measured after exposure stopped [tleg-li2018pfas], and the untreated comparison group in a firefighter programme showed apparent half-lives of 7.3-9.4 years [tleg-delaere2025]. Whether lowering serum PFAS improves health is untested: the interventions measure only the biomarker [tleg-moller2024, tleg-gasiorowski2022].

entries.headline: A Singapore preconception cohort found 5-10% lower fecundability per quartile of some PFAS and Chinese clinic studies link PFAS to PCOS and poorer embryo quality, but older time-to-pregnancy links were likely reverse causation, and PFAS did not track AMH or follicle counts.

dose.effective: No fertility intervention tested. For likely-exposed women, see [pfas] (testing, water filtration). Plasma donation and bile-acid sequestrants lower serum PFAS but have not been studied for fertility and sequestrants are not tested in pregnancy planning.
dose.studied_range: Plasma PFOS ~4-13 ng/mL in fertility cohorts; follicular fluid PFOA ~5-7 ng/mL.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk.
dose.timeframe: Years (PFAS half-lives 2.7-5.3 years).
dose.notes: PFAS cross readily into follicular fluid (65-92% of serum levels). Pregnancy and breastfeeding lower a woman's PFAS, which is why parity confounds time-to-pregnancy studies.

entries.mechanism: PFAS in follicular fluid may disrupt steroidogenesis, PPAR signalling and follicular lipid metabolism; one IVF study linked PFOA to altered follicular sphingolipids and organonitrogen metabolites.
entries.interactions: Coexists with other persistent pollutants; in one ovarian-tissue study organochlorines, not PFAS, tracked a smaller ovarian reserve. Women's PFAS falls with each pregnancy and breastfeeding period.
entries.caveats: Mostly case-control or single-centre clinic studies; PCOS itself alters menstruation and therefore PFAS excretion (reverse causation).
entries.debate: Time to pregnancy: the Danish birth cohort found longer TTP with PFOS/PFOA [env-fei2009], but the link appeared only in parous women in Norway [env-whitworth2012], the original authors raised reverse causation [env-fei2012], and a systematic review judged it most likely not causal [env-bach2016]. A preconception cohort that avoids this bias still found modestly lower fecundability [env-cohen2023]. PCOS: a mixture of PFAS, led by newer alternatives, was associated with PCOS [env-zhan2023], whereas an earlier study found only one congener associated [env-wangw2019]. IVF: follicular PFOA tracked poorer embryo quality [env-xu2025], but another IVF study found no clear outcome pattern [env-hong2022]; PFAS were not associated with AMH or follicle density in ovarian tissue [env-bjorvang2021].

entries.title: PFAS and female fertility

timing.summary: PFAS stay in the body for years (half-lives 2.7-5.3 years) and reach follicular fluid at 65-92% of blood levels. Cutting exposure before pregnancy barely changes the body burden in the time frame of a conception attempt.

onset.text: Not measured.

full.text: Body burden reflects years of exposure.

after_stopping.text: Half-lives after exposure ended: PFOA 2.7 y, PFOS 3.4 y, PFHxS 5.3 y [tegg-li2018]; menstruation adds an elimination route in women [tegg-wong2014].

frequency.text: Exposure reduction is ongoing; regular plasma donation every 6 weeks for a year lowered PFOS modestly (-2.9 ng/mL) [tegg-gasiorowski2022].

timing.debate: Early cohorts linked PFAS to longer time to pregnancy [tegg-fei2009], but the association appeared only in parous women, consistent with reverse causation [tegg-whitworth2012]; a preconception cohort measuring PFAS before pregnancy still found lower fecundability [tegg-cohen2023].

egg.late_start: Reducing exposure in the months before conception changes blood levels only slightly because of multi-year half-lives [tegg-li2018].
egg.text: PFAS cross into follicular fluid (ratio 0.65-0.92) [tegg-hong2022]; preconception levels were linked to 5-10% lower fecundability per quartile [tegg-cohen2023].

entries.headline: Pooled data link PFAS to slightly lower progressive motility and more sperm DNA fragmentation (r = 0.14 across 14 studies), but the effects are small, individual studies disagree, and a 604-man study found no consistent SDF effect.

dose.effective: No sperm-specific intervention tested. If exposure is likely, see [pfas] for testing and exposure reduction.
dose.studied_range: General-population serum PFOS ~5-25 ng/mL; occupational groups higher.
dose.too_much: NASEM serum sum >20 ng/mL = increased general health risk (not a fertility-specific threshold).
dose.timeframe: PFAS half-lives are years, so serum (and any sperm effect) changes slowly.
dose.notes: Effect sizes are correlations of about 0.06-0.14, i.e. small at the individual level.

entries.mechanism: PFAS reach the testis and seminal plasma; in animals they lower testosterone, disrupt Sertoli and Leydig cells and raise oxidative stress.
entries.interactions: Occurs alongside other persistent pollutants (PCBs, organochlorines) that confound associations; see [phthalates] for short-lived endocrine disruptors.
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional, single-sample designs; many congener-by-endpoint tests invite chance findings.
entries.debate: A 2026 meta-analysis found consistent inverse links with motility and DNA integrity [env-dinisio2026] and an earlier one found PFOA/PFNA linked to lower progressive motility [env-wangh2023a]; Danish young men with high PFOS+PFOA had fewer normal sperm [env-joensen2009]. Against this, a 604-man study found no consistent link with SCSA DNA fragmentation [env-specht2012], the LIFE study found associations in varying directions [env-louis2015], and a systematic review found little consistent evidence in men [env-bach2016].

entries.title: PFAS and sperm

timing.summary: PFAS stay in the blood for years after exposure ends, so any effect on sperm cannot be cut quickly. Plasma or blood donation lowered levels only modestly over a year.

onset.text: Not measured for sperm.

full.text: Not measured; weak links to motility and DNA damage are seen with long-term body burden [tsperm-dinisio2026].

after_stopping.text: Serum half-lives after exposure ended were 2.7 years (PFOA), 3.4 years (PFOS) and 5.3 years (PFHxS) [tsperm-li2018], 0.9-5 years across PFAS [tsperm-li2022].

frequency.text: Plasma donation every 6 weeks for 12 months lowered PFOS by 2.9 ng/mL [tsperm-gasiorowski2022].

sperm.late_start: Cutting exposure 2-4 weeks or even 3 months before barely changes blood levels, which fall about 13-26% per year [tsperm-li2018].
sperm.text: Body burden, not recent intake, drives exposure, so any reduction plan works on a scale of years (extrapolated from half-lives).

timing.debate: The pooled association with sperm DNA damage is small (r = 0.14) and individual studies disagree [tsperm-dinisio2026]; no study shows that lowering PFAS improves sperm.

factors.name: PFAS in cosmetics and dental floss

entries.headline: PFAS are added to some long-wear cosmetics and PTFE dental floss (FDA 2025: 51 PFAS in 1,744 cosmetic formulations, safety unestablished for most); one study linked Oral-B Glide flossing to higher serum PFHxS and short-chain PFAS cross skin models, but for most people water, food and dust dominate PFAS intake ([pfas]).

dose.effective: Check ingredient lists for 'PTFE', 'perfluoro-' or 'polyfluoro-' (common in waterproof or long-wear makeup and some floss); switch to nylon or silk floss and keep flossing. Deal first with bigger sources: contaminated water ([water-filtration]) and the steps in [pfas].
dose.studied_range: Product testing of tens of cosmetics; one cohort of 178 women with serum PFAS and product-use interviews.
dose.too_much: No cosmetic-specific threshold; serum guidance (NASEM 2 and 20 ng/mL for summed PFAS) is in [pfas].
dose.timeframe: Long-chain PFAS have serum half-lives of about 2.7-5.3 years, so body levels fall slowly after a source is removed.
dose.notes: Many cosmetic PFAS are polyfluoroalkyl phosphate esters that can break down to persistent acids.

entries.mechanism: PFAS act on PPAR nuclear receptors, lipid metabolism and immune function; oxidative-stress links in humans are inconsistent (see [pfas]). Short-chain PFAS permeate skin models while long chains lodge in skin tissue [epc-ragnarsdottir2024].
entries.interactions: Adds to the body burden described in [pfas], [pfas-sperm] and [pfas-egg]; flossing remains important for [periodontal-disease].
entries.caveats: The floss finding is from one study whose interviews came years after blood collection [epc-boronow2019]. Dermal-intake estimates come from skin models and assumed product concentrations [epc-wang2025].
entries.debate: Some modelling suggests cosmetics may rival diet for short-chain PFCA intake and add meaningfully to PFOA in regular users [epc-wang2025], while a European emissions study found cosmetics a smaller PFAS source than textiles [epc-putz2022]. FDA concluded it lacks data to judge safety of most cosmetic PFAS [epc-fda2025pfas]; products can contain very high levels of precursor PAPs [epc-harris2022].

entries.title: PFAS in cosmetics and dental floss

timing.summary: Long-chain PFAS stay in the blood for years, so removing a cosmetic or floss source lowers body levels only slowly. Short-chain PFAS clear faster but their dermal contribution is modelled, not measured.

onset.text: Not measured for cosmetics or floss.

full.text: Not measured; with half-lives of years, levels approach steady state over many years of use (extrapolated from [epc-li2018]).

after_stopping.text: Serum half-lives after a source is removed were 2.7 years (PFOA), 3.4 (PFOS) and 5.3 (PFHxS) [epc-li2018].

frequency.text: Because PFAS accumulate, cumulative use matters more than frequency; non-PTFE floss removes the floss source entirely.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: PGT-A does not raise live birth per woman and can lower it: in a 1212-woman NEJM trial cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% without; it lowers miscarriage per transfer (HFEA green for that) but HFEA rates it red for having a baby, and it roughly doubles IVF cost.

dose.effective: Not recommended routinely (ESHRE, HFEA). Distinct from PGT-M/PGT-SR for known genetic conditions, which are not add-ons.
dose.studied_range: Trophectoderm biopsy of day 5-6 blastocysts with NGS; older trials used day-3 or polar-body biopsy.
dose.too_much: Embryos labelled aneuploid or mosaic may be discarded although some could make healthy babies; some couples end with no transferable embryo.
dose.timeframe: Adds a freeze-all cycle and weeks of delay before transfer.
dose.notes: Per-transfer success looks higher because poor embryos are filtered out before transfer; the fair comparison is live birth per started cycle.

entries.mechanism: Selects embryos without whole-chromosome errors, which rise steeply with maternal age because of cohesin loss in eggs (see [maternal-age]). It cannot create euploid embryos, only choose among those already made, and a 5-10-cell biopsy may misrepresent the embryo (mosaicism).
entries.interactions: Most relevant with advanced [maternal-age]; does not fix egg quality. Combining with [time-lapse-egg] or [assisted-hatching-egg] adds nothing proven.
entries.caveats: Aneuploid calls are very accurate at predicting failure [fer-tiegs2021], which is why the debate is about efficacy per woman, not about test validity.
entries.debate: Supporters cite fewer miscarriages and shorter time to pregnancy in older women (Rubio RCT: miscarriage 2.7% vs 39%, delivery per first transfer 52.9% vs 24.2%) and the STAR post hoc gain at 35-40 [fer-rubio2017, fer-munne2019], plus near-perfect predictive value of aneuploid calls [fer-tiegs2021]. Critics point to unchanged or lower cumulative live birth [fer-yan2021, fer-munne2019, fer-cornelisse2020, fer-iwarsson2026], viable mosaic embryos being discarded (the mosaic study was run by a PGT company) [fer-capalbo2021], and per-transfer reporting that hides losses [fer-paulson2019]. HFEA red for live birth, green for miscarriage [fer-hfea2026]; ESHRE: not for routine use [fer-eshre2023addons].

entries.title: PGT-A (preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy)

audit.claim: PGT-A does not raise live birth per woman and can lower it, while reducing miscarriage per transfer; HFEA red for live birth.
audit.biases: Per-transfer reporting (denominator selection) inflates apparent benefit; post hoc age subgroups; company-run studies on mosaic embryos.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 BMJ RCT in 450 couples with severe male factor found identical cumulative live birth (60.4% vs 60.9%) with fewer pregnancy losses (5.8% vs 19.1% after first transfer) [afert-lin2025], matching the 2021 NEJM trial (77.2% vs 81.8%) [afert-yan2021]. ASRM's 2024 committee opinion says routine PGT-A's value has not been demonstrated [afert-asrm2024pgta]. Supporters point to low-quality data in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss suggesting more live births per patient [afert-mumusoglu2025] and a pilot RCT in women 35-42 with a non-significant cumulative gain (72% vs 52%, n=100) [afert-beebeejaun2025].
audit.bottom_line: Newer RCTs keep finding the same thing: fewer miscarriages, not more babies. A properly powered trial in older women and recurrent loss is still missing.

factors.name: Phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBzP, DiNP, DEP) and their replacements
aliases: Phthalates, egg yield, IVF and pregnancy

entries.headline: Nearly everyone excretes phthalates, which clear within a day; the most consistent human signals are slightly more preterm births (12-16% higher odds per interquartile rise, 16 pooled US cohorts) and shorter anogenital distance in baby boys, while headline mortality estimates rest on NHANES analyses that disagree with each other, and a 2026 randomized trial cut urinary DBP and BBzP metabolites by 38-54% in 7 days with low-plastic food.

dose.effective: Food is the main lever for DEHP and DiNP: cook from fresh, minimally packaged ingredients and eat less fast food and ultra-processed food (people getting 35% or more of calories from fast food had 24% higher DEHP and 39% higher DiNP metabolites); store and reheat food in glass or steel. A 7-day randomized diet of food sourced to avoid plastic contact plus plastic-free kitchenware cut MnBP 37.5% and MBzP 53.5%. For DEP (fragrance carrier) and DBP: pick fragrance-free lotions, deodorants and aftershave (cologne or aftershave users had about double urinary MEP; a 3-day switch cut MEP 27%). If you take an enteric-coated drug long term (some mesalamine, omeprazole, didanosine or theophylline products), ask a pharmacist whether a phthalate-free formulation exists; never stop a medicine on your own. Replace soft PVC flooring when renovating, and wet-mop and vacuum dust (PVC bedroom flooring went with higher infant MBzP).
dose.studied_range: Interventions from 3 days to 2 months, in 20-100 people per study; outcomes are urinary metabolites. Typical intakes in Germany: median 2.7 ug/kg/day DEHP, 2.1 DnBP, 1.5 DiBP, 0.6 DiNP.
dose.too_much: EFSA (2019) group tolerable daily intake 50 ug/kg body weight/day as DEHP equivalents for DBP, BBP, DEHP and DINP (individual TDI for DBP 10 ug/kg); average European diets supply 0.9-7.2 ug/kg/day. HBM4EU urinary guidance values (e.g. 0.5 mg/L for 5-oxo- plus 5-OH-MEHP in adults) were exceeded in up to 5% of European children and teens, and a mixture risk could not be excluded for about 17%. Very high exposures come from medical PVC in neonatal intensive care and from DBP-coated medicines (urinary MBP up to 50-fold higher).
dose.timeframe: Metabolite half-lives are about 2-18 hours, so urine levels fall within 1-3 days of removing a source and rise again as soon as it returns. Pregnancy associations concern exposure during pregnancy itself (DEHP: first and second trimester in the largest pool).
dose.notes: One spot urine sample is a poor measure of usual DEHP exposure (intraclass correlation 0.08-0.3), which blurs associations. US and German exposure to DEHP, DBP, BBzP and DEP fell after 2001 while the replacements DINCH and DEHTP rose quickly (DEHTP from under 10% to 100% detection in German 24-hour urine, 2009-2017).

entries.mechanism: Several ortho-phthalates (DBP, DEHP, BBzP, DiNP; DEP only weakly) are anti-androgenic: during a fetal window their monoesters suppress Leydig-cell testosterone and INSL3, producing the rat 'phthalate syndrome' (hypospadias, undescended testes, malformed accessory glands, shorter anogenital distance); EFSA's group TDI rests on this fetal-testosterone effect. In people, oxidative stress is the best-documented intermediate: across repeated pregnancy samples, phthalate metabolites tracked urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane (an IQR rise in MBP or MiBP went with about 50% more 8-isoprostane in Puerto Rico), and in mediation analysis 8-isoprostane accounted for an estimated 47-60% of the DEHP-preterm-birth association. In 1,034 Chinese men every metabolite tracked 8-OHdG, 8-isoPGF2a and HNE-MA.
entries.interactions: Shares food and packaging sources with [bisphenols] and [microplastics]; fast food and ultra-processed diets raise several at once, so diet quality ([mediterranean-diet]) confounds most associations. Fragrance-free products also cut parabens and triclosan. Persistent chemicals are covered under [pfas]. Fertility evidence is in [phthalates] and [phthalates].
entries.caveats: Most evidence is observational with single spot urines, so exposure is badly misclassified (DEHP ICC about 0.1-0.3), which usually biases toward the null but can also create chance findings when 11 or more metabolites are tested against many outcomes. Phthalates come with other exposures (processed food, low income, fragrance use, medical care), so residual confounding and reverse causation (sick people receive more medical PVC and coated drugs) are real threats in mortality studies. Exposure-reduction trials are short and small and none measured a health outcome. 'Phthalate-free' often means DINCH or DEHTP, which have far less human data.
entries.debate: Mortality: an NHANES analysis linked DEHP and high-molecular-weight metabolites to higher all-cause mortality and estimated 90,761-107,283 US deaths a year at ages 55-64 [ept-trasande2022], and burden models built on that hazard ratio attributed 356,238 global cardiovascular deaths and 1.97 million preterm births to DEHP [ept-hyman2025, ept-hyman2026] (the 2025 estimate was funded by Bloomberg Philanthropies and NIH, with the Beyond Petrochemicals campaign named in its disclosures). But other analyses of the same NHANES data found no link with cardiovascular death [ept-sturgeon2016], implicated different metabolites (MBzP and MnBP, not DEHP) [ept-beyer2022], or found the plasticizer-mixture link only in people with low vitamin D or folate [ept-zhang2025]; attributable-death figures assume the association is causal. Preterm birth: a 16-cohort pool [ept-welch2022], the ECHO cohort [ept-buckley2026] and an EPA systematic review [ept-radke2019] support a modest link, but the pool put the DEHP window in early pregnancy [ept-friedman2025] while a fertility cohort found it late [ept-yland2022]. Anogenital distance: shorter AGD with prenatal phthalates in US and Swedish cohorts [ept-swan2005, ept-swan2015, ept-bornehag2015] but no consistent association in a low-exposed Danish cohort [ept-jensen2016]. Sources: the PVC-flooring study [ept-carlstedt2013] drew a letter calling it 'anti-PVC advocacy' [ept-blakey2013]. Exposure reduction: food and personal-care swaps lowered metabolites in days [ept-rudel2011, ept-harley2016, ept-harray2026], but a catered low-exposure diet backfired on contaminated spices and milk [ept-sathyanarayana2013] and a plastic-free family saw mixed results [ept-hutter2016]; a scoping review concludes policy may matter more than individual action [ept-yang2023]. Replacements: DEHTP showed no developmental toxicity in older guideline rodent studies at hundreds of mg/kg [ept-faber2007] and intakes sit far below its TDI [ept-lessmann2019], yet a 2025 mouse study found ovarian effects from 10 ug/kg [ept-potts2025]; DINCH metabolites were unrelated to IVF outcomes in one cohort [ept-machtinger2018] but went with longer time to pregnancy, higher FSH and preterm birth in others [ept-blaauwendraad2025, ept-jiang2024, ept-yland2022], all single-study signals.

entries.title: Phthalates (DEHP, DBP, BBzP, DiNP, DEP) and their replacements

entries.headline: Men with higher urinary DBP and BBzP metabolites (MBP, MBzP) have roughly twice the odds of low sperm concentration in pooled data, and DEP and DEHP metabolites tracked 14-18% more Comet sperm DNA damage in one Boston clinic, but nearly all of it comes from single spot urines in fertility-clinic men, motility and morphology links are null in meta-analysis, and no trial shows that lowering exposure improves semen.

dose.effective: Same steps as [phthalates]: fresh rather than fast or ultra-processed food, glass or steel for hot food, fragrance-free toiletries and aftershave, and phthalate-free formulations of long-term enteric-coated medicines (with a pharmacist). Start about 3 months before trying to conceive.
dose.studied_range: General-population and fertility-clinic urinary levels; single spot urine in most studies, repeated samples in a 1,034-man Chinese cohort.
dose.too_much: No semen threshold established. EFSA group TDI 50 ug/kg/day (DEHP equivalents) is set on fetal testosterone, not adult sperm.
dose.timeframe: Urine falls within 1-3 days; any change in sperm would need roughly one spermatogenic cycle (about 64 days plus epididymal transit, so about 3 months).
dose.notes: No intervention study has measured semen or sperm DNA fragmentation.

entries.mechanism: Phthalate monoesters are Sertoli- and Leydig-cell toxicants in rodents and lower testosterone; in men from subfertile couples, every urinary phthalate metabolite tracked oxidative-stress markers (8-OHdG, 8-isoPGF2a, HNE-MA), and 8-isoPGF2a suggestively mediated about 12% of the MBP-sperm concentration association. Comet-assay damage is consistent with oxidative DNA breaks but was not measured alongside oxidative markers.
entries.interactions: Shares sources with [bisphenols] and [microplastics-sperm]; men with higher exposure also tend to eat more processed food, so [profertility-diet] confounds. Paternal DEHP was also linked to lower IVF live birth in couples (see [phthalates]).
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional fertility-clinic samples (selection into IVF clinics), one urine per man for metabolites with ICC 0.1-0.6, many metabolite-by-endpoint tests, and confounding by diet and BMI. The MEHP-DNA-damage finding appeared only after statistically adjusting for its own oxidative metabolite MEHHP, a modelling choice. Sperm DNA damage was measured with the neutral Comet assay, not the clinical SCSA/TUNEL tests.
entries.debate: For: an EPA systematic review rated evidence 'robust' for DEHP and DBP and male reproductive outcomes (AGD, semen, testosterone) [ept-radke2018]; clinic studies found dose-response links of MBP with low concentration [ept-hauser2006] and of MEP and MEHP with Comet DNA damage [ept-duty2003, ept-hauser2007]; a 2026 systematic review graded certainty low to moderate [ept-dhar2026]; oxidative stress may partly mediate [ept-liu2019]. Against or narrower: a meta-analysis found only MBP, MBzP and semen DEHP associated with concentration and nothing for motility or morphology [ept-wangh2023]; in 420 EARTH men a mixture analysis of 24 chemicals found the consistent signals were mercury and triclosan, not phthalates [ept-genardwalton2025]. Paternal exposure and couple outcomes: a few paternal metabolites predicted lower implantation and live birth but most did not [ept-dodge2015]; a paternal DEHP factor predicted IVF failure (HR 1.41) [ept-minguezalarcon2021].
