entries.title: Phthalates and sperm

entries.headline: In the Boston EARTH IVF cohort (256 women), the top quartile of urinary DEHP metabolites had fewer eggs and 19 percentage points lower live birth per cycle, but an Israeli IVF cohort confirmed fewer eggs without any drop in live birth, and the clearest pregnancy signal is modestly more preterm birth.

dose.effective: Same steps as [phthalates]: fresh, minimally packaged food, less fast and ultra-processed food, glass or steel for hot food, fragrance-free personal care. Keep it up through the roughly 3-month window before egg retrieval or conception and through pregnancy.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of urinary metabolites from one or two spot samples per IVF cycle.
dose.too_much: No established threshold. EFSA group TDI 50 ug/kg/day (DEHP equivalents).
dose.timeframe: Urine changes within days, but the follicle that ovulates grows for about 85 days, so lower exposure across about 3 months; pregnancy associations involve exposure across gestation.
dose.notes: IVF associations come from two clinic cohorts; general-population time-to-pregnancy studies point in opposite directions.

entries.mechanism: In mice, the replacement DEHTP altered follicle counts, follicle growth and ovarian gene expression at low doses, and DEHP metabolites tracked fewer oocytes in two IVF cohorts; in pregnancy, urinary phthalates track 8-isoprostane, which statistically mediated about half of the DEHP-preterm association.
entries.interactions: Usually co-exposed with [bisphenols]; paternal DEHP also predicted IVF failure ([phthalates]). Diet quality ([profertility-diet]) confounds.
entries.caveats: Clinic populations (selection into IVF), one or two spot urines per cycle, 11 metabolites x many endpoints, and residual confounding by diet and BMI. Pregnancy-loss estimates were imprecise.
entries.debate: IVF: DEHP linked to fewer oocytes and 19-point lower live birth [ept-hauser2016] and to biochemical pregnancy loss (top quartile RR 3.4, CI 0.97-11.7) [ept-messerlian2016], but in a second IVF cohort DEHP predicted fewer oocytes and embryos with no effect on implantation, pregnancy or live birth, and DINCH showed nothing [ept-machtinger2018]. Ovarian reserve: a phthalate-plus-DINCH mixture went with 8.6% lower antral follicle count [ept-jiang2024], and a 2026 meta-analysis reported lower AFC (SMD -0.38) [ept-majdi2026], though its very narrow confidence intervals despite high heterogeneity invite caution. Fecundity: one cohort found phthalates lengthened time to pregnancy [ept-charifson2024], another that several phthalate metabolites shortened it while a DINCH metabolite lengthened it [ept-blaauwendraad2025]. Preterm birth: moderate pooled evidence [ept-welch2022, ept-radke2019, ept-buckley2026], with disagreement over which trimester matters [ept-friedman2025, ept-yland2022].

key_numbers.label: Live birth per cycle, top vs bottom DEHP quartile (EARTH)
Lower antral follicle count with phthalate+DINCH mixture
Preterm-birth odds per IQR MiBP in pregnancy

entries.title: Phthalates, egg yield, IVF and pregnancy

timing.summary: Phthalates are cleared in hours, so urine reflects roughly the last day and a change of food or toiletries shows up within 3-7 days [ept-koch2004, ept-rudel2011, ept-harray2026]. The flip side is that the benefit lasts only while the change is kept up, and a single urine sample says little about the previous months [ept-johns2015].

onset.text: After a DEHP dose, urinary metabolites peak at 2-4 hours [ept-koch2004]. Reductions are equally fast: 3 days of fresh food cut DEHP metabolites 53-56% [ept-rudel2011], 3 days of fragrance-free products cut MEP 27% [ept-harley2016], and 7 days of low-plastic food cut MnBP 37.5% and MBzP 53.5% [ept-harray2026].

full.text: Urine reaches its new level within about 3-7 days of a sustained change [ept-rudel2011, ept-harray2026]; nothing builds beyond that.

after_stopping.text: Metabolite half-lives are about 2 hours in a first phase and 5-10 hours in a second phase for DEHP [ept-koch2004], 3-18 hours across phthalates [ept-johns2015]; DEHTP is 95% excreted within 24 hours [ept-lessmann2016]. Levels return to the old baseline within a day or two of going back to the old habits.

frequency.text: Because exposure is cleared in hours, avoidance protects only on the days it is practised; there is no carry-over [ept-johns2015]. Even careful diets can be undone by contaminated ingredients [ept-sathyanarayana2013].

timing.debate: Kinetics are not disputed, but their meaning for health studies is: because a spot urine has an ICC of only 0.08-0.3 for DEHP [ept-braun2012, ept-johns2015], studies of long-term outcomes are badly misclassified, and the pooled preterm-birth data put the sensitive window in early pregnancy [ept-friedman2025] while a fertility cohort found it in late pregnancy [ept-yland2022].

sperm.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks before still lowers exposure within days [ept-rudel2011], but covers only the last stages of sperm maturation; no trial shows any semen benefit at any lead time.
sperm.text: The 64-day spermatogenic cycle plus epididymal transit sets the lead time [ept-heller1963], not the chemistry, which clears in a day [ept-koch2004].

egg.late_start: Starting in the last 2-4 weeks still lowers exposure during dominant-follicle selection and the treatment cycle, which is when the IVF studies measured it [ept-hauser2016]; it cannot cover earlier follicle growth.
egg.text: Lead time follows the ~85-day follicle growth period [ept-gougeon1986]; for pregnancy, pooled data point to the first and second trimesters for DEHP [ept-friedman2025].

entries.headline: PCOS carries measurable systemic oxidative stress (malondialdehyde about 47% higher, glutathione about 50% lower than controls, independent of weight); fertility problems are mainly ovulatory, and IVF outcomes are worse when PCOS coexists with obesity.

dose.effective: Management per the 2023 international guideline: healthy lifestyle first, then evidence-based medical and fertility treatment. In overweight women, losing 5% or more of body weight improved insulin, SHBG and cycles in an early study.
dose.studied_range: Weight loss studies 5-22% of body weight; lifestyle RCTs mostly 3-12 months.
dose.timeframe: Metabolic and ovulatory improvement over 3-6 months of weight loss.
dose.notes: Insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism, not oocytes per se, drive most of the problem; egg quality in lean, ovulating PCOS is often normal.

entries.mechanism: Hyperinsulinaemia and hyperandrogenism alter the follicular environment; chronic low-grade inflammation and lower antioxidant reserve (glutathione, paraoxonase-1) increase lipid peroxidation. Obesity adds lipotoxicity and further insulin resistance.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [excess-adiposity] and [glycemic-control]; supplements studied mainly in PCOS: [myo-inositol], [n-acetylcysteine]. Weight loss is covered by [weight-loss].
entries.caveats: Raised oxidative markers in blood do not prove oxidative damage to eggs is the cause of infertility in PCOS; most infertility is anovulation, which is treatable. Lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth (Cochrane 2019 found none).
entries.title: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

timing.summary: In PCOS the fixable part is mostly ovulation, and it responds to weight loss over months: about 5% loss over 6-7 months restored menstrual function in most women, and 16 weeks of lifestyle change before ovulation induction raised ovulation and live birth.

onset.text: SHBG and insulin improve as weight falls [tegg-kiddy1992].

full.text: Ovulation gains after 16 weeks of preconception weight loss [tegg-legro2015]; menstrual recovery over 6-7 months [tegg-kiddy1992].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; follows weight regain.

frequency.text: Daily diet and activity; see weight-loss.

timing.debate: Weight loss before treatment helped anovulatory obese PCOS [tegg-legro2015, tegg-legro2016], but not unselected obese infertile women or IVF [tegg-mutsaerts2016, tegg-einarsson2017]; oral-contraceptive pretreatment worsened metabolic syndrome without gain [tegg-legro2015]. Systemic oxidative stress in PCOS is documented [tegg-murri2013] but not shown to change on a time course.

egg.late_start: Ovulation induction itself works within a cycle, so a late start loses the weight-loss benefit but not treatment.
egg.text: Delaying clomiphene 16 weeks for weight loss raised live birth from 10% to 25% in obese PCOS [tegg-legro2016].

audit.claim: PCOS carries systemic oxidative stress; fertility problems are mainly ovulatory; lifestyle RCTs in PCOS have not reported live birth.
audit.biases: Oxidative markers are cross-sectional and confounded by obesity and insulin resistance; weight-loss advice rests partly on observational data.
audit.newer_evidence: In obese women with PCOS, a secondary cross-trial comparison of two RCTs found lifestyle weight loss before clomiphene gave higher live birth (25% vs 10%) than immediate clomiphene [afert-legro2016]. In obese infertile women generally, the large LIFEstyle (NEJM 2016) and FIT-PLESE (2022) RCTs found no live-birth gain from preconception weight loss [afert-mutsaerts2016, afert-legro2022], and a 2024 meta-analysis found more pregnancies but not more live births (RR 1.19, 0.97-1.45) [afert-caldwell2024]. MR in MoBa supports a causal effect of higher BMI on longer time to conception [afert-wootton2023].
audit.bottom_line: Weight loss helps ovulation in PCOS, but randomised evidence that delaying treatment to lose weight raises live birth is weak outside PCOS-specific data.

entries.headline: An oral fern extract that modestly raises the skin's tolerance to UV: in 9 volunteers a single 7.5 mg/kg dose reduced sunburn redness, sunburn cells and DNA dimers, but the evidence is small trials, and there are no large trials showing less photoaging or fewer skin cancers.

dose.effective: No established dose; the key photoprotection study used a single 7.5 mg/kg dose (about 500 mg for a 70 kg adult) before UV exposure.
dose.studied_range: Single pre-exposure doses in photoprotection studies; daily use as an adjunct in small trials for melasma, vitiligo, polymorphous light eruption and atopic dermatitis.
dose.too_much: No safety signal in reviews; long-term data are limited.
dose.timeframe: Hours (taken before sun exposure).
dose.notes: An adjunct only; it does not replace [sunscreen].

entries.mechanism: The extract's polyphenols are thought to scavenge ROS; in human skin biopsies it reduced UV-induced CPDs, sunburn cells and mast-cell infiltration, with a trend toward preserved Langerhans cells.
entries.interactions: Similar systemic-photoprotection niche to dietary carotenoids ([tomatoes-lycopene]); neither approaches the protection of [sunscreen].
entries.caveats: The landmark study had 9 participants without a placebo group. Effect sizes are small (a modest rise in the dose needed to burn).
entries.debate: A 2025 systematic review describes strong therapeutic potential across many skin conditions [skb-zundell2025], but its evidence base is 21 small studies spread over six conditions; the core photoprotection data come from tiny within-person studies [skb-middelkamphup2004]. No independent large RCT has tested hard outcomes.
entries.title: Polypodium leucotomos extract (oral fern extract)

timing.summary: A single oral dose taken before sun exposure reduced sunburn and DNA damage measured the next day. Nothing is known about daily use or how long protection lasts.

onset.text: A single 7.5 mg/kg dose before UV reduced erythema, sunburn cells and DNA dimers at 24 h [tfood-middelkamphup2004].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Taken before planned sun exposure in the key study [tfood-middelkamphup2004].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: In 9 volunteers a single dose reduced sunburn redness, sunburn cells and DNA dimers; small trials only.
audit.biases: The landmark study had 9 participants and no placebo [anut-middelkamphup2004].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2026 randomized study replicated a modest 26% rise in the UVA burn threshold but found no reduction in UVA-induced thymidine dimers in skin or urine [anut-faisal2026].
audit.bottom_line: Modest sunburn protection replicated; the DNA-damage claim did not replicate for UVA.

entries.headline: In one 70-man RCT, pomegranate-fruit extract plus galangal tablets for 3 months raised the total number of motile sperm by 62%, vs 20% on placebo; it has not been replicated and pregnancy was not measured.

dose.effective: Daily standardised pomegranate-extract plus galangal tablets (Punalpin) for 3 months.
dose.studied_range: 3 months.
dose.timeframe: About 3 months (one spermatogenic cycle plus transit).
dose.notes: The extract was standardised for punicalagins, punicalin and ellagic acid; effect of pomegranate alone is unknown.

entries.mechanism: Not established in humans; candidates are ellagitannin-derived metabolites (urolithins, metabotype-dependent) and galangal's acetoxychavicol acetate.
entries.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]. Urolithin production varies by metabotype (see [urolithin-a]).
entries.caveats: Single trial; participants were men whose semen did not meet sperm-bank standards, not infertile couples; no pregnancy or DNA-fragmentation outcomes.

key_numbers.label: Total motile sperm increase, active vs placebo

entries.title: Pomegranate fruit extract (with galangal)

timing.summary: One 3-month trial reported more motile sperm with a pomegranate-galangal tablet. Nothing is known about faster effects or how long a benefit lasts.

onset.text: Not measured before the end of treatment.

full.text: After 3 months, total motile sperm rose 62% versus 20% on placebo [tsperm-fedder2014].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Daily tablets in the only trial; no schedule data [tsperm-fedder2014].

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: The trial lasted one cycle plus transit [tsperm-fedder2014].

timing.debate: The single trial has not been replicated and two authors commercialise the product [tsperm-fedder2014].

entries.headline: A famous 10-patient study reported dramatic falls in LDL oxidation and carotid thickness, but an 18-month RCT in 289 people found no effect on carotid progression and a meta-analysis found no lipid effect.

dose.effective: Not established; 240 mL/day was ineffective for carotid progression overall.
dose.studied_range: 50-240 mL/day for up to 3 years.
dose.too_much: Juice adds free sugar.
dose.notes: Punicalagins are converted by gut bacteria to urolithins, but people differ: across trials 25-80% make only urolithin A, 10-50% also make isourolithin A/urolithin B, and 5-25% make none, and the mix shifts with age. Purified urolithin A bypasses this (see [urolithin-a]).

entries.mechanism: Ellagitannins (punicalagin) -> ellagic acid -> urolithins; raised paraoxonase-1 in the small study.
entries.interactions: Ellagitannin source like [walnuts-nuts] and [blackberries]; downstream metabolite evidence is under [urolithin-a]. A pomegranate-plus-galangal extract increased motile sperm in one RCT (see [pomegranate-extract-sperm]).
entries.caveats: Industry-funded small studies drove early enthusiasm; possible benefit only in exploratory subgroups with high oxidative stress.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, Folin assay, pure juice
People producing no urolithins (metabotype 0), range across trials

entries.title: Pomegranate juice

timing.summary: Ellagic acid from pomegranate peaks in blood within about an hour and then gut bacteria turn it into urolithins, which only some people make. An 18-month trial found no effect on carotid thickening, so there is no proven benefit to time.

onset.text: Plasma ellagic acid peaks at about 0.65 h after juice [tfood-seeram2008]; urolithin production depends on a person's stable gut metabotype [tfood-tomasbarberan2014].

full.text: No overall effect on carotid intima-media progression after up to 18 months of 240 mL/day [tfood-davidson2009].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No outcome benefit has been shown, so there is no evidence-based schedule [tfood-davidson2009].

timing.debate: The null 18-month trial [tfood-davidson2009] contrasts with exploratory benefit in people with high oxidative stress in the same trial; metabotype differences [tfood-tomasbarberan2014] may explain inconsistent responses.

audit.claim: A famous 10-patient study was not replicated by an 18-month RCT and lipids are unchanged in meta-analysis.
audit.biases: Industry-funded small early studies.
audit.newer_evidence: Davidson 2009 and a 12-RCT lipid meta-analysis remain the best evidence [adiet-davidson2009, adiet-sahebkar2016].
audit.bottom_line: A small positive study was overturned by a larger trial.

entries.headline: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic (Group 1) and red meat as probably carcinogenic (2A); independent 2022-2025 reviews find the processed-meat link consistent but modest (at least ~7% higher colorectal cancer risk) and the unprocessed-red-meat link weak, with heme-driven lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso formation as the likely mechanism.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat rare and red meat to a few modest portions per week.
dose.studied_range: 0-420 g/day red meat in controlled feeding (dose-response for fecal N-nitroso compounds); white meat at 420-600 g/day had no effect.
dose.too_much: Each 50 g/day of processed meat raised colorectal cancer risk ~18% (IARC). Highest vs lowest heme intake: colon cancer RR 1.18.
dose.timeframe: Fecal markers change within days; cancer risk over years.
dose.notes: Meat eaten with red-wine polyphenols or polyphenol-rich spices produced less postprandial MDA in animal and human meal studies.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron catalyses peroxidation of dietary PUFA in the stomach and colon, producing malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal, and promotes endogenous N-nitrosation; processed meats add nitrite and pre-formed nitrosamines; high-heat cooking adds HCAs and PAHs.
entries.interactions: Worse with [high-temperature-cooking]; partly offset by [herbs-spices] and polyphenol-rich foods eaten in the same meal.
entries.caveats: Oxidative mechanism evidence is strongest for the gut lumen; effects on systemic markers are less studied. For sperm, only processed meat (not unprocessed red meat) has been linked to worse semen; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

key_numbers.label: Colon cancer RR, highest vs lowest heme iron
Fecal N-nitroso compounds per g red meat/day

entries.title: Processed and red meat

timing.summary: The gut chemistry changes within days - faecal N-nitroso compounds rise in proportion to red-meat intake under controlled feeding [tleg-bingham2002] - and plasma TMAO rises over about 4 weeks of daily red meat and falls again within 4 weeks of stopping [tleg-wang2019tmao]. The cancer risk that drives the IARC classification accrues over decades and has no short-term readout.

onset.text: Faecal apparent total N-nitroso compounds rose linearly with red meat from 0 to 420 g/day within days of controlled feeding [tleg-bingham2002]; white meat had no such effect.

full.text: Plasma and urinary TMAO roughly tripled after 4 weeks of a red-meat diet, through more precursor, more microbial conversion and less renal clearance [tleg-wang2019tmao]. Colorectal cancer risk, the basis of the Group 1 classification for processed meat, reflects years to decades of intake [tleg-bouvard2015, tleg-bastide2011].

after_stopping.text: TMAO returned to baseline within 4 weeks of stopping red meat [tleg-wang2019tmao], and faecal nitrosation markers fall as soon as intake does [tleg-bingham2002]. Cumulative cancer risk does not reverse on that timescale.

frequency.text: The measurable markers track current intake, not a lifetime store, so cutting back works whenever you do it and reverting undoes it within weeks [tleg-wang2019tmao]. White meat at the same quantity did not raise faecal nitrosation [tleg-bingham2002], so substitution rather than schedule is the lever.

timing.debate: Whether the slow clock justifies acting at all is disputed: IARC classifies processed meat as Group 1 and red meat as Group 2A [tleg-bouvard2015] and heme intake carries an 18% higher colon cancer risk [tleg-bastide2011], but the NutriRECS panel reviewed the same literature and issued weak recommendations that adults continue their current intake, judging the certainty of benefit from cutting back to be low [tleg-johnston2019]. The fast biomarkers (TMAO, faecal nitrosation) have never been shown to mediate the cancer risk.

audit.claim: IARC classes processed meat as carcinogenic and red meat as probably carcinogenic, with heme-driven lipid peroxidation and N-nitroso formation; evidence rated strong.
audit.biases: Cohort associations come from food-frequency questionnaires and heavy meat eaters differ in smoking, obesity, alcohol and fibre intake (residual confounding, measurement error) [adiet-zeraatkar2019, adiet-ioannidis2018]. IARC classifies how certain a hazard is, not how large it is [adiet-bouvard2015].
audit.newer_evidence: NutriRECS (2019) rated the evidence low certainty and advised people to continue current intake [adiet-johnston2019, adiet-zeraatkar2019]; nutrition epidemiologists replied that GRADE is unsuited to diet and that substitution matters [adiet-qian2020]. Substitution analyses suggest replacing red meat with nuts, legumes or soy is associated with 13-17% lower CHD risk [adiet-alshaar2020]. The independent Burden of Proof analyses found only weak evidence for unprocessed red meat (2022) [adiet-lescinsky2022], and for processed meat a conservative minimum of 11% higher diabetes and 7% higher colorectal cancer risk, rated two stars (2025) [adiet-haile2025]. Mechanistic support (haem iron) is unchanged [adiet-bastide2011].
audit.bottom_line: Processed meat probably raises colorectal cancer and diabetes risk modestly; for unprocessed red meat the case is weak and depends on what replaces it. 'Strong' overstates how certain and how large the effect is.

entries.headline: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: men eating the most had fewer normal-shaped sperm (1.7 points) and, in young men, about 78 million fewer sperm per ejaculate. Unprocessed red meat was not linked to worse semen.

dose.effective: Keep processed meat (bacon, ham, sausages, deli meats) to less than one serving a week; replace with fish or legumes.
dose.studied_range: Quartiles of intake in 155 clinic patients.
dose.too_much: Highest quartile associated with worse morphology.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.

entries.mechanism: Heme iron, nitrites and advanced glycation/lipoxidation products may increase oxidative stress; may also mark a Western diet.
entries.interactions: Replace with [omega3-fish] or unprocessed meat/poultry; see [unprocessed-red-meat].
entries.caveats: Observational only, small effects, and confounding by overall diet and abstinence time is possible (the young-men study noted heavy meat eaters also had shorter abstinence). The finding is specific to processed meat; see [unprocessed-red-meat].

key_numbers.label: Fewer normal forms, highest vs lowest quartile

entries.title: Processed meat (bacon, ham, hot dogs, deli meats)

timing.summary: Semen reflects the diet of the preceding 2-3 months, not of last week, because a sperm takes about 74-90 days to make. The processed-meat associations come from questionnaires covering the previous year [tleg-afeiche2014a, tleg-afeiche2014b], so one spermatogenic cycle is the minimum honest trial period - and no trial has been done.

onset.text: Not measured. No study has fed or withdrawn processed meat and followed semen over time; the association comes from cross-sectional and repeated-measures cohorts using food-frequency questionnaires [tleg-afeiche2014a, tleg-afeiche2014b].

full.text: Extrapolated from spermatogenesis: a complete change in the sperm population takes about 74-90 days, so changes in diet should be judged after roughly 3 months, as air-pollution window studies over the same 74-day window demonstrate [tleg-russo2025].

after_stopping.text: Not measured; by the same logic, going back to a high processed-meat diet would take about one spermatogenic cycle to show in semen. Nothing suggests a lasting effect after that.

frequency.text: No study has compared schedules. The quantity signal is in the top versus bottom quartile of habitual intake (about 1.7 percentage points fewer normal forms [tleg-afeiche2014a], and about 78 million fewer sperm per ejaculate in young men [tleg-afeiche2014b]), which implies average weekly intake over months rather than any single meal.

sperm.late_start: Starting 2-4 weeks before conception can only affect the last stages of maturation and epididymal transit; the cell divisions most plausibly affected happened 1-3 months earlier.
sperm.text: Lead time is set by the 74-90 day spermatogenic cycle, which is also the window over which environmental exposures have measurable semen effects [tleg-russo2025]. Unprocessed red meat was not associated with worse semen in the same cohorts [tleg-afeiche2014b].

timing.debate: The timing claim is entirely extrapolated: no intervention study exists. The association itself is contested - the young-men study's authors noted that it was strongest in men with under 2 days' abstinence and was driven by ejaculate volume, so residual confounding by abstinence time cannot be excluded [tleg-afeiche2014b], and the broader meat-and-health literature is disputed [tleg-johnston2019].

audit.claim: Processed meat is the meat signal for sperm: high intake is linked to fewer normal-form sperm and lower counts; observational only.
audit.biases: Two small US studies with food-frequency questionnaires; confounding by overall diet, BMI and abstinence time is plausible [adiet-afeiche2014a, adiet-afeiche2014b].
audit.newer_evidence: No randomized or genetic study of meat and semen quality was found. The general-health evidence on processed meat is consistent but modest [adiet-haile2025].
audit.bottom_line: A reasonable, low-cost precaution, correctly labelled limited and observational.

entries.headline: Fasts of 2-10+ days push ketones into the millimolar range and lowered lipid peroxidation (TBARS) in uncontrolled cohorts, but half or more of the weight lost is lean tissue and water, uric acid rises 100-200 umol/L, and no controlled trial shows lasting oxidative stress or health benefit beyond weight loss.

dose.effective: No proven effective dose. Medically supervised Buchinger-type fasts of 5-10 days at 200-250 kcal/day, or water-only fasts, have been studied; a refeeding period of at least half the fast length is used in clinics.
dose.studied_range: 2-21 days, water-only or 75-250 kcal/day, usually 1-2 times per year.
dose.too_much: Beyond ~5 days of little or no intake, refeeding-syndrome criteria apply (NICE: >5 days plus another risk factor, or >10 days alone). Risks: hyponatraemia, orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, gout and urate stones, gallstones, lean-mass loss. Never unsupervised with diabetes medication, low BMI, eating disorder, pregnancy, gout or kidney disease.
dose.timeframe: Ketosis from day 2-4; systemic proteome changes appear only after ~3 days; most weight is regained within weeks.
dose.notes: Ketonaemia reaches roughly 2-4 mmol/L by day 3-5 in many adults (higher in lean people and with exercise) and keeps rising for ~2-3 weeks.

entries.mechanism: Glycogen depletion (largely by ~24-42 h), lipolysis and ketogenesis; insulin and IGF-1 fall, growth hormone rises ~5-fold. Beta-hydroxybutyrate signalling (HDAC inhibition) and lower substrate flux may reduce ROS production; the rise in uric acid, an antioxidant, inflates total antioxidant capacity readings.
entries.interactions: Exercise during a fast speeds ketosis; light activity was used to protect muscle in the 10-day trial. Does not replace sustained [calorie-restriction] or [weight-loss]. Avoid stacking with [vigorous-exercise-low-energy] in women.
entries.caveats: Evidence comes mostly from clinic cohorts run by fasting-clinic staff, without control groups. 'Autophagy peaks at day 2-3' is extrapolated from mice; human muscle and blood studies show ambiguous flux changes. TAC increases partly reflect uric acid.

key_numbers.label: Share of 10-day weight loss that was lean soft tissue

entries.title: Prolonged (multi-day) fasting

timing.summary: Systemic changes need about three days of fasting to appear, and muscle becomes temporarily insulin resistant by day three. There are no controlled data on how long any benefit lasts after refeeding.

onset.text: Plasma proteome changes appeared only after ~3 days of water-only fasting [tbody-pietzner2024]; a 72-h fast markedly reduced muscle insulin sensitivity [tbody-vendelbo2012]; ketones rose in clinic fasts [tbody-wilhelmidetoledo2019].

full.text: Weight, waist and blood pressure fell over 5-20 day clinic fasts (uncontrolled) [tbody-wilhelmidetoledo2019].

after_stopping.text: Not measured in controlled trials.

frequency.text: No evidence-based schedule; any repeat interval is untested.

timing.debate: Autophagy is often claimed after 1-3 days, but a 36-h fast changed human muscle autophagy markers only modestly [tbody-dethlefsen2018], while blood-cell autophagy gene expression rose with early daily time-restricted eating [tbody-jamshed2019].

audit.claim: Multi-day fasts lowered TBARS in uncontrolled cohorts, but much of the weight lost is lean tissue and no controlled trial shows lasting benefit.
audit.biases: Clinic-run uncontrolled cohorts (selection, no comparator) [adiet-wilhelmidetoledo2019].
audit.newer_evidence: Controlled physiology work confirms large lean-tissue loss [adiet-laurens2021]; no RCT found.
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: The most sedentary quarter of adults had about 2.6x the mortality of the least sedentary in accelerometer studies, and walking breaks in sitting cut post-meal glucose and insulin by a moderate amount (SMD about -0.5); direct evidence that sitting itself raises oxidative stress is weak.

dose.effective: Break up sitting every 20-30 min with 2-5 min of light walking (better than just standing); aim to replace sitting with any movement. About 60-75 min/day of moderate activity offset the extra mortality of sitting 8+ h/day.
dose.studied_range: Acute crossover trials: 2-min light or moderate walking every 20-30 min over 5-9 h; cohorts: under 4 to over 8 h/day sitting.
dose.too_much: More than 8 h/day sitting combined with low activity; more than 20 h/week TV was linked to 44% lower sperm concentration in young men.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin effects within a single day; insulin resistance appears within days of bed rest or step reduction.
dose.notes: Even high activity only attenuated, not eliminated, the risk tied to heavy TV viewing, perhaps because TV time travels with snacking and other habits.

entries.mechanism: Inactive muscle takes up little glucose (less GLUT4 translocation, lower lipoprotein lipase activity); repeated post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive mitochondrial superoxide and NADPH oxidase activity. Over time, lost fitness, fat gain and inflammation add chronic ROS sources. Short-term disuse lowers mitochondrial content without raising muscle H2O2.
entries.interactions: Countered by [aerobic-exercise-moderate], [post-meal-walking] and [exercise-snacks]; worsens [glycemic-control] and [excess-adiposity]. In men, prolonged sitting may add scrotal heat ([everyday-scrotal-heat]).
entries.caveats: Bed rest cut insulin sensitivity 42% but did not raise mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers, so 'sitting causes oxidative stress' is not established directly; the one oxidative crossover study used a crude marker (d-ROMs) and only showed trends. Sedentary-time associations with mortality are rated weak in umbrella reviews and are hard to separate from low activity and poor health.
entries.debate: Whether sitting is an independent risk or mainly a marker of low activity is debated. A harmonised meta-analysis of 1 million adults found 60-75 min/day of moderate activity eliminated the excess mortality of high sitting time (but not of high TV time) [exr-ekelund2016]; accelerometer data still show a steep gradient for sedentary time [exr-ekelund2019], while an umbrella review graded the sedentary-mortality evidence as weak [exr-rahmati2025]. For metabolism, activity breaks lower glucose and insulin versus continuous sitting [exr-loh2020, exr-dunstan2012, exr-buffey2022], but when energy expenditure was matched the advantage of breaks over a single continuous bout was small for glucose and absent for insulin and triglycerides [exr-loh2020]. Direct oxidative effects are unproven: disuse lowered mitochondrial capacity without increasing muscle H2O2 [exr-dirks2020, exr-edwards2021], and the only sitting/oxidative crossover trial was small with borderline results [exr-takahashi2015].

key_numbers.label: Mortality HR, most vs least sedentary quarter (accelerometer)
Glucose SMD, activity breaks vs continuous sitting
Insulin sensitivity change after short bed rest
Sperm concentration, >20 h/week TV vs none

entries.title: Prolonged sitting and physical inactivity

timing.summary: Long sitting raises that day's post-meal glucose, and a week or two of very low activity cuts insulin sensitivity and fitness. Young people bounce back quickly, but in older prediabetic adults two weeks of normal activity were not enough to recover.

onset.text: Breaking up sitting lowered same-day post-meal glucose and insulin [tbody-dunstan2012]; short bed rest cut insulin-stimulated glucose disposal 42% [tbody-dirks2020].

full.text: Two weeks at ~1,350 steps/day lowered insulin sensitivity 17% and VO2max 7% [tbody-kroghmadsen2010].

after_stopping.text: In trained young people one exercise bout almost restored glucose responses after 10 inactive days [tbody-heath1983]; in prediabetic older adults glycaemic control and muscle protein synthesis had not recovered after 2 weeks of normal activity [tbody-mcglory2018].

frequency.text: Short walking breaks every 20-30 min [tbody-dunstan2012].

timing.debate: Bed-rest insulin resistance occurred without a rise in mitochondrial H2O2 or oxidative markers [tbody-dirks2020], so the oxidative-stress route for sitting harms is unproven; no substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: The most sedentary quarter has about 2.6x the mortality of the least sedentary, and breaking up sitting lowers glucose; direct oxidative evidence is weak.
audit.biases: Sitting time travels with low activity, poor health, obesity and lower education (confounding and reverse causation).
audit.newer_evidence: Device-measured cohorts show steep gradients [abody-ekelund2019], but an umbrella review rates the sedentary-mortality evidence weak [abody-rahmati2025]. Mendelian randomization disagrees: genetically predicted TV watching raised coronary disease (OR 1.44 per 1.5 h) [abody-vandevegte2020], whereas other MR analyses found no effect of sedentary behaviour on CAD, stroke or mortality [abody-bahls2021, abody-han2026]. TV-watching genetics overlap heavily with education and BMI [abody-vandevegte2020].
audit.bottom_line: Long sitting is a robust marker of risk; whether sitting itself causes harm independent of low activity is still unsettled. The glucose benefit of breaking up sitting is trial-based and holds.

entries.headline: Two or more years of PPIs is linked to B12 deficiency (OR 1.65), iron deficiency (OR 2.49) and low magnesium (RR 1.43) in observational studies, but the 17,598-person COMPASS RCT found no excess harm over 3 years except slightly more gut infections.

dose.effective: As prescribed (e.g. omeprazole 20-40 mg/day, pantoprazole 40 mg/day), ideally at the lowest effective dose and for a defined duration.
dose.studied_range: Pantoprazole 40 mg/day for ~3 years (COMPASS); >=2 years' supply in case-control studies.
dose.too_much: Associations strengthen above ~1.5 pills/day and with longer use (iron deficiency OR 4.27 at >1.5 pills/day for >=10 years).
dose.timeframe: Nutrient effects appear over years; iron-deficiency association weakens after stopping.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Ask the prescriber how to step down rather than stopping on your own. On long-term use, ask whether B12, iron (ferritin) and magnesium checks make sense.

entries.mechanism: Gastric acid frees food-bound B12 and keeps non-heme iron soluble, so chronic acid suppression reduces their absorption; magnesium loss reflects impaired intestinal uptake. Higher gastric pH also lets oral bacteria colonize the gut and reduces microbial diversity [med-imhann2016].
entries.interactions: Adds to the B12 drain of [metformin]. Iron deficiency interacts with [iron-excess] advice (supplementing iron when deficient is different from excess). Microbiome shifts overlap [antibiotics-microbiome] and may affect polyphenol metabolism ([dietary-fiber-microbiome]).
entries.caveats: Observational associations are prone to confounding by indication and illness; the RCT used pantoprazole in older adults with cardiovascular disease and did not measure nutrient levels.
entries.debate: Harms: large case-control studies link long-term PPIs to B12 and iron deficiency [med-lam2013, med-lam2017] and a meta-analysis to hypomagnesemia [med-cheungpasitporn2015]; a B12 meta-analysis found only a modest, heterogeneous association with no difference in serum B12 in most studies [med-choudhury2023], and the COMPASS RCT found no excess harms besides enteric infection [med-moayyedi2019]. Sperm: a Dutch registry linked PPI use 6-12 months earlier to threefold odds of low motile sperm count [med-huijgen2016], while a US clinic study of 248 users found no effect [med-keihani2018b].
entries.title: Proton-pump inhibitors & acid suppressants

timing.summary: Acid suppression has a fast microbiological effect and a slow nutritional one: specific gut taxa shift within 4 weeks [tleg-freedberg2015], while magnesium deficiency appeared after a median 5.5 years of use [tleg-hess2012] and B12 deficiency is associated with 2 or more years [tleg-lam2013]. Stopping has its own clock: magnesium recovers within about 4 days, but rebound acid symptoms appear in the weeks after withdrawal and can be mistaken for the original problem [tleg-reimer2009].

onset.text: Four weeks of high-dose omeprazole reproducibly increased Enterococcaceae and Streptococcaceae and decreased Clostridiales without changing overall diversity [tleg-freedberg2015]. Nutrient effects start much later - hypomagnesaemia onset ranged from 14 days to 13 years with a median of 5.5 years [tleg-hess2012].

full.text: Nutrient depletion accrues with duration: B12 deficiency was associated with 2 or more years of use and with higher doses [tleg-lam2013], and the magnesium cases clustered around 5.5 years [tleg-hess2012]. Microbiome changes appear established by 4-8 weeks [tleg-freedberg2015, tleg-imhann2016].

after_stopping.text: Magnesium recovered within about 4 days of stopping and fell again within about 4 days of re-challenge [tleg-hess2012]. But 8 weeks of a PPI caused clinically relevant acid-related symptoms in 21-22% of previously healthy volunteers during the 4 weeks after withdrawal, versus 2-7% on placebo - so expect 2-4 weeks of rebound [tleg-reimer2009].

frequency.text: Duration, not dosing pattern, is what the harm signals track [tleg-lam2013, tleg-hess2012], so the practical rule is the shortest course that does the job and periodic review. Tapering matters because of rebound hypersecretion in the weeks after stopping [tleg-reimer2009].

sperm.late_start: A late stop may not be enough: the association was with use 6-12 months before the semen analysis, not with use in the preceding 6 months, which is the opposite of a short-lag effect [tleg-huijgen2016].
sperm.text: In a primary-care registry, PPI use 6-12 months before semen analysis carried threefold higher odds of a low total motile count while recent use did not [tleg-huijgen2016] - an unexplained pattern that, taken at face value, implies a lead time of 6-12 months rather than one spermatogenic cycle.

timing.debate: The long-term harms are contested. Observational studies link 2 or more years of use to B12, iron and magnesium deficiency [tleg-lam2013, tleg-hess2012] and to large microbiome shifts [tleg-imhann2016], but the randomized COMPASS trial of 3 years of pantoprazole found no excess harm apart from slightly more enteric infections, and the controlled microbiome study found taxon shifts without any loss of diversity [tleg-freedberg2015]. The semen association has a biologically odd lag that its own authors could not explain [tleg-huijgen2016].

audit.claim: Long-term PPIs are linked to B12, iron and magnesium deficiency in observational data, but the COMPASS RCT found no excess harm except gut infections.
audit.biases: Confounding by indication and illness in observational studies.
audit.newer_evidence: COMPASS (17,598) remains the key trial [abody-moayyedi2019]; the B12 case-control association [abody-lam2013] persists. For dementia, a frequently publicised harm, MR found no robust causal effect [abody-xie2024].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: nutrient monitoring on long-term use is sensible; most feared harms are not supported by the trial.

entries.headline: Chronic stress and depression are associated with higher oxidative damage markers (depression: F2-isoprostanes effect size ~0.5), but causality and the size of any modifiable effect are uncertain.

dose.effective: Treat depression and anxiety with proven methods (therapy, medication when indicated, exercise, sleep); reduce chronic stressors where possible.
dose.studied_range: Cross-sectional comparisons of high vs low perceived stress and depressed vs non-depressed groups.
dose.timeframe: Unknown for oxidative markers.
dose.notes: Exercise and sleep improvements are the best-evidenced stress interventions that also affect oxidative stress.

entries.mechanism: Chronic stress raises cortisol and catecholamines, increases metabolic rate and inflammatory signalling (NF-kB), and is associated with lower telomerase activity; catecholamine auto-oxidation produces ROS.
entries.interactions: Stress worsens [short-sleep], drinking ([alcohol]), smoking and eating, which are likely bigger oxidative contributors than stress itself.
entries.caveats: The famous Epel 2004 study was cross-sectional in 58 women; it shows association, not cause. Confounding by health behaviours is likely in most studies.
entries.title: Chronic psychological stress and depression

entries.headline: A high salivary alpha-amylase stress marker was linked to 29% lower fecundability in one cohort, but a meta-analysis of 3583 IVF patients found pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not affect pregnancy rates.

dose.effective: Stress management for wellbeing (counselling, CBT, mindfulness, exercise); not proven to raise pregnancy rates.
dose.notes: Reassure people that stress caused by infertility does not ruin their IVF chances.

entries.mechanism: Sympathetic and HPA-axis activation can suppress GnRH/LH and raise systemic oxidative stress, but direct evidence of oocyte damage in humans is lacking.
entries.interactions: Linked with [short-sleep].
entries.caveats: Reverse causation (infertility causes stress) is likely in many studies; avoid blaming patients.
entries.title: Psychological stress

timing.summary: Stress episodes lasting weeks were linked to lower seminal glutathione and poorer sperm that had recovered three months later, and years of chronic stress track with oxidative damage and shorter telomeres. For egg and IVF outcomes, pre-treatment distress showed no effect.

onset.text: Not precisely measured; during an exam period seminal glutathione and sperm motility were lower than 3 months later [tbody-eskiocak2005].

full.text: Chronic stress over years was associated with higher oxidative stress and shorter telomeres (cross-sectional) [tbody-epel2004].

after_stopping.text: Sperm measures and seminal glutathione had recovered 3 months after exams [tbody-eskiocak2005], consistent with sperm production time [tbody-misell2006].

frequency.text: Stress-reduction practices are studied as regular programmes [tbody-pascoe2017].

sperm.late_start: Reducing stress late may not change sperm already formed.
sperm.text: Stress was linked to lower sperm concentration [tbody-nordkap2016] and reversed within one sperm cycle after exams [tbody-eskiocak2005].

timing.debate: Stress is associated with poorer semen [tbody-nordkap2016, tbody-eskiocak2005], but pre-treatment anxiety or depression did not predict IVF pregnancy [tbody-boivin2011].

audit.claim: Stress is linked to oxidative markers with uncertain causality; for eggs, a meta-analysis found pre-treatment distress did not affect IVF pregnancy.
audit.biases: Reverse causation (infertility and failed cycles cause distress) and confounding by health behaviours.
audit.newer_evidence: The 2011 meta-analysis found pre-treatment distress unrelated to IVF pregnancy [abody-boivin2011], whereas a 2018 meta-analysis found lower depression and anxiety scores during treatment in women who conceived (SMD about -0.3), though changes from baseline did not predict outcome [abody-purewal2018]. Salivary alpha-amylase predicted lower fecundability in one cohort [abody-lynch2014].
audit.bottom_line: Stress before treatment does not appear to doom IVF; scores measured during treatment may partly reflect how the cycle is going.

entries.headline: Pyrethroids replaced many organophosphates and are found in most people's urine; one NHANES cohort linked the top tertile of urinary 3-PBA to 56% higher all-cause and 3-fold cardiovascular mortality, but it rests on a single urine sample of a metabolite with half-life about 6 hours and has not been replicated.

dose.effective: Peel, juice or cook produce where practical (peeling removes 60-100% of pyrethroid residues; tap-water washing 10-70%); choose organic for high-residue items; use indoor insect sprays, pet flea products and treated clothing sparingly and ventilate after use.
dose.studied_range: General-population urinary 3-PBA (NHANES); residential and dietary exposure.
dose.too_much: No human threshold established. Mortality excess was in the top NHANES tertile of urinary 3-PBA.
dose.timeframe: 3-PBA half-life about 6 h; urine reflects the last day or so.
dose.notes: Pyrethroids are less acutely toxic to people than organophosphates; the concern is chronic, low-level exposure, which is poorly measured.

entries.mechanism: Pyrethroids prolong sodium-channel opening in nerves; in animals and cells they raise ROS, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction and have anti-androgenic activity. In pregnant women and Cypriot children, urinary 3-PBA tracked 8-OHdG [efw-wang2024, efw-makris2022].
entries.interactions: Sperm data: [pyrethroids]. Co-exposure with [organophosphates] and [neonicotinoids]. Lower intake via [washing-produce] and [organic-food].
entries.caveats: Single spot urine has ICC <0.22 for 3-PBA [efw-morgan2016]; at least four samples months apart are needed [efw-lin2021], so cohort exposure groups are badly misclassified. 3-PBA is also formed from pyrethroid breakdown in food and the environment. Residual confounding by income, diet and health status is likely in NHANES.
entries.debate: For harm: the NHANES mortality cohort [efw-bao2020] and an invited commentary urging closer scrutiny [efw-stellman2020]; urinary pyrethroid metabolites track oxidative DNA damage markers [efw-wang2024, efw-makris2022]. Against: reliability studies show one urine sample cannot classify long-term pyrethroid exposure [efw-morgan2016, efw-lin2021], and no independent cohort has replicated the mortality finding.

key_numbers.label: All-cause mortality, top vs bottom 3-PBA tertile
CVD mortality, top vs bottom 3-PBA tertile

entries.title: Pyrethroid insecticides

entries.headline: Cross-sectional clinic studies link urinary pyrethroid metabolites to lower sperm concentration and more sperm DNA damage, but meta-analyses of 12 cross-sectional studies are inconsistent (lower motility overall; concentration lower in Poland but higher in the US).

dose.effective: No intervention tested on sperm. Use the exposure steps in [pyrethroids]: peel or cook produce, choose organic for high-residue items, and limit indoor insecticide, flea-treatment and treated-clothing use.
dose.studied_range: Urinary 3-PBA and DCCA metabolites in clinic men (n = 207-240 per study).
dose.too_much: Not defined.
dose.timeframe: Metabolites clear within a day; any sperm effect would follow the ~64-day course of spermatogenesis [efw-heller1963].
dose.notes: Studies used a single urine sample against a semen sample that reflects about 3 months of exposure.

entries.mechanism: Pyrethroids show anti-androgenic and oxidative effects in rodent testes. In men, 3-PBA tracked sperm DNA fragmentation (beta 0.27) [efw-ji2011] and comet-assay DNA damage [efw-meeker2008].
entries.interactions: General exposure: [pyrethroids]. Often studied together with [organophosphates]; occupational data in [pesticides].
entries.caveats: All studies are cross-sectional with one urine sample and poor exposure reliability [efw-lin2021]; small clinic samples; publication bias untested.
entries.debate: Positive studies found lower concentration and more sperm DNA damage [efw-meeker2008, efw-ji2011]. Meta-analyses disagree: one found pyrethroids linked only to fewer normal-morphology sperm [efw-giulioni2021], another to lower motility with region-dependent, sometimes opposite, effects on concentration [efw-akhigbe2024].
entries.title: Pyrethroid insecticides and sperm

entries.headline: Marketed for 'mitochondrial biogenesis', PQQ raised muscle PGC-1alpha but not aerobic performance in a 23-man trial; cognition trials are small and manufacturer-linked.

dose.effective: No proven clinical dose; 20 mg/day is typical
dose.studied_range: 0.2-0.3 mg/kg in a 10-person study; 20-21.5 mg/day for 6-12 weeks
dose.too_much: EFSA judged up to 20 mg/day safe for healthy adults, excluding pregnant and breastfeeding women
dose.timeframe: Trials ran 6-12 weeks
dose.notes: The proposed supplement dose is at least 250 times typical dietary intake.

entries.mechanism: A redox-cycling quinone made by bacteria and present in trace amounts in foods. In animals it influences mitochondrial biogenesis signalling (PGC-1alpha) and acts as a redox cofactor; it is not a confirmed vitamin in humans.
entries.interactions: Often sold with [coq10]; no evidence for the combination. Exercise is a far stronger trigger of mitochondrial biogenesis ([aerobic-exercise-moderate]).
entries.caveats: Human data are tiny and short. The 'longevity vitamin' label is a hypothesis, not evidence.
entries.debate: Supporters cite lower CRP and IL-6 in a 10-person study [lon-harris2013], better cognitive test scores in two small Japanese RCTs of branded PQQ products [lon-itoh2016, lon-shiojima2022], and Ames's proposal of PQQ as a longevity vitamin [lon-ames2018]. In the only exercise trial, PQQ raised PGC-1alpha protein but did not improve aerobic performance beyond training alone [lon-hwang2020]. EFSA addressed safety, not efficacy [lon-efsa2017pqq].
entries.title: Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)

timing.summary: In one tiny study PQQ appeared in plasma after a single dose, and 3 days of daily intake lowered inflammatory markers. Longer time courses are unknown.

onset.text: CRP and IL-6 lower after about 76 h of daily PQQ [tnut-harris2013].

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: No schedule data beyond daily dosing for 3 days [tnut-harris2013].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: PQQ raised muscle PGC-1alpha but not aerobic performance; cognition trials small and manufacturer-linked.
audit.biases: Manufacturer-linked trials; tiny inflammation study [anut-harris2013].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer decisive trial; the exercise null stands [anut-hwang2020].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: At 500 mg/day or more, quercetin lowers blood pressure by about 4/3 mmHg in pooled RCTs, but it did not reduce colds in a 1002-person trial, improves endurance by a trivial ~2%, and left oxidative-stress markers unchanged even when it lowered blood pressure.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day for blood-pressure effects.
dose.studied_range: 100-1250 mg/day for 2-12 weeks; senolytic protocols used 1000-1250 mg for 3 days with dasatinib.
dose.too_much: Long-term safety above 1000 mg/day beyond 12 weeks is not established; quercetin alters the bioavailability of some drugs, and animal data raise kidney concerns.
dose.timeframe: Blood pressure change within 4 weeks.
dose.notes: Quercetin glucosides from onions were 52% absorbed vs 24% for the aglycone used in most pills; almost all circulates as conjugates.

entries.mechanism: Quercetin conjugates act on vascular signalling (nitric oxide availability, NADPH oxidase) rather than by scavenging radicals in plasma; in senolytic regimens it is paired with the kinase inhibitor dasatinib.
entries.interactions: Same flavonol class as [fisetin]. Flavonol foods overlap [green-tea], [black-tea] and onions in [garlic-alliums]. Unlike resveratrol, 1000 mg/day for 2 weeks did not blunt mitochondrial markers in untrained men (see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]).
entries.caveats: The often-quoted '~1% bioavailability' understates absorption from onion glucosides, but plasma levels stay low-micromolar. The infection benefit appeared only in a post-hoc subgroup. Dasatinib plus quercetin trials are small and mostly open-label; the one RCT (bone) missed its primary endpoint, and quercetin was not detected in CSF in the Alzheimer's pilot.
entries.title: Quercetin (supplement; onions, capers, apples, tea)

timing.summary: Quercetin peaks within hours and has a half-life of about 11 hours, so daily intake builds modestly higher fasting levels over days. As a senolytic it is given in short bursts ('hit and run'), but the first randomised trial of that schedule missed its main endpoint.

onset.text: Plasma peak about 0.7 h after quercetin glucosides (4-7 h after rutin) [tnut-graefe2001].

full.text: Fasting plasma quercetin raised up to 570% after 2 weeks of daily intake [tnut-egert2008]; extrapolated steady state in 2-3 days.

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated from the 11 h half-life: back to baseline within 2-3 days [tnut-graefe2001]; senolytic effects proposed to last weeks [tnut-kirkland2020].

frequency.text: BP effects came from daily doses of 500 mg or more [tnut-serban2016]. Senolytic use is intermittent (3 days of dasatinib plus quercetin, effects 11 days later) [tnut-hickson2019, tnut-justice2019] and experimental.

timing.debate: Pilot studies and reviews support intermittent 'hit and run' senolytic dosing [tnut-hickson2019, tnut-kirkland2020], but a phase 2 RCT of intermittent dasatinib plus quercetin found no effect on bone resorption at 20 weeks, with a bone-formation rise only at 2-4 weeks [tnut-farr2024].

audit.claim: At 500 mg/day or more quercetin lowers BP ~4/3 mmHg; no cold prevention; trivial endurance benefit.
audit.biases: Infection benefit was post hoc only [anut-heinz2010].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer trial changes the BP meta-analysis [anut-serban2016].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Rapamycin is the most reproducible drug for extending mouse lifespan, but in humans the year-long PEARL trial (5-10 mg weekly) found no change in its primary outcome, visceral fat; it is a prescription immunosuppressant with real risks.

dose.effective: No proven longevity dose in humans; PEARL used 5 or 10 mg compounded rapamycin once weekly
dose.studied_range: Weekly 5-10 mg (PEARL, 48 weeks); low-dose everolimus or combined TORC1 inhibitors for 6 weeks in immune-function trials
dose.too_much: Transplant-level daily dosing causes immunosuppression, infections, raised cholesterol and triglycerides, and impaired glucose control (mTORC2 disruption in mice)
dose.timeframe: Immune effects after 6 weeks; PEARL ran 48 weeks
dose.notes: Prescription-only; off-label use should be medically supervised with monitoring of lipids, glucose and blood counts. Compounded products vary in bioavailability.

entries.mechanism: Inhibits mTORC1, the nutrient-sensing kinase that drives growth and suppresses autophagy; this mimics aspects of calorie restriction. Chronic exposure also disrupts mTORC2, which causes insulin resistance. Effects on oxidative stress are indirect, through improved mitochondrial quality control.
entries.interactions: Has many drug interactions; review all medicines with a prescriber. Overlaps conceptually with energy restriction and exercise, which also lower mTORC1 signalling.
entries.caveats: Human data are short and mostly surrogate. The off-label user survey is self-selected and partly authored by people with commercial interests in longevity medicine.
entries.debate: Mouse data are robust: rapamycin extended lifespan even when started late in life [lon-harrison2009], and low-dose mTOR inhibitors improved vaccine responses and reduced infections in older adults [lon-mannick2014, lon-mannick2018]. But PEARL missed its primary endpoint, with benefits only in subgroups [lon-moel2025]; a systematic review found some immune and cardiovascular improvements but more infections and higher lipids in patients [lon-lee2024]; and insulin resistance via mTORC2 is a known mechanism-based risk [lon-lamming2012]. Supporters cite a survey of 333 off-label users as evidence of safety [lon-kaeberlein2023], but that design cannot detect benefits or uncommon harms.
entries.title: Rapamycin (sirolimus), off-label for longevity

timing.summary: Rapamycin's long half-life means blood levels build over days, and the rationale for weekly rather than daily dosing is to hit mTORC1 while sparing mTORC2 (mainly mouse data). A 6-week rapalog course was linked to fewer infections for a year, but a year of weekly rapamycin did not change its primary outcome.

onset.text: Steady-state blood levels take at least 4 days [tbody-mahalati2001]; immune effects were measured after 6 weeks of a rapalog [tbody-mannick2014].

full.text: No plateau defined; 48 weeks of 5-10 mg weekly did not change visceral fat [tbody-moel2025].

after_stopping.text: After a 6-week course of a TORC1 inhibitor combination (not rapamycin), fewer infections were reported over the year after starting [tbody-mannick2018].

frequency.text: In mice, intermittent dosing spared glucose tolerance and immunity compared with daily dosing, because chronic exposure also inhibits mTORC2 [tbody-arriolaapelo2016, tbody-lamming2012]; daily 1 mg was tolerated for 8 weeks in older humans [tbody-kraig2018]. No human trial has compared schedules.

timing.debate: The weekly-dosing rationale rests on mouse data [tbody-arriolaapelo2016], and the only year-long human trial of weekly rapamycin missed its primary outcome [tbody-moel2025].

entries.headline: A glass of red wine contains well under 1 mg trans-resveratrol, oral resveratrol is almost entirely conjugated before it reaches blood, and urinary resveratrol levels did not predict mortality; the ethanol itself raises lipid peroxidation in a dose-dependent way.

dose.effective: No antioxidant reason to drink. If you drink, wine polyphenols taken with a fatty meal may limit postprandial lipid oxidation in the stomach (animal data).
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol supplements in trials range from tens to thousands of mg; a 25 mg oral dose left <5 ng/mL free resveratrol in plasma.
dose.too_much: Alcohol raises urinary isoprostanes dose-dependently; see [alcohol].
dose.notes: Trans-resveratrol ~0.18 mg/100 mL (about 0.3 mg per 150 mL glass), so reaching supplement doses would take hundreds of glasses.

entries.mechanism: Resveratrol is absorbed (~70%) but rapidly sulfated and glucuronidated; wine's other polyphenols (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols) are similar to those in grapes and berries without the ethanol.
entries.interactions: Ethanol counteracts the polyphenols; grapes, berries or dealcoholised wine provide the polyphenols without it. Supplement-dose resveratrol is covered under [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements]: meta-analyses find no overall blood-pressure effect and only trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects, and 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men.
entries.caveats: Associations of urinary resveratrol metabolites with better lipids in PREDIMED are cross-sectional and confounded by wine drinking patterns.

key_numbers.label: Total polyphenols, chromatography, red wine (sum of compounds)
Free resveratrol in plasma after 25 mg oral dose

entries.title: Red wine and resveratrol

timing.summary: Resveratrol is well absorbed but almost all is conjugated at once; only metabolites circulate, with a half-life of about 9 h. A glass of wine supplies far too little for any timed effect.

onset.text: Metabolites peak within hours of a 25 mg dose; unchanged resveratrol is only a trace [tfood-walle2004].

full.text: Not applicable.

after_stopping.text: Metabolites have a plasma half-life of 9.2 h, so they clear within about 2 days [tfood-walle2004].

frequency.text: No antioxidant reason to drink on any schedule [tfood-walle2004].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Red wine has negligible resveratrol, resveratrol is poorly bioavailable, and alcohol raises lipid peroxidation; no antioxidant reason to drink.
audit.biases: The old 'French paradox' and J-curve rested on cohorts where 'non-drinkers' include sick former drinkers (abstainer bias) and light drinkers are healthier [adiet-zhao2023].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 meta-analysis of 107 cohorts correcting for former-drinker bias found no mortality benefit from low-volume drinking [adiet-zhao2023]. Linear and non-linear Mendelian randomization in UK Biobank found alcohol raised hypertension and coronary risk at all intakes, and that light drinkers' apparent benefit was explained by healthier lifestyles [adiet-biddinger2022]. Resveratrol metabolites did not predict mortality [adiet-semba2014].
audit.bottom_line: Treating red wine as a harm is better supported now than before: the apparent protection was mostly abstainer bias.

factors.name: Refined sugar, sugary drinks & high-GI meals

entries.headline: A 75 g glucose drink more than doubled leukocyte ROS generation at 2 h in healthy people and lowered plasma vitamin E; large post-meal glucose and triglyceride spikes drive transient oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction.

dose.effective: Limit sugary drinks and large refined-starch meals; pair carbohydrates with fiber, protein, fat and vinegar or acidic foods.
dose.studied_range: 75 g oral glucose; single high-fat or high-carbohydrate meals.
dose.too_much: Repeated large spikes; sugar-sweetened beverages.
dose.timeframe: Peaks at 1-3 h after the meal.
dose.notes: Cream (fat) and casein (protein) also raised leukocyte ROS, so the size of the meal matters, not only sugar.

entries.mechanism: Nutrient surges increase leukocyte NADPH oxidase (p47phox) and mitochondrial superoxide; hyperglycemia fuels AGE and polyol pathways and NF-kB activation.
entries.interactions: Additive with [overfeeding]. Blunted by [whole-grains], [legumes], [dietary-fiber-microbiome] and polyphenol-rich foods with the meal (e.g. [tomatoes-lycopene], [herbs-spices]).
entries.caveats: Acute leukocyte ROS assays are not the same as chronic tissue damage; whether postprandial spikes in non-diabetic people cause disease independent of overall diet is debated.

key_numbers.label: Peak leukocyte (PMNL) ROS after 75 g glucose

entries.title: Refined sugar and high-glycemic meals

entries.headline: Young men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had about 10 points lower progressive motility.

dose.effective: Under one sugary drink a week; water, unsweetened tea or coffee instead.
dose.studied_range: <0.2 to >=1.3 servings/day.
dose.too_much: >=1.3 servings/day associated with lower motility.
dose.timeframe: ~3 months.
dose.notes: Caffeinated soft drinks also looked worse than coffee in reviews.

entries.mechanism: Glycaemic load drives insulin resistance, advanced glycation end-products and inflammation.
entries.interactions: Linked with [excess-adiposity].
entries.caveats: Cross-sectional, single semen sample; association only in lean men.
entries.title: Sugar-sweetened beverages

timing.summary: A sugary load raises white-cell ROS output within one to two hours, and repeated spikes across a day do more harm than steady high glucose. Each spike passes in hours, but habitual intake shows up in HbA1c over about three months.

onset.text: 75 g glucose doubled leukocyte ROS at 2 h and lowered vitamin E within 1 h [tbody-mohanty2000].

full.text: Glucose oscillating over 24 h worsened endothelial function and oxidative stress more than constant high glucose [tbody-ceriello2008].

after_stopping.text: Each spike resolves within hours [tbody-mohanty2000]; HbA1c reflects intake over the past ~3 months [tbody-tahara1995].

frequency.text: Effects are per meal or drink; fewer and smaller spikes matter more than occasional treats.

sperm.late_start: Unknown.
sperm.text: Men drinking 1.3+ sugary drinks a day had lower motility (cross-sectional) [tbody-chiu2014]; lead time extrapolated from sperm production [tbody-misell2006].

timing.debate: Glucose swings drove oxidative stress in clamp and type 2 diabetes studies [tbody-ceriello2008, tbody-monnier2006] but not in a type 1 diabetes CGM study [tbody-wentholt2008].

audit.claim: A glucose load transiently raises leukocyte ROS; sugary drinks linked to ~10 points lower motility in young men.
audit.biases: The ROS data are acute mechanistic studies [adiet-mohanty2000]; the semen link is cross-sectional with a single sample [adiet-chiu2014].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2023 umbrella review found many harmful associations, the strongest (moderate quality) for weight gain and ectopic fat [adiet-huang2023]; Burden of Proof rated SSB-diabetes evidence two stars [adiet-haile2025]. For sperm, results conflict: a 2024 preconception cohort found ~22% lower concentration with 7+ SSBs/week [adiet-joseph2024], while 1,047 Danish young men showed no strong association [adiet-meldgaard2022]; SSBs were linked to lower fecundability in both partners [adiet-hatch2018].
audit.bottom_line: Limiting sugary drinks is well supported for general health; the semen effect is plausible but inconsistent.

entries.headline: Donating lowers iron stores, and donors live longer, but most of that is the 'healthy donor effect': in 1.2 million donors the 18.6% lower mortality per annual donation shrank to 7.5% after adjustment, a large cohort found no heart benefit, and frequent donation often causes iron deficiency.

dose.effective: Donate for altruism, not as a health intervention. Standard whole-blood intervals (in the UK about 12 weeks for men and 16 for women), with ferritin checks or iron supplementation for frequent donors.
dose.studied_range: One donation removes ~200-250 mg iron. RCT of 550-800 mL phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome; donation intervals of 8-16 weeks (INTERVAL).
dose.too_much: Each week shorter donation interval lowered ferritin ~5-6.5% and raised low-haemoglobin deferrals; frequent donors reported more tiredness and restless legs.
dose.timeframe: Ferritin falls within months of regular donation.
dose.notes: Therapeutic phlebotomy for haemochromatosis is a medical treatment and is clearly beneficial in that condition; this entry is about healthy people.

entries.mechanism: Removes iron (as haemoglobin) and thereby lowers ferritin and, in theory, the labile iron available for Fenton chemistry. Short-term blood-pressure falls after phlebotomy may reflect volume and haemodynamic effects rather than iron.
entries.interactions: Lowers [iron-status-ferritin]; can cause [iron-deficiency], especially in young women and frequent donors.
entries.caveats: Donors are pre-screened for good health and continue donating only while healthy, so observational comparisons overstate benefits. No study has shown that donation reduces oxidative-stress outcomes or disease in healthy people.
entries.debate: For a benefit: the Kuopio cohort found 88% fewer heart attacks in recent donors [nut-salonen1998], a small RCT of phlebotomy in metabolic syndrome lowered systolic BP by 16.6 mmHg [nut-houschyar2012] (commentary noted design drawbacks [nut-manco2012]), and FeAST suggested fewer cancers [nut-zacharski2008]. Against: the 38,244-man Health Professionals cohort found no CHD benefit despite lower ferritin [nut-ascherio2001], FeAST was null for death and CV events [nut-zacharski2007], and Scandinavian and Dutch data show a strong healthy donor effect [nut-ullum2015, nut-atsma2011]. INTERVAL showed the harms side: more symptoms and iron deficiency with frequent donation [nut-diangelantonio2017, nut-kaptoge2019, nut-vandenhurk2018].

Mortality per extra annual donation, healthy-donor adjusted
Systolic BP change after phlebotomy (metabolic syndrome)

entries.title: Regular blood donation

timing.summary: One whole-blood donation removes iron at once, and without iron tablets most donors had not rebuilt their iron stores 6 months later. With a small daily iron dose, haemoglobin recovered in about a month and stores in about 2.5 months.

onset.text: Iron stores drop on the day of donation; haemoglobin falls about 1.3-1.4 g/dL [tnut-kiss2015].

full.text: Not applicable; the iron loss is immediate.

after_stopping.text: Without iron, 80% haemoglobin recovery took 78-158 days and 67% had not restored iron stores by 168 days; with 37.5 mg/day iron, stores recovered in a median 76 days [tnut-kiss2015]; full recovery took over 100 days even with iron [tnut-mast2020].

frequency.text: Data suggest intervals of at least 3-6 months without iron, or iron supplements for frequent donors with ferritin below about 50 ng/mL [tnut-kiss2015, tnut-mast2020].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the trials show the US 8-week minimum interval is too short for many donors to recover without iron [tnut-kiss2015].

audit.claim: Donors live longer mostly because of the healthy-donor effect; donation is not a proven health intervention.
audit.biases: Healthy-donor selection and retention.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 target-trial emulation in 121,967 Australians found crude donor mortality lower (HR 0.57) but no effect after full adjustment (HR 1.0) [abody-rahman2025]; Danish data show donors are healthier and more engaged from the start [abody-brodersen2023], consistent with the earlier Scandinavian analysis [abody-ullum2015].
audit.bottom_line: Holds and is strengthened: donation does not lower mortality once selection is handled.

entries.headline: Muscle-strengthening is associated with 10-27% lower mortality, with the biggest drop at about 30-60 min/week and the best results when combined with aerobic exercise (41% lower vs neither); it reliably builds strength (about 25-30% in older adults) and fights sarcopenia, while its 'antioxidant' effects are small.

dose.effective: 2-3 sessions/week (about 30-60 min/week total) on non-consecutive days, covering major muscle groups; 1-3 sets of 8-12 reps at a load you could lift a couple more times. Older adults benefit most from progressively heavier loads.
dose.studied_range: Cohorts: 0 to 150+ min/week; RCTs in older adults: 2-3 sessions/week for 8-24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Some cohorts show the mortality benefit fading above about 60 min/week (J-shape), but the largest cohort found no upturn. Rapid jumps in volume caused a 7-fold rise in urinary isoprostanes and a performance drop in an overreaching study.
dose.timeframe: Strength gains within 4-8 weeks; muscle mass in 8-12 weeks; antioxidant enzyme changes (glutathione peroxidase) in 8-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Do it in addition to aerobic activity: in NIH-AARP weight training was not associated with lower mortality in people doing no aerobic exercise. Avoid high-dose vitamin C/E and post-workout cold plunges if muscle gain is the goal.

entries.mechanism: Mechanical tension and metabolic stress activate mTOR and satellite cells; local ROS and NOX-derived signals contribute to hypertrophy signalling (p38, ERK, p70S6K, which vitamin C/E blunted). Added muscle increases glucose disposal, lowering glycemic oxidative stress, and repeated sessions modestly up-regulate glutathione peroxidase.
entries.interactions: High-dose vitamin C/E blunted lean-mass and bone-density gains in older men and hypertrophy signalling in younger adults ([antioxidant-megadoses-during-training]); post-workout [cold-water-immersion] blunted strength gains. Strength appears to feed fitness: genetic analyses suggest grip strength raises [cardiorespiratory-fitness], not the reverse. Combines with [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Mortality data are self-reported and observational; people who lift weights differ in many ways. In older adults, muscle and function benefits are well proven by RCTs, but mortality benefit is not. Meta-analysis found a small decrease in SOD and no change in catalase, so 'strength training is an antioxidant' is an overstatement.
entries.debate: Whether 'more is worse' is disputed. Two meta-analyses found J-shaped curves with maximal benefit at about 30-60 min/week [exr-momma2022, exr-shailendra2022], echoed in older women [exr-kamada2017]; but the largest single cohort (216,339 older adults) found any weight training lowered mortality with no clear upturn, just diminishing returns [exr-shailendra2024], and the J-shape rests on few people at high volumes with wide confidence intervals. An umbrella review rated the resistance-training mortality evidence only 'suggestive' [exr-rahmati2025]. On causality, Mendelian randomization supports grip strength protecting against coronary disease and AF [exr-tikkanen2018], while grip strength's mortality association comes from observational data [exr-leong2015]. For oxidative stress, only glutathione peroxidase rose reliably [exr-cordeiro2025]; a 2026 meta-analysis in older adults found redox data from just 6 trials with moderate-to-high bias [exr-chenhuichen2026].

Mortality HR, aerobic guideline + weightlifting 1-2x/week vs neither
Mortality HR per 5 kg lower grip strength

entries.title: Resistance (strength) training

timing.summary: Each session raises muscle protein synthesis for about two days; strength rises in the first weeks mainly through the nervous system and muscle growth takes over after 3-5 weeks and continues for months. Muscle size is lost over months off, but much of the strength and some cellular 'memory' remain.

onset.text: Muscle protein synthesis stayed raised 48 h after a bout [tbody-phillips1997]; early strength gains in the first 3-5 weeks are mainly neural [tbody-moritani1979].

full.text: Protein synthesis tracks hypertrophy from about week 3 once muscle damage subsides [tbody-damas2016]; gains continue over months of progressive training.

after_stopping.text: After 20 weeks off, muscle size was back to baseline but ~60% of the strength gain remained [tbody-psilander2019]; extra myonuclei persisted 16 weeks [tbody-cumming2024] and methylation changes 7 weeks [tbody-seaborne2018].

frequency.text: 2-3 sessions a week to build. Once built, one-third or even one-ninth of the dose (about 1 session a week) kept muscle in young adults for 32 weeks, but older adults needed more [tbody-bickel2011, tbody-spiering2021].

timing.debate: One study found previously trained muscle did not regrow faster [tbody-psilander2019], while others found persistent myonuclei and epigenetic marks that favour regrowth [tbody-cumming2024, tbody-seaborne2018].

audit.claim: Muscle-strengthening is associated with 10-27% lower mortality; strength and function gains are proven by RCTs; mortality benefit is observational.
audit.biases: Self-reported, observational mortality data with healthy-user bias.
audit.newer_evidence: An umbrella review rates resistance-training mortality evidence only suggestive [abody-rahmati2025]; trial evidence for strength and function stands.
audit.bottom_line: Holds as written: strength gains are causal, the mortality number is not established.

entries.headline: Despite the sirtuin story, resveratrol supplements show trivial or very-low-certainty metabolic effects in meta-analyses, 250 mg/day blunted training gains in older men, and pterostilbene 250 mg/day lowered blood pressure but raised LDL by 17 mg/dL.

dose.effective: None established for health outcomes.
dose.studied_range: Resveratrol 10 mg to 2 g/day; pterostilbene 100-250 mg/day for 6-8 weeks.
dose.too_much: Gram doses cause nausea, diarrhoea and weight loss. Avoid around training if adaptation is the goal. See [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements] for embryo-transfer concerns.
dose.timeframe: Weeks.
dose.notes: Food supplies well under 1 mg/day (see [red-wine-resveratrol]); supplements are a pharmacological, not dietary, exposure.

entries.mechanism: Resveratrol activates AMPK and indirectly SIRT1 and acts as a mild hormetic stressor at low micromolar levels; in muscle it can dampen the reactive-oxygen signalling that drives training adaptation.
entries.interactions: Can antagonise exercise adaptation (contrast [quercetin], which did not blunt mitochondrial markers short-term). Part of the broader [isolated-polyphenol-supplements] picture.
entries.caveats: Positive single trials exist (150 mg/day in 11 obese men; 200 mg/day for memory; 500 mg/day augmenting muscle response to training in 65-80-year-olds), but other trials were null, and in the 52-week Alzheimer's trial (up to 1 g twice daily) brain-volume loss was greater on resveratrol. Exercise results conflict by age, dose and training type.

key_numbers.label: VO2max gain blunted by 250 mg/day during training
LDL change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily
Systolic BP change, pterostilbene 125 mg twice daily

entries.title: Resveratrol and pterostilbene supplements

entries.headline: The only human data are an uncontrolled 20-man pilot of a multivitamin with 150 mg/day resveratrol, which reported motility rising from 48% to 59%; with no placebo group the effect cannot be attributed to resveratrol.

dose.effective: Not established.
dose.studied_range: 150 mg/day resveratrol within a multivitamin for 3-6 months.
dose.timeframe: 3-6 months.

entries.mechanism: Proposed SIRT1 and mitochondrial effects in sperm, from animal work.
entries.interactions: Overlaps [male-antioxidant-combination]; see [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements] for general resveratrol evidence.
entries.caveats: Uncontrolled, small, multi-ingredient, no pregnancy outcomes; regression to the mean is likely.
entries.title: Resveratrol (multivitamin-based) for sperm

entries.headline: Resveratrol may improve some follicular markers (an 800 mg/day RCT in PCOS raised oocyte maturity without changing pregnancy rates), but it suppresses endometrial decidualization, and 200 mg/day during embryo-transfer cycles was associated with lower pregnancy (OR 0.54) and more miscarriage (OR 2.60).

dose.effective: Not recommended while trying to conceive or around embryo transfer.
dose.studied_range: 200 mg/day (retrospective IVF cohort); 800 mg/day for 60 days (PCOS RCT, 56 women).
dose.too_much: Any use in the luteal phase or early pregnancy (possible anti-implantation effect; teratogenicity not excluded).
