entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli extract supplements

entries.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane or broccoli sprouts on sperm DNA fragmentation, motility or fertility; protection is shown only in rodents exposed to toxins, diabetes or high-fat diets and in human sperm treated in the lab.

dose.effective: Unknown for sperm. General-health doses (30-70 g fresh sprouts, or 40-150 µmol sulforaphane/day) are the only human-tested amounts.
dose.studied_range: Rodents: injected or oral sulforaphane for weeks to months; in vitro: 5 µM added to human semen before freezing.
dose.too_much: Not established; in cell culture sulforaphane becomes cytotoxic above about 10-15 µM, far above blood levels from food.
dose.timeframe: One spermatogenic cycle (about 74 days) would be needed to see any effect.
dose.notes: The in vitro cryopreservation result applies to sperm-freezing media, not to eating broccoli.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2-driven antioxidant genes in testis, AMPK-dependent relief of ER stress in sperm, and reduced testicular apoptosis in diabetic or toxin-exposed animals.
entries.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]; no data on combining with other sperm antioxidants such as [n-acetylcysteine].
entries.caveats: All evidence is animal or in vitro; rodent models used toxic exposures (phthalates, diabetes, high-fat diet) and often injected doses. Do not expect measurable improvement in semen analysis from broccoli in healthy men.
entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for sperm quality

entries.headline: No human trial has tested sulforaphane on egg quality, ovarian reserve, PCOS or IVF outcomes; it protects human granulosa cells and animal oocytes from oxidative stress in the lab, but becomes cytotoxic to granulosa cells at higher concentrations.

dose.effective: Unknown for ovarian outcomes; only general-health doses have been tested in people.
dose.studied_range: In vitro: about 1-5 µM in oocyte maturation or granulosa-cell culture.
dose.too_much: Bovine granulosa cells lost viability above about 15 µM in culture.
dose.timeframe: Follicle development takes about 3 months, so any dietary effect would need at least that long.
dose.notes: In vitro maturation results apply to IVF lab media, not diet.

entries.mechanism: Nrf2 activation (SOD, catalase, GCLC/GCLM, HO-1, NQO1) and AMPK/AKT signalling in granulosa cells and oocytes; reduced ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction and spindle defects after toxin exposure.
entries.interactions: Same redundancy considerations as [broccoli-sprouts] and [sulforaphane-supplements]. The modest glucose-lowering seen in obese people with poorly controlled diabetes ([glycemic-control]) is the only human finding with plausible indirect relevance to PCOS, and it has not been tested in PCOS.
entries.caveats: Cell and animal data only; biphasic (protective at low, harmful at high concentrations) responses argue against high-dose supplementation around conception without data.
entries.title: Sulforaphane / broccoli sprouts for egg and ovarian function

timing.summary: Each capsule is a pulse cleared within a day, but blood glutathione and Nrf2-target mRNA rise within days to weeks of daily use. Clinical effects in trials took 4-18 weeks to show and faded within weeks of stopping.

onset.text: Blood-cell HMOX1, NQO1 and glutathione rose within 7 days to 1 month of daily dosing [tfood-sedlak2018, tfood-doss2016, tfood-ribeiro2024]; nasal inflammation to diesel particles fell after 4 days [tfood-heber2014].

full.text: Behavioural effects in autism were measured at 18 weeks [tfood-singh2014]; no trial mapped when biomarkers plateau beyond the first days of dosing.

after_stopping.text: Autism behaviour scores rose back toward baseline during 4 weeks off sulforaphane [tfood-singh2014]; detox biomarkers lose the effect within 5 days [tfood-kensler2012].

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily; one or two doses a day gave the same blood-cell marker response [tfood-atwell2015]. Every-other-day dosing is untested in humans (it worked in mice [tfood-xu2016]).

sperm.late_start: Unknown: no human data. Because Nrf2 induction appears within a day, a late start could in theory protect sperm already maturing, but this is untested.
sperm.text: No human sperm trial exists. Sperm take about 64 days (range 42-76) from labelled precursor to ejaculate [tfood-misell2006], and the classic ~74-day estimate is uncertain by about a week [tfood-amann2008], so a diet change needs roughly 2.5-3 months to reach every stage of the sperm in a given ejaculate.

egg.late_start: Unknown: no human data on eggs or IVF.
egg.text: No human egg or IVF trial exists. A follicle grows for several months before ovulation, including about 70 days from the preantral stage to 2 mm [tfood-gougeon2010], so anything acting on the growing follicle needs roughly 3-4 months to cover the whole final growth phase.

timing.debate: Lasting benefit is questioned: autism gains reverted within weeks of stopping [tfood-singh2014], and Nrf2 feedback could limit long-term activation [tfood-lee2007], although 12 weeks of daily dosing showed no tolerance [tfood-egner2014]. Permanent maximal Nrf2 activation is harmful in mice [tfood-wakabayashi2003], an argument against chasing constant high exposure.

audit.claim: Product type decides delivery; trials at 50-200 umol/day are mixed with several nulls; about half of registered trials unpublished.
audit.biases: Publication bias: only 39 of 84 registered trials published [anut-saito2025].
audit.newer_evidence: No new large trial; nulls (COPD Nrf2) and modest positives (obese T2D) stand [anut-wise2016, anut-axelsson2017].
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

factors.name: Sun/UV exposure (photoaging and skin DNA damage)

entries.headline: Chronic unprotected UV is the main driver of visible skin aging and of skin cancer: a single exposure switched on collagen-degrading MMPs and raised collagen breakdown 58% in human skin, and identical twins with more sun exposure looked older.

dose.effective: Avoid sunburn. Around midday and whenever the UV index is high, use shade, clothing and a hat, plus daily broad-spectrum sunscreen on exposed skin (see [sunscreen]).
dose.studied_range: Experimental studies used single or repeated (every 2 days) erythemal UV doses on buttock skin; twin and cohort data reflect lifetime exposure.
dose.too_much: Any sunburn, tanning beds, and long cumulative outdoor exposure without protection.
dose.timeframe: MMP induction within hours of one exposure, sustained about 7 days with repeated exposure; visible photoaging accrues over years to decades.
dose.notes: Vitamin D: a consensus panel concluded that sunscreen used to prevent sunburn is unlikely to compromise vitamin D status; people with low levels or strict photoprotection needs should test and supplement rather than tan.

entries.mechanism: UVB (290-320 nm) is absorbed directly by DNA, forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs) and 6-4 photoproducts. UVA (320-400 nm) penetrates deeper into the dermis and is absorbed by cellular chromophores that generate singlet oxygen and superoxide, producing 8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial DNA deletions; in whole human skin UVA also forms CPDs, which outnumber 8-oxo-dG and are repaired more slowly. ROS-activated MAP kinase signalling drives AP-1, which induces MMP-1 (collagenase), MMP-3 and MMP-9 and suppresses new procollagen, while NF-kB drives inflammation. Repeated sub-burning exposures leave behind fragmented collagen: photoaging.
entries.interactions: [tobacco-smoking] and traffic-related [outdoor-air-pollution] add to extrinsic skin aging. Oral antioxidants do not replace UV protection: 30 mg/day beta-carotene ([beta-carotene-supplement]) had no effect on photoaging or skin cancer in Nambour, and the SU.VI.MAX antioxidant capsule raised skin cancer in women. Protection and repair options: [sunscreen], [topical-retinoids], and in high-risk people [nicotinamide].
entries.caveats: Whole-body oxidative-marker effects of ordinary sun exposure are not well documented; the evidence concerns skin. Visible light and near-infrared also generate ROS in skin in lab and biopsy studies, but whether everyday doses cause visible aging is unproven (visible light does matter for melasma and darker skin types). Twin and survey studies are observational and partly self-reported.
entries.debate: Mechanism weighting: the textbook picture of UVA as an 'oxidative' waveband is complicated by evidence that CPDs, not 8-oxo-dG, are the predominant UVA lesion in whole human skin [skb-mouret2006]. Beyond UV: visible light induced ROS and MMP-1 in skin equivalents [skb-liebel2012] and IR-A induced MMP-1 in human skin in vivo [skb-schroeder2008], but Diffey and Cadars argue solar IR doses equal those of furnace workers who show little chronic damage, so IR-protection claims are premature [skb-diffey2016]. Vitamin D: concern that sun avoidance causes deficiency is countered by a consensus review concluding normal sunscreen use does not compromise status [skb-passeron2019], though that panel included cosmetics-industry scientists.

MMP induction blocked by tretinoin pretreatment

entries.title: Sun/UV exposure (photoaging and skin DNA damage)

timing.summary: One unprotected exposure switches on collagen-degrading enzymes within hours and raises collagen breakdown by 58%, and with repeated exposures that enzyme activity stays up for about 7 days [tleg-fisher1997]. What accumulates from those episodes is structural and effectively permanent: identical twins with more sun exposure look older [tleg-guyuron2009], and skin cancer risk reflects decades.

onset.text: Matrix metalloproteinases are induced within hours of a single UV exposure, with collagen breakdown up 58% [tleg-fisher1997].

full.text: With repeated exposure, MMP activity remains elevated for about 7 days, so frequent exposures keep skin in a continuously degradative state [tleg-fisher1997]. Visible photoageing accumulates over years to decades [tleg-guyuron2009], and particulate air pollution adds to the same extrinsic ageing score [tleg-vierkotter2010].

after_stopping.text: The enzymatic response subsides over about a week once exposure stops [tleg-fisher1997], but the structural damage does not reverse on its own - which is why prevention trials measure effects over years and why the only partial reversal comes from treatment, not time [tleg-hughes2013].

frequency.text: Because MMP induction persists about 7 days, exposures more often than weekly keep the degradative state continuous [tleg-fisher1997]. There is no threshold below which repeated unprotected midday exposure stops contributing; protection has to be routine rather than occasional [tleg-hughes2013].

timing.debate: The acute molecular response is well measured [tleg-fisher1997]; what is debated is attribution of long-term ageing, since observational twin and cohort studies cannot fully separate sun from smoking, weight and pollution, all of which independently predicted older appearance or worse extrinsic ageing scores [tleg-guyuron2009, tleg-vierkotter2010].

audit.claim: Chronic unprotected UV drives photoaging and skin cancer; sunscreen use is unlikely to compromise vitamin D.
audit.biases: Claims that sun avoidance shortens life come from cohorts where healthier, more active people spend more time outdoors (healthy-user, reverse causation).
audit.newer_evidence: A Swedish cohort reported twice the mortality in sun avoiders [abody-lindqvist2014]; this observational finding is often cited against sun protection but cannot separate sun from health and activity.
audit.bottom_line: Holds; avoid burning, and test vitamin D rather than seek UV.

factors.name: Supplement-drug interactions (anticoagulants, nitrates, St John's wort)

entries.headline: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke 22% in trials, NAC with nitroglycerin caused symptomatic hypotension and intolerable headache in a third of patients, and St John's wort sped up oral-contraceptive breakdown (breakthrough bleeding in 7 of 12 women); fish oil, by contrast, did not raise bleeding overall in 120,643 trial patients.

dose.effective: Not applicable: this is about avoiding harmful combinations.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 50-800 IU/day (stroke trials) and 100-400 IU/day with warfarin; NAC 10 g/day IV or oral with nitroglycerin; high-hyperforin St John's wort (>10 mg hyperforin/day); omega-3 up to 4 g/day purified EPA.
dose.too_much: Vitamin E above ~400 IU/day with anticoagulants; any NAC with nitrate therapy without supervision; any St John's wort with hormonal contraceptives, transplant drugs or other CYP3A substrates; high-dose purified EPA (bleeding RR ~1.5, absolute +0.6%).
dose.timeframe: Interactions act within days of starting the combination.
dose.notes: Informs, does not prescribe: do not stop, start or change the dose of a prescribed medication without talking to the prescriber. Bring a list of all supplements to every prescriber and pharmacist; ask before combining supplements with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, nitrates, hormonal contraception or immunosuppressants.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin E may antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting factors at high doses [med-corrigan1981]; omega-3s alter platelet function without clearly raising bleeding [med-wachira2014]; NAC supplies thiols that potentiate nitroglycerin's vasodilation [med-horowitz1988]; St John's wort's hyperforin induces CYP3A, accelerating breakdown of ethinyl estradiol and progestins [med-hall2003, med-whitten2006].
entries.interactions: Applies to [vitamin-e-supplement], [omega3-fish], [n-acetylcysteine], [turmeric-curcumin] and [curcumin-supplements]. Contraceptive failure from St John's wort parallels the oral-contraceptive interaction of tirzepatide ([glp1-agonists]).
entries.caveats: Curcumin is often listed as a warfarin potentiator, but the evidence is case-level; it was not among the higher-risk items named in a 2021 systematic review of warfarin interactions [med-tan2021]. Vitamin E 400 IU/day did not change prothrombin time in a small warfarin study.
entries.debate: Fish oil: reviews and a 2024 meta-analysis found no increase in clinically significant bleeding even with antithrombotic drugs [med-wachira2014, med-javaid2024], though high-dose purified EPA showed a small dose-related signal [med-javaid2024]. Vitamin E: no prothrombin-time change at <=400 IU/day with warfarin [med-corrigan1981], but a 9-trial meta-analysis found more haemorrhagic strokes [med-schurks2010]. NAC with nitrates: the combination reduced cardiac events in angina trials yet was limited by hypotension and headache [med-horowitz1988, med-ardissino1997]. Warfarin and herbs: most supplements are safe in moderation but dozens potentiate warfarin [med-tan2021].
entries.title: Supplement-drug interactions (anticoagulants, nitrates, St John's wort)

timing.summary: Enzyme-inducing herbs like St John's wort change drug levels within the first cycle of use, and the induction fades about a week after stopping.

onset.text: CYP3A induction after 14 days [tnut-imai2008]; breakthrough bleeding on the pill within the first cycles of St John's wort [tnut-hall2003].

full.text: Induction established within 2 weeks [tnut-imai2008].

after_stopping.text: CYP3A activity back to baseline about 7 days after stopping (recovery half-life 46 h) [tnut-imai2008].

frequency.text: Avoid the combination; allow about a week after stopping an inducer before relying on affected drugs [tnut-imai2008].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Vitamin E raised haemorrhagic stroke 22%, NAC with nitroglycerin caused hypotension and headache, St John's wort speeds contraceptive breakdown; fish oil did not raise bleeding overall in 120,643 trial patients, with a small signal for high-dose purified EPA.
audit.biases: The fish-oil bleeding signal comes mainly from REDUCE-IT, whose mineral-oil placebo raised LDL, hs-CRP (+21.9%) and IL-1beta in the control arm [anut-ridker2022], which may distort comparisons; STRENGTH, with a corn-oil placebo, found no cardiovascular benefit [anut-nicholls2020].
audit.newer_evidence: An often-missed omega-3 harm: a 2021 meta-analysis of 7 cardiovascular RCTs (81,210 patients) found marine omega-3 supplements raised atrial fibrillation (HR 1.25; 1.49 above 1 g/day; +11% per extra gram) [anut-gencer2021]; REDUCE-IT also had more AF hospitalisation (3.1% vs 2.1%) and borderline more serious bleeding (2.7% vs 2.1%) [anut-bhatt2019]. The bleeding meta-analysis remains reassuring overall [anut-javaid2024]; vitamin E stroke data are unchanged [anut-schurks2010].
audit.bottom_line: Add atrial fibrillation: people with AF risk, or on anticoagulants for AF, should discuss gram-dose fish oil with their prescriber.

factors.name: Tampons, pads, cups and intimate-care products

entries.headline: A 2024 study found lead (about 120 ng/g), arsenic and cadmium in all 30 tampons tested, but it measured content, not absorption; FDA's 2026 laboratory study judged releases far below harmful levels and the only biomarker study found no significant differences; douching, by contrast, tracked 81% higher blood 1,4-dichlorobenzene and has no health benefit.

dose.effective: Use the lowest-absorbency tampon you need and change it as directed (toxic shock prevention); menstrual cups were safe in a meta-analysis (watch for IUD dislodgement); skip douches, feminine sprays and powders; choose unscented products to avoid added fragrance chemicals.
dose.studied_range: Content testing of 30 tampons (14 brands) and 11 US products; NHANES questionnaires; 259 women in a biomarker cohort.
dose.too_much: No harm threshold from tampon metals is established. FDA's extraction study under exaggerated conditions found margins of safety indicating negligible concern for all 19 metals detected.
dose.timeframe: Not measured; no study has tracked body metal levels before and after changing products.
dose.notes: Organic tampons were not consistently lower in metals: lead was higher in non-organic tampons but arsenic higher in organic ones.

entries.mechanism: Vaginal tissue is permeable and bypasses first-pass liver metabolism [epc-upson2022], so absorption of contaminants is plausible. In the only biomarker study, tampon users had non-significantly higher blood mercury and urinary isoprostane [epc-singh2019]. Modelling suggests lead released into menstrual fluid binds red cells and is largely reabsorbed by the tampon [epc-ellison2026].
entries.interactions: Metals overlap with [heavy-metals]; scented products overlap with [fragrance-musks]; PFAS-treated period underwear overlaps with [pfas-personal-care].
entries.caveats: Content is not exposure: only 19 of 55 extractable chemicals leached under realistic simulated use [epc-marcelis2025]. Dioxin exposure from tampons is thousands of times lower than from diet [epc-devito2002]. The douching-VOC link is cross-sectional and douching itself marks other exposures.
entries.debate: The tampon-metal authors argue that, with no 'safe' lead level, content warrants concern until absorption is studied [epc-shearston2024, epc-shearston2024b]. FDA's laboratory risk assessment [epc-jin2026, epc-fdatampon] and a model by scientists from a major tampon manufacturer [epc-ellison2026] conclude releases are negligible; the latter is industry-authored. A systematic review lists many chemical classes in menstrual products but no exposure-per-cycle data [epc-marroquin2024].

key_numbers.label: Modelled lead available to vaginal tissue per tampon

entries.title: Tampons, pads, cups and intimate-care products

timing.summary: No study has measured how body levels of metals or other chemicals change with tampon use or after switching products. Timing is unknown.

onset.text: Not measured.

full.text: Not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; the only biomarker study compared users and non-users cross-sectionally [epc-singh2019].

frequency.text: Change tampons as directed and use the lowest absorbency needed; no evidence on chemical exposure by frequency.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: Taurine extended mouse lifespan in a 2023 Science study, but a 2025 NIH study found blood taurine does not fall with age in humans; human trials show only small drops in blood pressure (about 4 mmHg systolic), glucose and triglycerides.

dose.effective: 1.5-3 g/day; 1.6 g/day for 12 weeks lowered clinic systolic BP by 7.2 vs 2.6 mmHg (placebo) in prehypertension
dose.studied_range: 0.5-6 g/day for 5 days to 1 year in RCTs
dose.too_much: Observed safe level 3 g/day for long-term use; no systematic adverse effects in trials up to 6 g/day
dose.timeframe: Blood-pressure and metabolic effects measured at 8-12 weeks; endurance effects seen after a single dose
dose.notes: Diet supplies taurine mainly from meat, fish and shellfish. Mouse doses, scaled per kg of body weight, are much higher than typical human supplement doses. Energy drinks contain taurine plus caffeine and sugar; those are not a sensible source.

entries.mechanism: Taurine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is not built into proteins. It conjugates bile acids, regulates cell volume and calcium, and modifies mitochondrial tRNAs, which supports translation of respiratory-chain proteins. It is a weak direct antioxidant; its proposed anti-aging effects in mice act through less mitochondrial dysfunction, less cellular senescence, less DNA damage and lower inflammation. In humans it may lower blood pressure partly through hydrogen sulfide and improved endothelial function.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with exercise, which raised blood taurine acutely in the Singh study; there is no evidence that taurine adds to the benefits of [aerobic-exercise-moderate]. Often stacked with [glycine] and [n-acetylcysteine] in 'longevity' blends with no trial of the combination.
entries.caveats: The 'taurine deficiency drives aging' claim rests on mouse and monkey data plus human cross-sectional associations. Monkeys showed health-span markers, not lifespan. Human blood taurine varies with diet and was not consistently lower in older people in larger longitudinal cohorts. No trial has tested taurine on aging outcomes in humans.
entries.debate: Singh et al. reported that circulating taurine declines with age in mice, monkeys and humans and that supplementation extended mouse median lifespan and improved monkey health span [lon-singh2023], a result welcomed as a reason for human trials [lon-mcgaunn2023]. An NIH group led by Fernandez and de Cabo measured taurine longitudinally in three human cohorts, monkeys and mice and found it increased or stayed flat with age, with inconsistent links to health outcomes, arguing taurine is not a universal aging biomarker [lon-fernandez2025]. On the clinical side, a meta-analysis of 25 small RCTs found modest metabolic benefits [lon-tzang2024], consistent with one well-run BP trial [lon-sun2016], but the trials are short and heterogeneous.
entries.title: Taurine

timing.summary: Taurine is cleared from plasma with a half-life of about an hour and a week of dosing did not raise muscle taurine, yet daily intake lowered blood pressure over 12 weeks.

onset.text: Plasma peaks at 1.5 h, half-life ~1 h [tnut-ghandforoush2010]; no muscle change after 7 days [tnut-galloway2008].

full.text: BP lowered at 12 weeks (7.2 vs 2.6 mmHg systolic) [tnut-sun2016].

after_stopping.text: Plasma back to baseline within hours; persistence of BP effect not measured.

frequency.text: Daily dosing was used [tnut-sun2016]; the 1-hour half-life suggests split doses keep plasma higher (extrapolated) [tnut-galloway2008].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Taurine extended mouse lifespan (2023 Science), but a 2025 NIH study found blood taurine does not fall with age in humans; human trials show small BP, glucose and triglyceride effects.
audit.biases: The 'deficiency drives ageing' human evidence was cross-sectional [anut-singh2023]; longitudinal data contradicted it [anut-fernandez2025].
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 Malmo cohort (27,786 people, 25 years) found neither dietary nor plasma taurine predicted dementia, and plasma taurine barely tracked intake [anut-zhang2025], further weakening taurine as a human ageing biomarker. Metabolic RCT meta-analysis unchanged [anut-tzang2024].
audit.bottom_line: Up to date; a 2025 cohort also found no link between taurine and dementia.

factors.name: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

entries.headline: Testicular sperm have about 25 points less DNA fragmentation, and non-randomised studies report more live births with ICSI, but the only randomised comparison did not favour it and the HFEA rates it red; consider only after other causes are fixed.

dose.effective: Testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE) for ICSI in non-azoospermic men with confirmed high SDF, usually after failed IVF/ICSI or recurrent miscarriage.
dose.studied_range: 5 studies with paired SDF (143 men); 4 studies, 507 cycles with clinical outcomes.
dose.too_much: Invasive; small risks of bleeding, infection and testicular damage; testicular sperm have higher aneuploidy in some studies.
dose.timeframe: Single procedure at the time of egg retrieval.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM 2024: may consider. EAU: experimental (weak). Try reversible causes and short-abstinence ejaculates first; a meta-analysis found testicular SDF ~9.5 points lower than short-abstinence ejaculates.

entries.mechanism: Much oxidative DNA damage occurs during epididymal transit and storage, where defective sperm and leukocytes generate ROS; testicular sperm bypass this exposure.
entries.interactions: Compare with [short-abstinence], which reduces epididymal storage time non-invasively.
entries.caveats: Evidence is from small, mostly non-randomised studies. Not appropriate as first-line care.
entries.title: Testicular sperm for ICSI when ejaculated SDF stays high

audit.claim: Testicular sperm carry about 25 points less DNA fragmentation, and pooled studies show higher pregnancy and live birth with ICSI in men with high ejaculated SDF.
audit.biases: Confounding by indication and selection: the pooled data are non-randomised comparisons in couples chosen after failed cycles, often from the same centres that promote the technique, and with regression to the mean in SDF [afert-esteves2017, afert-khoo2024]. Lower SDF in the sample is a surrogate; testicular sperm may carry more aneuploidy.
audit.newer_evidence: A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 studies (>536 men) found higher pregnancy (OR 2.51) and live birth (OR 2.59) but judged the evidence too weak to recommend outside trials [afert-khoo2024]. The only multi-arm RCT that included a testicular arm (Hozyen 2022, 302 couples) found testicular sperm gave lower cleavage, blastulation and top-blastocyst rates, with PICSI and MACS ejaculated-sperm arms doing best [afert-hozyen2022]. A small RCT found TESA and MACS similar but lacked an untreated control [afert-mantravadi2024]. Reviews call the evidence non-conclusive [afert-romano2023]. The HFEA now rates TESE/TESA with ICSI after SDF testing RED (insufficient evidence plus surgical risk) [afert-hfea2026sdf].
audit.bottom_line: Testicular sperm do have less fragmented DNA, but whether that means more babies is unproven; the one randomised comparison did not favour it and the UK regulator rates it red. It is a last-resort option for selected couples, ideally within a trial.

entries.headline: Two large double-blind RCTs (TILT, 1575 women; SelecTIMO, 1731 couples) found no live-birth or cumulative-pregnancy gain from time-lapse culture or time-lapse-based selection; HFEA rates it black (no effect).

dose.effective: No benefit for live birth; harmless if the clinic includes it at no extra cost.
dose.studied_range: Time-lapse incubators with manual or algorithmic (e.g. EEVA, KIDScore) embryo selection.
dose.too_much: No known extra risk; cost only.
dose.timeframe: Embryo culture days 0-5.
dose.notes: Useful as a lab-management tool (undisturbed culture, records), not as a success booster.

entries.mechanism: Continuous imaging avoids taking embryos out of the incubator (stable temperature, pH and oxygen, i.e. less culture stress) and adds timing data for selection.
entries.interactions: Often bundled with AI embryo selection; same lack of live-birth data applies.
entries.caveats: Earlier Cochrane evidence was low quality and inconclusive.
entries.debate: Proponents point to the non-significant +3.6 points with undisturbed culture in TILT [fer-bhide2024]; trialists conclude widespread use 'should be questioned' [fer-kieslinger2023]. Cochrane found low-quality, inconclusive evidence [fer-armstrong2019]; HFEA and ESHRE say it does not improve live birth [fer-hfea2026, fer-eshre2023addons].

key_numbers.label: 12-month ongoing pregnancy, time-lapse selection vs standard (SelecTIMO)

entries.title: Time-lapse embryo imaging and incubation

audit.claim: TILT and SelecTIMO found no live-birth gain from time-lapse; HFEA black.
audit.biases: Earlier positive data were small or industry-sponsored; the large trials are independent and double-blind.
audit.newer_evidence: TILT (2024): live birth 33.7% time-lapse, 36.6% undisturbed culture, 33.0% standard [afert-bhide2024]. HFEA black [afert-hfea2026].
audit.bottom_line: Holds.

entries.headline: Eating within an 8-10 h window cuts intake by roughly 170-550 kcal/day and gives weight loss similar to calorie counting; when calories are matched (Liu 2022 NEJM, Peters 2025) it adds little or nothing, and 4-6 h windows lowered 8-isoprostane ~35% only alongside ~3% weight loss.

dose.effective: An 8-10 h daily window, ideally early (e.g., 8:00-16:00 or 7:00-15:00), at least 5-6 days/week, for 12 weeks or more.
dose.studied_range: 4-10 h windows, early (ending 14:00-16:00), mid-day or late (12:00-20:00), 4 days to 12 months.
dose.too_much: Windows of 4-6 h increased lean-mass loss (6-h TRE: -1.5 kg lean in 8 weeks); 16:8 without resistance training reduced appendicular lean mass. An observational NHANES analysis linked <8 h eating to CV mortality (HR 2.35) but is heavily confounded.
dose.timeframe: Glucose and insulin changes within 4 days to 5 weeks; weight loss over 3-12 months.
dose.notes: Early windows look better than late ones in some trials (Xie 2022) but not when calories are held constant (Peters 2025). The overnight fast in a 16:8 schedule barely raises ketones (~0.1-0.15 mmol/L).

entries.mechanism: Mainly spontaneous energy reduction. Early windows align meals with daytime insulin sensitivity and lower evening glucose exposure; a longer overnight fast lowers insulin and slightly raises fat oxidation and ketones. eTRF raised blood SIRT1 and LC3A expression in one 4-day study.
entries.interactions: Equivalent to [calorie-restriction] at matched intake; benefits track [weight-loss]. Combine with [resistance-training] and ~1.6 g/kg protein to keep lean mass. Late windows that push dinner close to bedtime may conflict with [short-sleep] and [shift-work-circadian]. Useful as a weight-loss tool in [pcos].
entries.caveats: Many trials are small and short. TREAT (Lowe 2020) found 16:8 alone no better than three meals. Manoogian 2024 found only a -0.10% HbA1c effect in metabolic syndrome. The 2024 AHA abstract (published as Chen 2025) used two days of dietary recall; the <8 h group was ~2% of participants, more often smokers, food-insecure and habitual breakfast-skippers, and the CV association lost significance when <8 h was required on both recall days (HR 1.78, 0.85-3.74).

16:8 TRE vs 3 meals, weight at 12 weeks (NS)
Early TRE + ER extra weight loss vs >=12 h window

entries.title: Time-restricted eating (8-10 h eating window)

timing.summary: A daily eating window changes glucose within days and gives about 3% weight loss over two months, mostly by cutting calories. Over a year it adds little beyond the calorie deficit, and benefits would fade as weight returns.

onset.text: Four days of eating 8 am-2 pm lowered 24-h glucose [tbody-jamshed2019].

full.text: Five weeks of early 6-h eating improved insulin sensitivity and oxidative stress [tbody-sutton2018]; 8 weeks of 4-6 h windows cut weight ~3% [tbody-cienfuegos2020]; 12 months gave no significant extra weight loss over calorie restriction alone [tbody-liu2022].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: Studied daily; no trial compared fewer days per week.

timing.debate: Weight-stable early TRE improved insulin sensitivity [tbody-sutton2018], but intended-isocaloric TRE did not [tbody-peters2025] and calorie-matched TRE added no significant benefit over 12 months [tbody-liu2022].

audit.claim: An 8-10 h window cuts intake and gives weight loss similar to calorie counting; it adds little when calories are matched; the NHANES 'HR 2.35' finding is heavily confounded.
audit.biases: The 2024 AHA abstract, published 2025, used two 24-h dietary recalls, the all-cause association did not survive sensitivity analyses, and the authors themselves flag residual confounding; reverse causation (illness, food insecurity, skipped meals) is plausible [adiet-chen2025].
audit.newer_evidence: Randomized trials: TRE plus calorie restriction was no better than calorie restriction (2022) [adiet-liu2022c]; TRE without counting matched counting (2023) [adiet-lin2023]; in metabolic syndrome only -0.10% HbA1c (2024) [adiet-manoogian2024]; isocaloric TRE did not improve cardiometabolic health (2025) [adiet-peters2025].
audit.bottom_line: The newest trials show eating windows work mainly through eating less; the NHANES '91% higher heart death' claim should be discounted.

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles plasma F2-isoprostanes, which fall measurably within 2 weeks of quitting. It raises urinary 8-OHdG and turns beta-carotene supplements harmful.

dose.effective: Complete cessation.
dose.too_much: Any smoking
dose.timeframe: F2-isoprostanes fell significantly after 2 weeks of abstinence
dose.notes: Smokers should avoid beta-carotene and high-dose vitamin A supplements.

entries.mechanism: Cigarette smoke delivers large amounts of radicals and oxidants directly and recruits activated inflammatory cells to the lung. Tumours with activating NRF2 mutations are enriched in smokers.
entries.interactions: Strongly interacts with [beta-carotene-supplement] (lung cancer RR 1.18-1.28). NRF2-mutant tumours occur especially in smokers.
entries.caveats: No antioxidant supplement offsets smoking.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking roughly doubles circulating F2-isoprostanes in a dose-dependent way; quitting lowers them within 2 weeks and to a new steady state by about 4 weeks, making it the single largest lifestyle lever.

dose.effective: Quit completely. In an RCT, cutting down from ~27 to ~18 cigarettes/day did not lower F2-isoprostanes or any other harm marker except carbon monoxide.
dose.studied_range: Studies compared heavy, moderate and non-smokers; cessation studies followed people from 2 weeks to 1 year.
dose.too_much: No safe level: urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was ~1.7x the nonsmoker level in moderate and ~3.3x in heavy smokers.
dose.timeframe: Isoprostanes fall within days, are ~20-40% lower at 2-3 weeks, and plateau about 4 weeks after quitting; cardiovascular risk falls ~39% within 5 years but takes 10-15+ years to approach never-smoker levels.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement did not prevent the fall in isoprostanes, suggesting combustion products, not nicotine, drive most of it.

entries.mechanism: Each puff delivers large amounts of free radicals in the gas and tar phases (semiquinone radicals, NO, peroxynitrite, H2O2), plus metals and aldehydes. Smoke also activates neutrophils and vascular NADPH oxidase, depletes vitamin C and E, and uncouples eNOS.
entries.interactions: Effects add to [alcohol], [secondhand-smoke] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Weight gain after quitting does not cancel the drop in oxidative markers. Smoking is also the main source of cadmium ([heavy-metals]) and worsens [periodontal-disease].
entries.caveats: Five days of 2 g/day vitamin C lowered smokers' isoprostanes in Reilly 1996 (vitamin E alone did not), but that is not a substitute for quitting. Smoking harms sperm parameters (meta-analysis) and is relevant to egg health (cross-link to fertility areas).
entries.title: Smoking tobacco (and quitting)

entries.headline: Smokers average about 9 percentage points higher SDF and lower count, motility and morphology; quitting improves semen within 3-6 months.

dose.effective: Quit completely; harm rises with cigarettes per day (moderate/heavy smokers, roughly >10/day, show larger effects).
dose.studied_range: Light (<10/day) to heavy (>20/day) smokers in clinic and population samples.
dose.too_much: No safe level identified; avoid second-hand smoke too.
dose.timeframe: Semen improved at 3 months and further at 6 months after quitting.
dose.notes: Nicotine replacement is far less harmful than smoking. Vaping data for sperm are sparse.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers oxidants, cadmium, lead and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; seminal leukocytes and ROS rise, antioxidant levels fall, and sperm show more 8-OHdG and strand breaks.
entries.interactions: Stacks with [varicocele] and [outdoor-air-pollution]. Non-responders to stopping heat exposure in one series were mostly smokers. Antioxidant pills do not offset smoking.
entries.caveats: Effects on standard semen parameters are moderate; the clearest harm is on DNA integrity and on offspring and partner health.
entries.title: Tobacco smoking

entries.headline: Smoking is the largest avoidable toxic exposure for eggs: about 60% higher odds of infertility, roughly halved odds of IVF live birth (OR 0.54), lower AMH and twice the risk of early menopause.

dose.effective: Zero. Risk is dose-dependent (cigarettes/day, years smoked, pack-years).
dose.studied_range: Current vs never smokers; dose-response up to >20 cigarettes/day and 15-20+ years.
dose.too_much: Any active smoking. 11-15 pack-years: ~4-fold risk of premature menopause; 15-20 years' duration: much higher.
dose.timeframe: Quitting at least 3 months before trying covers one follicle-growth cycle; menopause-timing risk normalises about 10 years after quitting.
dose.notes: ASRM's 2024 opinion also reviews nicotine and marijuana as potential reproductive harms.

entries.mechanism: Tobacco smoke delivers polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cadmium and other oxidants that accelerate follicle loss (lower AMH), raise follicular oxidative stress and impair oocyte maturation.
entries.interactions: Adds to [maternal-age]. Cadmium overlaps with [heavy-metals]. Cessation is covered by [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: Evidence is observational, but consistent across designs and dose-dependent, which supports causation.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth per cycle, smokers

entries.title: Cigarette smoking

entries.headline: Quitting removes the biggest avoidable egg toxin; former smokers' excess menopause risk is much smaller than current smokers' and disappears about 10 years after quitting.

dose.effective: Complete cessation, ideally at least 3 months before trying or before IVF stimulation.
dose.studied_range: Former vs current smokers, years since quitting.
dose.timeframe: One follicle-growth cycle (~3 months) for the follicular environment; longer for ovarian-reserve effects.
dose.notes: Lost follicles are not regained, so earlier is better. Use evidence-based cessation support.

entries.mechanism: Removes the exogenous oxidant and toxicant load (PAHs, cadmium) on growing follicles.
entries.interactions: See [tobacco-smoking].
entries.caveats: No RCT has randomised women to quit and measured egg quality; the benefit is inferred from the dose-response and former-smoker data.
entries.title: Stopping smoking

timing.summary: Quitting lowers whole-body oxidative stress within days to 4 weeks, but semen improves over months: clearly at 3 months and further at 6. Smokers carry about 9 points more sperm DNA fragmentation.

onset.text: Not timed for sperm; smokers average 9.2 points higher SDF [tsperm-szabo2023].

full.text: Not timed; harms are larger in moderate and heavy smokers [tsperm-sharma2016].

after_stopping.text: Isoprostanes fell within days and plateaued about 4 weeks after quitting [tsperm-pilz2000]; semen improved at 3 months and further at 6 months [tsperm-ragheb2025].

frequency.text: Dose-dependent: heavier smoking, larger effect [tsperm-sharma2016].

sperm.late_start: Quitting 2-4 weeks before already lowers systemic oxidative stress [tsperm-pilz2000], which may help stored sperm, but semen gains were measured only at 3 and 6 months.
sperm.text: Smoking affects all stages; semen improvement kept growing to 6 months after quitting [tsperm-ragheb2025].

egg.late_start: Quitting 2-4 weeks before still removes smoke exposure from the final follicular phase and the early embryo, and active smoking at the time of ART carries the clearest penalty (live birth OR 0.54) [tegg-waylen2009]; it cannot undo earlier loss of follicles.
egg.text: Smoking acts across the whole follicle path: tobacco markers reach follicular fluid [tegg-benedict2011], and longer, heavier smoking speeds depletion of the follicle pool, raising early-menopause risk, which falls with time since quitting and reaches never-smoker levels after >10 years [tegg-zhu2018, tegg-whitcomb2018]. Stopping at least ~3 months before covers the 85-day growth path (extrapolated).

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found; the only cessation time course is a 60-man uncontrolled study [tsperm-ragheb2025].

audit.claim: Smoking roughly doubles F2-isoprostanes and is the largest lifestyle lever for oxidative stress, sperm and eggs.
audit.biases: Fertility data are observational, but dose-response, cessation reversal and genetic evidence argue against confounding.
audit.newer_evidence: Isoprostane doubling is long established [abody-morrow1995]; a 2022 meta-analysis of MR studies confirms smoking causes a wide range of diseases, including type 2 diabetes, periodontitis and PCOS [abody-larsson2022].
audit.bottom_line: Holds; genetic evidence strengthens causality.

factors.name: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: Lycopene is 2.5-3.8x more bioavailable from tomato paste than fresh tomatoes and needs fat to be absorbed; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6, improve FMD, and blunted LDL oxidation after a high-fat meal.

dose.effective: A serving of cooked tomato product (sauce, paste, puree) with a little olive oil most days.
dose.studied_range: 21 intervention trials of tomato products or lycopene; single meals with processed tomato.
dose.timeframe: Postprandial (same meal) for oxLDL; weeks for lipids and FMD.
dose.notes: Tomato puree has ~8x the lycopene of raw tomato per 100 g (USDA). Fat-free dressing gave essentially no carotenoid absorption from salad.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a lipid-phase singlet-oxygen quencher carried in LDL; processing breaks cell walls and isomerises lycopene, improving absorption; tomato also supplies vitamin C and naringenin chalcone.
entries.interactions: Pair with [extra-virgin-olive-oil] or avocado; eat with high-fat meals to blunt postprandial oxidation.
entries.caveats: Lycopene supplements lowered systolic BP in pooled trials but tomato products, not pills, gave the lipid and FMD effects. Most trials are short.

key_numbers.label: Lycopene AUC, paste vs fresh tomato

entries.title: Tomatoes and tomato products (cooked with oil)

entries.headline: A placebo-controlled trial of 14 mg/day lycopene improved fast motility and morphology, but missed its primary endpoint; no SDF data.

dose.effective: About 14 mg lycopene/day, roughly half a cup of tomato sauce or passata (content varies by product); cooked tomato with some oil is better absorbed than raw.
dose.studied_range: 14 mg/day lactolycopene for 12 weeks in 60 healthy men.
dose.timeframe: 12 weeks.
dose.notes: Getting lycopene from food also brings other carotenoids and fibre.

entries.mechanism: Lycopene is a potent singlet-oxygen quencher concentrated in the testes and seminal fluid.
entries.interactions: Part of [mediterranean-diet]; included in the MOXI supplement (10 mg), which was null.
entries.caveats: Single small trial in healthy men; primary outcome (motile sperm concentration) not significant (p=0.058).
entries.title: Tomatoes and lycopene

timing.summary: Only a few milligrams of lycopene are absorbed per serving however much is eaten, so regular servings build up blood and tissue levels over weeks. Levels then fade over weeks; a sperm trial ran 12 weeks.

onset.text: Plasma lycopene rose within 8 days of 20 mg/day [tnut-cohn2004].

full.text: Depletion half-life about 26 days implies a plateau after 2-4 months (extrapolated) [tnut-burri2001]; sperm effects at 12 weeks [tnut-williams2020].

after_stopping.text: Effective half-life 5-9 days after short dosing [tnut-cohn2004] but about 26 days on longer depletion [tnut-burri2001].

frequency.text: Absorption saturates at about 4-6 mg per dose [tnut-diwadkar2003], so spreading cooked tomato over most days beats one large serving (extrapolated).

sperm.late_start: Not measured.
sperm.text: Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963]; the RCT ran 12 weeks [tnut-williams2020].

timing.debate: Short dosing studies give lycopene half-lives of 5-9 days [tnut-cohn2004], long depletion studies about 26 days [tnut-burri2001]; both are true for different body pools.

audit.claim: Lycopene is more bioavailable from cooked paste; tomato interventions lower LDL and IL-6; one lycopene trial missed its semen primary endpoint.
audit.biases: Short trials; the sperm trial was underpowered [adiet-williams2020].
audit.newer_evidence: No newer contrary synthesis found [adiet-cheng2017].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: The best-proven topical treatment for photoaging: tretinoin improved 14 of 15 treated faces versus none on vehicle in 16 weeks, retinol 0.4% smoothed fine wrinkles even at age 87, and tretinoin blocked 70-80% of UV-induced collagenase; it does not prevent skin cancer.

dose.effective: Prescription tretinoin cream at night (0.1% in the classic trials; lower strengths if irritated), or over-the-counter retinol (0.4% lotion up to 3 times a week in the elderly-skin trial); build up from every second or third night.
dose.studied_range: Tretinoin 0.1% daily for 16 weeks to 5.5 years; retinol 0.4% up to 3 times weekly for 24 weeks.
dose.too_much: Irritation, redness and peeling (retinoid dermatitis) are common and dose-related. Avoid during pregnancy as a precaution, although first-trimester topical tretinoin exposure showed no excess birth defects in a 106-pregnancy cohort.
dose.timeframe: Visible improvement from about 16-24 weeks, with continued use needed to maintain it.
dose.notes: Retinoids are not antioxidants: they work downstream of UV-generated ROS by blocking AP-1-driven MMPs and rebuilding matrix. Use with daily [sunscreen].

entries.mechanism: Retinoic acid binds nuclear retinoic acid receptors, which antagonize AP-1 (c-Jun/c-Fos). This blocks the UV- and ROS-triggered induction of MMP-1, MMP-3 and MMP-9, while increasing procollagen I and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and normalizing epidermal turnover.
entries.interactions: Complements [sunscreen] (prevention) and [uv-sun-exposure] avoidance; stronger evidence than [topical-vitamin-c] for wrinkles. Oral retinoid-like compounds such as high-dose [beta-carotene-supplement] are a different story and are not a substitute.
entries.caveats: Most photoaging trials are small and vehicle-controlled over months, with clinician-graded outcomes. In the large VATTC trial, high-dose tretinoin did not prevent basal- or squamous-cell carcinoma, and the trial stopped early because of excess deaths in the tretinoin arm.
entries.debate: Efficacy for photoaging is not seriously disputed [skb-weiss1988, skb-kafi2007, skb-fisher1997]. The disputes concern cancer and safety: VATTC showed no prevention of keratinocyte carcinoma [skb-weinstock2012] and an unexpected mortality excess [skb-weinstock2009]; the investigators judged it unlikely to be causal given minor baseline imbalances and no plausible mechanism for a topical cream, but the signal has never been explained. Pregnancy: systemic retinoids are teratogens, yet a prospective cohort found no excess malformations after topical tretinoin [skb-loureiro2005], so advice to avoid it is precautionary.

key_numbers.label: Fine-wrinkle score change, retinol vs vehicle
BCC at 5 years, tretinoin vs vehicle

entries.title: Topical retinoids (tretinoin, retinol)

timing.summary: Retinoids are slow to work and need maintenance: 16 weeks of daily tretinoin improved 14 of 15 treated faces versus none on vehicle [tleg-weiss1988], improvement continued or held through 48 weeks [tleg-olsen1997a], and after that three applications a week maintained it while once a week did less well and stopping led to partial regression [tleg-olsen1997b].

onset.text: Clinical improvement becomes evident over about 16 weeks of daily use [tleg-weiss1988]; the protective molecular effect is faster, with tretinoin pretreatment blocking 70-80% of UV-induced MMP induction [tleg-fisher1997].

full.text: Benefit continued to build to 24-48 weeks of daily use, with side effects becoming less common in the second half [tleg-olsen1997a]; retinol 0.4% applied up to three times weekly for 24 weeks reduced fine wrinkles even in people with a mean age of 87 [tleg-kafi2007].

after_stopping.text: Partial regression: in the 24 weeks after 48 weeks of daily tretinoin, people who stopped tended to lose their improvement, while three-times-weekly users held or improved [tleg-olsen1997b].

frequency.text: This is the one factor in the group with a direct schedule comparison. Daily to build, then three times a week to maintain - once a week was clearly weaker and stopping lost ground, and side effects tracked application frequency [tleg-olsen1997b]. Retinol at 0.4% worked at up to three times weekly from the start [tleg-kafi2007].

timing.debate: Retinoids treat appearance, not cancer: a trial of 1,131 high-risk veterans found topical 0.1% tretinoin for 1.5-5.5 years did not reduce basal-cell or invasive squamous-cell carcinoma or actinic keratosis counts [tleg-weinstock2012], so the fast molecular protection against UV-induced collagenase [tleg-fisher1997] does not translate into cancer prevention.

factors.name: Topical vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid serum), alone or with vitamin E and ferulic acid

entries.headline: Vitamin C only gets into skin as L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5 (best at about 20%); small vehicle-controlled trials (7 RCTs, 139 people in total) show modest smoothing of wrinkles and lighter pigment, and a 15% C + 1% E + ferulic acid mix doubled UV protection in pig skin, an add-on to sunscreen rather than a replacement.

dose.effective: 10-20% L-ascorbic acid at pH below 3.5, applied once daily in the morning under sunscreen; the best-studied combination is 15% L-ascorbic acid + 1% alpha-tocopherol + ferulic acid.
dose.studied_range: 5-20% L-ascorbic acid for 3-6 months in clinical trials; 4 days of pretreatment in photoprotection studies.
dose.too_much: Concentrations above 20% did not increase skin uptake; the low pH can sting or irritate.
dose.timeframe: Skin levels saturate after about 3 daily applications and fall with a half-life of about 4 days; visible change needs 3-6 months.
dose.notes: Common derivatives (magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, ascorbyl palmitate) did not raise skin vitamin C in pig skin. L-ascorbic acid is unstable in solution; ferulic acid improved the stability of the C+E formula. Eating or swallowing vitamin C does not deliver comparable skin levels ([vitamin-c-supplement]).

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble antioxidant in skin, scavenging UV-generated radicals and regenerating alpha-tocopherol from the tocopheroxyl radical. It is also the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases needed to make stable collagen, and it inhibits tyrosinase, which explains the pigment-lightening effect.
entries.interactions: Synergy with vitamin E and ferulic acid in the same formula. Complements [sunscreen] (blocks photons) by mopping up ROS from the photons that get through, including visible and IR-A light. [topical-retinoids] have stronger evidence for wrinkles.
entries.caveats: The trials are small, short, split-face or split-arm, and often run or funded by the product developers. There are no long-term trials of visible aging and none on skin cancer. 'Doubled photoprotection' means a protection factor of about 8, measured in pig skin, well below a typical sunscreen.
entries.debate: Supporters point to vehicle-controlled improvements in wrinkles and pigmentation [skb-humbert2003, skb-correia2023] and to a 31-study Bayesian pooling showing dose-dependent prevention of UV pigmentation [skb-dedormael2019]. Sceptics note the pooled studies were all run in-house by L'Oreal, the key formulation papers come from the group that developed the C+E+ferulic serum [skb-lin2003, skb-lin2005, skb-pinnell2001], and the only independent systematic review found just 139 participants across 7 trials [skb-correia2023]. No independent large RCT exists.
entries.title: Topical vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid serum), alone or with vitamin E and ferulic acid

timing.summary: The skin reservoir fills fast and empties slowly for a topical: L-ascorbic acid saturates skin levels after three daily applications and then disappears with a tissue half-life of about 4 days [tleg-pinnell2001]. Visible change is a different, much slower matter - small vehicle-controlled trials assessed benefit at 3 and 6 months [tleg-humbert2003, tleg-correia2023].

onset.text: Skin levels saturate after about three daily applications [tleg-pinnell2001]; measurable antioxidant photoprotection is present once the reservoir is loaded, and adding ferulic acid to 15% vitamin C plus 1% vitamin E doubled that protection in skin [tleg-lin2005].

full.text: Clinically visible smoothing and pigment change were assessed at 3 and 6 months of daily use in the vehicle-controlled trials [tleg-humbert2003], and the systematic review of 7 trials in 139 volunteers used similar 3-6 month timeframes [tleg-correia2023].

after_stopping.text: The skin reservoir falls with a half-life of about 4 days, so most of the loaded vitamin C is gone within 1-2 weeks of stopping [tleg-pinnell2001]; whether the clinical gains fade as fast has not been measured.

frequency.text: Daily is the practical schedule and the one used in trials, but the kinetics suggest why: three consecutive daily applications are needed to saturate skin, and levels then decay with a 4-day half-life, so skipping several days lets the reservoir drain [tleg-pinnell2001]. Formulation matters more than frequency - it must be L-ascorbic acid below pH 3.5, best around 20% [tleg-pinnell2001].

timing.debate: The pharmacokinetics are from pig skin rather than people [tleg-pinnell2001], and the clinical evidence is thin: 7 small vehicle-controlled trials with 139 volunteers in total, with the reviewers calling for better studies and noting the ideal concentration is unresolved [tleg-correia2023]. The photoprotection data are also laboratory measurements rather than clinical outcomes [tleg-lin2005].

factors.name: Triclosan and triclocarban (antibacterial soaps and products)

entries.headline: Antibacterial soaps with triclosan worked no better than plain soap, so the FDA removed triclosan and triclocarban from consumer washes from 2017 (wastewater loads then fell 80-90%); the remaining exposure has weak, inconsistent links to thyroid, birth weight and fertility, while triclosan toothpaste modestly reduces gingivitis.

dose.effective: Wash hands with plain soap and water (or alcohol sanitizer away from a sink); skip products marketed as 'antibacterial' for everyday home use; check toothpaste, deodorant, cosmetics and imported products for triclosan. Products labelled triclosan-free lowered urinary triclosan by 36% in 3 days.
dose.studied_range: Urinary triclosan geometric means of about 1-100 ng/mL across countries; toothpaste use raised plasma triclosan from under 1 to 26-296 ng/g.
dose.too_much: No human harm threshold established. Top-quartile triclosan (over 72 ng/mL in a post-conception urine) went with 16% lower fecundability in one cohort; EU allows at most 0.3% in specified products.
dose.timeframe: Plasma half-life about 21 h; most of a dose is excreted within 24 h.
dose.notes: The 2016 FDA rule covered consumer washes, not toothpaste or hand sanitizers; it deferred benzalkonium chloride, benzethonium chloride and chloroxylenol, which have become the common replacements.

entries.mechanism: Triclosan disrupts thyroid hormone homeostasis and shows estrogenic/androgenic activity in animals and cells; it is a mitochondrial uncoupler and raises ROS experimentally. In humans, triclosan tracked higher urinary 8-OHdG and isoprostane in pregnancy, but not independently of phthalates [epc-ferguson2019], and went with 31% higher IL-6 [epc-watkins2015]; triclocarban correlated non-significantly with 8-OHdG [epc-iyer2018].
entries.interactions: Co-occurs with parabens and BP-3 in personal-care products ([parabens], [uv-filters]). Relevant to [periodontal-disease] because triclosan toothpaste reduces gingivitis. See [triclosan-triclocarban], [triclosan-triclocarban].
entries.caveats: Most outcome studies use one spot urine (intraclass correlation about 0.47 [epc-meeker2013]); higher-income groups have higher triclosan [epc-han2016], a confounding risk. A 14-day toothpaste study found no thyroid change despite large plasma rises [epc-allmyr2009], and a systematic review could not conclude that current exposure affects thyroid function [epc-homburg2022]. A birth-weight meta-analysis found no clear overall effect, with stronger inverse links only in higher-exposure populations [epc-patti2021, epc-zhong2020].
entries.debate: Over 200 scientists' Florence Statement called triclosan and triclocarban persistent endocrine disruptors without benefit in most uses [epc-halden2017], and a systematic review found triclosan soaps no better than plain soap [epc-aiello2007]; the FDA agreed for consumer washes [epc-fda2016]. On the other side, a Cochrane review found triclosan/copolymer toothpaste reduced plaque, gingivitis and caries slightly, with no serious safety concerns over up to 3 years [epc-riley2013]. After the ban, triclosan fell in wastewater by 89% but parabens rose 72% [epc-adhikari2022] and other antibacterials replaced it in soaps [epc-rundle2019].

key_numbers.label: Wastewater triclosan after the FDA ban
Urinary triclosan after 3 days of labelled-free products

entries.title: Triclosan and triclocarban (antibacterial soaps and products)

entries.headline: A 2024 meta-analysis of 5 small case-control and cross-sectional studies linked triclosan to lower sperm concentration and motility (high heterogeneity); the larger Boston study found only about 1 percentage point fewer normal-shaped sperm without dose-response, and a 443-couple Shanghai cohort linked higher male triclosan to 23% lower fecundability.

dose.effective: Use plain soap and triclosan-free toothpaste, deodorant and cosmetics; most US consumer washes have been triclosan-free since 2017.
dose.studied_range: Urinary or seminal-plasma triclosan in 262-471 men; one preconception cohort of 443 couples.
dose.too_much: No human threshold.
dose.timeframe: Triclosan clears in about 1-4 days; sperm effects, if any, would take a spermatogenic cycle.
dose.notes: Exposure in the US has fallen since the FDA rule, so older studies reflect higher exposure.

entries.mechanism: Endocrine disruption (androgen and thyroid pathways) and oxidative stress in animal and in vitro testis models.
entries.interactions: See [triclosan-triclocarban] for sources; co-exposure with [parabens].
entries.caveats: Small, mainly clinic-based, cross-sectional studies with single urines; pooled estimates are dominated by heterogeneity.
entries.debate: Positive: meta-analysis SMD -0.42 for concentration and -1.30 for motility [epc-adegbola2024]; modest motility links in 471 men [epc-zhu2016]; lower fecundability with male triclosan [epc-zhu2022]. Weak or null: limited (none or modest) effects in 406 men [epc-yuan2022]; only slightly lower morphology without dose-response in 262 Boston men [epc-nassan2019]; a systematic review found little to no indication that triclosan affects time to pregnancy [epc-hipwell2019].
entries.title: Triclosan and sperm

entries.headline: Two fertility-clinic studies found higher urinary triclosan with fewer antral follicles (about 4% fewer with higher triclosan in Boston), and a Canadian pregnancy cohort linked the top quartile to 16% lower fecundability; but a systematic review found little overall link with time to pregnancy, and one preconception cohort found the opposite direction.

dose.effective: Avoid triclosan-containing products (check toothpaste, deodorant, cosmetics); use plain soap.
dose.studied_range: Urinary triclosan in 109-2,001 women.
dose.too_much: Top quartile (over 72 ng/mL in a post-conception urine) had fecundability odds ratio 0.84.
dose.timeframe: Triclosan clears within days; antral follicle count reflects follicles growing over the previous months.
dose.notes: US exposure has fallen since 2017.

entries.mechanism: Thyroid and estrogen-pathway disruption in animals; human mechanism unknown.
entries.interactions: See [triclosan-triclocarban].
entries.caveats: Antral follicle count is a marker of ovarian reserve, not of egg quality or live birth. The Canadian cohort measured triclosan once, after conception.
entries.debate: Harm: lower antral follicle count in Boston [epc-minguez2017] and Poland [epc-jurewicz2019]; lower fecundability in MIREC [epc-velez2015]. Null or opposite: little to no indication for time to pregnancy in a systematic review [epc-hipwell2019]; higher fecundability with higher triclosan using pooled daily urines [epc-rosenvollmar2023].

key_numbers.label: Antral follicle count change with higher triclosan

entries.title: Triclosan, ovarian reserve and fecundability

timing.summary: Triclosan has a plasma half-life of about a day, so personal levels fall within days of switching products. Population levels fell after the 2016-2017 FDA rule removed it from consumer washes.

onset.text: Plasma triclosan peaked 1-3 h after an oral dose [epc-sandborgh2006]; toothpaste use raised plasma levels markedly within 14 days [epc-allmyr2009].

full.text: Steady state with daily use within a few days, given a 21-h half-life [epc-sandborgh2006] (extrapolated).

after_stopping.text: Most of a dose is excreted within 24 h and 24-83% within 4 days [epc-sandborgh2006]; labelled-free products cut urinary triclosan 36% in 3 days [epc-harley2016].

frequency.text: Exposure tracks daily product use; there is no benefit of antibacterial soap over plain soap at any frequency [epc-aiello2007].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

sperm.late_start: Stopping late still lowers exposure of sperm in the final maturation stages; benefit is unproven either way.
sperm.text: Spermatogenesis takes about 64 days plus epididymal transit [epc-heller1963], so a chemical that affected developing sperm would need roughly 2-3 months off exposure before a full cohort of unexposed sperm is ejaculated.

egg.late_start: Stopping late still lowers exposure during final follicle growth and early pregnancy.
egg.text: The ovulated follicle began its final growth phase about 85 days earlier and is recruited 15-20 days before ovulation [epc-gougeon1986], so a follicle-level effect would need about 3 months off exposure to clear.

entries.headline: A teaspoon (2-3 g) of ground turmeric holds roughly 60-100 mg curcumin, and eating it in food produces only nanomolar curcumin conjugates in blood (free curcumin mostly undetectable), so culinary turmeric is a pleasant spice with plausible gut-local effects but no demonstrated systemic antioxidant effect.

dose.effective: No proven systemic dose from cooking. Normal culinary use (about 1/2-2 teaspoons, 1.5-6 g ground turmeric/day in curries) is safe; one small haemodialysis trial used 2.5 g turmeric in juice three times a week.
dose.studied_range: Culinary-level feeding studies used a few grams of turmeric per meal; supplement trials use 80 mg-3 g/day of curcuminoids, mostly far above what food provides.
dose.too_much: Food amounts are within the EFSA ADI of 3 mg curcumin/kg/day (about 210 mg/day for a 70 kg adult). Turmeric is relatively high in soluble oxalate, a consideration for people with calcium-oxalate kidney stones. Cheap or imported ground turmeric can be adulterated with lead chromate.
dose.timeframe: Plasma conjugates peak about 30 min after a turmeric meal and persist for at least 8 h; no long-term human outcome data.
dose.notes: Pure turmeric powder averages about 3% curcumin by weight; most curry powders contain much less and vary widely. Black pepper and fat are often recommended, but in a head-to-head human study piperine-type adjuvants did not significantly raise curcumin exposure at a 207 mg dose. Buy from suppliers that test for lead; avoid unusually bright, cheap loose turmeric from markets with documented adulteration.

entries.mechanism: Curcumin is an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (Michael acceptor) that can modify KEAP1 Cys151 and activate Nrf2/HO-1 in cells, inhibits NF-kB signalling in vitro, and scavenges radicals in a test tube. In people, food doses are rapidly glucuronidated and sulfated in gut wall and liver; circulating forms are mainly conjugates that lack the parent compound's activity in cell assays. The gut lumen and intestinal wall are the only tissues likely to see meaningful concentrations.
entries.interactions: Redundant with, and far weaker than, food Nrf2 activators such as [broccoli-sprouts] and [broccoli-seed-powder]. Part of the general [herbs-spices] pattern within a [mediterranean-diet]-style or South Asian diet. Not interchangeable with [curcumin-supplements], which deliver 10-100x more curcuminoids in formulations designed to be absorbed. No known meaningful drug interactions at culinary amounts.
entries.caveats: Population associations (e.g. curry eaters with better cognitive scores in Singapore) cannot separate turmeric from the rest of diet and lifestyle. Claims that 'golden milk' or a pinch of pepper turns kitchen turmeric into a systemic antioxidant are not supported by pharmacokinetic data. In-vitro antioxidant capacity of turmeric says nothing about in-vivo effect. Lead chromate adulteration has been documented in turmeric from Bangladesh, India and Pakistan and has caused childhood lead poisoning in the US.

entries.title: Turmeric as a spice (culinary use)

timing.summary: Culinary or capsule curcumin barely reaches blood as free curcumin; its conjugates peak at about 3 h with a half-life of about 7 h. Leukocyte Nrf2-target mRNA peaked 4-6 h after a large single dose, so any effect is short-lived.

onset.text: Conjugates peak at about 3 h [tfood-vareed2008]; leukocyte NRF2, HO-1 and NQO1 mRNA peaked 4-6 h after 4 g curcumin [tfood-cheng2019].

full.text: No long-term human outcome data for culinary turmeric.

after_stopping.text: Conjugate half-life about 6.8 h [tfood-vareed2008], so exposure ends within about 2 days.

frequency.text: No outcome-based schedule exists for culinary use.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Culinary turmeric produces only nanomolar curcumin conjugates in blood; no systemic antioxidant effect shown.
audit.biases: Population 'curry eater' associations are confounded.
audit.newer_evidence: Pharmacokinetic data remain decisive [adiet-mahale2018].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

factors.name: Unneeded iron supplements / excess iron intake

entries.headline: Iron pills taken without a deficiency mostly pass unabsorbed into the colon, where 19 mg/day raised faecal free-radical production by ~40% and, in infant trials, shifted gut bacteria toward pathogens and inflammation; genetic studies link lifelong higher iron to shorter lifespan and more diabetes.

dose.effective: Take iron only to correct documented deficiency (ferritin below ~30 ug/L, or below ~50 ug/L with symptoms such as fatigue), then stop or reduce once ferritin is replete. Most iron-replete men and postmenopausal women need no supplemental iron; a multivitamin 'for men' or '50+' formula without iron is the sensible default.
dose.studied_range: 19 mg/day ferrous sulfate for 2 weeks (adults, gut markers); 2.5-12.5 mg/day in infant micronutrient powders; >100 mg/day high-dose supplements (cross-sectional microbiome data).
dose.too_much: IOM UL 45 mg/day elemental iron (GI side effects); EFSA set no UL but a safe level of 40 mg/day total iron for adults including pregnancy. Untargeted iron in malaria-endemic settings raised severe illness and death in young children. Never self-supplement with known or suspected haemochromatosis.
dose.timeframe: Gut changes within 2 weeks; systemic store build-up over years.
dose.notes: Absorption is regulated (hepcidin) but there is no excretion route, so stores accumulate in iron-replete people, especially men. Vitamin C taken with iron raises non-heme absorption; tea, coffee and calcium lower it.

entries.mechanism: Unabsorbed ferrous iron in the colon catalyses Fenton chemistry (Fe2+ + H2O2 -> hydroxyl radical) and lipid peroxidation, and favours iron-hungry Enterobacteriaceae over bifidobacteria and butyrate producers. Systemically, surplus iron expands the labile iron pool that feeds Fenton reactions and ferroptosis.
entries.interactions: Heme iron from red and processed meat acts similarly in the gut [processed-red-meat]. Do not pair high-dose vitamin C with iron in people with high stores [vitamin-c-status]. Overlaps with [iron-status-ferritin]; the opposite risk is [iron-deficiency]. Multivitamins often contain 8-18 mg iron [multivitamin-mineral].
entries.caveats: Faecal radical generation is an ex vivo assay and the infant microbiome trials were done in low-income settings with high pathogen loads; adult outcome data are thin. The harm signal is for iron the body does not need: in deficient people, including many pregnant women, iron is clearly beneficial.
entries.debate: Harm from untargeted iron is shown by infant trials (Pemba mortality [nut-sazawal2006]; Kenyan microbiome and calprotectin [nut-jaeggi2015]) and by gut-biology commentaries [nut-weiss2015, nut-simonytesjodin2019], with Mendelian randomization suggesting lifelong higher iron shortens lifespan [nut-daghlas2021]. On the other side, a 2023 meta-analysis found daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women still reduced iron-deficiency anaemia and low birthweight [nut-hansen2023], and EFSA could not identify a dose-response for chronic disease, setting only a conservative safe level [nut-efsa2024iron]. Adult evidence for harm at typical multivitamin doses (8-18 mg) is lacking.
