entries.title: Unneeded iron supplements / excess iron intake

timing.summary: Unneeded iron pills mostly pass into the colon, where they raise free-radical generation within 2 weeks; this gut effect clears within about 2 weeks of stopping. Body iron stores, by contrast, build and fall over months to years.

onset.text: 19 mg/day raised faecal free iron and radical generation during 2 weeks [tnut-lund1999].

full.text: Infant microbiome shifts were seen over 4 months of iron-fortified powders [tnut-jaeggi2015].

after_stopping.text: Faecal iron returned to baseline within 2 weeks of stopping [tnut-lund1999].

frequency.text: Without documented deficiency, avoid routine iron; when needed, alternate-day dosing lowers unabsorbed iron per dose (extrapolated) [tnut-stoffel2017].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Iron pills without deficiency raise faecal free-radical production and, in infant trials, shift gut bacteria toward pathogens; genetic studies link lifelong higher iron to shorter lifespan and more diabetes.
audit.biases: Adult evidence is mostly mechanistic or genetic; MR on serum iron [anut-daghlas2021] estimates lifelong exposure and may involve pleiotropy of iron-regulating variants, so it does not directly quantify the effect of a few years of supplements.
audit.newer_evidence: A natural experiment supports the genetic arm: HFE C282Y homozygotes (lifelong iron loading) in UK Biobank had more liver disease, arthritis and diabetes (OR 1.53 in men) and more incident morbidity [anut-pilling2019]. Against over-generalising, iron in iron-replete pregnancy still reduced anaemia and low birthweight [anut-hansen2023].
audit.bottom_line: Iron the body does not need is not harmless, but the clearest harm is from genetic overload; at multivitamin doses adult harm is unproven.

entries.headline: Not linked to worse semen quality. In young US men unprocessed red meat showed no association with any semen measure, and a Chinese case-control study linked higher unprocessed meat intake to lower odds of poor motility (OR 0.61). The negative meat signal for sperm comes from processed meat.

dose.effective: No evidence-based target. Normal portions of unprocessed red meat are compatible with sperm health; cooking method may matter more than the meat itself.
dose.studied_range: Food-frequency quartiles/tertiles of habitual intake.
dose.timeframe: ~2-3 months (one spermatogenic cycle) for any dietary change to show in semen.
dose.notes: Red meat is a dense source of zinc, vitamin B12, iron and carnitine, which sperm production needs. That matters most if intake is low (e.g. restrictive diets). In men who were not deficient, adding 30 mg/day zinc (with folic acid) did not improve semen or live birth in the large FAZST trial.

entries.mechanism: No direct human evidence that red meat improves spermatogenesis or spermiogenesis. The plausible route is nutrient supply (zinc, B12, iron, carnitine) in people with low intake. The oxidative concerns that apply to processed meat (nitrites, preformed N-nitroso compounds) do not apply to fresh meat, while high-heat or stir-fry cooking can add oxidized products.
entries.interactions: Contrast with [processed-meat]. High-heat cooking was associated with worse motility in the case-control study. Extra zinc on top of an adequate diet did not help ([folate-zinc]).
entries.caveats: Two observational studies with different populations; no trials. The case-control result could reflect overall diet or recall bias. Absence of harm is not proof of benefit.
entries.title: Unprocessed red meat (beef, pork, lamb)

timing.summary: There is no effect on semen to time: in young men, unprocessed red meat showed no association with any semen measure, while processed meat did [tleg-afeiche2014b]. If you change intake anyway, judge the result after one spermatogenic cycle of about 74-90 days.

onset.text: No measurable semen effect to appear [tleg-afeiche2014b].

full.text: Not applicable. Any dietary change would need about 74-90 days to show in semen, by analogy with measured exposure windows for spermatogenesis [tleg-russo2025].

after_stopping.text: Not applicable: nothing to reverse [tleg-afeiche2014b].

frequency.text: No schedule evidence and no semen signal to act on [tleg-afeiche2014b]. Gut-level effects of red meat (faecal nitrosation, TMAO) are a separate question handled under [processed-red-meat] and do respond within days to weeks [tleg-bingham2002, tleg-wang2019tmao].

sperm.late_start: Nothing to start: no benefit has been shown from reducing unprocessed red meat for semen quality [tleg-afeiche2014b].
sperm.text: No measured time course exists because no effect has been demonstrated.

timing.debate: Whether unprocessed red meat is harmless for fertility is a question of absent evidence rather than conflicting evidence; the general-health debate about red meat is live, with IARC's Group 2A classification [tleg-bouvard2015] against the NutriRECS panel's weak recommendation to continue current intake [tleg-johnston2019].

audit.claim: Unprocessed red meat is not linked to worse semen quality.
audit.biases: Absence of association in small observational studies, with recall bias in the case-control study [adiet-afeiche2014b, adiet-liu2022b].
audit.newer_evidence: Nothing newer on semen. For general health, the 2022 Burden of Proof review rated unprocessed red meat's links with disease as weak [adiet-lescinsky2022].
audit.bottom_line: A neutral rating fits: the evidence for harm from unprocessed red meat is weak.

entries.headline: Repeated night-time oxygen drops and re-oxygenation act like ischemia-reperfusion; CPAP treatment raised total antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis.

dose.effective: Get tested if you snore loudly, stop breathing during sleep, or have daytime sleepiness; use CPAP or other prescribed therapy nightly.
dose.studied_range: CPAP studies of weeks to months.
dose.timeframe: Changes within weeks to months of consistent CPAP use.
dose.notes: Weight loss often reduces apnea severity.

entries.mechanism: Cycles of hypoxia and re-oxygenation activate NADPH oxidase and xanthine oxidase and cause mitochondrial ROS bursts, much like ischemia-reperfusion injury.
entries.interactions: Strongly linked to [weight-loss]; worsened by [alcohol] at night.
entries.caveats: Total antioxidant capacity is a crude marker; studies are heterogeneous.
entries.title: Untreated obstructive sleep apnea

timing.summary: Effective CPAP lowers blood pressure and improves blood vessel function within weeks, and lowered an oxidative marker after 12 weeks in one trial but not after 8 weeks in a larger one. Stopping CPAP brings apnoea back within days and blood pressure up within two weeks.

onset.text: Blood-pressure and endothelial benefits are evident within 2 weeks (inferred from withdrawal) [tbody-kohler2011].

full.text: Plasma 8-isoprostane fell after 12 weeks of CPAP versus sham [tbody-alonsofernandez2009]; total antioxidant capacity rose across therapy durations [tbody-hosseini2023].

after_stopping.text: OSA returned within days and morning blood pressure rose +8.5/6.9 mmHg within 2 weeks [tbody-kohler2011], but blood oxidative markers did not rise in 2 weeks [tbody-stradling2015].

frequency.text: Nightly use; the benefit is lost within days of stopping [tbody-kohler2011].

timing.debate: CPAP lowered 8-isoprostane at 12 weeks [tbody-alonsofernandez2009] and raised antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis [tbody-hosseini2023], but a 153-person sham-controlled trial found no change in F2-isoprostanes after 2 months [tbody-pazymar2016] and withdrawal did not raise oxidative markers [tbody-stradling2015].

audit.claim: Night-time hypoxia-reoxygenation acts like ischaemia-reperfusion; CPAP raised total antioxidant capacity in a meta-analysis.
audit.biases: Marker studies are uncontrolled; adherence analyses suffer healthy-adherer bias.
audit.newer_evidence: The TAC finding stands [abody-hosseini2023], but in RCTs CPAP did not prevent cardiovascular events (SAVE, HR 1.10) [abody-mcevoy2016]; an IPD meta-analysis was null overall (HR 1.01), with benefit only in good adherers in an on-treatment analysis [abody-sanchezdelatorre2023].
audit.bottom_line: CPAP improves sleepiness, mood and some markers, but it has not been shown to prevent heart attacks or strokes in randomised trials.

factors.name: Uranium in well and tap water

entries.headline: Natural uranium in groundwater is under-recognised in US public and private water, especially in the West, Great Plains and in Hispanic and American Indian communities; it mainly affects kidney tubules and blood pressure in observational studies, with no clear effect on diabetes at low levels.

dose.effective: Test private wells in uranium-bearing regions together with arsenic; reverse osmosis or anion exchange removes uranium.
dose.studied_range: Finnish drilled wells median 25 ug/L (up to 1,500); US public systems mostly <30 ug/L.
dose.too_much: Finnish data suggest tubular effects without a clear threshold and a safe level possibly within 2-30 ug/L; some Navajo Nation wells exceeded US standards.
dose.timeframe: Not measured in intervention studies; kidney and blood-pressure associations reflect long-term intake.
dose.notes: Toxicity from natural uranium in water is chemical (kidney) rather than radiological.

entries.mechanism: Uranyl ions accumulate in proximal tubules and bone and cause oxidative stress and tubular injury in animals.
entries.interactions: Co-occurs with [arsenic-drinking-water] in private wells; the same reverse-osmosis systems remove both.
entries.caveats: Few cohorts with individual exposure; findings mix weak tubular markers and blood pressure; region-specific results vary in direction.
entries.debate: Tubular effects without a threshold were reported in Finnish well users [efw-kurttio2002], but a later Finnish study at higher exposures found no kidney cytotoxicity, only higher blood pressure [efw-kurttio2006]. Hypertension was linked in Strong Heart [efw-patterson2025], while diabetes was not in two cohorts [efw-spaur2026]. Water is a major driver of urinary uranium [efw-spaur2024], with environmental-justice concerns [efw-ravalli2022, efw-corlin2016].

factors.name: Urolithin A (supplement; gut metabolite of ellagitannins in pomegranate, berries, walnuts)

entries.headline: In company-funded RCTs, 500-1000 mg/day of urolithin A for 1-4 months improved muscle endurance or strength (about 12% for leg strength) and lowered CRP and acylcarnitines in older and middle-aged adults, but most primary endpoints were not met and trained runners gained no performance.

dose.effective: 500-1000 mg/day purified urolithin A (the Mitopure product in all major trials).
dose.studied_range: 250-1000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 4 months.
dose.too_much: No safety signal up to 1000 mg/day for 4 months; long-term data lacking.
dose.timeframe: Plasma and muscle biomarker changes by 4 weeks; muscle endurance differences at 2 months.
dose.notes: Ellagitannin foods only yield urolithin A if your gut bacteria can make it: across trials 5-25% of people make none and 10-50% partly divert to isourolithin A/urolithin B, and the distribution shifts with age. Taking urolithin A directly bypasses this metabotype problem.

entries.mechanism: Urolithin A, made by gut bacteria from ellagic acid, induces mitophagy (selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and mitochondrial gene expression; it is not a meaningful radical scavenger at the concentrations reached in plasma.
entries.interactions: Food precursors overlap [pomegranate], [walnuts-nuts], [blackberries] and [berries-other], but only help producers. Unlike high-dose vitamins C and E, there is no sign that it blunts training adaptations; in trained runners it lowered creatine kinase.
entries.caveats: All major human trials were sponsored by the manufacturer. In the 66-person JAMA Network Open trial the primary endpoints (6-minute walk, maximal muscle ATP production) were null; in the middle-aged trial peak power (primary) was null. Oxidative-damage markers have not been measured directly. The immune study reports 4-week changes in cell phenotypes, not infections.

key_numbers.label: Leg muscle strength gain, middle-aged adults (4 months)
People producing no urolithins (metabotype 0), upper bound across trials

entries.title: Urolithin A (supplement; gut metabolite of ellagitannins in pomegranate, berries, walnuts)

timing.summary: Urolithin A shifted blood and muscle mitochondrial markers within 4 weeks, muscle endurance by 2 months and strength by 4 months in company-funded trials. Four weeks did nothing for trained runners' performance.

onset.text: Plasma acylcarnitines and muscle gene expression changed after 4 weeks [tnut-andreux2019].

full.text: Muscle endurance at 2 months [tnut-liu2022]; strength (~12%) at 4 months [tnut-singh2022].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: All trials dosed daily [tnut-liu2022, tnut-singh2022].

timing.debate: Benefits in older and middle-aged adults at 2-4 months [tnut-liu2022, tnut-singh2022] contrast with no performance gain after 4 weeks in trained runners [tnut-whitfield2025].

audit.claim: In company-funded RCTs 500-1000 mg/day improved some muscle endurance or strength measures and lowered CRP, but most primary endpoints were missed.
audit.biases: All major trials sponsored by the manufacturer; primary endpoints null [anut-liu2022, anut-singh2022].
audit.newer_evidence: In trained runners 4 weeks gave no performance benefit [anut-whitfield2025]; no independent outcome trial found.
audit.bottom_line: Unchanged.

entries.headline: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 percentage points on average, and more when SDF starts high.

dose.effective: One procedure (microsurgical subinguinal varicocelectomy is the reference technique) in men with a palpable varicocele plus abnormal semen or high SDF.
dose.studied_range: 19 studies, 1070 men; SCSA, TUNEL and SCD all showed reductions.
dose.timeframe: Re-test semen/SDF about 3-6 months after surgery; one spermatogenic cycle is ~64-74 days.
dose.notes: AUA/ASRM: consider varicocelectomy in men trying to conceive with palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen (not azoospermia). EAU adds that the female partner should have good ovarian reserve, because the benefit takes months.

entries.mechanism: Removes venous reflux, restoring testicular cooling and oxygenation and cutting seminal ROS, which lowers oxidative DNA damage in newly made sperm.
entries.interactions: Lifestyle changes ([tobacco-smoking], [sauna]) should be made in parallel. If the female partner is older, time may favour going straight to ART, optionally with [testicular-sperm-icsi] or short abstinence [short-abstinence].
entries.caveats: The SDF drop is solid; the pregnancy benefit is less certain (Cochrane: pregnancy RR 1.55, low certainty; live birth uncertain). Not useful for subclinical varicocele with normal semen.
entries.title: Varicocele repair (microsurgical varicocelectomy or embolisation)

timing.summary: After varicocele repair, sperm DNA fragmentation falls within 3 months and a little more by 6 months, with no further gain at 12 months. Motile counts improve mostly in the first 3-6 months.

onset.text: DFI 3.7 points lower within 3 months [tsperm-wang2024]; total motile count up at 3-6 months [tsperm-masterson2019].

full.text: A further 1.5-point DFI fall by 6 months and no significant gain by 12 months [tsperm-wang2024]; no significant count gain after 3-6 months [tsperm-masterson2019]. Average total fall about 7 points [tsperm-liraneto2021].

after_stopping.text: Not applicable; the repair is permanent unless the varicocele recurs.

frequency.text: One procedure.

sperm.late_start: Surgery 2-4 weeks before achieves nothing for that cycle.
sperm.text: Repair must be followed by at least one full cycle; DFI keeps improving to about 6 months [tsperm-wang2024].

timing.debate: A pooled analysis suggests 6 months is the best time to conceive or test after surgery [tsperm-wang2024], but it rests on 4 studies; count data from 33 men show most of the gain by 3-6 months [tsperm-masterson2019].

audit.claim: Repairing a clinical varicocele lowers SDF by about 7 points, more when SDF starts high; pregnancy benefit less certain.
audit.biases: SDF studies are before-after without untreated controls (regression to the mean, since men are selected for high SDF); ART-outcome studies compare men who chose repair with men who did not (confounding by indication, healthy-user).
audit.newer_evidence: A 2025 meta-analysis of 86 studies found SDF fell 6.7 points at 3 months and 12.4 at 6 months after varicocelectomy, larger in grade II-III [afert-szabo2025]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 9 observational studies linked repair before ICSI with higher live birth (OR 2.07) [afert-palani2025], but Cochrane 2021 remains uncertain about live birth from randomised data (RR 2.27, 0.19-26.6) [afert-persad2021].
audit.bottom_line: The SDF drop is consistent; a live-birth gain is plausible but still rests mostly on non-randomised data.

factors.name: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)

entries.headline: Minute for minute, intervals raise VO2max and muscle mitochondria more than steady moderate exercise (about +1-3 mL/kg/min extra VO2max; 1.7-3.9x more mitochondrial gain per hour), and vigorous training improved redox markers where gentle training did not; total mitochondrial gains converge when volume is matched.

dose.effective: 75-150 min/week of vigorous activity, or 2-3 interval sessions/week, e.g. 4 x 4 min at 85-95% HRmax with 3 min easy between (similar to the ~90%-of-peak-heart-rate intervals used in Generation 100), or 4-6 x 4-6 min at >90% HRmax (Paulsen 2014). Sprint intervals (3 x 20 s all-out) work too.
dose.studied_range: Trials: 2-4 sessions/week for 2-16 weeks; Generation 100 used 2 sessions/week for 5 years in 70-77-year-olds.
dose.too_much: Oxidative load rises with intensity x volume. Ramping HIIT to daily hard sessions over 4 weeks cut mitochondrial respiration and worsened glucose tolerance. Keep hard sessions to about 2-3 per week with easy days between.
dose.timeframe: VO2max and mitochondrial gains within 2-6 weeks; antioxidant-enzyme changes in 6-12 weeks.
dose.notes: Intensity is one of the surest ways to abolish fitness 'non-response'. People with heart disease should get medical clearance first.

entries.mechanism: Higher intensity recruits more fibres and produces larger calcium, AMP/AMPK and ROS signals per minute (NOX2-derived ROS were required for full HIIT adaptation in mice), driving PGC-1alpha, Nrf2 and mitochondrial protein synthesis. Volume is a separate driver of mitochondrial content, while relative intensity matters more for mitochondrial respiratory function. Excess intensity x volume leads to sustained ROS, glutathione depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction.
entries.interactions: Same caution about [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training] (resveratrol blunted HIIT gains in two trials). Combines with [resistance-training]. The most efficient route to [cardiorespiratory-fitness]. Excess volume leads to [overtraining-ultraendurance]. In men, the one large semen RCT found moderate continuous training beat HIIT for sperm markers.
entries.caveats: Hard mortality data for HIIT specifically are thin: Generation 100's HIIT advantage was not statistically significant. Many HIIT-vs-moderate comparisons are small, short and not matched for energy. 'Zone 2 is special' and 'only intensity matters' are both overstatements.
entries.debate: Intensity versus volume is a live argument. MacInnis, Skelly and Gibala argue intensity matters more for mitochondrial content [exr-macinnis2019, exr-macinnis2017a], while Bishop's group argues volume matters more [exr-bishop2019, exr-granata2018]. A 353-study meta-regression found similar total mitochondrial gains for continuous (23%), HIIT (27%) and sprint training (27%) after adjustment, with intervals far more time-efficient [exr-molmen2025]. A 2025 review rejects the popular claim that 'Zone 2' is uniquely good for mitochondria in the general public [exr-storoschuk2025]. HIIT beats moderate training for VO2max by a small margin in healthy adults [exr-milanovic2015] and a larger one in cardiometabolic patients [exr-weston2014], but gives similar fat loss [exr-wewege2017]. For redox markers, vigorous protocols looked better [exr-torresrojo2025], but the meta-analysis held only 7 RCTs, and HIIT and moderate exercise carried the lowest risk of large oxidative damage when volume was moderate [exr-zhou2022].

entries.title: Vigorous exercise and high-intensity interval training (HIIT)

timing.summary: Interval sessions trigger mitochondrial signalling after the first bout and raise fitness within two weeks, with gains building over months. Fitness built this way needs intensity kept up to be maintained, and too much hard work too fast damages mitochondria.

onset.text: PGC-1alpha protein rose after one session and plateaued after 3-7 sessions, with VO2peak +12% after 7 interval sessions in 2 weeks [tbody-perry2010].

full.text: Across trials of 2 weeks or more, interval training raised VO2max ~5.5 mL/kg/min versus ~4.9 for continuous training [tbody-milanovic2015]; a long-term plateau is not well defined.

after_stopping.text: Same detraining as other aerobic training: recent gains are lost after more than 4 weeks [tbody-mujika2000b]; VO2max fell 7% in 3 weeks in trained people [tbody-coyle1984].

frequency.text: 2-3 hard sessions a week; maintaining fitness needs intensity kept [tbody-hickson1985]. Ramping load too quickly impaired mitochondrial function and glucose tolerance within the peak week [tbody-flockhart2021].

sperm.late_start: Unknown; only late maturation stages are covered.
sperm.text: Extrapolated from the ~64-day sperm production time [tbody-misell2006]; no reliable trial of interval training on semen exists.

timing.debate: Intervals give more fitness per minute [tbody-milanovic2015], but rapidly escalating high-intensity load reduced mitochondrial function [tbody-flockhart2021], so more is not always better on short timescales.

audit.claim: Intervals raise VO2max and mitochondria more per minute than steady exercise; hard mortality data for HIIT are thin.
audit.biases: Mostly RCT physiology, so confounding is not the main issue; small, short trials and unmatched energy expenditure are.
audit.newer_evidence: Generation 100 found a non-significant mortality advantage for HIIT over control (HR 0.63) [abody-stensvold2020], consistent with a possible but unproven benefit.
audit.bottom_line: The physiological benefits rest on trials and hold; a mortality benefit specific to HIIT remains unproven.

entries.headline: Correcting B12 or folate deficiency is essential (anaemia, neuropathy, neural tube defects), and folic acid cut first stroke by 21% in unfortified China; but lowering homocysteine with B vitamins did not prevent heart attacks or death in 71,422 trial participants, and high-dose folic acid plus B12 raised cancer in Norway. Women with higher B12 and folate before IVF had ~26 points higher live birth.

dose.effective: Folate RDA 400 ug DFE/day; anyone who could become pregnant: 400-800 ug folic acid daily from at least 1 month (ideally 3) before conception [folic-acid]. B12 RDA 2.4 ug/day; vegans need a reliable source every day (fortified foods or a B12 supplement); adults over 50 should get B12 from fortified foods or supplements.
dose.studied_range: Folic acid 0.4-5 mg/day; B12 0.4-1 mg/day in homocysteine-lowering trials.
dose.too_much: Folic acid UL 1000 ug/day (IOM and EFSA): high folic acid can mask B12 deficiency and let neuropathy progress. Norwegian trial of 0.8 mg folic acid + 0.4 mg B12 saw more cancer; 1 mg/day folic acid did not prevent adenomas and may have raised advanced lesions. No UL for B12.
dose.timeframe: Homocysteine falls within weeks; neural tube closes by day 28 after conception.
dose.notes: At risk of B12 deficiency: vegans, older adults (atrophic gastritis), metformin users (B12 ~57 pmol/L lower), long-term PPI or H2-blocker users (OR 1.65), bariatric surgery, pernicious anaemia, nitrous oxide use. Serum B12 is imperfect; methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are functional markers.

entries.mechanism: Folate (as 5-methyl-THF) and B12 (methionine synthase) remethylate homocysteine to methionine, sustaining SAM-dependent DNA methylation and thymidine synthesis for DNA repair. Homocysteine not remethylated can enter transsulfuration (B6-dependent) to cysteine, the rate-limiting precursor of glutathione. Elevated homocysteine auto-oxidises, generating H2O2, and impairs endothelial nitric oxide.
entries.interactions: Riboflavin is the FAD cofactor of MTHFR [riboflavin]. Folic acid is the core of [profertility-diet] and [folic-acid]. High-dose folic acid in men: [folate-zinc]. NAC and glycine bypass the transsulfuration route to glutathione [n-acetylcysteine] [glynac].
entries.caveats: The homocysteine hypothesis largely failed for heart attacks; benefits concentrate where folate status is low (unfortified populations). Fertility data are observational and from a fortified population.
entries.debate: Cochrane finds homocysteine lowering does not prevent MI or death but modestly reduces stroke [nut-marticarvajal2017]; CSPPT showed a 21% stroke reduction in an unfortified population [nut-huo2015], which an editorial argued outweighs earlier null trials [nut-stampfer2015]. Safety concerns come from excess cancer with folic acid + B12 in Norway [nut-ebbing2009] (editorial urged caution on interpretation [nut-drake2009]) and a possible rise in advanced adenomas [nut-cole2007], although EFSA judged cancer links insufficient while keeping the 1000 ug UL [nut-efsa2023folate]. For eggs, higher serum folate/B12 predicted IVF live birth [nut-gaskins2015] and folic acid predicted fecundability [nut-cueto2016], but no RCT tests B12 for fertility.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, top vs bottom quartile serum B12

entries.title: Vitamin B12 and folate status (homocysteine)

timing.summary: Folate status responds within months: plasma folate plateaus at about 3 months, red-cell folate keeps rising for 6 months, and both fall within months of stopping. B12 is stored in milligram amounts, so deficiency takes years to develop.

onset.text: Plasma folate up within 1 month, plateau at 3 months [tnut-hao2008].

full.text: Red-cell folate still rising at 6 months [tnut-daly1997].

after_stopping.text: Blood folate fell rapidly over 3 months [tnut-hao2008]; B12 deficiency symptoms can take several years [tnut-ods2025b12].

frequency.text: Single vs split daily folic acid made no difference [tnut-hao2008]; B12 stores tolerate gaps, but vegans need a reliable regular source [tnut-ods2025b12].

egg.late_start: One month before conception still raises folate before neural tube closure at day 28, but red-cell folate keeps rising for months [tnut-daly1997].
egg.text: Neural tube risk depends on red-cell folate at day 28 of pregnancy [tnut-crider2014]; serum folate and B12 before IVF were linked to live birth [tnut-gaskins2015].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Correcting deficiency is essential and folic acid cut stroke in unfortified China, but homocysteine lowering did not prevent heart attacks.
audit.biases: Homocysteine associations were confounded and genetic studies showed effect modification by population folate.
audit.newer_evidence: MTHFR effects on homocysteine and stroke were large only in low-folate Asia, and trials in folate-replete regions matched the genetic prediction of no benefit [abody-holmes2011].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: benefit depends on baseline folate status.

factors.name: Vitamin C + E in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia

entries.headline: Four large RCTs (VIP, WHO, US MFMU, DAPIT; about 14,700 women) found vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU did not prevent pre-eclampsia, and pooled data show more low birthweight, gestational hypertension and term rupture of membranes.

dose.effective: None; do not take high-dose C+E for pre-eclampsia.
dose.studied_range: 1000 mg vitamin C + 400 IU vitamin E daily from 9-22 weeks.
dose.too_much: Low birthweight RR 1.15 (VIP); term prelabour rupture of membranes RR 1.77 (Cochrane).
dose.timeframe: From second trimester to delivery in trials.
dose.notes: A standard prenatal vitamin at RDA levels is different and fine.

entries.mechanism: Placental ischaemia-reperfusion and syncytiotrophoblast stress generate oxidative stress in pre-eclampsia, but the disease is driven upstream by defective placentation and antiangiogenic factors that bulk antioxidants do not correct.
entries.interactions: Same failure pattern as [vitamin-c-e-combined] in fertility and cardiovascular trials; [aspirin-preeclampsia-egg] works through a different mechanism.
entries.caveats: A textbook antioxidant paradox: strong biomarker rationale, null hard outcomes.
entries.debate: DAPIT authors suggested women with low antioxidant status might still benefit (pre-eclampsia 15% vs 19%, NS) [fer-mccance2010], and Cochrane found less placental abruption (RR 0.64) [fer-rumbold2015e]. But the large trials were null [fer-poston2006, fer-villar2009, fer-roberts2010], including in low-nutrition populations, and meta-analysis found no benefit with some harms [fer-condeagudelo2011].
entries.title: Vitamin C + E in pregnancy to prevent pre-eclampsia

timing.summary: Vitamins C and E were tested to prevent pre-eclampsia starting either at 9-16 weeks or in the second trimester; neither start time worked. The placenta goes through a natural oxidative burst at 8-12 weeks, which some argued the trials missed, but the earlier-start trial was also null.

onset.text: Trials started at 9-16 weeks [tegg-roberts2010] or in the second trimester [tegg-poston2006]; no benefit appeared at either start.

full.text: No benefit at any point to delivery.

after_stopping.text: Not applicable (no benefit to persist).

frequency.text: High-dose vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU daily is not recommended in pregnancy; the VIP trial found more low birthweight [tegg-poston2006, tegg-rumbold2015].

timing.debate: The oxidative-stress model of pre-eclampsia places the key event at the onset of maternal placental blood flow (8-12 weeks) [tegg-jauniaux2000, tegg-burton2011], which led to the argument that antioxidants started in the second trimester were too late; however, starting at 9-16 weeks in 10,154 women was also null [tegg-roberts2010].

audit.claim: Large RCTs found vitamin C 1000 mg + E 400 IU did not prevent pre-eclampsia and raised some harms.
audit.biases: Not applicable; the claim rests on large RCTs.
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analysis of 9 trials (19,810 women) confirms RR 1.00 for pre-eclampsia with more gestational hypertension and membrane rupture [afert-condeagudelo2011].
audit.bottom_line: Holds: a textbook case of RCTs overturning the antioxidant hypothesis.

factors.name: Vitamin C + E supplements (fertility trials)
aliases: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

entries.headline: An uncontrolled study found 1 g vitamin C + 1 g vitamin E for 2 months lowered SDF and boosted the next ICSI's pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null.

dose.effective: If used before ICSI for high SDF: about 500-1000 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E daily for 2-3 months, under medical advice.
dose.studied_range: 1 g C + 1 g E daily for 2 months (38 men).
dose.too_much: Vitamin C contributed to opening protamine disulphide bridges (sperm decondensation) in one study; vitamin E above 1000 mg/day raises bleeding risk.
dose.timeframe: 2-3 months.
dose.notes: Both are in MOXI at lower doses, which was null.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin C is the main water-soluble antioxidant of seminal plasma; vitamin E protects PUFA-rich membranes from lipid peroxidation.
entries.interactions: See [male-antioxidant-combination] and [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: Greco 2005 was a before-after comparison after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean and cycle-to-cycle variation can explain much of the effect.
entries.title: Vitamins C and E

entries.headline: Vitamin E (600 mg/day) lowered follicular oxidative markers in a tiny study, and supplement use was associated with slightly shorter time to pregnancy in some subgroups, but there is no convincing RCT evidence of more live births.

dose.effective: Meet needs from food (nuts, seeds, vegetable oils, fruit, vegetables); routine high-dose supplements are not supported.
dose.studied_range: Vitamin E 600 mg/day (Tamura); vitamin C and E in mixed antioxidant trials in the Cochrane review.
dose.too_much: No benefit shown, so there is no reason to take high-dose supplements.
dose.notes: Typical prenatal vitamins already contain modest amounts.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin E is the main lipid-phase chain-breaking antioxidant; vitamin C regenerates it. Neither targets mitochondrial ROS production.
entries.interactions: Part of [female-antioxidant-supplements].
entries.caveats: Classic antioxidant paradox: big mechanistic story, no clinical proof.
entries.title: Vitamin E and vitamin C supplements

timing.summary: Vitamin C saturates blood within weeks and vitamin E has a plasma half-life of about 2.4 days, so both reach steady blood levels quickly. A 2-month course lowered sperm DNA fragmentation, which is shorter than a full sperm cycle.

onset.text: Vitamin E plasma half-life 57 h [tnut-leonard2005]; steady plasma levels within about 10 days (extrapolated).

full.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation fell from 22% to 9% after 2 months [tnut-greco2005].

after_stopping.text: Not measured for sperm; plasma vitamin E falls over days (extrapolated) [tnut-leonard2005].

frequency.text: Trials dosed daily [tnut-greco2005].

sperm.late_start: Not measured.
sperm.text: A 2-month course was enough in one trial [tnut-greco2005], suggesting protection of late-stage sperm; Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: An uncontrolled study found 1 g C + 1 g E lowered sperm DNA fragmentation and boosted the next ICSI pregnancy rate, but controlled trials of similar mixes are null; no RCT shows more live births in women.
audit.biases: Greco 2005 is a before-after design after a failed cycle, so regression to the mean drives much of the effect [anut-greco2005]. Female data rest on a Cochrane review that included trials later retracted [anut-showell2020].
audit.newer_evidence: MOXI found no semen or DNA-fragmentation benefit and numerically fewer live births (15% vs 24%) [anut-steiner2020]; Cochrane 2022 found no effect in low-risk-of-bias trials [anut-deligny2022]; a 2025 meta-analysis of 50 studies found no supplement improved pregnancy or live birth [anut-michaelsen2025].
audit.bottom_line: Controlled trials don't support high-dose vitamin C and E for men with high DNA fragmentation before ICSI.

factors.name: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

entries.headline: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day (white cells saturate at 100 mg), easily reached from foods; extra beyond that is excreted and high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.

dose.effective: About 200 mg/day from food: e.g. 1 red pepper, or 2 kiwifruit, or 1 orange + 1 cup strawberries.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; at 1000 mg/day oxalate and urate excretion rise (kidney stone risk).
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: Benefit is concentrated in people with low intake (smokers, low produce eaters).

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant and regenerates vitamin E; kiwifruit also raised lymphocyte DNA resistance to H2O2 ex vivo beyond what its vitamin C explained.
entries.interactions: Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption (good if iron-deficient; avoid iron + vitamin C supplements in iron overload, see [iron-excess]). High-dose vitamin C + E blunted exercise adaptation (covered in exercise sections).
entries.caveats: In the Cochrane review vitamin C supplements had no effect on mortality; beta-carotene and vitamin E increased it.

key_numbers.label: Dose at which plasma vitamin C plateaus

entries.title: Vitamin C foods (citrus, kiwi, peppers, strawberries)

timing.summary: Plasma vitamin C is tightly regulated: it rises steeply between 30 and 100 mg/day and saturates at about 400-1000 mg/day, with excess excreted. The body pool fills at about 100 mg/day, and turnover slows when intake is low.

onset.text: Not timed in verified abstracts; plasma rises the same day after a dose.

full.text: Extrapolated: inpatient depletion-repletion studies stepped through seven doses over 4-6 months, implying steady state within a few weeks at each dose [tnut-levine1996, tnut-levine2001].

after_stopping.text: Half-life lengthens as intake falls [tnut-kallner1979], so plasma drops quickly from saturation but the remaining pool is conserved; exact times not in verified abstracts.

frequency.text: Water-soluble with saturable absorption: daily food sources keep tissues saturated [tnut-levine1996].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Plasma vitamin C saturates near 200 mg/day from food; high-dose pills show no mortality benefit.
audit.biases: None material; depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics are experimental [adiet-levine1996].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane supplement data unchanged [adiet-bjelakovic2012].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate.

entries.headline: Plasma vitamin C rises steeply between 30 and 100 mg/day and plateaus by about 200 mg/day; about 7% of Americans (more among smokers and low-income groups) are deficient, but once tissues are saturated, extra vitamin C did not lower F2-isoprostanes at any dose up to 2500 mg/day.

dose.effective: About 100-200 mg/day from food (e.g. one red pepper, two kiwifruit, or an orange plus a cup of strawberries). Smokers need at least 35 mg/day more than non-smokers. RDA 90 mg men, 75 mg women.
dose.studied_range: 30-2500 mg/day in inpatient depletion-repletion pharmacokinetics.
dose.too_much: UL 2000 mg/day (IOM; diarrhoea). Doses above ~400 mg/day have no evident value; oxalate excretion rises at 1000 mg/day, and supplements are linked to kidney stones in men. EFSA set no UL.
dose.timeframe: Steady state in 2-3 weeks.
dose.notes: At risk of deficiency: smokers, low fruit and vegetable intake, alcohol use disorder, restrictive diets, dialysis.

entries.mechanism: Ascorbate is the main water-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant, regenerates vitamin E, and is a cofactor for collagen and carnitine synthesis and iron absorption. Tissue and white-cell uptake is transporter-limited, so above saturation extra intake is excreted.
entries.interactions: Food sources are covered in [vitamin-c-foods]; pills in [vitamin-c-supplement]. Raises non-heme iron absorption (useful in [iron-deficiency], unhelpful with high [iron-status-ferritin]). High-dose C plus E belongs to [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
entries.caveats: The 'more is better' view rests on observational associations; in saturated people neither oxidative-stress biomarkers nor outcomes improve with more.
entries.debate: Levine's pharmacokinetic studies argue for ~200 mg/day and no value above ~400 mg [nut-levine1996, nut-levine2001], while Carr and Frei argued from epidemiology for ~120 mg/day [nut-carr1999]; the IOM settled on 75-90 mg [nut-iom2000]. Both camps agree megadoses add nothing for replete people, and limited evidence links vitamin C supplements to kidney stones [nut-oconnor2022].

entries.title: Vitamin C status (deficiency vs saturation)

timing.summary: Plasma vitamin C is tightly regulated: it rises steeply between 30 and 100 mg/day and saturates at about 400-1000 mg/day, with excess excreted. The body pool fills at about 100 mg/day, and turnover slows when intake is low.

onset.text: Not timed in verified abstracts.

full.text: Extrapolated: steady state within a few weeks at each dose step [tnut-levine1996, tnut-levine2001]; pool of about 20 mg/kg reached at about 100 mg/day [tnut-kallner1979].

after_stopping.text: Half-life is longer at low intake [tnut-kallner1979]; exact depletion times not in verified abstracts.

frequency.text: Daily intake of about 100-200 mg from food keeps cells saturated [tnut-levine1996, tnut-levine2001].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Plasma vitamin C plateaus at ~200 mg/day; once saturated, more vitamin C does not lower F2-isoprostanes; 'more is better' rests on observational data.
audit.biases: Plasma vitamin C is a marker of fruit and vegetable intake, smoking and SES (confounding).
audit.newer_evidence: Measured plasma vitamin C predicted lower diabetes risk but genetically predicted vitamin C did not (HR 1.03) [abody-zheng2021]; genetic estimates for heart disease and mortality were non-significant [abody-kobylecki2015].
audit.bottom_line: Holds and is strengthened: high plasma vitamin C mostly marks a healthy diet.

entries.headline: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs. Shortens colds by about 8% and halves cold risk only under extreme physical stress. About 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men.

dose.effective: Body stores saturate with diet alone: cells saturate at ~100 mg/day and plasma at ~1,000 mg/day. 1-2 servings of fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C cover the steep part of the curve (30-100 mg).
dose.studied_range: 120 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 500 mg/day (PHS II) for outcomes; 200 mg to 2 g/day for colds
dose.too_much: ≥1,000 mg/day: about twice the kidney-stone risk in men (RR 1.95); 1 g/day blunted endurance-training adaptations.
dose.timeframe: Outcome trials ran for ~8 years with no effect
dose.notes: Oral absorption is tightly controlled (1.25 g oral peak ~135 µmol/L vs ~885 µmol/L IV), so megadoses mostly end up in urine. Pharmacological levels need IV dosing.

entries.mechanism: Water-soluble electron donor that regenerates vitamin E and is a cofactor for many enzymes. A true antioxidant at physiological levels, but once someone is replete, extra intake does not raise tissue levels and cannot compete with peroxiredoxins and GPx for H2O2. Large doses can blunt ROS-dependent training signals (PGC-1α, mitochondrial biogenesis).
entries.interactions: Taken around training it can cancel adaptive signalling, the same issue as [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Combined with vitamin E it showed no benefit in PHS II. Correcting deficiency is useful; adding more on top of a vegetable-rich diet adds nothing measurable.
entries.caveats: The 'megadose vitamin C' claims come from oral pharmacokinetics that cannot reach the plasma levels seen with IV dosing. Cold prevention works only for marathon runners, skiers and soldiers in subarctic conditions. Kidney-stone risk is relevant for men and people prone to stones.
entries.title: Vitamin C supplements (ascorbic acid)

timing.summary: Oral vitamin C cannot push plasma much above about 200 umol/L because absorption falls and excretion rises above about 500 mg per dose. Above that, extra vitamin C is mostly excreted.

onset.text: Plasma peaks within hours of a dose (1.25 g gave 135 umol/L) [tnut-padayatty2004].

full.text: Plasma saturates at about 400-1000 mg/day [tnut-levine1996, tnut-levine2001].

after_stopping.text: Excess above saturation is excreted; return to food-level steady state not timed in verified abstracts.

frequency.text: If used, split doses absorb better than one large dose because bioavailability falls above 500 mg (extrapolated) [tnut-levine1996].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs; shortens colds about 8%; about 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men; megadoses need IV dosing.
audit.biases: The kidney-stone figure (RR 1.95) is from one Swedish cohort [anut-thomas2013], open to confounding by who takes high-dose supplements and to self-report error. The outcome-null findings are from RCTs [anut-sesso2008] and the cold data from a Cochrane review [anut-hemila2013].
audit.newer_evidence: A larger US analysis of three cohorts replicated a smaller kidney-stone association in men only (HR 1.19 for 1000 mg/day or more supplemental; none in women) [anut-ferraro2016]. Mendelian randomization found genetically higher plasma ascorbate did not lower coronary disease [anut-luo2021]. The IV megadose route has now been tested in a large RCT: in sepsis, IV vitamin C increased death or persistent organ dysfunction (RR 1.21) [anut-lamontagne2022].
audit.bottom_line: Oral vitamin C beyond what food provides does not prevent chronic disease; high doses carry a modest kidney-stone risk in men, and IV megadoses are not harmless.

entries.headline: In a 330-man RCT, high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen quality in men with low vitamin D, though live birth rose in a small oligozoospermic subgroup.

dose.effective: Correct deficiency (25OHD <50 nmol/L) for general health; not a sperm treatment.
dose.studied_range: 300,000 IU loading dose then 1400 IU/day plus 500 mg calcium for 150 days.
dose.too_much: Avoid chronic intake above 4000 IU/day without monitoring.
dose.timeframe: 150 days studied.

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in testis and sperm; proposed effects on calcium signalling and inhibin B.
entries.caveats: The subgroup benefit is hypothesis-generating only.
entries.title: Vitamin D

entries.headline: Low vitamin D is linked to poorer IVF results in cohort studies, but randomized trials in deficient women (630 and 876 women) found supplementation did not raise pregnancy or live birth (52% vs 50%), so the link is probably confounding by overall health.

dose.effective: Correct a known deficiency for general health; it is not an IVF treatment. Randomized trials in deficient women found no gain in pregnancy or live birth, and the Endocrine Society (2024) advises against routine 25(OH)D testing in healthy adults.
dose.studied_range: Observational: replete vs deficient 25(OH)D. RCTs: a single 600,000 IU dose in 630 deficient women; 4000 IU/day in 876 women with PCOS.
dose.too_much: Avoid unsupervised megadoses.
dose.timeframe: Not applicable for IVF outcomes; see the Timing card for how fast blood levels change.
dose.notes: The cohort link most likely reflects overall health (confounding).

entries.mechanism: Vitamin D receptors are present in granulosa cells and endometrium; vitamin D influences AMH signalling and immune tolerance.
entries.interactions: Part of [profertility-diet].
entries.caveats: Observational links are confounded by overall health, BMI and outdoor activity, and the randomized trials did not confirm them.

key_numbers.label: IVF live birth, replete vs deficient

entries.title: Vitamin D (correcting deficiency)

timing.summary: Blood 25(OH)D has a half-life of about 2 weeks, so daily or weekly doses reach a new steady level in about 2-3 months, while fat stores keep levels up long after a large dose. Large intermittent boluses spike levels and were linked to more falls and less benefit than daily dosing in several trials.

onset.text: 25(OH)D rose by day 7 with daily, weekly or monthly dosing [tnut-ishshalom2008].

full.text: Extrapolated from a 15-day half-life: about 75 days to steady state [tnut-jones2014]; daily, weekly and monthly dosing converged at 2 months [tnut-ishshalom2008]; winter trial ran 20 weeks [tnut-heaney2003].

after_stopping.text: 25(OH)D3 half-life about 15 days [tnut-jones2014], but stored vitamin D (body half-life ~2 months) [tnut-jones2008] kept 25(OH)D above placebo 12 months after a 500,000 IU dose [tnut-sanders2010].

frequency.text: Daily or weekly doses are preferred: bolus doses gave no respiratory protection [tnut-martineau2017] and no cancer-mortality benefit [tnut-keum2022], and an annual 500,000 IU dose raised falls, most in the first 3 months [tnut-sanders2010].

sperm.late_start: A loading dose raises 25(OH)D within days, but semen did not improve even after 150 days [tnut-blombergjensen2018].
sperm.text: Correcting deficiency did not improve semen quality [tnut-blombergjensen2018]; Sperm take about 64 days to form (42-76 days in a labelling study) plus epididymal transit [tnut-misell2006, tnut-heller1963].

egg.late_start: A clinician-supervised loading dose can correct deficiency within weeks (extrapolated) [tnut-ishshalom2008].
egg.text: Vitamin D-replete women had more IVF live births [tnut-chu2018]; reaching steady state takes about 2-3 months [tnut-jones2014].

timing.debate: Several trials and meta-analyses favour daily dosing over boluses [tnut-martineau2017, tnut-keum2022, tnut-sanders2010, tnut-bischoff2016, tnut-hollis2013], but a short trial found equal blood levels across schedules [tnut-ishshalom2008], the 2025 meta-analysis found no effect modification by frequency [tnut-jolliffe2025, tnut-jolliffe2021], monthly dosing borderline reduced cardiovascular events [tnut-thompson2023], and daily 2000 IU was null in VITAL [tnut-manson2019] while monthly dosing in D-Health showed a cancer-mortality signal [tnut-neale2022].

audit.claim: Vitamin D-replete women have about 33% higher odds of IVF live birth than deficient women, RCTs show only a chemical-pregnancy gain, so test and correct deficiency before IVF (general impact 2); in men high-dose vitamin D did not improve semen.
audit.biases: The IVF association [anut-chu2018] is observational and exposed to reverse causation and confounding: low 25(OH)D tracks obesity, inactivity, less time outdoors, inflammation and chronic illness, and a systematic review of 290 cohorts and 172 trials concluded low 25(OH)D is mainly a marker of ill health because trials did not reproduce cohort associations even in people starting below 50 nmol/L [anut-autier2014]; a letter questioned whether the IVF association had been demonstrated at all [anut-iliuta2018]. Causal genetic evidence is weaker than it looked: the 2021 non-linear Mendelian randomization paper suggesting deficiency causally raised mortality was retracted and republished in 2024 with null results at every 25(OH)D level [anut-sofianopoulou2021, anut-erfc2024], because the residual stratification method is biased when the genetic effect on 25(OH)D varies [anut-burgess2023]; a similar 2022 analysis using the same method [anut-sutherland2022] carries the same caveat.
audit.newer_evidence: Fertility: a 2021 double-blind RCT in 630 women with 25(OH)D below 30 ng/mL found a 600,000 IU dose did not raise clinical pregnancy (RR 0.91) in any subgroup [anut-somigliana2021], and a 2026 BMJ multicentre RCT of 876 women with PCOS and mean 25(OH)D of 16 ng/mL found 4000 IU/day before IVF doubled 25(OH)D but left live birth unchanged (52.0% vs 50.2%; RR 1.03) [anut-hu2026]; these supersede the small 2022 trial-sequential meta-analysis [anut-zhou2022]. Male: the 330-man RCT remains null for semen quality [anut-blomberg2018]. General health: VITAL (2019) [anut-manson2019], D-Health (2022 mortality HR 1.04; 2023 CVD HR 0.91, borderline) [anut-neale2022, anut-thompson2023] and DO-HEALTH (2020) [anut-bischoffferrari2020] were null on primary outcomes. The Endocrine Society (2024) now suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing and against supplementing above the DRI in healthy adults under 75 [anut-demay2024]. On the other side, 2026 UK Biobank target-trial emulations argue the big trials enrolled mostly replete people and predict real benefit in deficient people [anut-wang2026a, anut-wang2026b], but these rely on the same observational associations that trials and corrected MR have not confirmed.
audit.bottom_line: Correcting true deficiency is reasonable for bone and general health, but there is now good randomized evidence that vitamin D does not raise IVF live birth, even in women with low levels; the observational IVF link is probably confounding.

entries.headline: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants; 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer by 17% and haemorrhagic stroke by 22%; meta-analyses disagree on whether high doses slightly raise overall mortality.

dose.effective: No supplemental dose has shown an outcome benefit; get vitamin E from food (nuts, seeds, plant oils).
dose.studied_range: 50 mg/day (ATBC) to 400 IU/day (HOPE, SELECT) or 600 IU every other day (WHS); 200-3,200 IU in biomarker studies
dose.too_much: ≥400 IU/day: +39 deaths per 10,000 (meta-analysis); risk rises above ~150 IU/day. Prostate cancer HR 1.17 at 400 IU/day (SELECT).
dose.timeframe: Lowering F2-isoprostanes needed ≥1,600 IU/day for 16 weeks; outcome trials ran 4.5-10 years
dose.notes: Doses used in outcome trials (400 IU) were too low to change oxidative-stress markers but high enough for bleeding effects. USPSTF grade D (recommends against).

entries.mechanism: Lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes and LDL. In replete people extra intake does not lower lipid peroxidation at practical doses. The pattern of more hemorrhagic and fewer ischemic strokes is consistent with an antithrombotic effect, though the exact mechanism was not established in these trials.
entries.interactions: Effect on prostate cancer depended on selenium status (risk raised in low-selenium men) [selenium-supplement]. Combined with vitamin C it blunted exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gains [vitamin-c-supplement]. Combined with NAC it accelerated tumour growth in mice [n-acetylcysteine].
entries.caveats: Observational data (supplement users had less heart disease) were confounded by healthy-user bias, and RCTs reversed the conclusion. WHS showed a 24% reduction in CV death as a secondary outcome, which was not replicated. Hemorrhagic stroke risk matters for people on anticoagulants.
entries.title: Vitamin E supplements (alpha-tocopherol)

timing.summary: Plasma vitamin E turns over in days (half-life about 2.4 days), but tissues lag for months and fat stores take 2 years or more to reach a new steady state. Harm signals also played out over years.

onset.text: Plasma half-life 57 h, so plasma levels shift within a week [tnut-leonard2005].

full.text: Tissues lagged plasma after 41 days and matched it only after about a year [tnut-burton1998]; adipose needed 2 years or more [tnut-handelman1994].

after_stopping.text: Adipose ratio fell only gradually over a year after stopping [tnut-handelman1994]; in a radiotherapy trial, excess second cancers did not persist after supplementation ended [tnut-bairati2005].

frequency.text: No supplemental schedule shows benefit; prostate-cancer excess emerged with longer follow-up in SELECT [tnut-klein2011].

timing.debate: In SELECT the prostate-cancer excess became clearer with longer follow-up [tnut-klein2011], whereas in a radiotherapy trial the second-cancer excess was limited to the supplementation period [tnut-bairati2005].

audit.claim: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants; 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer 17% and haemorrhagic stroke, and high doses slightly raise mortality.
audit.biases: The original belief in vitamin E came from cohorts where supplement users were healthier (healthy-user bias); RCTs reversed it [anut-hope2000, anut-lee2005, anut-sesso2008, anut-klein2011]. The mortality part of the claim rests on trial-level meta-analysis [anut-miller2005, anut-bjelakovic2012], which is sensitive to which trials are pooled and how doses are modelled.
audit.newer_evidence: The no-benefit and prostate-cancer findings hold [anut-klein2011], and USPSTF kept a grade D recommendation in 2022 [anut-uspstf2022]. Haemorrhagic stroke harm is supported by a 9-trial meta-analysis (RR 1.22) [anut-schurks2010]. The mortality signal is contested: a Bayesian re-analysis concluded vitamin E is unlikely to affect mortality at any dose [anut-berry2009], and a 57-trial meta-analysis with 246,371 people found RR 1.00 with no dose-response [anut-abner2011]. Proponents argue the trials were flawed because doses did not lower oxidative stress [anut-blumberg2007], but the dose needed (1600 IU/day or more) is itself a bleeding-risk dose. Mendelian randomization found no protective effect of genetically higher tocopherols on coronary disease [anut-luo2021].
audit.bottom_line: Vitamin E pills do not prevent heart disease or cancer and raise prostate cancer and haemorrhagic stroke risk; whether they raise overall mortality is genuinely disputed and probably small at most.

factors.name: VOCs and formaldehyde (new furniture, paint, air fresheners, candles, incense)

entries.headline: Formaldehyde and other VOCs from new materials, fragranced products and burning are linked to childhood asthma (OR about 1.1-1.2 per 10 ug/m3 formaldehyde) and urinary oxidative-DNA markers, but the evidence is mostly cross-sectional; heavy long-term incense use is linked to respiratory squamous-cell cancers.

dose.effective: Air out new furniture, flooring and freshly painted rooms (VOCs are highest at first occupancy and fall over months); choose low-VOC paint and solid wood or certified low-formaldehyde composite wood; skip plug-in air fresheners and fragranced sprays; burn candles and incense rarely, away from draughts, with a window open; do not rely on potted plants.
dose.studied_range: Asthma meta-analyses spanned roughly 10-60 ug/m3 indoor formaldehyde (median of studies about 22.5 ug/m3).
dose.too_much: WHO indoor guideline for formaldehyde: 0.1 mg/m3 (0.08 ppm), set to prevent sensory irritation and considered protective against nasal cancer. Formaldehyde is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen at occupational levels.
dose.timeframe: Concentrations fall within hours of ventilating; emissions from new materials decline over months to about a year.
dose.notes: Terpenes from essential oils and "natural" air fresheners react with ozone indoors to make formaldehyde and fine particles. Plants would need 10-1000 per m2 of floor to matter.

entries.mechanism: Formaldehyde and acrolein are reactive aldehydes that form DNA and protein adducts and deplete glutathione; aromatic VOCs (benzene, toluene) are metabolized by CYP2E1 with ROS release. In 128 Chinese adults, 16 urinary VOC metabolites tracked urinary 8-OHdG and 8-OHG after false-discovery correction [eia-qian2021].
entries.interactions: Ventilation ([ventilation-co2]) lowers every indoor-sourced VOC; activated-carbon filters adsorb some VOCs, HEPA alone does not ([hepa-air-purifier]). Candles and incense also emit particles like [indoor-combustion-smoke]. Occupational formaldehyde and solvents: see [occupational-solvents].
entries.caveats: Home formaldehyde correlates with new construction, renovation, damp, smoking and income; the asthma meta-analyses pool mostly cross-sectional studies with large heterogeneity. Fragranced-product harm is mostly inferred from emission chemistry, not health outcomes. The reproductive data for formaldehyde come from occupational settings (see [occupational-solvents] and [occupational-solvents]).
entries.debate: Three meta-analyses agree on a modest asthma association (OR 1.17, 1.10 and 1.20 per 10 ug/m3) [eia-mcgwin2010, eia-yu2020, eia-lam2021], but all note that most studies are cross-sectional, so the direction of causation and confounding by housing cannot be excluded [eia-mcgwin2010]. Whether the WHO 0.1 mg/m3 guideline protects against cancer is argued from non-linear animal dose-response [eia-nielsen2010]; linear unit-risk approaches give lower acceptable levels. For incense, a 61,320-person cohort found more respiratory squamous carcinomas but no overall lung cancer excess [eia-friborg2008]. The claim that houseplants clean indoor air is contradicted by a quantitative re-analysis of the chamber studies [eia-cummings2020].

entries.title: VOCs and formaldehyde (new furniture, paint, air fresheners, candles, incense)

timing.summary: Indoor VOCs and formaldehyde follow their sources: concentrations fall within hours of ventilating, while emissions from new building materials decline over the first months to a year [eia-yamaguchi2006]. The health effects studied (asthma, oxidative markers) reflect ongoing exposure.

onset.text: Urinary VOC metabolites and oxidative DNA markers co-vary over days in repeated samples [eia-qian2021].

full.text: New-home VOC concentrations were highest at first occupancy and declined over a year of monthly sampling [eia-yamaguchi2006].

after_stopping.text: Not measured for health outcomes; airborne levels fall within hours of removing the source or ventilating, and VOCs are metabolized within hours to days.

frequency.text: Avoid frequent fragranced sprays, candles and incense; ventilate continuously for the first months after new furniture, flooring or paint [eia-yamaguchi2006].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

entries.headline: A 10-15 minute walk after each main meal lowered post-meal glucose 12% more than one daily 30-minute walk in type 2 diabetes (22% after dinner), and post-meal exercise reliably blunts glucose spikes (effect size about -0.3); oxidative-stress benefits are inferred, not measured directly.

dose.effective: 10-15 min of easy-to-brisk walking after each main meal, especially the largest (often evening) meal; longer bouts (over 30 min) did more in meta-analysis.
dose.studied_range: Crossover trials: 2-min walks every 20-30 min, 10 min after each meal, 3 x 15 min post-meal, up to 60 min.
dose.too_much: None known at walking intensity.
dose.timeframe: Acute: lowers the glucose curve of that meal and 24-h mean glucose; long-term HbA1c effects are not well established.
dose.notes: Effects are biggest in people with type 2 diabetes, prediabetes or obesity and after carbohydrate-heavy meals. Light walking beat standing breaks. Evidence on the ideal start time is inconsistent.

entries.mechanism: Contracting muscle takes up glucose independently of insulin (AMPK, NOX2-ROS and calcium-mediated GLUT4 translocation), flattening the post-meal glucose and triglyceride peaks that drive mitochondrial superoxide, NADPH oxidase activation and AGE formation.
entries.interactions: Directly supports [glycemic-control] and blunts spikes from [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] meals. A practical way to break [sedentary-time]. Complements, but does not replace, [aerobic-exercise-moderate].
entries.caveats: Most trials are short crossover studies with continuous glucose monitors in small groups; long-term outcome trials are lacking. Oxidative-marker evidence is limited to small studies with crude markers.
entries.debate: That post-meal activity lowers glucose is well replicated [exr-reynolds2016, exr-dipietro2013, exr-kang2023, exr-buffey2022, exr-dunstan2012]. Debated: whether timing or just total movement matters. Breaks beat continuous exercise only modestly once energy expenditure is matched [exr-loh2020], and one meta-analysis found longer bouts mattered more than early start times [exr-kang2023]. Whether lower glucose spikes translate into less oxidative stress in people is mostly inferred; a small crossover found only trends in a crude oxidative marker [exr-takahashi2015].

entries.title: Walking after meals

timing.summary: A walk after a meal lowers that meal's glucose rise within the hour and trims the whole day's average. The effect does not carry over much, so it works best as a daily habit after main meals.

onset.text: Lowers the glucose curve of the meal it follows [tbody-reynolds2016, tbody-kang2023].

full.text: Also lowers 24-h mean glucose [tbody-kang2023]; three 15-min walks after meals improved 24-h glycaemia [tbody-reynolds2016].

after_stopping.text: Extrapolated: single-bout effects on insulin action last at most 1-2 days [tbody-hawley2008].

frequency.text: After each main meal, especially the largest; bouts over 30 min did more [tbody-kang2023].

timing.debate: Most advice is to walk straight after eating [tbody-reynolds2016], while a meta-analysis suggested starting after the first hour may lower 24-h glucose more [tbody-kang2023].

audit.claim: A 10-15 minute walk after meals lowers post-meal glucose more than one daily walk; oxidative benefits are inferred.
audit.biases: Randomised crossover trials, so confounding is minimal; small samples and short duration are the limits.
audit.newer_evidence: The key randomised crossover showed 12% lower post-meal glucose with after-meal walks [abody-reynolds2016]; no newer trial overturns it.
audit.bottom_line: Holds for glucose; long-term outcome and oxidative-stress effects are untested.

entries.headline: A handful a day (30 g) lowers LDL and apoB and, in PREDIMED, cut major CVD events by ~28%; walnuts improved endothelial function, but direct oxidation markers were unchanged in several trials.

dose.effective: 30 g (a small handful) of mixed nuts or walnuts daily.
dose.studied_range: 30 g/day mixed nuts (PREDIMED); walnuts replacing ~32% of monounsaturated-fat energy for 4 weeks; 26 walnut trials (1059 people).
dose.too_much: Calories; walnut-enriched diets did not cause weight gain in trials.
dose.timeframe: 4 weeks for lipids and endothelial function.
dose.notes: Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid and gamma-tocopherol.

entries.mechanism: Lipid lowering (fewer oxidizable LDL particles), gamma-tocopherol, ellagitannins (converted to urolithins), ALA.
entries.interactions: Walnut PUFAs are oxidizable; store nuts cool and dark. Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet].
entries.caveats: In the walnut endothelial trial, oxidation biomarkers did not differ from the Mediterranean control diet; in PREDIMED the nut arm did not improve LDL oxidation traits (the EVOO arm did).

key_numbers.label: PREDIMED major CVD events HR, MedDiet + nuts

entries.title: Walnuts and other nuts

entries.headline: Two RCTs found that adding 60-75 g of nuts a day improved sperm vitality, motility and morphology, and one also lowered sperm DNA fragmentation.

dose.effective: 60 g/day mixed nuts (walnuts, almonds, hazelnuts) or 75 g/day walnuts (about a large handful to two handfuls), added to the usual diet.
dose.studied_range: 60 g/day for 14 weeks (FERTINUTS, n=119); 75 g/day walnuts for 12 weeks (n=117).
dose.too_much: 75 g walnuts is about 490 kcal; swap for other snacks to avoid weight gain. Avoid if allergic.
dose.timeframe: 12-14 weeks.
dose.notes: Unsalted, unroasted or dry-roasted nuts were used. Walnuts are rich in alpha-linolenic acid (plant omega-3).

entries.mechanism: Provides ALA omega-3, vitamin E, polyphenols, magnesium, selenium and zinc; raised blood omega-3 and correlated with lower sperm aneuploidy; FERTINUTS showed lower SDF and miR-34b-3p expression.
entries.interactions: Overlaps with [mediterranean-diet] and [omega3-fish].
entries.caveats: Healthy young men on Western diets; not infertile men; no pregnancy outcomes; FERTINUTS was partly funded by the nut industry.
entries.title: Walnuts and mixed nuts

timing.summary: Nuts lowered oxidized LDL within 3 months and improved sperm quality, including DNA fragmentation, after 12-14 weeks, about one full sperm cycle. Long-term cardiovascular benefit in PREDIMED accrued over about 5 years.

onset.text: Oxidized LDL fell after 3 months on a Mediterranean diet with 30 g/day nuts [tfood-fito2007].

full.text: Sperm vitality, motility and morphology improved after 12 weeks of 75 g/day walnuts [tfood-robbins2012], and count plus DNA fragmentation after 14 weeks of 60 g/day nuts [tfood-salashuetos2018]; CVD events lower over a median 4.8 years [tfood-estruch2018].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: All trials used a daily handful or more [tfood-robbins2012, tfood-salashuetos2018].

sperm.late_start: Unknown: the trials measured only at the end (12-14 weeks), so how much a 2-4 week start helps was not tested.
sperm.text: Effects were measured after 12-14 weeks, matching one spermatogenic cycle [tfood-robbins2012, tfood-salashuetos2018]. Sperm take about 64 days (range 42-76) from labelled precursor to ejaculate [tfood-misell2006], and the classic ~74-day estimate is uncertain by about a week [tfood-amann2008], so a diet change needs roughly 2.5-3 months to reach every stage of the sperm in a given ejaculate.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: A handful of nuts a day lowers LDL and apoB, PREDIMED's nut arm cut CVD events by ~28%, and 60-75 g/day nuts improved sperm quality in two RCTs.
audit.biases: PREDIMED caveats apply [adiet-agarwal2019]; nut trials are often nut-industry funded, including FERTINUTS [adiet-salashuetos2018b].
audit.newer_evidence: Lipid lowering is consistent across 26 walnut trials [adiet-guaschferre2018]. A 2024 meta-analysis pooled the two sperm RCTs (223 men) and confirmed better motility, vitality and morphology, but found no link with ART outcomes in observational studies [adiet-cardoso2024, adiet-robbins2012].
audit.bottom_line: Nuts reliably improve blood lipids and probably sperm parameters in healthy men; fertility outcomes are untested.

factors.name: Wasabi, horseradish and mustard (allyl and other short-chain isothiocyanates)

entries.headline: Pungent condiments supply isothiocyanates that are well absorbed (in animals) and concentrate in urine, and one 72-person RCT found a wasabi 6-MSITC extract improved memory in older adults, but there are no human oxidative-stress or disease trials.

dose.effective: Not established; culinary amounts.
dose.studied_range: Wasabi 6-MSITC supplement for 12 weeks; cabbage meals for allyl isothiocyanate kinetics.
dose.too_much: Large amounts irritate the gut.
dose.notes: Isothiocyanates form only when the plant's myrosinase acts on crushed tissue, so freshly grated root or prepared mustard delivers them; lightly cooked cabbage gave more allyl isothiocyanate than fully cooked.

entries.mechanism: Allyl isothiocyanate and 6-MSITC are electrophiles that conjugate glutathione and activate Nrf2; allyl isothiocyanate is excreted as an N-acetylcysteine conjugate concentrated in urine.
entries.interactions: Mustard powder also restores myrosinase activity to cooked broccoli: see [mustard-seed-myrosinase]. Same pathway as [broccoli-sprouts] and [watercress-peitc].
entries.caveats: Bioavailability figures for allyl isothiocyanate come mainly from animals. The memory trial is a single study with improvement in 2 of several cognitive domains. Erucin (rocket) and sulforaphene (radish) have essentially no human outcome data.
entries.title: Wasabi, horseradish and mustard (allyl and other short-chain isothiocyanates)

timing.summary: The only human outcome trial gave a wasabi isothiocyanate supplement daily for 12 weeks and measured memory only at the end. When effects start and how long they last are unknown.

onset.text: Not measured; memory improved at the single 12-week assessment [tfood-nouchi2023].

full.text: Not measured beyond 12 weeks [tfood-nouchi2023].

after_stopping.text: Not measured.

frequency.text: The trial used a daily supplement [tfood-nouchi2023]; no schedule data.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

factors.name: Washing and peeling produce to remove pesticide residues

entries.headline: Tap-water washing removes roughly 40% of fruit pesticide residues on average and a baking-soda soak removes surface residues better, but systemic pesticides that have entered the peel or flesh stay; peeling removes most residues (and some nutrients), and no study has shown that washing changes urinary pesticide levels or health.

dose.effective: Rinse produce under running water while rubbing for about 30 s; for firm fruit like apples, soak 12-15 min in 1% baking soda (about 1 teaspoon per 500 mL water) and rinse. Peel high-residue items when the peel adds little. Discard outer leaves of leafy vegetables.
dose.studied_range: Laboratory processing studies on fruit and vegetables; 1% sodium bicarbonate soak on apples.
dose.too_much: Do not wash produce with soap, detergent or bleach; residues of these are not food-safe and a 2-min bleach wash did not remove surface residues from apples.
dose.timeframe: Immediate (per meal).
dose.notes: Peeling removes fibre, vitamins and polyphenols concentrated in the skin. Most EU-sampled foods are within legal residue limits, and eating more produce matters more than its residue level.

entries.mechanism: Physical removal and, for some pesticides, alkaline hydrolysis by baking soda; residues inside the plant (systemic pesticides such as neonicotinoids and glyphosate) cannot be reached.
entries.interactions: Complements [organic-food] for lowering [organophosphates] and [pyrethroids] intake; does little for [glyphosate] and [neonicotinoids]. Never trade away [high-fruit-vegetable-intake].
entries.caveats: Evidence is from laboratory spiking studies, often with residues applied at high concentrations shortly before testing; real residues may be older and more penetrated. No human biomonitoring trial of washing exists.
entries.debate: Washing helps: a meta-analysis gives a tap-water processing factor of 0.59 [efw-liang2014], and baking soda removed surface residues fully on apples [efw-yang2017]. Limits: residues that penetrated the peel were not removed [efw-yang2017], reviews conclude washing gives only partial reduction while peeling and cooking remove more [efw-chung2018, efw-chauhan2014], and EU monitoring finds residue risk already very low for most consumers [efw-efsa2025].

entries.title: Washing and peeling produce to remove pesticide residues

entries.headline: 85 g/day of raw watercress for 8 weeks cut lymphocyte DNA damage by 17% (oxidative purine damage by 24%, more in smokers), and watercress or pure PEITC shifted a tobacco lung carcinogen toward detoxification in smokers.

dose.effective: About 85 g (a large bowl) of raw watercress daily.
dose.studied_range: 85-170 g/day for 3 days to 8 weeks; pure PEITC 40 mg/day for 1 week.
dose.timeframe: Carcinogen-metabolism shift within 2-3 days; DNA-damage changes at 8 weeks.
dose.notes: Eat raw or barely wilted so chewing releases PEITC via the plant's myrosinase. Watercress also doubled plasma lutein and raised beta-carotene, so not all of the effect is PEITC.

entries.mechanism: PEITC inhibits cytochrome P450 activation of the tobacco nitrosamine NNK and, like other isothiocyanates, conjugates glutathione and activates Nrf2-driven phase II enzymes; the carotenoids add lipid-phase antioxidant capacity.
entries.interactions: Same pathway family as [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other] and [moringa]. The carotenoid boost overlaps [leafy-greens].
entries.caveats: Trials are small; in the 82-smoker PEITC trial the change in carcinogen activation was only 7.7%. The exercise study had 10 men. There are no cancer-outcome data.

key_numbers.label: Urinary detoxified NNK metabolites in smokers
NNK activation ratio with 40 mg/day PEITC

entries.title: Watercress (phenethyl isothiocyanate, PEITC)

timing.summary: Watercress shifted a tobacco carcinogen toward detoxification within 2-3 days, and the effect was gone 1-2 weeks after stopping. A drop in DNA damage was seen after 8 weeks of daily intake.

onset.text: Detoxified NNK metabolites rose 33.5% on days 2-3 of eating watercress at each meal [tfood-hecht1995].

full.text: Lymphocyte DNA damage was 17% lower after 8 weeks of 85 g/day (the only time point) [tfood-gill2007].

after_stopping.text: NNK detox metabolites were back near baseline 1-2 weeks after stopping [tfood-hecht1995].

frequency.text: Both trials used daily or every-meal intake [tfood-hecht1995, tfood-gill2007]; the detox effect fades within a week or two, so regular intake is needed to keep it.

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: 85 g/day watercress cut lymphocyte DNA damage 17% in 60 adults; PEITC modestly shifted carcinogen metabolism in smokers.
audit.biases: Small trials; single-centre.
audit.newer_evidence: No replication found [adiet-gill2007, adiet-yuan2016].
audit.bottom_line: Accurate and appropriately limited.

entries.headline: Each 90 g/day (3 servings) of whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower all-cause mortality; the oxidative-stress link is indirect, through lower glycemic spikes and fermentable fiber.

dose.effective: 3 servings (90 g) per day or more; associations continued up to ~210-225 g/day.
dose.studied_range: Cohort intakes; RCTs show lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol with higher fiber and whole grain.
dose.timeframe: Long-term.
dose.notes: Oats contain avenanthramides and beta-glucan; most grain phenolics (ferulic acid) are bound to fiber and released by gut bacteria.

entries.mechanism: Fiber-bound ferulic acid released in the colon, short-chain fatty acids, lower glycemic load.
entries.interactions: Replaces [refined-sugar-high-glycemic] carbohydrate.
entries.caveats: Observational for hard outcomes; refined grains and white rice showed little association.

key_numbers.label: CHD RR per 90 g/day whole grain

entries.title: Whole grains

timing.summary: Eight weeks of whole grains lowered IL-6, CRP and body weight without major microbiome change. Lower heart disease and mortality in cohorts reflect years of habitual intake.

onset.text: IL-6 and CRP lower after 8 weeks (only time point) [tfood-roager2019].

full.text: Cohort benefits reflect long-term intake [tfood-aune2016]; plateau not measured.

after_stopping.text: Not measured; the crossover used a washout of at least 6 weeks [tfood-roager2019].

frequency.text: Associations are with daily servings (90 g/day = 3 servings) [tfood-aune2016].

timing.debate: No substantive published debate on timing found.

audit.claim: Each 90 g/day whole grain is associated with ~19% lower CHD and 17% lower mortality; evidence rated moderate.
audit.biases: Whole-grain eaters are more educated and health-conscious; a UK Biobank genetic analysis suggested the wholemeal-vs-white-bread pattern is driven by education-linked factors and is not strongly causal for heart disease or diabetes [adiet-cole2020].
audit.newer_evidence: Cochrane (2017) found no RCT with cardiovascular outcomes, and trials up to 16 weeks showed no difference in total cholesterol and insufficient evidence on blood pressure, with partial cereal-industry funding [adiet-kelly2017]. The cohort association itself is consistent [adiet-aune2016], and the Lancet carbohydrate-quality reviews found trial support for higher fibre more than for whole grain per se [adiet-reynolds2019].
audit.bottom_line: Whole grains are a sensible choice over refined grains, but the size of the mortality benefit is uncertain and may be partly confounded.

entries.headline: About 17% of the world is at risk of low zinc intake, and infertile men have lower seminal zinc, yet zinc supplements in replete people do little: 30 mg zinc plus folic acid did nothing for semen or live birth in 2370 men, and doses of 50 mg/day already depress copper-dependent SOD1, with 100+ mg/day causing copper-deficiency anaemia and myelopathy.

dose.effective: RDA 11 mg/day men, 8 mg/day women (11-12 in pregnancy/lactation). Get it from meat, shellfish (oysters), dairy, legumes, seeds and whole grains; vegans may need up to ~50% more because phytate blocks absorption. If supplementing, 8-15 mg/day in a multivitamin with ~1-2 mg copper.
dose.studied_range: 15-66 mg/day elemental zinc in trials; 30 mg/day in FAZST; 50 mg/day lowered SOD1 in 6 weeks.
