pmid:32517172.title: Influence of Long-Term Fasting on Blood Redox Status in Humans.
pmid:32517172.finding: A 10-day Buchinger fast lowered plasma TBARS and raised total antioxidant capacity alongside rising uric acid; erythrocyte GSH, GR, GPx and catalase were unchanged.

pmid:35194047.authors: Xie Z, Sun Y, Ye Y, et al.
pmid:35194047.title: Randomized controlled trial for time-restricted eating in healthy volunteers without obesity.
pmid:35194047.finding: 5 weeks of early TRE improved insulin sensitivity, fasting glucose, adiposity and inflammation more than mid-day TRE.

pmid:37466280.authors: Barnes LL, Dhana K, Liu X, et al.
pmid:37466280.title: Trial of the MIND Diet for Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Older Persons.
pmid:37466280.n: 604 adults 65+ with family history of dementia
pmid:37466280.finding: The 3-year MIND trial: global cognition improved similarly with the MIND diet and a control diet, both with mild caloric restriction (difference 0.035 SD, P=0.23); MRI outcomes did not differ.

pmid:36224029.authors: Glans I, Sonestedt E, Nägga K, et al.
pmid:36224029.title: Association Between Dietary Habits in Midlife With Dementia Incidence Over a 20-Year Period.
pmid:36224029.finding: Over 20 years, midlife adherence to conventional dietary guidelines or a modified Mediterranean diet was not associated with dementia, Alzheimer disease or amyloid accumulation.

pmid:30826160.authors: Hosking DE, Eramudugolla R, Cherbuin N, et al.
pmid:30826160.title: MIND not Mediterranean diet related to 12-year incidence of cognitive impairment in an Australian longitudinal cohort study.
pmid:30826160.finding: MIND-diet adherence, but not Mediterranean-diet adherence, was associated with lower 12-year odds of cognitive impairment (OR 0.47).

pmid:25681666.authors: Morris MC, Tangney CC, Wang Y, et al.
pmid:25681666.title: MIND diet associated with reduced incidence of Alzheimer's disease.
pmid:25681666.finding: Highest vs lowest tertile of MIND-diet score was associated with 53% lower Alzheimer incidence (HR 0.47); moderate adherence was associated with 35% lower risk.

pmid:25961184.authors: Valls-Pedret C, Sala-Vila A, Serra-Mir M, et al.
pmid:25961184.title: Mediterranean Diet and Age-Related Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:25961184.finding: PREDIMED-Barcelona substudy: Mediterranean diet plus olive oil or nuts improved memory or frontal composites versus a low-fat control diet over about 4 years, in which cognition declined.

pmid:30422212.authors: Baudry J, Assmann KE, Touvier M, et al.
pmid:30422212.title: Association of Frequency of Organic Food Consumption With Cancer Risk: Findings From the NutriNet-Santé Prospective Cohort Study.
pmid:30422212.finding: The highest quartile of organic food consumption was associated with 25% lower cancer risk (HR 0.75; absolute risk reduction 0.6%).

pmid:41862000.authors: Berlivet J, Meyer E, Allès B, et al.
pmid:41862000.title: Consumption of organic compared with conventional fruits and vegetables in relation to cancer risk: findings from the NutriNet-Santé cohort study.
pmid:41862000.finding: Substituting organic for conventional fruit and vegetables (per 100 g/day) was associated with lower postmenopausal breast cancer (HR 0.90) but not robustly with overall cancer.

pmid:29084307.authors: Chiu YH, Williams PL, Gillman MW, et al.
pmid:29084307.title: Association Between Pesticide Residue Intake From Consumption of Fruits and Vegetables and Pregnancy Outcomes Among Women Undergoing Infertility Treatment With Assisted Reproductive Technology.
pmid:29084307.finding: Women eating the most high-pesticide-residue produce (>=2.3 servings/day) had 18% lower probability of clinical pregnancy and 26% lower probability of live birth than those eating <1 serving/day.

pmid:37803657.authors: González N, Pàmies C, Martinez P, et al.
pmid:37803657.title: Effects of an organic diet intervention on the levels of organophosphorus metabolites in an adult cohort.
pmid:37803657.finding: An organic diet intervention significantly lowered urinary dialkyl phosphate (organophosphate) metabolites, e.g. total DAP by about 75%.

pmid:30422205.authors: Hemler EC, Chavarro JE, Hu FB
pmid:30422205.title: Organic Foods for Cancer Prevention-Worth the Investment?
pmid:30422205.finding: Invited commentary questioning whether the NutriNet-Sante organic-cancer association justifies the cost of organic food.

pmid:30765100.authors: Hyland C, Bradman A, Gerona R, et al.
pmid:30765100.title: Organic diet intervention significantly reduces urinary pesticide levels in U.S. children and adults.
pmid:30765100.finding: Switching to an organic diet cut urinary levels of 13 pesticide metabolites, e.g. malathion metabolite -95%, chlorpyrifos metabolite -61%, clothianidin -83%.

pmid:37493357.authors: Hyland C, Spivak M, Sheppard L, et al.
pmid:37493357.title: Urinary Glyphosate Concentrations among Pregnant Participants in a Randomized, Crossover Trial of Organic and Conventional Diets.
pmid:37493357.finding: An organic grocery week modestly lowered urinary glyphosate in women living >0.5 km from fields but not in those living near fields.

pmid:41338693.authors: Kazemi M, Salas-Huetos A, Mitsunami M, et al.
pmid:41338693.title: Male partner pesticide residue exposure from fruit and vegetable intake in relation to outcomes of infertility treatment: a prospective cohort study.
pmid:41338693.finding: Male intake of high-pesticide-residue produce was associated with lower fertilization rates and live birth in conventional IVF; low-residue produce with higher fertilization.

pmid:39101594.authors: Komati N, Cravedi JP, Lecerf JM, et al.
pmid:39101594.title: Potential Health Benefits of a Diet Rich in Organic Fruit and Vegetables versus a Diet Based on Conventional Produce: A Systematic Review.
pmid:39101594.finding: Current data do not allow a firm conclusion that diets rich in organic fruit and vegetables are healthier; results were contradictory with methodological limitations.

pmid:39261657.authors: Poulia KA, Bakaloudi DR, Alevizou M, et al.
pmid:39261657.title: Impact of organic foods on chronic diseases and health perception: a systematic review of the evidence.
pmid:39261657.finding: Organic food consumption was linked to lower cardiometabolic risk in prospective studies and consistently lower pesticide exposure in trials; cancer data inconclusive.

pmid:32259756.authors: Wesselink AK, Hatch EE, Rothman KJ, et al.
pmid:32259756.title: Pesticide residue intake from fruits and vegetables and fecundability in a North American preconception cohort study.
pmid:32259756.finding: Intake of high- or low-pesticide-residue produce was not related to fecundability; inverse links seen only in women already trying for 3-6 cycles suggested reverse causation.

pmid:32690432.title: Genetically predicted iron status and life expectancy
pmid:32690432.n: Mendelian randomization using parental lifespan GWAS
pmid:32690432.finding: Each SD of genetically higher serum iron corresponded to 0.7 fewer years of parental lifespan and lower odds of reaching the 90th age percentile (OR 0.81).

pmid:38868106.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
pmid:38868106.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for iron
pmid:38868106.finding: EFSA could not set an iron UL; it set a safe level of 40 mg/day total iron for adults including pregnant women.

pmid:16413858.title: Iron and folic acid supplementation and malaria risk
pmid:16413858.finding: Lancet comment on the Pemba trial discussing risks of untargeted iron supplementation where malaria is common.

pmid:37403900.authors: Hansen R, Sejer EPF, Holm C, et al.
pmid:37403900.title: Iron supplements in pregnant women with normal iron status: A systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:37403900.finding: Daily iron in iron-replete pregnant women probably reduced iron-deficiency anaemia at term and low birthweight.

pmid:20200263.title: Iron bioavailability and dietary reference values
pmid:20200263.finding: Iron bioavailability is ~14-18% from mixed diets and 5-12% from vegetarian diets; body iron status influences absorption more than diet composition.

pmid:25143342.authors: Jaeggi T, Kortman GA, Moretti D, et al.
pmid:25143342.title: Iron fortification adversely affects the gut microbiome, increases pathogen abundance and induces intestinal inflammation in Kenyan infants
pmid:25143342.finding: Iron-containing micronutrient powders increased enterobacteria and pathogenic E. coli, lowered bifidobacteria and raised faecal calprotectin (gut inflammation).

pmid:16413877.authors: Sazawal S, Black RE, Ramsan M, et al.
pmid:16413877.title: Effects of routine prophylactic supplementation with iron and folic acid on admission to hospital and mortality in preschool children in a high malaria transmission setting: community-based, randomised, placebo-controlled trial
pmid:16413877.finding: Routine iron (12.5 mg) plus folic acid in a high-malaria setting raised death or hospitalisation by 12%; the arm was stopped early.

pmid:38542697.authors: Shearer J, Shah S, MacInnis MJ, et al.
pmid:38542697.title: Dose-Responsive Effects of Iron Supplementation on the Gut Microbiota in Middle-Aged Women
pmid:38542697.finding: High-dose iron supplements (>100 mg/day) were associated with more Proteobacteria and fewer butyrate producers (e.g. Faecalibacterium).

pmid:30343273.authors: Simonyté Sjödin K, Domellöf M, Lagerqvist C, et al.
pmid:30343273.title: Administration of ferrous sulfate drops has significant effects on the gut microbiota of iron-sufficient infants: a randomised controlled study
pmid:30343273.finding: Ferrous sulfate drops significantly changed the gut microbiota of infants who were not iron deficient.

pmid:25331454.title: Dietary iron supplementation: a proinflammatory attack on the intestine?
pmid:25331454.finding: Gut commentary describing dietary iron supplementation as a potential pro-inflammatory insult to the intestine.

pmid:32169997.authors: Adani G, Filippini T, Wise LA, et al.
pmid:32169997.title: Dietary Intake of Acrylamide and Risk of Breast, Endometrial, and Ovarian Cancers: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-analysis.
pmid:32169997.finding: Higher acrylamide intake was associated with slightly higher ovarian and endometrial cancer risk, mainly in never-smokers; no association with breast cancer except possibly in premenopausal women.

pmid:17935291.authors: Allouche Y, Jiménez A, Gaforio JJ, et al.
pmid:17935291.title: How heating affects extra virgin olive oil quality indexes and chemical composition.
pmid:17935291.finding: Heating EVOO at 180 °C for 36 h degraded tocopherols and polyphenols (cultivar-dependent), but oleic acid, sterols, squalene and triterpenes stayed stable; oil kept most minor compounds.

pmid:37224552.authors: Ampem G, Le Gresley A, Grootveld M, et al.
pmid:37224552.title: High-resolution (1)H NMR analysis of continuous and discontinuous thermo-oxidative susceptibility of culinary oils during frying at 180 °C.
pmid:37224552.finding: NMR showed PUFA-rich culinary oils were the most susceptible to thermo-oxidation at 180 °C and coconut oil the most resistant; continuous heating caused more change than intermittent episodes.

pmid:28646140.authors: Baye E, de Courten MP, Walker K, et al.
pmid:28646140.title: Effect of dietary advanced glycation end products on inflammation and cardiovascular risks in healthy overweight adults: a randomised crossover trial.
pmid:28646140.finding: Two weeks of low vs high AGE diets did not change blood pressure, lipids or inflammatory markers (IL-6, MCP-1, TNF-alpha, CRP, NF-kB).

pmid:24944061.authors: Cahill LE, Pan A, Chiuve SE, et al.
pmid:24944061.title: Fried-food consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease: a prospective study in 2 cohorts of US women and men.
pmid:24944061.finding: Fried food ≥7 times/week vs <1: type 2 diabetes RR 1.55 and CAD RR 1.21; associations largely attenuated after adjusting for BMI, hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia.

pmid:20678538.authors: Casal S, Malheiro R, Sendas A, et al.
pmid:20678538.title: Olive oil stability under deep-frying conditions.
pmid:20678538.finding: In domestic deep-frying, olive oils (including EVOO) lasted 24-27 h before reaching the 25% total polar compound legal limit vs 15 h for a vitamin-E-rich vegetable oil blend, which was far more susceptible to oxidation.

pmid:28524104.authors: Chiavarini M, Bertarelli G, Minelli L, et al.
pmid:28524104.title: Dietary Intake of Meat Cooking-Related Mutagens (HCAs) and Risk of Colorectal Adenoma and Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:28524104.finding: Meat-cooking mutagens were associated with colorectal adenoma (PhIP OR 1.20) and cancer (MeIQx OR 1.14, DiMeIQx 1.12, mutagenicity 1.12), with high heterogeneity in some analyses.

pmid:17995742.title: Chemistry of deep-fat frying oils.
pmid:17995742.finding: Deep-fat frying causes hydrolysis, oxidation and polymerisation; high temperature, number of fryings, free fatty acids, metals and unsaturation reduce oil stability.

pmid:20215514.authors: Cross AJ, Ferrucci LM, Risch A, et al.
pmid:20215514.title: A large prospective study of meat consumption and colorectal cancer risk: an investigation of potential mechanisms underlying this association.
pmid:20215514.finding: Red and processed meat were associated with colorectal cancer; heme iron, nitrate/nitrite and HCAs (MeIQx HR 1.19, DiMeIQx HR 1.17 top vs bottom quintile) were candidate mechanisms.

pmid:41300535.authors: Crupi P, Clodoveo ML, Desantis A, et al.
pmid:41300535.title: Effect of Long-Term Storage Temperature on the Quality of Extra-Virgin Olive Oil (Coratina cv.): A Multivariate Discriminant Approach.
pmid:41300535.finding: In 21 EVOOs stored in the dark for 18 months, peroxide values rose and polyphenols declined markedly after 6 months at room temperature, much less at 4 °C.

pmid:33022698.authors: Dashti HS, Gómez-Abellán P, Qian J, et al.
pmid:33022698.title: Late eating is associated with cardiometabolic risk traits, obesogenic behaviors, and impaired weight loss.
pmid:33022698.finding: Late eaters had higher BMI, triglycerides and lower insulin sensitivity at baseline and lost ~80 g/week less weight than early eaters.

pmid:27030534.authors: de Courten B, de Courten MP, Soldatos G, et al.
pmid:27030534.title: Diet low in advanced glycation end products increases insulin sensitivity in healthy overweight individuals: a double-blind, randomized, crossover trial.
pmid:27030534.finding: Double-blind crossover: 2 weeks of a low-AGE diet raised insulin sensitivity (clamp) by 1.3 mg/kg/min vs the high-AGE diet, without weight change.

pmid:30364556.title: Omega-6 vegetable oils as a driver of coronary heart disease: the oxidized linoleic acid hypothesis.
pmid:30364556.finding: Argues that oxidized linoleic acid in LDL drives coronary heart disease and that omega-6 vegetable oils should be limited; authors disclose commercial interests (books, nutraceutical company).

pmid:33412921.title: Formation and mitigation of PAHs in barbecued meat - a review.
pmid:33412921.finding: PAH mitigation in barbecued meat: remove visible char, minimise fat dripping onto the heat source, use acidic marinades and leaner cuts; exposure estimation is hampered by varied practices.

doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4104.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM)
doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4104.title: Scientific Opinion on acrylamide in food
doi:10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4104.finding: EFSA CONTAM Panel: mean adult dietary acrylamide exposure 0.4-0.9 µg/kg bw/day (95th percentile 0.6-2.0); BMDL10 0.17 mg/kg bw/day for tumours in mice; margins of exposure indicate a concern for neoplastic effects, while neurotoxicity and reproductive effects are not a concern at current exposure.

pmid:35540797.authors: Benford D, Bignami M, Chipman JK, et al.
pmid:35540797.title: Assessment of the genotoxicity of acrylamide.
pmid:35540797.finding: EFSA statement: newer studies confirm acrylamide and glycidamide are genotoxic (glycidamide DNA adducts also seen in humans), with additional ROS-mediated and non-genotoxic effects; the 2015 margin-of-exposure approach and conclusions still stand.

pmid:25161045.authors: Farvid MS, Ding M, Pan A, et al.
pmid:25161045.title: Dietary linoleic acid and risk of coronary heart disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
pmid:25161045.finding: Highest vs lowest linoleic acid intake: 15% lower CHD events and 21% lower CHD deaths; 5% energy LA replacing saturated fat linked to 9% fewer events.

pmid:7959444.authors: Felton JS, Fultz E, Dolbeare FA, et al.
pmid:7959444.title: Effect of microwave pretreatment on heterocyclic aromatic amine mutagens/carcinogens in fried beef patties.
pmid:7959444.finding: Microwaving beef patties for 1-3 min before frying (and discarding the juice) removed up to 30% of HCA precursors and cut the four main HCAs 3- to 9-fold and mutagenicity up to 95%.

pmid:35548558.authors: Filippini T, Halldorsson TI, Capitão C, et al.
pmid:35548558.title: Dietary Acrylamide Exposure and Risk of Site-Specific Cancer: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Epidemiological Studies.
pmid:35548558.finding: No association between highest vs lowest dietary acrylamide exposure (median 23 µg/day) and any site-specific non-gynaecological cancer, except lung cancer in smokers.

pmid:28967343.authors: Fong M, Caterson ID, Madigan CD
pmid:28967343.title: Are large dinners associated with excess weight, and does eating a smaller dinner achieve greater weight loss? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:28967343.finding: Observational links between large evening intake and BMI were inconsistent and trials showed no significant difference in weight change between small and large dinners.

pmid:23357955.authors: Garaulet M, Gómez-Abellán P, Alburquerque-Béjar JJ, et al.
pmid:23357955.title: Timing of food intake predicts weight loss effectiveness.
pmid:23357955.finding: Late lunch eaters (after 15:00) lost less weight over 20 weeks than early eaters despite similar energy intake, expenditure and sleep.

pmid:35015083.authors: Garaulet M, Lopez-Minguez J, Dashti HS, et al.
pmid:35015083.title: Interplay of Dinner Timing and MTNR1B Type 2 Diabetes Risk Variant on Glucose Tolerance and Insulin Secretion: A Randomized Crossover Trial.
pmid:35015083.finding: An evening glucose load 1 h before habitual bedtime vs 4 h before gave 3.5-fold higher melatonin, 6.7% lower insulin AUC and 8.3% higher glucose AUC, worse in MTNR1B G-allele carriers.

pmid:17988088.title: Effect of oil marinades with garlic, onion, and lemon juice on the formation of heterocyclic aromatic amines in fried beef patties.
pmid:17988088.finding: In oil marinades for fried beef patties, garlic and onion (not lemon juice) dose-dependently reduced MeIQx by up to ~70%; HCA levels were low overall (MeIQx 0.38-1.22 ng/g).

pmid:18729379.authors: Goicoechea E, Van Twillert K, Duits M, et al.
pmid:18729379.title: Use of an in vitro digestion model to study the bioaccessibility of 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal and related aldehydes present in oxidized oils rich in omega-6 acyl groups.
pmid:18729379.finding: In an in vitro digestion model, part of the toxic alpha,beta-unsaturated aldehydes (including 4-HNE) in oxidized omega-6-rich oils survived digestion and were bioaccessible.

pmid:35071288.title: Evidence-Based Challenges to the Continued Recommendation and Use of Peroxidatively-Susceptible Polyunsaturated Fatty Acid-Rich Culinary Oils for High-Temperature Frying Practises: Experimental Revelations Focused on Toxic Aldehydic Lipid Oxidation Products.
pmid:35071288.finding: Argues that PUFA-rich culinary oils generate the most toxic aldehydic lipid oxidation products during frying and calls for tolerable daily intakes and epidemiological studies of these compounds.

pmid:32525525.authors: Gu C, Brereton N, Schweitzer A, et al.
pmid:32525525.title: Metabolic Effects of Late Dinner in Healthy Volunteers-A Randomized Crossover Clinical Trial.
pmid:32525525.finding: Dinner at 22:00 vs 18:00 raised nocturnal glucose, delayed the triglyceride peak and reduced fatty acid oxidation, especially in habitually early sleepers; sleep architecture unchanged.

pmid:22275385.authors: Guallar-Castillón P, Rodríguez-Artalejo F, Lopez-Garcia E, et al.
pmid:22275385.title: Consumption of fried foods and risk of coronary heart disease: Spanish cohort of the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition study.
pmid:22275385.finding: No association between fried food intake and CHD (HR top vs bottom quarter 1.08) or all-cause mortality, whether olive or sunflower oil was used for frying.

pmid:19663427.title: Contribution to further understanding of the evolution of sunflower oil submitted to frying temperature in a domestic fryer: study by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance.
pmid:19663427.finding: Sunflower oil held at 190 °C in a domestic fryer produced aldehydes very early, including genotoxic 4-hydroxy-trans-2-alkenals, well before reaching 25% polar compounds.

pmid:28526025.title: The effect of replacing saturated fat with mostly n-6 polyunsaturated fat on coronary heart disease: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
pmid:28526025.n: RCTs replacing SFA with n-6 PUFA
pmid:28526025.finding: In adequately controlled trials, replacing saturated fat with mostly n-6 PUFA did not reduce CHD events, CHD mortality or total mortality; benefits in earlier meta-analyses came from inadequately controlled trials.

pmid:18006919.authors: Hogervorst JG, Schouten LJ, Konings EJ, et al.
pmid:18006919.title: A prospective study of dietary acrylamide intake and the risk of endometrial, ovarian, and breast cancer.
pmid:18006919.finding: Top vs bottom quintile of acrylamide intake (40 vs 9 µg/day): ovarian cancer HR 1.78 and, in never-smokers, endometrial HR 1.99 and ovarian HR 2.22; no breast cancer association.

pmid:30488422.authors: Hooper L, Al-Khudairy L, Abdelhamid AS, et al.
pmid:30488422.title: Omega-6 fats for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
pmid:30488422.finding: Increasing omega-6 fats made little or no difference to all-cause mortality (RR 1.00) or CVD events (RR 0.97); may reduce myocardial infarction; low to very low quality evidence.

pmid:32827219.authors: Hooper L, Martin N, Jimoh OF, et al.
pmid:32827219.title: Reduction in saturated fat intake for cardiovascular disease.
pmid:32827219.finding: Reducing saturated fat lowered combined cardiovascular events by 17% (RR 0.83), more with greater cholesterol reduction; no clear difference between replacement by PUFA or carbohydrate.

pmid:23512957.authors: Jakubowicz D, Barnea M, Wainstein J, et al.
pmid:23512957.title: High caloric intake at breakfast vs. dinner differentially influences weight loss of overweight and obese women.
pmid:23512957.finding: On a 1,400 kcal diet, a 700 kcal breakfast/200 kcal dinner pattern produced more weight and waist loss and larger falls in glucose, insulin, HOMA-IR and triglycerides than the reverse.

pmid:21233108.authors: Jinno M, Takeuchi M, Watanabe A, et al.
pmid:21233108.title: Advanced glycation end-products accumulation compromises embryonic development and achievement of pregnancy by assisted reproductive technology.
pmid:21233108.finding: Higher serum toxic AGEs and follicular-fluid pentosidine correlated with fewer follicles, oocytes and embryos and lower ongoing pregnancy rates.

pmid:22889633.title: Effect of dietary linoleic acid on markers of inflammation in healthy persons: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:22889633.finding: Virtually no evidence from RCTs in healthy adults that adding linoleic acid raises inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-alpha, etc.).

pmid:23361161.title: Dietary advanced glycation end-product restriction for the attenuation of insulin resistance, oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction: a systematic review.
pmid:23361161.finding: Some evidence that AGE restriction lowers HOMA-IR and AGE-LDL in type 2 diabetes, but 75% of trials lasted <6 weeks, over half were low quality, and evidence was low to very low.

pmid:31782659.authors: Leung GKW, Huggins CE, Ware RS, et al.
pmid:31782659.title: Time of day difference in postprandial glucose and insulin responses: Systematic review and meta-analysis of acute postprandial studies.
pmid:31782659.finding: Postprandial glucose after an identical meal was lower in the day than at night (SMD -1.66), consistent with poorer glucose tolerance at night.

pmid:32020162.authors: Li J, Guasch-Ferré M, Li Y, et al.
pmid:32020162.title: Dietary intake and biomarkers of linoleic acid and mortality: systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies.
pmid:32020162.finding: Highest vs lowest LA intake: total mortality RR 0.87, CVD mortality 0.87, cancer mortality 0.89; similar inverse associations for LA biomarkers.

pmid:35133989.authors: Linkens AM, Houben AJ, Niessen PM, et al.
pmid:35133989.title: A 4-week high-AGE diet does not impair glucose metabolism and vascular function in obese individuals.
pmid:35133989.finding: Despite 2.7- to 5.3-fold differences in CML, CEL and MG-H1 intake, 4 weeks of low vs high AGE diets did not change insulin sensitivity, secretion, micro/macrovascular function, inflammation or lipids.

pmid:34581759.authors: Linkens AMA, Houben AJHM, Kroon AA, et al.
pmid:34581759.title: Habitual intake of dietary advanced glycation end products is not associated with generalized microvascular function-the Maastricht Study.
pmid:34581759.finding: Habitual intake of CML, CEL and MG-H1 (LC-MS/MS database) was not meaningfully associated with generalised microvascular function.

pmid:37302878.authors: Linkens AMA, Eussen SJMP, Houben AJHM, et al.
pmid:37302878.title: Habitual intake of advanced glycation endproducts is not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, worse beta cell function, or presence of prediabetes or type 2 diabetes: The Maastricht Study.
pmid:37302878.finding: Higher habitual dietary AGE intake was not associated with worse insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

pmid:28455106.authors: Lopez-Minguez J, Saxena R, Bandín C, et al.
pmid:28455106.title: Late dinner impairs glucose tolerance in MTNR1B risk allele carriers: A randomized, cross-over study.
pmid:28455106.finding: Eating dinner late, when melatonin is high, impaired glucose tolerance, significantly so only in MTNR1B risk-allele carriers.

pmid:30971107.authors: Marklund M, Wu JHY, Imamura F, et al.
pmid:30971107.title: Biomarkers of Dietary Omega-6 Fatty Acids and Incident Cardiovascular Disease and Mortality.
pmid:30971107.finding: Higher blood/tissue linoleic acid was associated with lower total CVD (HR 0.93), CVD mortality (0.78) and ischaemic stroke (0.88); arachidonic acid was not associated with higher risk.

pmid:30275115.authors: Martínez Góngora V, Matthes KL, Castaño PR, et al.
pmid:30275115.title: Dietary Heterocyclic Amine Intake and Colorectal Adenoma Risk: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
pmid:30275115.finding: Highest vs lowest intake of PhIP (OR 1.20), MeIQx (1.20), DiMeIQx (1.16), benzo(a)pyrene (1.15) and meat mutagenicity (1.22) were associated with colorectal adenoma, with dose-response for PhIP and MeIQx.

pmid:25870289.authors: Morris CJ, Yang JN, Garcia JI, et al.
pmid:25870289.title: Endogenous circadian system and circadian misalignment impact glucose tolerance via separate mechanisms in humans.
pmid:25870289.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:25870289.finding: Postprandial glucose was 17% higher in the biological evening than morning, and circadian misalignment itself raised it a further 6%, via reduced insulin sensitivity.

pmid:20351774.authors: Mozaffarian D, Micha R, Wallace S
pmid:20351774.title: Effects on coronary heart disease of increasing polyunsaturated fat in place of saturated fat: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:20351774.finding: Increasing PUFA (mostly LA) in place of saturated fat reduced CHD events by 19% (RR 0.81), about 10% per 5% energy.

pmid:12556964.authors: Mucci LA, Dickman PW, Steineck G, et al.
pmid:12556964.title: Dietary acrylamide and cancer of the large bowel, kidney, and bladder: absence of an association in a population-based study in Sweden.
pmid:12556964.finding: No association between dietary acrylamide and cancers of the bowel, bladder or kidney; an unexpected inverse trend for large-bowel cancer.

pmid:26598536.authors: Obón-Santacana M, Lujan-Barroso L, Travis RC, et al.
pmid:26598536.title: Acrylamide and Glycidamide Hemoglobin Adducts and Epithelial Ovarian Cancer: A Nested Case-Control Study in Nonsmoking Postmenopausal Women from the EPIC Cohort.
pmid:26598536.finding: Acrylamide and glycidamide haemoglobin adducts showed no clear association with epithelial ovarian cancer and no dose-response.

pmid:18183576.authors: Olesen PT, Olsen A, Frandsen H, et al.
pmid:18183576.title: Acrylamide exposure and incidence of breast cancer among postmenopausal women in the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health Study.
pmid:18183576.n: Nested in Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort
pmid:18183576.finding: Acrylamide-haemoglobin adducts were not associated with breast cancer overall, but after smoking adjustment were associated with ER-positive breast cancer (IRR 2.7 per 10-fold increase).

pmid:22438055.authors: Ollberding NJ, Wilkens LR, Henderson BE, et al.
pmid:22438055.title: Meat consumption, heterocyclic amines and colorectal cancer risk: the Multiethnic Cohort Study.
pmid:22438055.finding: No association between total or specific HCA intake (RR Q5 vs Q1 0.90, 0.76-1.05), red meat or processed meat and colorectal cancer; a modest effect could not be ruled out.

pmid:23092936.authors: Pedersen M, von Stedingk H, Botsivali M, et al.
pmid:23092936.title: Birth weight, head circumference, and prenatal exposure to acrylamide from maternal diet: the European prospective mother-child study (NewGeneris).
pmid:23092936.finding: Highest vs lowest quartile of cord-blood acrylamide adducts was associated with 132 g lower birth weight and 0.33 cm smaller head circumference, also in non-smokers; fried potatoes predicted adducts.

pmid:25403648.authors: Pelucchi C, Bosetti C, Galeone C, et al.
pmid:25403648.title: Dietary acrylamide and cancer risk: an updated meta-analysis.
pmid:25403648.finding: Dietary acrylamide was not related to most common cancers; borderline kidney cancer RR 1.20 (1.00-1.45), and in never-smokers endometrial RR 1.23 and ovarian RR 1.39 (CI crossing 1).

pmid:33468573.authors: Qin P, Zhang M, Han M, et al.
pmid:33468573.title: Fried-food consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of observational studies.
pmid:33468573.finding: Highest vs lowest fried-food intake: major CVD RR 1.28, CHD 1.22, heart failure 1.37; no association with CVD or all-cause mortality; high heterogeneity.

pmid:26041214.authors: Ramírez-Anaya Jdel P, Samaniego-Sánchez C, Castañeda-Saucedo MC, et al.
pmid:26041214.title: Phenols and the antioxidant capacity of Mediterranean vegetables prepared with extra virgin olive oil using different domestic cooking techniques.
pmid:26041214.finding: Cooking vegetables in EVOO (frying, sautéing) transferred olive phenols into the vegetables and kept or increased their phenolic content, while boiling reduced it.

pmid:22959954.authors: Ramsden CE, Ringel A, Feldstein AE, et al.
pmid:22959954.title: Lowering dietary linoleic acid reduces bioactive oxidized linoleic acid metabolites in humans.
pmid:22959954.finding: A 12-week low-LA diet reduced plasma oxidized linoleic acid metabolites (OXLAMs) and LA content of circulating lipid pools.

pmid:23386268.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Leelarthaepin B, et al.
pmid:23386268.title: Use of dietary linoleic acid for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease and death: evaluation of recovered data from the Sydney Diet Heart Study and updated meta-analysis.
pmid:23386268.n: 458 men after coronary event (Sydney Diet Heart Study)
pmid:23386268.finding: Replacing saturated fat with safflower oil/margarine raised all-cause (17.6% vs 11.8%, HR 1.62) and CHD death (HR 1.74); updated meta-analysis showed non-significant trends to harm.

pmid:27071971.authors: Ramsden CE, Zamora D, Majchrzak-Hong S, et al.
pmid:27071971.title: Re-evaluation of the traditional diet-heart hypothesis: analysis of recovered data from Minnesota Coronary Experiment (1968-73).
pmid:27071971.finding: A corn-oil diet lowered cholesterol 13.8% but gave no mortality benefit; each 30 mg/dL fall in cholesterol was associated with 22% higher death risk; meta-analysis of 5 RCTs showed no mortality benefit.

pmid:8432867.authors: Reaven P, Parthasarathy S, Grasse BJ, et al.
pmid:8432867.title: Effects of oleate-rich and linoleate-rich diets on the susceptibility of low density lipoprotein to oxidative modification in mildly hypercholesterolemic subjects.
pmid:8432867.finding: After 8 weeks, LDL from oleate-rich diets was less susceptible to copper-induced oxidation than LDL from linoleate-rich diets.

pmid:36087576.authors: Ruddick-Collins LC, Morgan PJ, Fyfe CL, et al.
pmid:36087576.title: Timing of daily calorie loading affects appetite and hunger responses without changes in energy metabolism in healthy subjects with obesity.
pmid:36087576.finding: Morning- vs evening-loaded calorie distribution for 4 weeks did not change energy expenditure or weight loss; morning loading reduced hunger.

pmid:28620111.authors: Sacks FM, Lichtenstein AH, Wu JHY, et al.
pmid:28620111.title: Dietary Fats and Cardiovascular Disease: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association.
pmid:28620111.finding: AHA Presidential Advisory: RCTs replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated vegetable oil reduced CVD by ~30%; recommends replacing saturated with unsaturated, especially polyunsaturated, fats.

pmid:9216741.authors: Salmon CP, Knize MG, Felton JS
pmid:9216741.title: Effects of marinating on heterocyclic amine carcinogen formation in grilled chicken.
pmid:9216741.finding: A brown sugar/olive oil/cider vinegar/garlic/mustard/lemon marinade cut PhIP in grilled chicken by 92-99% and total HCAs from 56 to 1.7 ng/g (20 min) and 330 to 44 ng/g (40 min), but MeIQx rose >10-fold at 30-40 min cooking.

pmid:11058620.authors: Salmon CP, Knize MG, Panteleakos FN, et al.
pmid:11058620.title: Minimization of heterocyclic amines and thermal inactivation of Escherichia coli in fried ground beef.
pmid:11058620.finding: Turning beef patties every minute at lower pan temperatures greatly reduced HCAs versus a single turn, while still reaching the 70 °C internal temperature that fully inactivated E. coli, with little or no extra cooking time.

pmid:25872656.authors: Sansano M, Juan-Borrás M, Escriche I, et al.
pmid:25872656.title: Effect of pretreatments and air-frying, a novel technology, on acrylamide generation in fried potatoes.
pmid:25872656.finding: Air-frying potatoes at 180 °C produced about 90% less acrylamide than deep-oil frying; for deep frying, pretreatment soaks (citric acid, nicotinic acid, glycine 1%, NaCl 2%) cut acrylamide 80-90%.

pmid:26213088.authors: Scheijen JLJM, Clevers E, Engelen L, et al.
pmid:26213088.title: Analysis of advanced glycation endproducts in selected food items by ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry: Presentation of a dietary AGE database.
pmid:26213088.finding: UPLC-MS/MS database of CML, CEL and MG-H1 in 190 foods: highest in high-heat-processed nut and grain products and canned meats, lowest in fruit, vegetables, butter and coffee.

pmid:24744309.authors: Semba RD, Gebauer SK, Baer DJ, et al.
pmid:24744309.title: Dietary intake of advanced glycation end products did not affect endothelial function and inflammation in healthy adults in a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:24744309.finding: Six weeks of a high- vs low-AGE diet (same foods, different cooking) had no effect on endothelial function (peripheral arterial tonometry) or inflammatory mediators.

pmid:10485479.authors: Sinha R, Chow WH, Kulldorff M, et al.
pmid:10485479.title: Well-done, grilled red meat increases the risk of colorectal adenomas.
pmid:10485479.finding: Each 10 g/day of well-done/very-well-done red meat was associated with 29% higher odds of colorectal adenoma (OR 1.29) versus 10% (NS) for rare/medium; grilled red meat OR 1.26 per 10 g/day.

pmid:42279734.authors: Sordini B, Urbani S, Selvaggini R, et al.
pmid:42279734.title: Evaluating the Effect of Packaging Materials on Extra Virgin Olive Oil Quality Under Simulated Household Use and Storage Conditions.
pmid:42279734.finding: Under simulated household use (25 °C, 12 h light, daily withdrawal over 40 days), EVOO in green PET bottles lost 44% of alpha-tocopherol and 26% of phenols and exceeded the legal peroxide limit after 30 days, vs 1-5% and 11-12% in bag-in-box or tin.

pmid:15072585.authors: Sugimura T, Wakabayashi K, Nakagama H, et al.
pmid:15072585.title: Heterocyclic amines: Mutagens/carcinogens produced during cooking of meat and fish.
pmid:15072585.finding: HCAs are potent mutagens and rodent carcinogens, but their content in ordinary dishes is low and not sufficient by itself to explain human cancer; reducing exposure is still recommended.

pmid:30674467.authors: Sun Y, Liu B, Snetselaar LG, et al.
pmid:30674467.title: Association of fried food consumption with all cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality: prospective cohort study.
pmid:30674467.finding: At least one serving of fried food per day vs none: all-cause mortality HR 1.08; fried chicken ≥1/week HR 1.13 all-cause, 1.12 CVD mortality.

pmid:24722128.authors: Tantalaki E, Piperi C, Livadas S, et al.
pmid:24722128.title: Impact of dietary modification of advanced glycation end products (AGEs) on the hormonal and metabolic profile of women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
pmid:24722128.finding: A high-AGE diet raised serum AGEs, testosterone, insulin, HOMA-IR and oxidative stress compared with a low-AGE diet, without BMI change.

pmid:21709297.authors: Uribarri J, Cai W, Ramdas M, et al.
pmid:21709297.title: Restriction of advanced glycation end products improves insulin resistance in human type 2 diabetes: potential role of AGER1 and SIRT1.
pmid:21709297.finding: AGE restriction for 4 months lowered insulin, HOMA, TNF-alpha, serum AGEs and 8-isoprostanes in type 2 diabetes and normalised AGER1 and SIRT1.

pmid:24605876.authors: Viegas O, Yebra-Pimentel I, Martínez-Carballo E, et al.
pmid:24605876.title: Effect of beer marinades on formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in charcoal-grilled pork.
pmid:24605876.finding: Marinating pork in black beer cut the EFSA PAH8 marker group in charcoal-grilled meat by 53% (non-alcoholic Pilsner 25%, Pilsner 13%), in line with each marinade's radical-scavenging activity.

pmid:36198293.authors: Vujović N, Piron MJ, Qian J, et al.
pmid:36198293.title: Late isocaloric eating increases hunger, decreases energy expenditure, and modifies metabolic pathways in adults with overweight and obesity.
pmid:36198293.finding: Under tightly controlled conditions, isocaloric late eating increased hunger and ghrelin:leptin ratio and decreased waketime energy expenditure and core temperature.

pmid:18855107.authors: Wilson KM, Vesper HW, Tocco P, et al.
pmid:18855107.title: Validation of a food frequency questionnaire measurement of dietary acrylamide intake using hemoglobin adducts of acrylamide and glycidamide.
pmid:18855107.finding: FFQ-estimated acrylamide intake correlated only moderately (r = 0.31-0.34) with haemoglobin adducts of acrylamide and glycidamide, illustrating exposure misclassification in diet studies.

pmid:39145124.authors: Yoon H, Jung MY, Choi SH, et al.
pmid:39145124.title: Effect of air-frying on formation and correlations of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, acrylamide, and heterocyclic aromatic amines in foods and risk assessment.
pmid:39145124.finding: In 184 air-fried foods, root and tuber crops had the most acrylamide and sea algae the most PAH4 and HCAs; margins of exposure for acrylamide suggested possible concern in some food groups.

pmid:36530130.authors: Young IE, Poobalan A, Steinbeck K, et al.
pmid:36530130.title: Distribution of energy intake across the day and weight loss: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:36530130.finding: In energy-reduced diets, shifting intake earlier gave 1.23 kg more weight loss and improvements in HOMA-IR, fasting glucose and LDL.

pmid:36740972.authors: Zhang Y, Zhang H, An W, et al.
pmid:36740972.title: Regulatory effect of dietary nitrate on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pmid:36740972.finding: Dietary nitrate lowered systolic BP by 2.4 mmHg in healthy people but did not lower office or 24-h BP in hypertensive patients.

pmid:33641343.authors: Wang DD, Li Y, Bhupathiraju SN, et al.
pmid:33641343.title: Fruit and Vegetable Intake and Mortality: Results From 2 Prospective Cohort Studies of US Men and Women and a Meta-Analysis of 26 Cohort Studies
pmid:33641343.finding: Fruit and vegetable intake was associated with lower mortality up to about 5 servings/day (HR 0.87 vs 2 servings), with no further reduction above that; starchy vegetables, juices and potatoes were not associated with benefit.

pmid:29310543.authors: Abt E, Fong Sam J, Gray P, et al.
pmid:29310543.title: Cadmium and lead in cocoa powder and chocolate products in the US Market.
pmid:29310543.journal: Food Addit Contam Part B Surveill
pmid:29310543.finding: Cadmium (0.004-3.15 mg/kg) and lead (up to 0.38 mg/kg) rose with % cocoa solids; cadmium was higher in products from Latin America than Africa.

pmid:32293881.title: Perspective on Cadmium and Lead in Cocoa and Chocolate.
pmid:32293881.finding: Perspective from FDA scientists: cadmium in cocoa comes mainly from soil (high in parts of Latin America), lead from post-harvest contamination; mitigation methods are still being developed.

pmid:31077049.authors: Ai CE, Li CJ, Tsou MC, et al.
pmid:31077049.title: Blood and seminal plasma mercury levels and predatory fish intake in relation to low semen quality.
pmid:31077049.finding: Predatory fish intake and higher blood mercury were associated with fewer morphologically normal sperm.

pmid:33917988.authors: Al-Jaal B, Latiff A, Salama S, et al.
pmid:33917988.title: Analysis of Multiple Mycotoxins in the Qatari Population and Their Relation to Markers of Oxidative Stress.
pmid:33917988.finding: Mycotoxins were detected in 37% of serum samples and their presence correlated with oxidative stress markers.

pmid:23873074.authors: Banerjee M, Banerjee N, Bhattacharjee P, et al.
pmid:23873074.title: High arsenic in rice is associated with elevated genotoxic effects in humans.
pmid:23873074.finding: Eating cooked rice with >200 ug/kg arsenic as a staple was associated with more micronuclei in urothelial cells, a marker of genetic damage, in people with safe drinking water.

pmid:34637914.authors: Branch FM, Perry MJ, Chen Z, et al.
pmid:34637914.title: Metal(loid)s and human semen quality: The LIFE Study.
pmid:34637914.finding: Among many metal-semen associations in both directions, cadmium was associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation.

pmid:32554271.authors: Butts CD, Bloom MS, McGough A, et al.
pmid:32554271.title: Seafood consumption is associated with higher follicular fluid arsenic (As) and mercury (Hg) concentrations in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF).
pmid:32554271.finding: Higher seafood intake was associated with higher follicular fluid mercury and arsenic.

pmid:42516822.authors: Cataldo N, Weed BD, Lewis K, et al.
pmid:42516822.title: International Investigation of Lead and Chromium Contamination in Imported Apple Puree.
pmid:42516822.finding: FDA/CDC investigation: lead chromate in ground cinnamon from an Ecuadorian processor contaminated apple-cinnamon puree pouches at 100-600 times FDA's action level.

pmid:38922145.authors: Charusalaipong P, Gordon MJ, Cantlay L, et al.
pmid:38922145.title: Frequent Dietary Multi-Mycotoxin Exposure in UK Children and Its Association with Dietary Intake.
pmid:38922145.finding: UK children were frequently exposed to several mycotoxins at once; deoxynivalenol exceeded its tolerable daily intake in 34% of samples.

pmid:24515811.authors: Chauhan R, Kumari B, Rana MK
pmid:24515811.title: Effect of fruit and vegetable processing on reduction of synthetic pyrethroid residues.
pmid:24515811.finding: Peeling removed 60-100% of pyrethroid residues, juicing 70-100%, cooking 75-98%, washing with tap water only 10-70%, and detergent or saline washes 34-60%.

pmid:30158148.authors: Chowdhury R, Ramond A, O'Keeffe LM, et al.
pmid:30158148.title: Environmental toxic metal contaminants and risk of cardiovascular disease: systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:30158148.finding: Top vs bottom thirds of arsenic, lead and cadmium were associated with 30%, 43% and 33% higher cardiovascular disease risk, with linear dose-response; mercury was not associated.

pmid:12387464.authors: Choy CM, Lam CW, Cheung LT, et al.
pmid:12387464.title: Infertility, blood mercury concentrations and dietary seafood consumption: a case-control study.
pmid:12387464.finding: Infertile couples had higher blood mercury than fertile couples, and higher mercury tracked seafood intake.

pmid:29222908.title: How effective are common household preparations on removing pesticide residues from fruit and vegetables? A review.
pmid:29222908.finding: Washing and soaking produce gives only partial residue reduction; peeling, chemical-bath soaking and blanching remove residues more effectively, depending on the pesticide's properties.

pmid:23008276.authors: Davis MA, Mackenzie TA, Cottingham KL, et al.
pmid:23008276.title: Rice consumption and urinary arsenic concentrations in U.S. children.
pmid:23008276.finding: Each extra quarter cup of cooked rice was associated with 14.2% higher total urinary arsenic in children who had not eaten seafood.

pmid:42006064.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM)
pmid:42006064.title: Statement on tolerable weekly intake for cadmium.
pmid:42006064.finding: EFSA maintained a tolerable weekly intake for cadmium of 2.5 ug/kg body weight, based on kidney effects.

pmid:32874256.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM), Schrenk D, Bignami M, et al.
pmid:32874256.title: Risk assessment of aflatoxins in food.
pmid:32874256.finding: EFSA 2020: margins of exposure for aflatoxin B1 in Europe were 5,000 to 29, below the 10,000 threshold, which raises a health concern.

pmid:38239496.authors: EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM), Schrenk D, Bignami M, et al.
pmid:38239496.title: Update of the risk assessment of inorganic arsenic in food.
pmid:38239496.finding: EFSA 2024: inorganic arsenic is a genotoxic carcinogen; using a reference point of 0.06 ug/kg bw/day (skin cancer), margins of exposure for European adults are 0.4-2, which raises a health concern.

pmid:40371318.authors: European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), Carrasco Cabrera L, Di Piazza G, et al.
pmid:40371318.title: The 2023 European Union report on pesticide residues in food.
pmid:40371318.finding: In 2023 EU monitoring, 1.0% of randomly sampled foods (2.0% of risk-based samples) exceeded legal residue limits, and estimated acute and chronic dietary risk was very low for most population groups.

pmid:11724948.authors: Egner PA, Wang JB, Zhu YR, et al.
pmid:11724948.title: Chlorophyllin intervention reduces aflatoxin-DNA adducts in individuals at high risk for liver cancer.
pmid:11724948.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:11724948.finding: Chlorophyllin 100 mg three times daily for 4 months lowered urinary aflatoxin-DNA adducts by 55% vs placebo.

pmid:999342.authors: Elinder CG, Lind B, Kjellström T, et al.
pmid:999342.title: Cadmium in kidney cortex, liver, and pancreas from Swedish autopsies. Estimation of biological half time in kidney cortex, considering calorie intake and smoking habits.
pmid:999342.finding: The biological half-time of cadmium in kidney cortex in non-smokers was estimated at about 30 years; smokers accumulated more.

pmid:35690180.title: Updated interim reference levels for dietary lead to support FDA's Closer to Zero action plan.
pmid:35690180.finding: FDA updated its interim reference levels for dietary lead to 2.2 ug/day for children and 8.8 ug/day for women of childbearing age.

pmid:37286126.authors: Forsyth JE, Baker M, Nurunnahar S, et al.
pmid:37286126.title: Food safety policy enforcement and associated actions reduce lead chromate adulteration in turmeric across Bangladesh.
pmid:37286126.finding: After enforcement and media campaigns, market turmeric with detectable lead fell from 47% to 0% and blood lead in exposed people dropped a median 30%.

pmid:35504404.authors: Golding J, Taylor C, Iles-Caven Y, et al.
pmid:35504404.title: The benefits of fish intake: Results concerning prenatal mercury exposure and child outcomes from the ALSPAC prebirth cohort.
pmid:35504404.finding: In ALSPAC, prenatal mercury was associated with beneficial outcomes in fish-eating mothers, attributed to fish nutrients.

pmid:9392777.authors: Grandjean P, Weihe P, White RF, et al.
pmid:9392777.title: Cognitive deficit in 7-year-old children with prenatal exposure to methylmercury.
pmid:9392777.finding: Prenatal methylmercury (mostly from pilot whale) was associated with deficits in language, attention and memory at age 7, even below 10 ug/g maternal hair.

pmid:39144282.authors: Hands JM, Anderson ML, Cooperman T, et al.
pmid:39144282.title: A multi-year heavy metal analysis of 72 dark chocolate and cocoa products in the USA.
pmid:39144282.finding: 43% of products exceeded California's Prop 65 daily lead limit and 35% the cadmium limit per serving, 97% were below FDA's lead reference level, and organic products had higher cadmium and lead.

pmid:26233555.authors: Heyndrickx E, Sioen I, Huybrechts B, et al.
pmid:26233555.title: Human biomonitoring of multiple mycotoxins in the Belgian population: Results of the BIOMYCO study.
pmid:26233555.finding: Deoxynivalenol, ochratoxin A and citrinin were widely detected in urine; 16-69% possibly exceeded the DON tolerable daily intake.

pmid:17307104.authors: Hibbeln JR, Davis JM, Steer C, et al.
pmid:17307104.title: Maternal seafood consumption in pregnancy and neurodevelopmental outcomes in childhood (ALSPAC study): an observational cohort study.
pmid:17307104.finding: Children of mothers eating <340 g seafood a week in pregnancy had higher risk of suboptimal verbal IQ and development than those eating more.

pmid:30588341.authors: Hoffmann V, Jones K, Leroy JL
pmid:30588341.title: The impact of reducing dietary aflatoxin exposure on child linear growth: a cluster randomised controlled trial in Kenya.
pmid:30588341.finding: Providing aflatoxin-tested maize lowered children's serum aflatoxin-albumin adducts but did not improve linear growth or stunting at endline.

pmid:30507772.authors: Hore P, Alex-Oni K, Sedlar S, et al.
pmid:30507772.title: A Spoonful of Lead: A 10-Year Look at Spices as a Potential Source of Lead Exposure.
pmid:30507772.finding: Of spices collected in New York City lead investigations, over half had detectable lead and over 30% had >2 ppm; spices bought abroad (Georgia, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nepal, Morocco) were highest.

pmid:7951403.authors: Ibeh IN, Uraih N, Ogonar JI
pmid:7951403.title: Dietary exposure to aflatoxin in human male infertility in Benin City, Nigeria.
pmid:7951403.finding: Aflatoxins were found in semen of 40% of infertile and 8% of fertile men, and infertile men with aflatoxin had more abnormal sperm.

pmid:26264017.authors: Jo S, Woo HD, Kwon HJ, et al.
pmid:26264017.title: Estimation of the Biological Half-Life of Methylmercury Using a Population Toxicokinetic Model.
pmid:26264017.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
pmid:26264017.finding: The population half-life of methylmercury in blood was about 80 days.

pmid:27111102.authors: Karagas MR, Punshon T, Sayarath V, et al.
pmid:27111102.title: Association of Rice and Rice-Product Consumption With Arsenic Exposure Early in Life.
pmid:27111102.finding: Infants eating rice cereal had urinary arsenic of 9.5 ug/L vs 2.9 ug/L in those eating no rice; rice snacks contained 5-201 ng/g inorganic arsenic.

pmid:25005864.authors: Liang Y, Liu Y, Ding Y, et al.
pmid:25005864.title: Meta-analysis of food processing on pesticide residues in fruits.
pmid:25005864.journal: Food Addit Contam Part A Chem Anal Control Expo Risk Assess
pmid:25005864.finding: Across studies of fruit, tap-water washing left 59% of residues (processing factor 0.59), boiling 0.71, while peeling (0.11) and juicing (0.14) removed most; oven drying could concentrate residues.

pmid:20172840.title: Global burden of aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma: a risk assessment.
pmid:20172840.finding: Aflatoxin may cause 4.6-28.2% of global liver cancer (25,200-155,000 cases a year), mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Asia and China where hepatitis B is common.

pmid:22405700.authors: Liu Y, Chang CC, Marsh GM, et al.
pmid:22405700.title: Population attributable risk of aflatoxin-related liver cancer: systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:22405700.finding: Aflatoxin and hepatitis B multiply liver cancer risk (combined OR 73 vs 11 for HBV alone and 6.4 for aflatoxin alone).

pmid:28572075.authors: Mantha M, Yeary E, Trent J, et al.
pmid:28572075.title: Estimating Inorganic Arsenic Exposure from U.S. Rice and Total Water Intakes.
pmid:28572075.finding: A mean Asian/Pacific/Tribal US rice eater gets as much inorganic arsenic from rice as someone drinking 1.5 L/day of water with several ug/L arsenic.

pmid:33153748.authors: Menon M, Dong W, Chen X, et al.
pmid:33153748.title: Improved rice cooking approach to maximise arsenic removal while preserving nutrient elements.
pmid:33153748.finding: Parboiling rice in fresh water for 5 min, draining, then cooking by absorption removed 54% (brown) and 73% (white) of inorganic arsenic while keeping most zinc and other nutrients.

pmid:38176556.authors: Menon M, Nicholls A, Smalley A, et al.
pmid:38176556.title: A comparison of the effects of two cooking methods on arsenic species and nutrient elements in rice.
pmid:38176556.finding: Excess-water and parboil-absorb cooking both removed inorganic arsenic (about 50% vs 39% in parboiled rice); cooking with arsenic-contaminated water raised rice arsenic.

pmid:29102416.authors: Mínguez-Alarcón L, Afeiche MC, Williams PL, et al.
pmid:29102416.title: Hair mercury (Hg) levels, fish consumption and semen parameters among men attending a fertility center.
pmid:29102416.finding: Men in the top hair-mercury quartile had 50% higher sperm concentration than the bottom quartile, stronger in high fish eaters, i.e. confounded by fish benefits.

pmid:17047219.title: Fish intake, contaminants, and human health: evaluating the risks and the benefits.
pmid:17047219.finding: Modest fish intake (1-2 servings/week) lowers coronary death by 36%; women of childbearing age should eat 2 servings/week while limiting a few high-mercury species; benefits exceed risks.

pmid:21428767.authors: Mozaffarian D, Shi P, Morris JS, et al.
pmid:21428767.title: Mercury exposure and risk of cardiovascular disease in two U.S. cohorts.
pmid:21428767.n: 3,427 cases and matched controls from two US cohorts
pmid:21428767.finding: Toenail mercury was not associated with coronary heart disease, stroke or total CVD (RR top vs bottom quintile 0.85).

pmid:25527760.authors: Muraki I, Wu H, Imamura F, et al.
pmid:25527760.title: Rice consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease: results from a pooled analysis of 3 U.S. cohorts.
pmid:25527760.finding: Eating >=5 servings a week of white or brown rice was not associated with cardiovascular disease (HR 0.98 and 1.01).

pmid:29882885.authors: Mwale T, Rahman MM, Mondal D
pmid:29882885.title: Risk and Benefit of Different Cooking Methods on Essential Elements and Arsenic in Rice.
pmid:29882885.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
pmid:29882885.finding: High-water (1:6) cooking lowered arsenic but also cut potassium (50%), magnesium (22%), selenium (12%), iron (8%) and zinc (8%).

pmid:12767734.authors: Myers GJ, Davidson PW, Cox C, et al.
pmid:12767734.title: Prenatal methylmercury exposure from ocean fish consumption in the Seychelles child development study.
pmid:12767734.finding: At mean prenatal hair mercury of 6.9 ppm from ocean fish, there was no consistent neurodevelopmental deficit at age 9.

pmid:36671421.authors: Peana M, Pelucelli A, Chasapis CT, et al.
pmid:36671421.title: Biological Effects of Human Exposure to Environmental Cadmium.
pmid:36671421.finding: Review of cadmium toxicity: carcinogenic mechanisms include oxidative stress with inhibition of antioxidant enzymes, lipid peroxidation and interference with DNA repair.

pmid:39012763.authors: Porterfield K, Hore P, Whittaker SG, et al.
pmid:39012763.title: A Snapshot of Lead in Consumer Products Across Four US Jurisdictions.
pmid:39012763.finding: Lead-containing consumer products (spices, cosmetics, remedies) found by four US health departments, often brought by travellers, put immigrant communities at higher risk.

pmid:19137137.authors: Raab A, Baskaran C, Feldmann J, et al.
pmid:19137137.title: Cooking rice in a high water to rice ratio reduces inorganic arsenic content.
pmid:19137137.finding: Rinsing removed about 10% of arsenic; cooking in a high water-to-rice ratio (draining excess) removed about 45% of inorganic arsenic; low-water absorption cooking removed none.

pmid:16203244.authors: Rankin CW, Nriagu JO, Aggarwal JK, et al.
pmid:16203244.title: Lead contamination in cocoa and cocoa products: isotopic evidence of global contamination.
pmid:16203244.finding: Lead isotopes showed cocoa beans are low in lead and shells adsorb lead during fermentation and sun-drying; most lead in finished products comes from shipping and processing.

pmid:34710078.authors: Ruckart PZ, Jones RL, Courtney JG, et al.
pmid:34710078.title: Update of the Blood Lead Reference Value - United States, 2021.
pmid:34710078.finding: CDC lowered its childhood blood lead reference value from 5 to 3.5 ug/dL in 2021.

pmid:7828289.authors: Salonen JT, Seppänen K, Nyyssönen K, et al.
pmid:7828289.title: Intake of mercury from fish, lipid peroxidation, and the risk of myocardial infarction and coronary, cardiovascular, and any death in eastern Finnish men.
pmid:7828289.finding: Hair mercury >=2 ug/g (from freshwater fish) was associated with 2.0-fold MI and 2.9-fold cardiovascular death risk and with antibodies to oxidised LDL.

pmid:40018851.title: Arsenic content and exposure in brown rice compared to white rice in the United States.
pmid:40018851.finding: Brown rice carries more total and inorganic arsenic than white rice; regular brown-rice eaters, especially young children, have higher estimated exposure, but no acute risk was indicated.

pmid:20045048.authors: Shuaib FM, Ehiri J, Abdullahi A, et al.
pmid:20045048.title: Reproductive health effects of aflatoxins: a review of the literature.
pmid:20045048.finding: Review of aflatoxin reproductive effects: one study found aflatoxin in semen of 40% of infertile vs 8% of fertile men; several linked aflatoxin to low birth weight.

pmid:34842923.authors: Sun Y, Liu B, Rong S, et al.
pmid:34842923.title: Association of Seafood Consumption and Mercury Exposure With Cardiovascular and All-Cause Mortality Among US Adults.
pmid:34842923.finding: Neither seafood intake nor blood mercury was associated with all-cause or cardiovascular mortality.

pmid:40273027.authors: Troeschel AN, Buser MC, Winquist A, et al.
pmid:40273027.title: Investigation of Lead and Chromium Exposure After Consumption of Contaminated Cinnamon-Containing Applesauce - United States, November 2023-April 2024.
pmid:40273027.finding: The 2023 cinnamon-applesauce pouch event produced 566 reported cases in 44 states (55% under 2 years), median maximum blood lead 7.2 ug/dL (up to 39.3).

pmid:24236891.authors: Wei Y, Zhu J, Nguyen A
pmid:24236891.title: Rice consumption and urinary concentrations of arsenic in US adults.
pmid:24236891.finding: Eating rice more than twice a week was associated with higher urinary total arsenic (OR 1.51) and DMA (OR 2.24).

pmid:25601638.authors: Wright DL, Afeiche MC, Ehrlich S, et al.
pmid:25601638.title: Hair mercury concentrations and in vitro fertilization (IVF) outcomes among women from a fertility clinic.
pmid:25601638.n: women in an IVF clinic, 229 cycles
pmid:25601638.finding: Hair mercury (median 0.62 ppm; 33% above 1 ppm) tracked fish intake but was not related to oocyte yield, embryo quality, clinical pregnancy or live birth.

pmid:29067814.authors: Yang T, Doherty J, Zhao B, et al.
pmid:29067814.title: Effectiveness of Commercial and Homemade Washing Agents in Removing Pesticide Residues on and in Apples.
pmid:29067814.finding: On apples, a 1% baking-soda (10 mg/mL) wash removed surface thiabendazole and phosmet in 12-15 min, better than tap water or bleach, but 20% of thiabendazole and 4.4% of phosmet had penetrated the peel and could not be washed off; peeling removed more.

pmid:24492839.authors: Paulsen G, Cumming KT, Holden G, et al.
pmid:24492839.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation hampers cellular adaptation to endurance training in humans: a double-blind, randomised, controlled trial.
pmid:24492839.finding: 1000 mg vitamin C plus 235 mg vitamin E daily for 11 weeks of endurance training did not change VO2max gains (8% in both groups) but blunted training-induced increases in muscle mitochondrial markers.

pmid:21325105.authors: Yfanti C, Nielsen AR, Akerström T, et al.
pmid:21325105.title: Effect of antioxidant supplementation on insulin sensitivity in response to endurance exercise training.
pmid:21325105.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 400 IU vitamin E during 12 weeks of intense endurance training (5x/week) did not change the ~17-19% training-induced gain in insulin-stimulated glucose uptake or VO2max.

pmid:26129928.authors: Bjørnsen T, Salvesen S, Berntsen S, et al.
pmid:26129928.title: Vitamin C and E supplementation blunts increases in total lean body mass in elderly men after strength training.
pmid:26129928.finding: 500 mg vitamin C plus 117.5 mg vitamin E around each of three weekly strength sessions for 12 weeks blunted lean-mass gain (1.4% vs 3.9% on placebo) but not strength gains.

pmid:31851538.authors: Clifford T, Jeffries O, Stevenson EJ, et al.
pmid:31851538.title: The effects of vitamin C and E on exercise-induced physiological adaptations: a systematic review and Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:31851538.finding: Across 9 aerobic and 9 resistance-training RCTs, vitamin C and/or E did not significantly attenuate gains in VO2max, endurance performance, lean mass or strength; trials were small.

pmid:32127289.authors: Mason SA, Trewin AJ, Parker L, et al.
pmid:32127289.title: Antioxidant supplements and endurance exercise: Current evidence and mechanistic insights.
pmid:32127289.finding: Review concluding that chronic intake of 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E is not recommended during heavy training, and that most marketed antioxidant compounds lack supportive human evidence.

pmid:17869589.authors: Radak Z, Chung HY, Koltai E, et al.
pmid:17869589.title: Exercise, oxidative stress and hormesis.
pmid:17869589.finding: Review framing exercise as a hormetic stressor: repeated moderate ROS exposure up-regulates antioxidant and repair systems, with a bell-shaped dose-response curve.

pmid:26893258.authors: Powers SK, Radak Z, Ji LL
pmid:26893258.title: Exercise-induced oxidative stress: past, present and future.
pmid:26893258.finding: Review of sources of exercise-induced ROS (mitochondria, NADPH oxidases, xanthine oxidase) and evidence that these ROS act as signals required for training adaptation.

pmid:27770706.title: Nrf2 mediates redox adaptations to exercise.
pmid:27770706.finding: Review of evidence that acute exercise activates Nrf2 and that repeated bouts up-regulate Nrf2-controlled antioxidant defences, with emerging human data.

pmid:40834031.authors: Torres-Rojo FI, Enríquez-Del Castillo LA, González-Chávez SA, et al.
pmid:40834031.title: Effect of exercise intensity on redox biomarkers in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
pmid:40834031.finding: Chronic exercise training raised antioxidant capacity and lowered pro-oxidant markers in healthy adults; the effect was significant for vigorous protocols but not for non-vigorous ones.

pmid:36139825.authors: Zhou Z, Chen C, Teo EC, et al.
pmid:36139825.title: Intracellular Oxidative Stress Induced by Physical Exercise in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:36139825.finding: Exercise-induced oxidative damage (8-OHdG, F2-isoprostanes, protein carbonyls) depends on intensity times volume; moderate continuous exercise and low-volume HIIT carried the lowest probability of large oxidative stress in unhealthy adults.

pmid:39914379.authors: Cordeiro LS, Linhares DG, Castro JBP, et al.
pmid:39914379.title: Impacts of Resistance Training on Endogenous Antioxidants in Older Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
pmid:39914379.finding: Resistance training in healthy older adults raised glutathione peroxidase (SMD 0.57) but did not significantly change catalase or total antioxidant activity.

pmid:20139793.authors: Campbell PT, Gross MD, Potter JD, et al.
pmid:20139793.title: Effect of exercise on oxidative stress: a 12-month randomized, controlled trial.
pmid:20139793.finding: 12 months of aerobic exercise (>=45 min/day, 5 days/week, 60-75% HRmax) lowered F2-isoprostanes 6% vs controls (not significant overall); women whose VO2max rose >15% had a 14% reduction.

pmid:33740420.authors: Flockhart M, Nilsson LC, Tais S, et al.
pmid:33740420.title: Excessive exercise training causes mitochondrial functional impairment and decreases glucose tolerance in healthy volunteers.
pmid:33740420.n: healthy volunteers (small progressive-load training study) plus elite athletes
pmid:33740420.finding: When training load was ramped up over 4 weeks, the highest-load week caused a sharp fall in intrinsic mitochondrial function and impaired glucose tolerance.

pmid:17697935.authors: Margonis K, Fatouros IG, Jamurtas AZ, et al.
pmid:17697935.title: Oxidative stress biomarkers responses to physical overtraining: implications for diagnosis.
pmid:17697935.finding: An overreaching resistance-training block raised urinary isoprostanes 7-fold, TBARS 56% and protein carbonyls 73% and lowered GSH 31%; markers tracked the performance decline.

pmid:11585710.authors: Mastaloudis A, Leonard SW, Traber MG
pmid:11585710.title: Oxidative stress in athletes during extreme endurance exercise.
pmid:11585710.finding: A 50 km ultramarathon (~6.5 h) raised plasma F2-isoprostanes from 75 to 131 pg/ml, with return to baseline by 24 h.

pmid:33239350.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
pmid:33239350.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour.
pmid:33239350.finding: WHO 2020 guidelines: adults should do 150-300 min/week of moderate or 75-150 min/week of vigorous aerobic activity, muscle strengthening on >=2 days/week, and limit sedentary time.

pmid:31721213.authors: Dirks ML, Miotto PM, Goossens GH, et al.
pmid:31721213.title: Short-term bed rest-induced insulin resistance cannot be explained by increased mitochondrial H(2) O(2) emission.
pmid:31721213.finding: Short-term bed rest cut insulin sensitivity by 42% and lowered mitochondrial respiration, but did not raise resting mitochondrial H2O2 emission or oxidative stress markers.

pmid:32502393.authors: Vaccaro A, Kaplan Dor Y, Nambara K, et al.
pmid:32502393.title: Sleep Loss Can Cause Death through Accumulation of Reactive Oxygen Species in the Gut.
pmid:32502393.finding: In flies and mice, severe sleep deprivation caused ROS accumulation in the gut; oral antioxidants or gut-targeted antioxidant enzymes prevented early death.

pmid:37717072.authors: Shah R, Shah VK, Emin M, et al.
pmid:37717072.title: Mild sleep restriction increases endothelial oxidative stress in female persons.
pmid:37717072.finding: Six weeks of sleeping 1.5 h less than habitual (randomized crossover) increased endothelial-cell oxidative stress without a compensatory antioxidant response.

pmid:28738082.authors: Trivedi MS, Holger D, Bui AT, et al.
pmid:28738082.title: Short-term sleep deprivation leads to decreased systemic redox metabolites and altered epigenetic status.
pmid:28738082.finding: One night of total sleep deprivation significantly lowered plasma glutathione, cysteine, ATP and homocysteine.

pmid:28933565.authors: Nagata C, Tamura T, Wada K, et al.
pmid:28933565.title: Sleep duration, nightshift work, and the timing of meals and urinary levels of 8-isoprostane and 6-sulfatoxymelatonin in Japanese women.
pmid:28933565.finding: Women sleeping 6 h or less had about 12% higher urinary 8-isoprostane than women sleeping more than 8 h.

pmid:26039963.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al.
pmid:26039963.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society.
pmid:26039963.finding: AASM/SRS consensus statement: adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis.

pmid:28652381.authors: Bhatti P, Mirick DK, Randolph TW, et al.
pmid:28652381.title: Oxidative DNA damage during night shift work.
pmid:28652381.finding: During night work (low melatonin) urinary 8-OH-dG excretion was only 20% of that during night sleep, interpreted as reduced repair of oxidative DNA lesions.

pmid:39993913.authors: Zanif U, Lai AS, Parks J, et al.
pmid:39993913.title: Melatonin supplementation and oxidative DNA damage repair capacity among night shift workers: a randomised placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:39993913.finding: Melatonin taken before day sleep for 4 weeks gave a borderline-significant 1.8-fold increase in urinary 8-OH-dG during day sleep, suggesting improved oxidative DNA repair.

pmid:36322225.authors: Hosseini H, Homayouni-Tabrizi M, Amiri H, et al.
pmid:36322225.title: The effect of continuous positive airway pressure on total antioxidant capacity in obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:36322225.finding: CPAP treatment of obstructive sleep apnea increased total antioxidant capacity (SMD 0.50).

pmid:8964113.authors: Reilly M, Delanty N, Lawson JA, et al.
pmid:8964113.title: Modulation of oxidant stress in vivo in chronic cigarette smokers.
pmid:8964113.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a rose with smoking dose (heavy 177, moderate 93, nonsmokers 54 pmol/mmol) and fell within 2-3 weeks of quitting; high-dose vitamin C lowered it, vitamin E alone did not.

pmid:10944241.authors: Pilz H, Oguogho A, Chehne F, et al.
pmid:10944241.title: Quitting cigarette smoking results in a fast improvement of in vivo oxidation injury (determined via plasma, serum and urinary isoprostane).
pmid:10944241.finding: Isoprostanes in plasma, serum and urine dropped within days of quitting and reached a new steady state about 4 weeks after cessation.

pmid:27932354.authors: King CC, Piper ME, Gepner AD, et al.
pmid:27932354.title: Longitudinal Impact of Smoking and Smoking Cessation on Inflammatory Markers of Cardiovascular Disease Risk.
pmid:27932354.finding: Smoking heaviness was independently tied to urinary F2-isoprostanes; after one year, successful quitters had lower F2-isoprostanes and white-cell counts despite gaining weight.

pmid:18324566.authors: Joseph AM, Hecht SS, Murphy SE, et al.
pmid:18324566.title: Smoking reduction fails to improve clinical and biological markers of cardiac disease: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:18324566.finding: Cutting cigarettes from ~27 to ~18/day over 6 months did not change F2-isoprostanes, inflammatory markers or symptoms; only carbon monoxide fell.

pmid:11466122.authors: Otsuka R, Watanabe H, Hirata K, et al.
pmid:11466122.title: Acute effects of passive smoking on the coronary circulation in healthy young adults.
pmid:11466122.finding: A 30-minute exposure to environmental tobacco smoke reduced coronary flow velocity reserve in healthy nonsmokers (4.4 to 3.4), indicating acute coronary endothelial dysfunction.

pmid:31429895.authors: Duncan MS, Freiberg MS, Greevy RA Jr, et al.
pmid:31429895.title: Association of Smoking Cessation With Subsequent Risk of Cardiovascular Disease.
pmid:31429895.finding: Quitting was linked to 39% lower CVD risk within 5 years versus continued smoking, but heavy smokers' risk stayed above never-smokers for well over 5 years (10-15+ years).

pmid:9644196.authors: Bermúdez E, Stone K, Carter KM, et al.
pmid:9644196.title: Environmental tobacco smoke is just as damaging to DNA as mainstream smoke.
pmid:9644196.finding: Tar from environmental (secondhand) tobacco smoke generated hydrogen peroxide and nicked DNA in cells much like mainstream-smoke tar; catalase was protective.

pmid:15911719.title: Cardiovascular effects of secondhand smoke: nearly as large as smoking.
pmid:15911719.finding: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk ~30%; even brief exposure produces effects on platelets, endothelium and oxidative stress averaging 80-90% of those of chronic active smoking.

pmid:30356972.authors: Siti Hajar MH, Zulkefli S, Juwita S, et al.
pmid:30356972.title: Metabolic, inflammatory, and oxidative stress markers in women exposed to secondhand smoke.
pmid:30356972.finding: Women with modest secondhand-smoke exposure (>=15 min on >=2 days/week) did not differ from unexposed women in 8-isoprostane, oxidized LDL or inflammatory markers.

pmid:27108682.authors: Carnevale R, Sciarretta S, Violi F, et al.
pmid:27108682.title: Acute Impact of Tobacco vs Electronic Cigarette Smoking on Oxidative Stress and Vascular Function.
pmid:27108682.finding: A single e-cigarette and a single tobacco cigarette both acutely raised 8-iso-PGF2a and NOX2 activation and lowered flow-mediated dilation; the e-cigarette's oxidative effects were smaller.

pmid:34289969.authors: Christensen CH, Chang JT, Rostron BL, et al.
pmid:34289969.title: Biomarkers of Inflammation and Oxidative Stress among Adult Former Smoker, Current E-Cigarette Users-Results from Wave 1 PATH Study.
pmid:34289969.finding: Former smokers who now only vape had F2-isoprostane levels similar to former smokers using nothing; dual users had 9% higher levels than cigarette-only smokers.

pmid:27113031.authors: Sharma R, Harlev A, Agarwal A, et al.
pmid:27113031.title: Cigarette Smoking and Semen Quality: A New Meta-analysis Examining the Effect of the 2010 World Health Organization Laboratory Methods for the Examination of Human Semen.
pmid:27113031.finding: Smoking was associated with lower sperm count, motility and morphology, with larger effects in moderate/heavy smokers.

pmid:18078827.title: CYP2E1 and oxidative liver injury by alcohol.
pmid:18078827.finding: Review: chronic ethanol induces CYP2E1, which leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide and drives lipid peroxidation in alcoholic liver injury.

pmid:22859618.authors: Schrieks IC, van den Berg R, Sierksma A, et al.
pmid:22859618.title: Effect of red wine consumption on biomarkers of oxidative stress.
pmid:22859618.finding: Four weeks of 450 ml/day red wine (4 drinks, 41 g alcohol) raised urinary 8-iso-PGF2a versus the same wine dealcoholized (157 vs 141 pg/mg creatinine).

pmid:29676281.authors: Wood AM, Kaptoge S, Butterworth AS, et al.
pmid:29676281.title: Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption: combined analysis of individual-participant data for 599 912 current drinkers in 83 prospective studies.
pmid:29676281.finding: All-cause mortality was lowest at or below ~100 g alcohol per week and rose with higher intake; stroke, heart failure and fatal hypertensive disease rose roughly linearly.

pmid:17709633.authors: Pou KM, Massaro JM, Hoffmann U, et al.
pmid:17709633.title: Visceral and subcutaneous adipose tissue volumes are cross-sectionally related to markers of inflammation and oxidative stress: the Framingham Heart Study.
pmid:17709633.finding: Visceral fat was more strongly associated with urinary isoprostanes than subcutaneous abdominal fat.

pmid:27803047.authors: Duggan C, Tapsoba JD, Wang CY, et al.
pmid:27803047.title: Dietary Weight Loss, Exercise, and Oxidative Stress in Postmenopausal Women: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:27803047.finding: 12 months of calorie-restricted weight-loss diet lowered F2-isoprostanes by ~23% (diet) and ~24% (diet plus exercise) vs 3% in controls; greater weight loss gave greater reductions.

pmid:28319890.authors: Monzo-Beltran L, Vazquez-Tarragón A, Cerdà C, et al.
pmid:28319890.title: One-year follow-up of clinical, metabolic and oxidative stress profile of morbid obese patients after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. 8-oxo-dG as a clinical marker.
pmid:28319890.n: morbidly obese patients vs normal-weight controls
pmid:28319890.finding: Morbidly obese patients had raised urinary F2-isoprostanes and 8-oxo-dG; after sleeve gastrectomy these declined progressively and antioxidant enzymes recovered over one year.

pmid:21959342.authors: Il'yasova D, Wang F, Spasojevic I, et al.
pmid:21959342.title: Urinary F2-isoprostanes, obesity, and weight gain in the IRAS cohort.
pmid:21959342.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes were higher with obesity cross-sectionally, yet some isoprostanes predicted less weight gain over 5 years, cautioning against naive reading of the marker.

pmid:23242914.authors: Sermondade N, Faure C, Fezeu L, et al.
pmid:23242914.title: BMI in relation to sperm count: an updated systematic review and collaborative meta-analysis.
pmid:23242914.finding: Obesity was associated with higher odds of oligozoospermia or azoospermia (OR 1.28; morbid obesity OR 2.04).

pmid:32835677.authors: Li Z, Liu Q, Xu Z, et al.
pmid:32835677.title: Association between short-term exposure to ambient particulate air pollution and biomarkers of oxidative stress: A meta-analysis.
pmid:32835677.finding: Each 10 ug/m3 rise in short-term PM2.5 was associated with 1.6% higher malondialdehyde and a borderline 2.1% higher 8-OHdG.

pmid:28669628.title: Role of oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease outcomes following exposure to ambient air pollution.
pmid:28669628.finding: Review of epidemiological, controlled-exposure and experimental data concluding that oxidative stress is central to the cardiovascular effects of ambient air pollution.

pmid:26022815.authors: Chen R, Zhao A, Chen H, et al.
pmid:26022815.title: Cardiopulmonary benefits of reducing indoor particles of outdoor origin: a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of air purifiers.
pmid:26022815.finding: 48 h of real vs sham air purification cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% (96 to 41 ug/m3) and lowered inflammatory and thrombotic markers (e.g., myeloperoxidase -33%) and blood pressure.

pmid:33682970.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Xue L, et al.
pmid:33682970.title: Effects of air purification of indoor PM(2.5) on the cardiorespiratory biomarkers in young healthy adults.
pmid:33682970.finding: One week of real vs sham HEPA purification lowered diastolic blood pressure, exhaled NO and 8-isoprostane and improved lung function.

pmid:34630006.authors: Hoffmann B, Boogaard H, de Nazelle A, et al.
pmid:34630006.title: WHO Air Quality Guidelines 2021-Aiming for Healthier Air for all: A Joint Statement by Medical, Public Health, Scientific Societies and Patient Representative Organisations.
