pmid:30263756.finding: Vitamin C retention in cooked vegetables ranged from 0 to 91%, generally highest after microwaving and lowest after boiling.

pmid:37738616.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al.
pmid:37738616.title: Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study.
pmid:37738616.finding: More regular sleep (Sleep Regularity Index) was associated with 20-48% lower all-cause and 22-57% lower cardiometabolic mortality vs the least regular quintile; regularity predicted mortality better than duration.

pmid:26580236.authors: Wong PM, Hasler BP, Kamarck TW, et al.
pmid:26580236.title: Social Jetlag, Chronotype, and Cardiometabolic Risk.
pmid:26580236.finding: Greater social jetlag was associated with lower HDL, higher triglycerides, insulin resistance and adiposity, independent of sleep duration and quality.

pmid:29642757.title: Associations between chronotype, morbidity and mortality in the UK Biobank cohort.
pmid:29642757.finding: Definite evening types had 10% higher all-cause mortality than definite morning types (HR 1.10) over 6.5 years.

pmid:18772469.authors: Treuting PM, Linford NJ, Knoblaugh SE, et al.
pmid:18772469.title: Reduction of age-associated pathology in old mice by overexpression of catalase in mitochondria
pmid:18772469.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
pmid:18772469.finding: MCAT mice had lower malignant (non-blood) tumour burden and fewer cardiac lesions at death, but no effect on blood cancers or kidney disease.

pmid:23025341.authors: Lewis KN, Andziak B, Yang T, et al.
pmid:23025341.title: The naked mole-rat response to oxidative stress: just deal with it
pmid:23025341.finding: Naked mole-rats combine mouse-like ROS production and unexceptional antioxidant defences with high steady-state oxidative damage, yet stay healthy; they tolerate rather than prevent damage.

pmid:19411855.title: Antioxidant defense and aging in C. elegans: is the oxidative damage theory of aging wrong?
pmid:19411855.finding: Worm studies in which antioxidant defences were changed without changing lifespan challenge the oxidative damage theory of aging.

pmid:35190722.authors: Sies H, Belousov VV, Chandel NS, et al.
pmid:35190722.title: Defining roles of specific reactive oxygen species (ROS) in cell biology and physiology
pmid:35190722.finding: Expert recommendation: the generic term 'ROS' should not be used for specific molecules; H2O2 and superoxide have distinct signalling roles that need specific measurement.

pmid:22641614.title: The free-radical theory of ageing--older, wiser and still alive: modelling positional effects of the primary targets of ROS reveals new support
pmid:22641614.finding: Modelling of where ROS are generated relative to their targets suggests many negative experiments are misleading; the theory survives as one of several mechanisms of aging.

pmid:23434764.title: Reactive oxygen species and the free radical theory of aging
pmid:23434764.finding: Defends the traditional view that ROS cause direct damage contributing to aging, cautioning against an overcorrection that treats ROS mainly as beneficial signals.

pmid:21290398.title: The free-radical damage theory: Accumulating evidence against a simple link of oxidative stress to ageing and lifespan
pmid:21290398.finding: Antioxidant-gene knockout mice show more oxidative damage but no change in lifespan, and long-lived species do not have exceptional defences: evidence against a simple damage-lifespan link.

pmid:19730800.title: When a theory of aging ages badly
pmid:19730800.finding: Concludes the mitochondrial free-radical theory of aging should be considered refuted, citing long-lived Mclk1-/- mice and transgenic studies.

pmid:33644065.authors: Shields HJ, Traa A, Van Raamsdonk JM
pmid:33644065.title: Beneficial and Detrimental Effects of Reactive Oxygen Species on Lifespan: A Comprehensive Review of Comparative and Experimental Studies
pmid:33644065.finding: Comparative studies mostly show an inverse correlation between ROS damage and lifespan, but experimental manipulations show ROS can shorten, not affect, or extend lifespan depending on context.

pmid:36599349.authors: López-Otín C, Blasco MA, Partridge L, et al.
pmid:36599349.title: Hallmarks of aging: An expanding universe
pmid:36599349.finding: Updated framework of 12 hallmarks of aging, including mitochondrial dysfunction, genomic instability and chronic inflammation.

deep-longevity:lon-fda2025nmn.authors: US Food and Drug Administration, Human Foods Program
deep-longevity:lon-fda2025nmn.title: Response letter to Natural Products Association and Alliance for Natural Health USA regarding the regulatory status of beta-nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), Docket FDA-2023-P-0872
deep-longevity:lon-fda2025nmn.finding: FDA reversed its 2022 position and determined that NMN is not excluded from the dietary supplement definition, granting the industry petition in part (September 29, 2025).

deep-longevity:lon-fdandi.title: Submitted 75-Day Premarket Notifications for New Dietary Ingredients
deep-longevity:lon-fdandi.finding: Lists new-dietary-ingredient notifications for beta-NMN (NDIN 1444, filed November 2025, FDA response January 2026) and reduced NMN (NDIN 1451).

pmid:32090480.authors: Sammaritano LR, Bermas BL, Chakravarty EE, et al.
pmid:32090480.title: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Reproductive Health in Rheumatic and Musculoskeletal Diseases.
pmid:32090480.finding: ACR 2020 reproductive-health guideline: contraception, pre-pregnancy counselling, and continuing pregnancy-compatible medications; low-dose methotrexate may be continued in men planning conception.

deep-medications:med-fda-wegovy2021.authors: US Food and Drug Administration; Novo Nordisk
deep-medications:med-fda-wegovy2021.title: WEGOVY (semaglutide) injection, prescribing information (revised 06/2021)
deep-medications:med-fda-wegovy2021.finding: Label section 8.3: discontinue semaglutide at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy because of its long half-life; discontinue when pregnancy is recognized.

deep-medications:med-fda-zepbound2023.authors: US Food and Drug Administration; Eli Lilly
deep-medications:med-fda-zepbound2023.title: ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) injection, prescribing information (revised 11/2023)
deep-medications:med-fda-zepbound2023.finding: A single 5 mg tirzepatide dose cut ethinyl estradiol Cmax 59% and AUC 20%; users of oral contraceptives should switch to a non-oral method or add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation.

deep-medications:med-fda-statins2021.title: FDA requests removal of strongest warning against using cholesterol-lowering statins during pregnancy; still advises most pregnant patients should stop taking statins (Drug Safety Communication, 20 July 2021)
deep-medications:med-fda-statins2021.finding: FDA removed the pregnancy contraindication for statins because observational data showed no increase in birth defects, while advising most patients to stop on learning they are pregnant, allowing continuation in very high-risk patients, and advising against breastfeeding.

pmid:25439662.authors: Fang X, An P, Wang H, et al.
pmid:25439662.title: Dietary intake of heme iron and risk of cardiovascular disease: a dose-response meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies
pmid:25439662.finding: Each 1 mg/day of heme iron was associated with 7% higher cardiovascular risk; non-heme and total iron were not associated.

pmid:40526045.authors: Wang Y, Li J, Zhuang J, et al.
pmid:40526045.title: Manganese in health and disease
pmid:40526045.finding: Manganese is the MnSOD cofactor in mitochondria; dysregulated manganese accumulates in brain with neurotoxic effects.

pmid:25469382.title: Vitamin E inadequacy in humans: causes and consequences
pmid:25469382.finding: >90% of Americans eat less alpha-tocopherol than the EAR; plasma alpha-tocopherol <12 umol/L is linked to infection, anaemia and poor pregnancy outcomes.

pmid:39099617.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
pmid:39099617.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for vitamin E
pmid:39099617.finding: EFSA retained a vitamin E UL of 300 mg/day alpha-tocopherol for adults, based on bleeding risk.

pmid:7477116.authors: Rothman KJ, Moore LL, Singer MR, et al.
pmid:7477116.title: Teratogenicity of high vitamin A intake
pmid:7477116.finding: Supplemental preformed vitamin A >10,000 IU/day was associated with a 4.8-fold prevalence of cranial-neural-crest birth defects.

pmid:24700407.authors: Wu AM, Huang CQ, Lin ZK, et al.
pmid:24700407.title: The relationship between vitamin A and risk of fracture: meta-analysis of prospective studies
pmid:24700407.n: 8 intake studies (283,930 participants) and 4 blood studies
pmid:24700407.finding: High retinol intake was associated with higher hip fracture risk (RR 1.40); beta-carotene was not; both high and low blood retinol were risky.

pmid:38846679.authors: EFSA NDA Panel: Turck D, Bohn T, Castenmiller J, et al.
pmid:38846679.title: Scientific opinion on the tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A and β-carotene
pmid:38846679.finding: EFSA retained a 3000 ug RE/day UL for preformed vitamin A, based on teratogenicity.

deep-nutrients:nut-efsa2006.authors: EFSA Scientific Committee on Food / Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition and Allergies
deep-nutrients:nut-efsa2006.title: Tolerable Upper Intake Levels for Vitamins and Minerals
deep-nutrients:nut-efsa2006.finding: EFSA/SCF compendium of tolerable upper intake levels (e.g. zinc 25 mg, copper 5 mg, iodine 600 ug, supplemental magnesium 250 mg per day for adults).

pmid:18543123.authors: Son TG, Camandola S, Mattson MP
pmid:18543123.title: Hormetic dietary phytochemicals.
pmid:18543123.finding: Many phytochemicals act as mild stressors at dietary doses and activate adaptive pathways (Nrf2/ARE, sirtuin-FOXO, NF-kB): hormesis.

pmid:28483461.authors: Espín JC, González-Sarrías A, Tomás-Barberán FA
pmid:28483461.title: The gut microbiota: A key factor in the therapeutic effects of (poly)phenols.
pmid:28483461.finding: Most polyphenols reach the colon, where gut microbes convert them into metabolites that are often more active and better absorbed; metabotype stratification is needed in trials.

pmid:33388204.authors: Del Bo' C, Bernardi S, Cherubini A, et al.
pmid:33388204.title: A polyphenol-rich dietary pattern improves intestinal permeability, evaluated as serum zonulin levels, in older subjects: The MaPLE randomised controlled trial.
pmid:33388204.finding: A polyphenol-rich diet (812 to 1391 mg/day polyphenols) for 8 weeks lowered serum zonulin and diastolic BP and increased butyrate-producing bacteria (MaPLE trial).

pmid:40456886.authors: Parmenter BH, Thompson AS, Bondonno NP, et al.
pmid:40456886.title: High diversity of dietary flavonoid intake is associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality and major chronic diseases.
pmid:40456886.finding: Greater diversity of flavonoid intake was associated with 6-20% lower mortality and chronic disease, independently of total quantity.

pmid:34338114.authors: Gerli S, Della Morte C, Ceccobelli M, et al.
pmid:34338114.title: Biological and clinical effects of a resveratrol-based multivitamin supplement on intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycles: a single-center, randomized controlled trial.
pmid:34338114.finding: A resveratrol-based multivitamin for 3 months (vs folic acid) increased oocytes, MII oocytes, fertilisation and embryos, but not pregnancy or live birth.

deep-phytochemicals:phy-nct03675724.title: AFFIRM-LITE: A Phase 2 Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study of Alleviation by Fisetin of Frailty, Inflammation, and Related Measures in Older Adults (NCT03675724), record accessed 2026-10-01.
deep-phytochemicals:phy-nct03675724.finding: Fisetin 20 mg/kg/day orally for 2 consecutive days vs placebo; started November 2018 and still listed as enrolling, with primary completion estimated for November 2026.

pmid:11340098.authors: Stahl W, Heinrich U, Wiseman S, et al.
pmid:11340098.title: Dietary tomato paste protects against ultraviolet light-induced erythema in humans.
pmid:11340098.finding: 40 g/day tomato paste (~16 mg lycopene) with olive oil for 10 weeks reduced UV-induced erythema by 40% versus olive oil alone; no effect was seen at 4 weeks.

pmid:20854436.authors: Rizwan M, Rodriguez-Blanco I, Harbottle A, et al.
pmid:20854436.title: Tomato paste rich in lycopene protects against cutaneous photodamage in humans in vivo: a randomized controlled trial.
pmid:20854436.finding: 55 g/day tomato paste (16 mg lycopene) for 12 weeks raised the erythema threshold (D30) and reduced UV-induced MMP-1 and mitochondrial DNA damage versus olive oil alone.

pmid:18086246.title: Protection from sunburn with beta-Carotene--a meta-analysis.
pmid:18086246.finding: Beta-carotene supplements protected against sunburn, but only after at least 10 weeks, with protection growing about 0.5 SD per extra month.

pmid:36606553.authors: Zhang X, Zhou Q, Qi Y, et al.
pmid:36606553.title: The effect of tomato and lycopene on clinical characteristics and molecular markers of UV-induced skin deterioration: A systematic review and meta-analysis of intervention trials.
pmid:36606553.finding: Tomato and lycopene supplementation reduced UV erythema, MMP-1 and pigmentation and raised the minimal erythema dose in healthy people.

pmid:23924651.authors: Okada HC, Alleyne B, Varghai K, et al.
pmid:23924651.title: Facial changes caused by smoking: a comparison between smoking and nonsmoking identical twins.
pmid:23924651.finding: Smoking twins had worse upper-eyelid redundancy, lower-lid and malar bags, nasolabial folds, lip wrinkles and jowls than their non-smoking identical twins.

pmid:31531169.authors: Goodman GD, Kaufman J, Day D, et al.
pmid:31531169.title: Impact of Smoking and Alcohol Use on Facial Aging in Women: Results of a Large Multinational, Multiracial, Cross-sectional Survey.
pmid:31531169.finding: In a multinational self-rated survey, smoking was linked to worse forehead, crow's-feet and glabellar lines and other features, and heavy alcohol use to more severe under-eye puffiness, oral commissures, midface volume loss and blood vessels (funded by Allergan).

pmid:25266053.authors: Oyetakin-White P, Suggs A, Koo B, et al.
pmid:25266053.title: Does poor sleep quality affect skin ageing?
pmid:25266053.finding: Poor sleepers had higher intrinsic skin-aging scores, worse skin-barrier recovery (good sleepers recovered 30% better at 72 h) and slower recovery from UV erythema than good sleepers.

pmid:23997369.authors: Sundelin T, Lekander M, Kecklund G, et al.
pmid:23997369.title: Cues of fatigue: effects of sleep deprivation on facial appearance.
pmid:23997369.finding: After 31 hours awake, faces were rated as having more hanging eyelids, darker circles, paler skin and more wrinkles/fine lines than after normal sleep.

pmid:29413961.authors: Cobley JN, Fiorello ML, Bailey DM
pmid:29413961.title: 13 reasons why the brain is susceptible to oxidative stress.
pmid:29413961.finding: The brain uses about 20% of basal oxygen; reasons for its oxidative vulnerability include PUFA-rich membranes, mitochondria, calcium and glutamate signalling, modest antioxidant defences, redox-active metals and neurotransmitter auto-oxidation, with ROS also needed for normal signalling.

pmid:16805774.title: Oxidative stress and neurodegeneration: where are we now?
pmid:16805774.finding: The brain is poorly equipped with antioxidant defences, and oxidative damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, protein aggregation and inflammation are intertwined in neurodegeneration.

pmid:30737462.title: Oxidative stress, dysfunctional glucose metabolism and Alzheimer disease.
pmid:30737462.finding: Oxidative damage to glycolytic, TCA-cycle and ATP-synthase enzymes plausibly contributes to the sharp fall in brain glucose metabolism seen in Alzheimer disease and amnestic MCI.

pmid:11487050.authors: Nunomura A, Perry G, Aliev G, et al.
pmid:11487050.title: Oxidative damage is the earliest event in Alzheimer disease.
pmid:11487050.finding: Neuronal RNA oxidation (8-OHG) and nitrotyrosine were greatest early in Alzheimer disease and declined as amyloid deposition increased, suggesting oxidative damage precedes plaques and tangles.

pmid:9110909.authors: Sano M, Ernesto C, Thomas RG, et al.
pmid:9110909.title: A controlled trial of selegiline, alpha-tocopherol, or both as treatment for Alzheimer's disease. The Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study.
pmid:9110909.finding: Unadjusted outcomes were null; after adjusting for baseline MMSE imbalance, 2000 IU/day vitamin E delayed the composite end point (670 vs 440 days).

pmid:15829527.authors: Petersen RC, Thomas RG, Grundman M, et al.
pmid:15829527.title: Vitamin E and donepezil for the treatment of mild cognitive impairment.
pmid:15829527.finding: 2000 IU/day vitamin E for 3 years did not slow progression from MCI to Alzheimer disease (HR 1.02), including in APOE4 carriers.

pmid:24381967.authors: Dysken MW, Sano M, Asthana S, et al.
pmid:24381967.title: Effect of vitamin E and memantine on functional decline in Alzheimer disease: the TEAM-AD VA cooperative randomized trial.
pmid:24381967.finding: TEAM-AD: 2000 IU/day alpha-tocopherol slowed functional decline by 3.15 ADCS-ADL points (about 19% per year, ~6 months' delay) versus placebo over 2.3 years; memantine and the combination did not.

pmid:28418065.authors: Farina N, Llewellyn D, Isaac MGEKN, et al.
pmid:28418065.title: Vitamin E for Alzheimer's dementia and mild cognitive impairment.
pmid:28418065.finding: Cochrane: no evidence of clinically important cognitive benefit of vitamin E in AD or of preventing progression from MCI; moderate-quality evidence suggests possible slowing of functional decline in AD and no increase in serious adverse events.

pmid:28319243.authors: Kryscio RJ, Abner EL, Caban-Holt A, et al.
pmid:28319243.title: Association of Antioxidant Supplement Use and Dementia in the Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease by Vitamin E and Selenium Trial (PREADViSE).
pmid:28319243.finding: PREADViSE (within SELECT): vitamin E (400 IU/day) or selenium (200 ug/day) did not prevent dementia (HRs 0.88 and 0.83, non-significant).

pmid:22431837.authors: Galasko DR, Peskind E, Clark CM, et al.
pmid:22431837.title: Antioxidants for Alzheimer disease: a randomized clinical trial with cerebrospinal fluid biomarker measures.
pmid:22431837.finding: Vitamin E + C + alpha-lipoic acid lowered CSF F2-isoprostanes by 19% but did not change amyloid or tau and was associated with faster MMSE decline.

pmid:24664227.authors: Parkinson Study Group QE3 Investigators, Beal MF, Oakes D, et al.
pmid:24664227.title: A randomized clinical trial of high-dosage coenzyme Q10 in early Parkinson disease: no evidence of benefit.
pmid:24664227.finding: QE3: CoQ10 1200 or 2400 mg/day was stopped for futility, with slight adverse trends versus placebo (UPDRS worsening 7.5 and 8.0 vs 6.9 points).

pmid:12374491.authors: Shults CW, Oakes D, Kieburtz K, et al.
pmid:12374491.title: Effects of coenzyme Q10 in early Parkinson disease: evidence of slowing of the functional decline.
pmid:12374491.finding: The pilot trial suggested CoQ10 1200 mg/day slowed functional decline (UPDRS +6.7 vs +12.0 on placebo), the result QE3 later failed to confirm.

pmid:8417384.title: Effects of tocopherol and deprenyl on the progression of disability in early Parkinson's disease.
pmid:8417384.finding: DATATOP: 2000 IU/day tocopherol did not delay disability in early Parkinson's disease, whereas deprenyl did.

pmid:34519802.authors: Parkinson Study Group SURE-PD3 Investigators, Schwarzschild MA, Ascherio A, et al.
pmid:34519802.title: Effect of Urate-Elevating Inosine on Early Parkinson Disease Progression: The SURE-PD3 Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:34519802.finding: SURE-PD3: raising serum urate (an endogenous antioxidant) by 44% with inosine did not slow Parkinson's progression and increased kidney stones; the trial stopped for futility.

pmid:36449420.authors: Devos D, Labreuche J, Rascol O, et al.
pmid:36449420.title: Trial of Deferiprone in Parkinson's Disease.
pmid:36449420.finding: FAIRPARK-II: the iron chelator deferiprone lowered nigrostriatal iron but worsened parkinsonism (MDS-UPDRS +15.6 vs +6.3 points over 36 weeks).

pmid:39495531.authors: Ayton S, Barton D, Brew B, et al.
pmid:39495531.title: Deferiprone in Alzheimer Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:39495531.n: 81 people with MCI or early Alzheimer disease
pmid:39495531.finding: Deferiprone lowered hippocampal iron but accelerated cognitive decline, mainly executive function, versus placebo.

pmid:19451353.authors: Kang JH, Cook NR, Manson JE, et al.
pmid:19451353.title: Vitamin E, vitamin C, beta carotene, and cognitive function among women with or at risk of cardiovascular disease: The Women's Antioxidant and Cardiovascular Study.
pmid:19451353.finding: WACS cognitive substudy: vitamin E and beta-carotene did not slow cognitive change over 5.4 years; vitamin C gave inconsistent results.

pmid:17998490.authors: Grodstein F, Kang JH, Glynn RJ, et al.
pmid:17998490.title: A randomized trial of beta carotene supplementation and cognitive function in men: the Physicians' Health Study II.
pmid:17998490.finding: PHS II: short-term beta-carotene had no cognitive effect, but men randomized for about 18 years scored slightly higher on global cognition (0.047 SD) and verbal memory.

pmid:36102337.authors: Baker LD, Manson JE, Rapp SR, et al.
pmid:36102337.title: Effects of cocoa extract and a multivitamin on cognitive function: A randomized clinical trial.
pmid:36102337.finding: COSMOS-Mind: cocoa extract (500 mg flavanols/day) had no effect on global cognition over 3 years, while a daily multivitamin gave a small benefit (0.07 SD), most in people with cardiovascular disease.

pmid:37244291.authors: Yeung LK, Alschuler DM, Wall M, et al.
pmid:37244291.title: Multivitamin Supplementation Improves Memory in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:37244291.finding: COSMOS-Web: a daily multivitamin improved immediate word-list recall at 1 year and over 3 years, estimated as equivalent to 3.1 years of age-related memory change; secondary outcomes were null.

pmid:25344629.authors: Brickman AM, Khan UA, Provenzano FA, et al.
pmid:25344629.title: Enhancing dentate gyrus function with dietary flavanols improves cognition in older adults.
pmid:25344629.finding: A 3-month high-cocoa-flavanol drink improved dentate-gyrus function on fMRI and a matched memory task versus a low-flavanol drink (small, Mars-supported).

pmid:37035889.authors: Sachs BC, Williams BJ, Gaussoin SA, et al.
pmid:37035889.title: Impact of multivitamin-mineral and cocoa extract on incidence of mild cognitive impairment and dementia: Results from the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study for the Mind (COSMOS-Mind).
pmid:37035889.finding: COSMOS-Mind: neither multivitamin nor cocoa extract reduced incident MCI or dementia over 3 years (110 MCI and 14 dementia cases; low power).

pmid:20047325.authors: Krikorian R, Shidler MD, Nash TA, et al.
pmid:20047325.title: Blueberry supplementation improves memory in older adults.
pmid:20047325.finding: Wild blueberry juice for 12 weeks improved paired-associate learning and word-list recall in a tiny uncontrolled pilot with early memory changes.

pmid:28283823.authors: Miller MG, Hamilton DA, Joseph JA, et al.
pmid:28283823.title: Dietary blueberry improves cognition among older adults in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:28283823.finding: Freeze-dried blueberry (24 g/day, equivalent to 1 cup fresh) for 90 days reduced repetition errors in verbal learning and task-switching cost versus placebo, with no gait or balance benefit.

pmid:22535616.authors: Devore EE, Kang JH, Breteler MM, et al.
pmid:22535616.title: Dietary intakes of berries and flavonoids in relation to cognitive decline.
pmid:22535616.finding: Higher blueberry and strawberry intake was associated with slower cognitive decline, equivalent to up to 2.5 years of delayed cognitive aging.

pmid:41974068.authors: He Y, Yang J, Zhang S, et al.
pmid:41974068.title: Blueberry consumption enhances vascular function but not cognitive abilities in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:41974068.finding: Blueberry interventions improved flow-mediated dilation by 1.11% but did not significantly improve executive function, mood or blood pressure.

pmid:40856863.authors: da Silva ABN, de Oliveira GM, Gallo Ruelas M, et al.
pmid:40856863.title: Blueberries for brainpower: A systematic review and meta-analysis with Bayesian post hoc analysis of RCTS exploring cognitive function in the elderly with prior cognitive decline.
pmid:40856863.finding: In older adults with MCI or subjective decline, chronic blueberry intake improved episodic memory (SMD 0.34) but not processing speed, recognition, visuospatial or working memory.

pmid:27063583.authors: Burckhardt M, Herke M, Wustmann T, et al.
pmid:27063583.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the treatment of dementia.
pmid:27063583.finding: Cochrane: omega-3 supplements had no effect on cognition, daily activities or dementia severity (high-quality evidence).

pmid:26305649.authors: Chew EY, Clemons TE, Agrón E, et al.
pmid:26305649.title: Effect of Omega-3 Fatty Acids, Lutein/Zeaxanthin, or Other Nutrient Supplementation on Cognitive Function: The AREDS2 Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:26305649.finding: AREDS2: 1 g/day omega-3 (or lutein/zeaxanthin) for 5 years did not change cognitive decline.

pmid:21045096.authors: Quinn JF, Raman R, Thomas RG, et al.
pmid:21045096.title: Docosahexaenoic acid supplementation and cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease: a randomized trial.
pmid:21045096.finding: DHA 2 g/day for 18 months did not slow cognitive or functional decline or brain atrophy.

pmid:35415212.authors: Kang JH, Vyas CM, Okereke OI, et al.
pmid:35415212.title: Marine n-3 fatty acids and cognitive change among older adults in the VITAL randomized trial.
pmid:35415212.finding: 1 g/day marine omega-3 for 2-3 years did not affect cognitive change (pooled difference -0.01 SD/year).

pmid:26718417.authors: Zhang Y, Chen J, Qiu J, et al.
pmid:26718417.title: Intakes of fish and polyunsaturated fatty acids and mild-to-severe cognitive impairment risks: a dose-response meta-analysis of 21 cohort studies.
pmid:26718417.finding: Each extra weekly serving of fish was associated with 5% lower dementia and 7% lower Alzheimer risk, and each 0.1 g/day dietary DHA with 14% lower dementia risk, with high heterogeneity.

pmid:28114437.authors: Yassine HN, Braskie MN, Mack WJ, et al.
pmid:28114437.title: Association of Docosahexaenoic Acid Supplementation With Alzheimer Disease Stage in Apolipoprotein E ε4 Carriers: A Review.
pmid:28114437.finding: Mixed omega-3 trial results may reflect APOE4 genotype and disease stage: trials in symptomatic AD are negative, while predementia and APOE4-specific effects remain plausible but unproven.

pmid:28359749.authors: Andrieu S, Guyonnet S, Coley N, et al.
pmid:28359749.title: Effect of long-term omega 3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation with or without multidomain intervention on cognitive function in elderly adults with memory complaints (MAPT): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
pmid:28359749.n: 1680 older adults with memory complaints or frailty
pmid:28359749.finding: MAPT: 3 years of omega-3 (800 mg DHA + 225 mg EPA/day), with or without a multidomain intervention, did not significantly slow cognitive decline.

pmid:21282661.authors: Erickson KI, Voss MW, Prakash RS, et al.
pmid:21282661.title: Exercise training increases size of hippocampus and improves memory.
pmid:21282661.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:21282661.finding: One year of walking-based aerobic training increased anterior hippocampal volume by 2% (reversing 1-2 years of age-related loss) and improved spatial memory, whereas stretching controls lost volume.

pmid:29769247.authors: Lamb SE, Sheehan B, Atherton N, et al.
pmid:29769247.title: Dementia And Physical Activity (DAPA) trial of moderate to high intensity exercise training for people with dementia: randomised controlled trial.
pmid:29769247.finding: DAPA: 4 months of moderate-high intensity aerobic and strength training improved fitness but slightly worsened cognition at 12 months (ADAS-cog difference -1.4).

pmid:29113943.authors: Firth J, Stubbs B, Vancampfort D, et al.
pmid:29113943.title: Effect of aerobic exercise on hippocampal volume in humans: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:29113943.finding: Aerobic exercise had no significant effect on total hippocampal volume, but preserved left hippocampal volume by preventing age-related decline.

pmid:26305648.authors: Sink KM, Espeland MA, Castro CM, et al.
pmid:26305648.title: Effect of a 24-Month Physical Activity Intervention vs Health Education on Cognitive Outcomes in Sedentary Older Adults: The LIFE Randomized Trial.
pmid:26305648.finding: LIFE: a 24-month physical activity program did not improve cognition or reduce MCI/dementia versus health education.

pmid:24136970.authors: Xie L, Kang H, Xu Q, et al.
pmid:24136970.title: Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain.
pmid:24136970.finding: In mice, sleep and anesthesia expanded brain interstitial space by 60% and increased clearance of beta-amyloid and other solutes (the glymphatic hypothesis).

pmid:29632177.authors: Shokri-Kojori E, Wang GJ, Wiers CE, et al.
pmid:29632177.title: β-Amyloid accumulation in the human brain after one night of sleep deprivation.
pmid:29632177.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:29632177.finding: One night of sleep deprivation increased beta-amyloid PET signal in the right hippocampus and thalamus (crossover design).

pmid:33829232.authors: Eide PK, Vinje V, Pripp AH, et al.
pmid:33829232.title: Sleep deprivation impairs molecular clearance from the human brain.
pmid:33829232.finding: After intrathecal gadobutrol, one night of total sleep deprivation slowed tracer clearance from most brain regions on MRI, without catch-up on the next night's sleep.

pmid:38741022.authors: Miao A, Luo T, Hsieh B, et al.
pmid:38741022.title: Brain clearance is reduced during sleep and anesthesia.
pmid:38741022.finding: Measuring fluorescent tracers in mouse brains, clearance was reduced, not increased, during sleep and anesthesia, contradicting the glymphatic sleep-clearance model.

pmid:33879784.authors: Sabia S, Fayosse A, Dumurgier J, et al.
pmid:33879784.title: Association of sleep duration in middle and old age with incidence of dementia.
pmid:33879784.finding: Sleeping 6 hours or less at age 50-60 was associated with 22-37% higher dementia risk over 25 years, and persistent short sleep with about 30% higher risk.

pmid:37478886.authors: Lin FR, Pike JR, Albert MS, et al.
pmid:37478886.title: Hearing intervention versus health education control to reduce cognitive decline in older adults with hearing loss in the USA (ACHIEVE): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
pmid:37478886.finding: ACHIEVE: hearing aids plus audiology did not slow 3-year cognitive decline overall (difference 0.002 SD); a prespecified sensitivity analysis suggested benefit in the higher-risk ARIC cohort but not the healthier de novo cohort.

pmid:39096926.authors: Livingston G, Huntley J, Liu KY, et al.
pmid:39096926.title: Dementia prevention, intervention, and care: 2024 report of the Lancet standing Commission.
pmid:39096926.finding: Lancet Commission 2024: 14 potentially modifiable risk factors (adding high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss to the 2020 list) account for about 45% of dementia cases worldwide.

pmid:37019461.authors: Wilker EH, Osman M, Weisskopf MG
pmid:37019461.title: Ambient air pollution and clinical dementia: systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:37019461.finding: Each 2 ug/m3 of PM2.5 was associated with a dementia HR of 1.04 (0.99-1.09) overall and 1.42 in studies with active case finding; NO2 and NOx associations were weaker and ozone showed none.

pmid:19716187.title: Air pollution: mechanisms of neuroinflammation and CNS disease.
pmid:19716187.finding: Air pollution components reach the brain directly and via systemic inflammation, activating microglia and damaging the blood-brain barrier, a chronic source of ROS and neuroinflammation.

pmid:27601646.authors: Maher BA, Ahmed IA, Karloukovski V, et al.
pmid:27601646.title: Magnetite pollution nanoparticles in the human brain.
pmid:27601646.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:27601646.finding: Abundant rounded magnetite nanoparticles in human brain tissue matched combustion-derived airborne pollution particles, a potential redox-active iron source.

pmid:35246521.authors: Daviet R, Aydogan G, Jagannathan K, et al.
pmid:35246521.title: Associations between alcohol consumption and gray and white matter volumes in the UK Biobank.
pmid:35246521.finding: Alcohol intake was associated with lower global brain volume, regional grey matter and white-matter integrity, already at an average of 1-2 units a day, with stronger associations at higher intake.

pmid:35834561.authors: Topiwala A, Wang C, Ebmeier KP, et al.
pmid:35834561.title: Associations between moderate alcohol consumption, brain iron, and cognition in UK Biobank participants: Observational and mendelian randomization analyses.
pmid:35834561.finding: Drinking more than 7 units a week was associated with higher iron in the putamen, caudate and substantia nigra, which was associated with poorer executive function and fluid intelligence; Mendelian randomization evidence was weak.

pmid:28588063.authors: Topiwala A, Allan CL, Valkanova V, et al.
pmid:28588063.title: Moderate alcohol consumption as risk factor for adverse brain outcomes and cognitive decline: longitudinal cohort study.
pmid:28588063.finding: Over 30 years, 14-21 units a week carried 3.4 times the odds of right hippocampal atrophy compared with abstinence, over 30 units 5.8 times, and light drinking showed no protection.

pmid:30068508.authors: Sabia S, Fayosse A, Dumurgier J, et al.
pmid:30068508.title: Alcohol consumption and risk of dementia: 23 year follow-up of Whitehall II cohort study.
pmid:30068508.finding: Both midlife abstinence (HR 1.47) and drinking over 14 units/week (each extra 7 units +17%) were associated with higher dementia risk over 23 years.

pmid:40987604.authors: Topiwala A, Levey DF, Zhou H, et al.
pmid:40987604.title: Alcohol use and risk of dementia in diverse populations: evidence from cohort, case-control and Mendelian randomisation approaches.
pmid:40987604.finding: Observational analyses showed a U-shaped alcohol-dementia curve, but genetic analyses showed a monotonic rise in risk with drinking (OR 1.15 per SD) and suggested reverse causation explains the apparent benefit of light drinking.

pmid:11410599.authors: Heiss E, Herhaus C, Klimo K, et al.
pmid:11410599.title: Nuclear factor kappa B is a molecular target for sulforaphane-mediated anti-inflammatory mechanisms.
pmid:11410599.finding: In LPS-stimulated macrophages, sulforaphane cut NO, PGE2 and TNF-alpha by selectively reducing NF-kB DNA binding without blocking IkB degradation or NF-kB nuclear entry.

pmid:29242678.authors: Dinkova-Kostova AT, Fahey JW, Kostov RV, et al.
pmid:29242678.title: KEAP1 and Done? Targeting the NRF2 Pathway with Sulforaphane.
pmid:29242678.finding: Of the many proposed cellular targets of sulforaphane, only KEAP1-Nrf2 signalling can be considered validated; summarises animal carcinogenesis protection and short-term clinical endpoints.

pmid:32784785.authors: Yagishita Y, Gatbonton-Schwager TN, McCallum ML, et al.
pmid:32784785.title: Current Landscape of NRF2 Biomarkers in Clinical Trials.
pmid:32784785.finding: Reviews NRF2 biomarkers in trials of dimethyl fumarate, bardoxolone, oltipraz and sulforaphane; no biomarker yet excels at defining pharmacodynamic action in humans.

pmid:24287881.authors: Heber D, Li Z, Garcia-Lloret M, et al.
pmid:24287881.title: Sulforaphane-rich broccoli sprout extract attenuates nasal allergic response to diesel exhaust particles.
pmid:24287881.finding: Four days of a broccoli sprout extract delivering 100 µmol sulforaphane cut the nasal white-cell response to a diesel exhaust particle challenge by about half.

pmid:33920642.authors: Yusin J, Wang V, Henning SM, et al.
pmid:33920642.title: The Effect of Broccoli Sprout Extract on Seasonal Grass Pollen-Induced Allergic Rhinitis.
pmid:33920642.finding: Broccoli sprout extract for 3 weeks improved peak nasal inspiratory flow after pollen challenge, mainly when combined with a nasal steroid; nasal cytokines did not change.

pmid:22537070.authors: Bahadoran Z, Tohidi M, Nazeri P, et al.
pmid:22537070.title: Effect of broccoli sprouts on insulin resistance in type 2 diabetic patients: a randomized double-blind clinical trial.
pmid:22537070.finding: 10 g/day broccoli sprout powder for 4 weeks lowered serum insulin and HOMA-IR (P=0.05).

pmid:20805984.authors: Christiansen B, Bellostas Muguerza N, Petersen AM, et al.
pmid:20805984.title: Ingestion of broccoli sprouts does not improve endothelial function in humans with hypertension.
pmid:20805984.finding: 10 g/day dried broccoli sprouts for 4 weeks did not improve flow-mediated dilation or blood pressure.

pmid:29854372.authors: Bent S, Lawton B, Warren T, et al.
pmid:29854372.title: Identification of urinary metabolites that correlate with clinical improvements in children with autism treated with sulforaphane from broccoli.
pmid:29854372.finding: In a 12-week open-label study, Social Responsiveness Scale improved (-9.7 points) but the ABC change was not significant; 77 urinary metabolites correlated with clinical change.

pmid:32347624.authors: Momtazmanesh S, Amirimoghaddam-Yazdi Z, Moghaddam HS, et al.
pmid:32347624.title: Sulforaphane as an adjunctive treatment for irritability in children with autism spectrum disorder: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
pmid:32347624.finding: Sulforaphane (50 or 100 µmol/day by weight) added to risperidone for 10 weeks improved irritability and hyperactivity vs placebo, without differences in other ABC subscales or adverse events.

pmid:34034808.authors: Zimmerman AW, Singh K, Connors SL, et al.
pmid:34034808.title: Randomized controlled trial of sulforaphane and metabolite discovery in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder.
pmid:34034808.finding: 15 weeks of sulforaphane did not significantly improve the primary clinician scale (Cohen's d 0.21, CI crossing zero); caregiver ABC improved (d -0.96) but SRS-2 did not.

pmid:36427174.authors: Ou J, Smith RC, Tobe RH, et al.
pmid:36427174.title: Efficacy of Sulforaphane in Treatment of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Multi-center Trial.
pmid:36427174.finding: In a multicentre trial in China, caregiver-rated scales did not differ from placebo while clinician-rated scales improved; sulforaphane was well tolerated.

pmid:39144775.authors: Hei G, Smith RC, Li R, et al.
pmid:39144775.title: Sulforaphane Effects on Cognition and Symptoms in First and Early Episode Schizophrenia: A Randomized Double-Blind Trial.
pmid:39144775.finding: Two sulforaphane doses for 22 weeks did not improve the primary MATRICS composite or PANSS, though some cognitive domains (working memory, verbal learning) improved.

pmid:39832347.authors: Huang J, Chen A, Jin H, et al.
pmid:39832347.title: Efficacy and Safety of Sulforaphane Added to Antipsychotics for the Treatment of Negative Symptoms of Schizophrenia: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:39832347.finding: 24 weeks of high-dose sulforaphane (Avmacol Extra Strength) added to antipsychotics reduced PANSS negative symptoms more than placebo.

pmid:40133020.authors: Chen H, Lu J, Zou T, et al.
pmid:40133020.title: Effects of sulforaphane on negative symptoms and cognitive impairments in chronic schizophrenia patients: A randomized double-blind trial.
pmid:40133020.finding: 24 weeks of sulforaphane reduced PANSS negative symptom scores vs placebo but did not improve MATRICS cognition.

pmid:42154264.authors: Okazaki M, Sakuma K, Jo H, et al.
pmid:42154264.title: Efficacy and safety of Nrf2 activators for schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:42154264.finding: Across Nrf2 activators in schizophrenia (vitamin C, curcumin, resveratrol, sulforaphane), sulforaphane lowered all-cause discontinuation and some lipids; curcumin showed only marginal, non-robust symptom benefit.

pmid:34033171.authors: Ghazizadeh-Hashemi F, Bagheri S, Ashraf-Ganjouei A, et al.
pmid:34033171.title: Efficacy and safety of sulforaphane for treatment of mild to moderate depression in patients with history of cardiac interventions: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial.
pmid:34033171.finding: Six weeks of sulforaphane improved HAM-D scores and response rate (30% vs 6.7%) vs placebo; remission difference was not significant.

pmid:33503851.authors: Nouchi R, Hu Q, Saito T, et al.
pmid:33503851.title: Brain Training and Sulforaphane Intake Interventions Separately Improve Cognitive Performance in Healthy Older Adults, Whereas a Combination of These Interventions Does Not Have More Beneficial Effects: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:33503851.finding: 30 mg (~69 µmol) glucoraphanin daily for 12 weeks improved processing speed and working memory vs placebo; combining with brain training added nothing.

pmid:41669080.authors: Shimizu S, Kasai S, Suzuki C, et al.
pmid:41669080.title: Efficacy of 42-month oral administration of glucoraphanin in preventing cognitive decline in individuals at elevated risk of dementia, including those with mild cognitive impairment: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study.
pmid:41669080.finding: 30 mg/day glucoraphanin for 42 months gave greater improvement in memory performance index than placebo in a small pilot (19 completers).

pmid:15387326.authors: Galan MV, Kishan AA, Silverman AL
pmid:15387326.title: Oral broccoli sprouts for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection: a preliminary report.
pmid:15387326.finding: Broccoli sprouts twice daily for 7 days were followed by negative stool antigen in 7 of 9 patients, but durable eradication was confirmed in only about 3 of 9.

pmid:25287166.authors: Chang YW, Jang JY, Kim YH, et al.
pmid:25287166.title: The Effects of Broccoli Sprout Extract Containing Sulforaphane on Lipid Peroxidation and Helicobacter pylori Infection in the Gastric Mucosa.
pmid:25287166.finding: Broccoli sprout extract did not reduce H. pylori density (urea breath test) but lowered gastric mucosal MDA.

pmid:31830776.authors: Chang YW, Park YM, Oh CH, et al.
pmid:31830776.title: Effects of probiotics or broccoli supplementation on Helicobacter pylori eradication with standard clarithromycin-based triple therapy.
pmid:31830776.finding: Adding sulforaphane to clarithromycin triple therapy did not raise H. pylori eradication rates (ITT 81.6% vs 85.2%).

pmid:17956979.authors: Talalay P, Fahey JW, Healy ZR, et al.
pmid:17956979.title: Sulforaphane mobilizes cellular defenses that protect skin against damage by UV radiation.
pmid:17956979.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
pmid:17956979.finding: Topical sulforaphane-rich sprout extract induced phase 2 enzymes in human skin and reduced UV-induced erythema by a mean 37.7%.

pmid:27889290.authors: Kerns ML, Guss L, Fahey J, et al.
pmid:27889290.title: Randomized, split-body, single-blinded clinical trial of topical broccoli sprout extract: Assessing the feasibility of its use in keratin-based disorders.
pmid:27889290.finding: Topical broccoli sprout extract activated Nrf2 and induced keratin 17 in human epidermis without altering keratins 5/14, supporting feasibility for epidermolysis bullosa simplex.

pmid:31155953.authors: Zhang Z, Garzotto M, Davis EW 2nd, et al.
pmid:31155953.title: Sulforaphane Bioavailability and Chemopreventive Activity in Men Presenting for Biopsy of the Prostate Gland: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
pmid:31155953.finding: 200 µmol/day broccoli sprout extract raised sulforaphane levels but did not change blood HDAC activity or prostate tissue biomarkers; 40 genes changed in expression.

pmid:26511489.authors: Atwell LL, Zhang Z, Mori M, et al.
pmid:26511489.title: Sulforaphane Bioavailability and Chemopreventive Activity in Women Scheduled for Breast Biopsy.
pmid:26511489.finding: A glucoraphanin supplement for 2-8 weeks lowered blood-cell HDAC activity but did not change breast tissue biomarkers vs placebo.

pmid:40041932.authors: Yuan JM, Kensler TW, Dacic S, et al.
pmid:40041932.title: Randomized Phase II Clinical Trial of Sulforaphane in Former Smokers at High Risk for Lung Cancer.
pmid:40041932.finding: About 95 µmol/day sulforaphane for 12 months did not change bronchial histopathology but reduced the Ki-67 proliferation index (-20% vs +65% on placebo).

pmid:38074675.authors: ElKhalifa D, Al-Ziftawi N, Awaisu A, et al.
pmid:38074675.title: Efficacy and tolerability of sulforaphane in the therapeutic management of cancers: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
pmid:38074675.finding: Systematic review of sulforaphane in cancer patients: inconsistent PSA effects, some biomarker changes, no excess adverse events, heterogeneous dosing.

pmid:34927380.authors: Komine S, Miura I, Miyashita N, et al.
pmid:34927380.title: Effect of a sulforaphane supplement on muscle soreness and damage induced by eccentric exercise in young adults: A pilot study.
pmid:34927380.finding: Two weeks of a sulforaphane supplement raised NQO1 mRNA in blood cells and reduced muscle soreness and serum MDA 2 days after eccentric exercise.

pmid:41754227.authors: Cesanelli L, Thomas R, Mickevičius M, et al.
pmid:41754227.title: Short-Term Effects of Broccoli-Derived Glucoraphanin on Recovery from Eccentric Muscle Damage: A Double-Blind Randomized Crossover Study.
pmid:41754227.finding: Two weeks of high-glucoraphanin broccoli powder (reconstituted in hot water) did not change recovery from eccentric muscle damage.

pmid:42617706.authors: Traustadóttir T, Islam H, Ostrom EL
pmid:42617706.title: Exercise and phytochemicals as modulators of redox homeostasis in aging.
pmid:42617706.finding: Exercise-induced Nrf2 activation weakens with age; evidence that adding Nrf2-activating phytochemicals (curcumin, sulforaphane, astaxanthin) to exercise helps older adults is insufficient.

pmid:22946519.authors: Volz N, Boettler U, Winkler S, et al.
pmid:22946519.title: Effect of coffee combining green coffee bean constituents with typical roasting products on the Nrf2/ARE pathway in vitro and in vivo.
pmid:22946519.finding: 750 mL/day of a specially roasted coffee for 4 weeks increased Nrf2 transcription in blood lymphocytes on average, with large inter-individual variation.

pmid:39651986.authors: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
pmid:39651986.title: 2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes-2025.
pmid:39651986.finding: ADA Standards of Care 2025 diagnostic criteria: HbA1c 5.7-6.4% or fasting glucose 100-125 mg/dL defines prediabetes; HbA1c >=6.5% or fasting glucose >=126 mg/dL defines diabetes, with HbA1c unreliable in conditions that alter red-cell turnover.

pmid:31127824.authors: Shah VN, DuBose SN, Li Z, et al.
pmid:31127824.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring Profiles in Healthy Nondiabetic Participants: A Multicenter Prospective Study.
pmid:31127824.finding: In healthy people wearing a blinded Dexcom G6, mean glucose was 98-99 mg/dL (104 over age 60), 96% of time was 70-140 mg/dL, within-person CV was 17%, and glucose was >140 mg/dL for a median 30 minutes a day.

pmid:30040822.authors: Hall H, Perelman D, Breschi A, et al.
pmid:30040822.title: Glucotypes reveal new patterns of glucose dysregulation.
pmid:30040822.finding: Some people classed as normoglycemic by standard tests showed high CGM variability, reaching prediabetic ranges 15% and diabetic ranges 2% of the time; glucose responses to standardized meals varied widely between people.

pmid:32766882.authors: Howard R, Guo J, Hall KD
pmid:32766882.title: Imprecision nutrition? Different simultaneous continuous glucose monitors provide discordant meal rankings for incremental postprandial glucose in subjects without diabetes.
pmid:32766882.finding: Two CGM brands worn at the same time ranked the same person's meals discordantly (Kendall tau 0.43), so meal choices based on one device lost about half the glycemic benefit as judged by the other; CGM-guided precision nutrition may be premature.

pmid:26590418.authors: Zeevi D, Korem T, Zmora N, et al.
pmid:26590418.title: Personalized Nutrition by Prediction of Glycemic Responses.
pmid:26590418.n: 800-person cohort plus 100-person validation and a small RCT
pmid:26590418.finding: Glucose responses to identical meals varied widely between people; an algorithm using microbiome and clinical data predicted responses and a personalized diet lowered post-meal glucose in a small blinded trial.

pmid:35856435.authors: Klonoff DC, Nguyen KT, Xu NY, et al.
pmid:35856435.title: Use of Continuous Glucose Monitors by People Without Diabetes: An Idea Whose Time Has Come?
pmid:35856435.finding: Review arguing that CGM use by people without diabetes (prediabetes, wellness, athletics) is expanding and that CGM 'glucotypes' may come to predict diabetes risk, while noting the evidence base is still developing.

pmid:17994218.authors: Wentholt IM, Kulik W, Michels RP, et al.
pmid:17994218.title: Glucose fluctuations and activation of oxidative stress in patients with type 1 diabetes.
pmid:17994218.n: 25 type 1 diabetes patients plus healthy controls
pmid:17994218.finding: No relationship was found between CGM glucose variability (MODD, MAGE, CONGA) and urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha in type 1 diabetes, contradicting the type 2 diabetes finding.

pmid:12551878.authors: Pearson TA, Mensah GA, Alexander RW, et al.
pmid:12551878.title: Markers of inflammation and cardiovascular disease: application to clinical and public health practice: A statement for healthcare professionals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Heart Association.
pmid:12551878.finding: AHA/CDC statement: hs-CRP is the inflammatory marker of choice for optional cardiovascular risk assessment, with <1, 1-3 and >3 mg/L as low, average and high risk; values >10 mg/L should prompt a search for infection or inflammation and repeat testing.

pmid:20031199.authors: Kaptoge S, Di Angelantonio E, Lowe G, et al.
pmid:20031199.title: C-reactive protein concentration and risk of coronary heart disease, stroke, and mortality: an individual participant meta-analysis.
pmid:20031199.finding: CRP was continuously associated with coronary disease, stroke, vascular and non-vascular death and several cancers, but the associations with vascular disease depended considerably on conventional risk factors and other inflammatory markers.

pmid:29998297.authors: Curry SJ, Krist AH, Owens DK, et al.
pmid:29998297.title: Risk Assessment for Cardiovascular Disease With Nontraditional Risk Factors: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
pmid:29998297.finding: USPSTF found insufficient evidence (I statement) that adding hs-CRP, ankle-brachial index or coronary calcium to traditional risk models improves outcomes in asymptomatic adults.

pmid:31642874.authors: Sniderman AD, Thanassoulis G, Glavinovic T, et al.
pmid:31642874.title: Apolipoprotein B Particles and Cardiovascular Disease: A Narrative Review.
pmid:31642874.finding: Argues that the number of apoB-containing particles, not their cholesterol content, determines atherogenic risk, so apoB unifies and improves on conventional lipid markers.

pmid:31504418.authors: Mach F, Baigent C, Catapano AL, et al.
pmid:31504418.title: 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias: lipid modification to reduce cardiovascular risk.
pmid:31504418.finding: ESC/EAS 2019 dyslipidaemia guideline: LDL-C remains the primary target; apoB is recommended for risk assessment, especially with high triglycerides, diabetes, obesity or very low LDL-C, with secondary apoB goals of <65, <80 and <100 mg/dL by risk category.

pmid:15346644.authors: Lee DH, Blomhoff R, Jacobs DR Jr
pmid:15346644.title: Is serum gamma glutamyltransferase a marker of oxidative stress?
pmid:15346644.finding: Proposes that serum GGT within its normal range is an early marker of oxidative stress: it is inversely related to antioxidant vitamins and predicts F2-isoprostanes and CRP measured 5-15 years later in a dose-response manner.

pmid:15336318.authors: Lim JS, Yang JH, Chun BY, et al.
pmid:15336318.title: Is serum gamma-glutamyltransferase inversely associated with serum antioxidants as a marker of oxidative stress?
pmid:15336318.finding: Across all deciles of serum GGT, higher GGT was associated with lower serum carotenoids and vitamin C (not vitamin E), independent of alcohol, smoking and BMI.

pmid:24585856.authors: Kunutsor SK, Apekey TA, Seddoh D, et al.
pmid:24585856.title: Liver enzymes and risk of all-cause mortality in general populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:24585856.finding: Top versus bottom third of GGT was associated with 60% higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.60), roughly linear at 7% per 5 U/L.

pmid:28338987.authors: Nano J, Muka T, Ligthart S, et al.
pmid:28338987.title: Gamma-glutamyltransferase levels, prediabetes and type 2 diabetes: a Mendelian randomization study.
pmid:28338987.finding: Observationally GGT predicted prediabetes and diabetes, but genetically raised GGT did not (causal RR 0.96), suggesting confounding or reverse causation rather than a causal role.

pmid:18600514.title: Uric acid: the oxidant-antioxidant paradox.
pmid:18600514.finding: Uric acid is the main plasma antioxidant yet predicts obesity, hypertension and cardiovascular disease; the authors argue its intracellular pro-oxidant actions contribute to disease.

pmid:28592419.authors: Li X, Meng X, Timofeeva M, et al.
pmid:28592419.title: Serum uric acid levels and multiple health outcomes: umbrella review of evidence from observational studies, randomised controlled trials, and Mendelian randomisation studies.
pmid:28592419.finding: Despite hundreds of meta-analyses and Mendelian randomization studies, convincing evidence of a causal role of serum uric acid exists only for gout and kidney stones.

pmid:32579811.authors: Badve SV, Pascoe EM, Tiku A, et al.
pmid:32579811.title: Effects of Allopurinol on the Progression of Chronic Kidney Disease.
pmid:32579811.finding: CKD-FIX: allopurinol lowered urate but did not slow eGFR decline compared with placebo.

pmid:32579810.authors: Doria A, Galecki AT, Spino C, et al.
pmid:32579810.title: Serum Urate Lowering with Allopurinol and Kidney Function in Type 1 Diabetes.
pmid:32579810.n: 530 adults with type 1 diabetes and early kidney disease
pmid:32579810.finding: PERL: allopurinol lowered serum urate but had no clinically meaningful benefit on kidney function.

pmid:36216006.authors: Mackenzie IS, Hawkey CJ, Ford I, et al.
pmid:36216006.title: Allopurinol versus usual care in UK patients with ischaemic heart disease (ALL-HEART): a multicentre, prospective, randomised, open-label, blinded-endpoint trial.
pmid:36216006.finding: ALL-HEART: allopurinol did not reduce MI, stroke or cardiovascular death (HR 1.04) versus usual care over 4.8 years.

pmid:12387654.title: Homocysteine and risk of ischemic heart disease and stroke: a meta-analysis.
pmid:12387654.finding: A 25% lower homocysteine (about 3 umol/L) was associated with 11% lower ischaemic heart disease and 19% lower stroke risk; homocysteine is at most a modest independent predictor in healthy people.

pmid:16531613.authors: Lonn E, Yusuf S, Arnold MJ, et al.
pmid:16531613.title: Homocysteine lowering with folic acid and B vitamins in vascular disease.
pmid:16531613.n: 5,522 adults with vascular disease or diabetes
pmid:16531613.finding: HOPE-2: folic acid, B6 and B12 lowered homocysteine but did not reduce major cardiovascular events (RR 0.95); stroke was reduced (RR 0.75) and unstable-angina admissions rose.

pmid:16531614.authors: Bønaa KH, Njølstad I, Ueland PM, et al.
pmid:16531614.title: Homocysteine lowering and cardiovascular events after acute myocardial infarction.
pmid:16531614.finding: NORVIT: B vitamins cut homocysteine 27% but did not reduce recurrent cardiovascular events, with a trend toward harm for the combined folic acid-B12-B6 arm (RR 1.22).

pmid:15208005.title: The Omega-3 Index: a new risk factor for death from coronary heart disease?
pmid:15208005.finding: Proposes red-cell EPA+DHA (the Omega-3 Index) as a coronary risk factor: >=8% associated with the most and <=4% with the least cardioprotection.

pmid:30415637.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
pmid:30415637.title: Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer.
pmid:30415637.finding: VITAL: 1 g/day marine omega-3 did not reduce major cardiovascular events or cancer (HR 0.92 and 1.03); myocardial infarction was lower (HR 0.72) as a secondary outcome.

pmid:30415628.authors: Bhatt DL, Steg PG, Miller M, et al.
pmid:30415628.title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia.
pmid:30415628.finding: REDUCE-IT: 4 g/day icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) lowered ischaemic events and cardiovascular death (HR 0.80) versus mineral-oil placebo, with more atrial fibrillation.

pmid:33993205.authors: Nissen SE, Lincoff AM, Wolski K, et al.
pmid:33993205.title: Association Between Achieved ω-3 Fatty Acid Levels and Major Adverse Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With High Cardiovascular Risk: A Secondary Analysis of the STRENGTH Trial.
pmid:33993205.n: 10,382 STRENGTH participants with fatty acid levels
pmid:33993205.finding: In STRENGTH, the highest achieved plasma EPA or DHA levels on omega-3 carboxylic acids were not associated with fewer cardiovascular events (HR 0.98 and 1.02) versus corn oil.

pmid:38828931.authors: Demay MB, Pittas AG, Bikle DD, et al.
pmid:38828931.title: Vitamin D for the Prevention of Disease: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline.
pmid:38828931.finding: Endocrine Society 2024: suggests empiric vitamin D for children, adults over 75, pregnancy and high-risk prediabetes, and suggests against routine 25(OH)D testing in the absence of established indications.

pmid:21118827.authors: Ross AC, Manson JE, Abrams SA, et al.
pmid:21118827.title: The 2011 report on dietary reference intakes for calcium and vitamin D from the Institute of Medicine: what clinicians need to know.
pmid:21118827.finding: IOM 2011: a serum 25(OH)D of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) meets the needs of 97.5% of people; higher levels were not consistently linked to more benefit, and deficiency prevalence had been overestimated.

pmid:21646368.authors: Holick MF, Binkley NC, Bischoff-Ferrari HA, et al.
pmid:21646368.title: Evaluation, treatment, and prevention of vitamin D deficiency: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline.
pmid:21646368.finding: Endocrine Society 2011 guideline recommended 25(OH)D testing in people at risk of deficiency (defining deficiency as <20 ng/mL and insufficiency as 21-29 ng/mL) but not screening of people not at risk.

pmid:33847711.authors: Krist AH, Davidson KW, Mangione CM, et al.
pmid:33847711.title: Screening for Vitamin D Deficiency in Adults: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
pmid:33847711.finding: USPSTF found insufficient evidence (I statement) to recommend for or against screening asymptomatic adults for vitamin D deficiency and noted no consensus on the level that defines deficiency.

pmid:24942828.authors: Devalia V, Hamilton MS, Molloy AM
pmid:24942828.title: Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of cobalamin and folate disorders.
pmid:24942828.finding: British Society for Haematology: no gold-standard test for cobalamin deficiency; serum B12 is first-line, methylmalonic acid is a more specific second-line test than homocysteine, and fixed cut-offs are not possible.

pmid:23301732.title: Clinical practice. Vitamin B12 deficiency.
pmid:23301732.finding: NEJM clinical review of vitamin B12 deficiency covering causes (including metformin and acid suppression), the limits of serum B12 and the use of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine to confirm deficiency.

pmid:27446930.authors: Hannibal L, Lysne V, Bjørke-Monsen AL, et al.
pmid:27446930.title: Biomarkers and Algorithms for the Diagnosis of Vitamin B12 Deficiency.
pmid:27446930.finding: Serum B12 alone has limited diagnostic value; holotranscobalamin plus methylmalonic acid (>271 nmol/L suggesting deficiency in one algorithm) improve classification.

pmid:25835046.title: Biomarkers of selenium status.
pmid:25835046.finding: Plasma selenoproteins (GPX3, selenoprotein P) reach maximal expression at plasma selenium around 50-70 ng/mL; above that plasma selenium mainly reflects non-specific selenomethionine, and supplementation showed no cancer benefit in people above ~120 ng/mL.

pmid:26962190.authors: King JC, Brown KH, Gibson RS, et al.
pmid:26962190.title: Biomarkers of Nutrition for Development (BOND)-Zinc Review.
pmid:26962190.finding: Plasma zinc is the only recommended zinc biomarker, but it responds weakly to intake and is shifted by recent meals, time of day, inflammation, drugs and hormones; oxidative-stress markers are not recommended for assessing zinc status.

pmid:27995906.authors: Kwo PY, Cohen SM, Lim JK
pmid:27995906.title: ACG Clinical Guideline: Evaluation of Abnormal Liver Chemistries.
pmid:27995906.finding: ACG guideline on abnormal liver chemistries: healthy upper limits of ALT are lower than many laboratory ranges, and abnormal values should prompt evaluation for fatty liver, alcohol, viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis and drugs.

pmid:12093239.authors: Prati D, Taioli E, Zanella A, et al.
pmid:12093239.title: Updated definitions of healthy ranges for serum alanine aminotransferase levels.
pmid:12093239.finding: Updated healthy ALT upper limits (30 U/L men, 19 U/L women) were lower than conventional limits; ALT tracked BMI and lipid and glucose abnormalities.

pmid:23198723.authors: Barregard L, Møller P, Henriksen T, et al.
pmid:23198723.title: Human and methodological sources of variability in the measurement of urinary 8-oxo-7,8-dihydro-2'-deoxyguanosine.
pmid:23198723.finding: ELISA results for urinary 8-oxodG varied more than chromatographic assays and could not determine absolute levels; within-person day-to-day CV was about 17-20%.

pmid:26415143.authors: Frijhoff J, Winyard PG, Zarkovic N, et al.
pmid:26415143.title: Clinical Relevance of Biomarkers of Oxidative Stress.
pmid:26415143.finding: Oxidative-stress biomarkers are often measured with non-specific methods, while specific methods are too laborious for routine use; none is yet validated as a clinical diagnostic.

pmid:24984994.authors: Pompella A, Sies H, Wacker R, et al.
pmid:24984994.title: The use of total antioxidant capacity as surrogate marker for food quality and its effect on health is to be discouraged.
pmid:24984994.finding: Using total antioxidant capacity assays (ORAC, FRAP, TEAC) as markers of food quality or health effect should be discouraged; a higher plasma TAC is often wrongly read as beneficial.

pmid:21030466.authors: Mather KA, Jorm AF, Parslow RA, et al.
pmid:21030466.title: Is telomere length a biomarker of aging? A review.
pmid:21030466.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
pmid:21030466.finding: Evidence that leukocyte telomere length is a biomarker of human ageing is equivocal; longitudinal studies are needed.

pmid:25239152.authors: Martin-Ruiz CM, Baird D, Roger L, et al.
pmid:25239152.title: Reproducibility of telomere length assessment: an international collaborative study.
pmid:25239152.finding: Inter-laboratory CVs were about 10% for Southern blot and over 20% for qPCR telomere measurement, which precludes shared reference ranges between laboratories.

pmid:28241208.authors: Haycock PC, Burgess S, Nounu A, et al.
pmid:28241208.title: Association Between Telomere Length and Risk of Cancer and Non-Neoplastic Diseases: A Mendelian Randomization Study.
pmid:28241208.n: Mendelian randomization across 35 cancers and 48 non-neoplastic diseases
pmid:28241208.finding: Genetically longer telomeres were associated with higher risk of several cancers and lower risk of some non-neoplastic diseases such as coronary heart disease, so longer is not simply better.

deep-testing:tst-who2021.title: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, sixth edition
deep-testing:tst-who2021.finding: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, 6th edition (2021): standardized methods and fifth-centile values from fertile men (volume 1.4 mL, concentration 16 million/mL, total 39 million, total motility 42%, progressive 30%, vitality 54%, normal forms 4%), plus extended tests such as sperm DNA fragmentation and seminal oxidative stress.

pmid:33528873.authors: Campbell MJ, Lotti F, Baldi E, et al.
pmid:33528873.title: Distribution of semen examination results 2020 - A follow up of data collated for the WHO semen analysis manual 2010.
pmid:33528873.finding: Updated fertile-men fifth centiles were 16 million/mL, 30% progressive motility (42% total) and 4% normal forms; these do not draw a sharp line between fertile and subfertile men.

pmid:11794171.authors: Guzick DS, Overstreet JW, Factor-Litvak P, et al.
pmid:11794171.title: Sperm morphology, motility, and concentration in fertile and infertile men.
pmid:11794171.finding: Subfertile thresholds were <13.5 million/mL, <32% motility and <9% normal forms and fertile thresholds >48 million/mL, >63% and >12%, but fertile and infertile men overlapped extensively; no single measure was diagnostic.

pmid:34947899.authors: Boitrelle F, Shah R, Saleh R, et al.
pmid:34947899.title: The Sixth Edition of the WHO Manual for Human Semen Analysis: A Critical Review and SWOT Analysis.
pmid:34947899.finding: The 6th WHO manual strengthened methods and described SDF and oxidative-stress tests but replaced reference limits with 'decision limits' that it never actually provides.

pmid:33295257.authors: Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.
pmid:33295257.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline Part I.
pmid:33295257.finding: AUA/ASRM male infertility guideline part I: evaluation with at least two semen analyses, hormonal testing (FSH, testosterone) in men with abnormal semen parameters or symptoms, and recognition that male infertility marks higher risk of other health problems; routine DNA fragmentation and ROS testing are not recommended in the initial evaluation.

pmid:32777871.authors: Agarwal A, Majzoub A, Baskaran S, et al.
pmid:32777871.title: Sperm DNA Fragmentation: A New Guideline for Clinicians.
pmid:32777871.finding: Expert review proposing clinical indications for SDF testing (varicocele, unexplained infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, failed ART, lifestyle risk) while acknowledging professional societies do not recommend routine testing.

pmid:37118960.authors: Agarwal A, Farkouh A, Saleh R, et al.
pmid:37118960.title: Controversy and Consensus on Indications for Sperm DNA Fragmentation Testing in Male Infertility: A Global Survey, Current Guidelines, and Expert Recommendations.
pmid:37118960.finding: Global survey: ~75% of andrology experts test SDF in unexplained infertility and 39% routinely in recurrent pregnancy loss, despite very few society recommendations; practice is highly heterogeneous.

pmid:33108829.authors: Esteves SC, Zini A, Coward RM, et al.
pmid:33108829.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing: Summary evidence and clinical practice recommendations.
pmid:33108829.finding: Expert group formulated 41 recommendations on SDF testing in varicocele, unexplained infertility, recurrent loss, IUI and IVF/ICSI, noting supporting evidence is moderate to low quality.

pmid:17644094.authors: Collins JA, Barnhart KT, Schlegel PN
pmid:17644094.title: Do sperm DNA integrity tests predict pregnancy with in vitro fertilization?
pmid:17644094.finding: Sperm DNA integrity tests had a small association with IVF/ICSI pregnancy (DOR 1.44) but likelihood ratios were not predictive, too weak to justify routine use.

pmid:27832085.authors: Cissen M, Wely MV, Scholten I, et al.
pmid:27832085.title: Measuring Sperm DNA Fragmentation and Clinical Outcomes of Medically Assisted Reproduction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
pmid:27832085.finding: Current SDF tests have limited capacity to predict pregnancy after IVF, ICSI or IUI and should not be used routinely to predict outcome or choose treatment.

pmid:30893955.authors: Homa ST, Vassiliou AM, Stone J, et al.
pmid:30893955.title: A Comparison Between Two Assays for Measuring Seminal Oxidative Stress and their Relationship with Sperm DNA Fragmentation and Semen Parameters.
pmid:30893955.n: Semen samples from men attending an andrology service
pmid:30893955.finding: Chemiluminescent ROS and MiOXSYS ORP captured different aspects of oxidative stress; leukocyte-rich samples had high ROS but not high ORP or DFI, so neither assay suffices alone.

pmid:35204147.authors: Castleton PE, Deluao JC, Sharkey DJ, et al.
pmid:35204147.title: Measuring Reactive Oxygen Species in Semen for Male Preconception Care: A Scientist Perspective.
pmid:35204147.finding: Clinically marketed semen ROS tests (MiOXSYS, luminol chemiluminescence, OxiSperm) have inconsistent decision limits and no trials showing benefit on fertilization, pregnancy or live birth.

pmid:36009282.authors: Panner Selvam MK, Baskaran S, O'Connell S, et al.
pmid:36009282.title: Association between Seminal Oxidation-Reduction Potential and Sperm DNA Fragmentation-A Meta-Analysis.
pmid:36009282.finding: Seminal ORP correlated weakly with SDF (pooled r = 0.24).

pmid:35514536.authors: Joao F, Duval C, Bélanger MC, et al.
pmid:35514536.title: Reassessing the interpretation of oxidation-reduction potential in male infertility.
pmid:35514536.n: 134 men with normal and 574 with abnormal semen
pmid:35514536.finding: Differences in the sORP index between groups were driven mainly by sperm concentration, the index's denominator, rather than by oxidation itself.

pmid:36055912.authors: Henkel R, Morris A, Vogiatzi P, et al.
pmid:36055912.title: Predictive value of seminal oxidation-reduction potential analysis for reproductive outcomes of ICSI.
pmid:36055912.n: Fresh ICSI cycles at one centre
pmid:36055912.finding: Seminal ORP predicted fertilization, blastocyst development, clinical pregnancy and live birth after ICSI about as well as SDF (live birth AUC 0.73).

pmid:39100838.authors: Tan Y, Yuan Y, Yang X, et al.
pmid:39100838.title: Diagnostic value of oxidation-reduction potential for male infertility: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:39100838.finding: ORP had pooled sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.66 (AUC 0.80) for distinguishing infertile from fertile men.

pmid:24532220.authors: Iliodromiti S, Kelsey TW, Wu O, et al.
pmid:24532220.title: The predictive accuracy of anti-Müllerian hormone for live birth after assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature.
pmid:24532220.finding: AMH had a weak association with live birth after assisted conception (DOR 2.4) independent of age, but poor predictive accuracy.

pmid:28393651.authors: Depmann M, Broer SL, Eijkemans MJC, et al.
pmid:28393651.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone does not predict time to pregnancy: results of a prospective cohort study.
pmid:28393651.finding: After age adjustment, AMH, AFC and basal FSH did not predict time to ongoing pregnancy.

pmid:38964587.authors: Nelson SM, Shaw M, Ewing BJ, et al.
pmid:38964587.title: Antimüllerian hormone levels are associated with time to pregnancy in a cohort study of 3,150 women.
pmid:38964587.finding: Low AMH (<1 ng/mL) was independently associated with a modest reduction in per-cycle chance of conception (11.2% vs 14.3% at cycle four).

pmid:38196321.authors: Copp T, Thompson R, Hammarberg K, et al.
pmid:38196321.title: Attitudes, knowledge and practice regarding the anti-müllerian hormone test among general practitioners and reproductive specialists: A cross-sectional study.
pmid:38196321.finding: Many clinicians ordered AMH tests for reproductive planning or reassurance, uses not supported by evidence, and half lacked confidence interpreting results; direct-to-consumer testing is growing.

pmid:16891297.authors: Broekmans FJ, Kwee J, Hendriks DJ, et al.
pmid:16891297.title: A systematic review of tests predicting ovarian reserve and IVF outcome.
pmid:16891297.finding: Systematic review: ovarian reserve tests predict poor response only modestly and pregnancy very poorly; their use for IVF outcome prediction cannot be supported.

pmid:33849787.authors: Pipari A, Guillen A, Cruz M, et al.
pmid:33849787.title: Serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels are not associated with aneuploidy rates in human blastocysts.
pmid:33849787.finding: AMH was not associated with blastocyst aneuploidy rates; higher AMH gave more embryos, not better ones.

pmid:19064542.title: Target sequence polymorphism of human manganese superoxide dismutase gene and its association with cancer risk: a review.
pmid:19064542.finding: The SOD2 (MnSOD) Val16Ala polymorphism showed no overall association with breast or total cancer risk (OR 0.98-1.02).

pmid:22206979.authors: Ji G, Gu A, Wang Y, et al.
pmid:22206979.title: Genetic variants in antioxidant genes are associated with sperm DNA damage and risk of male infertility in a Chinese population.
pmid:22206979.finding: SOD2 Val16Ala and PON1 Arg192Glu variants were associated with male infertility and higher sperm DNA fragmentation and 8-OHdG in a Chinese population.

pmid:23288205.authors: Hickey SE, Curry CJ, Toriello HV
pmid:23288205.title: ACMG Practice Guideline: lack of evidence for MTHFR polymorphism testing.
pmid:23288205.finding: ACMG: MTHFR polymorphism testing has minimal clinical utility and should not be part of routine thrombophilia evaluation; meta-analyses disproved links with venous thrombosis and coronary disease.

pmid:29939939.authors: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists' Committee on Practice Bulletins–Obstetrics
pmid:29939939.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 197: Inherited Thrombophilias in Pregnancy.
pmid:29939939.finding: ACOG Practice Bulletin 197 on inherited thrombophilias: limited evidence guides screening; screening for MTHFR polymorphisms or fasting homocysteine is not recommended in pregnancy evaluation.

pmid:21508090.authors: Crider KS, Zhu JH, Hao L, et al.
pmid:21508090.title: MTHFR 677C->T genotype is associated with folate and homocysteine concentrations in a large, population-based, double-blind trial of folic acid supplementation.
pmid:21508090.finding: MTHFR TT women had lower folate and higher homocysteine at every folic acid dose, but genotype did not interact with dose: folic acid raised folate across all genotypes.

pmid:39478547.authors: Li F, Qi JJ, Li LX, et al.
pmid:39478547.title: MTHFR C677T、MTHFR A1298C、MTRR A66G and MTR A2756G polymorphisms and male infertility risk: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:39478547.finding: MTHFR C677T was associated with male infertility and abnormal semen, mainly in Asian studies; A1298C was not.

pmid:36873081.authors: Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
pmid:36873081.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022.
pmid:36873081.finding: ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline update: assess male lifestyle (strong); sperm DNA fragmentation testing can be considered for explanatory and diagnostic purposes (conditional); thrombophilia screening recommendations from 2017 were unchanged.

pmid:8782820.title: Apolipoprotein E allele-specific antioxidant activity and effects on cytotoxicity by oxidative insults and beta-amyloid peptides.
pmid:8782820.finding: In cell culture apoE isoforms protected against hydrogen peroxide toxicity with E2 > E3 > E4, suggesting lower antioxidant activity of apoE4.

pmid:17466101.authors: Minihane AM, Jofre-Monseny L, Olano-Martin E, et al.
pmid:17466101.title: ApoE genotype, cardiovascular risk and responsiveness to dietary fat manipulation.
pmid:17466101.finding: APOE4 carriers may have 40-50% higher CVD risk, but associations are highly heterogeneous and diet-genotype interaction evidence comes from small or retrospectively genotyped studies.

pmid:19085196.authors: Basu S, Helmersson J, Jarosinska D, et al.
pmid:19085196.title: Regulatory factors of basal F(2)-isoprostane formation: population, age, gender and smoking habits in humans.
pmid:19085196.n: 588 healthy adults in Sweden, Italy and Poland
pmid:19085196.finding: Urinary F2-isoprostanes differed by country, were higher in smokers, fell moderately with age, and were only slightly lower in women than men.

pmid:27957792.authors: Kander MC, Cui Y, Liu Z
pmid:27957792.title: Gender difference in oxidative stress: a new look at the mechanisms for cardiovascular diseases.
pmid:27957792.finding: Under physiological conditions women appear less susceptible to oxidative stress, possibly via estrogen and lower NADPH-oxidase activity, but hormone therapy did not reduce cardiovascular risk.

pmid:29731617.authors: Liguori I, Russo G, Curcio F, et al.
pmid:29731617.title: Oxidative stress, aging, and diseases.
pmid:29731617.finding: Review of oxidative stress as a contributor to ageing and age-related diseases; antioxidant therapy efficacy remains unproven.

pmid:12142263.authors: Block G, Dietrich M, Norkus EP, et al.
pmid:12142263.title: Factors associated with oxidative stress in human populations.
pmid:12142263.finding: Sex was the strongest predictor of lipid peroxidation (women higher F2-isoprostanes and MDA), stronger than smoking; plasma vitamin C was strongly inversely associated.

pmid:27524815.authors: Celis-Morales C, Livingstone KM, Marsaux CF, et al.
pmid:27524815.title: Effect of personalized nutrition on health-related behaviour change: evidence from the Food4Me European randomized controlled trial.
pmid:27524815.finding: Personalized nutrition advice improved diet more than generic advice, but adding phenotype or genotype (five diet-responsive variants) did not enhance its effect.

pmid:26681314.title: Direct-to-consumer genetic testing: a revised position statement of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics.
pmid:26681314.finding: ACMG position statement on direct-to-consumer genetic testing: consumers should be informed about test limitations, clinical validity and utility, and have access to a qualified genetics professional.

pmid:36779907.authors: King A, Graham CA, Glaister M, et al.
pmid:36779907.title: The efficacy of genotype-based dietary or physical activity advice in changing behavior to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, type II diabetes mellitus or obesity: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:36779907.finding: Genotype-based dietary or physical-activity advice did not change behaviour more than general or phenotype-based advice.

pmid:24439821.title: Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: nutritional genomics.
pmid:24439821.finding: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: nutritional genomics is an emerging science; for complex chronic disease, genetic variants are only partially predictive and DTC testing is loosely regulated, so evidence-based validation is required before clinical use.

pmid:6511559.authors: Coyle EF, Martin WH 3rd, Sinacore DR, et al.
