pmid:25948669.title: Genetically high plasma vitamin C, intake of fruit and vegetables, and risk of ischemic heart disease and all-cause mortality: a Mendelian randomization study.
pmid:25948669.finding: Fruit and vegetable intake predicted lower IHD and mortality; genetically 25% higher plasma vitamin C gave non-significant estimates (IHD OR 0.90, mortality 0.88).

pmid:33203707.authors: Zheng JS, Luan J, Sofianopoulou E, et al.
pmid:33203707.title: Plasma Vitamin C and Type 2 Diabetes: Genome-Wide Association Study and Mendelian Randomization Analysis in European Populations.
pmid:33203707.finding: Measured plasma vitamin C was inversely associated with type 2 diabetes (HR 0.88 per SD), but genetically predicted vitamin C was not (1.03).

pmid:29769070.authors: Larsson SC, Burgess S, Michaëlsson K
pmid:29769070.title: Serum magnesium levels and risk of coronary artery disease: Mendelian randomisation study.
pmid:29769070.finding: Genetically higher serum magnesium (per 0.1 mmol/L) was associated with lower coronary artery disease risk (OR 0.88).

pmid:36479702.authors: Brodersen T, Rostgaard K, Lau CJ, et al.
pmid:36479702.title: The healthy donor effect and survey participation, becoming a donor and donor career.
pmid:36479702.finding: Donors were more likely to answer health surveys and becoming and remaining a donor tracked better self-reported health and lifestyle, a mechanism of the healthy donor effect.

pmid:41088737.authors: Rahman MM, Karki S, Hayen A
pmid:41088737.title: A target trial emulation to estimate the effect of blood donation on mortality among blood donors in Australia.
pmid:41088737.finding: Crude donor mortality was lower (HR 0.57), but after adjusting for all baseline covariates donation had no effect on mortality (HR 1.0).

pmid:21303629.authors: Siegelaar SE, Barwari T, Kulik W, et al.
pmid:21303629.title: No relevant relationship between glucose variability and oxidative stress in well-regulated type 2 diabetes patients.
pmid:21303629.finding: No relevant relationship between glucose variability and urinary 8-iso-PGF2a.

pmid:18539917.authors: Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes Study Group, Gerstein HC, Miller ME, et al.
pmid:18539917.title: Effects of intensive glucose lowering in type 2 diabetes.
pmid:18539917.finding: Targeting HbA1c below 6.0% did not significantly reduce major cardiovascular events (HR 0.90) and increased mortality (HR 1.22).

pmid:27571048.authors: McEvoy RD, Antic NA, Heeley E, et al.
pmid:27571048.title: CPAP for Prevention of Cardiovascular Events in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
pmid:27571048.finding: CPAP (mean 3.3 h/night) did not prevent cardiovascular events (HR 1.10) but improved sleepiness, mood and quality of life.

pmid:37787793.authors: Sánchez-de-la-Torre M, Gracia-Lavedan E, Benitez ID, et al.
pmid:37787793.title: Adherence to CPAP Treatment and the Risk of Recurrent Cardiovascular Events: A Meta-Analysis.
pmid:37787793.finding: CPAP did not reduce recurrent cardiovascular events overall (HR 1.01); good adherence was associated with lower risk (HR 0.69) in an on-treatment analysis.

pmid:31887786.authors: Liu W, Cao Y, Dong L, et al.
pmid:31887786.title: Periodontal therapy for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease in people with periodontitis.
pmid:31887786.finding: Cochrane: evidence is insufficient (very low certainty) to know whether periodontal therapy prevents cardiovascular disease.

pmid:29622404.authors: Purewal S, Chapman SCE, van den Akker OBA
pmid:29622404.title: Depression and state anxiety scores during assisted reproductive treatment are associated with outcome: a meta-analysis.
pmid:29622404.finding: Women who conceived had lower depression and state-anxiety scores during treatment (SMD about -0.3), but changes from baseline did not predict outcome.

pmid:28031317.title: Coffee intake, cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomization analyses in 95 000-223 000 individuals
pmid:28031317.n: 95,366 Danes observational; up to 223,414 in genetic analyses
pmid:28031317.finding: Coffee intake showed U-shaped observational associations with CVD and mortality, but genetic variants that raise coffee intake by 42% were not associated with ischaemic heart disease, CVD mortality or all-cause mortality (Mendelian randomization), while an ApoE positive control worked.

pmid:34319429.title: Causal relationship from coffee consumption to diseases and mortality: a review of observational and Mendelian randomization studies including cardiometabolic diseases, cancer, gallstones and other diseases
pmid:34319429.finding: Review of observational and Mendelian randomization studies: lower mortality and cardiometabolic disease with high coffee intake in cohorts (HR 0.85-0.90) is not supported as causal by MR; MR supports only a lower gallstone risk and suggests higher colorectal cancer risk.

pmid:31055709.authors: Kim Y, Je Y, Giovannucci E
pmid:31055709.title: Coffee consumption and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: a meta-analysis by potential modifiers
pmid:31055709.finding: Non-linear inverse association of coffee with mortality, lowest at 3.5 cups/day (RR 0.85); the association persisted in strata by smoking status, age, weight, alcohol and caffeine content.

pmid:30838377.title: Long-term coffee consumption, caffeine metabolism genetics, and risk of cardiovascular disease: a prospective analysis of up to 347,077 individuals and 8368 cases
pmid:30838377.finding: Coffee-CVD association was non-linear: compared with 1-2 cups/day, CVD odds were 11% higher in non-drinkers, 7% higher in decaf drinkers and 22% higher above 6 cups/day; CYP1A2 caffeine-metabolism genotype did not modify risk.

pmid:35635846.authors: Liu D, Li ZH, Shen D, et al.
pmid:35635846.title: Association of Sugar-Sweetened, Artificially Sweetened, and Unsweetened Coffee Consumption With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality : A Large Prospective Cohort Study
pmid:35635846.finding: Unsweetened and moderately sugar-sweetened coffee were associated with about 16-31% lower mortality versus non-drinkers in a U-shaped pattern, including decaffeinated and instant coffee; a single baseline measure.

pmid:36947466.authors: Marcus GM, Rosenthal DG, Nah G, et al.
pmid:36947466.title: Acute Effects of Coffee Consumption on Health among Ambulatory Adults
pmid:36947466.finding: Randomly assigned coffee days did not significantly raise premature atrial contractions (RR 1.09) but increased premature ventricular contractions (RR 1.51) and daily steps (+1,058) and reduced nightly sleep (-36 min) versus caffeine-avoidance days.

pmid:32193382.authors: Cole JB, Florez JC, Hirschhorn JN
pmid:32193382.title: Comprehensive genomic analysis of dietary habits in UK Biobank identifies hundreds of genetic associations
pmid:32193382.finding: GWAS of 85 food-frequency items found 814 loci, many tied to taste, smell and education; MR suggested the top 'healthy' pattern (wholemeal vs white bread) is driven by education-correlated factors and is not strongly causal for coronary disease or diabetes.

pmid:31569213.authors: Zeraatkar D, Han MA, Guyatt GH, et al.
pmid:31569213.title: Red and Processed Meat Consumption and Risk for All-Cause Mortality and Cardiometabolic Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cohort Studies
pmid:31569213.finding: Low-certainty evidence that cutting red or processed meat by 3 servings/week is associated with very small reductions in mortality, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

pmid:31959642.authors: Qian F, Riddle MC, Wylie-Rosett J, et al.
pmid:31959642.title: Red and Processed Meats and Health Risks: How Strong Is the Evidence?
pmid:31959642.finding: Critique of NutriRECS: GRADE criteria designed for drug trials are inappropriate for diet; under NutriGRADE the evidence linking red/processed meat to type 2 diabetes is high quality and to mortality moderate; replacement foods matter.

pmid:36216940.authors: Lescinsky H, Afshin A, Ashbaugh C, et al.
pmid:36216940.title: Health effects associated with consumption of unprocessed red meat: a Burden of Proof study
pmid:36216940.finding: Burden of Proof analysis found only weak evidence linking unprocessed red meat with colorectal cancer, breast cancer, type 2 diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, and no evidence for stroke; the lowest-risk intake range spanned 0-200 g/day once heterogeneity was included.

pmid:40588677.authors: Haile D, Harding KL, McLaughlin SA, et al.
pmid:40588677.title: Health effects associated with consumption of processed meat, sugar-sweetened beverages and trans fatty acids: a Burden of Proof study
pmid:40588677.finding: Burden of Proof: processed meat was conservatively associated with at least 11% higher type 2 diabetes and 7% higher colorectal cancer risk, SSBs with at least 8% higher diabetes risk, and trans fat with at least 3% higher IHD risk; all rated two stars (weak or inconsistent evidence).

pmid:33268459.authors: Al-Shaar L, Satija A, Wang DD, et al.
pmid:33268459.title: Red meat intake and risk of coronary heart disease among US men: prospective cohort study
pmid:33268459.finding: Each daily serving of red meat was associated with 11-15% higher CHD risk; substituting nuts, legumes or soy for red meat was associated with 13-17% lower CHD risk.

pmid:30422271.title: The Challenge of Reforming Nutritional Epidemiologic Research
pmid:30422271.finding: Viewpoint arguing that nutritional epidemiology relies on unreliable self-report, finds implausibly large effects and needs radical reform.

pmid:25593140.authors: Satija A, Yu E, Willett WC, et al.
pmid:25593140.title: Understanding nutritional epidemiology and its role in policy
pmid:25593140.finding: Defends nutritional epidemiology: criticisms often misapply the drug-trial paradigm; diet is a complex, long-term exposure that cohorts with repeated measures and biomarkers can study.

pmid:23193004.title: Is everything we eat associated with cancer? A systematic cookbook review
pmid:23193004.finding: Of 50 random cookbook ingredients, 80% had studies linking them to cancer risk; single studies reported implausibly large effects that shrank to a median RR of 0.96 in meta-analyses.

pmid:30032218.title: Perspective: Limiting Dependence on Nonrandomized Studies and Improving Randomized Trials in Human Nutrition Research: Why and How
pmid:30032218.finding: Argues tiny effect sizes, massive confounding and measurement error make observational nutrition research unreliable and calls for large, long, streamlined randomized trials.

pmid:21118617.authors: Ramsden CE, Hibbeln JR, Majchrzak SF, et al.
pmid:21118617.title: n-6 fatty acid-specific and mixed polyunsaturate dietary interventions have different effects on CHD risk: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
pmid:21118617.finding: Trials that raised linoleic acid specifically (n-6 only) showed a non-significant 13% higher risk of MI or CHD death, versus 22% lower risk in mixed n-3/n-6 trials; trans fat displacement confounded older trials.

pmid:29032079.authors: Wu JHY, Marklund M, Imamura F, et al.
pmid:29032079.title: Omega-6 fatty acid biomarkers and incident type 2 diabetes: pooled analysis of individual-level data for 39 740 adults from 20 prospective cohort studies
pmid:29032079.finding: Higher linoleic acid biomarkers were associated with 35% lower risk of type 2 diabetes per interquintile range; arachidonic acid was neutral.

pmid:35692035.authors: Borges MC, Haycock PC, Zheng J, et al.
pmid:35692035.title: Role of circulating polyunsaturated fatty acids on cardiovascular diseases risk: analysis using Mendelian randomization and fatty acid genetic association data from over 114,000 UK Biobank participants
pmid:35692035.n: GWAS of 114,999 UK Biobank participants + MR
pmid:35692035.finding: Mendelian randomization did not support a protective effect of genetically higher circulating linoleic acid or omega-3 on cardiovascular disease; estimates for LA were inconsistent and pleiotropy via lipoproteins (FADS locus) is a likely bias.

pmid:31817859.authors: Yuan S, Bäck M, Bruzelius M, et al.
pmid:31817859.title: Plasma Phospholipid Fatty Acids, FADS1 and Risk of 15 Cardiovascular Diseases: A Mendelian Randomisation Study
pmid:31817859.finding: MR: genetically higher plasma linoleic, alpha-linolenic and oleic acid were associated with lower large-artery stroke and venous thromboembolism, but signals were driven by the pleiotropic FADS1 locus.

pmid:38578269.authors: Zhang Y, Sun Y, Yu Q, et al.
pmid:38578269.title: Higher ratio of plasma omega-6/omega-3 fatty acids is associated with greater risk of all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality: A population-based cohort study in UK Biobank
pmid:38578269.finding: Higher plasma omega-6/omega-3 ratio was associated with higher mortality, but both plasma omega-6 and omega-3 levels were individually associated with lower all-cause, cancer and CVD mortality.

pmid:29897867.authors: Estruch R, Ros E, Salas-Salvadó J, et al.
pmid:29897867.title: Retraction and Republication: Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease with a Mediterranean Diet. N Engl J Med 2013;368:1279-90
pmid:29897867.finding: NEJM retraction and republication notice for the 2013 PREDIMED report after non-random allocation of household members and at two of 11 sites.

pmid:35525255.authors: Delgado-Lista J, Alcala-Diaz JF, Torres-Peña JD, et al.
pmid:35525255.title: Long-term secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat diet (CORDIOPREV): a randomised controlled trial
pmid:35525255.finding: CORDIOPREV: over 7 years a Mediterranean diet reduced major cardiovascular events versus a low-fat diet (adjusted HR about 0.72-0.75), mainly in men.

pmid:9989963.authors: de Lorgeril M, Salen P, Martin JL, et al.
pmid:9989963.title: Mediterranean diet, traditional risk factors, and the rate of cardiovascular complications after myocardial infarction: final report of the Lyon Diet Heart Study
pmid:9989963.finding: Lyon Diet Heart Study final report: Mediterranean-type diet reduced cardiac death and non-fatal MI (14 vs 44 events) over 46 months.

pmid:30864165.authors: Rees K, Takeda A, Martin N, et al.
pmid:30864165.title: Mediterranean-style diet for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
pmid:30864165.finding: Cochrane: low-quality evidence of little or no effect of PREDIMED on CVD mortality or total mortality but fewer strokes; Lyon trial suggested benefit; two trials excluded for data-reliability concerns; overall uncertainty remains.

pmid:12433513.authors: Singh RB, Dubnov G, Niaz MA, et al.
pmid:12433513.title: Effect of an Indo-Mediterranean diet on progression of coronary artery disease in high risk patients (Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study): a randomised single-blind trial
pmid:12433513.finding: Indo-Mediterranean Diet Heart Study reported large cardiac benefits; PubMed links a 2005 Lancet expression of concern about the data.

pmid:35027106.authors: Guasch-Ferré M, Li Y, Willett WC, et al.
pmid:35027106.title: Consumption of Olive Oil and Risk of Total and Cause-Specific Mortality Among U.S. Adults
pmid:35027106.finding: Olive oil >7 g/day was associated with 19% lower total mortality versus rarely, but not when compared with other vegetable oils combined.

pmid:33478205.authors: Caruso P, Caputo M, Cirillo P, et al.
pmid:33478205.title: Effects of Mediterranean diet on semen parameters in healthy young adults: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:33478205.finding: Six months of Mediterranean diet versus low-fat diet modestly increased sperm concentration and total count; other parameters unchanged.

pmid:40593139.authors: Ghasemi A, Jaladat AM, Sharifi MH, et al.
pmid:40593139.title: The effects of mediterranean and Persian diet on sexual function and semen parameters quality among infertile men: a randomized controlled trial
pmid:40593139.finding: Two months of a Mediterranean diet improved sperm count, motility and morphology versus control in a single-blind Iranian trial.

pmid:28836672.authors: Kelly SA, Hartley L, Loveman E, et al.
pmid:28836672.title: Whole grain cereals for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
pmid:28836672.finding: Cochrane: no RCT reported cardiovascular events; trials of up to 16 weeks found no difference in total cholesterol and insufficient evidence on blood pressure; low-quality evidence and partial cereal-industry funding.

pmid:36811595.authors: Zargarzadeh N, Mousavi SM, Santos HO, et al.
pmid:36811595.title: Legume Consumption and Risk of All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Prospective Studies
pmid:36811595.finding: Higher legume intake was associated with 6% lower all-cause mortality and lower stroke mortality but not CVD, CHD or cancer mortality; low-to-moderate certainty.

pmid:30122560.authors: Seidelmann SB, Claggett B, Cheng S, et al.
pmid:30122560.title: Dietary carbohydrate intake and mortality: a prospective cohort study and meta-analysis
pmid:30122560.finding: U-shaped association of carbohydrate intake with mortality (lowest at 50-55% energy); replacing carbohydrate with animal fat/protein was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.18) and with plant sources lower mortality (HR 0.82).

pmid:39732588.authors: Hamsho M, Shkorfu W, Ranneh Y, et al.
pmid:39732588.title: Is isocaloric intermittent fasting superior to calorie restriction? A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
pmid:39732588.finding: Isocaloric intermittent fasting was not superior to calorie restriction overall; some fat-mass and insulin differences, with more hunger and fatigue on IF.

pmid:40966617.authors: Li S, Hamaya R, Zhu H, et al.
pmid:40966617.title: Effects of 2-year cocoa extract supplementation on inflammaging biomarkers in older US adults: findings from the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study randomised clinical trial
pmid:40966617.finding: Cocoa extract lowered hsCRP by 8.4% per year relative to placebo over 2 years; other inflammatory markers were unchanged except a rise in IFN-gamma.

pmid:34612056.authors: Gencer B, Djousse L, Al-Ramady OT, et al.
pmid:34612056.title: Effect of Long-Term Marine ɷ-3 Fatty Acids Supplementation on the Risk of Atrial Fibrillation in Randomized Controlled Trials of Cardiovascular Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:34612056.finding: Marine omega-3 supplements increased atrial fibrillation risk by 25%, more at doses above 1 g/day (HR 1.49).

pmid:38800667.authors: Chen G, Qian ZM, Zhang J, et al.
pmid:38800667.title: Regular use of fish oil supplements and course of cardiovascular diseases: prospective cohort study
pmid:38800667.finding: Regular fish-oil supplement use was associated with higher risk of incident atrial fibrillation (HR 1.13) and possibly stroke (HR 1.05) in people without CVD, but with better outcomes in people with existing CVD.

pmid:37977328.authors: Cardoso BR, Fratezzi I, Kellow NJ
pmid:37977328.title: Nut Consumption and Fertility: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:37977328.finding: Pooling 2 RCTs in 223 healthy men, at least 60 g/day nuts improved sperm motility, vitality and morphology but not concentration; observational studies found no links with ART outcomes.

pmid:32330233.authors: Filippou CD, Tsioufis CP, Thomopoulos CG, et al.
pmid:32330233.title: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) Diet and Blood Pressure Reduction in Adults with and without Hypertension: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
pmid:32330233.finding: DASH lowered systolic BP by 3.2 mmHg and diastolic by 2.5 mmHg versus control diets, in people with and without hypertension; moderate-quality evidence.

pmid:40326569.authors: Bensaaud A, Seery S, Gibson I, et al.
pmid:40326569.title: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular diseases
pmid:40326569.finding: Cochrane 2025: no trial had enough events to show whether DASH prevents myocardial infarction, stroke or death; evidence on clinical outcomes is very sparse.

pmid:36622248.authors: Li L, Li H, Gao Y, et al.
pmid:36622248.title: Effect of flaxseed supplementation on blood pressure: a systematic review, and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
pmid:36622248.finding: Flaxseed lowered systolic BP by 3.2 mmHg and diastolic by 2.6 mmHg on average, with very high heterogeneity (I2 >90%); larger effects at >=30 g/day, >20 weeks and in hypertension.

pmid:37019448.authors: Huang Y, Chen Z, Chen B, et al.
pmid:37019448.title: Dietary sugar consumption and health: umbrella review
pmid:37019448.finding: Umbrella review: high sugar intake associated with many adverse outcomes; strongest (moderate quality) for body weight and ectopic fat; most other evidence low quality.

pmid:38450974.authors: Joseph MD, Koenig MR, Kuriyama AS, et al.
pmid:38450974.title: A preconception cohort study of sugar-sweetened beverage consumption and semen quality
pmid:38450974.finding: Seven or more SSBs per week was associated with about 22% lower sperm concentration and total count versus none, using at-home semen kits.

pmid:35055501.authors: Meldgaard M, Brix N, Gaml-Sørensen A, et al.
pmid:35055501.title: Consumption of Sugar-Sweetened or Artificially Sweetened Beverages and Semen Quality in Young Men: A Cross-Sectional Study
pmid:35055501.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
pmid:35055501.finding: Sugar-sweetened or artificially sweetened beverage consumption was not strongly associated with semen volume, concentration, count or motility.

pmid:29384791.authors: Hatch EE, Wesselink AK, Hahn KA, et al.
pmid:29384791.title: Intake of Sugar-sweetened Beverages and Fecundability in a North American Preconception Cohort
pmid:29384791.finding: Seven or more SSBs per week by either partner was associated with about 20% lower fecundability.

pmid:37619675.authors: Ribeiro M, Cardozo LF, Paiva BR, et al.
pmid:37619675.title: Sulforaphane Supplementation Did Not Modulate NRF2 and NF-kB mRNA Expressions in Hemodialysis Patients
pmid:37619675.finding: 150 umol/day sulforaphane for 2 months did not change NRF2 or NF-kB expression, inflammatory markers or malondialdehyde.

pmid:30208394.authors: Morishita M, Adar SD, D'Souza J, et al.
pmid:30208394.title: Effect of Portable Air Filtration Systems on Personal Exposure to Fine Particulate Matter and Blood Pressure Among Residents in a Low-Income Senior Facility: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:30208394.finding: Three days of portable filtration lowered personal PM2.5 and systolic BP by 3.2 mmHg vs sham; most secondary outcomes did not improve.

pmid:40082868.authors: Margiana R, Odhar HA, Prasad K, et al.
pmid:40082868.title: Does outdoor air pollution cause poor semen quality? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
pmid:40082868.finding: Higher air pollution exposure was associated with lower semen volume, concentration and motility, with very high heterogeneity (I2 about 96-99%).

pmid:34532803.authors: Qian H, Xu Q, Yan W, et al.
pmid:34532803.title: Association between exposure to ambient air pollution and semen quality in adults: a meta-analysis.
pmid:34532803.finding: Air pollution was associated with small reductions in sperm concentration, count and total motility, but not progressive motility.

pmid:28657878.authors: Di Q, Wang Y, Zanobetti A, et al.
pmid:28657878.title: Air Pollution and Mortality in the Medicare Population.
pmid:28657878.finding: PM2.5 and ozone were associated with higher mortality even below current US standards, with no evident threshold.

pmid:20123611.authors: Hansen C, Luben TJ, Sacks JD, et al.
pmid:20123611.title: The effect of ambient air pollution on sperm quality.
pmid:20123611.finding: After adjusting for season and temperature, PM2.5 and ozone were not significantly associated with any semen outcome, including DNA integrity.

pmid:41936219.authors: Russo LM, Pilsner JR, Canty TP, et al.
pmid:41936219.title: Men's exposure to ambient air pollution and in vitro fertilization outcomes among an infertility treatment population.
pmid:41936219.finding: Men's air pollution exposure during spermatogenesis was not clearly associated with pregnancy, loss or live birth, though higher NO2 and ozone tracked fewer good-quality day-3 embryos.

deep-audit-env-plastics:ept-eu2024.title: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/3190 of 19 December 2024 on the use of bisphenol A (BPA) and other bisphenols and bisphenol derivatives in materials and articles intended to come into contact with food
deep-audit-env-plastics:ept-eu2024.journal: Official Journal of the European Union
deep-audit-env-plastics:ept-eu2024.finding: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/3190 bans BPA and its salts in food contact materials (plastics, coatings, varnishes, inks, adhesives, rubbers), with an 18-month transition to 20 July 2026 for most single-use items and 36 months (to 20 January 2028) for some uses; other hazardous bisphenols need authorization.

pmid:32381348.authors: Bordewijk EM, Wang R, Askie LM, et al.
pmid:32381348.title: Data integrity of 35 randomised controlled trials in women' health
pmid:32381348.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
pmid:32381348.finding: Of 35 women's-health RCTs published 2006-2016 by two authors from one institute, 26 shared many similar baseline and outcome values, and baseline distributions were unlikely to reflect proper randomisation.

pmid:32935841.authors: Bordewijk EM, Wang R, van Wely M, et al.
pmid:32935841.title: To share or not to share data: how valid are trials evaluating first-line ovulation induction for polycystic ovary syndrome?
pmid:32935841.finding: In PCOS ovulation-induction trials, RCTs that did not share individual data had more risk of bias (75% vs 24% not low risk), no adequate registration, more statistical problems and different pooled effects than trials that shared data.

pmid:32387277.authors: Li W, van Wely M, Gurrin L, et al.
pmid:32387277.title: Integrity of randomized controlled trials: challenges and solutions
pmid:32387277.finding: Review from the Monash group: compromised RCT integrity undermines systematic reviews; data can be checked via summary statistics and individual participant data, and reviewers should account for problematic trials.

pmid:38735122.authors: Mol BW, Bordewijk EM, Rogozińska E, et al.
pmid:38735122.title: Data integrity of 14 randomised controlled trials
pmid:38735122.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
pmid:38735122.finding: Integrity check of 14 RCTs by one Egyptian author (2004-2019): duplicated baseline tables, plagiarism and baseline p-values implying non-random allocation; unretracted trials should not inform practice until investigated.

pmid:33040331.title: False individual patient data and zombie randomised controlled trials submitted to Anaesthesia
pmid:33040331.finding: Of 526 RCTs submitted to Anaesthesia, 14% had false data and 8% were 'zombie' trials; when individual patient data were requested, 44% had false data and 26% were zombies.

pmid:40349737.authors: Wilkinson J, Heal C, Antoniou GA, et al.
pmid:40349737.title: Assessing the feasibility and impact of clinical trial trustworthiness checks via an application to Cochrane Reviews: Stage 2 of the INSPECT-SR project
pmid:40349737.finding: Applying 72 trustworthiness checks to RCTs in 50 Cochrane reviews raised some or serious concerns about authenticity for 25% and 6% of trials; removing them left 22% of meta-analyses empty, and concerns were unrelated to Risk-of-Bias or GRADE ratings.

pmid:41990228.authors: Zou H, Abdallah KS, Wirleitner B, et al.
pmid:41990228.title: Intrauterine human chorionic gonadotropin administration before embryo transfer (IHABT): an individual participant data meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pmid:41990228.n: 7 RCTs with IPD, 2244 women (28 RCTs found)
pmid:41990228.finding: IPD meta-analysis: intrauterine hCG before embryo transfer did not improve live birth (OR 0.99, 0.83-1.19); all 7 IPD trials passed trustworthiness checks, none of the trials without IPD did, and those untrustworthy trials produced the apparent benefit.

pmid:18462730.authors: Papaleo E, Unfer V, Baillargeon JP, et al.
pmid:18462730.title: RETRACTED: Myo-inositol may improve oocyte quality in intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycles. A prospective, controlled, randomized trial
pmid:18462730.finding: RETRACTED (2025) myo-inositol ICSI trial; retracted at the request of the ASRM Publications Committee after an undisclosed conflict of interest with the supplement maker was reported. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:39971415.title: Retraction notice to 'Myo-inositol may improve oocyte quality in intracytoplasmic sperm injection cycles. A prospective, controlled, randomized trial' [Fertility and Sterility 91 (2009) 1750-1754]
pmid:39971415.finding: Retraction notice (Fertil Steril 2025) for Papaleo 2009 myo-inositol RCT.

pmid:26963897.authors: Kotb MM, Hassan AM, AwadAllah AM
pmid:26963897.title: Does dehydroepiandrosterone improve pregnancy rate in women undergoing IVF/ICSI with expected poor ovarian response according to the Bologna criteria? A randomized controlled trial
pmid:26963897.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
pmid:26963897.finding: RETRACTED (2026) Egyptian RCT of DHEA in poor responders undergoing IVF/ICSI. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:41785717.authors: Kotb MMM, Hassan AMA, AwadAllah AMA
pmid:41785717.title: Retraction notice to "Does Dehydroepiandrosterone improve pregnancy rate in women undergoing IVF/ICSI with expected poor ovarian response according to the Bologna criteria? A randomized controlled trial" [Eur. J. Obstet. Gynecol. Reprod. Biol. 200 (2016) 11-15]
pmid:41785717.journal: Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
pmid:41785717.finding: Retraction notice (Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 2026) for the Kotb 2016 DHEA RCT.

pmid:32451660.authors: Elprince M, Kishk EA, Metawie OM, et al.
pmid:32451660.title: Ovarian stimulation after dehydroepiandrosterone supplementation in poor ovarian reserve: a randomized clinical trial
pmid:32451660.finding: RETRACTED (2024) RCT of DHEA before ovarian stimulation in poor ovarian reserve. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:24813752.authors: El Refaeey A, Selem A, Badawy A
pmid:24813752.title: Combined coenzyme Q10 and clomiphene citrate for ovulation induction in clomiphene-citrate-resistant polycystic ovary syndrome
pmid:24813752.finding: RETRACTED (2023, after an expression of concern) RCT of CoQ10 plus clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant PCOS. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:31273783.authors: El Sharkwy IA, Abd El Aziz WM
pmid:31273783.title: Randomized controlled trial of N-acetylcysteine versus l-carnitine among women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant polycystic ovary syndrome
pmid:31273783.finding: RETRACTED RCT of N-acetylcysteine vs L-carnitine in clomiphene-resistant PCOS; it was the only source for two outcomes in the Cochrane female-antioxidant review. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:29048754.authors: Maged AM, Rashwan H, AbdelAziz S, et al.
pmid:29048754.title: Randomized controlled trial of the effect of endometrial injury on implantation and clinical pregnancy rates during the first ICSI cycle
pmid:29048754.finding: RETRACTED (2024) Egyptian RCT reporting higher implantation and pregnancy with endometrial injury before first ICSI. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:28397981.authors: Helmy MEE, Maher MA, Elkhouly NI, et al.
pmid:28397981.title: A randomized trial of local endometrial injury during ovulation induction cycles
pmid:28397981.finding: RETRACTED (2024) Egyptian RCT of endometrial injury during clomiphene ovulation-induction cycles. Cited only to flag it.

pmid:40996763.authors: de Ligny WR, de Bruin JP, Smits RM, et al.
pmid:40996763.title: Antioxidant Treatment and the Chance to Conceive in Men Seeking Fertility Care: The SUMMER Randomized Clinical Trial
pmid:40996763.finding: SUMMER (21 Dutch centres): 6 months of an antioxidant/B-vitamin supplement vs placebo did not raise ongoing pregnancy (33.8% vs 37.5%; aOR 0.85, 0.66-1.09); in the 4-6 month window it was lower (15.5% vs 21.5%); no effect on semen or SDF.

pmid:36102104.authors: Agarwal A, Cannarella R, Saleh R, et al.
pmid:36102104.title: Impact of Antioxidant Therapy on Natural Pregnancy Outcomes and Semen Parameters in Infertile Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
pmid:36102104.finding: Meta-analysis by Agarwal's group: antioxidants associated with higher spontaneous pregnancy and better semen parameters, but no effect on live birth (4 studies) or SDF (3 studies).

pmid:40128318.authors: Szabó A, Váncsa S, Hegyi P, et al.
pmid:40128318.title: Assessing the efficacy of varicocelectomy, antioxidants, FSH treatment, and lifestyle modifications on sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:40128318.finding: SDF fell 6.7 points 3 months after varicocelectomy (12.4 at 6 months), about 4.3 points with antioxidants, 6.7 with FSH and 3.2 with lifestyle change; authors judged antioxidants 'questionable'.

pmid:42206761.authors: Melhem SJ, Melhem M, Haddad R, et al.
pmid:42206761.title: Pharmacologic and Nutritional Therapies in Idiopathic Male Infertility: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:42206761.finding: Antioxidants were associated with higher sperm concentration and motility in idiopathic infertility, but certainty was very low, heterogeneity >80% and prediction intervals crossed zero; live-birth data lacking.

pmid:37709593.authors: Khoo CC, Cayetano-Alcaraz AA, Rashid R, et al.
pmid:37709593.title: Does Testicular Sperm Improve Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection Outcomes for Nonazoospermic Infertile Men with Elevated Sperm DNA Fragmentation? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
pmid:37709593.finding: Testicular sperm associated with higher pregnancy (OR 2.51) and live birth (OR 2.59, SCSA studies) in high-SDF men, but evidence quality was too low to recommend it outside trials.

pmid:34076869.authors: Hozyen M, Hasanen E, Elqusi K, et al.
pmid:34076869.title: Reproductive Outcomes of Different Sperm Selection Techniques for ICSI Patients with Abnormal Sperm DNA Fragmentation: a Randomized Controlled Trial
pmid:34076869.finding: Egyptian 4-arm RCT in high-SDF ICSI: testicular sperm gave lower cleavage, blastulation and top-blastocyst rates than ejaculated-sperm methods; PICSI and MACS had the highest ongoing pregnancy.

pmid:37867514.authors: Romano M, Cirillo F, Spadaro D, et al.
pmid:37867514.title: High sperm DNA fragmentation: do we have robust evidence to support antioxidants and testicular sperm extraction to improve fertility outcomes? a narrative review
pmid:37867514.finding: Narrative review: evidence for antioxidants or testicular sperm in high SDF is non-conclusive because of small samples and risk of bias.

deep-audit-fertility:afert-hfea2026sdf.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation: treatment add-on rating
deep-audit-fertility:afert-hfea2026sdf.finding: HFEA (page updated 24 Sep 2026): after SDF testing, antioxidants and sperm selection rated grey; TESE/TESA with ICSI rated RED for male-factor infertility (insufficient evidence plus procedural risk).

pmid:39344117.authors: Palani A, Cannarella R, Saleh R, et al.
pmid:39344117.title: Impact of Varicocele Repair on Assisted Reproductive Technique Outcomes in Infertile Men: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:39344117.finding: Men who had varicocele repair before ICSI had higher fertilisation, clinical pregnancy (OR 1.38) and live birth (OR 2.07) than unrepaired men; all studies observational.

pmid:35690546.authors: Murugesu S, Kasaven LS, Petrie A, et al.
pmid:35690546.title: Does advanced paternal age affect outcomes following assisted reproductive technology? A systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:35690546.finding: Paternal age under 40 associated with higher clinical pregnancy and live birth in autologous IVF; under 50 with lower miscarriage and more blastocysts in donor-egg cycles where maternal age is controlled.

pmid:36652117.authors: Begon E, Lefebvre T, Arbo E, et al.
pmid:36652117.title: Does paternal age affect the live birth rate in donor oocyte cycles? A systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:36652117.finding: In egg-donation cycles live birth fell slightly but linearly with paternal age, with no threshold.

pmid:22914163.authors: Kong A, Frigge ML, Masson G, et al.
pmid:22914163.title: Rate of de novo mutations and the importance of father's age to disease risk
pmid:22914163.finding: De novo mutations rise by about two per year of father's age (doubling about every 16.5 years); father's age explains most variation in de novo mutation counts.

pmid:24577047.authors: D'Onofrio BM, Rickert ME, Frans E, et al.
pmid:24577047.title: Paternal age at childbearing and offspring psychiatric and academic morbidity
pmid:24577047.finding: Sibling- and cousin-comparison designs found paternal-age associations with autism, psychosis, bipolar disorder and academic problems as large or larger than population estimates, consistent with a causal mutation pathway.

pmid:30381468.authors: Khandwala YS, Baker VL, Shaw GM, et al.
pmid:30381468.title: Association of paternal age with perinatal outcomes between 2007 and 2016 in the United States: population based cohort study
pmid:30381468.finding: Fathers 45+ had 14% higher odds of preterm birth and partners 34% higher odds of gestational diabetes after adjustment for maternal age; population impact modest.

pmid:36377604.authors: Levine H, Jørgensen N, Martino-Andrade A, et al.
pmid:36377604.title: Temporal trends in sperm count: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis of samples collected globally in the 20th and 21st centuries
pmid:36377604.finding: Updated global meta-regression: mean sperm concentration among unselected men fell 51.6% between 1973 and 2018, with the decline appearing to steepen in recent decades.

pmid:33969777.authors: Boulicault M, Perret M, Galka J, et al.
pmid:33969777.title: The future of sperm: a biovariability framework for understanding global sperm count trends
pmid:33969777.finding: Critique of the sperm-count-decline hypothesis: proposes that sperm count varies widely and non-pathologically, and that trends need ecological and life-history interpretation rather than a decline narrative.

pmid:36460524.authors: Harris BS, Jukic AM, Truong T, et al.
pmid:36460524.title: Markers of ovarian reserve as predictors of future fertility
pmid:36460524.finding: Diminished ovarian reserve (AMH <0.7 or FSH >=10) was not associated with lower future live birth, infertility or fecundability.

pmid:37475164.authors: Peigné M, Bernard V, Dijols L, et al.
pmid:37475164.title: Using serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels to predict the chance of live birth after spontaneous or assisted conception: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:37475164.finding: AMH relates non-linearly to cumulative live birth after IVF/ICSI, with no threshold below which live birth is impossible; data lacking for natural conception.

pmid:38654466.authors: Hirsch A, Hirsh Raccah B, Rotem R, et al.
pmid:38654466.title: Planned oocyte cryopreservation: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis
pmid:38654466.finding: Planned egg freezing: 11% returned to use eggs; live birth per returning patient 28% overall, 52% if frozen at 35 or younger and 19% at 40+.

pmid:38964588.authors: Kirubarajan A, Patel P, Thangavelu N, et al.
pmid:38964588.title: Return rates and pregnancy outcomes after oocyte preservation for planned fertility delay: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:38964588.finding: Return rate after planned egg freezing 10.8% (median 7-year follow-up); live birth in 28.9% of those who thawed eggs.

pmid:38955888.authors: Cascante SD, Grifo JA, Licciardi F, et al.
pmid:38955888.title: The effects of age, mature oocyte number, and cycle number on cumulative live birth rates after planned oocyte cryopreservation
pmid:38955888.finding: Cumulative live birth 43% overall and >70% with >=20 mature eggs frozen before 38; age and number of eggs, not number of cycles, predicted success.

deep-audit-fertility:afert-hfea2026.title: Treatment add-ons with limited evidence (HFEA add-ons rating list)
deep-audit-fertility:afert-hfea2026.finding: HFEA add-on ratings for 'chances of having a baby' (page reviewed 28 Sep 2026): yellow for endometrial scratching, hyaluronate transfer medium, elective freeze-all; grey for assisted hatching, androgens, intralipids, IMSI, intrauterine culture, microbiome testing, SDF; black for time-lapse and PICSI; red for endometrial receptivity testing, IVIG, steroids, PRP and PGT-A. No green.

pmid:41436190.authors: Lin X, Wu D, Zhang C, et al.
pmid:41436190.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy versus no genetic testing in couples undergoing intracytoplasmic sperm injection for severe male infertility: multicentre, open label, randomised controlled trial
pmid:41436190.finding: BMJ RCT in severe male factor ICSI: PGT-A did not change cumulative live birth (60.4% vs 60.9%) but lowered pregnancy loss after first transfer (5.8% vs 19.1%).

pmid:38762806.authors: Practice Committees of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology. Electronic address: asrm@asrm.org
pmid:38762806.title: The use of preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy: a committee opinion
pmid:38762806.finding: ASRM 2024: value of PGT-A as routine screening for all IVF patients has not been demonstrated; multicentre RCTs found similar outcomes; miscarriage benefit unclear.

pmid:39151684.authors: Mumusoglu S, Telek SB, Ata B
pmid:39151684.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy in unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:39151684.finding: In unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss, low-quality evidence suggests PGT-A lowers pregnancy loss and raises live birth per transfer and per patient; RCTs needed.

pmid:40725861.authors: Beebeejaun Y, Bakalova D, Mania A, et al.
pmid:40725861.title: Preimplantation Genetic Testing for Aneuploidy Versus Morphological Selection in Women Aged 35-42: Results of a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
pmid:40725861.finding: Pilot RCT in women 35-42: PGT-A vs morphology gave cumulative live birth 72% vs 52% after up to three single transfers (not significant; feasibility trial).

pmid:42330177.authors: Rocha RM, Andrade MCR, Barcelos IDES, et al.
pmid:42330177.title: Hyaluronic Acid Enriched Medium for Embryo Transfer: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
pmid:42330177.finding: Hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium: live birth RR 1.14 (0.99-1.31, NS), 1.06 (0.85-1.31) after excluding high-risk-of-bias trials; certainty very low.

pmid:36414088.authors: Arian SE, Hessami K, Khatibi A, et al.
pmid:36414088.title: Endometrial receptivity array before frozen embryo transfer cycles: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:36414088.finding: ERA before frozen transfer did not change live birth or ongoing pregnancy (OR 1.38, 0.79-2.41).

pmid:38309515.title: Some common, fatal flaws in systematic reviews of observational studies
pmid:38309515.finding: Uses ERA systematic reviews as an example of common fatal flaws in meta-analyses of observational studies (critical appraisal and pooling errors).

pmid:37129654.authors: Sun Y, Cui L, Lu Y, et al.
pmid:37129654.title: Prednisone vs Placebo and Live Birth in Patients With Recurrent Implantation Failure Undergoing In Vitro Fertilization: A Randomized Clinical Trial
pmid:37129654.finding: JAMA RCT in recurrent implantation failure: prednisone did not improve live birth (37.8% vs 38.8%) and increased biochemical loss (17.3% vs 9.9%) and preterm delivery (11.8% vs 5.5%).

pmid:37348787.authors: Fancsovits P, Lehner A, Kaszas Z, et al.
pmid:37348787.title: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection does not improve the outcome of IVF treatments in patients with advanced maternal age or low oocyte number: A randomized controlled trial
pmid:37348787.finding: In women >=40 and/or with <=4 oocytes (non-severe male factor), ICSI gave lower fertilisation (53% vs 62%) and no better live birth than conventional IVF; worse with both age and few eggs.

pmid:39332623.authors: Conforti A, Carbone L, Di Girolamo R, et al.
pmid:39332623.title: Therapeutic management in women with a diminished ovarian reserve: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pmid:39332623.finding: In POSEIDON-defined diminished ovarian reserve, testosterone was the only adjuvant associated with higher live birth (OR 2.19).

pmid:41136866.authors: Etrusco A, Agrifoglio V, Castillo Farfán JC, et al.
pmid:41136866.title: Effectiveness of hormone add-on strategies in ovarian stimulation for women with poor ovarian response: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pmid:41136866.finding: Network meta-analysis of hormonal add-ons in poor responders: no significant live-birth differences among add-ons (very low evidence); growth hormone ranked best for oocyte numbers.

pmid:40190407.authors: Zhang J, Zhang H, Zhou W, et al.
pmid:40190407.title: Effect of myo-inositol supplementation in mixed ovarian response IVF cohort: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:40190407.finding: Myo-inositol associated with higher MII oocyte rate in PCOS IVF but not in poor responders; surrogate outcomes.

pmid:14629312.authors: Giannelli M, Doyle P, Roman E, et al.
pmid:14629312.title: The effect of caffeine consumption and nausea on the risk of miscarriage
pmid:14629312.finding: UK case-control: >300 mg/day caffeine in pregnancy roughly doubled miscarriage odds after adjusting for nausea; nausea itself was strongly protective; pre-pregnancy caffeine not associated.

pmid:34187701.authors: Yuan S, Liu J, Larsson SC
pmid:34187701.title: Smoking, alcohol and coffee consumption and pregnancy loss: a Mendelian randomization investigation
pmid:34187701.finding: Mendelian randomization: genetically predicted smoking raised pregnancy loss (OR 1.31) but genetically predicted coffee consumption did not (OR 0.96, 0.87-1.06).

pmid:35679582.authors: Brito Nunes C, Huang P, Wang G, et al.
pmid:35679582.title: Mendelian randomization study of maternal coffee consumption and its influence on birthweight, stillbirth, miscarriage, gestational age and pre-term birth
pmid:35679582.finding: Two-sample MR and genetic-risk-score analyses found no effect of coffee consumption on miscarriage, stillbirth or preterm birth.

pmid:37013617.authors: Wootton RE, Lawn RB, Magnus MC, et al.
pmid:37013617.title: Associations between health behaviours, fertility and reproductive outcomes: triangulation of evidence in the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa)
pmid:37013617.finding: Triangulating regression with MR for alcohol, caffeine, BMI and smoking: only smoking and BMI showed consistent effects on time to conception.

pmid:38408693.authors: Caldwell AE, Gorczyca AM, Bradford AP, et al.
pmid:38408693.title: Effectiveness of preconception weight loss interventions on fertility in women: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:38408693.finding: Preconception weight-loss interventions raised pregnancy (RR 1.24) but not live birth (RR 1.19, 0.97-1.45).

pmid:7979565.authors: Czeizel AE, Dudás I, Métneki J
pmid:7979565.title: Pregnancy outcomes in a randomised controlled trial of periconceptional multivitamin supplementation. Final report
pmid:7979565.finding: Hungarian RCT: periconceptional multivitamin with 0.8 mg folic acid increased cumulative conceptions and multiple births, with no other effect on pregnancy outcomes.

pmid:30920622.authors: Levie D, Korevaar TIM, Bath SC, et al.
pmid:30920622.title: Association of Maternal Iodine Status With Child IQ: A Meta-Analysis of Individual Participant Data
pmid:30920622.finding: IPD of 3 cohorts: UI/Creat <150 ug/g not significantly associated with lower verbal (-0.6) or nonverbal IQ; curvilinear association with verbal IQ only, limited to the first 14 weeks.

pmid:29030199.authors: Gowachirapant S, Jaiswal N, Melse-Boonstra A, et al.
pmid:29030199.title: Effect of iodine supplementation in pregnant women on child neurodevelopment: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
pmid:29030199.finding: 200 ug/day iodine in mildly deficient pregnant women (India, Thailand) did not improve child IQ or executive function at 5-6 years.

pmid:37299551.authors: Winter HG, Rolnik DL, Mol BWJ, et al.
pmid:37299551.title: Can Dietary Patterns Impact Fertility Outcomes? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:37299551.finding: Mediterranean adherence linked to better ART outcomes after excluding high-risk studies (2 studies); healthy-diet patterns too heterogeneous to pool.

pmid:35293975.authors: Kellow NJ, Le Cerf J, Horta F, et al.
pmid:35293975.title: The Effect of Dietary Patterns on Clinical Pregnancy and Live Birth Outcomes in Men and Women Receiving Assisted Reproductive Technologies: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:35293975.finding: All diet-pattern studies in ART had moderate-high risk of bias; Mediterranean and profertility diets associated with live birth in individual studies.

pmid:36979001.authors: Barbagallo F, Cannarella R, Crafa A, et al.
pmid:36979001.title: The Impact of a Very Short Abstinence Period on Assisted Reproductive Technique Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pmid:36979001.finding: A second ejaculate within 4 hours was associated with higher implantation, clinical pregnancy and live birth in ART.

pmid:38345682.authors: Cannarella R, Marino M, Crafa A, et al.
pmid:38345682.title: Impact of COVID-19 on testicular function: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:38345682.finding: Active or recent COVID-19 associated with lower sperm concentration, count and motility and altered hormones; mostly short-term follow-up.

pmid:7805903.authors: Yanushpolsky EH, Politch JA, Hill JA, et al.
pmid:7805903.title: Antibiotic therapy and leukocytospermia: a prospective, randomized, controlled study
pmid:7805903.finding: Leukocytospermia often resolved spontaneously; doxycycline or co-trimoxazole were no better than no treatment.

pmid:39104757.authors: Guo L, Yin S, Wei H, et al.
pmid:39104757.title: No evidence of genetic causation between iron and infertility: a Mendelian randomization study
pmid:39104757.finding: Mendelian randomization found no causal effect of serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation or TIBC on male or female infertility.

pmid:39817704.authors: Tulenheimo-Silfvast A, Ruokolainen-Pursiainen L, Simberg N
pmid:39817704.title: Association between iron deficiency and fertility
pmid:39817704.finding: Uncontrolled before-after clinic study: after IV iron for deficiency, live birth rose (51% vs 26% before); confounded by time and ongoing treatment.

pmid:32979078.authors: Alshehre SM, Narice BF, Fenwick MA, et al.
pmid:32979078.title: The impact of endometrioma on in vitro fertilisation/intra-cytoplasmic injection IVF/ICSI reproductive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pmid:32979078.finding: Endometrioma reduced oocytes and MII oocytes retrieved but not live birth or clinical pregnancy after IVF/ICSI.

pmid:33170239.authors: Bischoff-Ferrari HA, Vellas B, Rizzoli R et al.
pmid:33170239.title: Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation, Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation, or a Strength-Training Exercise Program on Clinical Outcomes in Older Adults: The DO-HEALTH Randomized Clinical Trial.
pmid:33170239.finding: DO-HEALTH: vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3 1 g/day or home exercise for 3 years had no significant benefit on blood pressure, physical performance, cognition, fractures or infections.

pmid:34717822.authors: Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration/EPIC-CVD/Vitamin D Studies Collaboration
pmid:34717822.title: Estimating dose-response relationships for vitamin D with coronary heart disease, stroke, and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomisation analyses.
pmid:34717822.finding: RETRACTED (2023 expression of concern, 2024 retraction and republication): original non-linear MR analysis that suggested vitamin D deficiency causally raised mortality; the residual stratification method was found to be biased.

pmid:38048800.authors: Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration/EPIC-CVD/Vitamin D Studies Collaboration
pmid:38048800.title: Estimating dose-response relationships for vitamin D with coronary heart disease, stroke, and all-cause mortality: observational and Mendelian randomisation analyses.
pmid:38048800.finding: Republished analysis using corrected non-linear MR methods: genetically predicted 25(OH)D had no association with coronary disease, stroke or all-cause mortality at any 25(OH)D level, including deficiency.

pmid:36279545.authors: Sutherland JP, Zhou A, Hyppönen E
pmid:36279545.title: Vitamin D Deficiency Increases Mortality Risk in the UK Biobank : A Nonlinear Mendelian Randomization Study.
pmid:36279545.finding: Non-linear MR using the residual method reported an L-shaped causal effect of low 25(OH)D on mortality (OR 1.25 at 25 vs 50 nmol/L); it relies on the stratification method later shown to be biased for vitamin D.

pmid:41719624.authors: Wang Y, Sha S, Gwenzi T et al.
pmid:41719624.title: Impact of vitamin D supplementation on all-cause mortality: Randomized trials revisited.
pmid:41719624.finding: Target-trial emulation of VITAL and D-Health in UK Biobank reproduced the null trial results in replete populations but predicted HR 0.75-0.85 for mortality if the same 25(OH)D rise were given to insufficient or deficient people (observational, modelled).

pmid:42484779.authors: Wang Y, Sha S, Gwenzi T et al.
pmid:42484779.title: Effect of vitamin D supplementation on cardiovascular outcomes: randomized trials revisited.
pmid:42484779.finding: Same emulation for cardiovascular outcomes: predicted cardiovascular mortality HR 0.74-0.79 in people with low 25(OH)D; relies on observational 25(OH)D-outcome associations.

pmid:24622671.authors: Autier P, Boniol M, Pizot C et al.
pmid:24622671.title: Vitamin D status and ill health: a systematic review.
pmid:24622671.finding: Strong inverse associations of 25(OH)D with many diseases in cohorts were not reproduced by trials, even in people starting below 50 nmol/L; concluded low 25(OH)D is mainly a marker of ill health (reverse causation, inflammation).

pmid:41702641.authors: Hu KL, Liao T, Wu Q et al.
pmid:41702641.title: Vitamin D supplementation before in vitro fertilisation in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: multicentre, double blind, placebo controlled, randomised clinical trial.
pmid:41702641.finding: Multicentre double-blind RCT: vitamin D 4000 IU/day for up to 90 days before IVF raised 25(OH)D from ~16 to 32 ng/mL but did not raise live birth after first transfer (52.0% vs 50.2%; RR 1.03, 0.91-1.18).

pmid:33894153.authors: Somigliana E, Sarais V, Reschini M et al.
pmid:33894153.title: Single oral dose of vitamin D(3) supplementation prior to in vitro fertilization and embryo transfer in normal weight women: the SUNDRO randomized controlled trial.
pmid:33894153.finding: SUNDRO: a single 600,000 IU vitamin D3 dose before IVF did not improve clinical pregnancy (37% vs 40%; RR 0.91, 0.75-1.11) in any subgroup, including low baseline 25(OH)D.

pmid:30010870.authors: Iliuta F, Pijoan JI, Matorras R
