tests:tst-who2021.title: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, sixth edition
tests:tst-who2021.finding: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, 6th edition (2021): standardized methods and fifth-centile values from fertile men (volume 1.4 mL, concentration 16 million/mL, total 39 million, total motility 42%, progressive 30%, vitality 54%, normal forms 4%), plus extended tests such as sperm DNA fragmentation and seminal oxidative stress.

options.label: Egg quality
options.note: Trying to conceive or pregnant: keep caffeine under about 200 mg/day (roughly 2 cups of coffee), mainly because of miscarriage risk. Take folic acid (400–800 µg/day) starting at least a month before conception.

options.label: Yes, tobacco
options.note: Quitting is the single largest lever on this site. In studies, F2-isoprostanes fell within 2–4 weeks of quitting; semen quality improves over about 3 months. Cutting down without quitting did not lower oxidative markers in an RCT. Avoid beta-carotene supplements while you smoke: they raised lung cancer risk in smokers.

questions.label: Body mass index (BMI)?
questions.help: Rough is fine. BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)².

options.label: Under 18.5
options.note: Being underweight or under-fuelled (low energy availability) can disrupt ovulation and hormone levels. Calorie restriction isn't for you.

questions.label: How would you describe your diet?

options.label: Lots of fast or processed food
Vegetarian or vegan
options.note: Plant-based diets need a reliable B12 source (supplement or fortified foods), and iodine and zinc deserve a check. See [vitamin-b12-folate-status] and [iodine-status].

options.label: Keto or very low carb
options.note: On a keto diet, recheck LDL cholesterol and apoB after 2-3 months: lean people often see large rises. When trying to conceive, switch to a less restrictive pattern: mouse studies found embryo harm at keto-level ketones, and very low carb intake in humans went with lower folate and more neural tube defects. See [ketogenic-diet].

options.label: Heavy traffic or wildfire smoke nearby
Wood stove, or gas cooking without a hood
Heavy periods, low ferritin, or anemia
Years on metformin or acid-suppressing drugs

questions.label: Are you taking any of these?

options.label: High-dose vitamin C/E or an 'antioxidant formula'
Sauna, hot tub, or hot baths weekly
Laptop on lap, tight underwear, hot job, or long sitting

questions.label: Using testosterone, anabolic steroids, or SARMs?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Exogenous testosterone shuts down sperm production. Come off it only with a doctor (often a urologist or reproductive endocrinologist); recovery can take many months to over a year.

questions.label: Has a doctor found a varicocele?

options.label: Never been examined
options.note: A urologist can check for a varicocele with a quick physical exam. Clinical varicocele is the most common correctable cause of high sperm DNA fragmentation.

questions.label: Fever or flu-like illness in the past 3 months?

options.label: Yes
options.note: Semen quality and DNA integrity can dip for 2–3 months after a fever. If you're getting a semen analysis or DNA fragmentation test, time it accordingly.

questions.label: Any results or treatment so far?

options.label: White cells in semen or a genital infection

questions.label: Age of the person whose eggs are being used?

options.note: Age is the dominant factor in egg quality, mostly through chromosome errors, and no supplement or lifestyle change has been shown to reverse it. Time matters more than any item below; if you're not pregnant after 6 months of trying, see a fertility specialist.

options.label: 40 or older
options.note: Age is the dominant factor in egg quality, mostly through chromosome errors, and nothing has been shown to reverse it in humans. See a fertility specialist promptly; the items below support the odds but won't offset age.

options.label: Planning IVF
options.note: Most IVF add-ons (endometrial scratching, PGT-A for live birth, receptivity tests, PRP, immune treatments) have no proven live-birth benefit; see [ivf-addons-egg].

options.label: IVF, told I'm a poor responder
options.note: For poor responders, CoQ10 (600 mg/day for about 60 days before stimulation) has the best trial support among supplements: more eggs and better embryos, but no significant difference in live birth yet. Discuss with your clinic. Most IVF add-ons (endometrial scratching, PGT-A for live birth, receptivity tests, PRP, immune treatments) have no proven live-birth benefit; see [ivf-addons-egg].

guide.footer: This plan is a starting point built from impact ratings and your answers, not a prescription. Effects on sperm show up after about 2–3 months (one spermatogenic cycle) and on eggs after about 3 months (folliculogenesis), so start early. Check any supplement with a clinician, especially when trying to conceive. For a month-by-month plan covering both partners, read the "Couple's 3-month plan" in the IVF add-ons deep dive.

tests.name: HbA1c and fasting glucose
tests.what: HbA1c is the share of hemoglobin that has picked up glucose, a 2-3 month average of blood sugar; fasting plasma glucose is a single-morning snapshot.
tests.why: High blood sugar is one of the best-documented drivers of systemic oxidative stress (glycation, AGE formation, NADPH-oxidase and mitochondrial superoxide). Diabetes also lowers fecundability in women and is linked to poorer semen quality, so finding prediabetes changes real levers (weight, diet, activity).
tests.who: Every adult at routine intervals, and anyone planning pregnancy who has overweight, PCOS, a family history of diabetes, or prior gestational diabetes.
tests.interpretation: ADA 2025: HbA1c below 5.7% is normal, 5.7-6.4% is prediabetes, 6.5% or higher (confirmed) is diabetes; fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL is normal, 100-125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose, 126 mg/dL or higher (confirmed) is diabetes [tst-ada2025]. A prediabetic result is an actionable signal: see [glycemic-control], [excess-adiposity] and [weight-loss].
tests.limits: HbA1c is distorted by anything that changes red-cell lifespan: iron-deficiency anemia (falsely high), hemolysis, recent transfusion, hemoglobin variants, pregnancy and advanced kidney disease [tst-ada2025]. It does not capture glucose swings.
tests.debate: Whether average glucose (HbA1c) or glucose swings matter more for oxidative stress is unresolved. In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha tracked glucose swings (r = 0.86) but not HbA1c [tst-monnier2006]; in type 1 diabetes the same kind of study found no link between variability and isoprostanes [tst-wentholt2008].
tests.access: Standard lab test, inexpensive, widely covered.

tests.name: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in people without diabetes
tests.what: A skin sensor that estimates interstitial glucose every few minutes for 10-14 days, showing post-meal peaks and day-to-day variability.
tests.why: Post-meal glucose spikes raise oxidative-stress markers acutely, so people use CGM to find meals that spike them. Whether this improves any outcome in healthy people is unknown.
tests.who: Not needed by most healthy people. Possibly informative for prediabetes, PCOS or gestational-diabetes risk under clinical guidance; mainly a curiosity or motivation tool otherwise.
tests.interpretation: Healthy reference (Dexcom G6, 153 non-diabetic people): mean glucose 98-99 mg/dL (104 over age 60), about 96% of time between 70 and 140 mg/dL, within-person CV about 17%, and a median 30 minutes a day above 140 mg/dL [tst-shah2019]. Brief rises to 140-160 mg/dL after carbohydrate meals are normal; a mean above about 105-110 mg/dL or frequent long excursions above 140 mg/dL are reasons to get a proper HbA1c and fasting glucose, not to self-diagnose.
tests.limits: Sensor accuracy is lowest in the normal range and after meals; two brands worn at the same time ranked the same person's meals differently (Kendall tau 0.43) [tst-howard2020]. Results are noisy from day to day, and there are no outcome trials in people without diabetes.
tests.debate: Proponents argue that CGM uncovers hidden dysregulation in 'normoglycemic' people, with glucose reaching prediabetic ranges 15% of the time [tst-hall2018], that responses to identical meals differ so much between people that personalized diets make sense [tst-zeevi2015], and that CGM use by people without diabetes is an idea whose time has come [tst-klonoff2023]. Critics show that meal rankings are not reproducible across simultaneous devices, so CGM-guided 'precision nutrition' may be premature [tst-howard2020]. The link between glucose variability and oxidative stress itself is inconsistent [tst-monnier2006, tst-wentholt2008].
tests.access: Over-the-counter sensors are now sold directly to consumers in several countries; otherwise prescription.

tests.name: High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP)
tests.what: A liver protein that rises with inflammation; the high-sensitivity assay measures the low range relevant to cardiovascular risk.
tests.why: Inflammation and oxidative stress feed each other (activated white cells are a major oxidant source), so persistently raised hs-CRP points to an inflammatory driver (visceral fat, smoking, gum disease, sleep apnea) worth addressing.
tests.who: Adults at intermediate cardiovascular risk where the result might change a statin decision; people curious about a chronic inflammatory load. Not useful during or soon after an infection.
tests.interpretation: AHA/CDC: below 1 mg/L low, 1-3 mg/L average, above 3 mg/L high relative cardiovascular risk; average two measurements about 2 weeks apart; above 10 mg/L suggests acute infection or inflammation and should be repeated [tst-pearson2003]. JUPITER showed that people with normal LDL but hs-CRP of 2 mg/L or more benefited from a statin [tst-ridker2008].
tests.limits: Rises with any infection, injury, hard exercise, hormonal contraception and pregnancy. Not specific for oxidative stress or for any organ. CRP is associated with many non-vascular outcomes too, and its vascular associations shrink after adjusting for conventional risk factors [tst-erfc2010].
tests.debate: AHA/CDC endorse optional hs-CRP testing for risk stratification [tst-pearson2003] and JUPITER supports acting on it [tst-ridker2008], but USPSTF found the evidence insufficient that adding hs-CRP to standard risk scores improves outcomes [tst-uspstf2018], and the large individual-participant meta-analysis concluded the relevance of CRP to such a range of disorders is unclear [tst-erfc2010].
tests.access: Standard lab test, inexpensive.

tests.name: Lipid panel and apolipoprotein B
tests.what: Standard panel (LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides, non-HDL-C) plus apoB, which counts the number of atherogenic particles (one apoB per LDL, VLDL, IDL or Lp(a) particle).
tests.why: Oxidized LDL is a central step in atherosclerosis; the more apoB particles in the blood, the more enter the artery wall and can be oxidized. This is a well-validated risk test, not an oxidative-stress test.
tests.who: All adults periodically; apoB is most informative with high triglycerides, diabetes, obesity or metabolic syndrome, where LDL-C can underestimate particle number.
tests.interpretation: ESC/EAS 2019 uses LDL-C as the primary target and apoB as a secondary target: apoB below 65 mg/dL for very-high-risk, below 80 mg/dL for high-risk and below 100 mg/dL for moderate-risk people [tst-mach2020].
tests.limits: Says nothing direct about oxidative stress. 'Oxidized LDL' tests sold to consumers are not standardized clinical tests.
tests.debate: Sniderman and colleagues argue apoB should replace cholesterol measures because particle number, not cholesterol content, drives risk [tst-sniderman2019]; the ESC/EAS guideline keeps LDL-C primary and apoB secondary [tst-mach2020]. Disagreement is about emphasis, not about apoB's validity.
tests.access: Lipid panel standard; apoB standard in Europe, less routine but widely available in the US.

tests.name: Ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT)
tests.what: Ferritin reflects stored iron; TSAT (serum iron divided by transferrin capacity) reflects iron in transit. Together they detect both iron deficiency and iron overload.
tests.why: Free iron drives Fenton chemistry (hydroxyl radicals), so iron overload is a direct pro-oxidant state; iron deficiency, on the other hand, harms energy, pregnancy outcomes and fetal development. Knowing which side you are on decides whether iron supplements are helpful or harmful.
tests.who: Anyone with fatigue, heavy periods, vegetarian diet or planning pregnancy (deficiency); men and postmenopausal women of northern European ancestry, people with a family history of hemochromatosis, unexplained liver enzyme rises, diabetes or arthritis (overload).
tests.interpretation: Ferritin below 30 ug/L is reasonably sensitive and very specific for iron deficiency [tst-garciacasal2021]. Overload: TSAT above 45% (women) or 50% (men) with ferritin above 200 ug/L (women) or 300 ug/L (men, postmenopausal women) in a C282Y homozygote is enough to diagnose haemochromatosis [tst-easl2022]. Ferritin below 1,000 ng/mL at diagnosis predicts low risk of advanced liver fibrosis [tst-kowdley2019]. Raised TSAT should trigger HFE genotyping; see [hfe-hemochromatosis].
tests.limits: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, raised by inflammation, infection, fatty liver and alcohol; high ferritin in a non-homozygote is more often fatty liver or alcohol than hemochromatosis [tst-kowdley2019]. TSAT varies with recent meals and time of day; repeat fasting. Evidence that high ferritin detects overload is very low certainty [tst-garciacasal2021].
tests.debate: Whether to screen the population for iron overload is contested. UK Biobank data show C282Y homozygosity causes substantial preventable morbidity in both sexes and argue for expanded case-finding [tst-pilling2019]; USPSTF's review found evidence insufficient to estimate benefit of screening [tst-whitlock2006], and penetrance in women is low [tst-allen2008].
tests.access: Standard lab test, inexpensive.

tests.name: Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT)
tests.what: A cell-surface enzyme that breaks down extracellular glutathione so cells can rebuild it; measured as a routine liver enzyme.
tests.why: Lee and colleagues proposed that GGT within the normal range is an early marker of oxidative stress: it predicted F2-isoprostanes and CRP 5-15 years later [tst-lee2004] and was inversely related to blood carotenoids and vitamin C in 9,083 NHANES adults [tst-lim2004].
tests.who: Already included in most liver panels. Worth noticing if it creeps up within the normal range alongside alcohol use, weight gain or fatty liver.
tests.interpretation: Typical laboratory upper limits are about 40-60 U/L for men and 30-40 U/L for women. In general-population cohorts the top third of GGT carried 60% higher all-cause mortality than the bottom third, about 7% per 5 U/L [tst-kunutsor2014]. Treat a rising GGT as a prompt to look at alcohol, body weight and fatty liver, not as an oxidative-stress score.
tests.limits: Raised by alcohol, fatty liver, biliary disease, many drugs (anticonvulsants, for example) and smoking. There is no validated GGT cut-off for oxidative stress.
tests.debate: Lee's group argues normal-range GGT tracks oxidative stress and explains its links with cardiometabolic disease [tst-lee2004, tst-lim2004]. Mendelian randomization found genetically higher GGT did not raise diabetes risk (causal RR 0.96), pointing to confounding or reverse causation [tst-nano2017], and the mortality association, though consistent, has unproven added prognostic value [tst-kunutsor2014].
tests.access: Standard lab test.

tests.name: Serum uric acid
tests.what: End product of purine breakdown and the single largest contributor to plasma antioxidant capacity.
tests.why: Uric acid is the oxidant-antioxidant paradox: an antioxidant in plasma but a predictor of obesity, hypertension and cardiovascular disease, possibly through pro-oxidant effects inside cells [tst-sautin2008]. It also dominates 'total antioxidant capacity' results [tst-sies2007].
tests.who: People with gout, kidney stones, metabolic syndrome or high fructose and alcohol intake.
tests.interpretation: Gout risk rises steeply when urate exceeds its solubility limit of about 6.8 mg/dL; treatment targets in gout are below 6 mg/dL. Outside gout and stones, a high value is a metabolic-health signal (weight, alcohol, sugary drinks), not a treatment target.
tests.limits: A high plasma antioxidant score caused by high urate is not good news. Varies with diet, alcohol, dehydration, diuretics and kidney function.
tests.debate: Johnson's group argues urate's intracellular pro-oxidant actions make it a causal contributor to cardiometabolic disease [tst-sautin2008]. An umbrella review found convincing evidence of causation only for gout and kidney stones [tst-li2017], and lowering urate with allopurinol did not protect the kidneys [tst-badve2020, tst-doria2020] or the heart [tst-mackenzie2022].
tests.access: Standard lab test.

tests.name: Total plasma homocysteine
tests.what: An amino acid that accumulates when folate, B12 or B6 are low, kidney function falls, or MTHFR activity is reduced.
tests.why: Homocysteine auto-oxidizes and is linked to endothelial dysfunction; high levels flag B-vitamin shortfalls that also matter for pregnancy (neural tube) and sperm DNA methylation.
tests.who: People with suspected B12 or folate deficiency, vegans, metformin or acid-suppressant users, kidney disease. Not a routine screening test.
tests.interpretation: Fasting levels of about 5-15 umol/L are typical; above 15 is raised and above 30 is intermediate to severe. Observationally, 3 umol/L lower homocysteine goes with 11% less ischaemic heart disease and 19% less stroke [tst-hsc2002]. A raised value calls for checking B12 (with MMA), folate and kidney function, then correcting deficiency.
tests.limits: Influenced by kidney function, thyroid status, age, sex and drugs. Lowering it with vitamins has not prevented heart attacks.
tests.debate: Large trials lowered homocysteine without preventing cardiovascular events (HOPE-2 RR 0.95 [tst-lonn2006]; NORVIT, with a hint of harm [tst-bonaa2006]), and Cochrane finds no effect on MI or death [tst-marticarvajal2017]. On the other side, stroke fell in HOPE-2 (RR 0.75) and in the Chinese CSPPT trial in an unfortified population (HR 0.79) [tst-huo2015], so benefit may depend on baseline folate status.
tests.access: Standard lab test, sometimes send-out; requires prompt processing.

tests.name: Omega-3 index (red-cell EPA + DHA)
tests.what: The percentage of EPA plus DHA in red-cell membrane fatty acids, a 2-3 month measure of fish or fish-oil intake.
tests.why: It tells you whether your omega-3 intake is actually low before you supplement; in IVF cohorts higher omega-3 levels went with higher live-birth rates (see [omega3-fish]).
tests.who: People who rarely eat oily fish, vegans, and those deciding whether to take fish oil.
tests.interpretation: The proposed risk zones are 8% or more (lowest coronary risk), 4-8% (intermediate) and 4% or less (highest risk) [tst-harris2004]. Two servings of oily fish a week typically moves people toward the middle zone.
tests.limits: Several assays exist and are not fully interchangeable. A low index identifies low intake; it does not prove that supplements will prevent disease.
tests.debate: Harris and von Schacky proposed the index as a modifiable risk factor [tst-harris2004], and high-dose purified EPA cut events in REDUCE-IT [tst-bhatt2019]. But 1 g/day omega-3 did not prevent major cardiovascular events in VITAL [tst-manson2019a], and in STRENGTH the highest achieved EPA or DHA levels were not linked to fewer events [tst-nissen2021], which questions whether raising the number itself is protective.
tests.access: Direct-to-consumer finger-prick kits and some specialty labs; rarely covered by insurance.

tests.name: 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D)
tests.what: The circulating storage form of vitamin D, reflecting sun exposure, diet and supplements.
tests.why: Vitamin D status is linked observationally to IVF outcomes and many diseases, but supplement trials in replete people are mostly null (see [vitamin-d]).
tests.who: People with established indications: osteoporosis, malabsorption, chronic kidney or liver disease, dark skin with little sun, obesity before bariatric surgery, or on drugs that alter vitamin D metabolism. Routine testing in healthy adults is not recommended.
tests.interpretation: IOM: 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) meets the needs of 97.5% of people; below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) is deficient [tst-ross2011]. The 2011 Endocrine Society guideline used below 20 ng/mL as deficiency and 21-29 ng/mL as insufficiency [tst-holick2011]; its 2024 successor suggests against routine testing and instead empiric supplementation for children, people over 75, pregnancy and high-risk prediabetes [tst-demay2024]. Above about 50 ng/mL (125 nmol/L) there is no added benefit and possible harm [tst-ross2011].
tests.limits: Assays differ by up to 10-20%. Seasonal variation is large. Low levels may partly reflect poor health rather than cause it.
tests.debate: The 30 ng/mL 'sufficiency' threshold [tst-holick2011] versus the 20 ng/mL population threshold [tst-ross2011] drove a decade of overtesting. USPSTF found insufficient evidence to screen [tst-uspstf2021], VITAL found no cancer or cardiovascular benefit from 2,000 IU/day [tst-manson2019b], and the Endocrine Society reversed its stance on routine testing in 2024 [tst-demay2024].
tests.access: Standard lab test; often not covered without an indication.

tests.name: Vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid (MMA) or holotranscobalamin
tests.what: Serum B12 measures total cobalamin; MMA and homocysteine rise when cells are actually short of B12; holotranscobalamin is the fraction delivered to cells.
tests.why: B12 deficiency raises homocysteine, impairs DNA synthesis and methylation, and matters before conception (neural tube risk, sperm production).
tests.who: Vegans and vegetarians, people over 60, metformin or long-term acid-suppressant users, after bariatric surgery, and anyone planning pregnancy with these risks [tst-stabler2013, tst-hannibal2016].
tests.interpretation: Serum B12 below about 148 pmol/L (200 pg/mL) usually indicates deficiency; 148-258 pmol/L (200-350 pg/mL) is a grey zone in which MMA or holotranscobalamin decides [tst-stabler2013]. MMA above about 271 nmol/L supports deficiency in one widely used algorithm [tst-hannibal2016]. Local reference ranges should be used because no single cut-off works across assays [tst-devalia2014].
tests.limits: There is no gold standard [tst-devalia2014]. Serum B12 can be normal or even high in true functional deficiency [tst-hannibal2016]. MMA rises with kidney impairment.
tests.debate: Whether serum B12 should remain first-line is disputed: the British guideline keeps it first-line with MMA as a more specific second-line test [tst-devalia2014], while others argue serum B12 alone has limited diagnostic value and favour holotranscobalamin-plus-MMA algorithms [tst-hannibal2016].
tests.access: Serum B12 standard; MMA and holotranscobalamin specialist or send-out.

tests.name: Selenium and zinc status (plasma levels)
tests.what: Plasma or serum selenium and zinc concentrations.
tests.why: Both are cofactors of antioxidant enzymes (glutathione peroxidases and selenoprotein P need selenium; Cu/Zn-SOD needs zinc) and both matter for sperm. Supplements are often taken on the assumption of deficiency.
tests.who: Rarely useful in healthy people. Consider with malabsorption, very restricted diets, parenteral nutrition, or living in low-selenium regions (parts of China, Malawi).
tests.interpretation: Plasma selenoproteins reach maximal expression at plasma selenium of about 50-70 ng/mL; above that, plasma selenium mostly reflects non-functional selenomethionine bound to albumin, and supplementation gave no cancer benefit above about 120 ng/mL [tst-combs2015]. Most people eating a Western diet are already above the plateau, so see [selenium-supplement] before adding more. Plasma zinc cut-offs exist for identifying populations at risk, but individual values are hard to interpret [tst-king2015].
tests.limits: Plasma zinc falls with inflammation, after meals, by time of day, and with some drugs and hormones, and responds only weakly to intake [tst-king2015]. Plasma selenium rises far more with selenomethionine than with inorganic selenium, so the form taken changes the number [tst-combs2015]. Hair and nail tests are not recommended.
tests.debate: Both BOND-style reviews conclude that status biomarkers for non-deficient people are poor [tst-combs2015, tst-king2015]; Combs notes it is still open whether higher-than-plateau intakes benefit immune cells, while trials in replete people show no cancer prevention [tst-combs2015].
tests.access: Specialist or send-out lab; not routine.

tests.name: Liver enzymes (ALT, AST)
tests.what: Enzymes released by damaged liver cells.
tests.why: Fatty liver is a major source of systemic oxidative stress and insulin resistance; mild ALT elevation is often its first sign. High-dose supplements such as green tea extract (EGCG) can also injure the liver.
tests.who: Part of routine panels; especially relevant with overweight, alcohol, diabetes, or when taking high-dose herbal or 'antioxidant' supplements.
tests.interpretation: Healthy-population upper limits are lower than many laboratory ranges: about 30 U/L for men and 19 U/L for women in the original blood-donor study [tst-prati2002]; ACG recommends evaluating abnormal values for fatty liver, alcohol, viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis and drugs [tst-kwo2017].
tests.limits: ALT rises after hard exercise (muscle), and normal values do not exclude fatty liver.
tests.debate: Lower 'healthy' ALT limits raise sensitivity for liver disease (76% vs 55% for HCV viremia) but lower specificity (89% vs 97%) [tst-prati2002]; laboratories have been slow to adopt them despite guideline support [tst-kwo2017].
tests.access: Standard lab test.

tests.name: Urinary F2-isoprostanes and 8-OHdG (research oxidative-damage markers)
tests.what: F2-isoprostanes are made when free radicals attack arachidonic acid in membranes; 8-OHdG (8-oxodG) is excreted after oxidative DNA damage is repaired.
tests.why: These are the best-validated markers of oxidative damage in the body and are used in most of the trials on this site. They are research tools, not clinical tests: no reference range, no treatment threshold, and no evidence that lowering them improves health.
tests.who: Research participants. Not recommended for individual decision-making.
tests.interpretation: No clinical cut-offs exist. In the multi-laboratory BOSS validation, F2-isoprostanes and MDA measured by GC-MS, and urinary 8-OHdG, rose reliably with a known oxidant insult in rats [tst-kadiiska2005]; F2-isoprostanes by mass spectrometry are considered accurate measures of lipid peroxidation [tst-milne2005]. Population levels depend on smoking, BMI, glucose, sex and country [tst-keaney2003, tst-basu2009].
tests.limits: ELISA kits for urinary 8-oxodG vary more than chromatographic methods and cannot give absolute levels [tst-barregard2013]; measuring 8-oxoguanine in DNA itself is plagued by artefactual oxidation during sample handling [tst-collins2004]. Within-person day-to-day variation is about 17-20% [tst-barregard2013].
tests.debate: Mass-spectrometry isoprostanes are the accepted reference marker [tst-milne2005, tst-kadiiska2005], but reviewers stress that no oxidative-stress biomarker is validated as a clinical diagnostic and many studies use non-specific methods [tst-frijhoff2015]. Whether women or men run higher isoprostanes, and whether levels rise or fall with age, differs between cohorts [tst-block2002, tst-keaney2003, tst-basu2009].
tests.access: Research-only (some specialty labs sell them, usually by ELISA, which is the least reliable method).

tests.name: 'Total antioxidant capacity' and direct-to-consumer oxidative-stress panels
tests.what: Assays such as ORAC, FRAP, TEAC, d-ROMs/BAP or urine MDA strips that claim to sum up the body's antioxidant or oxidant load in one number.
tests.why: They are marketed to guide supplement purchases. They should not be used for that.
tests.who: No one, for clinical decisions.
tests.interpretation: There is no meaningful interpretation. Plasma TAC mostly reflects uric acid, vitamin C and vitamin E, which can be measured directly; the main antioxidant defences are enzymes that these assays do not capture [tst-sies2007]. A higher plasma TAC is often wrongly read as healthy [tst-pompella2014]; a high urate (see uric acid) raises TAC while signalling metabolic risk.
tests.limits: Non-specific chemistry, arbitrary choice of oxidant, large dietary and urate confounding, no outcome data. USDA withdrew its food ORAC database in 2012 for similar reasons.
tests.debate: No published defence of consumer TAC or oxidative-stress panels was found among peer-reviewed sources; critiques argue that the 'total' concept is inappropriate and should be abandoned for food and health claims [tst-sies2007, tst-pompella2014], and broader reviews conclude no oxidative-stress marker is ready for routine clinical use [tst-frijhoff2015].
tests.access: Sold direct-to-consumer and by some integrative clinics; not offered by standard labs.

tests.name: Telomere-length tests
tests.what: Average length of the protective caps on chromosomes in white blood cells, sold as a 'biological age' test.
tests.why: Oxidative stress shortens telomeres in cell studies, so these tests are marketed as a readout of oxidative ageing.
tests.who: No one, for personal decisions.
tests.interpretation: No validated individual interpretation. The evidence that telomere length is a biomarker of human ageing is equivocal [tst-mather2011].
tests.limits: Inter-laboratory CV above 20% for qPCR, the method most commercial tests use, which excludes shared reference ranges [tst-martinruiz2015]. Genetically longer telomeres are linked to higher risk of several cancers [tst-tmrc2017], so 'longer is better' is not even directionally safe.
tests.debate: Telomere length predicts some outcomes in population studies, but reviewers find the case for it as an ageing biomarker equivocal [tst-mather2011], measurement reproducibility poor [tst-martinruiz2015], and Mendelian randomization shows a trade-off between cancer and cardiovascular risk [tst-tmrc2017]. No peer-reviewed support for consumer telomere testing was found.
tests.access: Direct-to-consumer only.

tests.name: Semen analysis (WHO 2021)
tests.what: Volume, sperm concentration and total count, motility, vitality and morphology, measured to WHO laboratory standards after 2-7 days of abstinence.
tests.why: It is the cornerstone of male fertility evaluation and the only way to know whether lifestyle or medical levers are needed; oxidative stress lowers motility and raises abnormal forms.
tests.who: The male partner in any couple not pregnant after 12 months (6 months if the woman is 35 or older), or earlier with known male risk factors; men wanting a baseline before lifestyle change.
tests.interpretation: WHO 2021 fifth-centile values from fertile men: volume 1.4 mL, concentration 16 million/mL, total count 39 million, total motility 42%, progressive motility 30%, vitality 54%, normal forms 4% [tst-who2021, tst-campbell2021]. Values below these are not diagnostic of infertility, and values above them do not guarantee fertility: in a large US study the subfertile thresholds were concentration below 13.5 million/mL, motility below 32% and normal forms below 9%, and fertile thresholds above 48 million/mL, 63% and 12%, with wide overlap in between [tst-guzick2001]. At least two analyses are needed because results vary [tst-schlegel2021].
tests.limits: Large within-man variation (fever, abstinence time, season). Morphology scoring is subjective. Reference limits describe fertile men, not a fertility threshold [tst-campbell2021].
tests.debate: WHO 2021 replaced reference limits with the idea of 'decision limits' but did not supply any, a gap critics call a major weakness [tst-boitrelle2021]; Guzick's study showed none of the parameters is a powerful discriminator on its own [tst-guzick2001].
tests.access: Standard (andrology lab); home kits measure concentration or motility only.

tests.name: Sperm DNA fragmentation (SCSA, TUNEL, SCD, Comet)
tests.what: Percentage of sperm with broken DNA strands. SCSA (DNA fragmentation index, DFI) and SCD (Halo) are indirect assays of DNA susceptibility to breakage; TUNEL and Comet detect breaks directly.
tests.why: Oxidative stress is the main cause of sperm DNA breaks; high fragmentation is linked to miscarriage and poorer ART outcomes and is the outcome most of this site's sperm factors target.
tests.who: Guidelines support it mainly for couples with recurrent pregnancy loss, and EAU also for unexplained infertility [tst-minhas2021, tst-eshrerpl2023]. Expert groups add clinical varicocele with normal semen, failed IUI or IVF, and men with lifestyle or environmental risks [tst-agarwal2020, tst-esteves2021]. Not recommended as a routine first-line test [tst-schlegel2021, tst-asrm2013, tst-eshre2023].
tests.interpretation: Assay-specific: SCSA DFI below about 15% is usually reported as low, 15-30% intermediate and above 25-30% high; TUNEL and SCD thresholds are lower (often around 20%) and are not interchangeable with SCSA [tst-agarwal2020, tst-esteves2021]. A 20% threshold best separated infertile from fertile men in one meta-analysis cited by ESHRE [tst-eshre2023]. High SDF doubled miscarriage risk overall (RR 2.16; TUNEL RR 3.94) [tst-robinson2012], and partners of women with recurrent loss averaged about 12 points higher SDF [tst-mcqueen2019]. A high result points to looking for varicocele, infection, heat, smoking, obesity or recent fever before considering testicular sperm for ICSI.
tests.limits: Assays measure different things and labs use different cut-offs; results vary with abstinence and fever. The tested sperm cannot be used, and a population DFI says nothing about the one sperm injected in ICSI [tst-eshre2023].
tests.debate: Supporters argue SDF identifies otherwise hidden male factors and has clear indications [tst-agarwal2020, tst-esteves2021], backed by miscarriage meta-analyses [tst-robinson2012, tst-mcqueen2019] and EAU recommendations [tst-minhas2021]. Sceptics note small diagnostic odds ratios and non-predictive likelihood ratios for IVF pregnancy [tst-collins2008, tst-cissen2016], and ASRM and ESHRE do not recommend routine use [tst-asrm2013, tst-eshre2023]. A global survey found highly heterogeneous practice and few society recommendations [tst-agarwal2023].
tests.access: Specialist andrology or fertility labs; usually self-pay.

tests.name: Seminal oxidation-reduction potential (MiOXSYS) and semen ROS tests
tests.what: MiOXSYS measures the net oxidation-reduction potential (ORP) of semen in millivolts, divided by sperm concentration; chemiluminescence assays measure ROS production directly.
tests.why: These are the only commercially available direct measures of seminal oxidative stress, proposed to identify men who might benefit from antioxidants.
tests.who: Optional adjunct in idiopathic infertility in specialist settings; not recommended routinely [tst-schlegel2021].
tests.interpretation: The manufacturer-studied cut-off of 1.34 mV/10^6 sperm/mL flagged abnormal semen with 98% sensitivity but only 41% specificity [tst-agarwal2019a]; a different cut-off (0.51) was used to predict ICSI outcomes [tst-henkel2022]. A pooled analysis found sensitivity 0.81 and specificity 0.66 for infertility [tst-tan2024].
tests.limits: Because ORP is divided by sperm concentration, low-count samples automatically score as 'oxidized' [tst-joao2022]. Leukocyte-rich samples can have high ROS but normal ORP [tst-homa2019]. Decision limits differ between studies and there are no trials showing that acting on the result improves live birth [tst-castleton2022].
tests.debate: Proponents propose 'Male Oxidative Stress Infertility' with ORP to target antioxidant therapy [tst-agarwal2019b], report correlations with SDF (pooled r = 0.24) [tst-pannerselvam2022] and with ICSI outcomes [tst-henkel2022], and good diagnostic accuracy [tst-tan2024]. Critics show the index is largely driven by sperm concentration [tst-joao2022], that ORP and ROS assays disagree [tst-homa2019], and that clinical utility is unproven [tst-castleton2022]; ESHRE notes little or no ORP-SDF correlation in some studies [tst-eshre2023].
tests.access: Specialist andrology labs; self-pay.

tests.name: Male hormone panel (FSH, LH, testosterone)
tests.what: Morning total testosterone, FSH and LH, sometimes with estradiol and prolactin.
tests.why: Separates testicular failure (high FSH) from pituitary or suppression causes (low FSH/LH), and reveals testosterone or anabolic-steroid suppression, which can drop sperm to zero.
tests.who: Men with abnormal semen parameters, low libido, erectile dysfunction, small testes, or a history of testosterone or anabolic steroid use [tst-schlegel2021].
tests.interpretation: AUA/ASRM recommend FSH and testosterone in men with impaired semen parameters or symptoms [tst-schlegel2021]; morning total testosterone below about 300 ng/dL should be repeated with LH. Raised FSH with low count suggests impaired spermatogenesis; very low FSH and LH with low sperm in a man taking testosterone points to exogenous suppression (see [testosterone-anabolic-steroids]). EAU advises screening infertile men for hypogonadism as a modifiable risk [tst-minhas2021].
tests.limits: Testosterone varies by time of day, sleep, illness and obesity; one value is not enough.
tests.debate: Little dispute about testing; the contested area is treatment, where hormone stimulation in hypergonadotropic or eugonadal men is controversial and not recommended outside trials [tst-minhas2021].
tests.access: Standard lab tests.

tests.name: Anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count (AFC)
tests.what: AMH is made by small growing follicles; AFC is the number of 2-10 mm follicles on a transvaginal ultrasound. Both estimate how many eggs remain (ovarian reserve).
tests.why: They predict how many eggs IVF stimulation will yield and help dose the drugs. They do NOT measure egg quality or natural fertility, the outcomes oxidative stress is thought to affect.
tests.who: Women starting IVF or egg freezing, or with suspected premature ovarian insufficiency. Not useful as a 'fertility test' for women trying naturally.
tests.interpretation: AMH below about 1 ng/mL or AFC below about 5-7 suggests reduced response to stimulation [tst-asrm2020]; ESHRE strongly recommends AMH or AFC over other tests to predict poor and high response [tst-eshre2020]. AMH or AFC predict poor response well (AUC 0.78 and 0.76) but add nothing to age for predicting ongoing pregnancy after IVF [tst-broer2013]. In 750 women aged 30-44 trying naturally, low AMH (below 0.7 ng/mL) did not lower the chance of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles (65% vs 62% at 6 cycles) [tst-steiner2017].
tests.limits: Assays differ; AMH falls on hormonal contraception and is high in PCOS. Higher AMH means more eggs, not better ones: AMH was unrelated to blastocyst aneuploidy [tst-pipari2021].
tests.debate: Steiner's cohort [tst-steiner2017] and a smaller Dutch study [tst-depmann2017] found AMH does not predict natural fertility, and ASRM calls reserve markers poor predictors of reproductive potential independent of age [tst-asrm2020]. A 3,150-woman cohort found low AMH (below 1 ng/mL) did carry a modest reduction in per-cycle conception (11.2% vs 14.3%) [tst-nelson2024], and AMH has a weak independent link to live birth after ART [tst-iliodromiti2014]. Clinicians still widely order AMH for reassurance or planning, uses the evidence does not support [tst-copp2024].
tests.access: AMH standard lab test (often self-pay, sold direct-to-consumer); AFC needs a fertility-clinic ultrasound.

tests.name: Day 2-4 FSH and estradiol
tests.what: Blood FSH and estradiol early in the menstrual cycle; the older way of estimating ovarian reserve.
tests.why: Raised early-cycle FSH signals that the brain is pushing harder on a shrinking follicle pool.
tests.who: Largely superseded by AMH and AFC for IVF planning [tst-eshre2020]; still used in evaluation of irregular cycles or suspected ovarian insufficiency.
tests.interpretation: FSH above about 10 IU/L on day 2-4 has high specificity but low sensitivity for poor IVF response, and a raised estradiol (above about 60-80 pg/mL) can falsely lower FSH, so the two are read together [tst-asrm2020]. In women trying naturally, FSH above 10 mIU/mL did not reduce conception by 6 or 12 cycles [tst-steiner2017].
tests.limits: Large cycle-to-cycle variability; only interpretable early in the cycle; misleading on hormonal contraception.
tests.debate: A systematic review concluded no ovarian reserve test can be supported for predicting IVF pregnancy and that entering a first IVF cycle without prior testing may be preferable [tst-broekmans2006]; current guidelines nonetheless use reserve tests to individualize stimulation dosing [tst-eshre2020].
tests.access: Standard lab test.

tests.name: 'Egg quality' and other unsupported tests (follicular-fluid oxidative markers, home fertility hormone kits, AMH as an egg-timer)
tests.what: Direct-to-consumer hormone panels marketed as fertility forecasts, oxidative-stress markers in follicular fluid, and similar add-on tests.
tests.why: There is no validated test of egg quality. Follicular-fluid oxidative markers are research measures taken during IVF, not decision tools.
tests.who: No one, for decisions about natural conception or supplements.
tests.interpretation: None validated. Home AMH kits answer an egg-count question, not a fertility or egg-quality question [tst-steiner2017, tst-asrm2020]; AMH does not track aneuploidy [tst-pipari2021]. ESHRE reviewed 42 add-ons and recommends against using unproven tests and treatments routinely, including antioxidant therapy in ART [tst-eshre2023].
tests.limits: False reassurance or false alarm; can drive unnecessary egg freezing or supplement spending.
tests.debate: Marketing presents AMH as a fertility clock, but prospective data show it does not predict natural conception in most women [tst-steiner2017], with only a modest association at very low levels [tst-nelson2024]; clinicians report requests driven by direct-to-consumer tests [tst-copp2024].
tests.access: Direct-to-consumer kits; research labs.

tests.name: HFE genotype (C282Y, H63D)
tests.what: Tests for the two common HFE variants behind type 1 hereditary hemochromatosis.
tests.why: C282Y homozygotes absorb too much iron; over decades free iron drives Fenton chemistry in liver, pancreas, joints and heart. It is the clearest case where a genetic test changes an oxidative-stress lever (stop iron and vitamin C supplements, give blood).
tests.who: People with raised transferrin saturation or ferritin, first-degree relatives of a known case, and people of northern European ancestry with unexplained liver disease, diabetes or arthritis [tst-easl2022, tst-kowdley2019].
tests.interpretation: C282Y/C282Y: diagnosis confirmed if TSAT above 45-50% and ferritin above 200-300 ug/L; treat with phlebotomy to ferritin below 50 ug/L, then keep below 100 ug/L [tst-easl2022]. About 28% of male but about 1% of female homozygotes had documented iron-overload disease in one cohort [tst-allen2008], though UK Biobank found excess morbidity in both sexes [tst-pilling2019]. C282Y/H63D: raised iron indices are common but progressive disease generally requires cofactors such as fatty liver, diabetes or alcohol [tst-walsh2006]. H63D/H63D or single carriers: usually no clinical consequence.
tests.limits: Incomplete penetrance: genotype alone does not mean disease. Non-HFE hemochromatosis exists but genetic testing for it is expensive and rarely useful [tst-kowdley2019].
tests.debate: Population genetic screening remains contested: UK Biobank data argue for expanded early case-finding [tst-pilling2019], while USPSTF judged the evidence insufficient to estimate benefit [tst-whitlock2006].
tests.access: Standard clinical genetic test; also in some consumer genotyping panels (confirm clinically).

tests.name: GSTM1 and GSTT1 null genotypes
tests.what: About half of people of European or East Asian ancestry carry two deleted copies of GSTM1 (and a smaller share of GSTT1), losing these glutathione S-transferases.
tests.why: GSTs conjugate isothiocyanates such as sulforaphane from broccoli, and electrophilic toxins, to glutathione. Genotype might change how much benefit people get from crucifers.
tests.who: Not clinically indicated. Of interest mainly in research and in consumer 'detox' panels.
tests.interpretation: GSTM1-null people handle sulforaphane differently (higher plasma levels and faster excretion in one crossover study [tst-gasper2005]; no substantial difference in a 114-person feeding study [tst-steck2007]). In Shanghai men, urinary isothiocyanates were linked to lower lung cancer risk mostly in GSTM1-null (RR 0.36) and double-null (RR 0.28) men [tst-london2000]. The practical message is the same whatever the result: eat crucifers (see [broccoli-sprouts], [cruciferous-other]).
tests.limits: Associations are inconsistent across populations; small studies dominate.
tests.debate: Whether null carriers benefit more (slower clearance, longer exposure [tst-london2000]) or less (less conjugated active metabolite [tst-gasper2005]) from crucifers is unresolved, and a feeding study found genotype mattered little [tst-steck2007]. GSTM1 null was associated with male infertility in a meta-analysis of 6,934 subjects [tst-wu2013], and GSTT1 null with endometriosis [tst-mear2020], but these case-control associations do not translate into any action.
tests.access: Research labs and consumer genetic panels.

tests.name: SOD2 (Val16Ala) and other antioxidant-enzyme polymorphisms (GPX1, CAT, NQO1, PON1)
tests.what: Common single-letter variants in genes for superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase, catalase and related enzymes.
tests.why: They are sold as revealing 'weak antioxidant genes' that justify specific supplements.
tests.who: No one, clinically.
tests.interpretation: No actionable interpretation. A meta-analysis of 7,366 cancer cases found no overall association of SOD2 Val16Ala with cancer risk (OR 0.98-1.02) [tst-bag2008]. A Chinese case-control study linked SOD2 Val16Ala and PON1 variants to male infertility and higher sperm DNA fragmentation [tst-ji2012], but such findings are not replicated in a way that guides treatment.
tests.limits: Small effect sizes, population-specific results, many tested variants (multiple-comparison problem), publication bias.
tests.debate: Positive single-population studies [tst-ji2012] versus null pooled analyses [tst-bag2008]; no trial shows that genotype-guided antioxidant use improves any outcome.
tests.access: Research labs and consumer genetic panels.

tests.name: MTHFR C677T (and A1298C) genotype
tests.what: A common variant (TT in roughly 10% of many populations) that lowers MTHFR enzyme activity and modestly raises homocysteine when folate is low.
tests.why: Heavily marketed as a reason to take 'methylfolate' instead of folic acid and as a cause of miscarriage and infertility. Professional bodies advise against testing.
tests.who: No one routinely. ACMG says it should not be part of thrombophilia work-ups [tst-hickey2013]; ACOG does not recommend MTHFR or homocysteine screening in pregnancy evaluation [tst-acog2018].
tests.interpretation: TT carriers have lower folate and higher homocysteine at every folic acid dose, but folic acid still raises their folate: genotype did not interact with dose in a 932-woman trial [tst-crider2011]. So standard folic acid advice (see [folic-acid]) applies regardless of genotype.
tests.limits: Testing invites unnecessary anticoagulation, supplement purchases and anxiety.
tests.debate: Meta-analyses of case-control studies link C677T to male infertility, mainly in Asian populations [tst-li2024], while ACMG concludes testing has minimal clinical utility after disproven links with thrombosis and heart disease [tst-hickey2013] and ACOG advises against testing [tst-acog2018]. ESHRE left its recurrent-loss thrombophilia recommendations unchanged in 2023 [tst-eshrerpl2023].
tests.access: Standard clinical genetic test and in nearly all consumer genotyping panels.

tests.name: G6PD deficiency test
tests.what: Enzyme-activity test (quantitative or point-of-care) or genotype for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, the enzyme that makes NADPH to keep glutathione reduced in red cells.
tests.why: Without G6PD, red cells cannot withstand oxidant loads; certain drugs, fava beans, infection and very high doses of some 'antioxidant' or 'mitochondrial' agents can cause acute hemolysis. One of the few tests that directly changes what someone should avoid.
tests.who: People of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South or Southeast Asian ancestry before high-risk drugs or high-dose IV vitamin C; anyone with unexplained hemolysis or neonatal jaundice in the family [tst-luzzatto2020, tst-nkhoma2009].
tests.interpretation: Deficient result: avoid fava beans [tst-beretta2023] and high-risk drugs (dapsone, methylene blue, pegloticase, primaquine, rasburicase, tafenoquine, toluidine blue), use nitrofurantoin with caution; vitamin C at standard doses is classed low-to-no risk [tst-gammal2023], but very high IV doses carry hemolysis risk and warrant pre-infusion testing [tst-alangari2026]. See [g6pd-deficiency].
tests.limits: Enzyme activity can read falsely normal during or just after hemolysis (young red cells have more enzyme); heterozygous women can have intermediate results; genotyping can miss rare variants.
tests.debate: The evidence linking several commonly listed drugs to hemolysis is sparse and regulatory warnings conflict; CPIC authors themselves disagreed on how strong the nitrofurantoin evidence is [tst-gammal2023]. Older reviews list a broader set of triggers [tst-cappellini2008].
tests.access: Standard lab test; point-of-care tests in malaria programmes.

tests.name: APOE genotype (e2/e3/e4)
tests.what: The three common forms of apolipoprotein E; e4 raises LDL and the risk of cardiovascular and Alzheimer's disease.
tests.why: In cell studies apoE4 has the weakest antioxidant activity (E2 > E3 > E4) [tst-miyata1996], and genotype may modify responses to dietary fat and fish oil.
tests.who: Not recommended for oxidative-stress or fertility decisions; Alzheimer's risk disclosure needs genetic counselling.
tests.interpretation: e4 carriers may have 40-50% higher cardiovascular risk, but individual studies are highly heterogeneous and diet-genotype trials are small [tst-minihane2007]. Practical advice (lipid-lowering diet, not smoking, exercise) does not change with genotype.
tests.limits: Mechanistic antioxidant data come from cell culture; outcome-based interaction evidence is weak.
tests.debate: Mechanistic work suggests apoE4 carriers face more oxidative damage [tst-miyata1996]; reviews of human data say the interaction evidence is too inconsistent to act on and call for prospectively genotyped trials [tst-minihane2007].
tests.access: Clinical genetic test and consumer panels.

tests.name: Direct-to-consumer genetic 'detox', antioxidant and nutrigenomic panels
tests.what: Consumer panels bundling MTHFR, GSTM1/GSTT1, SOD2, CAT, COMT and similar variants into 'detox' or 'antioxidant capacity' scores with supplement recommendations.
tests.why: They promise personalized antioxidant plans. Trials show genotype-based advice does not change behaviour or outcomes beyond ordinary personalized advice.
tests.who: No one, for oxidative-stress or fertility decisions. The exceptions are clinical tests with real actions: HFE and G6PD.
tests.interpretation: Ignore the composite scores. Personalized diet advice improved eating more than generic advice in Food4Me, but adding genotype added nothing [tst-celismorales2017]; a meta-analysis found genotype-based advice no better than general or phenotype-based advice [tst-king2023].
tests.limits: Weak or unreplicated variant-trait links, no validated algorithms, little regulation of DTC claims [tst-camp2014], and conflicts of interest when the same company sells the supplements.
tests.debate: Nutrigenomics is presented as an emerging science that may eventually personalize diets [tst-camp2014]; ACMG asks that consumers be told about limited clinical validity and have access to genetics professionals [tst-acmg2016], and RCT evidence shows no added value of genotype-based advice [tst-celismorales2017, tst-king2023].
tests.access: Direct-to-consumer only.

windows.name: Primordial follicle activation and early (primary) growth
windows.what: A resting follicle, part of a pool fixed before birth, starts to grow; it takes several months to reach the preantral stage (0.15 mm) [tegg-gougeon2010, tegg-mcgee2000]. The oocyte has been arrested in meiosis since fetal life and now enlarges and builds its large mitochondrial pool [tegg-maypanloup2016]. The 200-day start is an extrapolated lower bound from "several months"; the exact human duration has not been measured.
windows.sensitive_to: Mostly age: the pool shrinks to ~12% of its peak by 30 and ~3% by 40 [tegg-wallace2010], and chromosome cohesion, set in fetal life, decays with age [tegg-nagaoka2012, tegg-gruhn2019]. Androgens act mainly at these early stages, which is one argument for long (months) rather than short androgen courses [tegg-polyzos2018]. Chemotherapy hits growing follicles here, and smoking speeds depletion of the pool [tegg-zhu2018]. No preconception intervention has been shown in humans to change this stage within a planning horizon.

windows.name: Preantral to small antral growth (the ~85-day path)
windows.what: The ovulatory follicle comes from a preantral cohort that formed its theca about 85 days before ovulation [tegg-gougeon1986]; it needs about 70 days to grow from 0.15 mm to 2 mm [tegg-gougeon2010]. Growth is slow and gonadotropin-independent at first; the oocyte reaches near full size and finishes stocking mitochondria and maternal RNA [tegg-maypanloup2016].
windows.sensitive_to: This is the stage that pre-treatment trials of 2-4 months aim at: CoQ10 for 60 days [tegg-xu2018], DHEA for 12-17 weeks [tegg-yeung2014, tegg-barad2006], weight loss for 12-24 weeks [tegg-einarsson2017, tegg-legro2015]. In mice, oocyte spindle and mitochondrial defects from a high-fat diet persisted 8 weeks after diet reversal [tegg-reynolds2015]. Human evidence that this stage is more sensitive than the last two weeks is indirect.

windows.name: Antral recruitment, selection and dominance (the last cycle)
windows.what: At the end of the previous luteal phase, 15-20 days before ovulation, the next ovulatory follicle is recruited from 2-5 mm follicles [tegg-gougeon1986]; follicles grow in waves and one becomes dominant by mid-follicular phase [tegg-baerwald2012]. IVF stimulation acts in this window (about 11-12 days of FSH [tegg-mourad2025]). The follicular fluid bathing the oocyte is built now.
windows.sensitive_to: Follicular fluid mirrors current blood metabolites, insulin, lipids and CRP [tegg-valckx2012, tegg-robker2009]. Deep energy deficit disrupts LH pulses within 3-5 days and can make a cycle anovulatory [tegg-loucks2003, tegg-alvero1998]. Melatonin or vitamin E taken during the cycle lowered follicular oxidative-damage markers [tegg-tamura2008]. Alcohol in the month before IVF was linked to failure [tegg-klonoffcohen2003]; PFAS and cotinine reach the follicle [tegg-hong2022, tegg-benedict2011].

windows.name: LH surge, meiotic resumption and final oocyte maturation
windows.what: The LH surge (or the IVF trigger) restarts meiosis: the nuclear envelope breaks down, the first spindle forms and half the chromosomes are expelled in the first polar body. Ovulation follows on average 34 h after surge onset (range 22-56 h) [tegg-erden2022].
windows.sensitive_to: Chromosome segregation errors rise with age because cohesion has decayed over decades [tegg-gruhn2019, tegg-franasiak2014]; nothing done in the last days repairs that. Oxidative stress blocks maturation in vitro (mouse oocytes with H2O2) and melatonin protected them [tegg-tamura2008], but no human trial isolates this 1-2 day window.

windows.name: Fertilisation, early cleavage and implantation
windows.what: Conception needs intercourse in the 6 days ending on ovulation day [tegg-wilcox1995]. The embryo runs on the oocyte's stored mitochondria and RNA, then implants 6-12 days after ovulation, mostly on days 8-10 [tegg-wilcox1999].
windows.sensitive_to: Late implantation predicts loss (13% if by day 9, 82% after day 11) [tegg-wilcox1999]. A 6-week dietary change before IVF altered embryo cleavage timing [tegg-kermack2020]. One-carbon (folate/B12) status shapes the large epigenetic reprogramming of this period [tegg-steegerstheunissen2013]. Early-pregnancy caffeine and alcohol relate to miscarriage [tegg-hahn2015, tegg-sundermann2019].

windows.name: Neural tube closure
windows.what: Neural tube closure starts on day 22 after fertilisation and finishes at the posterior neuropore around day 26 [tegg-copp2015], usually before a period is missed by much more than a week.
windows.sensitive_to: Folate status must already be adequate: RBC folate takes a median 36 weeks to reach steady state on 400 ug/day [tegg-crider2019], and the lowest malformation risk was seen when folic acid started about 1.5 months before conception [tegg-dong2023]; hence USPSTF advice to take it daily whenever pregnancy is possible [tegg-uspstf2023].

windows.name: Embryonic organogenesis and the first-trimester placental oxygen transition
windows.what: Organs form through gestational week 10 (about 8 weeks after conception) [tegg-steegerstheunissen2013]. Placental oxygen tension rises from <20 mmHg at 8 weeks to >50 mmHg at 12 weeks of gestation as maternal blood flow starts, with a physiological burst of oxidative stress [tegg-jauniaux2000, tegg-burton2011].
windows.sensitive_to: Teratogens and drugs (GLP-1 agonists, chemotherapy) and maternal metabolism [tegg-cesta2024, tegg-fleming2018]. Antioxidant vitamins started at 9-16 weeks did not prevent pre-eclampsia [tegg-roberts2010]; aspirin works when started by 11-16 weeks [tegg-rolnik2017, tegg-roberge2017].

windows.name: The periconception period (umbrella window)
windows.what: Steegers-Theunissen and colleagues define periconception as a 5-6 month span from oocyte growth through fertilisation to gestational week 10 [tegg-steegerstheunissen2013]; 110 days before ovulation is the midpoint of that definition once the 56 days after conception are subtracted.
windows.sensitive_to: Parental nutrition, obesity, smoking, alcohol and one-carbon metabolism, with effects on fertility, miscarriage and long-term offspring health [tegg-steegerstheunissen2013, tegg-fleming2018].

windows.name: Spermatogonial proliferation (stem cell to last pre-meiotic DNA copy)
windows.what: Pale type A spermatogonia commit to divide, multiply through type B spermatogonia and copy their DNA one last time as preleptotene spermatocytes. This sets how many cells enter the pipeline. Heavy-water label taken up at that last DNA copy first reached semen after 64 +/- 8 days (range 42-76) [tsperm-misell2006], and the steps before it take roughly one 16-day cycle of the seminiferous epithelium [tsperm-heller1963], so this window sits about 64-90 days before ejaculation (extrapolated; the 1960s timings may be off by about 6 days [tsperm-amann2008]).
windows.sensitive_to: Killing or arrest of dividing cells: chemotherapy and testicular radiation (counts dip after as little as 0.2-0.7 Gy and recover in 12-24 months; after cisplatin only about half of men recover by 2 years) [tsperm-howell2005, tsperm-bujan2013]; outside testosterone, which blocks the type A to type B step within weeks [tsperm-mclachlan2002]. Damage here shows up as low counts 2-3 months later, not as instant DNA breaks.

windows.name: Meiosis (primary and secondary spermatocytes)
windows.what: Spermatocytes pair and recombine their chromosomes over a long pachytene stage, then divide twice to make round spermatids with half the chromosomes. In the original tracer study, labelled preleptotene cells were at mid-pachytene 16 days later and had become immature spermatids by 32 days [tsperm-heller1963]. Counting back from the 64-day label-to-semen lag [tsperm-misell2006] puts meiosis roughly 40-64 days before ejaculation (extrapolated).
windows.sensitive_to: Heat and fever: fever during meiosis lowered concentration in the sample formed from those cells by about a third (7% per fever day) [tsperm-carlsen2003], and mild sustained heat impaired meiosis and spermiogenesis [tsperm-abdelhamid2019]. Chemotherapy raises sperm aneuploidy that can persist 18-24 months [tsperm-tempest2008]. Heavy alcohol caused arrest at pachytene in one case [tsperm-sermondade2010]. Most natural germ-cell loss happens at the spermatocyte stage [tsperm-amann2008].

windows.name: Spermiogenesis (round spermatid to sperm, chromatin packing)
windows.what: Round spermatids grow an acrosome and tail and pack their DNA very tightly by swapping histones for transition proteins and then protamines. To do this, every elongating spermatid makes temporary DNA strand breaks that must be resealed [tsperm-laberge2005]. The cell loses most of its ability to repair DNA, so the quality of packing set here largely decides how vulnerable the sperm is later (timing extrapolated from [tsperm-heller1963, tsperm-misell2006]).
windows.sensitive_to: Fever and heat: a 1-day 39.9 C fever produced 36% sperm with denatured DNA 18 days later and an unprocessed protamine precursor at days 33-39 [tsperm-evenson2000]; a 2-day fever raised DFI at days 15-37 [tsperm-sergerie2007]; fever during spermiogenesis worsened count, morphology and motility [tsperm-carlsen2003]; sauna reduced histone-protamine exchange [tsperm-garolla2013]. Poorly protaminated sperm are the ones that later carry oxidative DNA damage [tsperm-deiuliis2009, tsperm-aitken2010], and most DNA-fragmented sperm show excess histones and apoptosis markers that point to a testicular origin [tsperm-muratori2015].

windows.name: Spermiation (release from the Sertoli cell)
windows.what: Finished spermatids shed their excess cytoplasm and are released from the Sertoli cells into the tubule over several days [tsperm-odonnell2011]. The exact position in days before ejaculation is extrapolated from the label-to-semen lag [tsperm-misell2006] minus epididymal transit [tsperm-amann1980] and is uncertain by about a week.
windows.sensitive_to: Loss of testosterone and FSH support: outside testosterone caused striking spermiation failure and cut sperm counts to 10% of baseline in about 24 days, faster than a full cycle [tsperm-mclachlan2002]. Failed or faulty release leaves sperm with retained cytoplasm and poor function [tsperm-odonnell2011].

windows.name: Epididymal transit and storage (to ejaculation)
windows.what: Sperm mature while passing through the caput and corpus of the epididymis (about 1.4 days) and then wait in the cauda (about 1.8 days) and vas deferens until ejaculation [tsperm-amann1980]; transit is faster in men who make more sperm per day [tsperm-johnson1988]. Human sperm reserves are small, so how long sperm sit in storage depends mostly on how often a man ejaculates (the 9-day start is an extrapolated upper estimate with infrequent ejaculation).
windows.sensitive_to: Oxidative and nuclease attack on stored, transcriptionally silent sperm: sperm taken straight from the testis have about 25 percentage points less SDF than ejaculated sperm [tsperm-esteves2017, tsperm-greco2005a]; a second ejaculate after 3 hours [tsperm-dahan2021] or 1-day abstinence [tsperm-pons2013] lowers SDF, and SDF rises about 0.65 points per extra day of abstinence [tsperm-logiudice2024]. In mice, fluid from the epididymis and vas activates chromatin fragmentation [tsperm-gawecka2015]. Genital-tract infection and white cells add ROS here [tsperm-gallegos2008]. Mild heating of testis plus epididymis raised DFI within 20 days [tsperm-ahmad2012], and paroxetine within 4 weeks [tsperm-tanrikut2010], consistent with late-stage effects.

rules.title: May blunt training adaptations
rules.message: High-dose antioxidants taken around training reduced gains in insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, and endurance markers in several trials, because the ROS pulse from exercise is part of the adaptation signal. If you keep them, take them away from workouts or drop the dose. Resveratrol blunted training benefits in older men, and the quercetin data are mixed. See [antioxidant-megadoses-during-training] and [resveratrol-pterostilbene-supplements].

rules.title: Beta-carotene raises lung cancer risk in smokers
rules.message: Beta-carotene supplements increased lung cancer in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (ATBC, CARET). Check that your formula has no beta-carotene or high-dose vitamin A. See [beta-carotene-supplement].

rules.title: Stacked antioxidants while trying to conceive
rules.message: The best fertility trials of antioxidant combinations (MOXI, FAZST) found no benefit for semen quality, DNA fragmentation, or live birth, and very high antioxidant loads can impair sperm chromatin compaction ('reductive stress'). ESHRE does not recommend antioxidants in IVF. If you use any, one modest-dose product is the evidence-based ceiling. See [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] and [male-antioxidant-combination].

rules.title: Iron only with a documented deficiency
rules.message: Iron catalyzes the most damaging oxidant reactions (Fenton chemistry). Supplement it only when ferritin or other tests show deficiency, and re-test. See [iron-excess].

rules.title: Selenium from more than one product
rules.message: Selenium has a narrow U-shaped curve: in people who are already replete, 200 µg/day was linked to higher type 2 diabetes risk. Add up the selenium across all your products and diet (Brazil nuts are very high). See [selenium-supplement].

rules.title: May add to bleeding risk
rules.message: Vitamin E raised hemorrhagic stroke risk in trials, and several polyphenol and curcumin supplements have antiplatelet effects. Tell your prescriber and pharmacist about these.

rules.title: Review every supplement with prenatal care
rules.message: Folic acid (and iodine, per many guidelines) is recommended in pregnancy. Most other supplements lack pregnancy safety data, and some (high-dose vitamin A, many herbal extracts) are best avoided. See [folic-acid].

rules.title: DIM / indole-3-carbinol with tamoxifen
rules.message: DIM lowered levels of tamoxifen's active metabolites in a trial in women taking tamoxifen. Don't combine without your oncologist. See [indole-3-carbinol-dim].

rules.title: Metformin may blunt some training gains
rules.message: In older adults, metformin reduced muscle gains from resistance training (MASTERS) and blunted aerobic fitness and mitochondrial gains; other trials found no blunting. If you take it for diabetes or PCOS, keep taking it, and raise the question with your prescriber. See [metformin].

rules.title: SGLT2 inhibitor + ketogenic diet: ketoacidosis risk
rules.message: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) combined with very low carbohydrate intake can cause euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, which is dangerous because blood glucose looks normal. Talk to your prescriber before starting keto. See [sglt2-inhibitors] and [ketogenic-diet].

rules.title: GLP-1 drugs and conception
rules.message: The semaglutide (Wegovy) label advises stopping at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy, and tirzepatide lowers oral contraceptive levels after starting and after each dose increase (use a non-oral or back-up method for 4 weeks). Plan timing with your prescriber. See [glp1-agonists].

rules.title: NSAIDs around ovulation
rules.message: Continuous NSAID use around mid-cycle was linked to luteinized unruptured follicles (the egg isn't released) in a substantial share of cycles in small studies, mostly with COX-2 inhibitors. Occasional use is unlikely to matter; ask about alternatives around ovulation if you use them daily. See [nsaids].

rules.title: Daily NSAIDs and muscle growth
rules.message: Daily high-dose ibuprofen roughly halved quadriceps growth from training in young adults, though not in older adults. See [nsaids].

rules.title: Medications that can affect sperm
rules.message: Some of these affect sperm DNA, counts, hormones, or ejaculation (for example paroxetine raised sperm DNA fragmentation in a small study; 5 mg finasteride and dutasteride lower counts; opioids lower testosterone). Don't stop any prescribed medication on your own; ask the prescriber whether there's a fertility-friendlier option while trying to conceive. Open each item for details.

rules.title: Testosterone shuts down sperm production
rules.message: Exogenous testosterone and anabolic steroids suppress the hormones that drive sperm production, often to zero. Come off only with medical help (often a urologist or reproductive endocrinologist); recovery can take months to over a year. See [testosterone-anabolic-steroids].

rules.title: Antioxidants during chemotherapy or radiation
rules.message: Some trials found worse outcomes with antioxidant supplements during cancer treatment (for example vitamin E during radiotherapy and more second primary cancers), while others found no harm. Clear every supplement with your oncology team. See [antioxidants-during-cancer-treatment].

rules.title: Long-term acid suppressants and nutrients
rules.message: Long-term PPI use is associated with lower B12, iron, and magnesium in observational studies, though a large RCT (COMPASS) found few harms. Worth checking B12 and ferritin if you've used them for years. See [ppi-acid-suppressants].

rules.title: High-dose zinc can cause copper deficiency
rules.message: At 50 mg/day zinc lowered the copper-dependent antioxidant enzyme SOD1 within weeks, and 100 mg/day or more over time causes copper-deficiency anemia and nerve damage. Stay under the upper limit (40 mg/day US, 25 mg/day EU) unless a clinician is treating a deficiency. See [zinc-status].

rules.title: Methylene blue with G6PD deficiency
rules.message: Methylene blue is classed as high-risk in G6PD deficiency because it can trigger hemolysis (red blood cell destruction). Don't take it. See [methylene-blue] and [g6pd-deficiency].

rules.title: Methylene blue + SSRI: serotonin toxicity
rules.message: Methylene blue is a potent MAO inhibitor; combined with SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs it has caused serotonin toxicity at doses around 1 mg/kg. Don't combine. See [methylene-blue].

rules.title: Off-label rapamycin
rules.message: Rapamycin's lifespan data are from mice; the human PEARL trial missed its primary endpoint, and the drug can cause infections, high lipids, and insulin resistance. Use only under medical supervision. See [rapamycin].
